# Part 1: Commodities and Money

## Chapter 1: Commodities

### Section 1: The Two Factors of a Commodity: Use-Value and Value (The Substance of Value and the Magnitude of Value)

<!-- ch01-p001 -->
In societies where the capitalist mode of production prevails, wealth presents itself as “an immense accumulation of commodities,”[^1.1] and its unit is a single commodity. Our investigation must therefore begin with the analysis of a commodity.

[^1.1]: Karl Marx, “Zur Kritik der Politischen Oekonomie.” Berlin, 1859, p. 3.

<!-- ch01-p002 -->
A commodity is, first of all, an object outside us, a thing that by its properties satisfies human wants of one sort or another. The nature of these wants makes no difference, for instance whether they spring from the stomach or from fancy.[^1.2] Nor are we concerned here with how the object satisfies these wants: whether directly, as means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live), or indirectly, as means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things).

[^1.2]: “Desire implies want, it is the appetite of the mind, and as natural as hunger to the body... The greatest number (of things) have their value from supplying the wants of the mind.” Nicholas Barbon: “A Discourse Concerning Coining the New Money Lighter. In Answer to Mr. Locke’s Considerations, &c.”, London, 1696, pp. 2, 3.

<!-- ch01-p003 -->
Every useful thing, such as iron, paper, etc., may be looked at from two points of view: quality and quantity. Each is a collection of many properties, and so it may be useful in various ways. Discovering the various uses of things is the work of history.[^1.3] So is setting up socially recognized standards of measure for the quantities of these useful objects. These measures differ partly because the objects to be measured differ in nature, and partly because of convention.

[^1.3]: “Things have an intrinsick vertue” (this is Barbon’s special term for use-value) “which in all places have the same vertue; as the loadstone [magnet] to attract iron” (cited above, p. 6). The magnet’s property of attracting iron became useful only after the polarity of the magnet had been discovered by means of that property.

<!-- ch01-p004 -->
The usefulness of a thing makes it a use-value.[^1.4] But this usefulness is not something made of air. It is limited by the physical properties of the commodity, and it does not exist apart from that commodity. A commodity, such as iron, grain, or a diamond, is therefore, so far as it is a material thing, a use-value, something useful. This property of a commodity does not depend on how much labor is needed to make its useful qualities our own. When dealing with use-values, we always assume that we are dealing with definite quantities, such as dozens of watches, yards of linen, or tons of iron. The use-values of commodities provide the material for a special field of study, the trade knowledge of commodities.[^1.5] Use-values become real only by being used or consumed. They also make up the substance of all wealth, whatever the social form of that wealth may be. In the form of society we are about to examine, they are in addition the material bearers of exchange-value.

[^1.4]: “The natural worth of anything consists in its fitness to supply the necessities, or serve the conveniencies of human life.” (John Locke, “Some Considerations on the Consequences of the Lowering of Interest, 1691,” in Works Edit. London, 1777, Vol. II., p. 28.) In English writers of the 17th century we often find “worth” used in the sense of use-value, and “value” in the sense of exchange-value. This fits the spirit of a language that likes to use a Germanic word for the actual thing and a Romance word for its reflection.

[^1.5]: In bourgeois societies (societies shaped by the capitalist class and its way of thinking) the economic *fictio juris* [legal fiction] prevails that everyone, as a buyer, has an encyclopedic knowledge of commodities.

<!-- ch01-p005 -->
At first sight, exchange-value presents itself as a quantitative relation: the proportion in which use-values of one sort are exchanged for use-values of another sort,[^1.6] a relation that constantly changes with time and place. So exchange-value appears to be something accidental and purely relative. Consequently an intrinsic value, that is, an exchange-value that is inseparably connected with commodities and built into them, seems a contradiction in terms.[^1.7] Let us look at the matter a little more closely.

[^1.6]: “La valeur consiste dans le rapport d’échange qui se trouve entre telle chose et telle autre entre telle mesure d’une production et telle mesure d’une autre.” [“Value consists in the exchange relation between one thing and another, between a given amount of one product and a given amount of another”] (Le Trosne: “De l’Intérêt Social.” Physiocrates, Ed. Daire. Paris, 1846. p. 889.)

[^1.7]: “Nothing can have an intrinsick value.” (N. Barbon, cited above, p. 6); or as Butler says – “For what is worth in any thing, / But so much money as ’twill bring?” (from *Hudibras*).

<!-- ch01-p006 -->
A given commodity, for example a quarter of wheat, is exchanged for x blacking, y silk, or z gold, etc. In short, it is exchanged for other commodities in the most varied proportions. So the wheat has not one exchange-value but a great many. But x blacking, y silk, z gold, etc., each represents the exchange-value of one quarter of wheat. So x blacking, y silk, z gold, etc., must, as exchange-values, be able to replace each other, or be equal to each other. It follows, first, that the valid exchange-values of a given commodity express something equal. Second, exchange-value in general is only the way of expressing, the form of appearance of, something contained in it, yet distinguishable from it.

<!-- ch01-p007 -->
Let us take two commodities, for example grain and iron. Whatever the proportions in which they can be exchanged, those proportions can always be represented by an equation in which a given quantity of grain is set equal to some quantity of iron: for example, 1 quarter corn = x cwt. iron. What does this equation tell us? It tells us that in two different things, in 1 quarter of grain and in x cwt. of iron, there exists something common to both, in equal quantities. The two things must therefore be equal to a third thing, which in itself is neither the one nor the other. So each of them, so far as it is an exchange-value, must be reducible to this third thing.

<!-- ch01-p008 -->
A simple example from geometry will make this clear. To calculate and compare the areas of straight-sided figures, we break them down into triangles. But the area of the triangle itself is expressed by something totally different from its visible shape, namely by half the base multiplied by the height. In the same way, the exchange-values of commodities must be capable of being expressed in terms of something common to them all, of which they represent a greater or smaller quantity.

<!-- ch01-p009 -->
This common “something” cannot be a geometrical, a chemical, or any other natural property of commodities. Such properties concern us only to the extent that they affect the usefulness of those commodities, that is, make them use-values. But the exchange of commodities is clearly an act marked by a total abstraction from use-value: use-value is left out of account entirely. Then one use-value is just as good as another, provided only that there is enough of it. Or, as old Barbon says,

<!-- ch01-p010 -->
> “one sort of wares are as good as another, if the values be equal. There is no difference or distinction in things of equal value ... An hundred pounds’ worth of lead or iron, is of as great value as one hundred pounds’ worth of silver or gold.”[^1.8]

[^1.8]: N. Barbon, cited above, p. 53 and 7.

<!-- ch01-p011 -->
As use-values, commodities are above all of different qualities. But as exchange-values they are merely different quantities, and so they do not contain an atom of use-value.

<!-- ch01-p012 -->
If, then, we leave the use-value of commodities out of consideration, they have only one common property left: they are products of labor. But even the product of labor itself has been changed in our hands. If we set aside its use-value, we also set aside the material elements and shapes that make the product a use-value. We no longer see in it a table, a house, yarn, or any other useful thing. Its existence as a material thing is put out of sight. Nor can it any longer be regarded as the product of the labor of the joiner, the mason, the spinner, or any other definite kind of productive labor. Along with the useful qualities of the products themselves, we put out of sight both the useful character of the various kinds of labor embodied in them and the concrete forms of that labor. Nothing is left but what is common to them all. All are reduced to one and the same sort of labor, abstract human labor.

<!-- ch01-p013 -->
Let us now look at what remains of each of these products. In each it is the same insubstantial reality: a mere congealed mass of uniform human labor, of labor-power (a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything) spent without regard to the way it was spent. All that these things now tell us is that human labor-power has been spent in producing them, that human labor is embodied in them. Looked at as crystals of this social substance, which is common to them all, they are – Values.

<!-- ch01-p014 -->
We have seen that when commodities are exchanged, their exchange-value shows itself as something totally independent of their use-value. But if we abstract from their use-value, what remains is their Value as defined above. Therefore the common substance that shows itself in the exchange-value of commodities, whenever they are exchanged, is their value. As our investigation goes on, it will show that exchange-value is the only form in which the value of commodities can show itself or be expressed. For the present, however, we have to consider the nature of value independently of this, its form.

<!-- ch01-p015 -->
A use-value, or useful article, therefore has value only because abstract human labor has been embodied or materialized in it. How, then, is the magnitude of this value to be measured? Plainly, by the quantity of the value-creating substance, the labor, contained in the article. The quantity of labor, however, is measured by its duration, and labor-time in turn is measured in weeks, days, and hours.

<!-- ch01-p016 -->
Some people might think that if the value of a commodity is determined by the quantity of labor spent on it, then the lazier and less skillful the worker, the more valuable his commodity would be, because he would need more time to produce it. The labor, however, that forms the substance of value is uniform human labor, the spending of one and the same labor-power. The total labor-power of society, which is embodied in the sum total of the values of all the commodities that society produces, counts here as one uniform mass of human labor-power, even though it is made up of countless individual units. Each of these units is the same as any other, so far as it has the character of the average labor-power of society and works as such; that is, so far as it needs no more time to produce a commodity than is needed on average, no more than is socially necessary. The labor-time socially necessary is the time needed to produce an article under the normal conditions of production, and with the average degree of skill and intensity usual at the time. In England the introduction of power-looms probably cut by one-half the labor needed to weave a given quantity of yarn into cloth. In fact, the hand-loom weavers went on needing the same time as before. But even so, after the change the product of one hour of their labor represented only half an hour’s social labor, and so it fell to one-half of its former value.

<!-- ch01-p017 -->
We see, then, that what determines the magnitude of the value of any article is the amount of labor socially necessary, or the socially necessary labor-time, for its production.[^1.9] In this connection each individual commodity is to be considered as an average sample of its kind.[^1.10] Commodities in which equal quantities of labor are embodied, or which can be produced in the same time, therefore have the same value. The value of one commodity is to the value of any other as the labor-time necessary to produce the one is to the labor-time necessary to produce the other. “As values, all commodities are only definite masses of congealed labour time.”[^1.11]

[^1.9]: “The value of them (the necessaries of life), when they are exchanged the one for another, is regulated by the quantity of labour necessarily required, and commonly taken in producing them.” (“Some Thoughts on the Interest of Money in General, and Particularly in the Publick Funds, &c.” London, p. 36) This remarkable anonymous work, written in the last century, bears no date. It is clear, however, from evidence inside the work that it appeared in the reign of George II, about 1739 or 1740.

[^1.10]: “Toutes les productions d’un même genre ne forment proprement qu’une masse, dont le prix se détermine en général et sans égard aux circonstances particulières.” [“Properly speaking, all products of the same kind form only one mass, whose price is determined in general and without regard to particular circumstances”] (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 893.)

[^1.11]: K. Marx. cited above, p.6

<!-- ch01-p018 -->
The value of a commodity would therefore stay constant if the labor-time required to produce it also stayed constant. But that labor-time changes with every change in the productivity of labor (how much a given amount of labor produces in a given time). This productivity is determined by various circumstances, among others: the average skill of the workers; the state of science and how far it is applied in practice; the social organization of production; the extent and capabilities of the means of production; and physical conditions. For example, the same amount of labor is embodied in 8 bushels of grain in good seasons, and in only four in bad ones. The same labor extracts more metal from rich mines than from poor ones. Diamonds are very rarely found on the earth’s surface, and so finding them costs, on average, a great deal of labor-time. Consequently much labor is represented in a small space. Jacob doubts whether gold has ever been paid for at its full value. This applies still more to diamonds. According to Eschwege, the total output of the Brazilian diamond mines for the eighty years ending in 1823 had not brought in the price of one-and-a-half years’ average output of the sugar and coffee plantations of the same country, although the diamonds cost much more labor and therefore represented more value. With richer mines, the same quantity of labor would embody itself in more diamonds, and their value would fall. If we could manage to turn carbon into diamonds with a small expenditure of labor, their value might fall below that of bricks. In general, the greater the productivity of labor, the less labor-time is needed to produce an article, the less labor is crystallized in that article, and the less its value. And the other way round: the less the productivity of labor, the more labor-time is needed to produce an article, and the greater its value. So the value of a commodity varies directly as the quantity, and inversely as the productivity, of the labor embodied in it.[^1.*1]

[^1.*1]: The following passage appeared only in the first edition. “Now we know the substance of value. It is labour. We know the measure of its magnitude. It is labour time. The form, which stamps value as exchange-value, remains to be analysed. But before this we need to develop the characteristics we have already found somewhat more fully.” Taken from the Penguin edition of “Capital,” translated by Ben Fowkes.

<!-- ch01-p019 -->
A thing can be a use-value without having value. This is the case whenever its usefulness to people is not due to labor. Examples are air, virgin soil, natural meadows, etc. A thing can be useful, and a product of human labor, without being a commodity. Whoever directly satisfies his wants with the product of his own labor does create use-values, but not commodities. To produce commodities, he must produce not only use-values, but use-values for others, social use-values. (And not simply for others, with nothing more. The medieval peasant produced quit-rent grain for his feudal lord and tithe grain for his parson. But neither the quit-rent grain nor the tithe grain became commodities just because they had been produced for others. To become a commodity, a product must be transferred by means of an exchange to someone else, for whom it will serve as a use-value.)[^1.12] Lastly, nothing can have value without being an object of utility. If the thing is useless, so is the labor contained in it; the labor does not count as labor, and so it creates no value.

[^1.12]: I am inserting the parenthesis because leaving it out has often led to the misunderstanding that, in Marx, every product consumed by someone other than its producer counts as a commodity. [Engels, 4th German Edition]

### Section 2: The Two-fold Character of the Labor Embodied in Commodities

<!-- ch01-p020 -->
At first sight a commodity presented itself to us as a complex of two things: use-value and exchange-value. Later on, we also saw that labor, too, has the same two-fold nature. For insofar as labor finds expression in value, it does not have the same characteristics that belong to it as a creator of use-values. I was the first to point out this two-fold nature of the labor contained in commodities and to examine it critically. This point is the pivot on which a clear understanding of political economy (the science of economics as it was then called) turns, so we must go into it in more detail.

<!-- ch01-p021 -->
Let us take two commodities, such as a coat and 10 yards of linen, and let the coat have double the value of the linen, so that, if 10 yards of linen = W, the coat = 2W.

<!-- ch01-p022 -->
The coat is a use-value that satisfies a particular want. It exists as the result of a special sort of productive activity, whose nature is determined by its aim, its way of operating, its object, its means, and its result. Labor whose usefulness is represented in this way by the use-value of its product, or which shows itself by making its product a use-value, we call useful labor. In this connection we consider only its useful effect.

<!-- ch01-p023 -->
Just as the coat and the linen are two use-values that differ in quality, so too are the two forms of labor that produce them, tailoring and weaving. If these two objects did not differ in quality, and were not produced by labor of different quality, they could not stand to each other in the relation of commodities. Coats are not exchanged for coats; one use-value is not exchanged for another of the same kind.

<!-- ch01-p024 -->
To all the different kinds of use-values there correspond as many different kinds of useful labor. These are classified according to the order, genus, species, and variety to which they belong in the social division of labor. This division of labor is a necessary condition for the production of commodities. But it does not follow, the other way round, that the production of commodities is a necessary condition for the division of labor. In the primitive Indian community there is a social division of labor, without production of commodities. Or, to take an example nearer home, in every factory the labor is divided according to a system, but this division is not brought about by the factory workers exchanging their individual products with one another. Only products that result from different kinds of labor, each kind carried on independently and on the account of private individuals, can become commodities in relation to each other.

<!-- ch01-p025 -->
To sum up, then: in the use-value of each commodity there is contained useful labor, that is, productive activity of a definite kind, carried out with a definite aim. Use-values cannot face each other as commodities unless the useful labor embodied in them differs in quality in each of them. Take a community whose produce in general takes the form of commodities, that is, a community of commodity producers. There, this difference in quality between the useful forms of labor, which individual producers carry on independently, each on their own account, develops into a complex system, a social division of labor.

<!-- ch01-p026 -->
In any case, whether the coat is worn by the tailor or by his customer, in either case it works as a use-value. Nor is the relation between the coat and the labor that produced it changed by the fact that tailoring may have become a special trade, an independent branch of the social division of labor. Wherever the need for clothing forced them to it, the human race made clothes for thousands of years without a single man becoming a tailor. But coats and linen, like every other element of material wealth that is not produced spontaneously by Nature, must always owe their existence to a special productive activity, carried out with a definite aim. This activity takes particular materials given by nature and makes them serve particular human wants. So insofar as labor is a creator of use-value, is useful labor, it is a necessary condition for the existence of the human race, independent of all forms of society. It is an eternal necessity imposed by nature, without which there can be no material exchanges between man and Nature, and therefore no life.

<!-- ch01-p027 -->
The use-values coat, linen, etc., that is, the bodies of commodities, are combinations of two elements: matter and labor. If we take away the useful labor spent on them, a material base is always left, which Nature supplies without the help of man. Man can work only as Nature does, that is, by changing the form of matter.[^1.13] Indeed, more than that: in this work of changing form he is constantly helped by natural forces. We see, then, that labor is not the only source of material wealth, of the use-values that labor produces. As William Petty puts it, labor is its father and the earth its mother.

[^1.13]: Tutti i fenomeni dell’universo, sieno essi prodotti della mano dell’uomo, ovvero delle universali leggi della fisica, non ci danno idea di attuale creazione, ma unicamente di una modificazione della materia. Accostare e separare sono gli unici elementi che l’ingegno umano ritrova analizzando l’idea della riproduzione: e tanto e riproduzione di valore (value in use, although Verri in this passage of his controversy with the Physiocrats is not himself quite certain of the kind of value he is speaking of) e di ricchezze se la terra, l’aria e l’acqua ne’ campi si trasmutino in grano, come se colla mano dell’uomo il glutine di un insetto si trasmuti in velluto ovvero alcuni pezzetti di metalio si organizzino a formare una ripetizione.” [“All the phenomena of the universe, whether produced by the hand of man or by the universal laws of physics, are not actual new creations, but merely a modification of matter. Joining together and separating are the only elements that the human mind always finds when it analyzes the idea of reproduction. And it is just the same with the reproduction of value” (use-value, although in this passage of his dispute with the Physiocrats Verri is not himself quite sure what kind of value he is speaking of) “and of wealth, when earth, air and water in the fields are changed into grain, or when the hand of man changes the secretions of an insect into silk, or some pieces of metal are arranged to make the mechanism of a watch.”] – Pietro Verri, “Meditazioni sulla Economia Politica” [first printed in 1773] in Custodi’s edition of the Italian Economists, Parte Moderna, t. XV., p. 22.

<!-- ch01-p028 -->
Let us now pass from the commodity considered as a use-value to the value of commodities.

<!-- ch01-p029 -->
By our assumption, the coat is worth twice as much as the linen. But this is a merely quantitative difference, which does not concern us for the present. We bear in mind, however, that if the value of the coat is double that of 10 yds of linen, 20 yds of linen must have the same value as one coat. Insofar as they are values, the coat and the linen are things of a like substance, objective expressions of essentially identical labor. But tailoring and weaving are kinds of labor that differ in quality. There are, however, states of society in which one and the same man does tailoring and weaving by turns. In that case these two forms of labor are mere variations of the labor of the same individual, not special and fixed functions of different persons. In just the same way, the coat our tailor makes one day and the trousers he makes another day imply only a variation in the labor of one and the same individual. Moreover, we see at a glance that in our capitalist society a given portion of human labor is supplied, according to the varying demand, at one time in the form of tailoring, at another in the form of weaving. This change may possibly not take place without friction, but take place it must.

<!-- ch01-p030 -->
Productive activity, if we leave aside its special form, namely the useful character of the labor, is nothing but the spending of human labor-power. Tailoring and weaving, though they are productive activities that differ in quality, are each a productive spending of human brains, nerves, and muscles, and in this sense are human labor. They are merely two different ways of spending human labor-power. Of course, this labor-power, which stays the same through all its variations, must have reached a certain level of development before it can be spent in many different ways. But the value of a commodity represents abstract human labor, the spending of human labor in general. In society, a general or a banker plays a great part, while mere man, on the other hand, plays a very shabby part,[^1.14] and it is the same here with mere human labor. It is the spending of simple labor-power, that is, of the labor-power that, on average, exists in the body of every ordinary individual, apart from any special development. Simple average labor, it is true, varies in character in different countries and at different times, but in a particular society it is given. Skilled labor counts only as simple labor intensified, or rather as multiplied simple labor, so that a given quantity of skilled labor is considered equal to a greater quantity of simple labor. Experience shows that this reduction is constantly being made. A commodity may be the product of the most skilled labor, but its value equates it to the product of simple unskilled labor, and so represents a definite quantity of that simple labor alone.[^1.15] The different proportions in which different sorts of labor are reduced to unskilled labor as their standard are set by a social process that goes on behind the backs of the producers. Consequently, these proportions appear to be fixed by custom. For simplicity’s sake we shall from now on count every kind of labor as unskilled, simple labor. By doing this we do no more than save ourselves the trouble of making the reduction.

[^1.14]: Compare Hegel, “Philosophie des Rechts.” Berlin, 1840. p. 250.

[^1.15]: The reader must note that we are not speaking here of the wages or value that the worker gets for a given labor-time, but of the value of the commodity in which that labor-time is materialized. Wages is a category that does not yet exist at the present stage of our investigation.

<!-- ch01-p031 -->
So, just as we abstract from the different use-values of the coat and the linen when we view them as values, so it is with the labor represented by those values: we disregard the difference between its useful forms, weaving and tailoring. The use-values coat and linen are combinations of special productive activities with cloth and yarn. The values coat and linen, on the other hand, are mere uniform, congealed quantities of undifferentiated labor. In the same way, the labor embodied in these values does not count because of its productive relation to cloth and yarn, but only as being the spending of human labor-power. Tailoring and weaving are necessary factors in creating the use-values coat and linen precisely because these two kinds of labor differ in quality. But tailoring and weaving form the substance of the values of these same articles only insofar as we abstract from their special qualities, only insofar as both have the same quality of being human labor.

<!-- ch01-p032 -->
Coats and linen, however, are not merely values, but values of a definite magnitude, and according to our assumption, the coat is worth twice as much as the ten yards of linen. Where does this difference in their values come from? It comes from the fact that the linen contains only half as much labor as the coat. Consequently, in producing the coat, labor-power must have been spent for twice the time needed to produce the linen.

<!-- ch01-p033 -->
So, with reference to use-value, the labor contained in a commodity counts only by its quality, while with reference to value it counts only by its quantity, and must first be reduced to human labor pure and simple. In the first case, it is a question of How and What; in the second, of How much? How long a time? Since the magnitude of the value of a commodity represents only the quantity of labor embodied in it, it follows that all commodities, when taken in certain proportions, must be equal in value.

<!-- ch01-p034 -->
If the productive power of all the different sorts of useful labor needed to produce a coat stays unchanged, the sum of the values of the coats produced increases with their number. If one coat represents x days’ labor, two coats represent 2x days’ labor, and so on. But assume that the time of the labor needed to produce a coat is doubled or halved. In the first case one coat is worth as much as two coats were before. In the second case two coats are worth only as much as one was before, although in both cases one coat gives the same service as before, and the useful labor embodied in it remains of the same quality. But the quantity of labor spent on producing it has changed.

<!-- ch01-p035 -->
An increase in the quantity of use-values is an increase of material wealth. With two coats two men can be clothed, with one coat only one man. Nevertheless, an increased quantity of material wealth may go together with a simultaneous fall in the magnitude of its value. This antagonistic movement has its origin in the two-fold character of labor. Productive power, of course, refers only to labor of some useful concrete form: how effective any special productive activity is during a given time depends on its productivity. So useful labor becomes a more or less abundant source of products, in proportion to the rise or fall of its productivity. On the other hand, no change in this productivity affects the labor represented by value. Since productive power is a property of the concrete useful forms of labor, it of course can no longer have any bearing on that labor as soon as we abstract from those concrete useful forms. However much productive power may vary, then, the same labor, carried on for equal periods of time, always yields equal amounts of value. But during equal periods of time it will yield different quantities of use-values: more if the productive power rises, fewer if it falls. The same change in productive power that increases the fruitfulness of labor, and so the quantity of use-values that labor produces, will reduce the total value of this increased quantity of use-values, provided the change shortens the total labor-time needed to produce them; and the other way round.

<!-- ch01-p036 -->
On the one hand, all labor is, physiologically speaking, a spending of human labor-power, and in its character as identical abstract human labor it creates and forms the value of commodities. On the other hand, all labor is the spending of human labor-power in a special form and with a definite aim, and in this character, as concrete useful labor, it produces use-values.[^1.16]

[^1.16]: To prove that labor alone is that all-sufficient and real measure by which the value of all commodities can at all times be estimated and compared, Adam Smith says: “Equal quantities of labour must at all times and in all places have the same value for the labourer. In his normal state of health, strength, and activity, and with the average degree of skill that he may possess, he must always give up the same portion of his rest, his freedom, and his happiness.” (“Wealth of Nations,” b. I. ch. V.) On the one hand, Adam Smith here (but not everywhere) confuses two things: fixing value by the quantity of labor spent in producing commodities, and fixing the values of commodities by the value of labor. As a result he tries to prove that equal quantities of labor always have the same value. On the other hand, he has an inkling that labor, insofar as it shows itself in the value of commodities, counts only as the spending of labor-power. But he treats this spending as merely the sacrifice of rest, freedom, and happiness, not also as the normal activity of living beings. But then, he has the modern wage worker in view. Much more aptly, the anonymous predecessor of Adam Smith, quoted above in note 9 of this chapter, says: “one man has employed himself a week in providing this necessary of life ... and he that gives him some other in exchange cannot make a better estimate of what is a proper equivalent, than by computing what cost him just as much labour and time; which in effect is no more than exchanging one man’s labour in one thing for a time certain, for another man’s labour in another thing for the same time.” (cited above, p. 39.) [The English language has the advantage of having different words for the two aspects of labor considered here. The labor that creates use-value and counts qualitatively is Work, as distinguished from Labour; the labor that creates Value and counts quantitatively is Labour, as distinguished from Work ‒ Engels]

### Section 3: The Form of Value or Exchange-Value

<!-- ch01-p037 -->
Commodities come into the world in the shape of use-values, articles, or goods, such as iron, linen, grain, etc. This is their plain, homely, bodily form. They are commodities, however, only because they are something twofold: both useful objects and, at the same time, containers of value. So they show themselves as commodities, or have the form of commodities, only insofar as they have two forms: a physical or natural form, and a form of value (the way the value of one commodity is expressed in another commodity).

<!-- ch01-p038 -->
The reality of the value of commodities differs in one respect from Dame Quickly (the hostess in Shakespeare's *Henry IV*): we don't know “where to have it” [how to get hold of it]. The value of commodities is the exact opposite of the coarse material stuff they are made of. Not an atom of matter goes into it. We can turn a single commodity over and examine it by itself as much as we like, yet insofar as it remains an object of value, it seems impossible to grasp. But suppose we bear in mind that the value of commodities has a purely social reality. They acquire this reality only insofar as they are expressions or embodiments of one identical social substance, namely, human labor. Then it follows as a matter of course that value can show itself only in the social relation of commodity to commodity. In fact we started from exchange-value, or the exchange relation of commodities, in order to get at the value that lies hidden behind it. We must now return to this form in which value first appeared to us.

<!-- ch01-p039 -->
Everyone knows, if he knows nothing else, that commodities have a form of value common to them all, which stands in marked contrast with the varied bodily forms of their use-values. I mean their money form (the form of value in which one commodity, gold, has become the universal equivalent). Here, however, we are set a task that *bourgeois* economics has never yet even attempted. The task is to trace the origin of this money form. That means developing the expression of value contained in the value relation of commodities, from its simplest, almost invisible outline, up to the dazzling money form. By doing this we shall, at the same time, solve the riddle that money presents.

<!-- ch01-p040 -->
The simplest value relation is clearly that of one commodity to some one other commodity of a different kind. So the relation between the values of two commodities gives us the simplest expression of the value of a single commodity.

#### A. Elementary or Accidental Form Of Value

<!-- ch01-p041 -->
x commodity A = y commodity B, or\
x commodity A is worth y commodity B.\
20 yards of linen = 1 coat, or\
20 Yards of linen are worth 1 coat.

##### 1. The two poles of the expression of value. Relative form and Equivalent form

<!-- ch01-p042 -->
The whole mystery of the form of value lies hidden in this elementary form. So analyzing it is our real difficulty.

<!-- ch01-p043 -->
Here two different kinds of commodities (in our example the linen and the coat) clearly play two different parts. The linen expresses its value in the coat. The coat serves as the material in which that value is expressed. The linen plays an active part, the coat a passive one. The value of the linen is represented as relative value, or appears in relative form. The coat acts as equivalent, or appears in equivalent form.

<!-- ch01-p044 -->
The relative form and the equivalent form are two closely connected elements of the expression of value. They depend on each other and cannot be separated. But at the same time they are mutually exclusive, opposed extremes, that is, poles of the same expression. They are assigned to the two different commodities that the expression brings into relation, one to each. It is not possible to express the value of linen in linen. 20 yards of linen = 20 yards of linen is no expression of value. On the contrary, such an equation says only that 20 yards of linen are nothing other than 20 yards of linen, a definite quantity of the use-value linen. So the value of the linen can be expressed only relatively, that is, in some other commodity. The relative form of value of the linen therefore presupposes that some other commodity, here the coat, is present in the form of an equivalent. On the other hand, the commodity that figures as the equivalent cannot at the same time take on the relative form. That second commodity is not the one whose value is expressed. Its function is only to serve as the material in which the value of the first commodity is expressed.

<!-- ch01-p045 -->
No doubt the expression 20 yards of linen = 1 coat, or 20 yards of linen are worth 1 coat, implies the opposite relation: 1 coat = 20 yards of linen, or 1 coat is worth 20 yards of linen. But in that case I must reverse the equation in order to express the value of the coat relatively. And as soon as I do that, the linen becomes the equivalent instead of the coat. So a single commodity cannot take on both forms at once in the same expression of value. The very polarity of these forms makes them mutually exclusive.

<!-- ch01-p046 -->
Whether a commodity takes on the relative form or the opposite, equivalent form, then, depends entirely on its accidental position in the expression of value. That is, it depends on whether it is the commodity whose value is being expressed, or the commodity in which value is being expressed.

##### 2. The Relative Form of value

<!-- ch01-p047 -->
(a.) The nature and meaning of this form

<!-- ch01-p048 -->
We want to discover how the elementary expression of the value of a commodity lies hidden in the value relation of two commodities. To do so, we must first consider that relation entirely apart from its quantitative side. The usual procedure is generally the reverse: in the value relation people see nothing but the proportion between definite quantities of two different sorts of commodities that are counted as equal to each other. It is easily forgotten that the magnitudes of different things can be compared in quantity only when those magnitudes are expressed in terms of the same unit. Only as expressions of such a unit are they of the same denomination, and therefore measurable against each other.[^1.17]

[^1.17]: The few economists, among them S. Bailey, who have busied themselves with analyzing the form of value have been unable to reach any result. First, because they confuse the form of value with value itself. Second, because, under the coarse influence of the practical bourgeois, they pay attention only to the quantitative side of the question. “The command of quantity ... constitutes value.” (“Money and its Vicissitudes.” London, 1837, p. 11. By S. Bailey.)

<!-- ch01-p049 -->
Whether 20 yards of linen = 1 coat or = 20 coats or = x coats, that is, whether a given quantity of linen is worth few coats or many, every such statement implies that the linen and the coats, as magnitudes of value, are expressions of the same unit, things of the same kind. Linen = coat is the basis of the equation.

<!-- ch01-p050 -->
But the two commodities whose sameness of quality is assumed in this way do not play the same part. Only the value of the linen is expressed. And how? By its reference to the coat as its equivalent, as something that can be exchanged for it. In this relation the coat is the form in which value exists, it is value embodied, for only as such is it the same as the linen. On the other hand, the linen's own value comes to the front and receives an independent expression. For it is only as value that the linen is comparable with the coat as a thing of equal value, or exchangeable with the coat. To borrow an illustration from chemistry: butyric acid is a different substance from propyl formate. Yet both are made up of the same chemical substances, carbon (C), hydrogen (H), and oxygen (O), and in the same proportions too, namely C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. Now suppose we equate butyric acid to propyl formate. Then, in the first place, propyl formate would be, in this relation, merely a form of existence of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. And in the second place, we would be stating that butyric acid also consists of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. So by equating the two substances in this way, we would express their chemical composition, while their different physical forms would be left out of account.

<!-- ch01-p051 -->
If we say that, as values, commodities are mere congealed amounts of human labor, our analysis does, it is true, reduce them to the abstraction, value. But we give this value no form apart from their bodily form. It is different in the value relation of one commodity to another. There, the one stands out in its character of value because of its relation to the other.

<!-- ch01-p052 -->
By making the coat the equivalent of the linen, we equate the labor embodied in the coat to the labor in the linen. Now, it is true that the tailoring that makes the coat is concrete labor of a different sort from the weaving that makes the linen. But the act of equating tailoring to weaving reduces the tailoring to what is really equal in the two kinds of labor, to their common character as human labor. In this roundabout way, then, the fact is expressed that weaving too, insofar as it weaves value, has nothing to distinguish it from tailoring, and so is abstract human labor. Only the expression of equivalence between different sorts of commodities brings out the specific character of value-creating labor. It does this by actually reducing the different kinds of labor embodied in the different kinds of commodities to their common quality of abstract human labor.[^1.18]

[^1.18]: The famous Franklin, one of the first economists after Wm. Petty to see through the nature of value, says: “Trade in general being nothing else but the exchange of labour for labour, the value of all things is ... most justly measured by labour.” (“The works of B. Franklin, &c.,” edited by Sparks. Boston, 1836, Vol. II., p. 267.) Franklin is not aware that, by estimating the value of everything in labor, he sets aside any difference in the sorts of labor exchanged, and so reduces them all to equal human labor. But although he does not know it, he says it. He speaks first of “the one labour,” then of “the other labour,” and finally of “labour,” with no further qualification, as the substance of the value of everything.

<!-- ch01-p053 -->
But something more is needed beyond expressing the specific character of the labor that the value of the linen consists of. Human labor-power in motion, or human labor, creates value, but is not itself value. It becomes value only in its congealed state, when it is embodied in the form of some object. To express the value of the linen as congealed human labor, that value must be expressed as something with an objective existence. It must be something materially different from the linen itself, and yet something common to the linen and all other commodities. The problem is already solved.

<!-- ch01-p054 -->
When the coat occupies the position of equivalent in the equation of value, it ranks in quality as the equal of the linen, as something of the same kind, because it is value. In this position it is a thing in which we see nothing but value, or whose tangible bodily form represents value. Yet the coat itself, the body of the commodity coat, is a mere use-value. A coat as such no more tells us that it is value than the first piece of linen we pick up does. This shows that when the coat is placed in a value relation to the linen, it signifies more than it does outside that relation. In the same way, many a man strutting about in a gorgeous uniform counts for more than he does in plain clothes.

<!-- ch01-p055 -->
In the production of the coat, human labor-power, in the shape of tailoring, must actually have been spent. So human labor has piled up in it. In this respect the coat is a container of value, but even when worn threadbare, it does not let this fact show through. And as the equivalent of the linen in the value equation, it exists in this respect alone, and so counts as embodied value, as a body that is value. A, for instance, cannot be “your majesty” to B unless, at the same time, majesty in B's eyes takes on the bodily form of A. What is more, majesty changes its features, hair, and many other things besides, with every new father of the people.

<!-- ch01-p056 -->
So in the value equation in which the coat is the equivalent of the linen, the coat serves as the form of value. The value of the commodity linen is expressed by the bodily form of the commodity coat, the value of one by the use-value of the other. As a use-value, the linen is something tangibly different from the coat. As value, it is the same as the coat, and now looks like a coat. In this way the linen acquires a form of value different from its physical form. The fact that it is value is made visible by its equality with the coat, just as the sheep's nature of a Christian is shown in his resemblance to the Lamb of God.

<!-- ch01-p057 -->
We see, then, that everything our analysis of the value of commodities has already told us is told us by the linen itself, as soon as it enters into dealings with another commodity, the coat. Only it gives away its thoughts in the one language it knows, the language of commodities. To tell us that its own value is created by labor in its abstract character as human labor, it says that the coat, insofar as it is worth as much as the linen, and therefore is value, consists of the same labor as the linen. To let us know that its sublime reality as value is not the same as its buckram body (its body of stiff cloth), it says that value looks like a coat, and so that, insofar as the linen is value, it and the coat are as like as two peas. We may remark here that the language of commodities has, besides Hebrew, many other more or less correct dialects. The German “Wertsein,” to be worth, for instance, expresses less strikingly than the Romance verbs “valere,” “valer,” “valoir” [each: to be worth] that the equating of commodity B to commodity A is commodity A's own way of expressing its value. *Paris vaut bien une messe*. [Paris is well worth a mass]

<!-- ch01-p058 -->
So, by means of the value relation expressed in our equation, the bodily form of commodity B becomes the form of value of commodity A. In other words, the body of commodity B acts as a mirror to the value of commodity A.[^1.19] Commodity A relates itself to commodity B as value in person, as the matter that human labor is made of. By doing so, commodity A turns the use-value B into the substance in which it expresses its own, A's, value. The value of A, expressed in this way in the use-value of B, has taken the form of relative value.

[^1.19]: In a way, it is with man as with commodities. Man does not come into the world with a looking glass in his hand, nor as a Fichtean philosopher, for whom “I am I” is enough. So he first sees and recognizes himself in other men. Peter establishes his own identity as a man only by first comparing himself with Paul as a being of the same kind. And in this way Paul, just as he stands, in his Pauline personality, becomes for Peter the type of the genus homo [the human kind].

<!-- ch01-p059 -->
(b.) How the quantity of relative value is determined

<!-- ch01-p060 -->
Every commodity whose value is to be expressed is a useful object of a given quantity, such as 15 bushels of grain, or 100 lbs of coffee. And a given quantity of any commodity contains a definite quantity of human labor. So the form of value must express not only value in general, but also value in a definite quantity. Therefore, in the value relation of commodity A to commodity B, of the linen to the coat, not only is the coat, as value in general, made the equal of the linen in quality, but a definite quantity of coat (1 coat) is made the equivalent of a definite quantity (20 yards) of linen.

<!-- ch01-p061 -->
The equation, 20 yards of linen = 1 coat, or 20 yards of linen are worth one coat, implies that the same quantity of value substance (congealed labor) is embodied in both. It implies that the two commodities have each cost the same amount of labor, of the same quantity of labor-time. But the labor-time necessary to produce 20 yards of linen or 1 coat changes with every change in the productivity of weaving or tailoring. We now have to consider how such changes affect the quantitative side of the relative expression of value.

<!-- ch01-p062 -->
I. Let the value of the linen vary,[^1.20] while that of the coat stays constant. Say the labor-time necessary to produce the linen is doubled, as a result, perhaps, of the exhaustion of the soil that grows flax. Then the value of the linen will also be doubled. Instead of the equation 20 yards of linen = 1 coat, we would have 20 yards of linen = 2 coats, since 1 coat would now contain only half the labor-time embodied in 20 yards of linen. If, on the other hand, this labor-time is cut by one-half, as a result, say, of improved looms, the value of the linen would fall by one-half. So we would have 20 yards of linen = ½ coat. The relative value of commodity A, that is, its value expressed in commodity B, rises and falls directly with the value of A, the value of B being assumed constant.

[^1.20]: Here, as now and then in the preceding pages, value is used in the sense of value determined as to quantity, or of magnitude of value.

<!-- ch01-p063 -->
II. Let the value of the linen stay constant, while the value of the coat varies. Under these conditions, suppose the labor-time necessary to produce a coat doubles, as a result, for instance, of a poor crop of wool. Then instead of 20 yards of linen = 1 coat, we have 20 yards of linen = ½ coat. If, on the other hand, the value of the coat sinks by one-half, then 20 yards of linen = 2 coats. So if the value of commodity A stays constant, its relative value expressed in commodity B rises and falls inversely with the value of B.

<!-- ch01-p064 -->
If we compare the different cases in I and II, we see that the same change in the magnitude of relative value may arise from completely opposite causes. Thus the equation 20 yards of linen = 1 coat becomes 20 yards of linen = 2 coats, either because the value of the linen has doubled, or because the value of the coat has fallen by one-half. And it becomes 20 yards of linen = ½ coat, either because the value of the linen has fallen by one-half, or because the value of the coat has doubled.

<!-- ch01-p065 -->
III. Let the quantities of labor-time necessary to produce the linen and the coat vary at the same time, in the same direction and in the same proportion. In this case 20 yards of linen continue to equal 1 coat, however much their values may have changed. Their change of value shows up as soon as they are compared with a third commodity whose value has stayed constant. If the values of all commodities rose or fell at the same time, and in the same proportion, their relative values would stay unchanged. Their real change of value would show in the smaller or larger quantity of commodities produced in a given time.

<!-- ch01-p066 -->
IV. The labor-time necessary to produce the linen and the coat, and therefore the value of these commodities, may vary at the same time in the same direction but at unequal rates, or in opposite directions, or in other ways. The effect of all these possible variations on the relative value of a commodity can be deduced from the results of I, II, and III.

<!-- ch01-p067 -->
So real changes in the magnitude of value are reflected in their relative expression, that is, in the equation that expresses the magnitude of relative value, neither unambiguously nor completely. The relative value of a commodity may vary, although its value stays constant. Its relative value may stay constant, although its value varies. And finally, changes that happen at the same time in the magnitude of value and in its relative expression by no means necessarily match in amount.[^1.21]

[^1.21]: Vulgar economists (economists who only describe and defend the surface appearances of the system, without investigating its real relations) have exploited this mismatch between the magnitude of value and its relative expression, with their customary ingenuity. For example – “Once admit that A falls, because B, with which it is exchanged, rises, while no less labour is bestowed in the meantime on A, and your general principle of value falls to the ground... If he [Ricardo] allowed that when A rises in value relatively to B, B falls in value relatively to A, he cut away the ground on which he rested his grand proposition, that the value of a commodity is ever determined by the labour embodied in it, for if a change in the cost of A alters not only its own value in relation to B, for which it is exchanged, but also the value of B relatively to that of A, though no change has taken place in the quantity of labour to produce B, then not only the doctrine falls to the ground which asserts that the quantity of labour bestowed on an article regulates its value, but also that which affirms the cost of an article to regulate its value’ (J. Broadhurst: “Political Economy,” London, 1842, pp. 11 and 14.) Mr. Broadhurst might just as well say: consider the fractions 10/20, 10/50, 10/100, etc.; the number 10 stays unchanged, and yet its proportional magnitude, its size relative to the numbers 20, 50, 100 etc., keeps getting smaller. Therefore the great principle that the magnitude of a whole number, such as 10, is “regulated” by the number of times unity (the number one) is contained in it, falls to the ground. [The author explains in section 4 of this chapter, pp. 80-81, note 2 (note 33 of this document), what he means by “Vulgar Economy.” – Engels]

##### 3. The Equivalent form of value

<!-- ch01-p068 -->
We have seen that commodity A (the linen) expresses its value in the use-value of a commodity of a different kind (the coat), and by doing so it at the same time stamps the coat with a specific form of value, namely the form of the equivalent. The commodity linen shows that it has value through the fact that the coat is equated to it, without the coat having taken on a form of value different from its bodily form. The fact that the linen therefore has value is expressed by saying that the coat is directly exchangeable with it. Therefore, when we say that a commodity is in the equivalent form, we are expressing the fact that it is directly exchangeable with other commodities.

<!-- ch01-p069 -->
When one commodity, such as a coat, serves as the equivalent of another, such as linen, and coats as a result acquire the characteristic property of being directly exchangeable with linen, we are far from knowing in what proportion the two can be exchanged. Since the magnitude of the linen's value is given, that proportion depends on the value of the coat. The coat may serve as the equivalent and the linen as relative value, or the linen may serve as the equivalent and the coat as relative value. Either way, the magnitude of the coat's value is fixed by the labor-time necessary to produce it, independently of its form of value. But whenever the coat takes the position of equivalent in the equation of value, its value gets no quantitative expression. On the contrary, the commodity coat now figures only as a definite quantity of some article.

<!-- ch01-p070 -->
For instance, 40 yards of linen are worth – what? 2 coats. The commodity coat here plays the part of equivalent, and the use-value coat, as opposed to the linen, figures as an embodiment of value. Because of this, a definite number of coats is enough to express the definite quantity of value in the linen. Two coats may therefore express the quantity of value of 40 yards of linen, but they can never express the quantity of their own value. The fact is that in the equation of value, the equivalent figures only as a simple quantity of some article, of some use-value. A superficial look at this fact has misled Bailey, and many others too, both before and after him, into seeing nothing but a quantitative relation in the expression of value. The truth is that when a commodity acts as equivalent, no fixing of the amount of its value is expressed.

<!-- ch01-p071 -->
The first peculiarity that strikes us when we consider the form of the equivalent is this: use-value becomes the form in which its opposite, value, shows itself, the form of appearance of value.

<!-- ch01-p072 -->
The bodily form of the commodity becomes its form of value. But note well that this taking of one thing for another exists for any commodity B only when some other commodity A enters into a value relation with it, and then only within the limits of this relation. No commodity can stand in the relation of equivalent to itself, and so turn its own bodily shape into the expression of its own value. So every commodity is compelled to choose some other commodity as its equivalent, and to accept the use-value, that is, the bodily shape, of that other commodity as the form of its own value.

<!-- ch01-p073 -->
One of the measures that we apply to commodities as material things, as use-values, will illustrate this point. A sugar-loaf is a body, so it is heavy and has weight; but we can neither see nor touch this weight. We then take various pieces of iron whose weight has been determined beforehand. The iron, as iron, is no more the form of appearance of weight than the sugar-loaf is. Nevertheless, in order to express the sugar-loaf as so much weight, we put it into a weight-relation with the iron. In this relation, the iron acts as a body that represents nothing but weight. So a certain quantity of iron serves as the measure of the sugar's weight, and, in relation to the sugar-loaf, it represents weight embodied, the form of appearance of weight. The iron plays this part only within this relation, which the sugar, or any other body whose weight has to be determined, enters into with the iron. If they were not both heavy, they could not enter into this relation, and so the one could not serve as the expression of the other's weight. When we throw both into the scales, we actually see that as weight they are both the same, and that therefore, taken in the right proportions, they have the same weight. Just as the substance iron, as a measure of weight, represents weight alone in relation to the sugar-loaf, so, in our expression of value, the material object coat represents value alone in relation to the linen.

<!-- ch01-p074 -->
Here, however, the analogy ends. In expressing the weight of the sugar-loaf, the iron represents a natural property common to both bodies, namely their weight. But in expressing the value of the linen, the coat represents a non-natural property of both, something purely social, namely their value.

<!-- ch01-p075 -->
The relative form of value of a commodity – the linen, for example – expresses the value of that commodity as something wholly different from its substance and properties, as something coat-like, for instance. So we see that this expression itself points to some social relation lying at the bottom of it. With the equivalent form it is just the opposite. The very essence of this form is that the material commodity itself – the coat – just as it is, expresses value, and is given the form of value by Nature itself. Of course this holds only so long as the value relation exists in which the coat stands in the position of equivalent to the linen.[^1.22] However, the properties of a thing do not result from its relations to other things; they only show themselves in such relations. So the coat seems to be endowed by Nature with its equivalent form, its property of being directly exchangeable, just as much as with the property of being heavy, or the capacity to keep us warm. Hence the puzzling character of the equivalent form. It escapes the notice of the bourgeois political economist until this form, fully developed, confronts him in the shape of money. He then tries to explain away the mystical character of gold and silver by putting less dazzling commodities in their place, and by reciting, with ever renewed satisfaction, the catalogue of all possible commodities that at one time or another have played the part of equivalent. He has not the least suspicion that the simplest expression of value, such as 20 yds of linen = 1 coat, already sets us the riddle of the equivalent form to solve.

[^1.22]: Such expressions of relations in general, which Hegel calls reflex categories, form a very curious class. For instance, one man is king only because other men stand in the relation of subjects to him. They, on the contrary, imagine that they are subjects because he is king.

<!-- ch01-p076 -->
The body of the commodity that serves as the equivalent figures as the materialization of abstract human labor, and at the same time it is the product of some specific useful, concrete labor. So this concrete labor becomes the medium for expressing abstract human labor. If, on the one hand, the coat counts as nothing but the embodiment of abstract human labor, so, on the other hand, the tailoring actually embodied in it counts as nothing but the form in which that abstract human labor is realized. In the expression of the linen's value, the usefulness of the tailoring lies not in making clothes, but in making an object that we at once recognize to be Value, and therefore to be a congealed mass of labor. But it is labor that cannot be told apart from the labor realized in the value of the linen. To act as such a mirror of value, the labor of tailoring must reflect nothing except its own abstract quality of being human labor in general.

<!-- ch01-p077 -->
In tailoring, as well as in weaving, human labor-power is spent. Both, therefore, have the general property of being human labor, and so, in certain cases, such as the production of value, they may have to be considered under this aspect alone. There is nothing mysterious in this. But in the expression of value the tables are completely turned. For instance, how is the fact to be expressed that weaving creates the value of the linen, not by virtue of being weaving as such, but because of its general property of being human labor? Simply by setting against weaving that other particular form of concrete labor (in this instance tailoring) which produces the equivalent of the product of weaving. Just as the coat in its bodily form became a direct expression of value, so now tailoring, a concrete form of labor, appears as the direct and tangible embodiment of human labor in general.

<!-- ch01-p078 -->
So the second peculiarity of the equivalent form is that concrete labor becomes the form in which its opposite, abstract human labor, shows itself.

<!-- ch01-p079 -->
But this concrete labor, tailoring in our case, counts as undifferentiated human labor and is directly identified with it. Because of this, it also counts as identical with any other sort of labor, and therefore with the labor embodied in the linen. So, although like all other commodity-producing labor it is the labor of private individuals, it nevertheless counts at the same time as labor directly social in its character. This is the reason why it results in a product directly exchangeable with other commodities. We have, then, a third peculiarity of the equivalent form, namely that the labor of private individuals takes the form of its opposite, labor directly social in its form.

<!-- ch01-p080 -->
The two last peculiarities of the equivalent form will become easier to understand if we go back to the great thinker who was the first to analyze so many forms, whether of thought, of society, or of Nature, and among them the form of value too. I mean Aristotle.

<!-- ch01-p081 -->
In the first place, he states clearly that the money form of commodities is only the further development of the simple form of value – that is, of the expression of the value of one commodity in some other commodity taken at random. For he says:

<!-- ch01-p082 -->
> 5 beds = 1 house (κλῖναι πέντε ἀντὶ οἰκίας) [five beds for a house]

<!-- ch01-p083 -->
cannot be distinguished from

<!-- ch01-p084 -->
> 5 beds = so much money. (κλῖναι πέντε ἀντὶ ... ὅσου αἱ πέντε κλῖναι) [five beds for ... as much as the five beds]

<!-- ch01-p085 -->
He further sees that the value relation that gives rise to this expression makes it necessary for the house to be made qualitatively equal to the bed. He sees that without such an equalization, these two clearly different things could not be compared with each other as commensurable quantities, that is, as quantities measurable by a common standard. “Exchange,” he says, “cannot take place without equality, and equality not without commensurability". (οὔτ᾿ ἰσότης μὴ οὔσης συμμετρίας) [nor equality where there is no commensurability]. Here, however, he comes to a stop, and gives up analyzing the form of value any further. “It is, however, in reality, impossible (τῇ μὲν οὖν ἀληθείᾳ ἀδύνατον) [in truth, then, impossible], that such unlike things can be commensurable” – that is, qualitatively equal. Such an equalization can only be something foreign to their real nature, and so only “a makeshift for practical purposes.”

<!-- ch01-p086 -->
So Aristotle himself tells us what blocked his further analysis: it was the absence of any concept of value. What is that equal something, that common substance, which allows the value of the beds to be expressed by a house? Such a thing, in truth, cannot exist, says Aristotle. And why not? Compared with the beds, the house does represent something equal to them, insofar as it represents what is really equal in both the beds and the house. And that is – human labor.

<!-- ch01-p087 -->
There was, however, an important fact that prevented Aristotle from seeing that to attribute value to commodities is merely a way of expressing all labor as equal human labor, and therefore as labor of equal quality. Greek society was founded on slavery, and therefore had as its natural basis the inequality of human beings and of their labor-powers. The secret of the expression of value, namely that all kinds of labor are equal and equivalent because, and so far as, they are human labor in general, cannot be deciphered until the notion of human equality has already become as firmly fixed as a popular prejudice. This, however, is possible only in a society in which the great mass of the products of labor takes the form of commodities, and in which, therefore, the dominant relation between one person and another is that of owners of commodities. The brilliance of Aristotle's genius is shown by this alone: that he discovered a relation of equality in the expression of the value of commodities. Only the particular conditions of the society in which he lived prevented him from discovering what, “in truth,” lay at the bottom of this equality.

##### 4. The Elementary Form of value considered as a whole

<!-- ch01-p088 -->
The elementary form of value of a commodity is contained in the equation that expresses its value relation to another commodity of a different kind, or its exchange relation to that commodity. The value of commodity A is expressed qualitatively by the fact that commodity B is directly exchangeable with it. Its value is expressed quantitatively by the fact that a definite quantity of B is exchangeable with a definite quantity of A. In other words, the value of a commodity gets an independent and definite expression by taking the form of exchange-value. At the beginning of this chapter we said, in everyday language, that a commodity is both a use-value and an exchange-value. Strictly speaking, we were wrong. A commodity is a use-value, or useful object, and a value. It shows itself as the twofold thing it is as soon as its value takes on an independent form, namely the form of exchange-value. It never takes on this form when isolated, but only when it is placed in a value relation or exchange relation with another commodity of a different kind. Once we know this, that way of speaking does no harm; it simply serves as an abbreviation.

<!-- ch01-p089 -->
Our analysis has shown that the form or expression of the value of a commodity arises from the nature of value, and not that value and its magnitude arise from the way they are expressed as exchange-value. This, however, is the delusion both of the mercantilists and their recent revivers, Ferrier, Ganilh,[^1.23] and others, and of their opposites, the modern traveling salesmen of Free-trade, such as Bastiat. The mercantilists lay special stress on the qualitative side of the expression of value, and so on the equivalent form of commodities, which reaches its full perfection in money. The modern peddlers of Free-trade, on the other hand, who must get rid of their goods at any price, lay most stress on the quantitative side of the relative form of value. So for them neither value nor magnitude of value exists anywhere except in its expression through the exchange relation of commodities, that is, in the daily list of current prices. Macleod, who has taken it upon himself to dress up the confused ideas of Lombard Street (the center of London banking) in the most learned finery, is a successful cross between the superstitious mercantilists and the enlightened Free-trade traveling salesmen.

[^1.23]: F. L. A. Ferrier, sous-inspecteur des douanes [sub-inspector of customs], “Du gouvernement considéré dans ses rapports avec le commerce,” Paris, 1805; and Charles Ganilh, “Des Systèmes d’Economie Politique, – 2nd ed., Paris, 1821.

<!-- ch01-p090 -->
A close examination of the expression of the value of A in terms of B, contained in the equation that expresses the value relation of A to B, has shown us the following: within that relation, the bodily form of A figures only as a use-value, and the bodily form of B only as the form or aspect of value. So the opposition, or contrast, that exists inside each commodity between use-value and value is made visible on the outside when two commodities are placed in a particular relation to each other. In that relation, the commodity whose value is to be expressed figures directly as a mere use-value, while the commodity in which that value is to be expressed figures directly as mere exchange-value. Hence the elementary form of value of a commodity is the elementary form in which the contrast contained in that commodity, between use-value and value, becomes visible.

<!-- ch01-p091 -->
Every product of labor is a use-value in all states of society. But only at a definite historical epoch in a society's development does such a product become a commodity, namely at the epoch when the labor spent on producing a useful article comes to be expressed as one of the objective qualities of that article, that is, as its value. It therefore follows that the elementary form of value is also the earliest form in which a product of labor appears historically as a commodity, and that the gradual transformation of such products into commodities proceeds at the same pace as the development of the form of value.

<!-- ch01-p092 -->
At first sight we see the shortcomings of the elementary form of value: it is a mere germ, which must go through a series of metamorphoses before it can ripen into the price form.

<!-- ch01-p093 -->
The expression of the value of commodity A in terms of any other commodity B merely distinguishes the value of A from its use-value, and so places A merely in a relation of exchange with one single different commodity, B. But it is still far from expressing A's qualitative equality with all commodities, and its quantitative proportionality to them. To the elementary relative form of value of one commodity there corresponds the single equivalent form of one other commodity. Thus, in the relative expression of the linen's value, the coat takes the form of equivalent, or of being directly exchangeable, only in relation to a single commodity, the linen.

<!-- ch01-p094 -->
Nevertheless, the elementary form of value passes over easily into a more complete form. It is true that through the elementary form the value of a commodity A is expressed in terms of one, and only one, other commodity. But that one may be a commodity of any kind: coat, iron, grain, or anything else. So, depending on whether A is placed in relation with one or another of them, we get different elementary expressions of value for one and the same commodity.[^1.24] The number of such possible expressions is limited only by the number of different kinds of commodities distinct from it. So the isolated expression of A's value can be turned into a series, prolonged to any length, of the different elementary expressions of that value.

[^1.24]: In Homer, for instance, the value of an article is expressed in a series of different things. *Iliad*. VII. 472-475.

#### B. Total or Expanded Form of value

<!-- ch01-p095 -->
> z Com. A = u Com. B or = v Com. C or = w Com. D or = Com. E or = &c.

<!-- ch01-p096 -->
(20 yards of linen = 1 coat or = 10 lbs tea or = 40 lbs. coffee or\
= 1 quarter corn or = 2 ounces gold or = ½ ton iron or = &c.)

##### 1. The Expanded Relative form of value

<!-- ch01-p097 -->
The value of a single commodity, the linen for example, is now expressed in terms of countless other elements of the world of commodities. Every other commodity now becomes a mirror of the linen’s value.[^1.25] So it is here that, for the first time, this value shows itself in its true light, as a congealed mass of undifferentiated human labor. For the labor that creates it now stands openly revealed as labor that ranks as equal with every other sort of human labor, whatever its form, whether tailoring, plowing, mining, etc., and so whether it is realized in coats, grain, iron, or gold. Through the form of its value, the linen now stands in a social relation, no longer with only one other kind of commodity, but with the whole world of commodities. As a commodity, it is a citizen of that world. At the same time, the endless series of value equations implies that, as regards the value of a commodity, it makes no difference in what particular form, or kind, of use-value it appears.

[^1.25]: For this reason we can speak of the coat value of the linen when its value is expressed in coats, or of its grain value when it is expressed in grain, and so on. Every such expression tells us that what appears in the use-values coat, grain, etc., is the value of the linen. “The value of any commodity denoting its relation in exchange, we may speak of it as ... corn [grain] value, cloth value, according to the commodity with which it is compared; and hence there are a thousand different kinds of value, as many kinds of value as there are commodities in existence, and all are equally real and equally nominal.” (“A Critical Dissertation on the Nature, Measures and Causes of Value: chiefly in reference to the writings of Mr. Ricardo and his followers.” By the author of “Essays on the Formation, &c., of Opinions.” London, 1825, p. 39.) S. Bailey, the author of this anonymous work, which caused a great stir in England in its day, fancied that by pointing out in this way the various relative expressions of one and the same value, he had proved that the concept of value could not be determined at all. However narrow his own views may have been, he did lay his finger on some serious defects in the Ricardian Theory. The proof is the hostility with which Ricardo’s followers attacked him. See, for example, the Westminster Review.

<!-- ch01-p098 -->
In the first form, 20 yds of linen = 1 coat, it might be pure accident, for all that appears otherwise, that these two commodities are exchangeable in definite quantities. In the second form, on the contrary, we see at once the background that determines this accidental appearance and is essentially different from it. The value of the linen stays the same in magnitude, whether it is expressed in coats, coffee, or iron, or in countless different commodities belonging to as many different owners. The accidental relation between two individual commodity-owners disappears. It becomes clear that it is not the exchange of commodities that regulates the magnitude of their value. On the contrary, it is the magnitude of their value that controls their exchange proportions.

##### 2. The particular Equivalent form

<!-- ch01-p099 -->
Each commodity, such as coat, tea, grain, iron, etc., figures in the expression of the linen’s value as an equivalent, and so as a thing that is value. The bodily form of each of these commodities now figures as a particular equivalent form, one out of many. In the same way, the many concrete, useful kinds of labor embodied in these different commodities now rank as so many different forms in which undifferentiated human labor is realized, or shows itself.

##### 3. Defects of the Total or Expanded form of value

<!-- ch01-p100 -->
First, the relative expression of value is incomplete, because the series that represents it never ends.
