The chain in which each equation of value is a link can at any moment be lengthened by each new kind of commodity that comes into existence and supplies the material for a fresh expression of value. Second, it is a many-colored mosaic of dissimilar and independent expressions of value. And lastly, if the relative value of each commodity in turn is expressed in this expanded form, as must be the case, we get for each of them a relative form of value that is different in every case and consists of an endless series of expressions of value. The defects of the expanded relative form of value are reflected in the corresponding equivalent form. The bodily form of each single commodity is one particular equivalent form among countless others. So, on the whole, we have nothing but fragmentary equivalent forms, each excluding the others. In the same way, the special, concrete, useful kind of labor embodied in each particular equivalent is presented only as a particular kind of labor, and so not as an exhaustive representative of human labor generally. Human labor generally does, indeed, find adequate expression in the totality of its many particular, concrete forms. But in that case its expression in an infinite series is always incomplete and lacks unity.

<!-- ch01-p101 -->
The expanded relative form of value, however, is nothing but the sum of the elementary relative expressions, or equations of the first kind, such as:

<!-- ch01-p102 -->
20 yards of linen = 1 coat\
20 yards of linen = 10 lbs of tea, etc.

<!-- ch01-p103 -->
Each of these implies the corresponding reversed equation,

<!-- ch01-p104 -->
1 coat = 20 yards of linen\
10 lbs of tea = 20 yards of linen, etc.

<!-- ch01-p105 -->
In fact, when a person exchanges his linen for many other commodities, and so expresses its value in a series of other commodities, it necessarily follows that the various owners of those other commodities exchange them for the linen, and so express the value of their various commodities in one and the same third commodity, the linen. If, then, we reverse the series 20 yards of linen = 1 coat or = 10 lbs of tea, etc., that is, if we express the converse relation already implied in the series, we get,

#### C. The General Form of Value

<!-- ch01-p106 -->
```text
1        coat
10       lbs of tea
40       lbs of coffee
1        quarter of corn           = 20 yards of linen
2        ounces of gold
½        a ton of iron
x        Commodity A, etc.
```

##### 1. The altered character of the form of value

<!-- ch01-p107 -->
All commodities now express their value (1) in an elementary form, because in a single commodity; (2) with unity, because in one and the same commodity. This form of value is elementary and the same for all, and therefore general.

<!-- ch01-p108 -->
Forms A and B were suited only to expressing the value of a commodity as something distinct from its use-value or material form.

<!-- ch01-p109 -->
The first form, A, supplies equations such as these: – 1 coat = 20 yards of linen, 10 lbs of tea = ½ a ton of iron. The value of the coat is equated to linen, the value of the tea to iron. But to be equated to linen, and again to iron, is to be as different as linen and iron are. Clearly, this form occurs in practice only at the very beginning, when the products of labor are turned into commodities by accidental and occasional exchanges.

<!-- ch01-p110 -->
The second form, B, distinguishes the value of a commodity from its use-value more adequately than the first form does. For there the value of the coat is set against the bodily form of the coat in every possible shape: it is equated to linen, to iron, to tea, in short to everything else, only not to itself, the coat. On the other hand, any general expression of value common to all is directly ruled out. For in the equation of value of each commodity, all other commodities now appear only in the form of equivalents. The expanded form of value first comes into actual existence as soon as a particular product of labor, such as cattle, is exchanged for various other commodities no longer as an exception, but habitually.

<!-- ch01-p111 -->
The third form, the last to be developed, expresses the values of the whole world of commodities in terms of a single commodity set apart for the purpose, namely the linen. So it represents their values to us by means of their equality with linen. By being equated to linen, the value of every commodity is now distinguished not only from its own use-value, but from all other use-values generally. By that very fact it is expressed as what is common to all commodities. Through this form, commodities are for the first time actually brought into relation with one another as values, or made to appear as exchange-values.

<!-- ch01-p112 -->
The two earlier forms express the value of each commodity either in terms of a single commodity of a different kind, or in a series of many such commodities. In both cases it is, so to speak, the special business of each single commodity to find an expression for its value, and it does this without the help of the others. In relation to it, these others play the passive parts of equivalents. The general form of value, C, results from the joint action of the whole world of commodities, and from that alone. A commodity can get a general expression of its value only if all other commodities, at the same time as it, express their values in the same equivalent; and every new commodity must follow suit. So it becomes clear that, since the existence of commodities as values is purely social, this social existence can be expressed only by the totality of their social relations, and so that the form of their value must be a socially recognized form.

<!-- ch01-p113 -->
Now that all commodities are equated to linen, they appear not only as qualitatively equal, as values in general, but also as values whose magnitudes can be compared. Because they express the magnitudes of their values in one and the same material, the linen, those magnitudes are also compared with each other. For instance, 10 lbs of tea = 20 yards of linen, and 40 lbs of coffee = 20 yards of linen. Therefore, 10 lbs of tea = 40 lbs of coffee. In other words, 1 lb of coffee contains only one-fourth as much substance of value – labor – as 1 lb of tea contains.

<!-- ch01-p114 -->
The general form of relative value, which takes in the whole world of commodities, turns the single commodity that is excluded from the rest and made to play the part of equivalent – here the linen – into the universal equivalent. The bodily form of the linen is now the form that the values of all commodities take in common. So it becomes directly exchangeable with every one of them. The substance linen becomes the visible incarnation, the social chrysalis state, of every kind of human labor. Weaving, which is the labor of certain private individuals producing a particular article, linen, therefore acquires a social character, the character of equality with all other kinds of labor. The countless equations that make up the general form of value equate, in turn, the labor embodied in the linen with the labor embodied in every other commodity. In this way they turn weaving into the general form in which undifferentiated human labor shows itself. In this manner the labor realized in the values of commodities is presented not only in its negative aspect, in which every concrete form and useful property of actual work is set aside; its own positive nature is also made to reveal itself expressly. The general form of value is the reduction of all kinds of actual labor to their common character of being human labor generally, of being the spending of human labor-power.

<!-- ch01-p115 -->
The general form of value, which represents all products of labor as mere congealed masses of undifferentiated human labor, shows by its very structure that it is the social summing-up of the world of commodities. So that form makes it beyond dispute that, in the world of commodities, the character that all labor has of being *human* labor is its specific social character.

##### 2. The Interdependent Development of the Relative Form of Value, and of the Equivalent Form

<!-- ch01-p116 -->
The degree of development of the relative form of value corresponds to that of the equivalent form. But we must remember that the development of the equivalent form is only the expression and result of the development of the relative form.

<!-- ch01-p117 -->
The primary or isolated relative form of value of one commodity turns some other commodity into an isolated equivalent. The expanded form of relative value, which is the expression of the value of one commodity in terms of all other commodities, gives those other commodities the character of particular equivalents of different kinds. And lastly, a particular kind of commodity acquires the character of universal equivalent, because all other commodities make it the material in which they uniformly express their value.

<!-- ch01-p118 -->
The opposition between the relative form of value and the equivalent form, the two poles of the form of value, develops along with that form itself.

<!-- ch01-p119 -->
The first form, 20 yds of linen = one coat, already contains this opposition, but does not yet fix it. Depending on whether we read this equation forwards or backwards, the linen and the coat play different parts. In one case the relative value of the linen is expressed in the coat; in the other, the relative value of the coat is expressed in the linen. So in this first form of value it is difficult to grasp the polar contrast.

<!-- ch01-p120 -->
Form B shows that only one single commodity at a time can fully expand its relative value, and that it gets this expanded form only because, and insofar as, all other commodities are equivalents with respect to it. Here we cannot reverse the equation, as we can the equation 20 yds of linen = 1 coat, without changing its general character and turning it from the expanded form of value into the general form of value.

<!-- ch01-p121 -->
Finally, form C gives the world of commodities a general social relative form of value, because, and insofar as, all commodities except one are thereby excluded from the equivalent form. So a single commodity, the linen, appears to have acquired the character of direct exchangeability with every other commodity because, and insofar as, this character is denied to every other commodity.[^1.26]

[^1.26]: It is by no means self-evident that this character of direct and universal exchangeability is, so to speak, a polar one, and as closely bound up with its opposite pole, the absence of direct exchangeability, as the positive pole of the magnet is with its negative counterpart. So one may imagine that all commodities can have this character stamped on them at the same time, just as one can imagine that all Catholics can be popes together. In the eyes of the petit bourgeois, for whom the production of commodities is the very height of human freedom and individual independence, it is of course highly desirable that the inconveniences resulting from this character of commodities, their not being directly exchangeable, should be removed. Proudhon’s socialism is a working out of this Philistine Utopia, a form of socialism which, as I have shown elsewhere, does not have even the merit of originality. Long before his time, Gray, Bray, and others attempted the task with much better success. But for all that, wisdom of this kind still flourishes in certain circles under the name of “science.” No school has ever played more tricks with the word science than the school of Proudhon, for “wo Begriffe fehlen, Da stellt zur rechten Zeit ein Wort sich ein.” [“Where concepts are lacking, a word turns up just at the right time,” Goethe’s, Faust, See Proudhon’s Philosophy of Poverty]

<!-- ch01-p122 -->
The commodity that figures as universal equivalent, on the other hand, is excluded from the relative form of value. If the linen, or any other commodity serving as universal equivalent, were at the same time to share in the relative form of value, it would have to serve as its own equivalent. We would then have 20 yds of linen = 20 yds of linen, and this tautology expresses neither value nor magnitude of value. To express the relative value of the universal equivalent, we must rather reverse form C. This equivalent has no relative form of value in common with other commodities; instead its value is expressed relatively by a never-ending series of other commodities. So the expanded form of relative value, or form B, now shows itself to be the specific form of relative value for the equivalent commodity.

##### 3. Transition from the General form of value to the Money form

<!-- ch01-p123 -->
The universal equivalent form is a form of value in general. So any commodity can take it on. On the other hand, if a commodity is found to have taken on the universal equivalent form (form C), this is only because, and insofar as, it has been excluded from all the other commodities as their equivalent, and excluded by their own act. And from the moment that this exclusion is finally restricted to one particular commodity, from that moment only, does the general form of relative value of the world of commodities gain real consistency and general social validity.

<!-- ch01-p124 -->
The particular commodity with whose bodily form the equivalent form is thus socially identified now becomes the money commodity, or serves as money. It becomes the special social function of that commodity, and so its social monopoly, to play the part of the universal equivalent within the world of commodities. Among the commodities that figure as particular equivalents of the linen in form B, and that in form C express their relative values in common in linen, one in particular has won this foremost place – namely, gold. If, then, in form C we replace the linen by gold, we get,

#### D. The Money-Form

<!-- ch01-p125 -->
```text
20 yards of linen    =
1 coat               =
10 lbs of tea        =
40 lbs of coffee     =
                           = 2 ounces of gold
1 quarter of corn =
½ a ton of iron      =
x Commodity A =
```

<!-- ch01-p126 -->
In passing from form A to form B, and from form B to form C, the changes are fundamental. On the other hand, there is no difference between forms C and D, except that in form D gold has taken on the equivalent form in place of linen. Gold is in form D what linen was in form C – the universal equivalent. The progress consists in this alone: the character of direct and universal exchangeability – in other words, the universal equivalent form – has now, by social custom, become finally identified with the substance gold.

<!-- ch01-p127 -->
Gold is now money with reference to all other commodities only because it was previously, with reference to them, a simple commodity. Like all other commodities, it was also able to serve as an equivalent, either as a simple equivalent in isolated exchanges, or as a particular equivalent alongside others. Gradually it began to serve, within varying limits, as universal equivalent. As soon as it monopolizes this position in the expression of value for the world of commodities, it becomes the money commodity. Then, and not until then, does form D become distinct from form C, and the general form of value turn into the money form.

<!-- ch01-p128 -->
The elementary expression of the relative value of a single commodity, such as linen, in terms of the commodity, such as gold, that plays the part of money, is the price form of that commodity. So the price form of the linen is

<!-- ch01-p129 -->
20 yards of linen = 2 ounces of gold, or, if 2 ounces of gold when\
coined are £2, 20 yards of linen = £2.

<!-- ch01-p130 -->
The difficulty in forming a concept of the money form lies in clearly understanding the universal equivalent form, and, as a necessary consequence, the general form of value, form C. Form C can be derived from form B, the expanded form of value, whose essential component element, as we saw, is form A, 20 yards of linen = 1 coat or x commodity A = y commodity B. So the simple commodity form is the germ of the money form.

### Section 4: The Fetishism of Commodities and the Secret Thereof

<!-- ch01-p131 -->
At first sight a commodity seems a very trivial thing, and easy to understand. Analysis shows that it is, in reality, a very strange thing, full of metaphysical subtleties and theological niceties. So far as it is a use-value, there is nothing mysterious about it. That holds whether we look at it from the point of view that its properties make it capable of satisfying human wants, or from the point of view that those properties are the product of human labor. It is as clear as noon-day that man, by his industry, changes the forms of the materials supplied by Nature in such a way as to make them useful to him. The form of wood, for instance, is altered when a table is made out of it. Yet, for all that, the table goes on being that common, everyday thing, wood. But as soon as it steps forward as a commodity, it is changed into something transcendent. It not only stands with its feet on the ground, but, in relation to all other commodities, it also stands on its head, and out of its wooden brain it spins grotesque ideas, far more wonderful than “table-turning” ever was.[^1.26a]

[^1.26a]: At this point the German edition has the following footnote: “One may recall that China and the tables began to dance when the rest of the world appeared to be standing still – pour encourager les autres [to encourage the others].” The defeat of the 1848-49 revolutions was followed by a period of grim political reaction in Europe. At that time spiritualism, and table-turning in particular, became the rage among the European aristocracy. In 1850-64, China was swept by an anti-feudal liberation movement in the form of a large-scale peasant war, the Taiping Revolt. – Note by editors of MECW.

<!-- ch01-p132 -->
So the mystical character of commodities does not come from their use-value. Just as little does it come from the nature of the factors that determine value. For, in the first place, however varied the useful kinds of labor, or productive activities, may be, it is a physiological fact that they are functions of the human organism. And each such function, whatever its nature or form, is essentially the spending of human brain, nerves, muscles, etc. Secondly, take the thing that forms the groundwork for fixing the amount of value, namely the duration of that spending, or the quantity of labor. Here it is quite clear that there is a tangible difference between its quantity and its quality. In all states of society, the labor-time that it costs to produce the means of subsistence must necessarily be an object of interest to mankind, though not of equal interest at different stages of development.[^1.27] And lastly, from the moment that men work for one another in any way, their labor takes on a social form.

[^1.27]: Among the ancient Germans the unit for measuring land was what could be harvested in a day. It was called Tagwerk [day’s work], Tagwanne [a day’s work] (jurnale, or terra jurnalis, or diornalis [day’s land]), Mannsmaad [a man’s mowing], etc. (See G. L. von Maurer, “Einleitung zur Geschichte der Mark, &c. Verfassung,” Munchen, 1854, p. 129 and following.)

<!-- ch01-p133 -->
Where, then, does the puzzling character of the product of labor come from, as soon as it takes the form of a commodity? Clearly from this form itself. The equality of all sorts of human labor is expressed objectively by the fact that their products are all equally values. The measure of the spending of labor-power by its duration takes the form of the quantity of value of the products of labor. And finally, the mutual relations of the producers, within which the social character of their labor asserts itself, take the form of a social relation between the products.

<!-- ch01-p134 -->
A commodity is therefore a mysterious thing, simply because in it the social character of men’s labor appears to them as an objective character stamped on the product of that labor. It is mysterious because the relation of the producers to the sum total of their own labor is presented to them as a social relation that exists not between themselves, but between the products of their labor. This is the reason why the products of labor become commodities: social things whose qualities are at the same time perceptible and imperceptible to the senses. In the same way, we perceive the light from an object not as a subjective stimulation of our optic nerve, but as the objective form of something outside the eye itself. But in the act of seeing, at any rate, light actually passes from one thing to another, from the external object to the eye. There is a physical relation between physical things. But it is different with commodities. There, the existence of the things as commodities, and the value relation between the products of labor that stamps them as commodities, have absolutely no connection with their physical properties, or with the material relations that arise from those properties. There it is a definite social relation between men that takes on, in their eyes, the fantastic form of a relation between things. So, to find an analogy, we must turn to the mist-covered regions of the religious world. In that world the products of the human brain appear as independent beings endowed with life, which enter into relations both with one another and with the human race. So it is in the world of commodities with the products of men’s hands. This I call the Fetishism that attaches itself to the products of labor as soon as they are produced as commodities, and which is therefore inseparable from the production of commodities.

<!-- ch01-p135 -->
This Fetishism of commodities has its origin, as the analysis so far has already shown, in the peculiar social character of the labor that produces them.

<!-- ch01-p136 -->
As a general rule, useful articles become commodities only because they are products of the labor of private individuals, or groups of individuals, who carry on their work independently of each other. The sum total of the labor of all these private individuals forms the total labor of society. The producers do not come into social contact with each other until they exchange their products. Because of this, the specific social character of each producer’s labor does not show itself except in the act of exchange. In other words, the labor of the individual asserts itself as a part of the labor of society only through the relations that the act of exchange sets up directly between the products, and indirectly, through them, between the producers. To the producers, therefore, the relations that connect the labor of one individual with that of the rest appear, not as direct social relations between individuals at work, but as what they really are: material relations between persons and social relations between things. It is only by being exchanged that the products of labor acquire, as values, one uniform social status, distinct from their varied forms of existence as useful objects. This division of a product into a useful thing and a value becomes important in practice only when exchange has spread so far that useful articles are produced for the purpose of being exchanged. At that point, their character as values therefore has to be taken into account in advance, during production. From this moment, the labor of the individual producer acquires socially a two-fold character. On the one hand, as a definite useful kind of labor, it must satisfy a definite social want. In this way it holds its place as part and parcel of the collective labor of all, as a branch of a social division of labor that has sprung up spontaneously. On the other hand, it can satisfy the many wants of the individual producer himself only insofar as the mutual exchangeability of all kinds of useful private labor is an established social fact, and the private useful labor of each producer therefore ranks as equal with that of all others. The most different kinds of labor can be made equal only by abstracting from their inequalities, or by reducing them to their common denominator, namely the spending of human labor-power, or abstract human labor. When this two-fold social character of the individual’s labor is reflected in his brain, it appears to him only in the forms that the exchange of products impresses on that labor in everyday practice. In this way, the socially useful character of his own labor takes the form of the condition that the product must be not only useful, but useful for others. And the social character that his particular labor has, of being equal to all other particular kinds of labor, takes the form that all the physically different articles that are products of labor have one common quality, namely that of having value.

<!-- ch01-p137 -->
So when we bring the products of our labor into relation with each other as values, it is not because we see these things as mere material containers of uniform human labor. Quite the opposite. Whenever we exchange our different products and so treat them as equal values, by that very act we also treat the different kinds of labor spent on them as equal, as human labor. We are not aware of this, but we do it.[^1.28] Value, then, does not walk around with a label saying what it is. Rather, it is value that turns every product into a social hieroglyph, a sign whose meaning is hidden. Later on, we try to decode the hieroglyph and get behind the secret of our own social products. For stamping a useful object as a value is just as much a social product as language is. Science has recently discovered that the products of labor, so far as they are values, are only the material expressions of the human labor spent in producing them. This discovery does mark an epoch in the history of human development. But it by no means clears away the mist through which the social character of labor looks to us like a property of the products themselves. In the particular form of production we are dealing with, namely the production of commodities, private labor is carried on independently, and its specific social character consists in the equality of every kind of such labor as human labor; in the product, this character therefore takes the form of value. To the producers, despite the discovery just mentioned, this fact seems just as real and final as another fact: that after science discovered the gases that make up air, the air itself stayed exactly as it was.

[^1.28]: So when Galiani says that value is a relation between persons – “La Ricchezza e una ragione tra due persone” [“Wealth is a relation between two persons”] – he ought to have added: a relation between persons expressed as a relation between things. (Galiani: Della Moneta, p. 221, V. III. of Custodi’s collection of “Scrittori Classici Italiani di Economia Politica.” Parte Moderna, Milano 1803.)

<!-- ch01-p138 -->
When producers make an exchange, what first of all concerns them in practice is the question: how much of some other product do they get for their own? In what proportions are the products exchangeable? When custom has made these proportions fairly stable, they appear to result from the nature of the products. For instance, one ton of iron and two ounces of gold then appear to be of equal value just as naturally as a pound of gold and a pound of iron appear to be of equal weight, in spite of their different physical and chemical qualities. Once the character of having value has been impressed on products, it becomes fixed only because they act and react on each other as quantities of value. These quantities vary continually, independently of the will, foresight and action of the producers. To the producers, their own social action takes the form of the action of objects, which rule the producers instead of being ruled by them. It takes a fully developed production of commodities before a scientific conviction springs up, from accumulated experience alone, that all the different kinds of private labor are continually being reduced to the quantitative proportions in which society requires them. These kinds of private labor are carried on independently of each other, and yet as branches of the social division of labor that have developed spontaneously. And why? Because, in the midst of all the accidental and ever-fluctuating exchange relations between the products, the labor-time socially necessary for their production forcibly asserts itself like an overriding law of Nature. In the same way, the law of gravity asserts itself when a house falls down around our ears.[^1.29] That the magnitude of value is determined by labor-time is therefore a secret, hidden under the apparent fluctuations in the relative values of commodities. Discovering this secret removes all appearance of mere chance from the way the magnitude of the values of products is determined. Yet it in no way changes the way in which that determining takes place.

[^1.29]: “What are we to think of a law that asserts itself only by periodical revolutions? It is just nothing but a law of Nature, founded on the want of knowledge of those whose action is the subject of it.” (Friedrich Engels: “Umrisse zu einer Kritik der Nationalökonomie,” in the “Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher,” edited by Arnold Ruge and Karl Marx. Paris. 1844.)

<!-- ch01-p139 -->
Man’s reflections on the forms of social life, and therefore also his scientific analysis of those forms, take a course directly opposite to that of their actual historical development. He begins after the event, with the results of the process of development already lying ready before him. Certain characters stamp products as commodities, and these characters must be established before there can be any circulation of commodities (the exchange of commodities through money: selling and buying). They have already acquired the stability of natural, self-evident forms of social life before man tries to decipher them. And what he tries to decipher is not their historical character, for in his eyes they are unchangeable, but their meaning. Consequently, it was only the analysis of the prices of commodities that led to determining the magnitude of value, and only the common expression of all commodities in money that led to establishing their character as values. But it is just this final money form of the world of commodities that actually conceals, instead of revealing, the social character of private labor and the social relations between the individual producers. When I state that coats or boots stand in a relation to linen because linen is the universal incarnation of abstract human labor, the absurdity of the statement is obvious. Nevertheless, the producers of coats and boots compare those articles with linen, or, what is the same thing, with gold or silver, as the universal equivalent. When they do, they express the relation between their own private labor and the collective labor of society in the same absurd form.

<!-- ch01-p140 -->
The categories of bourgeois economics consist of forms of just this kind. They are forms of thought that express, with social validity, the conditions and relations of a definite, historically determined mode of production, namely the production of commodities. So the whole mystery of commodities, all the magic and necromancy that surrounds the products of labor as long as they take the form of commodities, vanishes as soon as we come to other forms of production.

<!-- ch01-p141 -->
Since Robinson Crusoe’s experiences are a favorite theme with political economists,[^1.30] let us take a look at him on his island. Frugal though he is, he still has a few wants to satisfy, and so he must do a little useful work of various sorts, such as making tools and furniture, taming goats, fishing and hunting. We take no account of his prayers and the like, since they are a source of pleasure to him and he looks on them as so much recreation. In spite of the variety of his work, he knows that his labor, whatever its form, is only the activity of one and the same Robinson, and so that it consists of nothing but different modes of human labor. Necessity itself forces him to divide his time accurately between his different kinds of work. Whether one kind takes up more room in his overall activity than another depends on the difficulties, greater or less as the case may be, that he must overcome to get the useful effect he aims at. Our friend Robinson soon learns this by experience. He has rescued a watch, a ledger, and pen and ink from the wreck, and, like a true-born Briton, he starts to keep a set of books. His stock-book contains a list of the useful objects that belong to him, of the operations needed to produce them, and lastly of the labor-time that definite quantities of those objects have, on average, cost him. All the relations between Robinson and the objects that form this wealth of his own creation are here so simple and clear that anyone can understand them without effort, even Mr. Sedley Taylor. And yet those relations contain everything essential to the determination of value.

[^1.30]: Even Ricardo has his stories in Robinson’s style. “He makes the primitive hunter and the primitive fisher straightway, as owners of commodities, exchange fish and game in the proportion in which labour time is incorporated in these exchange values. On this occasion he commits the anachronism of making these men apply to the calculation, so far as their implements have to be taken into account, the annuity tables in current use on the London Exchange in the year 1817. The parallelograms of Mr. Owen appear to be the only form of society, besides the bourgeois form, with which he was acquainted.” (Karl Marx: “Zur Kritik, &c.,” pp. 38, 39)

<!-- ch01-p142 -->
Let us now move from Robinson’s island, bathed in light, to the European middle ages, shrouded in darkness. Here, instead of the independent man, we find everyone dependent: serfs and lords, vassals and suzerains (overlords), laymen and clergy. Personal dependence here marks the social relations of production just as much as it marks the other spheres of life that are organized on the basis of that production. But for the very reason that personal dependence forms the groundwork of society, there is no need for labor and its products to take on a fantastic form different from their reality. In the transactions of society they take the shape of services in kind and payments in kind. Here the immediate social form of labor is the particular and natural form of labor, and not its general abstract form, as it is in a society based on the production of commodities. Compulsory labor is measured by time just as properly as commodity-producing labor is. But every serf knows that what he spends in the service of his lord is a definite quantity of his own personal labor-power. The tithe (the tenth part of produce owed to the church) that has to be handed over to the priest is more of a plain fact than his blessing is. So, no matter what we may think of the parts played by the different classes of people themselves in this society, the social relations between individuals in the performance of their labor appear, at any rate, as their own mutual personal relations. They are not disguised under the shape of social relations between the products of labor.

<!-- ch01-p143 -->
For an example of labor in common, or directly associated labor, we have no need to go back to the spontaneously developed form of it that we find on the threshold of the history of all civilized peoples.[^1.31] We have one close at hand in the patriarchal industries of a peasant family that produces grain, cattle, yarn, linen, and clothing for home use. As far as the family is concerned, these different articles are so many products of its labor, but in relation to one another they are not commodities. The different kinds of labor that result in the various products, such as tilling the soil, tending cattle, spinning, weaving and making clothes, are, in themselves and just as they are, direct social functions. They are so because they are functions of the family. And the family, just as much as a society based on the production of commodities, has a spontaneously developed system of division of labor. The distribution of the work within the family, and the regulation of the labor-time of its several members, depend on differences of age and sex as well as on natural conditions that vary with the seasons. In this case the labor-power of each individual, by its very nature, works merely as a definite portion of the whole labor-power of the family. And therefore the measure of the spending of individual labor-power by its duration appears here, by its very nature, as a social character of their labor.

[^1.31]: A ridiculous presumption has lately spread that common property in its primitive form is specifically a Slavonian, or even exclusively Russian form. It is the primitive form that we can prove to have existed amongst Romans, Germanic peoples, and Celts, and even to this day we find numerous examples, ruins though they be, in India. A more exhaustive study of Asiatic, and especially of Indian forms of common property, would show how from the different forms of primitive common property, different forms of its dissolution have been developed. Thus, for instance, the various original types of Roman and Germanic private property are deducible from different forms of Indian common property.” (Karl Marx, “Zur Kritik, &c.,” p. 10.)

<!-- ch01-p144 -->
Let us now picture to ourselves, for a change, a community of free individuals, who carry on their work with the means of production held in common. In this community the labor-power of all the different individuals is consciously applied as the combined labor-power of the community. All the characteristics of Robinson’s labor are repeated here, but with this difference: they are social instead of individual. Everything Robinson produced was exclusively the result of his own personal labor, and therefore simply an object of use for himself. The total product of our community is a social product. One portion of it serves as fresh means of production and remains social. But another portion is consumed by the members as means of subsistence. So this portion has to be distributed among them. The way it is distributed will vary with the productive organization of the community and with the degree of historical development the producers have reached. We will assume, but only for the sake of a parallel with the production of commodities, that each individual producer’s share in the means of subsistence is determined by his labor-time. In that case labor-time would play a double part. Allotting it according to a definite social plan keeps the proper proportion between the different kinds of work to be done and the various wants of the community. On the other hand, labor-time also serves as a measure of the part of the common labor borne by each individual, and of his share in the part of the total product meant for individual consumption. In this case the social relations of the individual producers, both to their labor and to its products, are perfectly simple and understandable, and that holds not only for production but also for distribution.

<!-- ch01-p145 -->
The religious world is only the reflection of the real world. Take a society based on the production of commodities. In it the producers in general enter into social relations with one another by treating their products as commodities and values, and in this way reduce their individual private labor to the standard of uniform human labor. For such a society, Christianity, with its *cultus* [worship] of abstract man, is the most fitting form of religion, more especially in its bourgeois developments, Protestantism, Deism, etc. In the ancient Asiatic and other ancient modes of production, we find that turning products into commodities, and therefore turning men into producers of commodities, holds a subordinate place. Its importance, however, grows as the primitive communities come nearer and nearer to their dissolution. Trading nations, properly so called, exist in the ancient world only in its gaps, like the gods of Epicurus in the Intermundia [the spaces between the worlds], or like Jews in the pores of Polish society. Compared with bourgeois society, those ancient social organisms of production are extremely simple and transparent. But they are founded either on the immature development of man as an individual, who has not yet cut the umbilical cord that joins him to his fellow men in a primitive tribal community, or on direct relations of subjection. They can arise and exist only when the development of the productive power of labor has not risen beyond a low stage. And they can arise and exist only when, therefore, the social relations within the sphere of material life, between man and man and between man and Nature, are correspondingly narrow. This narrowness is reflected in the ancient worship of Nature and in the other elements of the popular religions. In any case, the religious reflection of the real world can finally vanish only when the practical relations of everyday life offer man nothing but perfectly understandable and reasonable relations with his fellow men and with Nature.

<!-- ch01-p146 -->
The life-process of society, which is based on the process of material production, does not strip off its mystical veil until it is treated as production by freely associated men and is consciously regulated by them according to a settled plan. This, however, requires that society have a certain material groundwork, or set of conditions of existence, and these in their turn are the spontaneous product of a long and painful process of development.

<!-- ch01-p147 -->
Political economy has indeed analyzed value and its magnitude, however incompletely,[^1.32] and has discovered what lies beneath these forms. But it has never once asked the question why labor is represented by the value of its product, and labor-time by the magnitude of that value.[^1.33] These formulas bear it stamped on them in unmistakable letters that they belong to a state of society in which the process of production has mastery over man, instead of being controlled by him. To the bourgeois mind, such formulas appear to be as much a self-evident necessity imposed by Nature as productive labor itself. So the bourgeoisie treat the forms of social production that came before the bourgeois form in much the same way as the Fathers of the Church treated pre-Christian religions.[^1.34]

[^1.32]: The inadequacy of Ricardo’s analysis of the magnitude of value – and his analysis is by far the best – will appear from the 3rd and 4th books of this work. As regards value in general, it is the weak point of the classical school of political economy (the economists from Petty to Ricardo who investigated the real relations of production) that nowhere does it distinguish, explicitly and with full awareness, between labor as it appears in the value of a product and the same labor as it appears in the use-value of that product. Of course the distinction is made in practice, since this school treats labor at one time under its quantitative aspect, at another under its qualitative aspect. But it has not the least idea that when the difference between various kinds of labor is treated as purely quantitative, this implies their qualitative unity or equality, and therefore their reduction to abstract human labor. For instance, Ricardo declares that he agrees with Destutt de Tracy in this proposition: “As it is certain that our physical and moral faculties are alone our original riches, the employment of those faculties, labour of some kind, is our only original treasure, and it is always from this employment that all those things are created which we call riches... It is certain, too, that all those things only represent the labour which has created them, and if they have a value, or even two distinct values, they can only derive them from that (the value) of the labour from which they emanate.” (Ricardo, “The Principles of Pol. Econ.,” 3 Ed. London 1821, p. 334.) We would only point out here that Ricardo puts his own deeper interpretation on Destutt’s words. What Destutt really says is that, on the one hand, all things that make up wealth represent the labor that creates them, but that, on the other hand, they acquire their “two different values” (use-value and exchange-value) from “the value of labour.” He thus falls into the commonplace error of the vulgar economists, who assume the value of one commodity (in this case labor) in order to determine the values of the rest. But Ricardo reads him as if he had said that labor (not the value of labor) is embodied both in use-value and in exchange-value. Nevertheless, Ricardo himself pays so little attention to the two-fold character of the labor that has a two-fold embodiment that he devotes the whole of his chapter on “Value and Riches, Their Distinctive Properties,” to a laborious examination of the trivialities of a J.B. Say. And at the end he is quite astonished to find that Destutt agrees with him, on the one hand, that labor is the source of value, and on the other hand agrees with J. B. Say about the notion of value.

[^1.33]: It is one of the chief failings of classical political economy that it has never succeeded, through its analysis of commodities, and in particular of their value, in discovering the form under which value becomes exchange-value. Even Adam Smith and Ricardo, the best representatives of the school, treat the form of value as a thing of no importance, as having no connection with the inner nature of commodities. The reason for this is not only that their attention is entirely absorbed by the analysis of the magnitude of value. It lies deeper. The form of value of the product of labor is not only the most abstract form that the product takes in bourgeois production, but also the most universal one. It stamps that production as a particular kind of social production, and in this way gives it its special historical character. If, then, we treat this mode of production as one fixed by Nature for all eternity, for every state of society, we necessarily overlook what is the differentia specifica [specific difference] of the form of value, and therefore of the commodity form, and of its further developments, the money form, the capital form, etc. So we find that economists who are thoroughly agreed that labor-time is the measure of the magnitude of value have the strangest and most contradictory ideas of money, the perfected form of the general equivalent. This shows up strikingly when they deal with banking, where the commonplace definitions of money no longer hold water. This led to the rise of a restored mercantile system (Ganilh, etc.), which sees in value nothing but a social form, or rather the unsubstantial ghost of that form. Let me state here, once and for all, that by classical political economy I mean the economics that, since the time of W. Petty, has investigated the real relations of production in bourgeois society. I contrast it with vulgar economics, which deals with appearances only. Vulgar economics endlessly chews over the materials that scientific economics provided long ago, and looks there for plausible explanations of the most glaring phenomena, for everyday bourgeois use. For the rest, it confines itself to systematizing, in a pedantic way, the trite ideas held by the self-satisfied bourgeoisie about their own world, which is to them the best of all possible worlds, and to proclaiming those ideas as everlasting truths.

[^1.34]: “Les économistes ont une singulière manière de procéder. Il n’y a pour eux que deux sortes d’institutions, celles de l’art et celles de la nature. Les institutions de la féodalité sont des institutions artificielles celles de la bourgeoisie sont des institutions naturelles. Ils ressemblent en ceci aux théologiens, qui eux aussi établissent deux sortes de religions. Toute religion qui n’est pas la leur, est une invention des hommes tandis que leur propre religion est une émanation de Dieu ‒ Ainsi il y a eu de l’histoire, mais il n’y en a plus.” [“Economists have a peculiar way of proceeding. For them there are only two kinds of institutions, artificial and natural. The institutions of feudalism are artificial institutions; those of the bourgeoisie are natural institutions. In this they are like the theologians, who likewise set up two kinds of religion. Every religion that is not theirs is an invention of men, while their own religion is an emanation from God. ... Thus there has been history, but there is no longer any”] (Karl Marx. Misère de la Philosophie. Réponse a la Philosophie de la Misère par M. Proudhon, 1847, p. 113.) Truly comical is M. Bastiat, who imagines that the ancient Greeks and Romans lived by plunder alone. But when people plunder for centuries, there must always be something at hand for them to seize; the objects of plunder must be continually reproduced. So it would appear that even the Greeks and Romans had some process of production, and therefore an economy, which formed the material basis of their world just as much as bourgeois economy forms that of our modern world. Or perhaps Bastiat means that a mode of production based on slavery is based on a system of plunder. In that case he is treading on dangerous ground. If a giant thinker like Aristotle erred in his judgment of slave labor, why should a dwarf economist like Bastiat be right in his judgment of wage labor? I take this opportunity to answer briefly an objection that a German paper in America raised against my work, “Zur Kritik der Pol. Oekonomie, 1859.” My view is that each special mode of production and the social relations corresponding to it, in short, the economic structure of society, is the real basis on which the legal and political superstructure is raised, and to which definite social forms of thought correspond. It is that the mode of production determines the character of social, political, and intellectual life generally. In the judgment of that paper, all this is very true for our own times, in which material interests predominate, but not for the middle ages, in which Catholicism reigned supreme, nor for Athens and Rome, where politics reigned supreme. In the first place, it strikes one as an odd thing for anyone to suppose that these well-worn phrases about the middle ages and the ancient world are unknown to anyone else. This much, however, is clear: the middle ages could not live on Catholicism, nor the ancient world on politics. On the contrary, it is the way in which they earned their living that explains why politics played the chief part in the ancient world, and Catholicism in the middle ages. For the rest, it takes only a slight acquaintance with the history of the Roman republic, for example, to be aware that its secret history is the history of its landed property. On the other hand, Don Quixote long ago paid the penalty for wrongly imagining that knight-errantry was compatible with all economic forms of society.

<!-- ch01-p148 -->
How far some economists are misled by the Fetishism inherent in commodities, or by the objective appearance of the social characteristics of labor, is shown, among other ways, by the dull and tedious quarrel over the part played by Nature in the formation of exchange-value. Exchange-value is a definite social way of expressing the amount of labor spent on an object. So Nature has no more to do with it than it has with fixing the exchange rate.

<!-- ch01-p149 -->
The mode of production in which the product takes the form of a commodity, or is produced directly for exchange, is the most general and most embryonic form of bourgeois production. So it makes its appearance early in history, though not in the same dominant and characteristic way as it does nowadays. Hence its Fetish character is comparatively easy to see through. But when we come to more concrete forms, even this appearance of simplicity vanishes. Where did the illusions of the monetary system come from? To the monetary system, gold and silver, when serving as money, did not represent a social relation between producers, but were natural objects with strange social properties. And modern economics, which looks down with such scorn on the monetary system: does its superstition not come out as clear as noon-day whenever it deals with capital? How long is it since economics discarded the illusion of the Physiocrats (a school of 18th-century French economists), that rents grow out of the soil and not out of society?

<!-- ch01-p150 -->
But, not to get ahead of ourselves, we will content ourselves with one more example relating to the commodity form. If commodities could speak, they would say: Our use-value may be a thing that interests men. It is no part of us as objects. What does belong to us as objects, however, is our value. Our natural dealings with each other as commodities prove it. In each other’s eyes we are nothing but exchange-values. Now listen to how those commodities speak through the mouth of the economist.

<!-- ch01-p151 -->
> “Value” – (that is, exchange-value) “is a property of things, riches” – (that is, use-value) “of man. Value, in this sense, necessarily implies exchanges, riches do not.”[^1.35] “Riches” (use-value) “are the attribute of men, value is the attribute of commodities. A man or a community is rich, a pearl or a diamond is valuable...” A pearl or a diamond is valuable as a pearl or a diamond.[^1.36]

[^1.35]: “Observations on certain verbal disputes in Pol. Econ., particularly relating to value and to demand and supply” London, 1821, p. 16.

[^1.36]: S. Bailey, cited above, p. 165.

<!-- ch01-p152 -->
So far no chemist has ever discovered exchange-value either in a pearl or in a diamond. The economic discoverers of this chemical element, by the way, lay special claim to critical sharpness. They find, however, that the use-value of objects belongs to them independently of their material properties, while their value, on the other hand, forms a part of them as objects. What confirms them in this view is a peculiar circumstance. The use-value of objects is realized without exchange, through a direct relation between the objects and man, while their value, on the other hand, is realized only through exchange, that is, through a social process. Who does not think here of our good friend Dogberry, the constable in Shakespeare’s *Much Ado About Nothing*, who informs neighbor Seacoal that “To be a well-favoured [good-looking] man is the gift of fortune; but reading and writing comes by Nature.”[^1.37]

[^1.37]: The author of “Observations” and S. Bailey accuse Ricardo of turning exchange-value from something relative into something absolute. The opposite is the case. He has explained the apparent relation between objects such as diamonds and pearls, the relation in which they appear as exchange-values. And he has revealed the true relation hidden behind the appearances, namely their relation to each other as mere expressions of human labor. If Ricardo’s followers answer Bailey somewhat rudely, and by no means convincingly, the reason is to be found in this: they could not find in Ricardo’s own works any key to the hidden relations that exist between value and its form, exchange-value.

## Chapter 2: Exchange

<!-- ch02-p001 -->
Clearly, commodities (things produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer’s own use) cannot go to market and make exchanges on their own account. We must therefore turn to their guardians, who are also their owners. Commodities are things, and so they have no power to resist man. If they are not docile, he can use force; in other words, he can take possession of them.[^2.1] For these objects to enter into relation with each other as commodities, their guardians must place themselves in relation to one another as persons whose will resides in those objects. They must behave in such a way that neither takes possession of the other’s commodity, or parts with his own, except by an act done by mutual consent. So they must recognize each other as having the rights of private owners. This legal relation expresses itself in a contract, whether or not that contract is part of a developed legal system. It is a relation between two wills, and it is only the reflection of the real economic relation between the two. It is this economic relation that decides the content of each such legal act.[^2.2]

[^2.1]: In the 12th century, so renowned for its piety, they counted some very delicate things among commodities. Thus a French poet of the period lists, among the goods to be found in the market of Landit, not only clothing, shoes, leather, farm tools, etc., but also “femmes folles de leur corps” [“women wanton with their bodies”].

[^2.2]: Proudhon begins by taking his ideal of Justice, of “justice éternelle” [“eternal justice”], from the legal relations that correspond to the production of commodities. In doing so, it may be noted, he proves, to the comfort of all good citizens, that the production of commodities is a form of production as everlasting as justice. Then he turns round and tries to reform the actual production of commodities, and the actual legal system that corresponds to it, in line with this ideal. What would we think of a chemist who, instead of studying the actual laws of the molecular changes in the composition and decomposition of matter, and on that basis solving definite problems, claimed to regulate the composition and decomposition of matter by means of the “eternal ideas” of “naturalité” [“naturalness”] and “affinité” [“affinity”]? Do we really know any more about “usury” when we say it contradicts “justice éternelle” [“eternal justice”], “équité éternelle” [“eternal equity”], “mutualité éternelle” [“eternal mutuality”], and other “vérités éternelles” [“eternal truths”], than the fathers of the church did when they said it was incompatible with “grâce éternelle” [“eternal grace”], “foi éternelle” [“eternal faith”], and “la volonté éternelle de Dieu” [“the eternal will of God”]?

<!-- ch02-p002 -->
The persons exist for one another merely as representatives of commodities, and therefore as owners of commodities. As our investigation goes on, we shall find, in general, that the characters who appear on the economic stage are only the personifications of the economic relations that exist between them.

<!-- ch02-p003 -->
What chiefly distinguishes a commodity from its owner is this: the commodity looks on every other commodity as merely the form of appearance of its own value. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) A born leveler and a cynic, the commodity is always ready to exchange not only soul but body with any and every other commodity, even one more repulsive than Maritornes herself, the inn servant in *Don Quixote*. The owner makes up for this lack of a sense of the concrete in the commodity with his own five and more senses. His commodity has no immediate use-value for him (use-value is the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties). Otherwise, he would not bring it to market. It has use-value for others. But for himself its only direct use-value is that it is a container of exchange-value (the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for), and so a means of exchange.[^2.3] So he makes up his mind to part with it for commodities whose use-value is of service to him. All commodities are non-use-values for their owners, and use-values for their non-owners. Consequently, they must all change hands. But this change of hands is what makes up their exchange, and exchange puts them in relation with each other as values, and realizes them as values. Hence commodities must be realized as values before they can be realized as use-values.

[^2.3]: For two-fold is the use of every object.... The one is peculiar to the object as such, the other is not, as a sandal which may be worn, and is also exchangeable. Both are uses of the sandal, for even he who exchanges the sandal for the money or food he is in want of, makes use of the sandal as a sandal. But not in its natural way. For it has not been made for the sake of being exchanged.” (Aristoteles, “De Rep.” l. i. c. 9.)

<!-- ch02-p004 -->
On the other hand, they must show that they are use-values before they can be realized as values. For the labor spent on them counts effectively only to the extent that it is spent in a form that is useful for others. Whether that labor is useful for others, and so whether its product can satisfy the wants of others, can be proved only by the act of exchange.

<!-- ch02-p005 -->
Every owner of a commodity wants to part with it in exchange only for those commodities whose use-value satisfies some want of his. Seen in this way, exchange is for him simply a private transaction. On the other hand, he wants to realize the value of his commodity, to turn it into any other suitable commodity of equal value, whether or not his own commodity has any use-value for the owner of the other. From this point of view, exchange is for him a social transaction of a general character. But one and the same set of transactions cannot be, at the same time and for all owners of commodities, both exclusively private and exclusively social and general.

<!-- ch02-p006 -->
Let us look at the matter a little more closely. To the owner of a commodity, every other commodity is, in relation to his own, a particular equivalent, and so his own commodity is the universal equivalent (a single commodity in which all other commodities express their values) for all the others. But since this applies to every owner, there is in fact no commodity acting as universal equivalent. The relative value of commodities then has no general form under which they can be equated as values and have the magnitude of their values compared. So far, therefore, they do not face each other as commodities, but only as products or use-values. In their difficulties our commodity owners think like Faust: “Im Anfang war die Tat.” [“In the beginning was the deed.” – Goethe, *Faust*.] They therefore acted and transacted before they thought. By instinct they conform to the laws imposed by the nature of commodities. They cannot bring their commodities into relation as values, and therefore as commodities, except by comparing them with some one other commodity as the universal equivalent. That we saw from the analysis of a commodity. But a particular commodity cannot become the universal equivalent except by a social act. So the social action of all other commodities sets apart the particular commodity in which they all represent their values. In this way the bodily form of this commodity becomes the form of the socially recognized universal equivalent. Through this social process, being the universal equivalent becomes the specific function of the commodity that the rest have excluded in this way. Thus it becomes – money. “Illi unum consilium habent et virtutem et potestatem suam bestiae tradunt. Et ne quis possit emere aut vendere, nisi qui habet characterem aut nomen bestiae aut numerum nominis ejus.” [“These have one mind, and shall give their power and strength unto the beast.” Revelations, 17:13; “And that no man might buy or sell, save he that had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name.” Revelations, 13:17.] (*Apocalypse*.)

<!-- ch02-p007 -->
Money is a crystal formed of necessity in the course of exchanges, in which different products of labor are in practice equated to one another and so, by practice, turned into commodities. As exchange develops and spreads through history, it develops the contrast, hidden in commodities, between use-value and value. Trade needs this contrast to be given an outward expression. That need pushes toward the setting up of an independent form of value (the way the value of one commodity is expressed in another commodity), and it does not rest until it is satisfied once and for all by the splitting of commodities into commodities and money. So at the same rate as products are turned into commodities, one special commodity is turned into money.[^2.4]

[^2.4]: From this we can judge the shrewdness of the petit-bourgeois (lower-middle-class) socialism which, while keeping the production of commodities going forever, aims to abolish the “antagonism” between money and commodities, and so, since money exists only by virtue of this antagonism, to abolish money itself. We might just as well try to keep Catholicism without the Pope. For more on this point see my work, “Zur Kritik der Pol. Oekon.,” p. 61, and following.

<!-- ch02-p008 -->
The direct barter of products reaches the elementary form of the relative expression of value in one respect, but not in another. That form is x Commodity A = y Commodity B. The form of direct barter is x use-value A = y use-value B.[^2.5] The articles A and B in this case are not yet commodities; they become commodities only by the act of barter. The first step an object of utility takes toward acquiring exchange-value is when it is a non-use-value for its owner. That happens when it is a surplus portion of some article needed for his immediate wants. Objects in themselves are external to man, and so he can alienate them, that is, part with them. For this alienation to be mutual, men only need, by a silent understanding, to treat each other as private owners of those alienable objects, and by implication as independent individuals. But such a state of mutual independence does not exist in a primitive society based on common property, whether that society takes the form of a patriarchal family, an ancient Indian community, or a Peruvian Inca State. The exchange of commodities therefore first begins on the boundaries of such communities, at their points of contact with other similar communities, or with members of those communities. But as soon as products become commodities in the external relations of a community, they also, by reaction, become commodities in its internal dealings. The proportions in which they are exchangeable are at first quite a matter of chance. What makes them exchangeable is their owners’ mutual desire to alienate them. Meanwhile the need for foreign objects of utility gradually takes hold. The constant repetition of exchange makes it a normal social act. In the course of time, therefore, some portion at least of the products of labor must be produced with exchange specially in view. From that moment the distinction becomes firmly fixed between the utility of an object for consumption and its utility for exchange. Its use-value becomes distinguished from its exchange-value. On the other hand, the quantitative proportion in which the articles are exchangeable comes to depend on their production itself. Custom stamps them as values with definite magnitudes.

[^2.5]: As long as, instead of two distinct use-values being exchanged, a chaotic mass of articles is offered as the equivalent of a single article, as often happens among savages, even the direct barter of products is only in its first infancy.

<!-- ch02-p009 -->
In the direct barter of products, each commodity is directly a means of exchange to its owner, and to all other persons an equivalent, but only to the extent that it has use-value for them. At this stage, therefore, the articles exchanged do not acquire a form of value independent of their own use-value, or of the individual needs of the people exchanging them. The need for a form of value grows as the number and variety of the commodities exchanged increase. The problem and the means of solving it arise at the same time. Commodity-owners never equate their own commodities to those of others, and exchange them on a large scale, without different kinds of commodities belonging to different owners being exchangeable for, and equated as values to, one and the same special article. This last article, by becoming the equivalent of various other commodities, at once acquires, though within narrow limits, the character of a general social equivalent. This character comes and goes with the passing social acts that called it into life. By turns and for a time it attaches itself first to this commodity and then to that. But as exchange develops, it fixes itself firmly and exclusively to particular sorts of commodities, and becomes crystallized by taking on the money form. The particular kind of commodity it sticks to is at first a matter of accident. Nevertheless there are two circumstances whose influence is decisive. The money form attaches itself either to the most important articles of exchange from outside, and these are in fact primitive and natural forms in which the exchange-value of home products finds expression; or else it attaches itself to the object of utility that forms, like cattle, the chief portion of the native wealth that can be alienated. Nomadic peoples are the first to develop the money form. This is because all their worldly goods consist of movable objects and so can be directly alienated, and because their way of life, by constantly bringing them into contact with foreign communities, invites the exchange of products. Man has often made man himself, in the form of slaves, serve as the primitive material of money, but has never used land for that purpose. Such an idea could only arise in a bourgeois society (bourgeois: belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it) that is already well developed. It dates from the last third of the 17th century, and the first attempt to put it into practice on a national scale was made a century later, during the French bourgeois revolution.

<!-- ch02-p010 -->
In proportion as exchange bursts its local bonds, and the value of commodities expands more and more into an embodiment of abstract human labor (labor counted simply as the spending of human effort, of brain, muscle, and nerve, whatever particular kind it is), in the same proportion the character of money attaches itself to commodities that are by Nature fitted to perform the social function of a universal equivalent. Those commodities are the precious metals.

<!-- ch02-p011 -->
The truth of the statement that “although gold and silver are not by Nature money, money is by Nature gold and silver”[^2.6] is shown by how well the physical properties of these metals suit the functions of money.[^2.7] So far, however, we know only one function of money: to serve as the form of appearance of the value of commodities, that is, as the material in which the magnitudes of their values are socially expressed. Only a material whose every sample shows the same uniform qualities can be an adequate form of appearance of value, a fit embodiment of abstract, undifferentiated, and therefore equal human labor. On the other hand, since the difference between magnitudes of value is purely quantitative, the money commodity must be capable of merely quantitative differences. It must therefore be divisible at will, and just as capable of being put back together. Gold and silver have these properties by Nature.

[^2.6]: Karl Marx, cited above, p. 135. “I metalli ... naturalmente moneta.” [“The metals ... are by their nature money.”] (Galiani, “Della moneta” in Custodi’s Collection: Parte Moderna t. iii.)

[^2.7]: For further details on this subject see the chapter on “The precious metals” in my work cited above.

<!-- ch02-p012 -->
The use-value of the money commodity becomes two-fold. Besides its special use-value as a commodity (gold, for instance, serves to fill teeth, to form the raw material of luxury articles, etc.), it acquires a formal use-value, which comes from its specific social function.

<!-- ch02-p013 -->
Since all commodities are merely particular equivalents of money, and money is their universal equivalent, they play the parts of particular commodities in relation to money as the universal commodity.[^2.8]

[^2.8]: “Il danaro è la merce universale" [“Money is the universal commodity”] (Verri, cited above, p. 16).

<!-- ch02-p014 -->
We have seen that the money form is only the reflection, thrown onto one single commodity, of the value relations between all the rest. So the claim that money is a commodity[^2.9] is a new discovery only for those who, when they analyze money, start from its fully developed shape. The act of exchange gives the commodity that is turned into money not its value, but its specific form of value. By confusing these two distinct things, some writers have been led to hold that the value of gold and silver is imaginary.[^2.10] The fact that money can, in certain functions, be replaced by mere symbols of itself gave rise to that other mistaken notion, that money is itself a mere symbol. Nevertheless, under this error lurked a sense that the money form of an object is not an inseparable part of that object, but is simply the form in which certain social relations show themselves. In this sense every commodity is a symbol, since, insofar as it is value, it is only the material envelope of the human labor spent on it.[^2.11] But if one declares that the social characters taken on by objects, or the material forms taken on by the social qualities of labor under the régime of a definite mode of production, are mere symbols, one declares in the same breath that these characteristics are arbitrary fictions approved by the so-called universal consent of mankind. This suited the kind of explanation in favor during the 18th century. People could not account for the origin of the puzzling forms taken on by social relations between man and man. So they tried to strip these forms of their strange appearance by tracing them back to an origin in convention.

[^2.9]: “Silver and gold themselves (which we may call by the general name of bullion) are ... commodities ... rising and falling in ... value ... Bullion, then, may be reckoned to be of higher value where the smaller weight will purchase the greater quantity of the product or manufacture of the countrey,” etc. (“A Discourse of the General Notions of Money, Trade, and Exchanges, as They Stand in Relation each to other.” By a Merchant. London, 1695, p. 7.) “Silver and gold, coined or uncoined, though they are used for a measure of all other things, are no less a commodity than wine, oil, tobacco, cloth, or stuffs.” (“A Discourse concerning Trade, and that in particular of the East Indies,” etc. London, 1689, p. 2.) “The stock and riches of the kingdom cannot properly be confined to money, nor ought gold and silver to be excluded from being merchandise.” ("The East-India Trade a Most Profitable Trade.” London, 1677, p. 4.)

[^2.10]: L’oro e l’argento hanno valore come metalli anteriore all’esser moneta.” [“Gold and silver have value as metals before they are money”] (Galiani, cited above.) Locke says, “The universal consent of mankind gave to silver, on account of its qualities which made it suitable for money, an imaginary value.” Law, on the other hand, asks: “How could different nations give an imaginary value to any single thing... or how could this imaginary value have maintained itself?” But the following shows how little he himself understood about the matter: “Silver was exchanged in proportion to the value in use it possessed, consequently in proportion to its real value. By its adoption as money it received an additional value (une valeur additionnelle).” (Jean Law: “Considérations sur le numéraire et le commerce” in E. Daire’s Edit. of “Economistes Financiers du XVIII siècle,” p. 470.)

[^2.11]: “L’Argent en (des denrées) est le signe.” [“Money is their (the commodities’) symbol”] (V. de Forbonnais: “Eléments du Commerce, Nouv. Edit. Leyde, 1766,” t. II., p. 143.) “Comme signe il est attiré par les denrées.” [“As a symbol it is attracted by the commodities”] (cited above, p. 155.) “L’argent est un signe d’une chose et la représente.” [“Money is a symbol of a thing and represents it.”] (Montesquieu: “Esprit des Lois,” (Oeuvres, London 1767, t. II, p. 2.) “L’argent n’est pas simple signe, car il est lui-même richesse, il ne représente pas les valeurs, il les équivaut.” [“Money is not a mere symbol, for it is itself wealth; it does not represent the values, it is their equivalent”] (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 910.) “The notion of value contemplates the valuable article as a mere symbol ‒ the article counts not for what it is, but for what it is worth.” (Hegel, cited above, p. 100.) Lawyers started the idea that money is a mere symbol, and that the value of the precious metals is purely imaginary, long before the economists did. They did this in the fawning service of the crowned heads. Throughout the middle ages they supported the kings’ right to debase the coinage, drawing on the traditions of the Roman Empire and on the ideas of money found in the Pandects (the digest of Roman law). “Qu’aucun puisse ni doive faire doute,” [“Let no one call into question,”] says an apt pupil of theirs, Philip of Valois, in a decree of 1346, “que à nous et à notre majesté royale n’appartiennent seulement ... le mestier, le fait, l’état, la provision et toute l’ordonnance des monnaies, de donner tel cours, et pour tel prix comme il nous plait et bon nous semble.” [“that the trade, the making, the condition, the supply and the whole regulation of the currency ... belongs only to us and to our royal majesty, to give it such a rate and such a price as pleases us and seems good to us”] It was a maxim of Roman Law that the value of money was fixed by decree of the emperor. It was expressly forbidden to treat money as a commodity. “Pecunias vero nulli emere fas erit, nam in usu publico constitutas oportet non esse mercem.” [“However, it shall not be lawful for anyone to buy money, for, as it was created for public use, it must not be a commodity”] Some good work on this question has been done by G. F. Pagnini: “Saggio sopra il giusto pregio delle cose, 1751"; Custodi “Parte Moderna,” t. II. In the second part of his work Pagnini aims his attacks especially at the lawyers.

<!-- ch02-p015 -->
It has already been remarked above that the equivalent form of a commodity does not imply how the magnitude of its value is determined. (In “20 yards of linen = 1 coat”, the linen’s value is expressed, so it is in the relative form of value, and the coat serves as the material that expresses it, so it is in the equivalent form.) So although we may know that gold is money, and so directly exchangeable for all other commodities, that fact by no means tells us how much 10 lbs. of gold, for instance, is worth. Money, like every other commodity, cannot express the magnitude of its value except relatively, in other commodities. Its value is determined by the labor-time required to produce it, and is expressed by the quantity of any other commodity that costs the same amount of labor-time.[^2.12] This quantitative fixing of its relative value takes place at the source of its production, by means of barter. When it steps into circulation (the exchange of commodities through money: selling and buying) as money, its value is already given.
