In the last decades of the 17th century it had already been shown that money is a commodity, but this step marks only the infancy of the analysis. The difficulty lies not in understanding that money is a commodity, but in discovering how, why, and by what means a commodity becomes money.[^2.13]

[^2.12]: “If a man can bring to London an ounce of Silver out of the Earth in Peru, in the same time that he can produce a bushel of Corn, then the one is the natural price of the other; now, if by reason of new or more easier mines a man can procure two ounces of silver as easily as he formerly did one, the corn will be as cheap at ten shillings the bushel as it was before at five shillings, caeteris paribus [other things being equal].” William Petty. “A Treatise of Taxes and Contributions.” London, 1667, p. 32.

[^2.13]: The learned Professor Roscher first informs us that “the false definitions of money may be divided into two main groups: those which make it more, and those which make it less, than a commodity.” He then gives us a long and very mixed catalogue of works on the nature of money, from which it appears that he has not the remotest idea of the real history of the theory. And then he moralizes thus: “For the rest, it is not to be denied that most of the later economists do not bear sufficiently in mind the peculiarities that distinguish money from other commodities” (so it is, after all, either more or less than a commodity!)... “So far, the semi-mercantilist reaction of Ganilh is not altogether without foundation.” (Wilhelm Roscher: “Die Grundlagen der Nationaloekonomie,” 3rd Edn. 1858, pp. 207-210.) More! less! not sufficiently! so far! not altogether! What clearness and precision of ideas and language! And Mr. Roscher modestly christens such eclectic professorial twaddle “the anatomico-physiological method” of political economy (the science of economics as it was then called)! He must, however, be given credit for one discovery, namely, that money is “a pleasant commodity.”

<!-- ch02-p016 -->
We have already seen, from the most elementary expression of value, x commodity A = y commodity B, that the object in which the magnitude of the value of another object is represented appears to have the equivalent form independently of this relation, as a social property given to it by Nature. We followed this false appearance up to the point where it becomes firmly established. That point is reached as soon as the universal equivalent form becomes identified with the bodily form of a particular commodity, and so is crystallized into the money form. What appears to happen is not that gold becomes money because all other commodities express their values in it. On the contrary, it appears that all other commodities universally express their values in gold because it is money. The intermediate steps of the process vanish in the result and leave no trace behind. Commodities find their own value already completely represented, without any initiative on their part, in another commodity existing alongside them. These objects, gold and silver, just as they come out of the bowels of the earth, are at once the direct incarnation of all human labor. Hence the magic of money. In the form of society we are now considering, the behavior of men in the social process of production is purely atomic. Hence their relations to each other in production take on a material character independent of their control and of their conscious individual action. These facts show themselves at first in products, as a general rule, taking the form of commodities. We have seen how the progressive development of a society of commodity-producers stamps one privileged commodity with the character of money. Hence the riddle presented by money is only the riddle presented by commodities; only now it strikes us in its most glaring form.

## Chapter 3: Money, Or the Circulation of Commodities

### Section 1: The Measure of Values

<!-- ch03-p001 -->
Throughout this work, for the sake of simplicity, I assume that gold is the money-commodity. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer's own use.)

<!-- ch03-p002 -->
The first main function of money is to supply commodities with the material for expressing their values. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) Or, put another way, its function is to represent their values as magnitudes of the same denomination: equal in quality and comparable in quantity. So money serves as a *universal measure of value*. And only through this function does gold, the equivalent commodity in the fullest sense, become money.

<!-- ch03-p003 -->
It is not money that makes commodities commensurable, that is, measurable by a common standard. Just the opposite. All commodities, as values, are realized human labor, and therefore commensurable. That is why their values can be measured by one and the same special commodity, and why this commodity can be turned into the common measure of their values, that is, into money. Money as a measure of value is the form of appearance that must necessarily be taken by the measure of value built into commodities: labor-time.[^3.1]

[^3.1]: The question, why does money not directly represent labor-time, so that a piece of paper might represent, for instance, x hours' labor, is at bottom the same as the question, why, given the production of commodities, must products take the form of commodities? This is clear, since their taking the form of commodities implies that they split into commodities and money. Or: why can private labor (labor for the account of private individuals) not be treated as its opposite, directly social labor? I have elsewhere examined thoroughly the Utopian idea of “labour-money” in a society founded on the production of commodities (cited above, p. 61, and following). On this point I will only add that Owen's “labour-money,” for instance, is no more “money” than a theater ticket is. Owen presupposes directly associated labor, a form of production that is entirely inconsistent with the production of commodities. The certificate of labor is merely evidence of the individual's share in the common labor, and of his right to a certain portion of the common product set aside for consumption. But it never enters Owen's head to presuppose the production of commodities and at the same time, by juggling with money, to try to dodge the necessary conditions of that production.

<!-- ch03-p004 -->
The expression of the value of a commodity in gold, *x* commodity A = *y* money-commodity, is its money form or price. A single equation, such as 1 ton of iron = 2 ounces of gold, is now enough to express the value of the iron in a socially valid way. This equation no longer needs to appear as one link in the chain of equations that express the values of all other commodities, because the equivalent commodity, gold, now has the character of money. The general form of relative value has gone back to its original shape of simple or isolated relative value. On the other hand, the expanded expression of relative value, the endless series of equations, has now become the form peculiar to the relative value of the money-commodity. The series itself, too, is now given, and is socially recognized in the prices of actual commodities. We have only to read the quotations of a price-list backwards to find the magnitude of the value of money expressed in all sorts of commodities. (The magnitude of value is how much value a commodity has, measured by the socially necessary labor-time needed to produce it.) But money itself has no price. To put it on an equal footing with all other commodities in this respect, we would have to equate it to itself as its own equivalent.

<!-- ch03-p005 -->
The price or money form of commodities is, like their form of value in general, a form quite distinct from their tangible bodily form. (The form of value is the way the value of one commodity is expressed in another commodity.) It is, therefore, a purely ideal or mental form. The value of iron, linen and grain is invisible, but it actually exists in these very articles. It is made perceptible, in an ideal way, by their equality with gold, a relation that, so to speak, exists only in their own heads. So their owner must lend them his tongue, or hang a ticket on them, before their prices can be communicated to the outside world.[^3.2] Since expressing the value of commodities in gold is a merely ideal act, we may use imaginary or ideal money for this purpose. Every trader knows that he is far from having turned his goods into money when he has expressed their value in a price, or in imaginary money. He also knows that it does not take the least bit of real gold to estimate millions of pounds' worth of goods in that metal. So when money serves as a measure of value, it is used only as imaginary or ideal money. This fact has given rise to the wildest theories.[^3.3] But although the money that performs the functions of a measure of value is only ideal money, price depends entirely on the actual substance that is money. The value of a ton of iron, in other words the quantity of human labor contained in it, is expressed in imagination by a quantity of the money-commodity that contains the same amount of labor as the iron. So, depending on whether the measure of value is gold, silver, or copper, the value of the ton of iron will be expressed by very different prices, or represented by very different quantities of those metals.

[^3.2]: Savages and half-civilized peoples use the tongue differently. Captain Parry says of the inhabitants of the west coast of Baffin's Bay: “In this case (he refers to barter) they licked it (the thing represented to them) twice to their tongues, after which they seemed to consider the bargain satisfactorily concluded.” In the same way, the Eastern Inuit licked the articles they received in exchange. If the tongue is used like this in the North as the organ of appropriation (of taking possession), no wonder that in the South the stomach serves as the organ of accumulated property, and that a Bantu-speaking southern African judges a man's wealth by the size of his belly. That these southern Africans know what they are about is shown by the following. At the same time as the official British Health Report of 1864 revealed the lack of fat-forming food among a large part of the working class, a certain Dr. Harvey (not, however, the famous discoverer of the circulation of the blood) did very well for himself by advertising recipes for reducing the excess fat of the bourgeoisie (the capitalist class) and the aristocracy.

[^3.3]: See Karl Marx: “Zur Kritik, &c.” “Theorien von der Masseinheit des Geldes,” p. 53, and following.

<!-- ch03-p006 -->
So if two different commodities, such as gold and silver, are measures of value at the same time, all commodities have two prices: one a gold-price, the other a silver-price. These exist quietly side by side as long as the ratio of the value of silver to that of gold stays unchanged, say at 15:1. Every change in that ratio disturbs the ratio between the gold-prices and the silver-prices of commodities. It thus proves, by the facts, that a double standard of value is inconsistent with the functions of a standard.[^3.4]

[^3.4]: “Wherever gold and silver have by law been made to perform the function of money or of a measure of value side by side, it has always been tried, but in vain, to treat them as one and the same material. To assume that there is an invariable ratio between the quantities of gold and silver in which a given quantity of labour-time is incorporated, is to assume in fact that gold and silver are of one and the same material, and that a given mass of the less valuable metal, silver, is a constant fraction of a given mass of gold. From the reign of Edward III. to the time of George II., the history of money in England consists of one long series of perturbations caused by the clashing of the legally fixed ratio between the values of gold and silver with the fluctuations in their real values. At one time gold was too high, at another, silver. The metal that for the time being was estimated below its value was withdrawn from circulation [the exchange of commodities through money: selling and buying], melted and exported. The ratio between the two metals was then again altered by law, but the new nominal ratio soon came into conflict again with the real one. In our own times, the slight and transient fall in the value of gold compared with silver, which was a consequence of the Indo-Chinese demand for silver, produced on a far more extended scale in France the same phenomena: export of silver, and its expulsion from circulation by gold. During the years 1855, 1856 and 1857, the excess in France of gold-imports over gold-exports amounted to £41,580,000, while the excess of silver-exports over silver-imports was £14,704,000. In fact, in those countries in which both metals are legally measures of value, and therefore both legal tender, so that everyone has the option of paying in either metal, the metal that rises in value is at a premium, and, like every other commodity, measures its price in the over-estimated metal, which alone serves in reality as the standard of value. The result of all experience and history with regard to this equation is simply that, where two commodities perform by law the functions of a measure of value, in practice one alone maintains that position.” (Karl Marx, cited above, pp. 52, 53.)

<!-- ch03-p007 -->
Commodities with definite prices appear in this form: *a* commodity A = x gold; *b* commodity B = z gold; *c* commodity C = y gold, etc. Here *a*, *b*, *c* stand for definite quantities of the commodities A, B, C, and x, z, y for definite quantities of gold. So the values of these commodities are changed in imagination into so many different quantities of gold. Hence, despite the confusing variety of the commodities themselves, their values become magnitudes of the same denomination: gold-magnitudes. They can now be compared with each other and measured. And the need is felt, as a technical matter, to compare them with some fixed quantity of gold as a unit of measure. This unit, by being further divided into equal fractions, itself becomes the standard or scale. Even before they become money, gold, silver, and copper already have such standard measures in their standards of weight. For example, a pound weight serves as the unit; on the one hand it can be divided into ounces, and on the other it can be combined to make up hundredweights.[^3.5] This is why, in all metallic currencies, the names given to the standards of money or of price were originally taken from the already existing names of the standards of weight.

[^3.5]: The peculiar fact that in England the ounce of gold serves as the unit of the standard of money, while the pound sterling does not form an equal fraction of it, has been explained as follows: “Our coinage was originally adapted to the employment of silver only, hence, an ounce of silver can always be divided into a certain adequate number of pieces of coin, but as gold was introduced at a later period into a coinage adapted only to silver, an ounce of gold cannot be coined into an aliquot [evenly dividing] number of pieces.” Maclaren, “A Sketch of the History of the Currency.” London, 1858, p. 16.

<!-- ch03-p008 -->
As *measure of Value* and as *standard of price*, money has two entirely distinct functions to perform. It is the measure of value insofar as it is the socially recognized incarnation of human labor. It is the standard of price insofar as it is a fixed weight of metal. As the measure of value, it serves to turn the values of all the many different commodities into prices, into imaginary quantities of gold. As the standard of price, it measures those quantities of gold. The measure of values measures commodities considered as values. The standard of price, on the contrary, measures quantities of gold by a unit quantity of gold, not the value of one quantity of gold by the weight of another. To make gold a standard of price, a certain weight must be fixed on as the unit. In this case, as in all cases of measuring quantities of the same denomination, establishing an unvarying unit of measure is all-important. Hence the less the unit varies, the better the standard of price does its job. But gold can serve as a measure of value only insofar as it is itself a product of labor, and therefore potentially variable in value.[^3.6]

[^3.6]: Among English writers the confusion between measure of value and standard of price (standard of value) is indescribable. Their functions, as well as their names, are constantly mixed up.

<!-- ch03-p009 -->
In the first place, it is quite clear that a change in the value of gold does not in any way affect its function as a standard of price. No matter how this value varies, the proportions between the values of different quantities of the metal stay constant. However far its value falls, 12 ounces of gold still have 12 times the value of 1 ounce; and in prices, the only thing considered is the relation between different quantities of gold. On the other hand, since no rise or fall in the value of an ounce of gold can change its weight, the weight of its equal fractions cannot change either. So gold always does the same service as an unvarying standard of price, however much its value may vary.

<!-- ch03-p010 -->
In the second place, a change in the value of gold does not interfere with its functions as a measure of value. The change affects all commodities at the same time. So, other things being equal, it leaves their relative values among themselves unchanged, although those values are now expressed in higher or lower gold-prices.

<!-- ch03-p011 -->
We may estimate the value of any commodity by a definite quantity of the use-value of some other commodity. (Use-value is the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties.) Just as when we do that, so when we estimate the first commodity's value in gold, we assume nothing more than that producing a given quantity of gold costs a given amount of labor at the given period. As for the fluctuations of prices in general, they are subject to the laws of elementary relative value examined in an earlier chapter.

<!-- ch03-p012 -->
A general rise in the prices of commodities can result only from one of two things: either from a rise in their values, while the value of money stays constant, or from a fall in the value of money, while the values of commodities stay constant. On the other hand, a general fall in prices can result only either from a fall in the values of commodities, while the value of money stays constant, or from a rise in the value of money, while the values of commodities stay constant. So it by no means follows that a rise in the value of money necessarily implies a proportional fall in the prices of commodities, or that a fall in the value of money implies a proportional rise in prices. Such a change of price holds good only for commodities whose value stays constant. With those, for example, whose value rises at the same time as, and in proportion to, that of money, there is no change in price. And if their value rises either more slowly or faster than that of money, the fall or rise in their prices will be determined by the difference between the change in their value and the change in that of money; and so on.

<!-- ch03-p013 -->
Let us now go back to examining the price form.

<!-- ch03-p014 -->
Gradually a gap arises between the current money-names of the various weights of the precious metal that serves as money, and the actual weights those names originally stood for. This gap is the result of historical causes, the chief of which are: (1) The import of foreign money into a community that is not fully developed. This happened in Rome in its early days, where gold and silver coins at first circulated as foreign commodities. The names of these foreign coins never match those of the native weights. (2) As wealth increases, the less precious metal is pushed out of its place as a measure of value by the more precious one: copper by silver, silver by gold, however much this order of sequence may contradict poetical chronology.[^3.7] The word pound, for instance, was the money-name given to an actual pound weight of silver. When gold replaced silver as a measure of value, the same name was applied, according to the ratio between the values of silver and gold, to perhaps 1-15th of a pound of gold. So the word pound, as a money-name, becomes distinct from the same word as a weight-name.[^3.8] (3) The debasing of money, carried on for centuries by kings and princes, to such an extent that nothing in fact remained of the original weights of the coins but the names.[^3.9]

[^3.7]: Moreover, it is not valid for history in general.

[^3.8]: This is how the pound sterling in English stands for less than one-third of its original weight; the pound Scot, before the union, only 1-36th; the French livre, 1-74th; the Spanish maravedi, less than 1-1,000th; and the Portuguese rei a still smaller fraction.

[^3.9]: “Le monete le quali oggi sono ideal, sono le piû antiche d’ogni nazione, e tutte furono un tempo real, e perche erano reali con esse si contava” [“The coins that are ideal today are the oldest coins of every nation, and all of them were once real, and because they were real, people counted with them”] (Galiani: Della moneta, cited above, p. 153.)

<!-- ch03-p015 -->
These historical causes turn the separation of the money-name from the weight-name into an established habit in the community. The standard of money is, on the one hand, purely conventional, and on the other hand it must be generally accepted. So in the end it is regulated by law. A given weight of one of the precious metals, an ounce of gold, for instance, is officially divided into equal fractions, which are given legal names such as pound, dollar, etc. These equal fractions, which from then on serve as units of money, are then subdivided into other equal fractions with legal names, such as shilling, penny, etc.[^3.10] But both before and after these divisions are made, a definite weight of metal is the standard of metallic money. The only change is in the subdivision and the naming.

[^3.10]: David Urquhart, in his “Familiar Words,” remarks on the monstrosity (!) that nowadays a pound (sterling), which is the unit of the English standard of money, equals about a quarter of an ounce of gold. “This is falsifying a measure, not establishing a standard.” In this “false denomination” of the weight of gold he sees, as in everything else, the falsifying hand of civilization.

<!-- ch03-p016 -->
So the prices, or quantities of gold, into which the values of commodities are ideally changed, are now expressed in the names of coins, or in the legally valid names of the subdivisions of the gold standard. Hence, instead of saying: A quarter of wheat is worth an ounce of gold, we say: it is worth £3 17s. 10 1/2d. In this way commodities express through their prices how much they are worth, and money serves as *money of account* whenever the value of an article has to be fixed in its money form.[^3.11]

[^3.11]: When Anacharsis was asked what the Greeks used money for, he replied, “For reckoning.” (Ashen. Deipn. 1. iv. 49 v. 2. ed. Schweighauser, 1802.)

<!-- ch03-p017 -->
The name of a thing is something distinct from the qualities of that thing. I know nothing about a man by knowing that his name is Jacob. In the same way, with money, every trace of a value-relation disappears in the names pound, dollar, franc, ducat, etc. Attributing a hidden meaning to these cabalistic (secret, magical) signs causes confusion. The confusion is all the greater because these money-names express both the values of commodities and, at the same time, equal fractions of the weight of the metal that is the standard of money.[^3.12] On the other hand, it is absolutely necessary that value, in order to be distinguished from the varied bodily forms of commodities, should take on this material and meaningless, but at the same time purely social, form.[^3.13]

[^3.12]: “Owing to the fact that money, when serving as the standard of price, appears under the same reckoning names as do the prices of commodities, and that therefore the sum of £3 17s. 10 1/2d. may signify on the one hand an ounce weight of gold, and on the other, the value of a ton of iron, this reckoning name of money has been called its mint-price. Hence there sprang up the extraordinary notion that the value of gold is estimated in its own material, and that, in contradistinction to all other commodities, its price is fixed by the State. It was erroneously thought that the giving of reckoning names to definite weights of gold is the same thing as fixing the value of those weights.” (Karl Marx, cited above, p. 52.)

[^3.13]: See “Theorien von der Masseinheit des Geldes” in “Zur Kritik der Pol Oekon. &c.,” p. 53, and following. There are fantastic notions about raising or lowering the mint-price of money by transferring the names already legally assigned to fixed weights of gold or silver to greater or smaller weights of those metals. Such notions, at least in those cases where they aim not at clumsy financial operations against creditors, both public and private, but at economic quack remedies, were treated so exhaustively by Wm. Petty in his “Quantulumcunque concerning money: To the Lord Marquis of Halifax, 1682,” that even his immediate followers, Sir Dudley North and John Locke, not to mention later ones, could only water him down. “If the wealth of a nation,” he remarks, “could be decupled [multiplied tenfold] by a proclamation, it were strange that such proclamations have not long since been made by our Governors.” (cited above, p. 36.)

<!-- ch03-p018 -->
Price is the money-name of the labor realized in a commodity. Hence to express the equivalence of a commodity with the sum of money that makes up its price is a tautology, a statement that says the same thing twice[^3.14], just as, in general, to express the relative value of a commodity is to state the equivalence of two commodities. Price, as the exponent (the indicator) of the magnitude of a commodity's value, is the exponent of its exchange-ratio with money. But although this is so, it does not follow that the exponent of this exchange-ratio is necessarily the exponent of the magnitude of the commodity's value. Suppose two equal quantities of socially necessary labor are represented by 1 quarter of wheat and £2 (nearly 1/2 oz. of gold) respectively. (Socially necessary labor-time is the time needed to produce an article under the normal conditions of production of the day, with the average skill and intensity of labor.) Then £2 is the expression in money of the magnitude of the value of the quarter of wheat, or its price. Now suppose circumstances allow this price to be raised to £3, or force it to be reduced to £1. Then £1 and £3 may be too small or too great to express the magnitude of the wheat's value properly; nevertheless they are its prices. For they are, in the first place, the form in which its value appears, that is, money; and in the second place, the exponents of its exchange-ratio with money. If the conditions of production, in other words the productive power of labor, stay constant, the same amount of social labor-time must be spent on reproducing a quarter of wheat both before and after the change in price. This fact depends neither on the will of the wheat producer nor on that of the owners of other commodities.

[^3.14]: “Ou bien, il faut consentir à dire qu’une valeur d’un million en argent vaut plus qu’une valeur égale en marchandises.” [“Or else we must agree to say that a value of a million in money is worth more than an equal value in commodities.”] (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 919), which amounts to saying “qu’une valeur vaut plus qu’une valeur égale.” [“that a value is worth more than an equal value.”]

<!-- ch03-p019 -->
Magnitude of value expresses a relation of social production: it expresses the connection that necessarily exists between a certain article and the portion of society's total labor-time required to produce it. As soon as magnitude of value is turned into price, this necessary relation takes the shape of a more or less accidental exchange-ratio between a single commodity and another, the money-commodity. But this exchange-ratio may express either the real magnitude of that commodity's value, or the quantity of gold, deviating from that value, for which, depending on circumstances, the commodity may be parted with. So the possibility of a quantitative mismatch between price and magnitude of value, that is, of price deviating from magnitude of value, is built into the price form itself. This is no defect. On the contrary, it makes the price form admirably suited to a mode of production whose built-in laws assert themselves only as the average of apparently lawless irregularities that cancel one another out.

<!-- ch03-p020 -->
The price form, however, is not only compatible with the possibility of a quantitative mismatch between magnitude of value and price, that is, between magnitude of value and its expression in money. It may also hide a qualitative inconsistency, so much so that price stops expressing value altogether, although money is nothing but the form of value of commodities. Things that in themselves are not commodities, such as conscience, honor, etc., can be offered for sale by their holders, and so acquire, through their price, the form of commodities. Hence a thing may have a price without having value. The price in that case is imaginary, like certain quantities in mathematics. On the other hand, the imaginary price form may sometimes hide either a direct or an indirect real value-relation; for instance, the price of uncultivated land, which is without value, because no human labor has been incorporated in it.

<!-- ch03-p021 -->
Price, like relative value in general, expresses the value of a commodity (for example, a ton of iron) by stating that a given quantity of the equivalent (for example, an ounce of gold) can be directly exchanged for iron. But it by no means states the reverse, that iron can be directly exchanged for gold. So, for a commodity to act effectively in practice as exchange-value, it must leave its bodily shape and transform itself from merely imaginary gold into real gold. (Exchange-value is the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for.) For the commodity, this transubstantiation (change of substance) may be harder than the transition from “necessity” to “freedom” is for the Hegelian “concept,” or than casting off its shell is for a lobster, or than putting off the old Adam was for Saint Jerome.[^3.15] A commodity may, alongside its actual form (iron, for instance), take the form of gold in our imagination, but it cannot actually be both iron and gold at one and the same time. To fix its price, it is enough to equate it to gold in imagination. But to enable it to do its owner the service of a universal equivalent (a single commodity in which all other commodities express their values), it must actually be replaced by gold. Suppose the owner of the iron went to the owner of some other commodity offered for exchange and pointed to the price of the iron as proof that it was already money. He would get the same answer that St. Peter gave Dante in heaven, when Dante recited the creed –

[^3.15]: Jerome had to wrestle hard, not only in his youth with the bodily flesh, as his fight in the desert with the beautiful women of his imagination shows, but also in his old age with the spiritual flesh. “I thought,” he says, “I was in the spirit before the Judge of the Universe.” “Who art thou?” asked a voice. “I am a Christian.” “Thou liest,” thundered back the great Judge, “thou art nought but a Ciceronian [a follower of Cicero].”

<!-- ch03-p022 -->
> “Assad bene e trascorsa\
> D’esta moneta gia la lega e’l peso,\
> Ma dimmi se tu l’hai nella tua borsa.”\
> [“The alloy and the weight of this coin have now been checked quite well, but tell me if you have it in your purse.”]

<!-- ch03-p023 -->
So a price implies both that a commodity can be exchanged for money and that it must be so exchanged. On the other hand, gold serves as an ideal measure of value only because it has already established itself as the money-commodity in the process of exchange. Under the ideal measure of values lurks hard cash.

### Section 2: The Medium of Circulation

##### A. The Metamorphosis of Commodities

<!-- ch03-p024 -->
We saw in an earlier chapter that the exchange of commodities involves conditions that contradict and exclude one another. The splitting of commodities into commodities and money does not sweep these inconsistencies away. Instead, it develops a *modus vivendi*, a form in which they can exist side by side. This is generally the way in which real contradictions are reconciled. For instance, it is a contradiction to depict one body as constantly falling towards another and, at the same time, as constantly flying away from it. The ellipse is a form of motion which lets this contradiction go on and at the same time reconciles it.

<!-- ch03-p025 -->
Insofar as exchange is a process that transfers commodities from hands in which they are not use-values to hands in which they become use-values, it is a social circulation of matter. The product of one form of useful labor (labor of a particular kind, such as tailoring or weaving, that makes a particular useful thing) replaces the product of another. Once a commodity has found a resting place where it can serve as a use-value, it falls out of the sphere of exchange and into the sphere of consumption. But only the sphere of exchange interests us at present. So we now have to consider exchange from the point of view of its form. We have to investigate the change of form, or metamorphosis, of commodities which brings about the social circulation of matter.

<!-- ch03-p026 -->
As a rule, this change of form is very poorly understood. Apart from unclear ideas about value itself, the cause is this: every change of form in a commodity results from the exchange of two commodities, an ordinary one and the money-commodity. If we keep in view only the material fact that a commodity has been exchanged for gold, we overlook the very thing we ought to observe, namely what has happened to the form of the commodity. We overlook the facts that gold, when it is a mere commodity, is not money, and that when other commodities express their prices in gold, this gold is only the money form of those commodities themselves.

<!-- ch03-p027 -->
To begin with, commodities enter the process of exchange just as they are. The process then splits them into commodities and money. It thus produces an external opposition that corresponds to the internal opposition built into them, as being at once use-values and values. Commodities as use-values now stand opposed to money as exchange-value. On the other hand, both opposing sides are commodities, unities of use-value and value. But this unity of differences shows itself at two opposite poles, and at each pole in an opposite way. Being poles, they are as necessarily opposite as they are connected. On one side of the equation we have an ordinary commodity, which is in reality a use-value. Its value is expressed only ideally, in its price. Through its price it is equated to its opponent, the gold, as to the real embodiment of its value. On the other side, the gold, in its metallic reality, counts as the embodiment of value, as money. Gold, as gold, is exchange-value itself. As for its use-value, that exists only ideally. It is represented by the series of expressions of relative value in which gold stands face to face with all other commodities, and the sum of the uses of all these commodities makes up the sum of the various uses of gold. These antagonistic forms of commodities are the real forms in which the process of their exchange moves and takes place.

<!-- ch03-p028 -->
Let us now go with the owner of some commodity, say our old friend the linen weaver, to the scene of action, the market. His 20 yards of linen has a definite price, £2. He exchanges it for the £2. Then, being a man of the good old sort, he parts with the £2 for a family Bible of the same price. In his eyes the linen is a mere commodity, a container of value. He gives it up in exchange for gold, which is the linen’s form of value, and he in turn parts with this form for another commodity, the Bible. The Bible is destined to enter his house as an object of utility and of moral improvement for his household. The exchange is completed by two metamorphoses of opposite yet complementary character: the conversion of the commodity into money, and the reconversion of the money into a commodity.[^3.16] The two phases of this metamorphosis are both separate transactions of the weaver: selling, or the exchange of the commodity for money; buying, or the exchange of the money for a commodity; and the unity of the two acts, selling in order to buy.

[^3.16]: 

    “εχ σε του ... πυροσ τ’ανταμεειβεσθαι παντα, ϕησιν δ’Ηραχλειτοσ, χαι πυρ απαντων, ωο περ χρυσου χρηματα χαι χρηματων χρυσοσ.” [“As Heraclitus says, all things are exchanged for fire and fire for all things, as goods are exchanged for gold and gold for goods.”] (F. Lassalle: “Die Philosophie Herakleitos des Dunkeln.” Berlin, 1858, Vol. I, p. 222.) In his note on this passage, p. 224, n. 3., Lassalle wrongly makes gold a mere symbol of value.

<!-- ch03-p029 -->
For the weaver, the result of the whole transaction is this: instead of the linen, he now has the Bible. Instead of his original commodity, he now owns another of the same value but of a different usefulness. In the same way he obtains his other means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live) and means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things). From his point of view, the whole process does nothing more than exchange the product of his labor for the product of someone else’s, nothing more than an exchange of products.

<!-- ch03-p030 -->
The exchange of commodities is therefore accompanied by the following changes in their form.

<!-- ch03-p031 -->
Commodity – Money – Commodity.\
C–––––– M ––––––C.

<!-- ch03-p032 -->
As far as the objects themselves are concerned, the result of the whole process is C – C, the exchange of one commodity for another, the circulation of materialized social labor. When this result is reached, the process is at an end.

##### C – M. *First metamorphosis, or sale*

<!-- ch03-p033 -->
The leap that value takes from the body of the commodity into the body of the gold is, as I have called it elsewhere, the salto mortale [death-defying leap] of the commodity. If the leap falls short, the commodity itself is not harmed, but its owner decidedly is. The social division of labor makes his labor as one-sided as his wants are many-sided. This is exactly why the product of his labor serves him only as exchange-value. But it cannot take on the properties of a socially recognized universal equivalent except by being converted into money. That money, however, is in someone else’s pocket. To coax the money out of that pocket, our friend’s commodity must, above all, be a use-value to the owner of the money. For this, the labor spent on it must be of a socially useful kind, a kind that forms a branch of the social division of labor. But division of labor is a system of production which has grown up spontaneously and goes on growing behind the backs of the producers. The commodity to be exchanged may possibly be the product of some new kind of labor that claims to satisfy newly arisen needs, or even to create new needs itself. A particular operation may yesterday, perhaps, have been one of the many operations carried out by one producer in making a given commodity. Today it may separate itself from this connection, set itself up as an independent branch of labor, and send its unfinished product to market as an independent commodity. The circumstances may or may not be ripe for such a separation. Today the product satisfies a social want. Tomorrow some other suitable product may wholly or partly take the article’s place. Moreover, our weaver’s labor may be a recognized branch of the social division of labor, but that fact is by no means enough to guarantee the usefulness of his 20 yards of linen. The community’s want of linen has a limit, like every other want. If it is already saturated by the products of rival weavers, our friend’s product is superfluous, redundant, and therefore useless. People do not look a gift horse in the mouth, but our friend does not go to market to hand out presents. But suppose his product turns out to be a real use-value, and so attracts money? The question arises: how much will it attract? No doubt the answer is already anticipated in the price of the article, the expression of its magnitude of value. Here we leave out of account any accidental miscalculation of value by our friend, a mistake that the market soon corrects. We suppose that he has spent on his product only the amount of labor-time that is, on average, socially necessary. The price, then, is merely the money name of the quantity of social labor realized in his commodity. But without our weaver’s leave, and behind his back, the old-fashioned way of weaving changes. The labor-time that yesterday was without doubt socially necessary to produce a yard of linen is no longer so today. The owner of the money is only too eager to prove this fact from the prices quoted by our friend’s competitors. Unluckily for him, weavers are not few and far between. Lastly, suppose that every piece of linen on the market contains no more labor-time than is socially necessary. Even so, all these pieces taken as a whole may have had superfluous labor-time spent on them. If the market cannot stomach the whole quantity at the normal price of 2 shillings a yard, this proves that too large a part of the community’s total labor has been spent in the form of weaving. The effect is the same as if each individual weaver had spent more labor-time on his particular product than is socially necessary. Here we may say, with the German proverb: caught together, hung together. All the linen on the market counts only as one article of trade, of which each piece is only a fractional part. And as a matter of fact, the value of each single yard, too, is only the materialized form of the same definite and socially fixed quantity of uniform human labor.[^3.17]

[^3.17]: *Note by the Institute of Marxism-Leninism in the Russian edition*. — In his letter of November 28, 1878, to N. F. Danielson (Nikolai-on), Marx proposed that this sentence be corrected to read as follows: “And, as a matter of fact, the value of each single yard is but the materialised form of a part of the social labour expended on the whole number of yards.” A similar correction was made in a copy of the second German edition of the first volume of “Capital” that belonged to Marx; however, it is not in his handwriting.

<!-- ch03-p034 -->
So we see that commodities are in love with money, but “the course of true love never did run smooth.” The quantitative division of labor comes about in exactly the same spontaneous and accidental way as its qualitative division. The owners of commodities therefore find out that the same division of labor that turns them into independent private producers also frees the social process of production, and the relations of the individual producers to each other within that process, from all dependence on the will of those producers. They also find out that the seeming independence of the individuals from one another is supplemented by a system of general and mutual dependence through, or by means of, the products.

<!-- ch03-p035 -->
The division of labor turns the product of labor into a commodity, and so makes it necessary for that product to be further turned into money. At the same time, it also makes it quite a matter of chance whether this transubstantiation is accomplished. Here, however, we are concerned only with the phenomenon in its complete form, and so we assume that it proceeds normally. Moreover, if the conversion takes place at all, that is, if the commodity is not absolutely unsellable, its metamorphosis does take place, although the price realized may be abnormally above or below the value.

<!-- ch03-p036 -->
The seller has his commodity replaced by gold; the buyer has his gold replaced by a commodity. The fact that stares us in the face here is that a commodity and gold, 20 yards of linen and £2, have changed hands and places, in other words, that they have been exchanged. But for what is the commodity exchanged? For the shape taken by its own value, for the universal equivalent. And for what is the gold exchanged? For a particular form of its own use-value. Why does gold take the form of money when it faces the linen? Because the linen’s price of £2, its name in money, has already equated the linen to gold in its character as money. A commodity strips off its original commodity form at the moment it is given up, that is, at the instant its use-value actually attracts the gold that before existed only ideally in its price. So the realization of a commodity’s price, or of its ideal form of value, is at the same time the realization of the ideal use-value of money. The conversion of a commodity into money is at the same time the conversion of money into a commodity. The apparently single process is in reality a double one. From the pole of the commodity owner it is a sale; from the opposite pole of the money owner it is a purchase. In other words, a sale is a purchase, C–M is also M–C.[^3.18]

[^3.18]: “Toute vente est achat.” [“Every sale is a purchase.”] (Dr. Quesnay: “Dialogues sur le Commerce et les Travaux des Artisans.” Physiocrates ed. Daire I. Partie, Paris, 1846, p. 170), or, as Quesnay puts it in his “Maximes générales,” “Vendre est acheter.” [“To sell is to buy.”]

<!-- ch03-p037 -->
So far we have considered people in only one economic capacity, that of owners of commodities. In this capacity they take possession of the produce of other people’s labor by giving up the produce of their own. So for one commodity owner to meet another who has money, one of two things is necessary. Either the product of the latter person’s labor (the buyer’s) must itself be money, must be gold, the material money consists of; or his product must already have changed its skin and stripped off its original form of a useful object. To play the part of money, gold must of course enter the market at some point or other. This point is found at the source where the metal is produced. There gold is bartered, as the immediate product of labor, for some other product of equal value. From that moment on, it always represents the realized price of some commodity.[^3.19] Apart from its exchange for other commodities at the source of its production, gold, in whoever’s hands it may be, is the transformed shape of some commodity that its owner has given up; it is the product of a sale, or of the first metamorphosis C–M.[^3.20] Gold, as we saw, became ideal money, or a measure of values, because all commodities measured their values by it. They thus set it ideally against their natural shape as useful objects, and made it the shape of their value. It became real money through the general giving-up of commodities, by actually changing places with their natural forms as useful objects, and so becoming in reality the embodiment of their values. When commodities take on this money shape, they strip off every trace of their natural use-value and of the particular kind of labor that created them. They do so in order to turn themselves into the uniform, socially recognized incarnation of human labor that is all of one kind. We cannot tell from the mere look of a piece of money what particular commodity it has been exchanged for. In their money form all commodities look alike. So money may be dirt, although dirt is not money. Let us assume that the two gold pieces for which our weaver has parted with his linen are the metamorphosed shape of a quarter of wheat. The sale of the linen, C–M, is at the same time its purchase, M–C. But the sale is the first act of a process that ends with a transaction of the opposite kind, namely the purchase of a Bible. The purchase of the linen, on the other hand, ends a movement that began with a transaction of the opposite kind, namely the sale of the wheat. C–M (linen–money), which is the first phase of C–M–C (linen–money–Bible), is also M–C (money–linen), the last phase of another movement C–M–C (wheat–money–linen). So the first metamorphosis of one commodity, its change from a commodity into money, is also always the second metamorphosis of some other commodity, its change back from money into a commodity.[^3.21]

[^3.19]: “Le prix d’une marchandise ne pouvant être payé que par le prix d’une autre marchandise” (Mercier de la Rivière: “L’Ordre naturel et essentiel des sociétés politiques.” [“The price of one commodity can only be paid by the price of another commodity”] Physiocrates, ed. Daire II. Partie, p. 554.)

[^3.20]: “Pour avoir cet argent, il faut avoir vendu,” [“In order to have this money, one must have made a sale,”] cited above, p. 543.

[^3.21]: As remarked before, the actual producer of gold or silver is an exception. He exchanges his product directly for another commodity, without having first sold it.

##### M–C, *or purchase.* *The second and concluding metamorphosis of a commodity*

<!-- ch03-p038 -->
Because money is the metamorphosed shape of all other commodities, the result of their being given up in general, it can itself be given up without restriction or condition. It reads all prices backwards, and so, as it were, depicts itself in the bodies of all other commodities, which offer it the material for realizing its own use-value. At the same time the prices, wooing glances cast at money by commodities, set the limits of its convertibility by pointing to its quantity. Since every commodity disappears as a commodity on becoming money, it is impossible to tell from the money itself how it got into the hands of its owner, or what article has been changed into it. Non olet [It does not smell], from whatever source it may come. Representing on the one hand a sold commodity, it represents on the other a commodity to be bought.[^3.22]

[^3.22]: “Si l’argent représente, dans nos mains, les choses que nous pouvons désirer d’acheter, il y représente aussi les choses que nous avons vendues pour cet argent.” [“If money represents, in our hands, the things we may wish to buy, it also represents the things we have sold to get that money”] (Mercier de la Rivière, cited above, p. 586.)

<!-- ch03-p039 -->
M–C, a purchase, is at the same time C–M, a sale; the concluding metamorphosis of one commodity is the first metamorphosis of another. As far as our weaver is concerned, the life of his commodity ends with the Bible, into which he has turned his £2 back. But suppose the seller of the Bible turns the £2 set free by the weaver into brandy: then M–C, the concluding phase of C–M–C (linen–money–Bible), is also C–M, the first phase of C–M–C (Bible–money–brandy). The producer of a particular commodity has only that one article to offer. He very often sells it in large quantities, but his many and various wants force him to split up the price he has realized, the sum of money set free, into numerous purchases. So one sale leads to many purchases of various articles. The concluding metamorphosis of a commodity thus makes up a collection of first metamorphoses of various other commodities.

<!-- ch03-p040 -->
If we now consider the completed metamorphosis of a commodity as a whole, it appears, in the first place, that it is made up of two opposite and complementary movements, C–M and M–C. These two opposed transmutations of a commodity are brought about by two opposed social acts on the part of the owner, and these acts in turn stamp the character of the economic parts he plays. As the person who makes a sale, he is a seller; as the person who makes a purchase, he is a buyer. But in every such transmutation of a commodity, its two forms, commodity form and money form, exist at the same time but at opposite poles. In just the same way, every seller has a buyer facing him, and every buyer a seller. While one particular commodity goes through its two transmutations one after the other, from a commodity into money and from money into another commodity, the owner of the commodity changes his part in turn from that of seller to that of buyer. So these characters of seller and buyer are not permanent. They attach themselves in turn to the various persons involved in the circulation of commodities.

<!-- ch03-p041 -->
In its simplest form, the complete metamorphosis of a commodity involves four extremes and three characters. First, a commodity comes face to face with money. Money is the form taken by the commodity’s value, and it exists, in all its hard reality, in the buyer’s pocket. A commodity owner is thus brought into contact with an owner of money. Now, as soon as the commodity has been changed into money, the money becomes its passing equivalent form (in “20 yards of linen = 1 coat”, the coat serves as the material that expresses the linen’s value: it is in the equivalent form). The use-value of this equivalent form is to be found in the bodies of other commodities. Money, the final term of the first transmutation, is at the same time the starting point for the second. So the person who is a seller in the first transaction becomes a buyer in the second, in which a third commodity owner appears on the scene as a seller.[^3.23]

[^3.23]: “Il y a donc ... quatre termes et trois contractants, dont l’un intervient deux fois” [“So there are ... four terms and three contracting parties, one of whom intervenes twice”] (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 909.)

<!-- ch03-p042 -->
The two phases that make up the metamorphosis of a commodity, each the reverse of the other, together form a circular movement, a circuit: the commodity form, the stripping off of this form, and the return to the commodity form. No doubt the commodity appears here in two different aspects. At the starting point it is not a use-value to its owner; at the finishing point it is. In the same way, the money appears in the first phase as a solid crystal of value, a crystal into which the commodity eagerly solidifies. In the second phase it dissolves into the mere passing equivalent form, destined to be replaced by a use-value.

<!-- ch03-p043 -->
The two metamorphoses that make up the circuit are at the same time two reverse partial metamorphoses of two other commodities. One and the same commodity, the linen, opens the series of its own metamorphoses and completes the metamorphosis of another (the wheat). In the first phase, or sale, the linen plays these two parts in its own person. But then, changed into gold, it completes its own second and final metamorphosis, and at the same time helps to carry out the first metamorphosis of a third commodity. So the circuit made by one commodity in the course of its metamorphoses is inseparably tangled up with the circuits of other commodities. The total of all the different circuits makes up *the circulation of commodities*.

<!-- ch03-p044 -->
The circulation of commodities differs from the direct exchange of products (barter) not only in form but in substance. Just consider the course of events. The weaver has, as a matter of fact, exchanged his linen for a Bible, his own commodity for someone else’s. But this is true only as far as he himself is concerned. The seller of the Bible, who prefers something to warm his insides, no more thought of exchanging his Bible for linen than our weaver knew that wheat had been exchanged for his linen. B’s commodity replaces A’s, but A and B do not exchange those commodities with each other. It may, of course, happen that A and B buy from each other at the same time; but such exceptional transactions are by no means the necessary result of the general conditions of the circulation of commodities. Here we see, on the one hand, how the exchange of commodities breaks through all the local and personal limits that are inseparable from direct barter, and develops the circulation of the products of social labor. On the other hand, we see how it develops a whole network of social relations that grow up spontaneously and are entirely beyond the control of the actors. It is only because the farmer has sold his wheat that the weaver is able to sell his linen; only because the weaver has sold his linen that our Hotspur is able to sell his Bible; and only because Hotspur has sold the water of everlasting life that the distiller is able to sell his *eau-de-vie* [brandy; literally “water of life”], and so on.

<!-- ch03-p045 -->
So the process of circulation does not, like the direct barter of products, die out once the use-values have changed places and hands. The money does not vanish when it drops out of the circuit of the metamorphosis of a given commodity. It is constantly being deposited in new places in the arena of circulation that other commodities have left empty. In the complete metamorphosis of the linen, for example, linen – money – Bible, the linen first falls out of circulation, and money steps into its place. Then the Bible falls out of circulation, and again money takes its place. When one commodity replaces another, the money-commodity always sticks to the hands of some third person.[^3.24] Circulation sweats money from every pore.

[^3.24]: Self-evident as this may be, political economists (the writers on political economy, the science of economics as it was then called) for the most part fail to notice it, and the “Free-trader Vulgaris” especially.

<!-- ch03-p046 -->
Nothing can be more childish than the dogma that, because every sale is a purchase and every purchase a sale, the circulation of commodities necessarily implies a balance of sales and purchases. If this means that the number of actual sales equals the number of purchases, it is mere tautology. But its real purpose is to prove that every seller brings his buyer to market with him. Nothing of the kind. The sale and the purchase are one identical act, an exchange between a commodity owner and an owner of money, between two persons as opposed to each other as the two poles of a magnet. When they are performed by one single person, they form two distinct acts, of polar and opposite character. So the identity of sale and purchase implies that the commodity is useless if, once thrown into the alchemist’s retort of circulation, it does not come out again in the shape of money; in other words, if its owner cannot sell it, and the owner of the money therefore cannot buy it. That identity further implies that the exchange, if it does take place, forms a period of rest, an interval, long or short, in the life *of* the commodity. Since the first metamorphosis of a commodity is at once a sale and a purchase, it is also an independent process in itself. The purchaser has the commodity, the seller has the money, that is, a commodity ready to go into circulation at any time. No one can sell unless someone else buys. But no one is immediately bound to buy just because he has just sold. Circulation bursts through all the limits of time, place, and individuals imposed by direct barter. It does this by splitting into the opposition of a sale and a purchase the direct identity that does exist in barter between giving up one’s own product and acquiring someone else’s. To say that these two independent and opposed acts have an inner unity, that they are essentially one, is the same as saying that this inner oneness expresses itself in an external opposition. If the interval in time between the two complementary phases of the complete metamorphosis of a commodity becomes too great, if the split between the sale and the purchase becomes too pronounced, the close connection between them, their oneness, asserts itself by producing – a crisis. The opposition of use-value and value; the contradictions that private labor has to show itself as direct social labor, and that a particularized concrete kind of labor has to count as abstract human labor (labor counted simply as the spending of human effort, of brain, muscle, and nerve, whatever particular kind it is); the contradiction between the personification of objects and the representation of persons by things: all these oppositions and contradictions, which are built into commodities, assert themselves and develop their modes of motion in the opposed phases of the metamorphosis of a commodity. So these modes imply the possibility, and no more than the possibility, of crises. The conversion of this mere possibility into a reality is the result of a long series of relations that, from our present standpoint of simple circulation, do not yet exist.[^3.25]

[^3.25]: See my remarks on James Mill in “Zur Kritik, &c.,” pp. 74-76. On this subject, we may note two methods typical of apologetic economics (the economics of the defenders of the system). The first is to identify the circulation of commodities with the direct barter of products, simply by leaving out the points in which they differ. The second is the attempt to explain away the contradictions of capitalist production by reducing the relations between the persons engaged in that mode of production to the simple relations that arise out of the circulation of commodities. But the production and circulation of commodities are phenomena that occur, to a greater or lesser extent, in the most diverse modes of production. If we know nothing but the abstract categories of circulation, which are common to all these modes of production, we cannot possibly know anything of the specific points in which those modes differ, nor pass any judgment on them. In no science is such a big fuss made over commonplace truisms as in political economy. For instance, J. B. Say sets himself up as a judge of crises because, if you please, he knows that a commodity is a product.

#### B. The currency of money[^3.26]

<!-- ch03-p047 -->
The change of form C–M–C brings about the circulation of the material products of labor. It requires that a given value, in the shape of a commodity, begin the process, and that it also end the process in the shape of a commodity. The movement of the commodity is therefore a circuit. On the other hand, the form of this movement rules out any circuit made by the money. The result is not that the money returns, but that it moves further and further away from its starting-point. As long as the seller holds on tight to his money, which is the changed shape of his commodity, that commodity is still in the first phase of its metamorphosis and has completed only half its course. But as soon as he completes the process, as soon as he follows up his sale with a purchase, the money leaves its owner’s hands again. It is true that if the weaver, after buying the Bible, sells more linen, money comes back into his hands. But this return is not due to the circulation of the first 20 yards of linen. That circulation ended with the money in the hands of the seller of the Bible. Money returns to the weaver’s hands only because the process of circulation is renewed or repeated with a fresh commodity, and this renewed process ends with the same result as the one before it. So the movement that the circulation of commodities directly gives to money takes the form of a constant motion away from its starting-point, a course from the hands of one commodity-owner into those of another. This course makes up its currency (cours de la monnaie [course of money]).

[^3.26]: *Translator’s note*. — Here this word is used in its original meaning: the course or track that money follows as it passes from hand to hand. This course is essentially different from circulation.

<!-- ch03-p048 -->
The currency of money is the constant and monotonous repetition of the same process. The commodity is always in the hands of the seller; the money, as a means of purchase, is always in the hands of the buyer. And money serves as a means of purchase by realizing the price of the commodity. This realization moves the commodity from the seller to the buyer, and moves the money from the buyer’s hands into the seller’s, where it goes through the same process again with another commodity. This one-sided character of the money’s motion arises out of the two-sided character of the commodity’s motion, but that fact is veiled over. The very nature of the circulation of commodities produces the opposite appearance. The first metamorphosis of a commodity is visibly a movement not only of the money but also of the commodity itself. In the second metamorphosis, on the contrary, the movement appears to us as the movement of the money alone. In the first phase of its circulation the commodity changes places with the money. Then the commodity, as a useful object, falls out of circulation into consumption.[^3.27] In its place we have its value-shape, the money. The commodity then goes through the second phase of its circulation, not in its own natural shape, but in the shape of money. So the continuity of the movement is kept up by the money alone. The same movement that, for the commodity, consists of two opposite processes is, when seen as the movement of the money, always one and the same process: a continual change of places with ever fresh commodities. So the result that the circulation of commodities brings about, namely the replacing of one commodity by another, appears to have been achieved not through the change of form of the commodities, but rather by the money acting as a medium of circulation (that is, in its role of passing from hand to hand to carry out sales and purchases). It looks as though an action of the money circulates the commodities, which to all appearance are motionless in themselves, and moves them from hands in which they are non-use-values to hands in which they are use-values, always in the direction opposite to the money’s. The money is continually withdrawing commodities from circulation and stepping into their places, and in this way it continually moves further and further from its starting-point. So although the movement of the money is merely the expression of the circulation of commodities, the opposite appears to be the actual fact, and the circulation of commodities seems to be the result of the movement of the money.[^3.28]

[^3.27]: Even when the commodity is sold over and over again (something that, for the present, does not exist for us), when it is finally sold for the last time it falls out of the sphere of circulation into that of consumption. There it serves either as means of subsistence or as means of production.

[^3.28]: “Il (l’argent) n’a d’autre mouvement que celui qui lui est imprimé par les productions.” [“It” (money) “has no other motion than the one given to it by the products”] (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 885.)

<!-- ch03-p049 -->
Again, money functions as a medium of circulation only because in money the values of commodities have an independent reality. So its movement as the medium of circulation is in fact merely the movement of commodities while they change their forms. This fact must therefore show itself plainly in the currency of money. Thus the linen, for instance, first changes its commodity-form into its money-form. The second term of its first metamorphosis, C–M, the money form, then becomes the first term of its final metamorphosis, M–C, its change back into the Bible. But each of these two changes of form is carried out by an exchange between commodity and money, by their *changing places with each other*. The same coins come into the seller’s hand *as the form of the commodity that has been parted with*, and leave it as *the form of the commodity that can be parted with absolutely*. They change places twice. The first metamorphosis of the linen puts these coins into the weaver’s pocket; the second draws them out of it. The two opposite changes that the same commodity goes through are reflected in the displacement of the same coins, repeated twice, but in opposite directions.

<!-- ch03-p050 -->
If, on the contrary, only one phase of the metamorphosis is gone through, if there are only sales or only purchases, then a given piece of money changes its place only once. Its second change of place always expresses the second metamorphosis of the commodity, its change back from money. The frequent repetition of the displacement of the same coins reflects not only the series of metamorphoses that a single commodity has gone through, but also the intertwining of the countless metamorphoses in the world of commodities in general. It goes without saying that all this applies only to the simple circulation of commodities, the only form we are now considering.

<!-- ch03-p051 -->
Every commodity, when it first steps into circulation and goes through its first change of form, does so only to fall out of circulation again and be replaced by other commodities. Money, on the contrary, as the medium of circulation, stays continually within the sphere of circulation and moves about in it. So the question arises: how much money does this sphere constantly absorb?

<!-- ch03-p052 -->
In a given country, numerous one-sided metamorphoses of commodities take place every day at the same time, but in different places; in other words, numerous sales and numerous purchases. The commodities are equated beforehand in imagination, by their prices, with definite quantities of money. And in the form of circulation we are now considering, money and commodities always come bodily face to face, one at the positive pole of purchase, the other at the negative pole of sale. Since this is so, the amount of the medium of circulation required is clearly fixed beforehand by the sum of the prices of all these commodities. In fact, the money in reality represents the quantity or sum of gold that was expressed ideally beforehand by the sum of the prices of the commodities. The equality of these two sums is therefore self-evident. We know, however, that if the values of commodities stay constant, their prices vary with the value of gold (the material of money): they rise as it falls, and fall as it rises. Now if, because of such a rise or fall in the value of gold, the sum of the prices of commodities falls or rises, the quantity of money in currency must fall or rise to the same extent. In this case, it is true, the change in the quantity of the medium of circulation is caused by the money itself. Yet it is caused not by money’s function as a medium of circulation, but by its function as a measure of value. First the price of the commodities varies inversely with the value of the money, and then the quantity of the medium of circulation varies directly with the price of the commodities. Exactly the same thing would happen if, for instance, instead of the value of gold falling, gold were replaced by silver as the measure of value; or if, instead of the value of silver rising, gold were to push silver out of its place as the measure of value. In the one case, more silver would be current than gold was before; in the other case, less gold would be current than silver was before. In each case the value of the material of money, that is, the value of the commodity that serves as the measure of value, would have changed. So, too, would the prices of commodities, which express their values in money, and so, too, would the quantity of money current, whose function is to realize those prices. We have already seen that the sphere of circulation has an opening through which gold (or the material of money generally) enters it as a commodity with a given value. So when money takes up its functions as a measure of value, when it expresses prices, its value is already fixed. If its value now falls, this first shows itself in a change in the prices of those commodities that are directly bartered for the precious metals at the places where those metals are produced. Most other commodities, especially in the less developed stages of civil society, will go on for a long time being valued by the former, outdated and illusory value of the measure of value. Nevertheless, one commodity infects another through their common value-relation. So their prices, expressed in gold or in silver, gradually settle into the proportions fixed by their comparative values, until finally the values of all commodities are estimated in terms of the new value of the metal that makes up money. This process goes along with a continued increase in the quantity of the precious metals, an increase caused by their streaming in to replace the articles directly bartered for them at their sources of production. So in the same proportion as commodities in general acquire their true prices, as their values come to be estimated according to the fallen value of the precious metal, the quantity of that metal needed to realize those new prices is provided beforehand. Some economists in the 17th, and particularly in the 18th century, observed the results that followed the discovery of fresh supplies of gold and silver from one side only. This one-sided observation led them to the false conclusion that the prices of commodities had gone up because of the increased quantity of gold and silver serving as the medium of circulation. From now on we shall take the value of gold as given, as in fact it is at that moment whenever we estimate the price of a commodity.

<!-- ch03-p053 -->
On this assumption, then, the quantity of the medium of circulation is fixed by the sum of the prices to be realized. If we further assume that the price of each commodity is given, the sum of the prices clearly depends on the mass of commodities in circulation. It takes very little racking of brains to understand that if one quarter of wheat costs £2,100 quarters will cost £200, 200 quarters £400, and so on. Consequently, the quantity of money that changes places with the wheat when it is sold must increase with the quantity of that wheat.

<!-- ch03-p054 -->
If the mass of commodities stays constant, the quantity of circulating money varies with the ups and downs in the prices of those commodities. It increases and decreases because the sum of the prices increases or decreases as a result of the change of price. To produce this effect, it is by no means necessary that the prices of all commodities rise or fall at the same time. A rise or a fall in the prices of a number of leading articles is enough, in the one case to increase, in the other to reduce, the sum of the prices of all commodities, and therefore to put more or less money into circulation. The effect on the quantity of the medium of circulation stays the same whether the change in price corresponds to an actual change of value in the commodities, or is the result of mere fluctuations in market-prices. Suppose the following articles are sold, or partly metamorphosed, at the same time in different places: say, one quarter of wheat, 20 yards of linen, one Bible, and 4 gallons of brandy. If the price of each article is £2, and the sum of the prices to be realized is therefore £8, it follows that £8 in money must go into circulation. If, on the other hand, these same articles are links in the following chain of metamorphoses: 1 quarter of wheat – £2 – 20 yards of linen – £2 – 1 Bible – £2 – 4 gallons of brandy – £2, a chain we already know well, then the £2 make the different commodities circulate one after the other. After realizing their prices one after another, and therefore the sum of those prices, £8, they come to rest at last in the pocket of the distiller. So the £2 make four moves. This repeated change of place of the same pieces of money corresponds to the double change in form of the commodities, to their motion in opposite directions through two stages of circulation, and to the interlacing of the metamorphoses of different commodities.[^3.29] The process of metamorphosis consists of these opposite and complementary phases, and they are gone through not at the same time but one after another. So time is needed to complete the series. Hence the velocity of the currency of money is measured by the number of moves made by a given piece of money in a given time. Suppose the circulation of the 4 articles takes a day. The sum of the prices to be realized in the day is £8, the number of moves of the two pieces of money is four, and the quantity of money circulating is £2. So for a given period of time during the process of circulation, we have the following relation: the quantity of money functioning as the medium of circulation is equal to the sum of the prices of the commodities divided by the number of moves made by coins of the same denomination. This law holds generally.

[^3.29]: “Ce sont les productions qui le (l’argent) mettent en mouvement et le font circuler ... La célérité de son mouvement (c. de l’argent) supplée à sa quantité. Lorsqu’il en est besoin il ne fait que glisser d’une main dans l’autre sans s’arrêter un instant.” [“It is products which set it” (money) “in motion and make it circulate ... The speed of its” (money’s) “motion makes up for its quantity. When necessary, it does nothing but slide from one hand into the other, without stopping for a moment”] (Le Trosne, cited above, pp. 915, 916.)

<!-- ch03-p055 -->
The total circulation of commodities in a given country during a given period is made up of two parts. On the one hand, there are numerous isolated and simultaneous partial metamorphoses, sales which are at the same time purchases, in which each coin changes its place only once, or makes only one move. On the other hand, there are numerous distinct series of metamorphoses, partly running side by side and partly merging with each other; in each of these series each coin makes a number of moves, more or fewer according to circumstances. Given the total number of moves made by all the circulating coins of one denomination, we can work out the average number of moves made by a single coin of that denomination, or the average velocity of the currency of money. The quantity of money thrown into circulation at the beginning of each day is of course fixed by the sum of the prices of all the commodities circulating at the same time, side by side. But once in circulation, coins are, so to speak, made responsible for one another. If one speeds up, the other either slows down or drops out of circulation altogether. For circulation can absorb only such a quantity of gold as, multiplied by the average number of moves made by one single coin or element, equals the sum of the prices to be realized. So if the number of moves made by the separate pieces increases, the total number of those pieces in circulation decreases. If the number of moves decreases, the total number of pieces increases.
