Since the quantity of money that circulation can absorb is given for a given average velocity of currency, all you need to do to withdraw a given number of sovereigns from circulation is to throw the same number of one-pound notes into it, a trick well known to all bankers.

<!-- ch03-p056 -->
Just as the currency of money, considered generally, is only a reflection of the circulation of commodities, or of the opposite metamorphoses they go through, so, too, the velocity of that currency reflects the speed with which commodities change their forms. It reflects the continual interlacing of one series of metamorphoses with another, the hurried social interchange of matter, the rapid disappearance of commodities from the sphere of circulation, and the equally rapid substitution of fresh ones in their places. So in the velocity of the currency we have the flowing unity of the opposite and complementary phases: the unity of the conversion of the useful aspect of commodities into their value-aspect and their conversion back from the value-aspect to the useful aspect, or the unity of the two processes of sale and purchase. On the other hand, the slowing down of the currency reflects the separation of these two processes into isolated, opposed phases. It reflects the stagnation in the change of form, and therefore in the social interchange of matter. The circulation itself, of course, gives no clue to the origin of this stagnation; it merely displays the phenomenon itself. At the same time as the currency slows down, the general public sees money appear and disappear less often at the edges of circulation. So it naturally blames this slowing down on a shortage in the quantity of the medium of circulation.[^3.30]

[^3.30]: “Money being ... the common measure of buying and selling, everybody who hath anything to sell, and cannot procure chapmen [buyers] for it, is presently [at once] apt to think, that want [lack] of money in the kingdom, or country, is the cause why his goods do not go off; and so, want of money is the common cry; which is a great mistake... What do these people want, who cry out for money? ... The farmer complains ... he thinks that were more money in the country; he should have a price for his goods. Then it seems money is not his want, but a price for his corn and cattel, which he would sell, but cannot... Why cannot he get a price? ... (1) Either there is too much corn and cattel in the country, so that most who come to market have need of selling, as he hath, and few of buying; or (2) There wants the usual vent [outlet] abroad by transportation [export]..., or (3) The consumption fails, as when men, by reason of poverty, do not spend so much in their houses as formerly they did; wherefore it is not the increase of specific money, which would at all advance the farmer’s goods, but the removal of any of these three causes, which do truly keep down the market... The merchant and shopkeeper want money in the same manner, that is, they want a vent for the goods they deal in, by reason that the markets fail” ... [A nation] “never thrives better, than when riches are tost from hand to hand.” (Sir Dudley North: “Discourses upon Trade,” London 1691, pp. 11-15, passim.) Herrenschwand’s fanciful notions come down merely to this: that the antagonism which has its origin in the nature of commodities, and is reproduced in their circulation, can be removed by increasing the medium of circulation. But if, on the one hand, it is a popular delusion to blame stagnation in production and circulation on too little medium of circulation, it by no means follows, on the other hand, that an actual scarcity of the medium, caused, for example, by bungling legislative interference with the regulation of currency, may not give rise to such stagnation.

<!-- ch03-p057 -->
The total quantity of money functioning as the medium of circulation during a given period is fixed, on the one hand, by the sum of the prices of the circulating commodities, and on the other hand, by how quickly the opposite phases of the metamorphoses follow one another. On this speed depends what proportion of the sum of the prices each single coin can, on average, realize. But the sum of the prices of the circulating commodities depends on the quantity of the commodities as well as on their prices. These three factors, however (the state of prices, the quantity of circulating commodities, and the velocity of the currency of money), are all variable. So the sum of the prices to be realized, and therefore the quantity of the medium of circulation that depends on that sum, will vary with the numerous variations of these three factors in combination. Of these variations we shall consider only those that have been the most important in the history of prices.

<!-- ch03-p058 -->
While prices stay constant, the quantity of the medium of circulation may increase because the number of circulating commodities increases, or because the velocity of currency decreases, or because of a combination of the two. On the other hand, the quantity of the medium of circulation may decrease with a decreasing number of commodities, or with an increasing speed of their circulation.

<!-- ch03-p059 -->
With a general rise in the prices of commodities, the quantity of the medium of circulation will stay constant, provided the number of commodities in circulation decreases in proportion to the increase in their prices; or provided the velocity of currency increases at the same rate as prices rise, while the number of commodities in circulation stays constant. The quantity of the medium of circulation may decrease, because the number of commodities decreases faster than prices rise, or because the velocity of currency increases faster than prices rise.

<!-- ch03-p060 -->
With a general fall in the prices of commodities, the quantity of the medium of circulation will stay constant, provided the number of commodities increases in proportion to their fall in price, or provided the velocity of currency decreases in the same proportion. The quantity of the medium of circulation will increase, provided the number of commodities increases faster, or the speed of circulation decreases faster, than prices fall.

<!-- ch03-p061 -->
The variations of the different factors may balance each other out, so that despite their continued instability, the sum of the prices to be realized and the quantity of money in circulation stay constant. Consequently we find, especially if we take long periods into account, that the deviations of the quantity of money current in any country from its average level are much smaller than we would at first sight expect. This of course leaves aside the excessive disturbances that arise periodically from industrial and commercial crises or, less often, from fluctuations in the value of money.

<!-- ch03-p062 -->
The law that the quantity of the medium of circulation is fixed by the sum of the prices of the commodities circulating and the average velocity of currency[^3.31] may also be stated as follows: given the sum of the values of commodities, and the average speed of their metamorphoses, the quantity of precious metal current as money depends on the value of that precious metal. There is a mistaken opinion that, on the contrary, it is prices that are fixed by the quantity of the medium of circulation, and that this quantity depends on the quantity of the precious metals in a country.[^3.32] Those who first held this opinion based it on the absurd hypothesis that commodities have no price, and money no value, when they first enter into circulation, and that, once they are in circulation, a fractional part of the jumble of commodities is exchanged for a fractional part of the heap of precious metals.[^3.33]

[^3.31]: “There is a certain measure and proportion of money requisite to drive the trade of a nation, more or less than which would prejudice the same. Just as there is a certain proportion of farthings necessary in a small retail trade, to change silver money, and to even such reckonings as cannot be adjusted with the smallest silver pieces.... Now, as the proportion of the number of farthings requisite in commerce is to be taken from the number of people, the frequency of their exchanges: as also, and principally, from the value of the smallest silver pieces of money; so in like manner, the proportion of money [gold and silver specie] requisite in our trade, is to be likewise taken from the frequency of commutations [exchanges], and from the bigness of the payments.” (William Petty, “A Treatise of Taxes and Contributions.” London 1667, p. 17.) Hume’s theory was defended against the attacks of J. Steuart and others by A. Young, in his “Political Arithmetic,” London 1774. That work has a special chapter entitled “Prices depend on quantity of money, at p. 112, and following. I have stated in “Zur Kritik, &c.,” p. 149: “He (Adam Smith) passes over without remark the question as to the quantity of coin in circulation, and treats money quite wrongly as a mere commodity.” This statement applies only insofar as Adam Smith deals with money officially. Now and then, however, as in his criticism of the earlier systems of political economy, he takes the right view. “The quantity of coin in every country is regulated by the value of the commodities which are to be circulated by it.... The value of the goods annually bought and sold in any country requires a certain quantity of money to circulate and distribute them to their proper consumers, and can give employment to no more. The channel of circulation necessarily draws to itself a sum sufficient to fill it, and never admits any more.” (“Wealth of Nations.” Bk. IV., ch. 1.) In the same way, officially, he opens his work with a glorification of the division of labor. Later, in the last book, which deals with the sources of public revenue, he occasionally repeats the denunciations of the division of labor made by his teacher, A. Ferguson.

[^3.32]: “The prices of things will certainly rise in every nation, as the gold and silver increase amongst the people, and consequently, where the gold and silver decrease in any nation, the prices of all things must fall proportionately to such decrease of money.” (Jacob Vanderlint: “Money Answers all Things.” London 1734, p. 5.) A careful comparison of this book with Hume’s “Essays” proves to my mind, beyond doubt, that Hume knew and made use of Vanderlint’s work, which is certainly an important one. The opinion that prices are determined by the quantity of the medium of circulation was also held by Barbon and by other, much earlier writers. “No inconvenience,” says Vanderlint, “can arise by an unrestrained trade, but very great advantage; since, if the cash of the nation be decreased by it, which prohibitions are designed to prevent, those nations that get the cash will certainly find everything advance in price, as the cash increases amongst them. And ... our manufactures, and everything else, will soon become so moderate as to turn the balance of trade in our favour, and thereby fetch the money back again.” (cited above, pp. 43, 44.)

[^3.33]: It is a self-evident proposition that the price of each single kind of commodity forms a part of the sum of the prices of all the commodities in circulation. But it is quite incomprehensible how use-values that cannot be measured against each other are to be exchanged, all together, for the total sum of gold and silver in a country. If we start from the notion that all commodities together form one single commodity, of which each is only an aliquot part, a fractional part, we get the following beautiful result: The total commodity = x cwt. of gold; commodity A = an aliquot part of the total commodity = the same aliquot part of x cwt. of gold. Montesquieu states this in all seriousness: “Si l’on compare la masse de l’or et de l’argent qui est dans le monde avec la somme des marchandises qui s’y vend il est certain que chaque denrée ou marchandise, en particulier, pourra être comparée à une certaine portion de la masse entière. Supposons qu’il n’y ait qu’une seule denrée ou marchandise dans le monde, ou qu’il n’y ait qu’une seule qui s’achète, et qu’elle se divise comme l’argent: Cette partie de cette marchandise répondra à une partie de la masse de l’argent; la moitié du total de l’une à la moitié du total de l’autre, &c.... L’établissement du prix des choses dépend toujours fondamentalement de la raison du total des choses au total des signes.” [“If one compares the mass of gold and silver in the world with the sum of the commodities sold in it, it is certain that each product or commodity, taken by itself, could be compared with a certain portion of the whole mass. Let us suppose that there is only one product, or commodity, in the world, or only one that is bought, and that it can be divided in the same way as money: this part of this commodity would then correspond to a part of the mass of money; half the total of the one to half the total of the other, etc. ... The setting of the prices of things always depends, fundamentally, on the ratio of the total of things to the total of signs”] (Montesquieu, cited above, t. III, pp. 12, 13.) As to the further development of this theory by Ricardo and his followers, James Mill, Lord Overstone, and others, see “Zur Kritik, &c.,” pp. 140-146, and p. 150, and following. John Stuart Mill, with his usual eclectic logic, knows how to hold at the same time the view of his father, James Mill, and the opposite view. When we compare the text of his compendium, “Principles of Pol. Econ.,” with his preface to the first edition, in which he announces himself as the Adam Smith of his day, we do not know which to admire more: the simplicity of the man, or that of the public, who took him, in good faith, for the Adam Smith he announced himself to be, although he bears about as much resemblance to Adam Smith as, say, General Williams, of Kars, does to the Duke of Wellington. Mr. J. S. Mill’s original researches in the field of political economy, which are neither extensive nor profound, will be found mustered in rank and file in his little work, “Some Unsettled Questions of Political Economy,” which appeared in 1844. Locke states point blank the connection between the absence of value in gold and silver and the fixing of their values by quantity alone. “Mankind having consented to put an imaginary value upon gold and silver ... the intrinsic value, regarded in these metals, is nothing but the quantity." (“Some Considerations,” *&c*., 1691, Works Ed. 1777, Vol. II., p. 15.)

#### C. Coin and symbols of value

<!-- ch03-p063 -->
Money takes the shape of coin because of its function as the medium of circulation. The prices or money names of commodities represent a weight of gold in imagination. Within circulation, that gold must face those commodities in the shape of coins, or pieces of gold of a given denomination. Coining, like establishing a standard of price, is the business of the State. As coins, gold and silver wear different national uniforms at home, and take them off again in the world market. This shows the separation between the internal or national spheres of the circulation of commodities and their universal sphere.

<!-- ch03-p064 -->
So the only difference between coin and bullion (uncoined gold or silver) is one of shape, and gold can pass from one form to the other at any time.[^3.34] But no sooner does a coin leave the mint than it finds itself on the high road to the melting pot. During their currency, coins wear away, some more, others less. Name and substance, nominal weight and real weight, begin to separate. Coins of the same denomination come to differ in value, because they differ in weight. The weight of gold fixed as the standard of price drifts away from the weight that serves as the medium of circulation. So the gold that circulates stops being a real equivalent of the commodities whose prices it realizes. The history of coinage in the middle ages and down into the 18th century records the confusion that this cause produced again and again. Circulation has a natural tendency to turn coins into a mere semblance of what they claim to be, into a symbol of the weight of metal they are officially supposed to contain. Modern legislation recognizes this tendency: it fixes how much weight a gold coin must lose to be demonetized, or to stop being legal tender.

[^3.34]: It lies, of course, entirely outside my purpose to consider such details as seigniorage (the charge for coining) on minting. However, for the benefit of the romantic sycophant Adam Muller, who admires the “generous liberality” with which the English Government coins free of charge, I will cite the following opinion of Sir Dudley North: “Silver and gold, like other commodities, have their ebbings and flowings. Upon the arrival of quantities from Spain ... it is carried into the Tower, and coined. Not long after there will come a demand for bullion to be exported again. If there is none, but all happens to be in coin, what then? Melt it down again; there’s no loss in it, for the coining costs the owner nothing. Thus the nation has been abused, and made to pay for the twisting of straw for asses to eat. If the merchant were made to pay the price of the coinage, he would not have sent his silver to the Tower without consideration, and coined money would always keep a value above uncoined silver.” (North, cited above, p. 18.) North was himself one of the leading merchants in the reign of Charles II.

<!-- ch03-p065 -->
The currency of coins itself separates their nominal weight from their real weight. It creates a distinction between them as mere pieces of metal on the one hand, and as coins with a definite function on the other. This fact implies the hidden possibility of replacing metal coins by tokens of some other material, by symbols that serve the same purposes as coins. There are practical difficulties in coining extremely tiny quantities of gold or silver. Also, at first the less precious metal is used as a measure of value instead of the more precious one, copper instead of silver, silver instead of gold, and the less precious metal circulates as money until the more precious one dethrones it. All these facts explain the parts that silver and copper tokens have played in history as substitutes for gold coins. Silver and copper tokens take the place of gold in those regions of circulation where coins pass from hand to hand most rapidly and suffer the most wear and tear. This happens where very small sales and purchases are going on all the time. To prevent these satellites from settling permanently in the place of gold, laws expressly lay down how far people must accept them as payment instead of gold. The particular tracks followed by the different kinds of coin in currency naturally run into each other. The tokens keep company with gold, to pay fractional parts of the smallest gold coin. Gold, on the one hand, is constantly pouring into retail circulation, and on the other hand is just as constantly being thrown out again by being changed into tokens.[^3.35]

[^3.35]: “If silver never exceed what is wanted for the smaller payments it cannot be collected in sufficient quantities for the larger payments ... the use of gold in the main payments necessarily implies also its use in the retail trade: those who have gold coin offering them for small purchases, and receiving with the commodity purchased a balance of silver in return; by which means the surplus of silver that would otherwise encumber the retail dealer, is drawn off and dispersed into general circulation. But if there is as much silver as will transact the small payments independent of gold, the retail trader must then receive silver for small purchases; and it must of necessity accumulate in his hands.” (David Buchanan; “Inquiry into the Taxation and Commercial Policy of Great Britain.” Edinburgh, 1844, pp. 248, 249.)

<!-- ch03-p066 -->
The law fixes the weight of metal in silver and copper tokens arbitrarily. In currency they wear away even faster than gold coins. Hence their functions are totally independent of their weight, and therefore of all value. The function of gold as coin becomes completely independent of the metallic value of that gold. So things that are relatively without value, such as paper notes, can serve as coins in its place. In metal tokens this purely symbolic character is hidden to a certain extent. In paper money it stands out plainly. In fact, ce n’est que le premier pas qui coûte [it is only the first step that costs].

<!-- ch03-p067 -->
We are speaking here only of inconvertible paper money (paper money that cannot be exchanged for gold) which the State issues and gives compulsory circulation. It arises directly out of the metal currency. Money based on credit, on the other hand, presupposes conditions that are still totally unknown to us from our standpoint of the simple circulation of commodities. But we may say this much: just as true paper money arises from the function of money as the medium of circulation, so money based on credit takes root spontaneously in the function of money as the means of payment (money used to settle a debt after goods have changed hands on credit).[^3.36]

[^3.36]: The mandarin Wan-mao-in, the Chinese Chancellor of the Exchequer, one day took it into his head to put before the Son of Heaven a proposal whose secret aim was to turn the *assignats* (paper money) of the empire into convertible bank-notes. In its report of April, 1854, the assignats Committee gave him a severe snubbing. Whether he also received the traditional beating with bamboo canes is not stated. The report ends as follows: — “The Committee has carefully examined his proposal and finds that it is entirely in favour of the merchants, and that no advantage will result to the crown.” (“Arbeiten der Kaiserlich Russischen Gesandtschaft zu Peking über China.” Aus dem Russischen von Dr. K. Abel und F. A. Mecklenburg. Erster Band. Berlin, 1858, p. 47 and following.) In his evidence before the Committee of the House of Lords on the Bank Acts, a governor of the Bank of England says this about the wearing down of gold coins during currency: “Every year a fresh class of sovereigns becomes too light. The class which one year passes with full weight, loses enough by wear and tear to draw the scales next year against it.” (House of Lords’ Committee, 1848, n. 429.)

<!-- ch03-p068 -->
The State puts into circulation bits of paper with their various denominations printed on them, say £1, £5, etc. Insofar as they actually take the place of gold to the same amount, their movement is subject to the laws that govern the currency of money itself. A law peculiar to the circulation of paper money can arise only from the proportion in which that paper money represents gold. Such a law exists. Stated simply, it is this: the issue of paper money must not exceed the amount of gold (or silver, as the case may be) that would actually circulate if it were not replaced by symbols. Now, the quantity of gold that circulation can absorb constantly fluctuates around a given level. Still, the mass of the medium of circulation in a given country never sinks below a certain minimum, which is easily found by actual experience. This minimum mass is constantly changing in its component parts: the pieces of gold that make it up are constantly being replaced by fresh ones. But this of course causes no change either in its amount or in the continuity of its circulation. It can therefore be replaced by paper symbols. If, on the other hand, all the channels of circulation were filled today with paper money to the full extent of their capacity to absorb money, they might be overflowing tomorrow because of a fluctuation in the circulation of commodities. There would no longer be any standard. The proper limit of paper money is the amount of gold coins of the same denomination that can actually circulate. If the paper money exceeds that limit, then, apart from the danger of falling into general disrepute, it would represent only that quantity of gold which the laws of the circulation of commodities require, and which alone can be represented by paper. If the quantity of paper money issued is double what it ought to be, then, as a matter of fact, £1 would be the money name not of 1/4 of an ounce, but of 1/8 of an ounce of gold. The effect would be the same as if a change had taken place in the function of gold as a standard of price. Values that were previously expressed by the price of £1 would now be expressed by the price of £2.

<!-- ch03-p069 -->
Paper money is a token that represents gold or money. Its relation to the values of commodities is this: those values are ideally expressed in the same quantities of gold that the paper represents symbolically. Paper money is a symbol of value only insofar as it represents gold, which, like all other commodities, has value.[^3.37]

[^3.37]: The following passage from Fullarton shows how unclear even the best writers on money are in their understanding of its various functions: “That, as far as concerns our domestic exchanges, all the monetary functions which are usually performed by gold and silver coins, may be performed as effectually by a circulation of inconvertible notes paying no value but that factitious [artificial] and conventional value they derive from the law is a fact which admits, I conceive, of no denial. Value of this description may be made to answer all the purposes of intrinsic value, and supersede even the necessity for a standard, provided only the quantity of issues be kept under due limitation.” (Fullerton: “Regulation of Currencies,” London, 1845, p. 21.) Because the commodity that serves as money can be replaced in circulation by mere symbols of value, therefore its functions as a measure of value and a standard of price are declared to be superfluous!

<!-- ch03-p070 -->
Finally, someone may ask: why can gold be replaced by tokens that have no value? But, as we have already seen, it can be replaced in this way only insofar as it functions exclusively as coin, or as the medium of circulation, and as nothing else. Now, money has other functions besides this one. The isolated function of serving as the mere medium of circulation is not necessarily the only one attached to gold coin, although it is the only one for those worn coins that continue to circulate. Each piece of money is a mere coin, or medium of circulation, only so long as it actually circulates. But this is exactly the case with that minimum mass of gold which can be replaced by paper money. That mass stays constantly within the sphere of circulation, functions continually as a medium of circulation, and exists only for that purpose. So its movement represents nothing but the continued alternation of the opposite phases of the metamorphosis C–M–C. In these phases commodities face their forms of value, only to disappear again immediately. Here the independent existence of a commodity's exchange-value is a passing apparition, by means of which the commodity is immediately replaced by another commodity. Hence, in this process that keeps making money pass from hand to hand, the mere symbolic existence of money is enough. Its functional existence absorbs, so to speak, its material existence. As a passing and objective reflection of the prices of commodities, it serves only as a symbol of itself, and can therefore be replaced by a token.[^3.38] One thing, however, is needed: this token must have an objective social validity of its own, and the paper symbol gets this by its forced currency. This compulsory action of the State can take effect only within the inner sphere of circulation whose boundaries coincide with the territories of the community. But it is also only within that sphere that money fully performs its function as the medium of circulation, or becomes coin.

[^3.38]: Nicholas Barbon starts from the fact that gold and silver, so far as they are coins, or serve exclusively as the medium of circulation, become mere tokens of themselves. From this he deduces the right of Governments “to raise money,” that is, to give the weight of silver that is called a shilling the name of a greater weight, such as a crown, and so to pay creditors shillings instead of crowns. “Money does wear and grow lighter by often telling over [counting]... It is the denomination and currency of the money that men regard in bargaining, and not the quantity of silver...’Tis the public authority upon the metal that makes it money.” (N. Barbon, cited above, pp. 29, 30, 25.)

### Section 3: Money

<!-- ch03-p071 -->
The commodity that functions as a measure of value, and also, either in its own person or through a representative, as the medium of circulation, is money. Gold (or silver) is therefore money. On the one hand, it functions as money when it has to be present in its own golden person. It is then the money-commodity. It is neither merely ideal, as in its function as a measure of value, nor able to be represented by something else, as in its function as the medium of circulation. On the other hand, it also functions as money when, by virtue of its function, whether that function is performed in person or by a representative, it solidifies into the sole form of value. It then becomes the only adequate form of existence of exchange-value, in opposition to use-value, represented by all other commodities.

#### A. Hoarding

<!-- ch03-p072 -->
The two opposed metamorphoses of commodities move continually in circuits: sale and purchase alternate without end. This is reflected in the restless currency of money, or in the function money performs as a *perpetuum mobile* [perpetual motion machine] of circulation. But as soon as the series of metamorphoses is interrupted, as soon as sales are not followed up by later purchases, money stops being mobile. It is transformed, as Boisguillebert says, from “meuble” into “immeuble,” from movable into immovable, from coin into money.

<!-- ch03-p073 -->
As soon as the circulation of commodities first develops, there also develops the need, and the passionate desire, to hold on to the product of the first metamorphosis. This product is the commodity in its transformed shape, or its gold-chrysalis.[^3.39] So commodities are now sold not in order to buy others, but in order to replace their commodity-form by their money-form. This change of form was merely the means of carrying out the circulation of commodities; now it becomes the end and aim. The changed form of the commodity is thus prevented from functioning as the form in which it can be parted with unconditionally, or as its merely passing money-form. The money turns to stone as a hoard, and the seller becomes a hoarder of money.

[^3.39]: “Une richesse en argent n’est que ... richesse en productions, converties en argent.” [“Wealth in money is nothing but ... wealth in products, changed into money.”] (Mercier de la Rivière, cited above.) “Une valeur en productions n’a fait que changer de forme.” [“A value in products has only changed its form.”] (Id., p. 486.)

<!-- ch03-p074 -->
In the early stages of the circulation of commodities, only the surplus use-values are turned into money. Gold and silver thus become, of themselves, the social expressions of superfluity, or wealth. This naïve form of hoarding becomes permanent in those communities where the traditional mode of production is carried on to supply a fixed and limited circle of home needs. This is the case with the people of Asia, and particularly of the East Indies. Vanderlint imagines that the prices of commodities in a country are determined by the quantity of gold and silver to be found in it, and he asks himself why Indian commodities are so cheap. Answer: Because the Hindus bury their money. From 1602 to 1734, he remarks, they buried 150 millions of pounds sterling of silver, which had originally come from America to Europe.[^3.40] In the 10 years from 1856 to 1866, England exported £120,000,000 in silver to India and China, silver it had received in exchange for Australian gold. Most of the silver exported to China makes its way to India.

[^3.40]: “’Tis by this practice’ they keep all their goods and manufactures at such low rates.” (Vanderlint, cited above, pp. 95, 96.)

<!-- ch03-p075 -->
As the production of commodities develops further, every producer of commodities is forced to make sure of the nexus rerum [the bond of things], or the social pledge.[^3.41] His needs constantly make themselves felt and require him to keep buying other people’s commodities, while the production and sale of his own goods take time and depend on circumstances. So in order to be able to buy without selling, he must previously have sold without buying. This operation, carried out on a general scale, appears to imply a contradiction. But at the sources where they are produced, the precious metals are exchanged directly for other commodities. And here we have sales (by the owners of commodities) without purchases (by the owners of gold or silver).[^3.42] And later sales by other producers, not followed by purchases, merely bring about the distribution of the newly produced precious metals among all the owners of commodities. In this way, hoards of gold and silver of varying size are accumulated all along the line of exchange. With the possibility of holding and storing up exchange-value in the shape of a particular commodity, there also arises the greed for gold. As circulation extends, the power of money increases, money being that absolutely social form of wealth that is always ready for use. “Gold is a wonderful thing! Whoever possesses it is lord of all he wants. By means of gold one can even get souls into Paradise.” (Columbus in his letter from Jamaica, 1503.) Since gold does not reveal what has been transformed into it, everything, commodity or not, can be converted into gold. Everything becomes salable and buyable. Circulation becomes the great social retort (a chemist’s distilling vessel) into which everything is thrown, to come out again as a gold-crystal. Not even the bones of saints can withstand this alchemy, and still less can more delicate res sacrosanctae, extra commercium hominum [sacred things, outside the commerce of men].[^3.43] Just as every qualitative difference between commodities is wiped out in money, so money, for its part, being the radical leveler that it is, does away with all distinctions.[^3.43a] But money itself is a commodity, an external object that can become the private property of any individual. Thus social power becomes the private power of private persons. The ancients therefore denounced money as subversive of the economic and moral order of things.[^3.43b] Modern society, soon after its birth, pulled Plutus (the Greek god of wealth) by the hair of his head out of the bowels of the earth.[^3.44] It greets gold as its Holy Grail, as the glittering incarnation of the very principle of its own life.

[^3.41]: “Money ... is a pledge.” (John Bellers: “Essays about the Poor, Manufactures, Trade, Plantations, and Immorality,” London, 1699, p. 13.)

[^3.42]: A purchase, in a “categorical” sense, implies that gold and silver are already the converted form of commodities, or the product of a sale.

[^3.43]: Henry III, most Christian king of France, robbed cloisters of their relics and turned them into money. It is well known what part the plundering of the Delphic Temple by the Phocians played in the history of Greece. Among the ancients, temples served as the dwellings of the gods of commodities. They were “sacred banks.” For the Phoenicians, a trading people above all others, money was the transformed shape of everything. So it was quite in order that the virgins who gave themselves up to strangers at the feast of the Goddess of Love should offer the goddess the piece of money they received.

[^3.43a]: “Gold, yellow, glittering, precious gold!

    > Thus much of this, will make black white; foul, fair; Wrong, right; base, noble; old, young; coward, valiant. ... What this, you gods? Why, this Will lug your priests and servants from your sides; Pluck stout men’s pillows from below their heads; This yellow slave Will knit and break religions; bless the accurs’d; Make the hoar leprosy ador’d; place thieves, And give them title, knee and approbation, With senators on the bench; this is it, That makes the wappen’d [worn-out] widow wed again: ... Come damned earth, Though common whore of mankind.” (Shakespeare: Timon of Athens.)

[^3.43b]: “Money! Nothing worse

    > in our lives, so current, rampant, so corrupting. Money — you demolish cities, root men from their homes, you train and twist good minds and set them on to the most atrocious schemes. No limit, you make them adept at every kind of outrage, every godless crimes — money!” (Sophocles, Antigone.)

[^3.44]: “The desire of avarice to draw Pluto himself out of the bowels of the earth.” (The Deipnosophists, VI, 23, Athenaeus)

<!-- ch03-p076 -->
A commodity, in its capacity as a use-value, satisfies a particular need and is a particular element of material wealth. But the value of a commodity measures how strongly it attracts all other elements of material wealth, and therefore measures the social wealth of its owner. To a barbarian owner of commodities, and even to a West-European peasant, value is the same as the form of value. So to him, an increase in his hoard of gold and silver is an increase in value. It is true that the value of money varies, at one time because its own value changes, at another because the values of commodities change. But on the one hand, this does not stop 200 ounces of gold from still containing more value than 100 ounces. On the other hand, it does not stop the actual metallic form of this article from remaining the universal equivalent form of all other commodities, and the immediate social incarnation of all human labor. The urge to hoard is by its very nature insatiable. In its qualitative aspect, or considered as to its form, money has no limits to its power; that is, it is the universal representative of material wealth, because it can be converted directly into any other commodity. But at the same time, every actual sum of money is limited in amount, and so, as a means of purchase, has only limited power. This antagonism between the quantitative limits of money and its qualitative boundlessness keeps spurring the hoarder on in his Sisyphus-like labor of accumulating. It is with him as with a conqueror who sees in every new country he annexes only a new frontier.

<!-- ch03-p077 -->
For gold to be held as money and made to form a hoard, it must be prevented from circulating, or from turning itself into a means of enjoyment. The hoarder therefore sacrifices the lusts of the flesh to his gold fetish. He lives up to the Gospel of abstention in earnest. On the other hand, he can withdraw from circulation no more than he has thrown into it in the shape of commodities. The more he produces, the more he can sell. Hard work, saving, and avarice are therefore his three cardinal virtues, and to sell much and buy little is the sum of his political economy.[^3.45]

[^3.45]: “Accrescere quanto più si può il numero de’venditori d’ogni merce, diminuere quanto più si puo il numero dei compratori, questi sono i cardini sui quali si raggirano tutte le operazioni di economia politica.” [“To increase as much as one can the number of sellers of every commodity, to reduce as much as one can the number of buyers: these are the hinges on which all the operations of political economy turn.”] (Verri, cited above, p. 52.)

<!-- ch03-p078 -->
Alongside the crude form of the hoard, we also find its aesthetic form, the possession of gold and silver articles. This grows with the wealth of civil society. “Soyons riches ou paraissons riches” [“Let us be rich or appear rich”] (Diderot).

<!-- ch03-p079 -->
In this way there is created, on the one hand, a constantly expanding market for gold and silver, unconnected with their functions as money. On the other hand, there is created a dormant source of supply, which is drawn on mainly in times of crisis and social upheaval.

<!-- ch03-p080 -->
Hoarding serves various purposes in the economy of metallic circulation. Its first function arises out of the conditions that govern the currency of gold and silver coins. We have seen how the quantity of money in circulation constantly ebbs and flows, along with the continual fluctuations in the extent and speed of the circulation of commodities and in their prices. This mass must therefore be able to expand and contract. At one time money must be drawn in to act as circulating coin; at another, circulating coin must be pushed out to act again as more or less stagnant money. The mass of money actually in circulation must always fill the absorbing capacity of circulation to the full. For this, the quantity of gold and silver in a country must be greater than the quantity needed to function as coin. This condition is met by money taking the form of hoards. These reserves serve as channels for supplying money to circulation or withdrawing it from circulation, which in this way never overflows its banks.[^3.46]

[^3.46]: “There is required for carrying on the trade of the nation a determinate sum of specifick money which varies, and is sometimes more, sometimes less, as the circumstances we are in require.... This ebbing and flowing of money supplies and accommodates itself, without any aid of Politicians.... The buckets work alternately; when money is scarce, bullion is coined; when bullion is scarce, money is melted.” (Sir D. North, cited above, Postscript, p. 3.) John Stuart Mill, who was for a long time an official of the East India Company, confirms the fact that in India silver ornaments still directly perform the functions of a hoard. The silver ornaments are brought out and coined when the rate of interest is high, and go back again when the rate of interest falls. (J. S. Mill’s Evidence “Reports on Bank Acts,” 1857, 2084.) According to a Parliamentary document of 1864 on the import and export of gold and silver in India, the import of gold and silver in 1863 exceeded the export by £19,367,764. During the 8 years just before 1864, imports of the precious metals exceeded exports by £109,652,917. During this century far more than £200,000,000 has been coined in India.

#### B. Means of Payment

<!-- ch03-p081 -->
In the simple form of the circulation of commodities that we have considered so far, a given value always appeared to us in a double shape: as a commodity at one pole, and as money at the opposite pole. So the owners of commodities came into contact as the representatives of things that were already equivalents. But as circulation develops, conditions arise under which the handing over of commodities is separated by an interval of time from the realization of their prices. It will be enough to point out the simplest of these conditions. One sort of article takes a longer time to produce, another a shorter time. Again, the production of different commodities depends on different seasons of the year. One sort of commodity may be born in its own market place; another has to make a long journey to market. So commodity-owner No. 1 may be ready to sell before No. 2 is ready to buy. When the same transactions are continually repeated between the same persons, the terms of sale are regulated to match the conditions of production. On the other hand, the use of a given commodity, of a house, for instance, is sold (in everyday language, let) for a definite period. Here the buyer has actually received the use-value of the commodity only at the end of the term. So he buys it before he pays for it. The seller sells an existing commodity; the buyer buys as the mere representative of money, or rather of future money. The seller becomes a creditor, the buyer becomes a debtor. Since the metamorphosis of commodities, or the development of their form of value, appears here in a new aspect, money also takes on a new function: it becomes the means of payment.

<!-- ch03-p082 -->
Here the roles of creditor and debtor arise out of simple circulation. The change in the form of that circulation stamps buyer and seller with this new die. At first, therefore, these new roles are just as passing and changeable as those of seller and buyer, and the same actors play them in turn. But this opposition is not nearly so pleasant, and it is far more capable of crystallizing.[^3.47] The same roles can, however, also arise independently of the circulation of commodities. The class struggles of the ancient world took the form chiefly of a contest between debtors and creditors. In Rome this ended in the ruin of the plebeian debtors. They were replaced by slaves. In the middle ages the contest ended with the ruin of the feudal debtors, who lost their political power together with the economic basis on which it rested. Nevertheless, the money relation of debtor and creditor that existed in these two periods only reflected the deeper-lying antagonism between the general economic conditions of existence of the classes in question.

[^3.47]: The following shows the debtor and creditor relations among English traders at the beginning of the 18th century. “Such a spirit of crudity reigns here in England among the men of trade, that is not to be met with in any other society of men, nor in any other kingdom of the world.” (“An Essay on Credit and the Bankrupt Act,” London, 1707, p. 2.)

<!-- ch03-p083 -->
Let us return to the circulation of commodities. The two equivalents, commodities and money, no longer appear at the same time at the two poles of the sale. Money now functions, first, as a measure of value in fixing the price of the commodity sold. The price fixed by the contract measures the debtor’s obligation, that is, the sum of money he has to pay on a fixed date. Secondly, money serves as a means of purchase that exists only ideally. Although it exists only in the buyer’s promise to pay, it makes the commodity change hands. Not until the day fixed for payment does the means of payment actually step into circulation and leave the buyer’s hand for the seller’s. The medium of circulation was turned into a hoard because the process stopped short after the first phase, because the converted shape of the commodity, namely the money, was withdrawn from circulation. The means of payment enters circulation, but only after the commodity has left it. Money is no longer the means that brings the process about. It only brings it to a close, by stepping in as the absolute form of existence of exchange-value, or as the universal commodity. The seller turned his commodity into money in order to satisfy some need with it; the hoarder did the same in order to keep his commodity in its money-shape; and the debtor did it in order to be able to pay. If he does not pay, the sheriff will sell his goods. So the form of value of commodities, money, is now the end and aim of a sale, and this owing to a social necessity springing out of the process of circulation itself.

<!-- ch03-p084 -->
The buyer turns money back into commodities before he has turned commodities into money. In other words, he carries out the second metamorphosis of commodities before the first. The seller’s commodity circulates and realizes its price, but only in the shape of a legal claim to money. It is turned into a use-value before it has been turned into money. Its first metamorphosis is completed only later.[^3.48]

[^3.48]: The following quotation from my book that appeared in 1859 will show why I take no notice in the text of an opposite form: “Contrariwise, in the process in M—C, the money can be alienated as a real means of purchase, and in that way, the price of the commodity can be realised before the use-value of the money is realised and the commodity actually delivered. This occurs constantly under the every-day form of prepayments. And it is under this form, that the English government purchases opium from the ryots [peasant farmers] of India.... In these cases, however, the money always acts as a means of purchase.... Of course capital also is advanced in the shape of money.... This point of view, however, does not fall within the horizon of simple circulation.” (“Zur Kritik, *&c*.,” pp. 119, 120.)

<!-- ch03-p085 -->
The obligations falling due within a given period represent the sum of the prices of the commodities whose sale gave rise to those obligations. The quantity of gold needed to realize this sum depends, in the first place, on the rapidity of currency of the means of payment. That quantity is conditioned by two circumstances. The first is that the relations between debtors and creditors form a sort of chain, so that A, when he receives money from his debtor B, at once hands it over to C, his creditor, and so on. The second circumstance is the length of the intervals between the different due dates of the obligations. The continuous chain of payments, or of delayed first metamorphoses, is essentially different from the interlacing of the series of metamorphoses that we considered earlier. The currency of the medium of circulation does not merely express the connection between buyers and sellers. This connection arises in circulation, and exists in it alone. By contrast, the movement of the means of payment expresses a social relation that was in existence long before.

<!-- ch03-p086 -->
The fact that a number of sales take place at the same time and side by side limits how far the rapidity of currency can make up for coin. On the other hand, this fact is a new lever for economizing on the means of payment. In proportion as payments are concentrated in one place, special institutions and methods develop for settling them. Such in the middle ages were the *virements* [transfers] at Lyons. The debts owed to A by B, to B by C, to C by A, and so on, only have to be set against each other in order to cancel each other out to a certain extent, like positive and negative quantities. Only a single balance then remains to be paid. The greater the amount of payments concentrated, the smaller this balance is relative to that amount, and the smaller is the mass of the means of payment in circulation.

<!-- ch03-p087 -->
The function of money as the means of payment implies a contradiction without a terminus medius [middle term]. To the extent that the payments balance one another, money functions only ideally, as money of account, as a measure of value. To the extent that actual payments have to be made, money does not serve as a medium of circulation, as a mere passing agent in the exchange of products. It serves as the individual incarnation of social labor, as the independent form of existence of exchange-value, as the universal commodity. This contradiction comes to a head in those phases of industrial and commercial crises that are known as monetary crises.[^3.49] Such a crisis occurs only where the ever-lengthening chain of payments, and an artificial system for settling them, have been fully developed. Whenever there is a general and extensive disturbance of this mechanism, no matter what its cause, money is suddenly and immediately transformed from its merely ideal shape of money of account into hard cash. Profane commodities can no longer take its place. The use-value of commodities becomes valueless, and their value vanishes in the presence of its own independent form. On the eve of the crisis, the bourgeois, with the self-satisfaction that springs from intoxicating prosperity, declares money to be an empty fancy: commodities alone are money. But now the cry is everywhere: money alone is a commodity! As the hart pants after fresh water, so his soul pants after money, the only wealth.[^3.50] In a crisis, the opposition between commodities and their form of value, money, is heightened into an absolute contradiction. Hence, in such events, the form in which money appears does not matter. The money famine continues, whether payments have to be made in gold or in credit money such as bank-notes.[^3.51]

[^3.49]: The monetary crisis referred to in the text is a phase of every crisis. It must be clearly distinguished from that particular kind of crisis which is also called a monetary crisis, but which may arise by itself as an independent phenomenon, in such a way that it reacts only indirectly on industry and trade. The pivot of these crises is moneyed capital, and so their sphere of direct action is the sphere of that capital, namely banking, the stock exchange, and finance.

[^3.50]: “The sudden reversion from a system of credit to a system of hard cash heaps theoretical fright on top of the practical panic; and the dealers by whose agency circulation is affected, shudder before the impenetrable mystery in which their own economic relations are involved” (Karl Marx, cited above, p. 126.) “The poor stand still, because the rich have no money to employ them, though they have the same land and hands to provide victuals [food] and clothes, as ever they had; ...which is the true riches of a nation, and not the money.” John Bellers, *Proposals for Raising a College of Industry*, London, 1696, p3.

[^3.51]: The following shows how such times are exploited by the “amis du commerce” [“friends of trade”]. “On one occasion (1839) an old grasping banker (in the city) in his private room raised the lid of the desk he sat over, and displayed to a friend rolls of bank-notes, saying with intense glee there were £600,000 of them, they were held to make money tight, and would all be let out after three o’clock on the same day.” (“The Theory of Exchanges. The Bank Charter Act of 1844.” London 1864, p. 81). The *Observer*, a semi-official government paper, printed the following paragraph on 24th April, 1864: “Some very curious rumours are current of the means which have been resorted to in order to create a scarcity of banknotes.... Questionable as it would seem, to suppose that any trick of the kind would be adopted, the report has been so universal that it really deserves mention.”

<!-- ch03-p088 -->
If we now consider the total sum of money in circulation during a given period, we find the following. Given the rapidity of currency of the medium of circulation and of the means of payment, it is equal to the sum of the prices to be realized, plus the sum of the payments falling due, minus the payments that balance each other, minus finally the number of circuits in which the same piece of coin serves in turn as medium of circulation and as means of payment. Hence, even when prices, the rapidity of currency, and the extent of the economizing on payments are given, the quantity of money in circulation and the mass of commodities circulating during a given period, such as a day, no longer correspond. Money continues to circulate that represents commodities withdrawn from circulation long ago. Commodities circulate whose equivalent in money will not appear on the scene until some future day. Moreover, the debts contracted each day and the payments falling due on the same day are quantities that have no common measure at all.[^3.52]

[^3.52]: “The amount of purchases or contracts entered upon during the course of any given day, will not affect the quantity of money afloat on that particular day, but, in the vast majority of cases, will resolve themselves into multifarious drafts upon the quantity of money which may be afloat at subsequent dates more or less distant.... The bills granted or credits opened, to-day, need have no resemblance whatever, either in quantity, amount or duration, to those granted or entered upon to-morrow or next day, nay, many of today’s bills, and credits, when due, fall in with a mass of liabilities whose origins traverse a range of antecedent dates altogether indefinite, bills at 12, 6, 3 months or 1 often aggregating together to swell the common liabilities of one particular day....” (“The Currency Theory Reviewed; in a Letter to the Scottish People.” By a Banker in England. Edinburgh, 1845, pp. 29, 30 passim.)

<!-- ch03-p089 -->
Credit-money springs directly out of the function of money as a means of payment. Certificates of the debts owed for purchased commodities circulate in order to transfer those debts to others. On the other hand, the function of money as a means of payment extends to the same degree as the credit system extends. In that role it takes on various forms of its own, in which it makes itself at home in the sphere of large commercial transactions. Gold and silver coin, on the other hand, are mostly pushed off into the sphere of retail trade.[^3.53]

[^3.53]: As an example of how little ready money is needed in real commercial operations, I give below a statement by one of the largest London firms of its yearly receipts and payments. Its transactions during the year 1856 ran to many millions of pounds sterling; here they are reduced to the scale of one million.

    *Receipts.Payments*.Bankers’ and Merchants’£533,596Bills payable after date£302,674Cheques on Bankers, &c. payable on demand357,715Cheques on London Bankers663,672Country Notes9,627Bank of England Notes22,743Bank of England Notes68,554Gold9,427Gold28,089Silver and Copper1,484Silver and Copper1,486 Post Office Orders933 Total £1,000,000Total £1,000,000“Report from the Select Committee on the Bank Acts, July, 1858,” p. lxxi..

<!-- ch03-p090 -->
When the production of commodities has extended far enough, money begins to serve as the means of payment beyond the sphere of the circulation of commodities. It becomes the commodity that is the universal subject-matter of all contracts.[^3.54] Rents, taxes, and similar payments are turned from payments in kind into money payments. How far this transformation depends on the general conditions of production is shown, to take one example, by the fact that the Roman Empire twice failed in its attempt to levy all contributions in money. The unspeakable misery of the French farming population under Louis XIV, a misery so eloquently denounced by Boisguillebert, Marshal Vauban, and others, was due not only to the weight of the taxes, but also to the conversion of taxes in kind into money taxes.[^3.55] In Asia, on the other hand, state taxes consist chiefly of rents payable in kind, and this fact depends on conditions of production that are reproduced with the regularity of natural phenomena. And this mode of payment tends in its turn to maintain the ancient form of production. It is one of the secrets of the survival of the Ottoman Empire. If the foreign trade forced upon Japan by Europeans should lead to money rents replacing rents in kind, it will be all up with the model agriculture of that country. The narrow economic conditions under which that agriculture is carried on will be swept away.

[^3.54]: “The course of trade being thus turned, from exchanging of goods for goods, or delivering and taking, to selling and paying, all the bargains ... are now stated upon the foot of a Price in money.” (“An Essay upon Publick Credit.” 3rd Ed. London, 1710, p. 8.)

[^3.55]: “L’argent ... est devenu le bourreau de toutes choses.” Finance is the “alambic, qui a fait évaporer une quantité effroyable de biens et de denrées pour faire ce fatal précis.” “L’argent déclare la guerre à tout le genre humain.” [“Money ... has become the executioner of all things.” Finance is the “still that has boiled away a frightful quantity of goods and foodstuffs to make this fatal extract.” “Money declares war on the whole human race.”] (Boisguillebert: “Dissertation sur la nature des richesses, de l’argent et des tributs.” Edit. Daire. Economistes financiers. Paris, 1843, t. i., pp. 413, 419, 417.)

<!-- ch03-p091 -->
In every country, certain days of the year become, by habit, recognized settling days for various large payments that recur. Apart from other turns in the wheel of reproduction, these dates depend on conditions closely connected with the seasons. They also govern the dates for payments that have no direct connection with the circulation of commodities, such as taxes, rents, and so on. The quantity of money needed for the payments falling due on those dates all over the country causes periodic, though merely superficial, disturbances in the economy of the medium of payment.[^3.56]

[^3.56]: “On Whitsuntide [Pentecost], 1824,” says Mr. Craig before the Commons’ Committee of 1826, “there was such an immense demand for notes upon the banks of Edinburgh, that by 11 o’clock they had not a note left in their custody. They sent round to all the different banks to borrow, but could not get them, and many of the transactions were adjusted by slips of paper only; yet by three o’clock the whole of the notes were returned into the banks from which they had issued! It was a mere transfer from hand to hand. “Although the average effective circulation of bank-notes in Scotland is less than three millions sterling, yet on certain pay days in the year, every single note in the possession of the bankers, amounting in the whole to about £7,000,000, is called into activity. On these occasions the notes have a single and specific function to perform, and so soon as they have performed it, they flow back into the various banks from which they issued. (See John Fullarton, “Regulation of Currencies.” Lond. 1845, p. 86, note.) By way of explanation, it should be said that in Scotland, at the time of Fullarton’s work, deposits were withdrawn with notes, not with checks.

<!-- ch03-p092 -->
From the law of the rapidity of currency of the means of payment, it follows that the quantity of means of payment required for all periodic payments, whatever their source, is in inverse[^3.57] proportion to the length of their periods.[^3.58]

[^3.57]: *Note by the Institute of Marxism-Leninism in the Russian edition:* Apparently a slip of the pen. When the author wrote *inverse*, he evidently meant *direct*.

[^3.58]: To the question, “If there were occasion to raise 40 millions p. a. [per year], whether the same 6 millions (gold) ... would suffice for such revolutions and circulations thereof, as trade requires,” Petty replies in his usual masterly way, “I answer yes: for the expense being 40 millions, if the revolutions were in such short circles, viz., weekly, as happens among poor artisans and labourers, who receive and pay every Saturday, then 40/52 parts of 1 million of money would answer these ends, but if the circles be quarterly, according to our custom of paying rent, and gathering taxes, then 10 millions were requisite. Wherefore, supposing payments in general to be of a mixed circle between one week and 13, then add 10 millions to 40/52, the half of which will be 5½, so as if we have 5½ millions we have enough.” (William Petty: “Political Anatomy of Ireland.” 1672, Edit.: London 1691, pp. 13, 14.)

<!-- ch03-p093 -->
As money develops into a medium of payment, it becomes necessary to accumulate money against the dates fixed for paying the sums owed. Hoarding, as a distinct way of getting rich, vanishes as civil society progresses, while the formation of reserves of the means of payment grows with that progress.

#### C. Universal Money

<!-- ch03-p094 -->
When money leaves the home sphere of circulation, it strips off the local costumes it wears there: those of a standard of price, of coin, of tokens, and of a symbol of value. It goes back to its original form of bullion. In trade between the markets of the world, the value of commodities is expressed in a way that is recognized everywhere. So in these cases their independent form of value also confronts them in the shape of world money (gold and silver used as money between nations). Only in the markets of the world does money take on, to the full extent, the character of the commodity whose bodily form is also the direct social incarnation of abstract human labor. In this sphere, the real way money exists fully matches its ideal concept.

<!-- ch03-p095 -->
Within the sphere of home circulation, there can be only one commodity that becomes money by serving as the measure of value. In the markets of the world, a double measure of value rules: gold and silver.[^3.59]

[^3.59]: Hence the absurdity of every law that orders the banks of a country to form their reserves only of the precious metal that circulates at home. The “pleasant difficulties” that the Bank of England created for itself in this way are well known. On the great epochs in the history of the changes in the relative value of gold and silver, see Karl Marx, cited above, p. 136 and following. Sir Robert Peel, with his Bank Act of 1844, tried to get around the difficulty by allowing the Bank of England to issue notes against silver bullion, on condition that the reserve of silver should never exceed more than one-fourth of the reserve of gold. For that purpose, the value of silver was to be estimated at its price in the London market.

    *Added in the 4th German edition. —* [We find ourselves once more in a period of serious change in the relative values of gold and silver. About 25 years ago the ratio expressing the relative value of gold and silver was 15-1/2:1; now it is approximately 22:1, and silver is still falling steadily against gold. This is essentially the result of a revolution in the mode of production of both metals. Formerly gold was obtained almost entirely by washing it out of gold-bearing alluvial deposits, which are products of the weathering of gold-bearing rocks. Now this method has become inadequate. It has been pushed into the background by the processing of the quartz lodes themselves, a way of extraction that used to be only of secondary importance, although the ancients knew it well (Diodorus, III, 12-14) (Diodor’s v. Sicilien “Historische Bibliothek,” book III, 12-14. Stuttgart 1828, pp. 258-261). Moreover, not only were huge new silver deposits discovered in North America, in the western part of the Rocky Mountains, but these and the Mexican silver mines were really opened up by the building of railways. The railways made it possible to ship modern machinery and fuel, and so to mine silver on a very large scale at a low cost. However, there is a great difference in the way the two metals occur in the quartz lodes. The gold is mostly native (found as pure metal), but scattered through the quartz in tiny quantities. So the whole mass of the vein must be crushed, and the gold either washed out or extracted with mercury. Often 1,000,000 grams of quartz barely yield 1-3, and very seldom 30-60, grams of gold. Silver is seldom found native. But it occurs in special quartz that can be separated from the lode fairly easily and mostly contains 40-90% silver; or it is contained, in smaller quantities, in copper, lead and other ores that are worth working in themselves. From this alone it is clear that the labor spent on producing gold is rather increasing, while the labor spent on producing silver has decidedly decreased. This quite naturally explains the drop in the value of silver. This fall in value would show itself in a still greater fall in price, if the price of silver were not pegged even today by artificial means. But America’s rich silver deposits have so far barely been tapped, and so the prospects are that the value of this metal will keep on dropping for rather a long time to come. A still greater contributing factor here is the relative decrease in the need for silver for articles of general use and for luxuries, that is, its replacement by plated goods, aluminum, etc. From this one may judge how utopian the bimetallist idea is that compulsory international quotation will raise silver back to the old value ratio of 1:15-1/2. It is more likely that silver will lose its function as money more and more in the markets of the world. — *F E.*]

<!-- ch03-p096 -->
World money serves as the universal means of payment, as the universal means of purchase, and as the universally recognized embodiment of all wealth. Its chief function is as a means of payment in settling international balances. Hence the watchword of the mercantilists: balance of trade.[^3.60] Gold and silver serve as international means of purchase chiefly, and necessarily, in those periods when the usual balance in the exchange of products between different nations is suddenly upset. And lastly, world money serves as the universally recognized embodiment of social wealth whenever the question is not one of buying or paying, but of transferring wealth from one country to another. It does so whenever this transfer cannot be made in the form of commodities, either because of special conditions in the markets or because of the very purpose the transfer is meant to serve.[^3.61]

[^3.60]: Even the opponents of the mercantile system entirely misunderstood the functions of world money. (The mercantile system regarded the settlement of trade surpluses in gold and silver as the aim of international trade.) I have shown, using the example of Ricardo, how their false idea of the laws that regulate the quantity of the medium of circulation is reflected in their equally false idea of the international movement of the precious metals (cited above, pp. 150 and following). His mistaken dogma: “An unfavourable balance of trade never arises but from a redundant currency.... The exportation of the coin is caused by its cheapness, and is not the effect, but the cause of an unfavourable balance,” already occurs in Barbon: “The Balance of Trade, if there be one, is not the cause of sending away the money out of a nation; but that proceeds from the difference of the value of bullion in every country.” (N. Barbon; cited above, pp. 59, 60.) MacCulloch, in “The Literature of Political Economy, a classified catalogue, Lond. 1845,” praises Barbon for anticipating this, but prudently passes over the naïve forms in which Barbon dresses up the absurd assumption on which the “currency principle” is based. The lack of real criticism, and even of honesty, in that catalogue reaches its peak in the sections on the history of the theory of money. The reason is that in this part of the work MacCulloch is flattering Lord Overstone, whom he calls “facile princeps argentanorum” [easily the first of the money-men].

[^3.61]: For example, in subsidies, and in money loans for waging wars or for enabling banks to resume cash payments, etc., it may be the money form of value, and no other, that is wanted.

<!-- ch03-p097 -->
Just as every country needs a reserve of money for its home circulation, it also needs one for external circulation in the markets of the world. So the functions of hoards arise partly out of money’s function as the medium of home circulation and home payments, and partly out of its function as world money.[^3.62] For this last function, the genuine money-commodity, actual gold and silver, is necessary. That is why Sir James Steuart, to distinguish gold and silver from their purely local substitutes, calls them “money of the world.”

[^3.62]: “I would desire, indeed, no more convincing evidence of the competency of the machinery of the hoards in specie-paying [coin-paying] countries to perform every necessary office of international adjustment, without any sensible aid from the general circulation, than the facility with which France, when but just recovering from the shock of a destructive foreign invasion, completed within the space of 27 months the payment of her forced contribution of nearly 20 millions to the allied powers, and a considerable proportion of the sum in specie, without any perceptible contraction or derangement of her domestic currency, or even any alarming fluctuation of her exchanges.” (Fullerton, cited above, p. 141.) [*Added in the 4th German edition. —* We have a still more striking example in the ease with which the same France was able in 1871-73 to pay off, within 30 months, a forced contribution more than ten times as great, a considerable part of it likewise in specie. *— F. E.*]

<!-- ch03-p098 -->
The stream of gold and silver flows in two directions. On the one hand, it spreads out from its sources over all the markets of the world. There it is absorbed, to various extents, into the different national spheres of circulation: it fills the channels of currency, replaces worn gold and silver coins, supplies the material for luxury articles, and hardens into hoards.[^3.63] This first current is set going by the countries that exchange their labor, realized in commodities, for the labor embodied in the precious metals by the gold- and silver-producing countries. On the other hand, gold and silver flow continually back and forth between the different national spheres of circulation, a current whose motion depends on the ceaseless ups and downs of the exchange rate.[^3.64]

[^3.63]: “L’argent se partage entre les nations relativement au besoin qu’elles en ont ... étant toujours attiré par les productions.” [“Money is shared out among the nations according to their need for it ... since it is always drawn by the products”] (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 916.) “The mines which are continually giving gold and silver, do give sufficient to supply such a needful balance to every nation.” (J. Vanderlint, cited above, p. 40.)

[^3.64]: “Exchanges rise and fall every week, and at some particular times in the year run high against a nation, and at other times run as high on the contrary.” (N. Barbon, cited above, p. 39)

<!-- ch03-p099 -->
Countries in which the bourgeois form of production is developed to a certain extent limit the hoards concentrated in the strong rooms of the banks to the minimum needed to carry out their particular functions properly.[^3.65] Whenever these hoards are strikingly above their average level, this is, with some exceptions, a sign of stagnation in the circulation of commodities, of a break in the even flow of their metamorphoses.[^3.66]

[^3.65]: These various functions are liable to come into dangerous conflict with one another whenever gold and silver also have to serve as a fund for converting bank-notes.

[^3.66]: “What money is more than of absolute necessity for a Home Trade, is dead stock ... and brings no profit to that country it’s kept in, but as it is transported in trade, as well as imported.” (John Bellers, “Essays,” p. 13.) “What if we have too much coin? We may melt down the heaviest and turn it into the splendour of plate, vessels or utensils of gold or silver, or send it out as a commodity, where the same is wanted or desired; or let it out at interest, where interest is high.” (W. Petty: “Quantulumcunque,” p. 39.) “Money is but the fat of the Body Politick, whereof too much doth as often hinder its agility, as too little makes it sick ... as fat lubricates the motion of the muscles, feeds in want of victuals [food], fills up the uneven cavities, and beautifies the body; so doth money in the state quicken its action, feeds from abroad in time of dearth [scarcity] at home, evens accounts ... and beautifies the whole; altho more especially the particular persons that have it in plenty.” (W. Petty, “Political Anatomy of Ireland,” p. 14.)

# Part 2: Transformation of Money into Capital

## Chapter 4: The General Formula for Capital

<!-- ch04-p001 -->
The circulation of commodities is the starting point of capital. (Commodities are things produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer’s own use. Their circulation is their exchange through money: selling and buying.) The production of commodities, their circulation, and that more developed form of their circulation called trade, together form the historical groundwork from which capital rises. The modern history of capital dates from the creation, in the 16th century, of a trade and a market that embraced the whole world.

<!-- ch04-p002 -->
If we set aside the material substance of the circulation of commodities, that is, the exchange of the various use-values (the usefulness of things: what they can be used for, which comes from their physical properties), and look only at the economic forms that this process of circulation produces, we find that its final result is money. This final product of the circulation of commodities is the first form in which capital appears.

<!-- ch04-p003 -->
Historically, capital, as opposed to landed property, invariably takes the form of money at first. It appears as moneyed wealth, as the capital of the merchant and of the usurer.[^4.1] But we do not need to look back to the origin of capital to discover that capital’s first form of appearance is money. We can see it daily, before our very eyes. Even in our own day, all new capital first comes on the stage, that is, on the market, whether the market of commodities, of labor, or of money, in the shape of money: money that has to be turned into capital by a definite process.

[^4.1]: The contrast between the power conferred by landed property, which rests on personal relations of domination and servitude, and the impersonal power given by money, is well expressed by two French proverbs: “Nulle terre sans seigneur,” and “L’argent n’a pas de maître” [“No land without its lord,” and “Money has no master”].

<!-- ch04-p004 -->
The first difference we notice between money that is only money and money that is capital is nothing more than a difference in their form of circulation.

<!-- ch04-p005 -->
The simplest form of the circulation of commodities is C—M—C: commodities are turned into money, and the money is changed back into commodities. In other words, selling in order to buy. But alongside this form we find another, specifically different form: M—C—M. Here money is turned into commodities, and the commodities are changed back into money. In other words, buying in order to sell. Money that circulates in this second way is thereby transformed into capital, becomes capital, and is already potentially capital.

<!-- ch04-p006 -->
Now let us look a little more closely at the circuit M—C—M. Like the other circuit, it consists of two opposed phases. In the first phase, M—C, the purchase, the money is changed into a commodity. In the second phase, C—M, the sale, the commodity is changed back into money. These two phases combined make up a single movement. In it, money is exchanged for a commodity, and the same commodity is exchanged again for money. A commodity is bought in order to be sold. Or, if we ignore the difference in form between buying and selling, a commodity is bought with money, and then money is bought with a commodity.[^4.2] The result, in which the phases of the process vanish, is the exchange of money for money, M—M. If I buy 2,000 lbs. of cotton for £100, and resell the 2,000 lbs. of cotton for £110, I have in fact exchanged £100 for £110, money for money.

[^4.2]: “Avec de l’argent on achète des marchandises et avec des marchandises on achète de l’argent.” [“With money one buys commodities, and with commodities one buys money.”] (Mercier de la Rivière: “L’ordre naturel et essentiel des sociétés politiques,” p. 543.)

<!-- ch04-p007 -->
Now clearly the circuit M—C—M would be absurd and meaningless if the intention were to exchange two equal sums of money by this means, £100 for £100. The miser’s plan would be far simpler and surer: he holds on to his £100 instead of exposing it to the dangers of circulation. And yet, whether the merchant who paid £100 for his cotton sells it for £110, or lets it go for £100, or even for £50, his money has in any case gone through a characteristic and original movement.
