This movement is quite different in kind from the one money goes through in the hands of the peasant who sells grain and, with the money thus set free, buys clothes. We must therefore first examine the features that distinguish the forms of the circuits M—C—M and C—M—C. In doing this, the real difference that lies beneath the mere difference of form will reveal itself.

<!-- ch04-p008 -->
Let us see, first, what the two forms have in common.

<!-- ch04-p009 -->
Both circuits can be broken down into the same two opposed phases: C—M, a sale, and M—C, a purchase. In each of these phases the same material elements confront one another, a commodity and money, and so do the same economic characters in the drama, a buyer and a seller. Each circuit is the unity of the same two opposed phases. In each case this unity is brought about through the intervention of three contracting parties: one only sells, another only buys, and the third both buys and sells.

<!-- ch04-p010 -->
But what first and foremost distinguishes the circuit C—M—C from the circuit M—C—M is that the two phases come in reverse order. The simple circulation of commodities begins with a sale and ends with a purchase, while the circulation of money as capital begins with a purchase and ends with a sale. In the one case both the starting point and the goal are commodities; in the other, they are money. In the first form, the intervention of money brings about the movement; in the second, the intervention of a commodity does.

<!-- ch04-p011 -->
In the circulation C—M—C, the money is in the end converted into a commodity that serves as a use-value; it is spent once and for all. In the reversed form, M—C—M, on the contrary, the buyer lays out money so that, as a seller, he may get money back. By buying his commodity he throws money into circulation, in order to withdraw it again by selling the same commodity. He lets the money go, but only with the sly intention of getting it back again. So the money is not spent; it is merely advanced.[^4.3]

[^4.3]: “When a thing is bought in order to be sold again, the sum employed is called money advanced; when it is bought not to be sold, it may be said to be expended.” — (James Steuart: “Works,” etc. Edited by Gen. Sir James Steuart, his son. London, 1805, V. I., p. 274.)

<!-- ch04-p012 -->
In the circuit C—M—C, the same piece of money changes places twice. The seller gets it from the buyer and pays it out to another seller. The complete circulation begins when money is received for commodities and ends when money is paid for commodities. It is just the opposite in the circuit M—C—M. Here it is not the piece of money that changes places twice, but the commodity. The buyer takes it from the seller’s hands and passes it into the hands of another buyer. In the simple circulation of commodities, the double change of place of the same piece of money moves it from one hand into another. In just the same way, here the double change of place of the same commodity brings about the flowing back of the money to its point of departure.

<!-- ch04-p013 -->
This flowing back does not depend on the commodity being sold for more than was paid for it. That circumstance affects only the amount of money that comes back. The flowing back itself takes place as soon as the purchased commodity is resold, in other words, as soon as the circuit M—C—M is completed. So here we have a tangible difference between the circulation of money as capital and its circulation as mere money.

<!-- ch04-p014 -->
The circuit C—M—C comes completely to an end as soon as the money brought in by selling one commodity is withdrawn again by buying another.

<!-- ch04-p015 -->
If money nevertheless flows back to its starting point afterward, this can only happen through a renewal or repetition of the operation. If I sell a quarter of grain for £3, and with this £3 buy clothes, the money, as far as I am concerned, is spent and done with. It belongs to the clothes merchant. If I now sell a second quarter of grain, money does flow back to me, but not as a sequel to the first transaction; it flows back because that transaction is repeated. The money leaves me again as soon as I complete this second transaction with a new purchase. Therefore, in the circuit C—M—C, the spending of money has nothing to do with its flowing back. In M—C—M, on the other hand, the flowing back of the money is conditioned by the very way it is spent. Without this flowing back, the operation fails, or the process is interrupted and incomplete, because its complementary and final phase, the sale, is missing.

<!-- ch04-p016 -->
The circuit C—M—C starts with one commodity and finishes with another, which falls out of circulation and into consumption. Consumption, the satisfaction of wants, in one word, use-value, is its end and aim. The circuit M—C—M, on the contrary, begins with money and ends with money. Its leading motive, and the goal that draws it on, is therefore mere exchange-value (the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for).

<!-- ch04-p017 -->
In the simple circulation of commodities, the two extremes of the circuit have the same economic form. They are both commodities, and commodities of equal value (value being what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time). But they are also use-values of different qualities, for example grain and clothes. Here the basis of the movement is the exchange of products, of the different materials in which the labor of society is embodied. It is otherwise in the circulation M—C—M, which at first sight seems purposeless, because it merely repeats the same thing. Both extremes have the same economic form. They are both money, and so they are not use-values of different qualities; for money is only the converted form of commodities, in which their particular use-values vanish. To exchange £100 for cotton, and then this same cotton again for £100, is merely a roundabout way of exchanging money for money, the same for the same. It seems to be an operation just as purposeless as it is absurd.[^4.4] One sum of money can be told apart from another only by its amount. So the character and tendency of the process M—C—M come not from any difference in quality between its extremes, since both are money, but solely from their difference in quantity. More money is withdrawn from circulation at the finish than was thrown into it at the start. The cotton that was bought for £100 is perhaps resold for £100 + £10, or £110. The exact form of this process is therefore M—C—M', where M' = M + ∆ M = the original sum advanced, plus an increment. I call this increment, or excess over the original value, “surplus-value.” So the value originally advanced not only stays intact while in circulation, but adds a surplus-value to itself, or expands itself. It is this movement that turns it into capital.

[^4.4]: “On n’échange pas de l’argent contre de l’argent” [“One does not exchange money for money”], says Mercier de la Rivière to the Mercantilists (cited above, p. 486). A work that deals expressly with “trade” and “speculation” contains the following: “All trade consists in the exchange of things of different kinds; and the advantage” (to the merchant?) “arises out of this difference. To exchange a pound of bread against a pound of bread ... would be attended with no advantage; ... Hence trade is advantageously contrasted with gambling, which consists in a mere exchange of money for money.” (Th. Corbet, “An Inquiry into the Causes and Modes of the Wealth of Individuals; or the Principles of Trade and Speculation Explained.” London, 1841, p. 5.) Corbet does not see that M—M, the exchange of money for money, is the characteristic form of circulation not only of merchants’ capital but of all capital. Yet at least he admits that this form is common to gambling and to one kind of trade, namely speculation. But then along comes MacCulloch and makes out that to buy in order to sell is to speculate, and so the difference between Speculation and Trade vanishes. “Every transaction in which an individual buys produce in order to sell it again, is, in fact, a speculation.” (MacCulloch: “A Dictionary Practical, &c., of Commerce.” London, 1847, p. 1009.) With much more naïveté, Pinto, the Pindar of the Amsterdam Stock Exchange, remarks: “Le commerce est un jeu: (taken from Locke) et ce n’est pas avec des gueux qu’on peut gagner. Si l’on gagnait longtemps en tout avec tous, il faudrait rendre de bon accord les plus grandes parties du profit pour recommencer le jeu.” [“Trade is a game, and it is not from beggars that one can win. If one kept on winning everything from everyone for a long time, the greater part of the profit would have to be given back by common consent, in order to start the game again.”] (Pinto: “Traité de la Circulation et du Crédit.” Amsterdam, 1771. p. 231,)

<!-- ch04-p018 -->
Of course, it is also possible that in C—M—C the two extremes C-C, say grain and clothes, may represent different quantities of value. The farmer may sell his grain above its value, or may buy the clothes below their value. On the other hand, he may “be done” (cheated) by the clothes merchant. Yet in the form of circulation we are now considering, such differences in value are purely accidental. The fact that the grain and the clothes are equivalents does not rob the process of all meaning, as it does in M—C—M. Rather, the equality of their values is a necessary condition for its normal course.

<!-- ch04-p019 -->
The repetition or renewal of the act of selling in order to buy is kept within bounds by the very aim it pursues, namely consumption, or the satisfaction of definite wants, an aim that lies entirely outside the sphere of circulation. But when we buy in order to sell, we, on the contrary, begin and end with the same thing, money, exchange-value; and so the movement becomes endless. No doubt M becomes M + ∆M, £100 become £110. But looked at only in terms of quality, £110 are the same as £100, namely money. And looked at in terms of quantity, £110 is, like £100, a sum of definite and limited value. If the £110 are now spent as money, they stop playing their part. They are no longer capital. Withdrawn from circulation, they become petrified into a hoard, and even if they stayed in that state until doomsday, not a single farthing would be added to them. So, if the expansion of value is once aimed at, there is just the same incentive to increase the value of the £110 as of the £100. For both are only limited expressions of exchange-value, and so both have the same calling: to come as near as possible to absolute wealth by growing in quantity. For a moment, indeed, the value originally advanced, the £100, can be told apart from the surplus-value of £10 that is added to it during circulation; but the distinction vanishes at once. At the end of the process, we do not receive the original £100 in one hand and the surplus-value of £10 in the other. We simply get a value of £110, which is in exactly the same condition, and just as fit to begin the expanding process, as the original £100 was. Money ends the movement only to begin it again.[^4.5] Therefore the final result of every separate circuit, in which a purchase and the sale that follows it are completed, forms of itself the starting point of a new circuit. The simple circulation of commodities, selling in order to buy, is a means of carrying out a purpose unconnected with circulation, namely, the acquiring of use-values, the satisfaction of wants. The circulation of money as capital, on the contrary, is an end in itself, for the expansion of value takes place only within this constantly renewed movement. The circulation of capital therefore has no limits.[^4.6]

[^4.5]: “Capital is divisible ... into the original capital and the profit, the increment to the capital ... although in practice this profit is immediately turned into capital, and set in motion with the original.” (F. Engels, “Umrisse zu einer Kritik der Nationalökonomie, in: Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, herausgegeben von Arnold Ruge und Karl Marx.” Paris, 1844, p. 99.)

[^4.6]: Aristotle contrasts Œconomic with Chrematistic. He starts from Œconomic. Insofar as it is the art of making a living, it is limited to obtaining the articles that are necessary for existence and useful either to a household or to the state. “True wealth (ὁ ἀληθινὸς πλοῦτος) consists of such values in use; for the quantity of possessions of this kind, capable of making life pleasant, is not unlimited. There is, however, a second mode of acquiring things, to which we may by preference and with correctness give the name of Chrematistic, and in this case there appear to be no limits to riches and possessions. Trade (ἡ καπηλικὴ literally means retail trade, and Aristotle takes this kind because use-values predominate in it) does not in its nature belong to Chrematistic, for here the exchange has reference only to what is necessary to themselves (the buyer or seller).” Therefore, as he goes on to show, the original form of trade was barter, but as barter spread, the need for money arose. Once money was discovered, barter necessarily developed into καπηλικὴ, into trading in commodities, and this in turn, against its original tendency, grew into Chrematistic, into the art of making money. Now Chrematistic differs from Œconomic in this way: “in the case of Chrematistic circulation is the source of riches (ποιητικὴ χρημάτων ... διὰ χρημάτων μεταβολῆς). And it appears to revolve about money, for money is the beginning and end of this kind of exchange (τὸ γὰρ νόμισμα στοιχεῖον καὶ πέρας τῆς ἀλλαγῆς ἐστίν). Therefore also riches, such as Chrematistic strives for, are unlimited. Just as every art that is not a means to an end, but an end in itself, has no limit to its aims, because it seeks constantly to approach nearer and nearer to that end, while those arts that pursue means to an end, are not boundless, since the goal itself imposes a limit upon them, so with Chrematistic, there are no bounds to its aims, these aims being absolute wealth. Œconomic not Chrematistic has a limit ... the object of the former is something different from money, of the latter the augmentation of money.... By confounding these two forms, which overlap each other, some people have been led to look upon the preservation and increase of money ad infinitum [without end] as the end and aim of Œconomic.” (Aristoteles, De Rep. edit. Bekker, lib. I., c. 8, 9. passim.)

<!-- ch04-p020 -->
As the conscious representative of this movement, the owner of money becomes a capitalist. His person, or rather his pocket, is the point from which the money starts and to which it returns. The expansion of value is the objective basis or mainspring of the circulation M—C—M, and it becomes his subjective aim. Only insofar as the appropriation of more and more wealth in the abstract becomes the sole motive of his operations does he function as a capitalist, that is, as capital personified and endowed with consciousness and a will. Use-values must therefore never be looked upon as the real aim of the capitalist;[^4.7] nor must the profit on any single transaction. The restless, never-ending process of profit-making is all he aims at.[^4.8] This boundless greed for riches, this passionate chase after exchange-value,[^4.9] is common to the capitalist and the miser. But while the miser is merely a capitalist gone mad, the capitalist is a rational miser. The miser strives after the never-ending increase of exchange-value by seeking to save[^4.10] his money from circulation. The shrewder capitalist achieves it by constantly throwing his money afresh into circulation.[^4.11]

[^4.7]: “Commodities (here used in the sense of use-values) are not the terminating object of the trading capitalist, money is his terminating object.” (Th. Chalmers, On Pol. Econ. &c.*,* 2nd Ed., Glasgow, 1832, pp. 165, 166.)

[^4.8]: “Il mercante non conta quasi per niente il lucro fatto, ma mira sempre al futuro.” [“The merchant counts the gain he has made as almost nothing, but always looks to the future.”] (A. Genovesi, Lezioni di Economia Civile (1765), Custodi’s edit. of Italian Economists. Parte Moderna t. viii, p. 139.)

[^4.9]: “The inextinguishable passion for gain, the auri sacra fames [accursed hunger for gold], will always lead capitalists.” (MacCulloch: “The Principles of Polit. Econ.” London, 1830, p. 179.) This view, of course, does not stop the same MacCulloch and others of his kind, when they get into theoretical difficulties, for example over the question of over-production, from turning the same capitalist into a moral citizen whose sole concern is for use-values, and who even develops an insatiable hunger for boots, hats, eggs, calico, and other extremely familiar sorts of use-values.

[^4.10]: Σὠξειν [to save, to keep safe] is a characteristic Greek expression for hoarding. In the same way, in English “to save” has the same two meanings: sauver [to rescue] and épargner [to put by, to spare].

[^4.11]: “Questo infinito che le cose non hanno in progresso, hanno in giro.” [“That infinity which things do not have in progress, they have in circulation.”] (Galiani.)

<!-- ch04-p021 -->
In simple circulation, the value of commodities takes on an independent form, that is, the money form (the form of value in which one commodity, gold, has become the universal equivalent). This form serves only one purpose, namely, their exchange, and it vanishes in the final result of the movement. In the circulation M—C—M, on the other hand, both the money and the commodity represent only different modes of existence of value itself: the money its general mode, and the commodity its particular, or, so to speak, disguised mode.[^4.12] Value is constantly changing from one form to the other without being lost in the process, and so it takes on an automatically active character. If we now take in turn each of the two different forms that self-expanding value assumes, one after the other, in the course of its life, we arrive at these two propositions: Capital is money: Capital is commodities.[^4.13] In truth, however, value is here the active factor in a process. In this process, while it constantly takes the form of money and of commodities in turn, it at the same time changes in magnitude: it differentiates itself by throwing off surplus-value from itself. In other words, the original value expands spontaneously. For the movement in the course of which it adds surplus-value is its own movement, and so its expansion is automatic expansion. Because it is value, it has acquired the occult quality of being able to add value to itself. It brings forth living offspring, or, at the least, lays golden eggs.

[^4.12]: “Ce n’est pas la matière qui fait le capital, mais la valeur de ces matières.” [“It is not matter that makes capital, but the value of those materials.”] (J. B. Say: “Traité d’Econ. Polit.” 3ème éd. Paris, 1817, t. II., p. 429.)

[^4.13]: “Currency (!) employed in producing articles... is capital.” (Macleod: “The Theory and Practice of Banking.” London, 1855, v. 1, ch. i, p. 55.) “Capital is commodities.” (James Mill: “Elements of Pol. Econ.” London, 1821, p. 74.)

<!-- ch04-p022 -->
Value, then, is the active factor in such a process. At one time it takes the form of money, at another that of commodities, but through all these changes it preserves itself and expands. For this reason it needs some independent form by which its identity can be established at any time. And it has this form only in the shape of money. It is in the form of money that value begins and ends, and begins again, every act of its own spontaneous generation. It began as £100, it is now £110, and so on. But the money itself is only one of the two forms of value. Unless it takes the form of some commodity, it does not become capital. Here there is no antagonism between the money and commodities, as there is in the case of hoarding. The capitalist knows that all commodities, however shabby they may look, or however badly they may smell, are in faith and in truth money, inwardly circumcised Jews, and, what is more, a wonderful means of making more money out of money.

<!-- ch04-p023 -->
In simple circulation, C—M—C, the value of commodities attained at most a form independent of their use-values, that is, the form of money. But now, in the circulation M—C—M, or the circulation of capital, that same value suddenly presents itself as an independent substance, endowed with a motion of its own, passing through a life-process of its own, in which money and commodities are mere forms that it takes on and casts off in turn. Indeed, more than that: instead of simply representing the relations of commodities, it now enters, so to speak, into private relations with itself. It differentiates itself as original value from itself as surplus-value, as the father differentiates himself from himself as the son, yet both are one and of one age. For only by the surplus-value of £10 does the £100 originally advanced become capital. And as soon as this happens, as soon as the son is begotten, and through the son the father, their difference vanishes, and they become one again, £110.

<!-- ch04-p024 -->
So value now becomes value in process, money in process, and, as such, capital. It comes out of circulation, enters it again, preserves and multiplies itself within its circuit, comes back out of it increased in size, and begins the same round over and over again.[^4.14] M—M', money that begets money: such is the description of Capital from the mouths of its first interpreters, the Mercantilists.

[^4.14]: Capital: “portion fructifiante de la richesse accumulée... valeur permanente, multipliante.” [fruit-bearing portion of accumulated wealth ... permanent, multiplying value.] (Sismondi: “Nouveaux Principes d’Econ. Polit.,” t. i., p. 88, 89.)

<!-- ch04-p025 -->
Buying in order to sell, or, more exactly, buying in order to sell dearer, M—C—M', certainly appears to be a form peculiar to only one kind of capital, namely, merchants’ capital. But industrial capital too is money that is changed into commodities and, by the sale of these commodities, turned back into more money. The events that take place outside the sphere of circulation, in the interval between the buying and the selling, do not affect the form of this movement. Lastly, in the case of interest-bearing capital, the circulation M—C—M' appears shortened. We have its result without the stage in between, in the form M—M', “en style lapidaire” [in the style of an inscription], so to speak: money that is worth more money, value that is greater than itself.

<!-- ch04-p026 -->
M—C—M' is therefore in reality the general formula of capital as it appears at first sight within the sphere of circulation.

## Chapter 5: Contradictions in the General Formula of Capital

<!-- ch05-p001 -->
When money becomes capital (value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger), circulation (the exchange of commodities through money: selling and buying) takes a form that goes against all the laws we have investigated so far concerning the nature of commodities, value and money, and even concerning circulation itself. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer’s own use. Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) What sets this form apart from the simple circulation of commodities is that the two opposed processes, sale and purchase, come in reverse order. How can this purely formal difference between these processes change their character, as if by magic?

<!-- ch05-p002 -->
But that is not all. This reversal does not exist at all for two of the three persons who do business together. As a capitalist, I buy commodities from A and sell them again to B. But as a simple owner of commodities, I sell them to B and then buy new ones from A. A and B see no difference between the two sets of transactions. They are merely buyers or sellers. And each time I meet them, I am a mere owner of either money or commodities, a buyer or a seller. What is more, in both sets of transactions I face A only as a buyer and B only as a seller: the one only as money, the other only as commodities. I face neither of them as capital or as a capitalist, or as the representative of anything that is more than money or commodities, or that can produce any effect beyond what money and commodities can. For me, the purchase from A and the sale to B are parts of a series. But the connection between the two acts exists for me alone. A does not bother himself about my transaction with B, nor does B about my business with A. And if I offered to explain to them how meritorious I had been in reversing the order of the two acts, they would probably point out that I was mistaken about that order. They would say that the whole transaction did not begin with a purchase and end with a sale, but, on the contrary, began with a sale and ended with a purchase. In truth, my first act, the purchase, was a sale from A’s standpoint, and my second act, the sale, was a purchase from B’s standpoint. Not content with that, A and B would declare that the whole series was superfluous and nothing but Hokus Pokus, and that in future A would buy directly from B, and B sell directly to A. So the whole transaction would shrink to a single act: an isolated phase in the ordinary circulation of commodities, with no phase to complete it, a mere sale from A’s point of view and a mere purchase from B’s. Reversing the order, therefore, does not take us outside the sphere of the simple circulation of commodities. We must rather look to see whether there is anything in this simple circulation that allows the value entering circulation to expand, and so allows surplus-value to be created.

<!-- ch05-p003 -->
Let us take the process of circulation in a form in which it appears as a simple and direct exchange of commodities. This is always the case when two owners of commodities buy from each other, and on the settling day the amounts they owe each other are equal and cancel out. In this case the money is money of account. It serves to express the value of the commodities in their prices (a price is the money name of the value, that is, of the labor, embodied in a commodity), but it does not itself face them as hard cash. As far as use-values are concerned (a use-value is the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties), clearly both parties may gain some advantage. Both part with goods that, as use-values, are of no service to them, and receive others that they can use. And there may also be a further gain. A, who sells wine and buys grain, possibly produces more wine with a given labor-time than farmer B could. B, on the other hand, possibly produces more grain than wine-grower A could. So, for the same exchange-value (the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for), A may get more grain, and B more wine, than each would get without any exchange, by producing his own grain and wine. So with respect to use-value, there is good reason to say that “exchange is a transaction by which both sides gain.”[^5.1] It is different with exchange-value. “A man who has plenty of wine and no corn treats [negotiates] with a man who has plenty of corn and no wine; an exchange takes place between them of corn to the value of 50, for wine of the same value. This act produces no increase of exchange-value either for the one or the other; for each of them already possessed, before the exchange, a value equal to that which he acquired by means of that operation.”[^5.2] The result does not change if money is brought in between the commodities as a medium of circulation (money in its role of passing from hand to hand to carry out sales and purchases), so that the sale and the purchase become two separate acts.[^5.3] The value of a commodity is expressed in its price before the commodity goes into circulation. So that value is a precondition of circulation, not its result.[^5.4]

[^5.1]: “L’échange est une transaction admirable dans laquelle les deux contractants gagnent ‒ toujours (!)” [“Exchange is an admirable transaction in which the two contracting parties gain ‒ always (!)”] (Destutt de Tracy: “Traité de la Volonté et de ses effets.” Paris, 1826, p. 68.) This work later appeared as “Traité d’Econ. Polit.”

[^5.2]: “Mercier de la Rivière,” cited above, p. 544.

[^5.3]: “Que l’une de ces deux valeurs soit argent, ou qu’elles soient toutes deux marchandises usuelles, rien de plus indifférent en soi.” [“Whether one of these two values is money, or both are ordinary commodities, in itself nothing could matter less.”] (“Mercier de la Rivière,” cited above, p. 543.)

[^5.4]: “Ce ne sont pas les contractants qui prononcent sur la valeur; elle est décidée avant la convention.” [“It is not the parties to the contract who decide on the value; it is settled before the agreement.”] (Le Trosne, p. 906.)

<!-- ch05-p004 -->
Considered in the abstract, that is, apart from circumstances that do not follow directly from the laws of the simple circulation of commodities, an exchange contains nothing (if we leave aside the replacing of one use-value by another) but a metamorphosis, a mere change in the form of the commodity. The same exchange-value, that is, the same quantity of embodied social labor, stays in the hands of the owner of the commodity throughout: first in the shape of his own commodity, then in the form of the money he exchanged it for, and lastly in the shape of the commodity he buys with that money. This change of form does not imply a change in the magnitude of the value (the magnitude of value is how much value a commodity has, measured by the socially necessary labor-time needed to produce it). But the change that the value of the commodity goes through in this process is limited to a change in its money form. This form exists first as the price of the commodity offered for sale; then as an actual sum of money, which, however, was already expressed in the price; and lastly as the price of an equivalent commodity. Taken alone, this change of form no more implies a change in the quantity of value than changing a £5 note into sovereigns, half sovereigns and shillings does. So, to the extent that the circulation of commodities changes only the form of their values, and is free from disturbing influences, it must be the exchange of equivalents. Vulgar economics (economists who only describe and defend the surface appearances of the system, without investigating its real relations) knows little about the nature of value. Yet whenever it wishes to consider the phenomena of circulation in their pure form, it assumes that supply and demand are equal, which amounts to saying that their effect is nil. So if both buyer and seller may possibly gain something as regards the use-values exchanged, this is not the case as regards the exchange-values. Here we must rather say, “Where equality exists there can be no gain.”[^5.5] It is true that commodities may be sold at prices that deviate from their values. But these deviations must be regarded as breaches of the laws of the exchange of commodities,[^5.6] which in its normal state is an exchange of equivalents, and so is no method for increasing value.[^5.7]

[^5.5]: “Dove è egualità non è lucro.” [“Where there is equality there is no gain.”] (Galiani, “Della Moneta in Custodi, Parte Moderna,” t. iv., p. 244.)

[^5.6]: “L’échange devient désavantageux pour l’une des parties, lorsque quelque chose étrangère vient diminuer ou exagérer le prix; alors l’égalité est blessée, mais la lésion procède de cette cause et non de l’échange.” [“Exchange becomes unfavorable for one of the parties when something external comes to lower or raise the price; then equality is harmed, but the harm comes from that cause and not from the exchange.”] (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 904.)

[^5.7]: “L’échange est de sa nature un contrat d’égalité qui se fait de valeur pour valeur égale. Il n’est donc pas un moyen de s’enrichir, puisque l’on donne autant que l’on reçoit.” [“Exchange is by its nature a contract of equality, made value for equal value. So it is not a means of getting rich, since one gives as much as one receives.”] (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 903.)

<!-- ch05-p005 -->
So we see that behind every attempt to present the circulation of commodities as a source of surplus-value there lurks a mix-up, a confusing of use-value with exchange-value. For instance, Condillac says: “It is not true that on an exchange of commodities we give value for value. On the contrary, each of the two contracting parties in every case, gives a less for a greater value. ... If we really exchanged equal values, neither party could make a profit. And yet, they both gain, or ought to gain. Why? The value of a thing consists solely in its relation to our wants. What is more to the one is less to the other, and *vice versâ* [the other way round]. ... It is not to be assumed that we offer for sale articles required for our own consumption. ... We wish to part with a useless thing, in order to get one that we need; we want to give less for more. ... It was natural to think that, in an exchange, value was given for value, whenever each of the articles exchanged was of equal value with the same quantity of gold. ... But there is another point to be considered in our calculation. The question is, whether we both exchange something superfluous for something necessary.”[^5.8] We see in this passage how Condillac not only confuses use-value with exchange-value, but also, in a really childish way, assumes that in a society where the production of commodities is well developed, each producer produces his own means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live), and throws into circulation only what is left over beyond his own needs.[^5.9] Still, Condillac’s argument is often used by modern economists, especially when the point is to show that the exchange of commodities in its developed form, trade, produces surplus-value. For instance: “Commerce ... adds value to products, for the same products in the hands of consumers, are worth more than in the hands of producers, and it may strictly be considered an act of production.”[^5.10] But commodities are not paid for twice over, once for their use-value and again for their value. And though the use-value of a commodity is more useful to the buyer than to the seller, its money form is more useful to the seller. Would he otherwise sell it? So we might just as well say that the buyer performs “strictly an act of production” by turning stockings, for example, into money.

[^5.8]: Condillac: “Le Commerce et le Gouvernement” (1776). Edit. Daire et Molinari in the “Mélanges d’Econ. Polit.” Paris, 1847, pp. 267, 291.

[^5.9]: So Le Trosne rightly answers his friend Condillac as follows: “Dans une ... société formée il n’y a pas de surabondant en aucun genre.” [“In a ... developed society nothing of any kind is superfluous.”] At the same time he jokingly remarks: “If both the persons who exchange receive more to an equal amount, and part with less to an equal amount, they both get the same.” It is because Condillac has not the faintest idea of the nature of exchange-value that Herr Professor Wilhelm Roscher has chosen him as a fit person to vouch for the soundness of his own childish notions. See Roscher’s “Die Grundlagen der Nationalökonomie, Dritte Auflage,” 1858.

[^5.10]: S. P. Newman: “Elements of Polit. Econ.” Andover and New York, 1835, p. 175.

<!-- ch05-p006 -->
If commodities, or commodities and money, of equal exchange-value, and so equivalents, are exchanged, clearly no one takes more value out of circulation than he throws into it. No surplus-value is created. And in its normal form, the circulation of commodities requires the exchange of equivalents. But in actual practice, the process does not keep its normal form. So let us assume an exchange of non-equivalents.

<!-- ch05-p007 -->
In any case, the only people who visit the market for commodities are owners of commodities, and the power these persons exercise over each other is nothing other than the power of their commodities. The material variety of these commodities is the material incentive to exchange. It makes buyers and sellers dependent on one another, because none of them possesses the object of his own wants, and each holds in his hand the object of another’s wants. Besides these material differences between their use-values, there is only one other difference between commodities: the difference between their bodily form and the form into which they are changed by sale, the difference between commodities and money. And so the owners of commodities can be told apart only as sellers, who own commodities, and buyers, who own money.

<!-- ch05-p008 -->
Suppose, then, that by some inexplicable privilege the seller is able to sell his commodities above their value, what is worth 100 for 110, so that the price is raised nominally by 10%. The seller therefore pockets a surplus-value of 10. But after he has sold, he becomes a buyer. A third owner of commodities now comes to him as a seller, and in this capacity he too enjoys the privilege of selling his commodities 10% too dear. Our friend gained 10 as a seller only to lose it again as a buyer.[^5.11] The net result is that all owners of commodities sell their goods to one another at 10% above their value, which comes to exactly the same as if they sold them at their true value. Such a general and nominal rise in prices has the same effect as if values were expressed in weight of silver instead of in weight of gold. The nominal prices of commodities would rise, but the real relation between their values would stay unchanged.

[^5.11]: “By the augmentation of the nominal value of the produce... sellers not enriched... since what they gain as sellers, they precisely expend in the quality of buyers.” (“The Essential Principles of the Wealth of Nations.” etc., London, 1797, p. 66.)

<!-- ch05-p009 -->
Let us make the opposite assumption: that the buyer has the privilege of buying commodities below their value. In this case we no longer need to remember that he will become a seller in his turn. He was a seller before he became a buyer; he had already lost 10% as a seller before he gained 10% as a buyer.[^5.12] Everything is just as it was.

[^5.12]: “Si l’on est forcé de donner pour 18 livres une quantité de telle production qui en valait 24, lorsqu’on employera ce même argent à acheter, on aura également pour 18 l. ce que l’on payait 24.” [“If one is forced to give for 18 livres a quantity of some product that was worth 24, then when one uses this same money to buy, one will likewise get for 18 livres what one used to pay 24 for.”] (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 897.)

<!-- ch05-p010 -->
So the creation of surplus-value, and therefore the turning of money into capital, can be explained neither by assuming that commodities are sold above their value, nor by assuming that they are bought below their value.[^5.13]

[^5.13]: “Chaque vendeur ne peut donc parvenir à renchérir habituellement ses marchandises, qu’en se soumettant aussi à payer habituellement plus cher les marchandises des autres vendeurs; et par la même raison, chaque consommateur ne peut payer habituellement moins cher ce qu’il achète, qu’en se soumettant aussi à une diminution semblable sur le prix des choses qu’il vend.” [“So each seller can habitually raise the price of his commodities only by submitting, in turn, to habitually paying more for the commodities of the other sellers; and for the same reason each consumer can habitually pay less for what he buys only by submitting, in turn, to a similar reduction in the price of the things he sells.”] (Mercier de la Rivière, cited above, p. 555.)

<!-- ch05-p011 -->
Bringing in irrelevant matters, in the manner of Col. Torrens, does nothing to simplify the problem: “Effectual demand consists in the power and inclination (!), on the part of consumers, to give for commodities, either by immediate or circuitous barter, some greater portion of ... capital than their production costs.”[^5.14] In relation to circulation, producers and consumers meet only as buyers and sellers. To claim that the surplus-value the producer gets comes from the fact that consumers pay more than their value for commodities is only to say, in other words: The owner of commodities has, as a seller, the privilege of selling too dear. The seller has himself produced the commodities, or represents their producer. But the buyer has just as much produced the commodities represented by his money, or represents their producer. The difference between them is that one buys and the other sells. The fact that the owner of commodities, under the name of producer, sells them above their value and, under the name of consumer, pays too much for them, does not carry us a single step further.[^5.15]

[^5.14]: Torrens. “An Essay on the Production of Wealth.” London, 1821, p. 349.

[^5.15]: “The idea of profits being paid by the consumers, is, assuredly, very absurd. Who are the consumers?” (G. Ramsay: “An Essay on the Distribution of Wealth.” Edinburgh, 1836, p. 183.)

<!-- ch05-p012 -->
So, to be consistent, those who uphold the delusion that surplus-value comes from a nominal rise in prices, or from the seller’s privilege of selling too dear, must assume that there is a class that only buys and does not sell, that is, only consumes and does not produce. From the standpoint we have reached so far, namely that of simple circulation, the existence of such a class cannot be explained. But let us look ahead. The money with which such a class is constantly buying must constantly flow into its pockets from the pockets of the commodity owners themselves, without any exchange, free of charge, by might or by right. To sell commodities above their value to such a class is only to pinch back part of the money previously handed over to it.[^5.16] In this way the towns of Asia Minor paid a yearly money tribute to ancient Rome. With this money Rome bought commodities from them, and paid too much for them. The provincials cheated the Romans, and so, in the course of trade, got back from their conquerors a part of the tribute. Yet for all that, it was the conquered who were really cheated. Their goods were still paid for with their own money. That is not the way to get rich or to create surplus-value.

[^5.16]: “When a man is in want of a demand, does Mr. Malthus recommend him to pay some other person to take off his goods?” This question was put by an angry disciple of Ricardo to Malthus, who, like his disciple Parson Chalmers, glorifies this class of simple buyers or consumers in economic terms. (See “An Inquiry into those Principles Respecting the Nature of Demand and the Necessity of Consumption, lately advocated by Mr. Malthus,” etc. London, 1821, p. 55.)

<!-- ch05-p013 -->
So let us keep within the limits of exchange, where sellers are also buyers, and buyers are also sellers. Perhaps our difficulty has come from treating the actors as personifications instead of as individuals.

<!-- ch05-p014 -->
A may be clever enough to get the better of B or C without their being able to pay him back in kind. A sells wine worth £40 to B and gets from him in exchange grain worth £50. A has turned his £40 into £50, has made more money out of less, and has turned his commodities into capital. Let us look at this a little more closely. Before the exchange we had £40 worth of wine in A’s hands and £50 worth of grain in B’s, a total value of £90. After the exchange we still have the same total value of £90. The value in circulation has not increased by one iota; it is only distributed differently between A and B. What is a loss of value to B is surplus-value to A; what is “minus” to one is “plus” to the other. The same change would have taken place if A, without the formality of an exchange, had simply stolen the £10 from B. Clearly, the sum of the values in circulation cannot be increased by any change in their distribution, any more than the quantity of precious metals in a country is increased by a Jew selling a Queen Anne’s farthing for a guinea. The capitalist class of any country, taken as a whole, cannot cheat itself.[^5.17]

[^5.17]: Destutt de Tracy held the opposite view, although, or perhaps because, he was a member of the Institute. He says industrial capitalists make profits because “they all sell for more than it has cost to produce. And to whom do they sell? In the first instance to one another.” (cited above, p. 239.)

<!-- ch05-p015 -->
Turn and twist as we may, then, the fact stays the same. If equivalents are exchanged, no surplus-value results; and if non-equivalents are exchanged, still no surplus-value results.[^5.18] Circulation, or the exchange of commodities, creates no value.[^5.19]

[^5.18]: “L’échange qui se fait de deux valeurs égales n’augmente ni ne diminue la masse des valeurs subsistantes dans la société. L’échange de deux valeurs inégales ... ne change rien non plus à la somme des valeurs sociales, bien qu’il ajoute à la fortune de l’un ce qu’il ôte de la fortune de l’autre.” [“The exchange of two equal values neither increases nor decreases the mass of values existing in society. Nor does the exchange of two unequal values ... change anything in the sum of social values, although it adds to the fortune of one person what it takes from the fortune of the other.”] (J. B. Say, cited above, t. II, pp. 443, 444.) Say, not in the least troubled by the consequences of this statement, borrows it almost word for word from the Physiocrats. The following example will show how Monsieur Say made use of the writings of the Physiocrats, which in his day were quite forgotten, in order to expand the “value” of his own. His most famous saying, “On n’achète des produits qu’avec des produits” [“Products are bought only with products.”] (cited above, t. II. p. 441.), reads as follows in the original physiocratic work: “Les productions ne se paient qu’avec des productions.” [“Products are paid for only with products.”] (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 899.)

[^5.19]: “Exchange confers no value at all upon products.” (F. Wayland: “The Elements of Political Economy.” Boston, 1843, p. 169.)

<!-- ch05-p016 -->
So the reason is now clear why, in analyzing the standard form of capital, the form in which it determines the economic organization of modern society, we left entirely out of account its most popular forms, which date, so to speak, from before the Flood: merchants’ capital and money-lenders’ capital.

<!-- ch05-p017 -->
The circuit M—C—M, buying in order to sell dearer, is seen most clearly in genuine merchants’ capital. But the movement takes place entirely within the sphere of circulation. However, since it is impossible to explain the turning of money into capital, the formation of surplus-value, by circulation alone, it would seem that merchants’ capital is impossible as long as equivalents are exchanged;[^5.20] and that it can therefore only arise from the double advantage gained, over both the selling and the buying producers, by the merchant who shoves himself in between them like a parasite. It is in this sense that Franklin says, “war is robbery, commerce is generally cheating.”[^5.21] If the turning of merchants’ money into capital is to be explained otherwise than by the producers simply being cheated, a long series of intermediate steps would be needed. At present, when the simple circulation of commodities is our only assumption, these steps are entirely missing.

[^5.20]: Under the rule of invariable equivalents, trade would be impossible. (G. Opdyke: “A Treatise on Polit. Economy.” New York, 1851, pp. 66-69.) “The difference between real value and exchange-value is based upon this fact, namely, that the value of a thing is different from the so-called equivalent given for it in trade, i.e., that this equivalent is no equivalent.” (F. Engels, cited above, p. 96).

[^5.21]: Benjamin Franklin: Works, Vol. II, edit. Sparks in “Positions to be examined concerning National Wealth,” p. 376.

<!-- ch05-p018 -->
> What we have said about merchants’ capital applies even more to money-lenders’ capital. In merchants’ capital, the two extremes, the money thrown onto the market and the increased money withdrawn from the market, are at least connected by a purchase and a sale, in other words by the movement of circulation. In money-lenders’ capital, the form M—C—M is reduced to the two extremes with nothing in between, M—M , money exchanged for more money. This form is incompatible with the nature of money, and so it remains inexplicable from the standpoint of the circulation of commodities. Hence Aristotle: “since chrematistic [the art of money-making] is a double science, one part belonging to commerce, the other to economic [household management], the latter being necessary and praiseworthy, the former based on circulation and with justice disapproved (for it is not based on Nature, but on mutual cheating), therefore the usurer is most rightly hated, because money itself is the source of his gain, and is not used for the purposes for which it was invented. For it originated for the exchange of commodities, but interest makes out of money, more money. Hence its name (τοκος interest and offspring). For the begotten are like those who beget them. But interest is money of money, so that of all modes of making a living, this is the most contrary to Nature.”[^5.22]

[^5.22]: Aristotle, cited above, c. 10.

<!-- ch05-p019 -->
In the course of our investigation we shall find that both merchants’ capital and interest-bearing capital are derived forms. At the same time it will become clear why these two forms appear in the course of history before the modern standard form of capital.

<!-- ch05-p020 -->
We have shown that surplus-value cannot be created by circulation, and so that, for it to be formed, something must take place in the background that is not visible in circulation itself.[^5.23] But can surplus-value possibly arise anywhere else than in circulation, which is the sum total of all the relations between commodity owners, insofar as these are determined by their commodities? Outside circulation, the commodity owner is in relation only with his own commodity. As far as value is concerned, that relation is limited to this: the commodity contains a quantity of his own labor, and that quantity is measured by a definite social standard. This quantity is expressed by the value of the commodity. And since the value is reckoned in money of account, this quantity is also expressed by the price, which we will suppose to be £10. But his labor is not represented both by the value of the commodity and by a surplus over that value: not by a price of 10 that is also a price of 11, not by a value that is greater than itself. The commodity owner can create value by his labor, but not self-expanding value. He can increase the value of his commodity by adding fresh labor, and so more value, to the value already there, for instance by making leather into boots. The same material now has more value, because it contains a greater quantity of labor. So the boots have more value than the leather, but the value of the leather remains what it was. It has not expanded itself; it has not added surplus-value to itself while the boots were being made. It is therefore impossible for a producer of commodities, outside the sphere of circulation and without coming into contact with other commodity owners, to expand value, and so to turn money or commodities into capital.

[^5.23]: “Profit, in the usual condition of the market, is not made by exchanging. Had it not existed before, neither could it after that transaction.” (Ramsay, cited above, p. 184.)

<!-- ch05-p021 -->
So it is impossible for capital to be produced by circulation, and it is just as impossible for it to arise apart from circulation. It must have its origin both in circulation and yet not in circulation.

<!-- ch05-p022 -->
So we have a double result.

<!-- ch05-p023 -->
The turning of money into capital has to be explained on the basis of the laws that govern the exchange of commodities, in such a way that the starting point is the exchange of equivalents.[^5.24] Our friend Moneybags, who is as yet only a capitalist in embryo, must buy his commodities at their value and sell them at their value, and yet at the end of the process he must withdraw more value from circulation than he threw into it at the start. His growth into a full-grown capitalist must take place both within the sphere of circulation and outside it. These are the conditions of the problem. *Hic Rhodus, hic salta!* [Here is Rhodes, jump here!][^5.25]

[^5.24]: From the investigation above, the reader will see that this statement only means this: the formation of capital must be possible even if the price of a commodity and its value are the same, because its formation cannot be put down to any deviation of the one from the other. If prices actually differ from values, we must first reduce prices to values. In other words, we must treat the difference as accidental, so that the phenomena can be observed in their pure form, and our observations are not disturbed by circumstances that have nothing to do with the process in question. We know, moreover, that this reduction is not a merely scientific procedure. The constant swings in prices, their rising and falling, balance each other out and reduce themselves to an average price, which is their hidden regulator. This average price is the guiding star of the merchant or the manufacturer in every undertaking that takes time. He knows that when a long period of time is taken, commodities are sold neither above nor below their average price, but at it. So if he thought about the matter at all, he would put the problem of the formation of capital this way: How can we explain the origin of capital on the assumption that prices are regulated by the average price, that is, ultimately by the value of the commodities? I say “ultimately,” because average prices do not directly coincide with the values of commodities, as Adam Smith, Ricardo, and others believe.

[^5.25]: “Hic Rhodus, hic saltus!” – Latin, usually translated: “Rhodes is here, here is where you jump!”

    It comes from the traditional Latin translation of the punch line of Aesop’s fable The Boastful Athlete, which has been mistranslated in several ways. In Greek, the saying reads:

    > “ιδού η ρόδος, ιδού και το πήδημα” [“Here is Rhodes, here too is the jump”]

    The story is that an athlete boasts that when he was in Rhodes he made a stupendous jump, and that there were witnesses who could back up his story. A bystander then remarked, ‘Alright! Let’s say this is Rhodes, demonstrate the jump here and now.’ The fable shows that people must be known by their deeds, not by the claims they make for themselves. In the context in which Hegel used it in the *Philosophy of Right*, this could be taken to mean that the philosophy of right must deal with the *actuality* of modern society, not with the theories and ideals that societies create for themselves, nor, as Hegel goes on to say, with trying to “teach the world what it ought to be.”

    Hegel gives the saying first in Greek, then in Latin (in the form “*Hic* Rhodus, *hic* saltus”), and he then says: “With little change, the above saying would read (in German): “*Hier* ist die Rose, *hier* tanze”: “Here is the rose, dance here”

    This is taken to be an allusion to the ‘rose in the cross’ of the Rosicrucians (who claimed to possess secret knowledge with which they could transform social life), implying that the material for understanding and changing society is found in society itself, not in some other-worldly theory, punning first on the Greek (*Rhodos* = Rhodes, *rhodon* = rose), then on the Latin (*saltus* = jump [noun], *salta* = dance [imperative]). [MIA Editors.]

## Chapter 6: The Buying and Selling of Labor-Power

<!-- ch06-p001 -->
The change of value (value being what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time) that happens to money meant to be turned into capital (value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger) cannot take place in the money itself. In its function as a means of purchase and as a means of payment (money used to settle a debt after goods have changed hands on credit), money does no more than realize the price (the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity) of the commodity (a thing produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer’s own use) that it buys or pays for. And as hard cash, it is value turned to stone, never varying.[^6.1] Just as little can the change arise in the second act of circulation (the exchange of commodities through money: selling and buying), the resale of the commodity. That act does no more than change the article from its bodily form back again into its money form (the form of value in which one commodity, gold, has become the universal equivalent). The change must therefore take place in the commodity bought by the first act, M—C, but not in its value, for equivalents are exchanged, and the commodity is paid for at its full value. We are therefore forced to conclude that the change arises from the use-value (the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties) of the commodity as such, that is, from its consumption. To be able to extract value from the consumption of a commodity, our friend Moneybags must be lucky enough to find, within the sphere of circulation, in the market, a commodity whose use-value has the peculiar property of being a source of value, so that actually consuming it is itself an embodiment of labor, and therefore a creation of value. The owner of money does find such a special commodity on the market: the capacity for labor, or labor-power.

[^6.1]: “In the form of money ... capital is productive of no profit.” (Ricardo: “Princ. of Pol. Econ.,” p. 267.)

<!-- ch06-p002 -->
By labor-power, or capacity for labor, we are to understand the sum total of the mental and physical capabilities that exist in a human being, and that he exercises whenever he produces a use-value of any kind.

<!-- ch06-p003 -->
But for our owner of money to be able to find labor-power offered for sale as a commodity, various conditions must first be met. The exchange of commodities in itself implies no relations of dependence other than those that come from its own nature. On this assumption, labor-power can appear on the market as a commodity only if, and so far as, its owner, the individual whose labor-power it is, offers it for sale, or sells it, as a commodity. To be able to do this, he must have it at his disposal. He must be the free, unrestricted owner of his capacity for labor, that is, of his person.[^6.2] He and the owner of money meet in the market and deal with each other as people with equal rights, with this one difference alone: one is buyer, the other seller. Both, therefore, are equal in the eyes of the law. For this relation to continue, the owner of the labor-power must sell it only for a definite period. For if he were to sell it outright, all of it, once and for all, he would be selling himself. He would be turning himself from a free man into a slave, from an owner of a commodity into a commodity. He must always treat his labor-power as his own property, his own commodity. He can do this only by placing it at the buyer’s disposal temporarily, for a definite period of time. Only in this way can he avoid giving up his rights of ownership over it.[^6.3]

[^6.2]: In encyclopedias of classical antiquity we find such nonsense as this: that in the ancient world capital was fully developed, “except that the free labourer and a system of credit was wanting.” Mommsen too, in his “History of Rome,” makes one blunder after another on this point.

[^6.3]: Hence legislation in various countries fixes a maximum for labor contracts. Wherever free labor is the rule, the laws regulate how this contract is ended. In some States, particularly in Mexico (before the American Civil War, also in the territories taken from Mexico, and also, as a matter of fact, in the Danubian provinces until the revolution carried out by Kusa), slavery is hidden under the form of *peonage*. Through advances that are to be repaid in labor and are handed down from generation to generation, not only the individual worker but his family become, in fact, the property of other persons and their families. Juarez abolished *peonage*. The so-called Emperor Maximilian brought it back by a decree, which was fittingly denounced in the House of Representatives at Washington as a decree for re-introducing slavery into Mexico. “I may make over to another the use, for a limited time, of my particular bodily and mental aptitudes and capabilities; because in consequence of this restriction, they are impressed with a character of alienation with regard to me as a whole. But by the alienation of all my labour-time and the whole of my work, I should be converting the substance itself, in other words, my general activity and reality, my person, into the property of another.” (Hegel, “Philosophie des Rechts.” Berlin, 1840, p. 104, § 67.)

<!-- ch06-p004 -->
The second essential condition for the owner of money to find labor-power on the market as a commodity is this: the worker, instead of being in a position to sell commodities in which his labor is embodied, must be obliged to offer for sale, as a commodity, that very labor-power which exists only in his living self.

<!-- ch06-p005 -->
For a man to be able to sell commodities other than labor-power, he must of course have the means of production, such as raw material, tools, etc. No boots can be made without leather. He also needs the means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live). Nobody, not even “a musician of the future”, can live on future products, or on use-values in an unfinished state. Ever since man first appeared on the world’s stage, he always has been, and still must be, a consumer, both before and while he is producing. In a society where all products take the form of commodities, these commodities must be sold after they have been produced; only after their sale can they serve to satisfy the needs of their producer. The time needed for their sale is added on top of the time needed for their production.

<!-- ch06-p006 -->
So, to turn his money into capital, the owner of money must meet in the market with the free worker, free in a double sense: free in that, as a free man, he can dispose of his labor-power as his own commodity, and free in that, on the other hand, he has no other commodity for sale and lacks everything needed to put his labor-power into action.

<!-- ch06-p007 -->
The owner of money has no interest in the question of why this free worker confronts him in the market, since he regards the labor market as a branch of the general market for commodities. And for the present, the question interests us just as little. We hold to the fact in theory, as he does in practice. One thing, however, is clear. Nature does not produce owners of money or commodities on one side, and on the other side men who possess nothing but their own labor-power. This relation has no natural basis, nor is its social basis one that is common to all historical periods. It is clearly the result of a past historical development, the product of many economic revolutions, of the extinction of a whole series of older forms of social production.

<!-- ch06-p008 -->
In the same way, the economic categories we have already discussed bear the stamp of history. Definite historical conditions are needed for a product to become a commodity. It must not be produced as the immediate means of subsistence of the producer himself. If we had gone further and asked under what circumstances all products, or even most of them, take the form of commodities, we would have found that this can happen only with production of a very specific kind: capitalist production. But such an inquiry would have been out of place in the analysis of commodities. The production and circulation of commodities can take place even though the great mass of the objects produced are meant for the immediate needs of their producers and are not turned into commodities, so that social production is still far from being dominated, in its length and breadth, by exchange-value (the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for). For products to appear as commodities, the social division of labor must have developed so far that the separation of use-value from exchange-value, a separation that first begins with barter, has already been completed. But such a degree of development is common to many forms of society, which in other respects show the most varied historical features. On the other hand, if we consider money, its existence implies a definite stage in the exchange of commodities. Money performs particular functions: as the mere equivalent of commodities, or as medium of circulation (money in its role of passing from hand to hand to carry out sales and purchases), or means of payment, as hoard (money withdrawn from circulation and kept as a store of value) or as world money (gold and silver used as money between nations). Depending on the extent of one function or the other, and on which of them relatively predominates, these functions point to very different stages in the process of social production. Yet we know from experience that a relatively primitive circulation of commodities is enough to produce all these forms. It is otherwise with capital. The historical conditions of its existence are by no means given with the mere circulation of money and commodities. Capital can spring into life only when the owner of the means of production and subsistence meets in the market with the free worker selling his labor-power. And this one historical condition contains a world’s history. So capital, from its first appearance, announces a new epoch in the process of social production.[^6.4]

[^6.4]: The capitalist epoch is therefore marked by this: labor-power, in the eyes of the worker himself, takes the form of a commodity that is his property, and so his labor becomes wage labor. On the other hand, it is only from this moment that the product of labor universally becomes a commodity.

<!-- ch06-p009 -->
We must now look more closely at this peculiar commodity, labor-power. Like all others, it has a value.[^6.5] How is that value determined?

[^6.5]: “The value or worth of a man, is as of all other things his price — that is to say, so much as would be given for the use of his power.” (Th. Hobbes: “Leviathan” in Works, Ed. Molesworth. London 1839-44, v. iii. p. 76.)

<!-- ch06-p010 -->
The value of labor-power is determined, as with every other commodity, by the labor-time needed to produce, and so also to reproduce, this special article. So far as it has value, it represents no more than a definite quantity of the average labor of society (simple average labor: the labor that an average person without special training can do; skilled labor counts as a multiple of it) embodied in it. Labor-power exists only as a capacity, or power, of the living individual. Its production therefore presupposes his existence. Given the individual, the production of labor-power consists in his reproducing himself, or maintaining himself. To maintain himself he needs a given quantity of the means of subsistence. So the labor-time needed to produce labor-power comes down to the labor-time needed to produce those means of subsistence. In other words, the value of labor-power is the value of the means of subsistence needed to maintain the worker. Labor-power, however, becomes a reality only by being exercised; it sets itself in action only by working. But in this way a definite quantity of human muscle, nerve, brain, etc., is used up, and these must be restored. This increased expenditure demands a larger income.[^6.6] If the owner of labor-power works today, tomorrow he must again be able to repeat the same process in the same conditions of health and strength. So his means of subsistence must be enough to maintain him in his normal state as a working individual. His natural wants, such as food, clothing, fuel, and housing, vary with the climate and other physical conditions of his country. On the other hand, the number and extent of his so-called necessary wants, and also the ways of satisfying them, are themselves the product of historical development. They therefore depend to a great extent on a country’s degree of civilization, and more particularly on the conditions under which the class of free workers has been formed, and so on the habits and the degree of comfort in which it has been formed.[^6.7] So, unlike the case of other commodities, a historical and moral element enters into determining the value of labor-power. Nevertheless, in a given country, at a given period, the average quantity of the means of subsistence needed by the worker is known in practice.

[^6.6]: Hence the Roman Villicus, as overseer of the agricultural slaves, received “more meagre fare than working slaves, because his work was lighter.” (Th. Mommsen, Röm. Geschichte, 1856, p. 810.)

[^6.7]: Compare W. Th. Thornton: “Over-population and its Remedy,” London, 1846.

<!-- ch06-p011 -->
The owner of labor-power is mortal. If, then, he is to appear on the market continuously, as the continuous turning of money into capital assumes, the seller of labor-power must perpetuate himself, “in the way that every living individual perpetuates himself, by procreation.”[^6.8] The labor-power withdrawn from the market by wear and tear and by death must be continually replaced by at least an equal amount of fresh labor-power. So the sum of the means of subsistence needed to produce labor-power must include the means needed for the worker’s replacements, that is, his children, so that this race of peculiar commodity-owners may go on appearing in the market.[^6.9]

[^6.8]: Petty.

[^6.9]: “Its (labour’s) natural price ... consists in such a quantity of necessaries and comforts of life, as, from the nature of the climate, and the habits of the country, are necessary to support the labourer, and to enable him to rear such a family as may preserve, in the market, an undiminished supply of labour.” (R. Torrens: “An Essay on the External Corn Trade.” London 1815, p. 62.) Here the word “labour” is wrongly used for labor-power.

<!-- ch06-p012 -->
To modify the human organism so that it gains skill and handiness in a given branch of industry and becomes labor-power of a special kind, a special education or training is needed, and this in turn costs an equivalent in commodities of a greater or smaller amount. The amount varies with how complicated the labor-power is. The expenses of this education (extremely small in the case of ordinary labor-power) enter to that extent into the total value spent in producing it.

<!-- ch06-p013 -->
The value of labor-power comes down to the value of a definite quantity of the means of subsistence. It therefore varies with the value of these means, or with the quantity of labor needed to produce them.

<!-- ch06-p014 -->
Some of the means of subsistence, such as food and fuel, are consumed daily, and a fresh supply must be provided daily. Others, such as clothes and furniture, last for longer periods and need to be replaced only at longer intervals. One article must be bought or paid for daily, another weekly, another quarterly, and so on. But however the total of these outlays may be spread over the year, they must be covered by the average income, taking one day with another. If the total of the commodities required daily for the production of labor-power = A, those required weekly = B, those required quarterly = C, and so on, then the daily average of these commodities = (365A + 52B + 4C + &c) / 365. Suppose that 6 hours of social labor are embodied in this mass of commodities needed for the average day. Then half a day’s average social labor is embodied daily in labor-power; in other words, half a day’s labor is needed for the daily production of labor-power. This quantity of labor forms the value of a day’s labor-power, or the value of the labor-power reproduced daily. If half a day’s average social labor is embodied in three shillings, then three shillings is the price corresponding to the value of a day’s labor-power. So if its owner offers it for sale at three shillings a day, its selling price is equal to its value, and, according to our supposition, our friend Moneybags, who is set on turning his three shillings into capital, pays this value.

<!-- ch06-p015 -->
The minimum limit of the value of labor-power is determined by the value of the commodities without whose daily supply the worker cannot renew his vital energy, and so by the value of those means of subsistence that are physically indispensable. If the price of labor-power falls to this minimum, it falls below its value, since under such circumstances labor-power can be maintained and developed only in a crippled state. But the value of every commodity is determined by the labor-time needed to turn it out at normal quality.

<!-- ch06-p016 -->
It is a very cheap sort of sentimentality that declares this method of determining the value of labor-power, a method required by the very nature of the case, to be a brutal method, and that wails along with Rossi: “To comprehend capacity for labour (puissance de travail) at the same time that we make abstraction from the means of subsistence of the labourers during the process of production, is to comprehend a phantom (être de raison). When we speak of labour, or capacity for labour, we speak at the same time of the labourer and his means of subsistence, of labourer and wages.”[^6.10] When we speak of capacity for labor, we do not speak of labor, any more than we speak of digestion when we speak of capacity for digestion. Digestion requires something more than a good stomach. When we speak of capacity for labor, we do not leave the necessary means of subsistence out of account. On the contrary, their value is expressed in its value. If his capacity for labor remains unsold, the worker gets no benefit from it. Rather, he will feel it to be a cruel necessity imposed by nature that this capacity has cost a definite amount of the means of subsistence to produce, and that it will go on doing so to be reproduced. He will then agree with Sismondi: “that capacity for labour ... is nothing unless it is sold.”[^6.11]

[^6.10]: Rossi: “Cours d’Econ. Polit.,” Bruxelles, 1842, p. 370.

[^6.11]: Sismondi: “Nouv. Princ. etc.,” t. I, p. 112.

<!-- ch06-p017 -->
One consequence of the peculiar nature of labor-power as a commodity is that its use-value does not pass straight into the buyer’s hands when the contract between buyer and seller is concluded. Its value, like that of every other commodity, is already fixed before it goes into circulation, since a definite quantity of social labor has been spent on it. But its use-value consists in the later exercise of its force. The handing over (alienation) of labor-power and its actual appropriation by the buyer, its use as a use-value, are separated by an interval of time. But in cases where the formal handing over of a commodity’s use-value by sale does not happen at the same time as its actual delivery to the buyer, the buyer’s money usually functions as means of payment.[^6.12] In every country where the capitalist mode of production reigns, it is the custom not to pay for labor-power until it has been exercised for the period fixed by the contract, for example at the end of each week. In all cases, therefore, the worker advances the use-value of the labor-power to the capitalist: he lets the buyer consume it before he receives payment of its price. Everywhere, he gives credit to the capitalist. That this credit is no mere fiction is shown not only by the occasional loss of wages (the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself) when the capitalist goes bankrupt,[^6.13] but also by a series of more lasting consequences.[^6.14] Nevertheless, whether money serves as a means of purchase or as a means of payment makes no difference to the nature of the exchange of commodities. The price of the labor-power is fixed by the contract, although it is not realized until later, like the rent of a house. The labor-power is sold, although it is only paid for later. So, for a clear understanding of the relation between the parties, it will be useful to assume for the time being that the owner of labor-power, each time he sells it, immediately receives the price agreed for it.

[^6.12]: “All labour is paid after it has ceased.” (“An Inquiry into those Principles Respecting the Nature of Demand,” etc., p. 104.) Le crédit commercial a dû commencer au moment où l’ouvrier, premier artisan de la production, a pu, au moyen de ses économies, attendre le salaire de son travail jusqu’à la fin de la semaine, de la quinzaine, du mois, du trimestre, &c.” [“Commercial credit had to begin at the moment when the worker, the first artisan of production, could, by means of his savings, wait for the wages of his labor until the end of the week, the fortnight, the month, the quarter, etc.”] (Ch. Ganilh: “Des Systèmes d’Econ. Polit.” 2éme édit. Paris, 1821, t. II, p. 150.)

[^6.13]: “L’ouvrier prête son industrie,” but, Storch slyly adds, he “risks nothing” except “de perdre son salaire ... l’ouvrier ne transmet rien de matériel.” [“The worker lends his industry ... losing his wages ... the worker does not hand over anything material.”] (Storch: “Cours d’Econ. Polit.” Pétersbourg, 1815, t. II., p. 37.)

[^6.14]: One example. In London there are two sorts of bakers: the “full priced,” who sell bread at its full value, and the “undersellers,” who sell it below its value. The undersellers make up more than three-fourths of the total number of bakers. (p. xxxii in the Report of H. S. Tremenheere, commissioner to examine into “the grievances complained of by the journeymen bakers,” etc., London 1862.) The undersellers, almost without exception, sell bread adulterated with alum, soap, pearl ashes, chalk, Derbyshire stone-dust, and similar agreeable, nourishing, and wholesome ingredients. (See the Blue Book cited above, and also the report of “the committee of 1855 on the adulteration of bread,” and Dr. Hassall’s “Adulterations Detected,” 2nd Ed. London 1861.)
