Sir John Gordon stated before the committee of 1855 that “in consequence of these adulterations, the poor man, who lives on two pounds of bread a day, does not now get one fourth part of nourishing matter, let alone the deleterious [harmful] effects on his health.” Tremenheere states (cited above, p. xlviii) the reason why a very large part of the working class, although well aware of this adulteration, nevertheless accept the alum, stone-dust, etc., as part of their purchase: it is for them “a matter of necessity to take from their baker or from the chandler’s shop [small general store], such bread as they choose to supply.” As they are not paid their wages before the end of the week, they in their turn are unable “to pay for the bread consumed by their families, during the week, before the end of the week,” and Tremenheere adds, on the evidence of witnesses, “it is notorious that bread composed of those mixtures, is made expressly for sale in this manner.” In many English, and still more Scottish, agricultural districts, wages are paid fortnightly and even monthly; with such long intervals between the payments, the agricultural worker is obliged to buy on credit.... He must pay higher prices, and is in fact tied to the shop that gives him credit. Thus at Horningham in Wilts, for example, where wages are paid monthly, the same flour that he could buy elsewhere at 1s 10d per stone costs him 2s 4d per stone. (“Sixth Report” on “Public Health” by “The Medical Officer of the Privy Council, &c., 1864,” p.264.) “The block printers of Paisley and Kilmarnock enforced, by a strike, fortnightly, instead of monthly payment of wages.” (“Reports of the Inspectors of Factories for 31st Oct., 1853,” p. 34.) As a further pretty result of the credit given by the workers to the capitalist, we may point to the method common in many English coal mines. There the worker is not paid until the end of the month, and in the meantime receives sums on account from the capitalist, often in goods for which the miner is obliged to pay more than the market price (truck system). “It is a common practice with the coal masters to pay once a month, and advance cash to their workmen at the end of each intermediate week. The cash is given in the shop” (that is, the Tommy shop, which belongs to the employer); “the men take it on one side and lay it out on the other.” (“Children’s Employment Commission, III. Report,” London 1864, p. 38, n. 192.)

<!-- ch06-p018 -->
We now know how the value that the buyer pays to the owner of this peculiar commodity, labor-power, is determined. The use-value that the buyer gets in exchange shows itself only in the actual use, in the consumption, of the labor-power. The money-owner buys everything needed for this purpose, such as raw material, in the market, and pays its full value for it. The consumption of labor-power is at one and the same time the production of commodities and of surplus-value (the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it). The consumption of labor-power, as in the case of every other commodity, is completed outside the limits of the market, or of the sphere of circulation. So, accompanied by Mr. Moneybags and by the owner of labor-power, we take leave for a time of this noisy sphere, where everything takes place on the surface and in full view of everyone. We follow them both into the hidden abode of production, on whose threshold we are met by the words “No admittance except on business.” Here we shall see not only how capital produces, but how capital is produced. We shall at last force the secret of profit-making.

<!-- ch06-p019 -->
This sphere that we are leaving, within whose boundaries the sale and purchase of labor-power goes on, is in fact a very Eden of the innate rights of man. There alone rule Freedom, Equality, Property and Bentham. Freedom, because both buyer and seller of a commodity, say of labor-power, are bound only by their own free will. They make their contract as free agents, and the agreement they come to is only the form in which they give legal expression to their common will. Equality, because each enters into relation with the other as with a simple owner of commodities, and they exchange equivalent for equivalent. Property, because each disposes only of what is his own. And Bentham, because each looks only to himself. The only force that brings them together and puts them in relation with each other is the selfishness, the gain and the private interests of each. Each looks to himself only, and no one troubles himself about the rest. And just because they do so, they all, in accordance with the pre-established harmony of things, or under the guidance of an all-shrewd providence, work together to their mutual advantage, for the common good and in the interest of all.

<!-- ch06-p020 -->
On leaving this sphere of simple circulation, or of the exchange of commodities, which supplies the “Free-trader Vulgaris” with his views and ideas, and with the standard by which he judges a society based on capital and wages, we think we can see a change in the faces of our cast of characters. He who was the money-owner before now strides in front as capitalist; the owner of labor-power follows as his worker. The one has an air of importance, smirking, intent on business; the other is timid and holding back, like someone who is bringing his own hide to market and has nothing to expect but – a hiding.

# Part 3: The Production of Absolute Surplus-Value

## Chapter 7: The Labor-Process and the Process of Producing Surplus-Value

### Section 1: The Labor-Process or the Production of Use-Values

<!-- ch07-p001 -->
The capitalist buys labor-power in order to use it, and labor-power in use is labor itself. (Labor-power is a person’s capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist.) The buyer of labor-power consumes it by setting its seller to work. By working, the seller actually becomes what before he was only potentially: labor-power in action, a worker. For his labor to reappear in a commodity (a thing produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer’s own use), he must, before all else, spend it on something useful, on something able to satisfy a want of some sort. So what the capitalist sets the worker to produce is a particular use-value (the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties), a specific article. The production of use-values, or goods, is carried on under the control of a capitalist and on his behalf; but this fact does not change the general character of that production. So we must first consider the labor process apart from the particular form it takes under given social conditions.

<!-- ch07-p002 -->
Labor is, first of all, a process in which both man and Nature take part, and in which man, of his own accord, starts, regulates, and controls the material reactions between himself and Nature. He confronts Nature as one of her own forces. He sets in motion arms and legs, head and hands, the natural forces of his body, in order to make Nature’s products his own in a form suited to his wants. By acting on the external world in this way and changing it, he at the same time changes his own nature. He develops his sleeping powers and forces them to act under his command. We are not now dealing with those primitive, instinctive forms of labor that remind us of mere animals. An immeasurable stretch of time separates the state of things in which a man brings his labor-power to market for sale as a commodity from the state in which human labor was still in its first instinctive stage. We assume labor in a form that marks it as exclusively human. A spider carries out operations that resemble those of a weaver, and a bee puts many an architect to shame in building her cells. But what distinguishes the worst architect from the best of bees is this: the architect raises his structure in imagination before he builds it in reality. At the end of every labor process we get a result that already existed in the worker’s imagination when it began. He not only changes the form of the material he works on; he also realizes a purpose of his own. That purpose lays down the law for his way of working, and he must subordinate his will to it. And this subordination is no mere passing act. Besides the effort of the bodily organs, the process demands that the worker’s will stay steadily in tune with his purpose during the whole operation. This means close attention. The less he is attracted by the nature of the work and the way it is carried on, and so the less he enjoys it as something that gives play to his bodily and mental powers, the closer his attention is forced to be.

<!-- ch07-p003 -->
The elementary factors of the labor process are 1, the personal activity of man, that is, work itself, 2, the object of that work, and 3, its instruments.

<!-- ch07-p004 -->
The soil (and this, economically speaking, includes water), in the virgin state in which it supplies[^7.1] man with the necessaries of life, or the means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live), ready to hand, exists independently of him and is the universal object of human labor. All those things that labor merely separates from their immediate connection with their surroundings are objects of labor provided by Nature of her own accord. Such are fish that we catch and take from their element, water; timber that we fell in the virgin forest; and ores that we extract from their veins. If, on the other hand, the object of labor has, so to speak, been filtered through earlier labor, we call it raw material. Ore already extracted and ready for washing is an example. All raw material is an object of labor, but not every object of labor is raw material: it can become raw material only after labor has changed it in some way.

[^7.1]: “The earth’s spontaneous productions being in small quantity, and quite independent of man, appear, as it were, to be furnished by Nature, in the same way as a small sum is given to a young man, in order to put him in a way of industry, and of making his fortune.” (James Steuart: “Principles of Polit. Econ.” edit. Dublin, 1770, v. I, p.116.)

<!-- ch07-p005 -->
An instrument of labor is a thing, or a complex of things, that the worker places between himself and the object of his labor, and that serves as the conductor of his activity. He makes use of the mechanical, physical, and chemical properties of some substances in order to make other substances serve his aims.[^7.2] Leave aside such ready-made means of subsistence as fruits, which a man gathers with his own limbs as the instruments of his labor. Then the first thing the worker takes possession of is not the object of labor but its instrument. In this way Nature becomes one of the organs of his activity, one that he adds to his own bodily organs, adding to his stature in spite of the Bible. Just as the earth is his original pantry, so it is also his original toolshed. It supplies him, for instance, with stones for throwing, grinding, pressing, cutting, etc. The earth itself is an instrument of labor; but when it is used as one in agriculture, that implies a whole series of other instruments and a comparatively high development of labor.[^7.3] As soon as labor develops in the least, it needs specially prepared instruments. So in the oldest caves we find stone tools and weapons. In the earliest period of human history, domesticated animals, that is, animals that have been bred for the purpose and have been changed by means of labor, play the chief part as instruments of labor, along with specially prepared stones, wood, bones, and shells.[^7.4] The use and making of instruments of labor, although they exist in germ among certain species of animals, are specifically characteristic of the human labor process, and so Franklin defines man as a tool-making animal. Remains of past instruments of labor are as important for investigating extinct economic forms of society as fossil bones are for identifying extinct species of animals. It is not the articles made, but how they are made and with what instruments, that lets us distinguish different economic epochs.[^7.5] Instruments of labor not only give a standard for the degree of development that human labor has reached; they also indicate the social conditions under which that labor is carried on. Among the instruments of labor, those of a mechanical kind, which taken as a whole we may call the bones and muscles of production, show the characteristics of a given epoch of production much more clearly than those that serve only to hold the materials of labor, like pipes, tubs, baskets, jars, etc. In a general way we may call this second class the vascular system of production. It first begins to play an important part in the chemical industries.

[^7.2]: “Reason is just as cunning as she is powerful. Her cunning consists principally in her mediating activity, which, by causing objects to act and re-act on each other in accordance with their own nature, in this way, without any direct interference in the process, carries out reason’s intentions.” (Hegel: “Enzyklopädie, Erster Theil, Die Logik,” Berlin, 1840, p. 382.)

[^7.3]: In his otherwise miserable work (“Théorie de l’Econ. Polit.” Paris, 1815), Ganilh, arguing against the “Physiocrats,” lists in a striking way the long series of earlier processes that are needed before agriculture proper can begin.

[^7.4]: Turgot, in his “Réflexions sur la Formation et la Distribution des Richesses” (1766), brings out well the importance of domesticated animals to early civilization.

[^7.5]: The least important commodities of all for comparing the technology of different epochs of production are articles of luxury, in the strict sense of the term. Our written histories up to now take little notice of the development of material production, which is the basis of all social life, and therefore of all real history. Yet however little they notice it, prehistoric times have been classified according to the results not of so-called historical investigations but of materialistic ones. These periods have been divided according to the materials their tools and weapons were made from, namely into the stone, the bronze, and the iron ages.

<!-- ch07-p006 -->
In a wider sense we may count among the instruments of labor, besides the things used to transfer labor directly to its object, which therefore serve in one way or another as conductors of activity, all the objects needed for carrying on the labor process. These do not enter directly into the process, but without them it either cannot take place at all or can take place only in part. Here again we find the earth to be a universal instrument of this sort, for it gives the worker a place to stand and a field in which to employ his activity. Among the instruments that are the result of earlier labor and also belong to this class, we find workshops, canals, roads, and so on.

<!-- ch07-p007 -->
So in the labor process man’s activity, with the help of the instruments of labor, brings about a change in the material worked on, a change intended from the start. The process disappears in the product. The product is a use-value: Nature’s material adapted to man’s wants by a change of form. Labor has combined itself with its object: the labor is materialized, the object is transformed. What appeared in the worker as movement now appears in the product as a fixed quality without motion. The blacksmith forges, and the product is a forging.

<!-- ch07-p008 -->
If we look at the whole process from the point of view of its result, the product, clearly both the instruments and the object of labor are means of production,[^7.6] and the labor itself is productive labor.[^7.7]

[^7.6]: It seems paradoxical to say that uncaught fish, for instance, are a means of production in the fishing industry. But so far no one has discovered the art of catching fish in waters that contain none.

[^7.7]: This way of determining what productive labor is, from the standpoint of the labor process alone, is by no means directly applicable to the capitalist process of production.

<!-- ch07-p009 -->
Although a use-value, in the form of a product, comes out of the labor process, other use-values, products of earlier labor, go into it as means of production. The same use-value is both the product of an earlier process and a means of production in a later one. So products are not only results of labor but also its essential conditions.

<!-- ch07-p010 -->
Apart from the extractive industries, in which Nature directly provides the material for labor, such as mining, hunting, fishing, and agriculture (so far as agriculture is limited to breaking up virgin soil), all branches of industry work on raw material: objects already filtered through labor, already products of labor. Seed in agriculture is an example. Animals and plants, which we are used to thinking of as products of Nature, are in their present form not only products of, say, last year’s labor. They are the result of a gradual transformation, continued through many generations under man’s supervision and by means of his labor. But in the great majority of cases, instruments of labor show traces of the labor of past ages even to the most superficial observer.

<!-- ch07-p011 -->
Raw material may either form the principal substance of a product, or enter into its formation only as an accessory. An accessory may be consumed by the instruments of labor, as coal is under a boiler, oil by a wheel, hay by draft-horses. Or it may be mixed with the raw material in order to modify it in some way, as chlorine is put into unbleached linen, coal with iron, dye with wool. Or, again, it may help to carry on the work itself, as with the materials used for heating and lighting workshops. The distinction between principal substance and accessory vanishes in the true chemical industries, because there none of the raw material reappears, in its original composition, in the substance of the product.[^7.8]

[^7.8]: Storch calls true raw materials “matières” [substances], and accessory material “matériaux” [materials]. Cherbuliez describes accessories as “matières instrumentales” [instrumental substances].

<!-- ch07-p012 -->
Every object has various properties, and so it can be put to different uses. One and the same product may therefore serve as raw material in very different processes. Grain, for example, is a raw material for millers, starch-manufacturers, distillers, and cattle breeders. It also enters as raw material into its own production, in the form of seed. Coal, too, is at the same time the product of coal-mining and a means of production in it.

<!-- ch07-p013 -->
Again, a particular product may be used in one and the same process both as an instrument of labor and as raw material. Take, for instance, the fattening of cattle: the animal is the raw material, and at the same time an instrument for producing manure.

<!-- ch07-p014 -->
A product, though ready for immediate consumption, may still serve as raw material for a further product, as grapes do when they become the raw material for wine. On the other hand, labor may give us its product in such a form that we can use it only as raw material, as is the case with cotton, thread, and yarn. Such a raw material, though itself a product, may have to go through a whole series of different processes. In each of these in turn it serves as raw material, its form constantly changing, until the last process of the series leaves it a finished product, ready for individual consumption or for use as an instrument of labor.

<!-- ch07-p015 -->
So we see that whether a use-value is to be regarded as raw material, as instrument of labor, or as product is determined entirely by its function in the labor process, by the position it holds there. As that position varies, so does its character.

<!-- ch07-p016 -->
So whenever a product enters a new labor process as a means of production, it loses its character as a product and becomes a mere factor in the process. A spinner treats spindles only as tools for spinning, and flax only as the material that he spins. Of course it is impossible to spin without material and spindles, and so we must assume that these things exist as products when the spinning begins. But in the process itself, the fact that they are products of earlier labor does not matter in the least. In the same way, in digestion it makes no difference whatever that bread is the product of the earlier labor of the farmer, the miller, and the baker. On the contrary, it is generally through their imperfections as products that the means of production in any process make their character as products felt. A blunt knife or weak thread forcibly reminds us of Mr. A., the cutler, or Mr. B., the spinner. In the finished product, the labor through which it acquired its useful qualities cannot be detected; it has apparently vanished.

<!-- ch07-p017 -->
A machine that does not serve the purposes of labor is useless. On top of that, it falls prey to the destructive action of natural forces. Iron rusts and wood rots. Yarn that we neither weave nor knit is wasted cotton. Living labor (the labor of workers now at work) must seize on these things and wake them from their death-sleep, changing them from mere possible use-values into real and effective ones. Bathed in the fire of labor, taken over as part and parcel of labor’s organism, and, as it were, brought to life to perform their functions in the process, they are indeed consumed. But they are consumed with a purpose, as the elementary parts of new use-values, of new products, always ready to serve as means of subsistence for individual consumption or as means of production for some new labor process.

<!-- ch07-p018 -->
So if, on the one hand, finished products are not only results but also necessary conditions of the labor process, then, on the other hand, being taken into that process, coming into contact with living labor, is the only way they can be made to keep their character as use-values and be put to use.

<!-- ch07-p019 -->
Labor uses up its material factors, its object and its instruments. It consumes them, and so it is a process of consumption. Such productive consumption differs from individual consumption in this: individual consumption uses up products as means of subsistence for the living individual; productive consumption uses them up as the means through which alone labor, the labor-power of the living individual, is able to act. So the product of individual consumption is the consumer himself; the result of productive consumption is a product distinct from the consumer.

<!-- ch07-p020 -->
So to the extent that its instruments and objects are themselves products, labor consumes products in order to create products; in other words, it consumes one set of products by turning them into means of production for another set. But just as in the beginning the only participants in the labor process were man and the earth, which exists independently of man, so even now we still use in the process many means of production that Nature provides directly and that do not represent any combination of natural substances with human labor.

<!-- ch07-p021 -->
The labor process, broken down as above into its simple elementary factors, is human action aimed at producing use-values, the appropriation of natural substances for human needs. It is the necessary condition for the exchange of matter between man and Nature. It is the everlasting condition of human existence, imposed by Nature, and so it is independent of every social phase of that existence, or rather, it is common to every such phase. So it was not necessary to show our worker in connection with other workers; man and his labor on one side, Nature and its materials on the other, were enough. The taste of the porridge does not tell you who grew the oats, and no more does this simple process tell you of itself under what social conditions it is taking place: whether under the slave-owner’s brutal lash or the anxious eye of the capitalist, whether Cincinnatus carries it on in tilling his modest farm or a savage in killing wild animals with stones.[^7.9]

[^7.9]: By a wonderful feat of logical sharpness, Colonel Torrens has discovered the origin of capital in this stone of the savage. “In the first stone which he [the savage] flings at the wild animal he pursues, in the first stick that he seizes to strike down the fruit which hangs above his reach, we see the appropriation of one article for the purpose of aiding in the acquisition of another, and thus discover the origin of capital.” (R. Torrens: “An Essay on the Production of Wealth,” etc., pp. 70-71.)

<!-- ch07-p022 -->
Let us now return to our would-be capitalist. We left him just after he had bought, in the open market, all the necessary factors of the labor process: its objective factors, the means of production, as well as its subjective factor, labor-power. With an expert’s keen eye he has selected the means of production and the kind of labor-power best suited to his particular trade, be it spinning, bootmaking, or any other kind. He then proceeds to consume the commodity he has just bought, the labor-power, by making the worker, the personification of that labor-power, consume the means of production by his labor. The general character of the labor process is clearly not changed by the fact that the worker works for the capitalist instead of for himself. Moreover, the particular methods and operations used in bootmaking or spinning are not immediately changed by the capitalist’s stepping in. He must begin by taking labor-power as he finds it in the market, and so he must be satisfied with labor of the kind found in the period just before capitalists arose. Changes in the methods of production through the subordination of labor to capital (value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger) can take place only at a later period, and so they will have to be dealt with in a later chapter.

<!-- ch07-p023 -->
The labor process, turned into the process by which the capitalist consumes labor-power, shows two characteristic features. First, the worker works under the control of the capitalist, to whom his labor belongs. The capitalist takes good care that the work is done properly and that the means of production are used intelligently, so that there is no unnecessary waste of raw material and no wear and tear on the tools beyond what the work necessarily causes.

<!-- ch07-p024 -->
Secondly, the product is the property of the capitalist and not of the worker, its immediate producer. Suppose that a capitalist pays for a day’s labor-power at its value (value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time). Then the right to use that power for a day belongs to him, just as much as the right to use any other commodity, such as a horse he has hired for the day. The use of a commodity belongs to its buyer, and the seller of labor-power, by giving his labor, in reality does no more than part with the use-value he has sold. From the moment he steps into the workshop, the use-value of his labor-power, and therefore also its use, which is labor, belongs to the capitalist. By buying labor-power, the capitalist incorporates labor, as a living ferment, into the lifeless elements of the product. From his point of view, the labor process is nothing more than the consumption of the commodity he has bought, that is, of labor-power; but he cannot carry out this consumption except by supplying the labor-power with means of production. The labor process is a process between things that the capitalist has bought, things that have become his property. So the product of this process belongs to him, just as much as the wine that is the product of a process of fermentation completed in his cellar.[^7.10]

[^7.10]: “Products are appropriated before they are converted into capital; this conversion does not secure them from such appropriation.” (Cherbuliez: “Richesse ou Pauvreté,” edit. Paris, 1841, p. 54.) “The Proletarian [a member of the class of wage workers], by selling his labour for a definite quantity of the necessaries of life, renounces all claim to a share in the product. The mode of appropriation of the products remains the same as before; it is in no way altered by the bargain we have mentioned. The product belongs exclusively to the capitalist, who supplied the raw material and the necessaries of life; and this is a rigorous consequence of the law of appropriation, a law whose fundamental principle was the very opposite, namely, that every labourer has an exclusive right to the ownership of what he produces.” (cited above, p. 58.) “When the labourers receive wages for their labour ... the capitalist is then the owner not of the capital only” (he means the means of production) “but of the labour also. If what is paid as wages is included, as it commonly is, in the term capital, it is absurd to talk of labour separately from capital. The word capital as thus employed includes labour and capital both.” (James Mill: “Elements of Pol. Econ.,” etc., Ed. 1821, pp. 70, 71.)

### Section 2: The Production of Surplus-Value

<!-- ch07-p025 -->
The product that the capitalist appropriates (takes as his own) is a use-value, such as yarn, for example, or boots. Boots are, in one sense, the basis of all social progress, and our capitalist is a decided “progressist.” But even so, he does not manufacture boots for their own sake. In the production of commodities, use-value is by no means the thing “qu’on aime pour lui-même” [that one loves for its own sake]. Capitalists produce use-values only because, and only insofar as, they are the material base, the containers, of exchange-value (the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for). Our capitalist has two aims in view. First, he wants to produce a use-value that has an exchange-value, that is, an article meant to be sold: a commodity. Second, he wants to produce a commodity whose value will be greater than the sum of the values of the commodities used to produce it, that is, of the means of production and the labor-power that he bought with his good money on the open market. His aim is to produce not only a use-value, but also a commodity; not only use-value, but value; and not only value, but surplus-value at the same time (surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it).

<!-- ch07-p026 -->
We must keep in mind that we are now dealing with the production of commodities, and that so far we have looked at only one aspect of the process. Just as commodities are at the same time use-values and values, so the process of producing them must be a labor process and, at the same time, a process of creating value.[^7.11]

[^7.11]: As was stated in an earlier note, the English language has two different words for these two different aspects of labor. In the simple labor process, the process of producing use-values, it is *Work;* in the process of creating value, it is *Labour,* taking the term in its strictly economic sense. — *F. E.*

<!-- ch07-p027 -->
Let us now examine production as a creation of value.

<!-- ch07-p028 -->
We know that the value of each commodity is determined by the quantity of labor spent on it and materialized in it, that is, by the working time necessary, under given social conditions, to produce it. This rule also holds for the product that came to our capitalist as the result of the labor process carried on for him. Let us assume this product is 10 lbs. of yarn. Our first step is to calculate the quantity of labor realized in it.

<!-- ch07-p029 -->
To spin the yarn, raw material is needed; suppose in this case 10 lbs. of cotton. For now we have no need to investigate the value of this cotton, because our capitalist has, we will assume, bought it at its full value, say ten shillings. In this price, the labor needed to produce the cotton is already expressed in terms of the average labor of society. (A price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity.) We will further assume that the wear and tear of the spindle amounts to a value of 2s. For our present purpose, the spindle may stand for all the other instruments of labor used. So if twenty-four hours’ labor, or two working days, are needed to produce the quantity of gold represented by twelve shillings, then we have here, to begin with, two days’ labor already embodied in the yarn.

<!-- ch07-p030 -->
We must not let ourselves be misled by the fact that the cotton has taken a new shape, while the substance of the spindle has been used up to a certain extent. By the general law of value, if the value of 40 lbs. of yarn = the value of 40 lbs. of cotton + the value of a whole spindle, that is, if the same working time is needed to produce the commodities on either side of this equation, then 10 lbs. of yarn are an equivalent for 10 lbs. of cotton together with one-fourth of a spindle. In the case we are looking at, the same working time is materialized in the 10 lbs. of yarn on the one hand, and in the 10 lbs. of cotton and the fraction of a spindle on the other. So whether value appears in cotton, in a spindle, or in yarn makes no difference to the amount of that value. The spindle and cotton do not rest quietly side by side. Instead, they join together in the process, their forms are altered, and they are turned into yarn. But this affects their value no more than it would if they had simply been exchanged for their equivalent in yarn.

<!-- ch07-p031 -->
The labor needed to produce the cotton, the raw material of the yarn, is part of the labor necessary to produce the yarn, and so it is contained in the yarn. The same applies to the labor embodied in the spindle, since without the spindle’s wear and tear the cotton could not be spun.

<!-- ch07-p032 -->
Hence, in determining the value of the yarn, or the labor-time needed to produce it, all the special processes may together be looked on as different and successive phases of one and the same process. These are the processes, carried on at various times and in different places, that were necessary first to produce the cotton and the worn-away part of the spindle, and then to spin the yarn with the cotton and spindle. All the labor in the yarn is past labor. It is of no importance that the operations needed to produce its component elements were carried on at times further back from the present than the final operation of spinning. Suppose a definite quantity of labor, say thirty days, is needed to build a house. The total amount of labor embodied in it is not changed by the fact that the work of the last day is done twenty-nine days later than that of the first. Therefore the labor contained in the raw material and the instruments of labor can be treated just as if it were labor spent at an earlier stage of the spinning process, before the actual spinning began.

<!-- ch07-p033 -->
The values of the means of production, that is, of the cotton and the spindle, which are expressed in the price of twelve shillings, are therefore component parts of the value of the yarn, or, in other words, of the value of the product.

<!-- ch07-p034 -->
Two conditions must nevertheless be met. First, the cotton and spindle must work together to produce a use-value; in the present case they must become yarn. Value does not depend on the particular use-value that carries it, but it must be embodied in a use-value of some kind. Second, the time taken up by the labor of production must not exceed the time really necessary under the given social conditions of the case. So if no more than 1 lb. of cotton is needed to spin 1 lb. of yarn, care must be taken that no more than this weight of cotton is used up in producing 1 lb. of yarn; and the same goes for the spindle. Suppose the capitalist has a hobby and uses a gold spindle instead of a steel one. Even so, the only labor that counts for anything in the value of the yarn is the labor that would be needed to produce a steel spindle, because no more is necessary under the given social conditions.

<!-- ch07-p035 -->
We now know what part of the value of the yarn is due to the cotton and the spindle. It amounts to twelve shillings, or the value of two days’ work. The next point to consider is what part of the value of the yarn is added to the cotton by the labor of the spinner.

<!-- ch07-p036 -->
We must now look at this labor from a very different angle from the one it had during the labor process. There, we viewed it only as the particular kind of human activity that changes cotton into yarn. There, the better suited the labor was to the work, the better the yarn, other things being equal. The spinner’s labor was then seen as specifically different from other kinds of productive labor. It was different, on the one hand, in its special aim, namely spinning. On the other hand, it was different in the special character of its operations, in the special nature of its means of production, and in the special use-value of its product. Cotton and spindles are a necessity for spinning, but for making rifled cannon they would be of no use whatever. Here, on the contrary, we consider the spinner’s labor only insofar as it creates value, that is, only as a source of value. Seen this way, his labor does not differ in any respect from the labor of the man who bores cannon, or (what concerns us more closely here) from the labor of the cotton-planter and the spindle-maker embodied in the means of production. It is only because of this sameness that cotton planting, spindle making, and spinning can form the parts of one whole, parts that differ from each other only in quantity. That whole is the value of the yarn. Here we no longer have anything to do with the quality, the nature, and the specific character of the labor, but only with its quantity. And this simply has to be calculated. We proceed on the assumption that spinning is simple, unskilled labor, the average labor of a given state of society. Later we shall see that the opposite assumption would make no difference.

<!-- ch07-p037 -->
While the worker is at work, his labor constantly undergoes a transformation: from being motion, it becomes an object without motion; from being the worker working, it becomes the thing produced. At the end of one hour’s spinning, that act is represented by a definite quantity of yarn. In other words, a definite quantity of labor, namely one hour’s labor, has become embodied in the cotton. We say labor, that is, the spinner’s spending of his vital force, and not spinning labor. This is because the special work of spinning counts here only insofar as it is the expenditure of labor-power in general, and not insofar as it is the specific work of the spinner.

<!-- ch07-p038 -->
In the process we are now considering, it is extremely important that no more time be spent in turning the cotton into yarn than is necessary under the given social conditions. Suppose that under normal, that is, average social conditions of production, *a* pounds of cotton ought to be made into *b* pounds of yarn by one hour’s labor. Then a day’s labor does not count as 12 hours’ labor unless 12 *a* pounds of cotton have been made into 12 *b* pounds of yarn. For in the creation of value, only the time that is socially necessary counts.

<!-- ch07-p039 -->
Not only the labor, but also the raw material and the product now appear in quite a new light, very different from the one in which we saw them in the labor process pure and simple. The raw material now serves merely to absorb a definite quantity of labor. By this absorption it is in fact changed into yarn, because it is spun, because labor-power in the form of spinning is added to it. But the product, the yarn, is now nothing more than a measure of the labor absorbed by the cotton. If in one hour 1 2/3 lbs. of cotton can be spun into 1 2/3 lbs. of yarn, then 10 lbs. of yarn indicate the absorption of 6 hours’ labor. Definite quantities of product, quantities fixed by experience, now represent nothing but definite quantities of labor, definite masses of crystallized labor-time. They are nothing more than the materialization of so many hours or so many days of social labor.

<!-- ch07-p040 -->
Here we are no more concerned with the facts that the labor is the specific work of spinning, that its object is cotton, and that its product is yarn, than we are with the fact that the object itself is already a product, and therefore raw material. If the spinner were working in a coal mine instead of spinning, the object of his labor, the coal, would be supplied by Nature. Nevertheless, a definite quantity of extracted coal, a hundredweight for example, would represent a definite quantity of absorbed labor.

<!-- ch07-p041 -->
When the labor-power was sold, we assumed that the value of a day’s labor-power is three shillings, and that six hours’ labor is embodied in that sum. We assumed, therefore, that this amount of labor is needed to produce the necessaries of life that the worker requires daily on average. Now if our spinner, by working for one hour, can turn 1 2/3 lbs. of cotton into 1 2/3 lbs. of yarn,[^7.12] it follows that in six hours he will turn 10 lbs. of cotton into 10 lbs. of yarn. Hence, during the spinning process, the cotton absorbs six hours’ labor. The same quantity of labor is also embodied in a piece of gold worth three shillings. Consequently, the mere labor of spinning adds a value of three shillings to the cotton.

[^7.12]: These figures are quite arbitrary.

<!-- ch07-p042 -->
Let us now consider the total value of the product, the 10 lbs. of yarn. Two and a half days’ labor has been embodied in it. Two of these days were contained in the cotton and in the substance of the spindle that was worn away, and half a day was absorbed during the spinning process. This two and a half days’ labor is also represented by a piece of gold worth fifteen shillings. Hence fifteen shillings is an adequate price for the 10 lbs. of yarn, or the price of one pound is eighteenpence.

<!-- ch07-p043 -->
Our capitalist stares in astonishment. The value of the product is exactly equal to the value of the capital advanced. The value advanced has not expanded, no surplus-value has been created, and so money has not been turned into capital. The price of the yarn is fifteen shillings, and fifteen shillings were spent on the open market on the component elements of the product, or, what amounts to the same thing, on the factors of the labor process: ten shillings were paid for the cotton, two shillings for the substance of the spindle worn away, and three shillings for the labor-power. The swollen value of the yarn is no use, for it is merely the sum of the values that already existed in the cotton, the spindle, and the labor-power. Out of such a simple addition of existing values, no surplus-value can possibly arise.[^7.13] These separate values are now all concentrated in one thing. But so they were in the sum of fifteen shillings, too, before the purchase of the commodities split it into three parts.

[^7.13]: This is the fundamental proposition on which the Physiocrats based their doctrine that all labor that is not agriculture is unproductive. For the orthodox economist it is irrefutable. “Cette façon d’imputer à une seule chose la valeur de plusieurs autres” (par exemple au lin la consommation du tisserand), “d’appliquer, pour ainsi dire, couche sur couche, plusieurs valeurs sur une seule, fait que celle-ci grossit d’autant.... Le terme d’addition peint trés bien la maniere dont se forme le prix des ouvrages de main d’oeuvre; ce prix n’est qu’un total de plusieurs valeurs consommées et additionnées ensemble; or, additionner n’est pas multiplier.” [“This way of attributing to one single thing the value of several others” (for example, attributing to the flax the consumption of the weaver), “of applying, so to speak, layer upon layer, several values onto a single one, makes that one grow by just as much.... The term ‘addition’ paints very well the way in which the price of handmade goods is formed; this price is only a total of several values consumed and added together; but adding is not multiplying.”] (“Mercier de la Rivière,” cited above, p. 599.)

<!-- ch07-p044 -->
There is really nothing very strange in this result. Since the value of one pound of yarn is eighteenpence, if our capitalist buys 10 lbs. of yarn on the market, he must pay fifteen shillings for them. Clearly, whether a man buys his house ready built or has it built for him, in neither case will the way he acquires it increase the amount of money spent on the house.

<!-- ch07-p045 -->
Our capitalist, who is at home in his vulgar economics (economics that only describes and defends the surface appearances of the system, without investigating its real relations), exclaims: “Oh! but I advanced my money for the express purpose of making more money.” The road to Hell is paved with good intentions, and he might just as easily have intended to make money without producing at all.[^7.14] He threatens all sorts of things. He won’t be caught napping again. In future he will buy the commodities on the market, instead of manufacturing them himself. But if all his brother capitalists were to do the same, where would he find his commodities on the market? And he cannot eat his money. He tries persuasion. “Consider my abstinence. I might have played ducks and drakes with (frittered away) the 15 shillings; but instead I consumed it productively and made yarn with it.” Very well, and as his reward he now has good yarn instead of a bad conscience. As for playing the part of a miser, it would never do for him to slip back into such bad ways as that; we have seen before where such asceticism leads. Besides, where there is nothing, the king has lost his rights. Whatever the merit of his abstinence may be, there is nothing with which to reward it specially, because the value of the product is merely the sum of the values of the commodities that were thrown into the process of production. So let him console himself with the thought that virtue is its own reward. But no, he becomes insistent. He says: “The yarn is of no use to me: I produced it for sale.” In that case let him sell it. Or, better still, let him in future produce only things to satisfy his personal wants, a remedy that his physician MacCulloch has already prescribed as infallible against an epidemic of over-production. Now he gets obstinate. “Can the worker,” he asks, “produce commodities out of nothing, merely with his arms and legs? Did I not supply him with the materials by means of which, and in which alone, his labor could be embodied? And as the greater part of society consists of such ne’er-do-wells, have I not done society an incalculable service with my instruments of production, my cotton and my spindle? And not only society, but the worker too, whom I have also provided with the necessaries of life? And am I to be allowed nothing in return for all this service?” Well, but has not the worker done him the equivalent service of changing his cotton and spindle into yarn? Besides, there is no question of service here.[^7.15] A service is nothing more than the useful effect of a use-value, whether of a commodity or of labor.[^7.16] But here we are dealing with exchange-value. The capitalist paid the worker a value of 3 shillings, and the worker gave him back an exact equivalent: the value of 3 shillings that he added to the cotton. He gave him value for value. Our friend, until now so purse-proud, suddenly takes on the modest manner of his own worker, and exclaims: “Have I myself not worked? Have I not performed the labor of superintendence, of overseeing the spinner? And does not this labor, too, create value?” His overseer and his manager try to hide their smiles. Meanwhile, after a hearty laugh, he puts on his usual face again. He has chanted the whole creed of the economists to us, but in reality, he says, he would not give a brass farthing for it. He leaves this and all such evasions and juggling tricks to the professors of political economy (the science of economics as it was then called), who are paid for it. He himself is a practical man. He does not always consider what he says outside his business, but in his business he knows what he is about.

[^7.14]: Thus from 1844-47 he withdrew part of his capital from productive use in order to throw it away on railway speculation. And so too, during the American Civil War, he closed his factory and turned his workers out into the streets in order to gamble on the Liverpool cotton exchange.

[^7.15]: “Extol thyself, put on finery and adorn thyself ... but whoever takes more or better than he gives, that is usury, and is not service, but wrong done to his neighbour, as when one steals and robs. All is not service and benefit to a neighbour that is called service and benefit. For an adulteress and adulterer do one another great service and pleasure. A horseman does an incendiary [arsonist] a great service, by helping him to rob on the highway, and pillage land and houses. The papists do ours a great service, in that they don’t drown, burn, murder all of them, or let them all rot in prison; but let some live, and only drive them out, or take from them what they have. The devil himself does his servants inestimable service.... To sum up, the world is full of great, excellent, and daily service and benefit.” (Martin Luther: “An die Pfarrherrn wider den Wucher zu predigen,” Wittenberg, 1540.)

[^7.16]: In “Zur Kritik der Pol. Oek.,” p. 14, I make the following remark on this point: “It is not difficult to understand what ‘service’ the category ‘service’ must render to a class of economists like J. B. Say and F. Bastiat.”

<!-- ch07-p046 -->
Let us examine the matter more closely. The value of a day’s labor-power amounts to 3 shillings because, on our assumption, half a day’s labor is embodied in that quantity of labor-power; that is, because the means of subsistence needed daily for the production of labor-power cost half a day’s labor. But the past labor that is embodied in the labor-power and the living labor that it can set in motion, the daily cost of maintaining it and its daily expenditure in work, are two totally different things. The former determines the exchange-value of the labor-power; the latter is its use-value. The fact that half a day’s labor is necessary to keep the worker alive for 24 hours does not in any way prevent him from working a whole day. Therefore the value of labor-power, and the value which that labor-power creates in the labor process, are two entirely different magnitudes. This difference between the two values was what the capitalist had in view when he was buying the labor-power. The useful qualities that labor-power possesses, by which it makes yarn or boots, were to him nothing more than an indispensable condition; for in order to create value, labor must be spent in a useful way. What really influenced him was the specific use-value that this commodity possesses, of being *a source not only of value, but of more value than it has itself.* This is the special service that the capitalist expects from labor-power, and in this transaction he acts in accordance with the “eternal laws” of the exchange of commodities. The seller of labor-power, like the seller of any other commodity, realizes its exchange-value and parts with its use-value. He cannot take the one without giving the other. The use-value of labor-power, in other words labor, belongs just as little to its seller as the use-value of oil, once sold, belongs to the dealer who sold it. The owner of the money has paid the value of a day’s labor-power; so the use of it for a day is his; a day’s labor belongs to him. On the one hand, the daily upkeep of labor-power costs only half a day’s labor. On the other hand, the very same labor-power can work for a whole day, and consequently the value that its use creates during one day is double what he pays for that use. This circumstance is, without doubt, a piece of good luck for the buyer, but by no means an injury to the seller.

<!-- ch07-p047 -->
Our capitalist foresaw this state of things, and that was the cause of his laughter. So the worker finds in the workshop the means of production needed for working not only six hours, but twelve. Just as during the six hours’ process our 10 lbs. of cotton absorbed six hours’ labor and became 10 lbs. of yarn, so now 20 lbs. of cotton will absorb 12 hours’ labor and be changed into 20 lbs. of yarn. Let us now examine the product of this prolonged process. In these 20 lbs. of yarn the labor of five days is now materialized. Four days are due to the cotton and the lost steel of the spindle, and the remaining day was absorbed by the cotton during the spinning process. Expressed in gold, the labor of five days is thirty shillings. This is therefore the price of the 20 lbs. of yarn, giving, as before, eighteenpence as the price of a pound. But the sum of the values of the commodities that went into the process amounts to 27 shillings. The value of the yarn is 30 shillings. Therefore the value of the product is 1/9 greater than the value advanced for its production; 27 shillings have been transformed into 30 shillings; a surplus-value of 3 shillings has been created. The trick has worked at last; money has been turned into capital.

<!-- ch07-p048 -->
Every condition of the problem is satisfied, and the laws that regulate the exchange of commodities have been in no way violated. Equivalent has been exchanged for equivalent. For the capitalist, as buyer, paid its full value for each commodity: for the cotton, the spindle, and the labor-power. He then did what every buyer of commodities does: he consumed their use-value. The consumption of the labor-power, which was also the process of producing commodities, resulted in 20 lbs. of yarn with a value of 30 shillings. The capitalist, formerly a buyer, now returns to market as a seller of commodities. He sells his yarn at eighteenpence a pound, which is its exact value. Yet for all that, he draws 3 shillings more out of circulation (the exchange of commodities through money: selling and buying) than he originally threw into it. This metamorphosis, this conversion of money into capital, takes place both inside the sphere of circulation and outside it. It takes place inside circulation, because it depends on the purchase of the labor-power in the market. It takes place outside circulation, because what is done inside it is only a stepping-stone to the production of surplus-value, a process entirely confined to the sphere of production. Thus “tout est pour le mieux dans le meilleur des mondes possibles.” [“Everything is for the best in the best of all possible worlds.” – Voltaire, *Candide*]

<!-- ch07-p049 -->
By turning his money into commodities that serve as the material elements of a new product and as factors in the labor process, and by joining living labor to their dead substance, the capitalist at the same time turns value, that is, past, materialized, dead labor, into capital: into value pregnant with value, a live monster that is fruitful and multiplies.

<!-- ch07-p050 -->
If we now compare the two processes, producing value and creating surplus-value, we see that the second is nothing but the continuation of the first beyond a definite point. On the one hand, if the process is not carried beyond the point where the value paid by the capitalist for the labor-power is replaced by an exact equivalent, it is simply a process of producing value. On the other hand, if it is continued beyond that point, it becomes a process of creating surplus-value.

<!-- ch07-p051 -->
If we go further, and compare the process of producing value with the labor process pure and simple, we find that the labor process consists of the useful labor, the work, that produces use-values. Here we look at the labor as producing a particular article; we view it in its qualitative aspect alone, with regard to its end and aim. But viewed as a value-creating process, the same labor process presents itself in its quantitative aspect alone. Here it is merely a question of the time the worker takes to do the work, of the period during which the labor-power is usefully spent. Here, the commodities that take part in the process no longer count as necessary aids to labor-power in producing a definite, useful object. They count merely as containers of so much absorbed or materialized labor. That labor may have been embodied in the means of production before, or it may be incorporated in them for the first time during the process by the action of labor-power. In either case it counts only according to its duration: it amounts to so many hours or days, as the case may be.

<!-- ch07-p052 -->
Moreover, only as much of the time spent in producing any article is counted as is necessary under the given social conditions. This has various consequences. In the first place, the labor must be carried on under normal conditions. If a self-acting mule is the implement in general use for spinning, it would be absurd to supply the spinner with a distaff and spinning wheel. The cotton, too, must not be such rubbish as to cause extra waste in being worked; it must be of suitable quality. Otherwise the spinner would turn out to spend more time producing a pound of yarn than is socially necessary, and in that case the excess time would create neither value nor money. But whether the material factors of the process are of normal quality or not depends not on the worker, but entirely on the capitalist. Then again, the labor-power itself must be of average effectiveness. In the trade in which it is employed, it must have the average skill, dexterity, and speed usual in that trade, and our capitalist took good care to buy labor-power of such normal quality. This power must be applied with the average amount of effort and with the usual degree of intensity. The capitalist is as careful to see that this is done as he is to see that his workers are not idle for a single moment. He has bought the use of the labor-power for a definite period, and he insists on his rights. He has no intention of being robbed. Lastly, all wasteful consumption of raw material or instruments of labor is strictly forbidden, and for this purpose our friend has a penal code of his own. For what is wasted in this way represents labor spent needlessly, labor that does not count in the product or enter into its value.[^7.17]

[^7.17]: This is one of the circumstances that make production by slave labor such a costly process. Here the worker, to use a striking expression of the ancients, is distinguished only as instrumentum vocale [speaking tool] from an animal as instrumentum semi-vocale [half-speaking tool], and from an implement as instrumentum mutum [mute tool]. But he himself takes care to let both beast and implement feel that he is none of them, but is a man. He convinces himself, with immense satisfaction, that he is a different being, by treating the one mercilessly and damaging the other lovingly. Hence the principle, applied everywhere in this method of production, of using only the crudest and heaviest implements, ones that are hard to damage because of their sheer clumsiness. In the slave states bordering on the Gulf of Mexico, right up to the date of the Civil War, the only plows to be found were built on old Chinese models, which turned up the soil like a hog or a mole instead of making furrows. Compare J. E. Cairnes. “The Slave Power,” London, 1862, p. 46 and following. In his “Sea Board Slave States,” Olmsted tells us: “I am here shown tools that no man in his senses, with us, would allow a labourer, for whom he was paying wages, to be encumbered with; and the excessive weight and clumsiness of which, I would judge, would make work at least ten per cent greater than with those ordinarily used with us. And I am assured that, in the careless and clumsy way they must be used by the slaves, anything lighter or less rude could not be furnished them with good economy, and that such tools as we constantly give our labourers and find our profit in giving them, would not last out a day in a Virginia cornfield – much lighter and more free from stones though it be than ours. So, too, when I ask why mules are so universally substituted for horses on the farm, the first reason given, and confessedly the most conclusive one, is that horses cannot bear the treatment that they always must get from negroes; horses are always soon foundered [lamed] or crippled by them, while mules will bear cudgelling [beating with a club], or lose a meal or two now and then, and not be materially injured, and they do not take cold or get sick, if neglected or overworked. But I do not need to go further than to the window of the room in which I am writing, to see at almost any time, treatment of cattle that would ensure the immediate discharge of the driver by almost any farmer owning them in the North.”

<!-- ch07-p053 -->
We now see that the difference between labor considered on the one hand as producing useful things, and on the other hand as creating value, a difference we discovered by our analysis of a commodity, comes down to a distinction between two aspects of the process of production.

<!-- ch07-p054 -->
The process of production, considered on the one hand as the unity of the labor process and the process of creating value, is production of commodities. Considered on the other hand as the unity of the labor process and the process of producing surplus-value, it is the capitalist process of production, or capitalist production of commodities.

<!-- ch07-p055 -->
We stated on an earlier page that in the creation of surplus-value it does not matter in the least whether the labor the capitalist appropriates is simple unskilled labor of average quality or more complicated skilled labor. All labor of a higher or more complicated character than average labor is the expenditure of a more costly kind of labor-power: labor-power whose production has cost more time and labor, and which therefore has a higher value, than unskilled or simple labor-power. Since this power has a higher value, its consumption is labor of a higher class, labor that creates proportionally higher values in equal times than unskilled labor does. Whatever difference in skill there may be between the labor of a spinner and that of a jeweler, the part of his labor by which the jeweler merely replaces the value of his own labor-power does not differ in quality in any way from the additional part by which he creates surplus-value. In making jewelry, just as in spinning, the surplus-value results only from a quantitative excess of labor, from lengthening one and the same labor process: in the one case the process of making jewels, in the other the process of making yarn.[^7.18]

[^7.18]: The distinction between skilled and unskilled labor rests partly on pure illusion, or, to say the least, on distinctions that long ago ceased to be real and survive only through traditional convention. It rests partly on the helpless condition of some groups of the working class, a condition that prevents them from extracting the value of their labor-power as fully as the rest do. Accidental circumstances play so great a part here that these two forms of labor sometimes change places. Take, for instance, places where the physique of the working class has deteriorated and is, relatively speaking, exhausted, which is the case in all countries with a well-developed capitalist production. There, the lower forms of labor, which demand great expenditure of muscle, are in general considered skilled compared with much more delicate forms of labor, and the latter sink down to the level of unskilled labor. Take as an example the labor of a bricklayer, which in England ranks much higher than that of a damask-weaver. Again, although the labor of a fustian cutter demands great bodily effort and is unhealthy as well, it counts only as unskilled labor. And then we must not forget that so-called skilled labor does not take up a large space in the field of national labor. Laing estimates that in England (and Wales) the livelihood of 11,300,000 people depends on unskilled labor. If from the total population of 18,000,000 living at the time when he wrote we deduct 1,000,000 for the “genteel population,” 1,500,000 for paupers, vagrants, criminals, prostitutes, etc., and 4,650,000 who make up the middle class, there remain the above-mentioned 11,000,000. But in his middle class he includes people who live on the interest of small investments, officials, writers, artists, schoolmasters, and the like, and to swell the number he also includes among these 4,650,000 the better-paid part of the factory workers! The bricklayers, too, figure among them. (S. Laing: “National Distress,” etc., London, 1844). “The great class who have nothing to give for food but ordinary labour, are the great bulk of the people.” (James Mill, in art.: “Colony,” Supplement to the Encyclop. Brit., 1831.)

<!-- ch07-p056 -->
But on the other hand, in every process of creating value, the reduction of skilled labor to average social labor, for example of one day of skilled labor to six days of unskilled labor, is unavoidable.[^7.19] So we spare ourselves an unnecessary operation, and simplify our analysis, by assuming that the labor of the worker employed by the capitalist is unskilled average labor.

[^7.19]: “Where reference is made to labour as a measure of value, it necessarily implies labour of one particular kind ... the proportion which the other kinds bear to it being easily ascertained.” (“Outlines of Pol. Econ.,” London, 1832, pp. 22 and 23.)

## Chapter 8: Constant Capital and Variable Capital

<!-- ch08-p001 -->
The various factors of the labor process (the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things) play different parts in forming the value of the product. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.)

<!-- ch08-p002 -->
The worker adds fresh value to the object of his labor by spending a given amount of additional labor on it, whatever the specific character and usefulness of that labor may be. On the other hand, the values of the means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things) that are used up in the process are preserved. They show up again as parts of the value of the product. The values of the cotton and the spindle, for instance, reappear in the value of the yarn. So the value of the means of production is preserved by being transferred to the product. This transfer takes place while those means are being turned into a product, in other words, during the labor process. It is brought about by labor; but how?

<!-- ch08-p003 -->
The worker does not perform two operations at once, one to add value to the cotton, and the other to preserve the value of the means of production, or, what amounts to the same thing, to transfer to the yarn, to the product, the value of the cotton he works on and part of the value of the spindle he works with. But by the very act of adding new value, he preserves their former values. Adding new value to the object of his labor and preserving its former value are, however, two entirely distinct results. The worker produces them at the same time, during one operation. So clearly this two-sided result can be explained only by the two-sided nature of his labor. At one and the same time, his labor must create value in one capacity, and preserve or transfer value in another.

<!-- ch08-p004 -->
Now, how does every worker add new labor, and so new value? Clearly, only by working productively in a particular way: the spinner by spinning, the weaver by weaving, the smith by forging. But while he thus embodies labor in general, that is, value, it is only through the particular form of the labor, through the spinning, the weaving, and the forging respectively, that the means of production (the cotton and spindle, the yarn and loom, and the iron and anvil) become parts of the product, of a new use-value (the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties).[^8.1] Each use-value disappears, but only to reappear in a new form in a new use-value. Now, when we were looking at the process of creating value, we saw the following. If a use-value is effectively consumed in producing a new use-value, the quantity of labor spent in producing the consumed article forms part of the quantity of labor needed to produce the new use-value. So this part is labor transferred from the means of production to the new product. Hence the worker preserves the values of the consumed means of production, or transfers them to the product as parts of its value, not because of his additional labor considered abstractly, but because of the particular useful character of that labor, because of its special productive form. So insofar as labor is this kind of specific productive activity, insofar as it is spinning, weaving, or forging, it raises the means of production from the dead by mere contact. It makes them living factors of the labor process, and combines with them to form the new products.

[^8.1]: “Labour gives a new creation for one extinguished.” (“An Essay on the Polit. Econ. of Nations,” London, 1821, p. 13.)

<!-- ch08-p005 -->
If the special productive labor of the worker were not spinning, he could not turn the cotton into yarn, and so he could not transfer the values of the cotton and spindle to the yarn. Suppose the same worker changed his occupation and became a joiner. He would still add value to the material he works on by a day’s labor. So we see, first, that new value is added not because his labor is spinning in particular, or joinery in particular, but because it is abstract human labor (labor counted simply as the spending of human effort, of brain, muscle, and nerve, whatever particular kind it is), a portion of the total labor of society. And we see next that the value added is of a given, definite amount, not because his labor has a special usefulness, but because it is carried on for a definite time. On the one hand, then, spinning adds new value to the values of the cotton and the spindle because of its general character, as the spending of human labor-power in the abstract. (Labor-power is a person’s capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist.) On the other hand, the same labor of spinning both transfers the values of the means of production to the product and preserves them in the product, because of its special character, as a concrete, useful process. Hence a two-sided result is produced at one and the same time.

<!-- ch08-p006 -->
By simply adding a certain quantity of labor, new value is added; and by the quality of this added labor, the original values of the means of production are preserved in the product. This two-sided effect, which comes from the two-sided character of labor, can be traced in various phenomena.

<!-- ch08-p007 -->
Let us assume that some invention lets the spinner spin as much cotton in 6 hours as he could spin before in 36 hours. For the purposes of useful production, his labor is now six times as effective as it was. The product of 6 hours’ work has grown six-fold, from 6 lbs. to 36 lbs. But now the 36 lbs. of cotton absorb only the same amount of labor as the 6 lbs. did before. Each pound of cotton absorbs one-sixth as much new labor, and so the value added by the labor to each pound is only one-sixth of what it was before. On the other hand, in the product, in the 36 lbs. of yarn, the value transferred from the cotton is six times as great as before. Through the 6 hours’ spinning, the value of the raw material that is preserved and transferred to the product is six times as great as before, although the new value that the spinner’s labor adds to each pound of the very same raw material is one-sixth of what it was before. This shows that the two properties of labor that enable it in one case to preserve value, and in the other to create value, are essentially different. On the one hand, the longer the time needed to spin a given weight of cotton into yarn, the greater the new value added to the material. On the other hand, the greater the weight of cotton spun in a given time, the greater the value preserved by being transferred from it to the product.

<!-- ch08-p008 -->
Now let us assume that the productivity of the spinner’s labor, instead of varying, stays constant. So he needs the same time as before to turn one pound of cotton into yarn. But let us assume that the exchange-value of the cotton varies (exchange-value is the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for): either it rises to six times its former value, or it falls to one-sixth of that value. In both these cases the spinner puts the same quantity of labor into a pound of cotton, and so adds as much value as he did before the change in value. He also produces a given weight of yarn in the same time as he did before. Nevertheless, the value he transfers from the cotton to the yarn is either one-sixth of what it was before the change, or, as the case may be, six times as much as before. The same result occurs when the value of the instruments of labor rises or falls while their usefulness in the process stays the same.

<!-- ch08-p009 -->
Again, if the technical conditions of the spinning process stay the same, and the means of production undergo no change of value, the spinner goes on consuming, in equal working times, equal quantities of raw material and equal quantities of machinery of unchanging value. The value he preserves in the product is directly proportional to the new value he adds to the product. In two weeks he embodies twice as much labor, and therefore twice as much value, as in one week. During the same time he consumes twice as much material and wears out twice as much machinery, of double the value in each case. So in the product of two weeks he preserves twice as much value as in the product of one week. As long as the conditions of production stay the same, the more value the worker adds by fresh labor, the more value he transfers and preserves. But he does so merely because this addition of new value takes place under conditions that have not changed and that are independent of his own labor. Of course, it may be said in one sense that the worker always preserves old value in proportion to the quantity of new value he adds. Whether the value of cotton rises from one shilling to two shillings, or falls to sixpence, the worker always preserves in the product of one hour only half as much value as he preserves in two hours. In the same way, if the productivity of his own labor varies, rising or falling, he will spin more or less cotton in one hour than he did before, as the case may be. So he will preserve more or less value of cotton in the product of one hour. But all the same, he will preserve twice as much value by two hours’ labor as by one.

<!-- ch08-p010 -->
Value exists only in useful articles, in objects; we leave aside its purely symbolic representation by tokens. (Man himself, seen as the embodiment of labor-power, is a natural object, a thing, although a living, conscious thing; and labor is the outward expression of this power residing in him.) So if an article loses its usefulness, it also loses its value. The reason why means of production do not lose their value at the same time as they lose their use-value is this: in the labor process they lose the original form of their use-value only to take on the form of a new use-value in the product. But however important it may be for value to have some useful object in which to be embodied, it makes no difference at all which particular object serves this purpose. We saw this when we dealt with the metamorphosis of commodities. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer’s own use. A metamorphosis is a change of form: a commodity changing into money, a sale, C–M, or money changing into a commodity, a purchase, M–C.) Hence it follows that in the labor process the means of production transfer their value to the product only insofar as they lose their exchange-value along with their use-value. They give up to the product only the value that they themselves lose as means of production. But in this respect the material factors of the labor process do not all behave alike.

<!-- ch08-p011 -->
The coal burned under the boiler vanishes without leaving a trace; so, too, does the tallow used to grease the axles of wheels. Dyes and other auxiliary substances also vanish, but reappear as properties of the product. Raw material forms the substance of the product, but only after it has changed its form. So raw material and auxiliary substances lose the characteristic form they had when they entered the labor process. It is different with the instruments of labor. Tools, machines, workshops, and vessels are of use in the labor process only as long as they keep their original shape, ready each morning to start the process again with their shape unchanged. And just as they keep their shape independent of the product during their lifetime, that is, during the continued labor process in which they serve, so they do after their death too. The corpses of machines, tools, workshops, etc., always remain separate and distinct from the product they helped to turn out. Now take any instrument of labor over the whole period of its service, from the day it enters the workshop until the day it is banished to the junk room. We find that during this period its use-value has been completely consumed, and therefore its exchange-value has been completely transferred to the product. For instance, if a spinning machine lasts for 10 years, clearly its total value is gradually transferred during that working period to the product of the 10 years. So the lifetime of an instrument of labor is spent in repeating a greater or smaller number of similar operations. Its life may be compared with that of a human being. Every day brings a man 24 hours nearer to his grave; but no one can tell exactly, just by looking at him, how many days he still has to travel on that road. This difficulty, however, does not stop life insurance offices from drawing very accurate, and at the same time very profitable, conclusions by means of the theory of averages. It is the same with the instruments of labor. Experience tells us how long, on average, a machine of a particular kind will last. Suppose its use-value in the labor process lasts only six days. Then on average it loses one-sixth of its use-value each day, and so gives up one-sixth of its value to the daily product.
