The wear and tear of all instruments, their daily loss of use-value, and the corresponding quantity of value they give up to the product, are calculated accordingly on this basis.

<!-- ch08-p012 -->
So it is strikingly clear that means of production never transfer more value to the product than they themselves lose during the labor process through the destruction of their own use-value. If such an instrument has no value to lose, in other words, if it is not the product of human labor, it transfers no value to the product. It helps to create use-value without contributing to the formation of exchange-value. This class includes all means of production supplied by Nature without human help, such as land, wind, water, metals still in the ground, and timber in virgin forests.

<!-- ch08-p013 -->
Yet another interesting phenomenon shows itself here. Suppose a machine is worth £1,000 and wears out in 1,000 days. Then one-thousandth of the value of the machine is transferred each day to the day’s product. At the same time, though with dwindling vitality, the machine as a whole goes on taking part in the labor process. Thus it appears that one factor of the labor process, a means of production, continually enters that process as a whole, while it enters the process of forming value only by fractions. The difference between the two processes is reflected here in their material factors: the same instrument of production takes part as a whole in the labor process, while at the same time, as an element in the formation of value, it enters only by fractions.[^8.2]

[^8.2]: The subject of repairs to the implements of labor does not concern us here. A machine that is being repaired no longer plays the part of an instrument, but that of an object of labor. Work is no longer done with it, but on it. For our purpose it is quite permissible to assume that the labor spent on repairing instruments is included in the labor needed to produce them in the first place. But in the text we deal with the wear and tear that no doctor can cure, and that little by little brings about death: with “that kind of wear which cannot be repaired from time to time, and which, in the case of a knife, would ultimately reduce it to a state in which the cutler would say of it, it is not worth a new blade.” We have shown in the text that a machine takes part in every labor process as a whole machine, but that it enters the simultaneous process of creating value only bit by bit. How great, then, is the confusion of ideas shown in the following extract! “Mr. Ricardo says a portion of the labour of the engineer in making [stocking] machines” is contained, for example, in the value of a pair of stockings. “Yet the total labour, that produced each single pair of stockings ... includes the whole labour of the engineer, not a portion; for one machine makes many pairs, and none of those pairs could have been done without any part of the machine.” “Obs. on Certain Verbal Disputes in Pol. Econ., Particularly Relating to Value,” p. 54. The author, an uncommonly self-satisfied know-it-all, is right in his confusion, and therefore in his claim, to this extent only: neither Ricardo nor any other economist, before or since him, has accurately distinguished the two aspects of labor, and still less, therefore, the part labor plays under each of these aspects in the formation of value.

<!-- ch08-p014 -->
On the other hand, a means of production may take part as a whole in the formation of value, while it enters the labor process only bit by bit. Suppose that in spinning cotton, the waste for every 115 lbs. used amounts to 15 lbs., which is turned not into yarn but into “devil’s dust.” This 15 lbs. of cotton never becomes part of the yarn. Yet if we assume that this amount of waste is normal and unavoidable under average conditions of spinning, its value is transferred to the value of the yarn just as surely as the value of the 100 lbs. that form the substance of the yarn. The use-value of 15 lbs. of cotton must vanish into dust before 100 lbs. of yarn can be made. So the destruction of this cotton is a necessary condition for producing the yarn. And because it is a necessary condition, and for no other reason, the value of that cotton is transferred to the product. The same holds for every kind of waste that results from a labor process, at least insofar as such waste cannot be used further as a means of producing new and independent use-values. Such a use of waste can be seen in the large machine works at Manchester, where mountains of iron turnings are carted off to the foundry in the evening, to reappear in the workshops the next morning as solid masses of iron.

<!-- ch08-p015 -->
We have seen that the means of production transfer value to the new product only insofar as they lose value, in the shape of their old use-value, during the labor process. The most value they can lose in the process is clearly limited by the amount of original value they had when they came into the process, in other words, by the labor-time needed to produce them. So the means of production can never add more value to the product than they themselves have, independently of the process they assist in. However useful a given kind of raw material, or a machine, or other means of production may be, even if it costs £150, or, say, 500 days’ labor, it still cannot, under any circumstances, add more than £150 to the value of the product. Its value is determined not by the labor process it enters as a means of production, but by the process it came out of as a product. In the labor process it serves only as a mere use-value, a thing with useful properties. So it could not transfer any value to the product unless it already had such value.[^8.3]

[^8.3]: From this we may judge how absurd J. B. Say is. He claims to explain surplus-value (Interest, Profit, Rent) by the “services productifs” [“productive services”] that the means of production, soil, instruments, and raw material, perform in the labor process through their use-values. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it.) Mr. Wm. Roscher, who seldom misses a chance to record, in black and white, ingenious fancies that defend the system, records the following specimen: – “J. B. Say (Traité, t. 1, ch. 4) very truly remarks: the value produced by an oil mill, after deduction of all costs, is something new, something quite different from the labour by which the oil mill itself was erected.” (cited above, p. 82, note.) Very true, Mr. Professor! The oil produced by the oil mill is indeed something very different from the labor spent in building the mill! By value, Mr. Roscher understands such stuff as “oil,” because oil has value, even though “Nature” produces petroleum, though relatively “in small quantities.” He seems to be referring to this fact in his further remark: “It (Nature) produces scarcely any exchange-value.” Mr. Roscher’s “Nature” and the exchange-value it produces are rather like the foolish virgin who admitted, indeed, that she had had a child, but “it was such a little one.” This “savant sérieux” [“serious scholar”] goes on to remark: “Ricardo’s school is in the habit of including capital as accumulated labour under the head of labour. This is unskilful work, because, indeed, the owner of capital, after all, does something more than the merely creating and preserving of the same: namely, the abstention from the enjoyment of it, for which he demands, *e.g.*, interest.” (cited above) How very “skilful” is this “anatomico-physiological method” of political economy (the science of economics as it was then called), which, “indeed,” turns a mere desire “after all” into a source of value.

<!-- ch08-p016 -->
While productive labor is changing the means of production into parts of a new product, their value undergoes a metempsychosis. It leaves the consumed body to occupy the newly created one. But this transmigration takes place, as it were, behind the worker’s back. He cannot add new labor, cannot create new value, without at the same time preserving old values. This is because the labor he adds must be of a specific useful kind, and he cannot do useful work without using products as the means of production of a new product, and so transferring their value to the new product. So the property that labor-power in action, living labor, has of preserving value at the same time as it adds value is a gift of Nature that costs the worker nothing. But it is very advantageous to the capitalist, since it preserves the existing value of his capital (value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger).[^8.4] As long as trade is good, the capitalist is too absorbed in money-grubbing to notice this free gift of labor. A violent interruption of the labor process by a crisis makes him keenly aware of it.[^8.5]

[^8.4]: “Of all the instruments of the farmers’ trade, the labour of man ... is that on which he is most to rely for the repayment of his capital. The other two ... the working stock of the cattle and the ... carts, ploughs, spades, and so forth, without a given portion of the first, are nothing at all.” (Edmund Burke: “Thoughts and Details on Scarcity, originally presented to the Right Hon. W. Pitt, in the month of November 1795,” Edit. London, 1800, p. 10.)

[^8.5]: In *The Times* of 26th November, 1862, a manufacturer whose mill employed 800 workers and consumed on average 150 bales of East Indian, or 130 bales of American, cotton complains dolefully about the standing expenses of his factory when it is not working. He estimates them at £6,000 a year. Among them are a number of items that do not concern us here, such as rent, rates, and taxes, insurance, and the salaries of the manager, book-keeper, engineer, and others. Then he reckons £150 for coal used to heat the mill occasionally and to run the engine now and then. Besides this, he includes the wages of the people employed at odd times to keep the machinery in working order. Lastly, he puts down £1,200 for depreciation of machinery, because “the weather and the natural principle of decay do not suspend their operations because the steam-engine ceases to revolve.” He says emphatically that he does not estimate his depreciation at more than the small sum of £1,200, because his machinery is already nearly worn out.

<!-- ch08-p017 -->
As regards the means of production, what is really consumed is their use-value, and the consumption of this use-value by labor results in the product. There is no consumption of their value,[^8.6] and so it would be inaccurate to say that it is reproduced. Rather, it is preserved. This is not because of any operation it undergoes itself in the process, but because the article in which it originally exists vanishes, it is true, but vanishes into some other article. Hence in the value of the product the value of the means of production reappears, but strictly speaking there is no reproduction of that value. What is produced is a new use-value in which the old exchange-value reappears.[^8.7]

[^8.6]: “Productive consumption ... where the consumption of a commodity is a part of the process of production. ... In these instances there is no consumption of value.” (S. P. Newman, cited above, p. 296.)

[^8.7]: In an American handbook that has gone through perhaps 20 editions, this passage occurs: “It matters not in what form capital re-appears;” then, after a lengthy list of all the possible ingredients of production whose value reappears in the product, the passage ends like this: “The various kinds of food, clothing, and shelter, necessary for the existence and comfort of the human being, are also changed. They are consumed from time to time, and their value re-appears in that new vigour imparted to his body and mind, forming fresh capital, to be employed again in the work of production.” (F. Wayland, cited above, pp. 31, 32.) Leaving aside any other oddities, it is enough to note that what reappears in the fresh vigor is not the bread’s price (the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity), but its blood-forming substances. What reappears in the value of that vigor, on the other hand, is not the means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live), but their value. The same necessaries of life, at half the price, would form just as much muscle and bone, just as much vigor, but not vigor of the same value. This confusion of “value” and “vigour,” together with our author’s sanctimonious vagueness, marks an attempt, futile all the same, to work out an explanation of surplus-value from a mere reappearance of values that already existed.

<!-- ch08-p018 -->
It is different with the subjective factor of the labor process, with labor-power in action. Because his labor is of a specialized kind with a special object, the worker preserves the value of the means of production and transfers it to the product. At the same time, by the mere act of working, he creates an additional, new value at every instant. Suppose the process of production stops just when the worker has produced an equivalent for the value of his own labor-power: when, for example, by six hours’ labor, he has added a value of three shillings. This value is the surplus of the total value of the product over the part of its value that is due to the means of production. It is the only original bit of value formed during this process, the only part of the value of the product created by this process. Of course, we do not forget that this new value only replaces the money the capitalist advanced to buy the labor-power, and that the worker spent on the necessities of life. With regard to the money spent, the new value is merely a reproduction. But nevertheless it is an actual reproduction, and not, as in the case of the value of the means of production, only an apparent one. Here one value is replaced by another through the creation of new value.

<!-- ch08-p019 -->
We know, however, from what has gone before, that the labor process may continue beyond the time needed to reproduce, and embody in the product, a mere equivalent for the value of the labor-power. Instead of the six hours that are enough for that purpose, the process may continue for twelve hours. So the action of labor-power not only reproduces its own value, but produces value over and above it. This surplus-value is the difference between the value of the product and the value of the elements consumed in forming that product, in other words, of the means of production and the labor-power.

<!-- ch08-p020 -->
By explaining the different parts that the various factors of the labor process play in forming the value of the product, we have in fact revealed the character of the different functions assigned to the different elements of capital in the process of expanding its own value. The surplus of the total value of the product over the sum of the values of its constituent factors is the surplus of the expanded capital over the capital originally advanced. The means of production on the one hand, and labor-power on the other, are merely the different forms of existence that the value of the original capital took on when it was changed from money into the various factors of the labor process. So the part of capital that is represented by the means of production, by the raw material, auxiliary material, and the instruments of labor, does not undergo any quantitative change of value in the process of production. I therefore call it the constant part of capital, or, more briefly, *constant capital.*

<!-- ch08-p021 -->
On the other hand, the part of capital represented by labor-power does undergo a change of value in the process of production. It both reproduces the equivalent of its own value and also produces an excess, a surplus-value, which may itself vary, and may be greater or smaller according to circumstances. This part of capital is continually being changed from a constant into a variable quantity. I therefore call it the variable part of capital, or, briefly, *variable capital.* The same elements of capital which, from the point of view of the labor process, appear as the objective and subjective factors respectively, as means of production and labor-power, appear, from the point of view of the process of creating surplus-value, as constant and variable capital.

<!-- ch08-p022 -->
The definition of constant capital given above by no means rules out the possibility of a change of value in its elements. Suppose the price of cotton is sixpence a pound one day, and the next day, because the cotton crop has failed, a shilling a pound. Each pound of the cotton bought at sixpence, and worked up after the rise in value, transfers a value of one shilling to the product. And the cotton already spun before the rise, perhaps circulating in the market as yarn, likewise transfers twice its original value to the product. Clearly, however, these changes of value are independent of the increment, the surplus-value, that the spinning itself adds to the value of the cotton. If the old cotton had never been spun, it could, after the rise, be resold at a shilling a pound instead of at sixpence. Further, the fewer the processes the cotton has gone through, the more certain this result is. So we find that when such sudden changes in value occur, speculators make it a rule to speculate in the material on which the least possible quantity of labor has been spent: to speculate, therefore, in yarn rather than in cloth, and in cotton itself rather than in yarn. In the case we have been looking at, the change of value originates, not in the process in which the cotton plays the part of a means of production, and in which it therefore functions as constant capital, but in the process in which the cotton itself is produced. The value of a commodity, it is true, is determined by the quantity of labor contained in it, but this quantity is itself limited by social conditions. Suppose the time socially necessary for producing any commodity changes – and a given weight of cotton represents more labor after a bad harvest than after a good one. Then all previously existing commodities of the same class are affected, because they are, as it were, only individuals of the species,[^8.8] and their value at any given time is measured by the labor socially necessary, that is, by the labor needed to produce them under the social conditions existing at that time.

[^8.8]: “Toutes les productions d’un même genre ne forment proprement qu’une masse, dont le prix se détermine en général et sans égard aux circonstances particulières.” (Le Trosne, cited above, p. 893.) [“Properly speaking, all products of the same kind form a single mass, whose price is fixed in general and without regard to particular circumstances.”]

<!-- ch08-p023 -->
Just as the value of the raw material may change, so may the value of the instruments of labor, the machinery, etc., used in the process; and so the part of the value of the product that is transferred to it from them may also change. If a new invention means that machinery of a particular kind can be produced with less labor, the old machinery loses more or less of its value, and so transfers that much less value to the product. But here again the change in value originates outside the process in which the machine acts as a means of production. Once engaged in this process, the machine cannot transfer more value than it has apart from the process.

<!-- ch08-p024 -->
Just as a change in the value of the means of production, even after they have begun to take part in the labor process, does not alter their character as constant capital, so, too, a change in the proportion of constant to variable capital does not affect the respective functions of these two kinds of capital. The technical conditions of the labor process may be revolutionized to such an extent that where formerly ten men, using ten implements of small value, worked up a relatively small quantity of raw material, one man may now, with the help of one expensive machine, work up one hundred times as much raw material. In the latter case we have an enormous increase in the constant capital, represented by the total value of the means of production used, and at the same time a great reduction in the variable capital, invested in labor-power. Such a revolution, however, alters only the quantitative relation between the constant and the variable capital, that is, the proportions in which the total capital is split into its constant and variable parts. It has not in the least affected the essential difference between the two.

## Chapter 9: The Rate of Surplus-Value

### Section 1: The Degree of Exploitation of Labor-Power

<!-- ch09-p001 -->
The surplus-value (the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it) that is generated in the process of production by C, the capital advanced (capital: value that is used to make more value, money that is advanced in order to come back larger), is, in other words, the self-expansion of the value of the capital C. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) In the first place, this surplus-value presents itself to us as a surplus: the amount by which the value of the product is greater than the value of the elements that make it up.

<!-- ch09-p002 -->
The capital C is made up of two parts. One is the sum of money c laid out on the means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things). The other is the sum of money v spent on the labor-power (a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything; it is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist). c stands for the part that has become constant capital, and v for the part that has become variable capital. (Constant capital is the part of capital spent on means of production; its value is passed on to the product but does not grow. Variable capital is the part of capital spent on labor-power; it reproduces its own value and also produces surplus-value, so its size varies.) At first, then, C = c + v. For example, if £500 is the capital advanced, its parts may be such that the £500 = £410 const. + £90 var. When the process of production is finished, we get a commodity (a thing produced in order to be exchanged, that is, sold, not for the producer's own use) whose value = (c + v) + s, where s is the surplus-value. Or, using our earlier figures, the value of this commodity may be (£410 const. + £90 var.) + £90 surpl. The original capital has now changed from C to C', from £500 to £590. The difference is s, or a surplus-value of £90. The value of the elements that make up the product is equal to the value of the capital advanced. So it is a mere tautology, saying the same thing twice, to say that the excess of the value of the product over the value of its elements is equal to the expansion of the capital advanced, or to the surplus-value produced.

<!-- ch09-p003 -->
Even so, we must look at this tautology a little more closely. The two things compared are the value of the product and the value of its elements used up in the process of production. Now, we have seen how the part of the constant capital that consists of the instruments of labor passes on only a fraction of its value to what is being produced, while the rest of that value stays in those instruments. Since this rest plays no part in forming value, we may leave it aside for now. Bringing it into the calculation would make no difference. For instance, take our earlier example, c = £410. Suppose this sum consists of £312 value of raw material, £44 value of auxiliary material, and £54 value of the machinery worn away in the process. And suppose that the total value of the machinery employed is £1,054. Out of this last sum, then, we count as advanced for turning out the product only the £54 that the machinery loses by wear and tear in the process, because this is all it passes on to the product. Now if we also count the remaining £1,000, which still stays in the machinery, as transferred to the product, we ought also to count it as part of the value advanced, and so make it appear on both sides of our calculation.[^9.1] In this way we would get £1,500 on one side and £1,590 on the other. The difference between these two sums, or the surplus-value, would still be £90. Throughout this Book, therefore, by constant capital advanced for the production of value we always mean the value of the means of production actually used up in the process, and that value alone, unless the context rules this out.

[^9.1]: “If we reckon the value of the fixed capital employed as a part of the advances, we must reckon the remaining value of such capital at the end of the year as a part of the annual returns.” (Malthus, “Princ. of Pol. Econ.” 2nd. ed., London, 1836, p. 269.)

<!-- ch09-p004 -->
With this settled, let us return to the formula C = c + v, which, as we saw, was transformed into C' = (c + v) + s, C becoming C'. We know that the value of the constant capital is transferred to the product and merely reappears in it. So the new value actually created in the process, the value produced, or value-product, is not the same as the value of the product. It is not, as it would seem at first sight, (c + v) + s, or £410 const. + £90 var. + £90 surpl. It is v + s, or £90 var. + £90 surpl.: not £590 but £180. Suppose c = 0. In other words, suppose there were branches of industry in which the capitalist could do without all means of production made by previous labor, whether raw material, auxiliary material, or instruments of labor, and employed only labor-power and materials supplied by Nature. In that case there would be no constant capital to transfer to the product. This part of the value of the product, that is, the £410 in our example, would disappear. But the sum of £180, the amount of new value created, or the value produced, which contains £90 of surplus-value, would stay just as large as if c stood for the highest value imaginable. We would have C = (0 + v) = v, or C', the expanded capital, = v + s, and therefore C' - C = s, as before. On the other hand, suppose s = 0. In other words, suppose the labor-power, whose value is advanced in the form of variable capital, produced only its equivalent. Then we would have C = c + v, or C', the value of the product, = (c + v) + 0, or C = C'. In this case the capital advanced would not have expanded its value.

<!-- ch09-p005 -->
From what has gone before, we know that surplus-value is purely the result of a change in the value of v, the part of the capital that is turned into labor-power. Consequently, v + s = v + v', or v plus an increase of v. But the fact that it is v alone that varies, and the conditions of that variation, are hidden by a circumstance: because the variable part of the capital increases, the total of the capital advanced increases too. It was originally £500 and becomes £590. So, for our investigation to lead to accurate results, we must leave out of account the part of the value of the product in which only constant capital appears. That is, we must set the constant capital equal to zero, or make c = 0. This is merely an application of a mathematical rule, used whenever we work with constant and variable magnitudes that are related to each other only by the signs of addition and subtraction.

<!-- ch09-p006 -->
A further difficulty comes from the original form of the variable capital. In our example, C' = £410 const. + £90 var. + £90 surpl. But £90 is a given, and therefore a constant, quantity, so it seems absurd to treat it as variable. In fact, though, the term £90 var. is here merely a symbol to show that this value goes through a process. The part of the capital invested in buying labor-power is a definite quantity of materialized labor, a constant value, like the value of the labor-power bought. But in the process of production the place of the £90 is taken by labor-power in action: dead labor is replaced by living labor, something stagnant by something flowing, a constant by a variable. The result is the reproduction of v plus an increase of v. From the standpoint of capitalist production, then, the whole process appears as the spontaneous change of the originally constant value that is turned into labor-power. Both the process and its result appear to be due to this value. So if expressions such as “£90 variable capital” or “so much self-expanding value” seem contradictory, this is only because they bring to the surface a contradiction built into capitalist production.

<!-- ch09-p007 -->
At first sight it seems a strange thing to do, to set the constant capital equal to zero. Yet we do it every day. If, for example, we want to calculate the amount of England's profits from the cotton industry, we first of all deduct the sums paid for cotton to the United States, India, Egypt and other countries. In other words, the value of the capital that merely reappears in the value of the product is put = 0.

<!-- ch09-p008 -->
Of course, it is economically of very great importance to know the ratio of surplus-value not only to the part of the capital from which it directly springs, and whose change in value it represents, but also to the total capital advanced. We shall therefore treat this ratio exhaustively in the third book. For one part of a capital to expand its value by being turned into labor-power, another part must be turned into means of production. For variable capital to perform its function, constant capital must be advanced in the proper proportion, a proportion given by the special technical conditions of each labor process (the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things). But the fact that retorts (glass vessels for distilling) and other vessels are necessary to a chemical process does not compel the chemist to take notice of them in the result of his analysis. If we look at the means of production in their relation to the creation of value and to the change in the quantity of value, apart from anything else, they appear simply as the material in which labor-power, the value-creator, embodies itself. Neither the nature nor the value of this material is of any importance. The only requirement is that there be a sufficient supply of it to absorb the labor spent in the process of production. Once that supply is given, the material may rise or fall in value, or even, like land and the sea, have no value in itself; but this will have no influence on the creation of value or on the change in the quantity of value.[^9.2]

[^9.2]: What Lucretius says is self-evident: “nil posse creari de nihilo,” out of nothing, nothing can be created. Creating value is turning labor-power into labor. Labor-power itself is energy transferred to a human organism by means of nourishing matter.

<!-- ch09-p009 -->
So, in the first place, we set the constant capital equal to zero. The capital advanced is therefore reduced from c + v to v, and instead of the value of the product (c + v) + s we now have the value produced (v + s). Given that the new value produced = £180, this sum therefore represents the whole labor spent during the process. Subtracting from it £90, the value of the variable capital, we have £90 left, the amount of the surplus-value. This sum of £90, or s, expresses the absolute quantity of surplus-value produced. The relative quantity produced, or the percentage increase of the variable capital, is clearly determined by the ratio of the surplus-value to the variable capital, or is expressed by s/v. In our example this ratio is 90/90, which gives an increase of 100%. This relative increase in the value of the variable capital, or the relative magnitude of the surplus-value, I call “The rate of surplus-value.”[^9.3]

[^9.3]: In the same way as the English use the terms “rate of profit” and “rate of interest.” We shall see in Book III that the rate of profit is no mystery as soon as we know the laws of surplus-value. If we reverse the process, we can understand neither the one nor the other.

<!-- ch09-p010 -->
We have seen that during one part of the labor process the worker produces only the value of his labor-power, that is, the value of his means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live). Now, his work forms part of a system based on the social division of labor. So he does not directly produce the actual necessities that he himself consumes. Instead he produces a particular commodity, yarn for example, whose value is equal to the value of those necessities, or of the money with which they can be bought. The part of his day's labor spent on this will be greater or smaller in proportion to the value of the necessities he requires daily on average, or, what comes to the same thing, in proportion to the labor-time required on average to produce them. If the value of those necessities represents on average the expenditure of six hours' labor, the worker must on average work for six hours to produce that value. If, instead of working for the capitalist, he worked independently on his own account, he would, other things being equal, still have to labor for the same number of hours to produce the value of his labor-power, and so to gain the means of subsistence necessary for his maintenance or continued reproduction. But, as we have seen, during the part of his day's labor in which he produces the value of his labor-power, say three shillings, he produces only an equivalent for the value of his labor-power already advanced[^9.4] by the capitalist; the new value created only replaces the variable capital advanced. Because of this fact, the production of the new value of three shillings takes on the appearance of a mere reproduction. So the part of the working day during which this reproduction takes place I call “*necessary*” labor-time, and the labor spent during that time I call “*necessary*” labor.[^9.5] It is necessary as regards the worker, because it does not depend on the particular social form of his labor. It is necessary as regards capital and the world of capitalists, because their existence also depends on the continued existence of the worker.

[^9.4]: *Note added in the 3rd German edition.* — The author is using the economic language in current use here. It will be remembered that on p. 182 (present edition, p. 174) it was shown that in reality the worker “advances” to the capitalist, and not the capitalist to the worker. — *F. E.*

[^9.5]: In this work we have so far used the term “necessary labor-time” to mean the time necessary under given social conditions for producing any commodity. From now on we also use it to mean the time necessary for producing the particular commodity labor-power. Using one and the same technical term in different senses is inconvenient, but in no science can it be altogether avoided. Compare, for instance, the higher with the lower branches of mathematics.

<!-- ch09-p011 -->
During the second period of the labor process, the one in which his labor is no longer necessary labor, the worker does labor, it is true, and does spend labor-power. But since his labor is no longer necessary labor, he creates no value for himself. He creates surplus-value, which, for the capitalist, has all the charms of a creation out of nothing. This part of the working day I name surplus labor-time, and to the labor spent during that time I give the name of surplus labor. To understand surplus-value correctly, it is every bit as important to see it as merely surplus labor-time in congealed form, as nothing but materialized surplus labor, as it is, to understand value properly, to see value as merely so many hours of labor in congealed form, as nothing but materialized labor. The essential difference between the various economic forms of society, for instance between a society based on slave labor and one based on wage labor, lies only in the way in which this surplus labor is in each case extracted from the actual producer, the worker.[^9.6]

[^9.6]: Herr Wilhelm Thucydides Roscher has found a mare's nest (a great discovery that turns out to be nothing). He has made the important discovery that if, on the one hand, the formation of surplus-value, or surplus-produce, and the accumulation of capital that follows from it (accumulation of capital: turning surplus-value back into capital, so that capital grows) are nowadays due to the thrift of the capitalist, on the other hand, in the lowest stages of civilization, it is the strong who compel the weak to economize. (cited above, p. 78.) To economize what? Labor? Or superfluous wealth that does not exist? What is it that makes men like Roscher account for the origin of surplus-value by a mere reheating of the more or less plausible excuses the capitalist gives for appropriating surplus-value? It is, besides their real ignorance, their dread, as apologists for the system, of a scientific analysis of value and surplus-value, and of reaching a result that might not be altogether palatable to the powers that be.

<!-- ch09-p012 -->
On the one hand, the values of the variable capital and of the labor-power bought by that capital are equal, and the value of this labor-power determines the necessary part of the working day (the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor). On the other hand, the surplus-value is determined by the surplus part of the working day. It follows that surplus-value bears the same ratio to variable capital as surplus labor does to necessary labor. In other words, the rate of surplus-value s/v = (surplus labor)/(necessary labor). Both ratios, s/v and (surplus labor)/(necessary labor), express the same thing in different ways: the one by reference to materialized, embodied labor, the other by reference to living, flowing labor.

<!-- ch09-p013 -->
The rate of surplus-value is therefore an exact expression for the degree of exploitation of labor-power by capital, or of the worker by the capitalist.[^9.7]

[^9.7]: Although the rate of surplus-value is an exact expression for the degree of exploitation of labor-power, it is in no sense an expression for the absolute amount of exploitation. For example, if the necessary labor = 5 hours and the surplus labor = 5 hours, the degree of exploitation is 100%. The amount of exploitation is here measured by 5 hours. If, on the other hand, the necessary labor = 6 hours and the surplus labor = 6 hours, the degree of exploitation stays at 100%, as before, while the actual amount of exploitation has increased 20%, namely from five hours to six.

<!-- ch09-p014 -->
In our example we assumed that the value of the product = £410 const. + £90 var. + £90 surpl., and that the capital advanced = £500. Since the surplus-value = £90 and the capital advanced = £500, the usual way of reckoning would give us a rate of surplus-value (which is generally confused with the rate of profits) of 18%. That rate is so low that it might give a pleasant surprise to Mr. Carey and other harmonizers (economists who taught that the interests of all classes are in harmony). But in truth the rate of surplus-value is not equal to s/C or s/(c+v), but to s/v. So it is not 90/500 but 90/90, or 100%, which is more than five times the apparent degree of exploitation. In the case we have supposed, we do not know the actual length of the working day, or how long the labor process lasts in days or weeks, or the number of workers employed. Even so, the rate of surplus-value s/v accurately reveals to us, through its equivalent expression, surplus labor/necessary labor, the relation between the two parts of the working day. Here this relation is one of equality, the rate being 100%. Clearly, then, the worker in our example works one half of the day for himself and the other half for the capitalist.

<!-- ch09-p015 -->
So, in short, the method of calculating the rate of surplus-value is as follows. We take the total value of the product and set the constant capital, which merely reappears in it, equal to zero. What remains is the only value that has actually been created in the process of producing the commodity. If the amount of surplus-value is given, we have only to deduct it from this remainder to find the variable capital. And the other way round, if the variable capital is given and we need to find the surplus-value. If both are given, we have only to perform the final operation, namely to calculate s/v, the ratio of the surplus-value to the variable capital.

<!-- ch09-p016 -->
Simple as the method is, it may not be out of place to give the reader some practice, by means of a few examples, in applying the new principles that underlie it.

<!-- ch09-p017 -->
First let us take the case of a spinning mill with 10,000 mule spindles, spinning No. 32 yarn from American cotton and producing 1 lb. of yarn per spindle each week. We assume the waste to be 6%. Under these circumstances 10,600 lbs. of cotton are used up weekly, of which 600 lbs. go to waste. The price (the money name of the value – the labor – embodied in a commodity) of the cotton in April, 1871, was 7¾d. per lb., so the raw material costs, in round numbers, £342. The 10,000 spindles, including preparation machinery and motive power, cost, we will assume, £1 per spindle, a total of £10,000. We put the wear and tear at 10%, or £1,000 a year = £20 a week. We suppose the rent of the building to be £300 a year, or £6 a week. The coal used (for 100 horse-power indicated, at 4 lbs. of coal per horse-power per hour during 60 hours, including the coal used for heating the mill) comes to 11 tons a week at 8s. 6d. a ton, about £4½ a week; gas, £1 a week; oil, etc., £4½ a week. The total cost of these auxiliary materials is £10 a week. So the constant part of the value of the week's product is £378. Wages (the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself) amount to £52 a week. The price of the yarn is 12¼d. per lb., which gives £510 as the value of 10,000 lbs. So the surplus-value in this case is £510 - £430 = £80. We set the constant part of the value of the product = 0, since it plays no part in the creation of value. What remains is £132 as the value created each week, which = £52 var. + £80 surpl. The rate of surplus-value is therefore 80/52 = 153 11/13%. In a working day of 10 hours with average labor, the result is: necessary labor = 3 31/33 hours, and surplus labor = 6 2/33.[^9.8]

[^9.8]: The above data, which may be relied on, were given to me by a Manchester spinner. In England the horse-power of an engine used to be calculated from the diameter of its cylinder; now the actual horse-power shown by the indicator is taken.

<!-- ch09-p018 -->
One more example. Jacob gives the following calculation for the year 1815. Because several items were adjusted beforehand, it is very imperfect; nevertheless it is sufficient for our purpose. In it he assumes the price of wheat to be 8s. a quarter, and the average yield per acre to be 22 bushels.

<!-- ch09-p019 -->
```text
VALUE PRODUCED PER ACRE
Seed        £1 9s. 0d.       Tithes, Rates,   £1 1s. 0d.
                             and taxes,
Manure      £2 10s. 0d.      Rent             £1 8s. 0d.
Wages       £3 10s. 0d.      Farmer’s Profit  £1 2s. 0d.
                             and Interest
TOTAL       £7 9s. 0d.       TOTAL            £3 11s 0d.
```

<!-- ch09-p020 -->
Assuming that the price of the product is the same as its value, we find here the surplus-value divided up under the various headings of profit, interest, rent, etc. We have nothing to do with these in detail; we simply add them together, and the sum is a surplus-value of £3 11s. 0d. The sum of £3 19s. 0d. paid for seed and manure is constant capital, and we put it equal to zero. What is left is the sum of £3 10s. 0d., which is the variable capital advanced, and we see that a new value of £3 10s. 0d. + £3 11s. 0d. has been produced in its place. Therefore s/v = £3 11s. 0d. / £3 10s. 0d., giving a rate of surplus-value of more than 100%. The worker spends more than one half of his working day producing the surplus-value, which different persons share among themselves under different pretexts.[^9.9]

[^9.9]: The calculations given in the text are meant merely as illustrations. We have in fact assumed that prices = values. We shall see in Book III, however, that even in the case of average prices this assumption cannot be made in this very simple way.

### Section 2: The Representation of the Components of the Value of the Product by Corresponding Proportional Parts of the Product Itself

<!-- ch09-p021 -->
Let us now go back to the example that showed us how the capitalist turns money into capital.

<!-- ch09-p022 -->
The product of a working day of 12 hours is 20 lbs. of yarn, with a value of 30s. No less than 8/10ths of this value, or 24s., is due simply to the reappearance in the yarn of the value of the means of production (20 lbs. of cotton, value 20s., and spindle worn away, 4s.). So this part is constant capital. The remaining 2/10ths, or 6s., is the new value created during the spinning process. One half of this replaces the value of the day's labor-power, that is, the variable capital; the other half makes up a surplus-value of 3s. So the total value of the 20 lbs. of yarn is made up as follows:

<!-- ch09-p023 -->
30s. value of yarn = 24s. const. + 3s. var. + 3s. surpl.

<!-- ch09-p024 -->
Since the whole of this value is contained in the 20 lbs. of yarn produced, it follows that the various component parts of this value can be represented as contained in corresponding parts of the product, each in its own part.

<!-- ch09-p025 -->
If the value of 30s. is contained in 20 lbs. of yarn, then 8/10ths of this value, or the 24s. that make up its constant part, is contained in 8/10ths of the product, that is, in 16 lbs. of yarn. Of these, 13 1/3 lbs. represent the value of the raw material, the 20s. worth of cotton spun, and 2 2/3 lbs. represent the 4s. worth of spindle, etc., worn away in the process.

<!-- ch09-p026 -->
So the whole of the cotton used up in spinning the 20 lbs. of yarn is represented by 13 1/3 lbs. of yarn. It is true that, by weight, this amount of yarn contains no more than 13 1/3 lbs. of cotton, worth 13 1/3 shillings. But the additional value of 6 2/3 shillings contained in it is the equivalent of the cotton used up in spinning the remaining 6 2/3 lbs. of yarn. The effect is the same as if these 6 2/3 lbs. of yarn contained no cotton at all, and the whole 20 lbs. of cotton were packed into the 13 1/3 lbs. of yarn. On the other hand, this last-named weight of yarn does not contain a single atom either of the value of the auxiliary materials and implements, or of the value newly created in the process.

<!-- ch09-p027 -->
In the same way, the 2 2/3 lbs. of yarn in which the 4s., the rest of the constant capital, is embodied represent nothing but the value of the auxiliary materials and instruments of labor used up in producing the 20 lbs. of yarn.

<!-- ch09-p028 -->
So we have arrived at this result: although eight-tenths of the product, or 16 lbs. of yarn, is, as a useful article, just as much the work of the spinner's labor as the rest of the same product, yet, seen in this connection, it does not contain, and has not absorbed, any labor spent during the process of spinning. It is just as if the cotton had turned itself into yarn without help, as if the shape it had taken were mere trickery and deceit. For as soon as our capitalist sells it for 24s. and uses the money to replace his means of production, it becomes clear that these 16 lbs. of yarn are nothing more than so much cotton and spindle-waste in disguise.

<!-- ch09-p029 -->
On the other hand, the remaining 2/10ths of the product, or 4 lbs of yarn, represent nothing but the new value of 6s. created during the 12 hours' spinning process. All the value transferred to those 4 lbs from the raw material and instruments of labor used up was, so to speak, intercepted so that it could be built into the 16 lbs. spun first. In this case it is as if the spinner had spun 4 lbs. of yarn out of air, or as if he had spun them with the help of cotton and spindles that were a spontaneous gift of Nature and so transferred no value to the product.

<!-- ch09-p030 -->
Of these 4 lbs. of yarn, in which the whole of the value newly created during the process is condensed, one half represents the equivalent of the value of the labor used up, or the 3s. variable capital; the other half represents the 3s. surplus-value.

<!-- ch09-p031 -->
Since 12 working hours of the spinner are embodied in 6s., it follows that yarn with a value of 30s. must have 60 working hours embodied in it. And this amount of labor-time does in fact exist in the 20 lbs of yarn. For in 8/10ths, or 16 lbs, are materialized the 48 hours of labor that were spent on the means of production before the spinning process began; and in the remaining 2/10ths, or 4 lbs, are materialized the 12 hours' work done during the process itself.

<!-- ch09-p032 -->
On an earlier page we saw that the value of the yarn is equal to the sum of the new value created during the production of that yarn plus the value that already existed in the means of production.

<!-- ch09-p033 -->
It has now been shown how the various component parts of the value of the product, parts that differ from each other in function, may be represented by corresponding proportional parts of the product itself.

<!-- ch09-p034 -->
The product can be split up in this way into different parts. One part represents only the labor previously spent on the means of production, or the constant capital. Another represents only the necessary labor spent during the process of production, or the variable capital. A third and last part represents only the surplus labor spent during the same process, or the surplus-value. To do this is no less important than it is simple, as will be seen later on, when it is applied to complicated problems that have not been solved until now.

<!-- ch09-p035 -->
In the investigation above, we have treated the total product as the final result, ready for use, of a working day of 12 hours. But we can also follow this total product through all the stages of its production. In this way we shall arrive at the same result as before, if we represent the partial products turned out at the different stages as functionally different parts of the final or total product.

<!-- ch09-p036 -->
The spinner produces 20 lbs. of yarn in 12 hours, or 1⅔ lbs in 1 hour. So in 8 hours he produces 13⅔ lbs., a partial product equal in value to all the cotton that is spun in a whole day. In the same way, the partial product of the next period of 1 hour and 36 minutes is 2⅔ lbs. of yarn; this represents the value of the instruments of labor that are used up in 12 hours. In the following hour and 12 minutes, the spinner produces 2 lbs. of yarn worth 3 shillings, a value equal to the whole value he creates in his 6 hours' necessary labor. Finally, in the last hour and 12 minutes he produces another 2 lbs. of yarn, whose value is equal to the surplus-value created by his surplus labor during half a day. The English manufacturer uses this method of calculation in everyday practice. It shows, he will say, that in the first 8 hours, or ⅔ of the working day, he gets back the value of his cotton, and so on for the remaining hours. It is also a perfectly correct method. In fact it is the first method given above, with this difference: instead of being applied to space, in which the different parts of the finished product lie side by side, it deals with time, in which those parts are produced one after another. But it can also come with very barbarous notions, especially in the heads of people who are as interested, in practice, in the process of making value breed value as they are in misunderstanding that process in theory. Such people may get it into their heads that our spinner, for example, produces or replaces in the first 8 hours of his working day the *value* of the cotton; in the following hour and 36 minutes the *value* of the instruments of labor worn away; in the next hour and 12 minutes the *value* of the wages; and that he devotes only that well-known “last hour” to producing surplus-value for the manufacturer. In this way the poor spinner is made to perform a double miracle. He not only produces cotton, spindles, steam-engine, coal, oil, etc., at the same time as he spins with them, but also turns one working day into five. For in the example we are considering, producing the raw material and instruments of labor takes four working days of twelve hours each, and turning them into yarn takes another such day. That the love of gain makes people quick to believe in such miracles, and that fawning doctrinaire theorists are never lacking to prove them, is borne out by the following historically famous incident.

### Section 3: Senior’s “Last Hour”

<!-- ch09-p037 -->
One fine morning in the year 1836, Nassau W. Senior was summoned from Oxford to Manchester. Senior may be called the leading wit among English economists, and he was well known both for his economic “science” and for his beautiful style. He was summoned to learn in Manchester the political economy (the science of economics as it was then called) that he taught in Oxford. The manufacturers chose him as their champion, not only against the newly passed Factory Act, but against the still more threatening agitation for a ten-hour day. With their usual practical sharpness, they had found out that the learned Professor “wanted [needed] a good deal of finishing;” it was this discovery that made them write to summon him. For his part, the Professor wrote up the lecture he had received from the Manchester manufacturers in a pamphlet, entitled: “Letters on the Factory Act, as it affects the cotton manufacture.” London, 1837. In it we find, among other things, the following edifying passage:

<!-- ch09-p038 -->
> “Under the present law, no mill in which persons under 18 years of age are employed, ... can be worked more than 11½ hours a day, that is, 12 hours for 5 days in the week, and nine on Saturday.

<!-- ch09-p039 -->
> “Now the following analysis (!) will show that in a mill so worked, the whole net profit is derived *from the last hour*. I will suppose a manufacturer to invest £100,000: – £80,000 in his mill and machinery, and £20,000 in raw material and wages. The annual return of that mill, supposing the capital to be turned [turned over] once a year, and gross profits to be 15 per cent., ought to be goods worth £115,000.... Of this £115,000, each of the twenty-three half-hours of work produces 5-115ths or one twenty-third. Of these 23-23rds (constituting the whole £115,000) twenty, that is to say £100,000 out of the £115,000, simply replace the capital; – one twenty-third (or £5,000 out of the £115,000) makes up for the deterioration of the mill and machinery. The remaining 2-23rds, that is, the last two of the twenty-three half-hours of every day, produce the net profit of 10 per cent. If, therefore (prices remaining the same), the factory could be kept at work thirteen hours instead of eleven and a half, with an addition of about £2,600 to the circulating capital, the net profit would be more than doubled. On the other hand, if the hours of working were reduced by one hour per day (prices remaining the same), the *net* profit would be destroyed – if they were reduced by one hour and a half, even the *gross* profit would be destroyed.”[^9.10]

[^9.10]: Senior, cited above, pp. 12, 13. We pass over such extraordinary notions as do not matter for our purpose. One example is the claim that manufacturers count as part of their profit, gross or net, the amount needed to make good the wear and tear of machinery, or in other words, to replace a part of the capital. In the same way, we pass over any question of whether his figures are accurate. Leonard Horner has shown in “A Letter to Mr. Senior,” etc., London, 1837, that they are worth no more than the so-called “Analysis.” Leonard Horner was one of the Factory Inquiry Commissioners in 1833, and Inspector, or rather Censor, of Factories until 1859. He did undying service to the English working class. He fought a lifelong battle, not only with the embittered manufacturers, but also with the Cabinet, which cared far more about the number of votes the employers cast in the Lower House than about the number of hours the “hands” worked in the mills.

    Apart from questions of principle, Senior’s statement is muddled. What he really meant to say was this: The manufacturer employs the worker for 11½ hours, or for 23 half-hours, a day. Like the working day, the working year may be thought of as consisting of 11½ hours or 23 half-hours, but each multiplied by the number of working days in the year. On this assumption, the 23 half-hours yield an annual product of £115,000; one half-hour yields 1/23 × £115,000; 20 half-hours yield 20/23 × £115,000 = £100,000, that is, they replace no more than the capital advanced. There remain 3 half-hours, which yield 1/23 × £115,000 = £5,000 or the gross profit. Of these 3 half-hours, one yields 1/23 × £115,000 = £5,000; that is, it makes up for the wear and tear of the machinery; the remaining 2 half-hours, that is, the last hour, yield 2/23 × £115,000 = £10,000 or the net profit. In the text, Senior turns the last 2/23 of the product into portions of the working day itself.

<!-- ch09-p040 -->
And the Professor calls this an “analysis!” Suppose he trusted the outcries of the manufacturers, and believed that the workers spend the best part of the day producing, that is, reproducing or replacing, the value of the buildings, machinery, cotton, coal, etc. In that case his analysis was unnecessary. His answer would simply have been: – Gentlemen! if you work your mills for 10 hours instead of 11½, then, other things being equal, the daily consumption of cotton, machinery, etc., will decrease in proportion. You gain just as much as you lose. In future your workers will spend one hour and a half less in reproducing or replacing the capital that has been advanced. – Suppose, on the other hand, that he did not believe them without further inquiry, but, as an expert in such matters, thought an analysis necessary. In that case he ought, in a question that concerns only the relation of net profit to the length of the working day, first of all to have asked the manufacturers to be careful not to lump together machinery, workshops, raw material, and labor. He ought to have asked them to be good enough to place the constant capital, invested in buildings, machinery, raw material, etc., on one side of the account, and the capital advanced in wages on the other side. If the Professor then found that, according to the manufacturers’ calculation, the worker reproduced or replaced his wages in 2 half-hours, then he should have continued his analysis like this:

<!-- ch09-p041 -->
According to your figures, the worker produces his wages in the last hour but one, and your surplus-value or net profit in the last hour. Now, since he produces equal values in equal periods, the product of the last hour but one must have the same value as that of the last hour. Further, he produces value only while he labors, and the amount of his labor is measured by his labor-time. This, you say, amounts to 11½ hours a day. He uses one portion of these 11½ hours in producing or replacing his wages, and the remaining portion in producing your net profit. Beyond this he does absolutely nothing. But since, on your assumption, his wages and the surplus-value he yields are of equal value, it is clear that he produces his wages in 5¾ hours, and your net profit in the other 5¾ hours. Again, since the value of the yarn produced in 2 hours is equal to the sum of the values of his wages and of your net profit, the measure of the value of this yarn must be 11½ working-hours. Of these, 5¾ hours measure the value of the yarn produced in the last hour but one, and 5¾ the value of the yarn produced in the last hour. Now we come to a tricky point, so pay attention! The last working-hour but one is, like the first, an ordinary working-hour, neither more nor less. How then can the spinner produce in one hour, in the shape of yarn, a value that embodies 5¾ hours’ labor? The truth is that he performs no such miracle. The use-value he produces in one hour is a definite quantity of yarn. (Use-value is the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties.) The value of this yarn is measured by 5¾ working-hours. Of these, 4¾ were already embodied in the means of production, in the cotton, the machinery, and so on, without any help from him; he adds only the remaining one hour. So since his wages are produced in 5¾ hours, and the yarn produced in one hour also contains 5¾ hours’ work, there is no witchcraft in the result that the value created by his 5¾ hours of spinning is equal to the value of the product spun in one hour. You are altogether on the wrong track if you think that he loses a single moment of his working day in reproducing or replacing the values of the cotton, the machinery, and so on. On the contrary, it is because his labor turns the cotton and spindles into yarn, because he spins, that the values of the cotton and spindles pass over to the yarn of their own accord. This result is due to the quality of his labor, not to its quantity. It is true that in one hour he will transfer more value to the yarn, in the shape of cotton, than in half an hour; but that is only because in one hour he spins up more cotton than in half an hour. So you see, your assertion that the worker produces the value of his wages in the last hour but one, and your net profit in the last hour, amounts to no more than this: in the yarn he produces in 2 working-hours, whether they are the first 2 or the last 2 hours of the working day, in that yarn there are incorporated 11½ working-hours, or just a whole day’s work, that is, two hours of his own work and 9½ hours of other people’s. And my assertion that he produces his wages in the first 5¾ hours, and your net profit in the last 5¾ hours, amounts only to this: you pay him for the former, but not for the latter. When I speak of payment of labor, instead of payment of labor-power, I am only talking your own slang. Now, gentlemen, if you compare the working time you pay for with the working time you do not pay for, you will find that they are to one another as half a day is to half a day. This gives a rate of 100%, and a very pretty percentage it is. Further, there is not the least doubt that if you make your “hands” toil for 13 hours instead of 11½, and, as may be expected of you, treat the work done in that extra hour and a half as pure surplus labor, then surplus labor will rise from 5¾ hours’ labor to 7¼ hours’ labor, and the rate of surplus-value from 100% to 126 2/23%. So you are far too hopeful in expecting that adding 1½ hours to the working day will raise the rate from 100% to 200% and more, in other words that it will be “more than doubled.” On the other hand ‒ man’s heart is a wonderful thing, especially when carried in the purse – you take too pessimistic a view when you fear that, if the hours of labor are cut from 11½ to 10, the whole of your net profit will go to the dogs. Not at all. If all other conditions remain the same, surplus labor will fall from 5¾ hours to 4¾ hours, a period that still gives a very profitable rate of surplus-value, namely 82 14/23%. But this dreadful “last hour,” about which you have invented more stories than the millenarians have about the day of judgment, is “all bosh.” If it goes, it will cost neither you your net profit, nor the boys and girls you employ their “purity of mind.”[^9.11] Whenever your “last hour” strikes in earnest, think of the Oxford Professor. And now, gentlemen, “farewell, and may we meet again in yonder better world, but not before.”

[^9.11]: If, on the one hand, Senior proved that the manufacturer’s net profit, the existence of the English cotton industry, and England’s command of the markets of the world depend on “the last working-hour,” then, on the other hand, Dr. Andrew Ure showed the following. If children and young persons under 18 years of age are turned out an hour sooner into the heartless and frivolous outside world, instead of being kept the full 12 hours in the warm and pure moral atmosphere of the factory, idleness and vice will rob them of all hope of salvation for their souls. Since 1848, the factory inspectors have never tired of taunting the employers with this “last,” this “fatal hour.” Thus Mr. Hovell in his report of the 21st May, 1855: “Had the following ingenious calculation (he quotes Senior) been correct, every cotton factory in the United Kingdom would have been working at a loss since the year 1850.” (Reports of the Insp. of Fact., for the half-year, ending 30th April, 1855, pp. 19, 20.) In the year 1848, after the 10 hours’ bill was passed, the employers of some flax spinning mills, scattered few and far between over the country on the borders of Dorset and Somerset, foisted a petition against the bill onto the shoulders of a few of their workers. One of the clauses of this petition reads: “Your petitioners, as parents, conceive that an additional hour of leisure will tend more to demoralise the children than otherwise, believing that idleness is the parent of vice.” On this the factory report of 31st Oct., 1848, says: The atmosphere of the flax mills, in which the children of these virtuous and tender parents work, is so loaded with dust and fibre from the raw material, that it is exceptionally unpleasant to stand even 10 minutes in the spinning rooms: for you are unable to do so without the most painful sensation, owing to the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, and mouth, being immediately filled by the clouds of flax dust from which there is no escape. The labour itself, owing to the feverish haste of the machinery, demands unceasing application of skill and movement, under the control of a watchfulness that never tires, and it seems somewhat hard, to let parents apply the term “idling” to their own children, who, after allowing for meal-times, are fettered for 10 whole hours to such an occupation, in such an atmosphere.... These children work longer than the labourers in the neighbouring villages.... Such cruel talk about “idleness and vice” ought to be branded as the purest cant [hypocritical talk], and the most shameless hypocrisy.... That portion of the public, who, about 12 years ago, were struck by the assurance with which, under the sanction of high authority, it was publicly and most earnestly proclaimed, that the whole net profit of the manufacturer flows from the labour of the last hour, and that, therefore, the reduction of the working day by one hour, would destroy his net profit, that portion of the public, we say, will hardly believe its own eyes, when it now finds, that the original discovery of the virtues of “the last hour” has since been so far improved, as to include morals as well as profit; so that, if the duration of the labour of children, is reduced to a full 10 hours, their morals, together with the net profits of their employers, will vanish, both being dependent on this last, this fatal hour. (See Repts., Insp. of Fact., for 31st Oct., 1848, p. 101.) The same report then gives some examples of the morality and virtue of these same pure-minded manufacturers: of the tricks, the dodges, the coaxing, the threats, and the falsifications they used, first, to force a few defenseless workers to sign petitions of this kind, and then to pass them off on Parliament as the petitions of a whole branch of industry, or a whole country. It is highly typical of the present state of so-called economic science that neither Senior himself, who later, to his honor be it said, energetically supported the factory legislation, nor his opponents, from first to last, have ever been able to explain the false conclusions of the “original discovery.” They appeal to actual experience, but the why and wherefore remains a mystery.

<!-- ch09-p042 -->
Senior invented the battle cry of the “last hour” in 1836.[^9.12] In the London *Economist* of the 15th April, 1848, James Wilson, an economic mandarin of high standing, raised the same cry again: this time against the 10 hours’ bill.

[^9.12]: All the same, the learned professor did get some benefit from his journey to Manchester. In the “Letters on the Factory Act,” he makes the whole net gains, including “profit” and “interests” and even “something more,” depend on a single unpaid hour’s work by the worker. One year earlier, in his “Outlines of Political Economy,” written for the instruction of Oxford students and cultivated Philistines, he had also “discovered, in opposition to Ricardo’s determination of value by labour, that profit is derived from the labour of the capitalist, and interest from his asceticism, in other words, from his abstinence.” The trick was an old one, but the word “abstinence” was new. Herr Roscher translates it rightly by “Enthaltung” [abstention]. Some of his countrymen, the Browns, Jones, and Robinsons of Germany, less well versed in Latin than he is, have, monk-like, rendered it by “Entsagung” (renunciation).

### Section 4: Surplus-Produce

<!-- ch09-p043 -->
The part of the product that represents the surplus-value (one tenth of the 20 lbs., or 2 lbs. of yarn, in the example given in Sec. 2) we call “surplus-produce.” The rate of surplus-value is determined by its relation, not to the total sum of the capital, but to its variable part. In just the same way, the relative quantity of surplus-produce is determined by the ratio this produce bears, not to the remaining part of the total product, but to the part of it in which the necessary labor is embodied. Since the production of surplus-value is the chief end and aim of capitalist production, it is clear that the size of a man’s or a nation’s wealth should be measured, not by the absolute quantity produced, but by the relative size of the surplus-produce.[^9.13]

[^9.13]: “To an individual with a capital of £20,000, whose profits were £2,000 per annum, it would be a matter quite indifferent whether his capital would employ a 100 or 1,000 men, whether the commodity produced sold for £10,000 or £20,000, provided, in all cases, his profit were not diminished below £2,000. Is not the real interest of the nation similar? Provided its net real income, its rent and profits, be the same, it is of no importance whether the nation consists of 10 or of 12 millions of inhabitants.” (Ric. cited above, p. 416.) Long before Ricardo, Arthur Young, a fanatical champion of surplus-produce and, apart from that, a rambling, uncritical writer whose reputation stands in inverse ratio to his merit, says: “Of what use, in a modern kingdom, would be a whole province thus divided [in the old Roman manner, by small independent peasants], however well cultivated, except for the mere purpose of breeding men, which taken singly is a most useless purpose?” (Arthur Young: “Political Arithmetic, &c.” London, 1774, p. 47.)

    What is very curious is “the strong inclination... to represent net wealth as beneficial to the labouring class... though it is evidently not on account of being net.” (Th. Hopkins, “On Rent of Land, &c.” London, 1828, p. 126.)

<!-- ch09-p044 -->
The necessary labor and the surplus labor added together, that is, the periods of time during which the worker replaces the value of his labor-power and produces the surplus-value, make up the actual time during which he works, that is, the working day.

## Chapter 10: The Working Day

### Section 1: The Limits of the Working Day

<!-- ch10-p001 -->
We started from the assumption that labor-power is bought and sold at its value. (Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist. Value is what commodities, things produced in order to be exchanged and not for the producer's own use, have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) Like the value of all other commodities, the value of labor-power is determined by the working time necessary to produce it. If producing the worker's average daily means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live) takes 6 hours, he must work, on average, 6 hours every day to produce his daily labor-power, or to reproduce the value he received from selling it. The necessary part of his working day (the total hours a worker works in a day) amounts to 6 hours, and so, other things being equal, it is a given quantity. But this does not yet give us the length of the working day itself.

<!-- ch10-p002 -->
Let us assume that the line A–––B represents the length of the necessary working time, say 6 hours. If the labor is extended 1, 3, or 6 hours beyond A––B, we get 3 other lines:

<!-- ch10-p003 -->
```text
Working day I.     Working day II.     Working day III.
  A–––B–C.           A–––B––C.           A–––B–––C.
```

<!-- ch10-p004 -->
These represent 3 different working days, of 7, 9, and 12 hours. The extension B––C of the line A––B represents the length of the surplus labor. (Surplus labor is the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist. Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it.) Since the working day is A––B + B––C, or A––C, it varies with the variable quantity B––C. Since A––B is constant, the ratio of B––C to A––B can always be calculated. In working day I it is 1/6 of A––B, in working day II 3/6, and in working day III 6/6. Further, since the ratio (surplus working-time)/(necessary working-time) determines the rate of surplus-value, that rate is given by the ratio of B–-C to A–-B. In the 3 different working days it comes to 16 2/3, 50, and 100 percent respectively. On the other hand, the rate of surplus-value alone would not tell us the length of the working day. If this rate were, for example, 100 percent, the working day might be 8, 10, 12, or more hours long. The rate would show that the 2 parts that make up the working day, necessary labor-time and surplus labor-time, were equal in length, but not how long each of these two parts was.

<!-- ch10-p005 -->
So the working day is not a constant but a variable quantity. One of its parts, certainly, is determined by the working time required to reproduce the worker's own labor-power. But its total length varies with the duration of the surplus labor. The working day can therefore be determined, but in itself it is undetermined.[^10.1]

[^10.1]: “A day’s labour is vague, it may be long or short.” (“An Essay on Trade and Commerce, Containing Observations on Taxes, &c.” London. 1770, p. 73.)

<!-- ch10-p006 -->
Although the working day is not a fixed but a flowing quantity, it can, on the other hand, vary only within certain limits. Its minimum limit, however, cannot be determined. Of course, if we make the extension line B–-C, or the surplus labor, = 0, we get a minimum limit, that is, the part of the day which the worker must necessarily work to maintain himself. On the basis of capitalist production, however, this necessary labor can form only a part of the working day; the working day itself can never be cut down to this minimum. On the other hand, the working day has a maximum limit. It cannot be extended beyond a certain point. This maximum limit is set by two things. First, by the physical bounds of labor-power. Within the 24 hours of the natural day a man can spend only a definite amount of his vital force. In the same way, a horse can work, day after day, only 8 hours. During part of the day this force must rest and sleep; during another part the man has to satisfy other physical needs, to feed, wash, and clothe himself. Besides these purely physical limits, the extension of the working day runs into moral ones. The worker needs time to satisfy his intellectual and social wants, and the extent and number of these wants are conditioned by the general level of social progress. So the variation of the working day moves within physical and social bounds. But both of these limiting conditions are very elastic, and they leave the widest room. So we find working days of 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 hours, that is, of the most varied lengths.

<!-- ch10-p007 -->
The capitalist has bought the labor-power at its day-rate. Its use-value (its usefulness: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties) belongs to him for one working day. He has thus acquired the right to make the worker work for him for one day. But what is a working day?[^10.2]

[^10.2]: This question is far more important than Sir Robert Peel's famous question to the Birmingham Chamber of Commerce: What is a pound? Peel could only have asked that question because he was as much in the dark about the nature of money as the “little shilling men” of Birmingham.

<!-- ch10-p008 -->
At any rate, it is less than a natural day. By how much? The capitalist has his own views about this *ultima Thule* [farthest limit], the necessary limit of the working day. As capitalist, he is only capital personified (capital being value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger). His soul is the soul of capital. But capital has one single life impulse: the tendency to create value and surplus-value, to make its constant factor, the means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things), soak up the greatest possible amount of surplus labor.[^10.3]

[^10.3]: “It is the aim of the capitalist to obtain with his expended capital the greatest possible quantity of labour (d’obtenir du capital dépense la plus forte somme de travail possible).” J. G. Courcelle-Seneuil. “Traité théorique et pratique des entreprises industrielles.” 2nd ed. Paris, 1857, p. 63.

<!-- ch10-p009 -->
Capital is dead labor that, like a vampire, lives only by sucking living labor, and lives the more, the more labor it sucks. (Dead labor is labor already embodied in means of production; living labor is the labor of workers now at work.) The time during which the worker works is the time during which the capitalist consumes the labor-power he has bought from him.[^10.4]

[^10.4]: “An hour’s labour lost in a day is a prodigious injury to a commercial State.... There is a very great consumption of luxuries among the labouring poor of this kingdom: particularly among the manufacturing populace, by which they also consume their time, the most fatal of consumptions.” “An Essay on Trade and Commerce, &c.,” p. 47, and 15

<!-- ch10-p010 -->
If the worker consumes his disposable time for himself, he robs the capitalist.[^10.5]
