[^10.5]: “Si le manouvrier libre prend un instant de repos, l’économie sordide qui le suit des yeux avec inquiétude, prétend qu’il la vole.” [If the free laborer takes a moment's rest, the stingy management that anxiously follows him with its eyes claims that he is stealing from it.] N. Linguet, “Théorie des Lois Civiles. &c.” London, 1767, t. II., p. 466.

<!-- ch10-p011 -->
The capitalist then takes his stand on the law of the exchange of commodities. Like every other buyer, he tries to get the greatest possible benefit out of the use-value of his commodity. Suddenly the voice of the worker, which had been drowned out in the storm and stress of the process of production, rises:

<!-- ch10-p012 -->
The commodity that I have sold to you differs from the crowd of other commodities in that its use creates value, and a value greater than its own. That is why you bought it. What appears on your side as a spontaneous expansion of capital is, on mine, an extra spending of labor-power. You and I know only one law in the market, the law of the exchange of commodities. And the consumption of a commodity belongs not to the seller who parts with it, but to the buyer who acquires it. So the use of my daily labor-power belongs to you. But with the price that you pay for it each day, I must be able to reproduce it daily and to sell it again. Apart from natural wear through age, etc., I must be able to work tomorrow with the same normal amount of strength, health, and freshness as today. You constantly preach to me the gospel of “saving” and “abstinence.” Good! Like a sensible, saving owner, I will take good care of my only wealth, labor-power, and abstain from all foolish waste of it. Each day I will spend, set in motion, and put into action only as much of it as is compatible with its normal duration and healthy development. By extending the working day without limit, you may use up in one day a quantity of labor-power greater than I can restore in three. What you gain in labor, I lose in substance. Using my labor-power and plundering it are quite different things. If the average time that an average worker can live (doing a reasonable amount of work) is 30 years, the value of my labor-power that you pay me from day to day is 1/(365×30) or 1/10950 of its total value. But if you consume it in 10 years, you pay me daily 1/10950 instead of 1/3650 of its total value, that is, only 1/3 of its daily value. So you rob me every day of 2/3 of the value of my commodity. You pay me for one day's labor-power, while you use up that of 3 days. That is against our contract and against the law of exchange. I therefore demand a working day of normal length, and I demand it without any appeal to your heart, for in money matters sentiment has no place. You may be a model citizen, perhaps a member of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, and with a name for holiness to boot; but the thing that you represent when you face me has no heart in its breast. What seems to beat there is my own heartbeat. I demand the normal working day because, like every other seller, I demand the value of my commodity.[^10.6]

[^10.6]: During the great strike of the London builders in 1860-61, for cutting the working day to 9 hours, their Committee published a manifesto that contained, to some extent, the plea of our worker. The manifesto hints, not without irony, that the greatest profit-monger among the building employers, a certain Sir M. Peto, had a name for holiness. (This same Peto, after 1867, came to an end in Strousberg's style.)

<!-- ch10-p013 -->
So we see that, apart from extremely elastic bounds, the nature of the exchange of commodities itself sets no limit to the working day, no limit to surplus labor. The capitalist asserts his right as a buyer when he tries to make the working day as long as possible, and, whenever possible, to make two working days out of one. On the other hand, the special nature of the commodity sold implies a limit to its consumption by the buyer, and the worker asserts his right as a seller when he wants to reduce the working day to one of definite normal length. So there is an antinomy here, a clash of right against right, both equally bearing the seal of the law of exchange. Between equal rights, force decides. That is why, in the history of capitalist production, the fixing of what a working day is presents itself as the result of a struggle, a struggle between collective capital, that is, the class of capitalists, and collective labor, that is, the working class.

### Section 2: The Greed for Surplus-Labor. Manufacturer and Boyard

<!-- ch10-p014 -->
Capital did not invent surplus labor. Wherever one part of society holds a monopoly of the means of production, the worker, free or not free, must add extra working time to the working time needed to maintain himself. He must do so in order to produce the means of subsistence for the owners of the means of production[^10.7], whether this owner is the Athenian χαλος γαχαθος [well-to-do man], the Etruscan theocrat, the *civis Romanus* [Roman citizen], the Norman baron, the American slave-owner, the Wallachian Boyard, the modern landlord, or the capitalist.[^10.8] It is clear, however, that in any given economic formation of society where the use-value of the product predominates, and not its exchange-value (the proportion in which one commodity trades for others), surplus labor will be limited by a given set of wants, which may be larger or smaller. Here no boundless thirst for surplus labor arises from the nature of production itself. So in antiquity over-work becomes horrible only where the aim is to obtain exchange-value in its specific, independent money form (the form of value in which one commodity, gold, has become the universal equivalent): in the production of gold and silver. Here, compulsory working to death is the recognized form of over-work. Just read Diodorus Siculus.[^10.9] Still, these are exceptions in antiquity. But as soon as peoples whose production still moves within the lower forms of slave labor, corvée labor (forced unpaid labor that peasants had to perform for a lord), etc., are drawn into the whirlpool of an international market dominated by the capitalist mode of production, and the sale of their products for export becomes their main interest, the civilized horrors of over-work are grafted onto the barbaric horrors of slavery, serfdom, etc. So the labor of Black people in the Southern States of the American Union kept something of a patriarchal character as long as production was aimed chiefly at immediate local consumption. But to the extent that the export of cotton became of vital interest to these states, the over-working of the Black worker, and sometimes the using up of his life in 7 years of labor, became a factor in a calculated and calculating system. It was no longer a question of getting a certain quantity of useful products out of him. It was now a question of the production of surplus labor itself. The same was true of the corvée, for example in the Danubian Principalities (now Roumania).

[^10.7]: “Those who labour ... in reality feed both the pensioners ... [called the rich] and themselves.” (Edmund Burke, cited above, p. 2.)

[^10.8]: Niebuhr, in his “Roman History,” says very naïvely: “It is evident that works like the Etruscan, which in their ruins astound us, pre-suppose in little (!) states lords and vassals.” Sismondi says, far more to the point, that “Brussels lace” presupposes wage-lords and wage-slaves.

[^10.9]: “One cannot see these unfortunates (in the gold mines between Egypt, Ethiopia, and Arabia) who cannot even have their bodies clean, or their nakedness clothed, without pitying their miserable lot. There is no indulgence, no forbearance for the sick, the feeble, the aged, for woman’s weakness. All must, forced by blows, work on until death puts an end to their sufferings and their distress.” (“Diod. Sic. Bibl. Hist.,” lib. 2, c. 13.)

<!-- ch10-p015 -->
Comparing the greed for surplus labor in the Danubian Principalities with the same greed in English factories is of special interest, because in the corvée, surplus labor has an independent form that you can see and touch.

<!-- ch10-p016 -->
Suppose the working day consists of 6 hours of necessary labor and 6 hours of surplus labor. Then the free worker gives the capitalist 6 x 6, or 36, hours of surplus labor every week. It is the same as if he worked 3 days a week for himself and 3 days a week free of charge for the capitalist. But this does not show on the surface. Surplus labor and necessary labor flow into each other. So I can express the same relation by saying, for example, that the worker works 30 seconds of every minute for himself and 30 for the capitalist, etc. It is different with the corvée. The necessary labor that the Wallachian peasant does to maintain himself is clearly marked off from his surplus labor for the Boyard. He does the one on his own field, the other on the lord's estate. So the two parts of the labor-time exist independently, side by side. In the corvée, surplus labor is precisely marked off from necessary labor. This, however, makes no difference to the quantitative relation of surplus labor to necessary labor. Three days of surplus labor a week remain three days that bring the worker himself no equivalent, whether they are called corvée or wage labor. But in the capitalist, the greed for surplus labor shows itself in the striving for an unlimited extension of the working day; in the Boyard, more simply, in a direct hunt for days of corvée.[^10.10]

[^10.10]: What follows refers to the situation in the Rumanian provinces before the changes made since the Crimean war.

<!-- ch10-p017 -->
In the Danubian Principalities the corvée was mixed up with rents in kind and other trappings of bondage, but it was the most important tribute paid to the ruling class. Where this was so, the corvée rarely arose from serfdom; on the contrary, serfdom much more often arose from the corvée.[^10.11] This is what happened in the Roumanian provinces. Their original mode of production was based on common ownership of the soil, but not in the Slavonic or Indian form. The members of the community farmed part of the land separately, as freehold. Another part, the *ager publicus* [public land], they farmed in common. The products of this common labor served partly as a reserve fund against bad harvests and other accidents, and partly as a public store to cover the costs of war, religion, and other common expenses. In the course of time, military and church dignitaries seized, along with the common land, the labor spent on it. The labor of the free peasants on their common land was turned into corvée for the thieves of the common land. This corvée soon developed into a relation of servitude that existed in fact, though not in law, until Russia, the liberator of the world, made it legal under the pretense of abolishing serfdom. The code of the corvée that the Russian General Kisseleff proclaimed in 1831 was, of course, dictated by the Boyards themselves. So with one blow Russia conquered both the magnates of the Danubian provinces and the applause of liberal cretins all over Europe.

[^10.11]: This also holds for Germany, and especially for Prussia east of the Elbe. In the 15th century the German peasant was nearly everywhere a man who, while subject to certain rents paid in produce and labor, was otherwise at least practically free. The German colonists in Brandenburg, Pomerania, Silesia, and Eastern Prussia were even legally recognized as free men. The victory of the nobility in the peasants' war put an end to that. Not only were the conquered South German peasants enslaved again. From the middle of the 16th century the peasants of Eastern Prussia, Brandenburg, Pomerania, and Silesia, and soon after them the free peasants of Schleswig-Holstein, were reduced to the condition of serfs. (Maurer, Fronhöfe iv. vol., — Meitzen, “Der Boden des preussischen Staats” — Hanssen, “Leibeigenschaft in Schleswig-Holstein.” — *F. E.)*

<!-- ch10-p018 -->
This code of the corvée is called the “Règlement organique” [Organic Regulation]. According to it, every Wallachian peasant owes the so-called landlord, besides a mass of detailed payments in kind: *(1)*, 12 days of general labor; *(2)*, one day of field labor; *(3)*, one day of carrying wood. In all, 14 days a year. But with deep insight into political economy (the science of economics as it was then called), the working day is not taken in its ordinary sense. It is taken as the working day needed to produce an average daily product, and that average daily product is fixed so craftily that no Cyclops could finish it in 24 hours. In dry words, the Réglement itself declares, with true Russian irony, that by 12 working days one must understand the product of 36 days of manual labor; by 1 day of field labor, 3 days; and by 1 day of wood carrying, likewise three times as much. In all, 42 corvée days. To this had to be added the so-called jobagie, service owed to the lord on extraordinary occasions. Every village has to supply a fixed contingent to the jobagie each year, in proportion to the size of its population. This extra corvée is estimated at 14 days for each Wallachian peasant. So the prescribed corvée comes to 56 working days a year. But because of the harsh climate, the agricultural year in Wallachia has only 210 days. Of these, 40 for Sundays and holidays and 30 on average for bad weather, 70 days together, do not count. 140 working days remain. The ratio of the corvée to the necessary labor, 56/84 or 66 2/3 %, gives a much lower rate of surplus-value than the one that governs the labor of the English agricultural or factory worker. This, however, is only the corvée prescribed by law. And in a spirit even more “liberal” than the English Factory Acts, the “Règlement organique” has known how to make its own evasion easy. After turning 12 days into 56, it arranges the nominal day's work of each of the 56 corvée days so that part of it must spill over onto the next day. In one day, for example, an area of land must be weeded that needs twice as much time for this work, especially on maize plantations. For some kinds of agricultural labor, the legal day's work can be interpreted so that the day begins in May and ends in October. In Moldavia conditions are even harsher.

<!-- ch10-p019 -->
“The 12 corvée days of the ‘Règlement organique’,” cried a Boyard drunk with victory, “amount to 365 days in the year.”[^10.12]

[^10.12]: Further details can be found in E. Regnault’s “Histoire politique et sociale des Principautés Danubiennes,” Paris, 1855.

<!-- ch10-p020 -->
If the Règlement organique of the Danubian provinces was a positive expression of the greed for surplus labor which every one of its paragraphs made legal, the English Factory Acts are the negative expression of the same greed. These Acts curb capital's passion for draining labor-power without limit by forcibly limiting the working day through state regulations, made by a state ruled by capitalist and landlord. Apart from the working-class movement, which grew more threatening every day, the limiting of factory labor was dictated by the same necessity that spread guano (a fertilizer made of bird droppings) over the English fields. The same blind eagerness for plunder that in the one case exhausted the soil had, in the other, torn up the living force of the nation by the roots. Periodic epidemics speak as clearly on this point as the falling military standard in Germany and France.[^10.13]

[^10.13]: “In general and within certain limits, exceeding the medium size of their kind, is evidence of the prosperity of organic beings. As to man, his bodily height lessens if his due growth is interfered with, either by physical or local conditions. In all European countries in which the conscription holds, since its introduction, the medium height of adult men, and generally their fitness for military service, has diminished. Before the revolution (1789), the minimum for the infantry in France was 165 centimetres; in 1818 (law of March 10th), 157; by the law of March 21, 1832, 156 cm.; on the average in France more than half are rejected on account of deficient height or bodily weakness. The military standard in Saxony was in 1780, 178 cm. It is now 155. In Prussia it is 157. According to the statement of Dr. Meyer in the Bavarian Gazette, May 9th, 1862, the result of an average of 9 years is, that in Prussia out of 1,000 conscripts 716 were unfit for military service, 317 because of deficiency in height, and 399 because of bodily defects.... Berlin in 1858 could not provide its contingent of recruits, it was 156 men short.” J. von Liebig: “Die Chemie in ihrer Anwendung auf Agrikultur und Physiologie. 1862,” 7th Ed., vol. 1, pp. 117, 118.

<!-- ch10-p021 -->
The Factory Act of 1850, now in force (1867), allows an average working day of 10 hours. That is, for the first 5 days of the week, 12 hours from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., including ½ an hour for breakfast and an hour for dinner, which leaves 10½ working hours; and for Saturday 8 hours, from 6 a.m. to 2 p.m., of which ½ an hour is taken off for breakfast. That leaves 60 working hours: 10½ for each of the first 5 days, 7½ for the last.[^10.14]

[^10.14]: The history of the Factory Act of 1850 will be given in the course of this chapter.

<!-- ch10-p022 -->
Certain guardians of these laws are appointed: the Factory Inspectors, who report directly to the Home Secretary. Their reports are published every half-year, by order of Parliament. They provide regular, official statistics of the capitalist greed for surplus labor.

<!-- ch10-p023 -->
Let us listen to the Factory Inspectors for a moment.[^10.15]

[^10.15]: I only touch here and there on the period from the beginning of modern industry (large-scale production based on machinery and the factory system) in England to 1845. For this period I refer the reader to “Die Lage der arbeitenden Klasse in England,” [Condition of the Working Class in England] von Friedrich Engels, Leipzig, 1845. The Factory Reports, Reports on Mines, etc., that have appeared since 1845 show how completely Engels understood the nature of the capitalist mode of production. Even the most superficial comparison of his work with the official reports of the Children’s Employment Commission, published 18 to 20 years later (1863-1867), shows how wonderfully he painted the conditions in detail. These reports deal especially with the branches of industry in which the Factory Acts had not been introduced up to 1862, and in fact are still not introduced. Here, then, the authorities had enforced little or no change in the conditions Engels painted. I take my examples mainly from the Free-trade period after 1848, that age of paradise about which the traveling salesmen for the great firm of Free-trade, as loud-mouthed as they are ignorant, tell such fabulous tales. For the rest, England stands in the foreground here because she is the classic representative of capitalist production, and she alone has a continuous set of official statistics on the things we are considering.

<!-- ch10-p024 -->
> “The fraudulent mill-owner begins work a quarter of an hour (sometimes more, sometimes less) before 6 a.m., and leaves off a quarter of an hour (sometimes more, sometimes less) after 6 p.m. He takes 5 minutes from the beginning and from the end of the half hour nominally allowed for breakfast, and 10 minutes at the beginning and end of the hour nominally allowed for dinner. He works for a quarter of an hour (sometimes more, sometimes less) after 2 p.m. on Saturday. Thus his gain is –

<!-- ch10-p025 -->
```text
Before 6 a.m.,                                     15 minutes.
After 6 p.m.,                                      15 "
At breakfast time,                                 10 "
At dinner time,                                    20 "
             Five days – 300 minutes,              60 "
On Saturday before 6 a.m.,                         15 minutes.
At breakfast time,                                 10 "
After 2 p.m.,                                      15 "
                                                   40 minutes.
Total weekly,                                      340 minutes.
```

<!-- ch10-p026 -->
> Or 5 hours and 40 minutes weekly, which multiplied by 50 working weeks in the year (allowing two for holidays and occasional stoppages) is equal to 27 working days.”[^10.16]

[^10.16]: “Suggestions, &c. by Mr. L. Horner, Inspector of Factories,” in Factories Regulation Acts. Ordered by the House of Commons to be printed, 9th August, 1859, pp. 4, 5.

<!-- ch10-p027 -->
> “Five minutes a day’s increased work, multiplied by weeks, are equal to two and a half days of produce in the year.”[^10.17]

[^10.17]: Reports of the Inspector of Factories for the half year. October, 1856, p. 35.

<!-- ch10-p028 -->
> “An additional hour a day gained by small instalments before 6 a.m., after 6 p.m., and at the beginning and end of the times nominally fixed for meals, is nearly equivalent to working 13 months in the year.”[^10.18]

[^10.18]: Reports, &c., 30th April, 1858, p. 9.

<!-- ch10-p029 -->
Crises, during which production is interrupted and the factories work “short time,” that is, only part of the week, naturally do not affect the tendency to extend the working day. The less business there is, the more profit has to be made on the business that is done. The less time is spent working, the more of that time has to be turned into surplus labor-time.

<!-- ch10-p030 -->
So the Factory Inspector reports on the period of the crisis from 1857 to 1858:

<!-- ch10-p031 -->
> “It may seem inconsistent that there should be any overworking at a time when trade is so bad; but that very badness leads to the transgression by unscrupulous men, they get the extra profit of it. ... In the last half year, says Leonard Horner, 122 mills in my district have been given up; 143 were found standing,” yet, over-work is continued beyond the legal hours.”[^10.19]

[^10.19]: Reports, &c., cited above, p. 10.

<!-- ch10-p032 -->
> “For a great part of the time,” says Mr. Howell, “owing to the depression of trade, many factories were altogether closed, and a still greater number were working short time. I continue, however, to receive about the usual number of complaints that half, or three-quarters of an hour in the day, are snatched from the workers by encroaching upon the times professedly allowed for rest and refreshment.”[^10.20]

[^10.20]: Reports &c., cited above, p. 25.

<!-- ch10-p033 -->
The same thing happened again, on a smaller scale, during the terrible cotton crises from 1861 to 1865.[^10.21]

[^10.21]: Reports &c., for the half year ending 30th April, 1861. See Appendix No. 2; Reports, &c., 31st October, 1862, pp. 7, 52, 53. The violations of the Acts became more numerous during the last half year 1863. Compare Reports, &c., ending 31st October, 1863, p. 7.

<!-- ch10-p034 -->
> “It is sometimes advanced by way of excuse, when persons are found at work in a factory, either at a meal hour, or at some illegal time, that they will not leave the mill at the appointed hour, and that compulsion is necessary to force them to cease work [cleaning their machinery, &c.], especially on Saturday afternoons. But, if the hands remain in a factory after the machinery has ceased to revolve ... they would not have been so employed if sufficient time had been set apart specially for cleaning, &c., either before 6 a.m. *[sic.!]* or before 2 p.m. on Saturday afternoons.”[^10.22]

[^10.22]: Reports, &c., October 31st, 1860, p. 23. The following curious incident shows with what fanaticism, according to the manufacturers' evidence in courts of law, their hands set themselves against every interruption of factory labor. At the beginning of June, 1836, the magistrates of Dewsbury (Yorkshire) received information that the owners of 8 large mills near Batley had violated the Factory Acts. Some of these gentlemen were accused of having kept 5 boys between 12 and 15 years of age at work from 6 a.m. on Friday to 4 p.m. on the following Saturday, without allowing them any rest except for meals and one hour of sleep at midnight. And these children had to do this ceaseless labor of 30 hours in the “shoddyhole,” as the hole is called in which the woolen rags are pulled to pieces. There a dense atmosphere of dust, shreds, etc., forces even the adult worker to keep his mouth covered with handkerchiefs to protect his lungs! Instead of taking an oath — as quakers they were too scrupulously religious to take an oath — the accused gentlemen affirm that, in their great compassion for the unhappy children, they had allowed them four hours for sleep, but the obstinate children absolutely would not go to bed. The quaker gentlemen were fined £20. Dryden foresaw these gentry:

    Fox full fraught in seeming sanctity, That feared an oath, but like the devil would lie, That look’d like Lent, and had the holy leer, And durst not sin! before he said his prayer!”

<!-- ch10-p035 -->
> “The profit to be gained by it (over-working in violation of the Act) appears to be, to many, a greater temptation than they can resist; they calculate upon the chance of not being found out; and when they see the small amount of penalty and costs, which those who have been convicted have had to pay, they find that if they should be detected there will still be a considerable balance of gain....[^10.23] In cases where the additional time is gained by a multiplication of small thefts in the course of the day, there are insuperable difficulties to the inspectors making out a case.”[^10.24]

[^10.23]: Rep., 31st Oct., 1856, p. 34.

[^10.24]: Cited above, p. 35.

<!-- ch10-p036 -->
The factory inspectors also call these “small thefts” by capital from the worker's meal and recreation time “petty pilferings of minutes,”[^10.25] “snatching a few minutes,”[^10.26] or, as the workers technically called them, “nibbling and cribbling at meal-times.”[^10.27]

[^10.25]: Cited above, p. 48.

[^10.26]: Cited above, p. 48.

[^10.27]: Cited above, p. 48.

<!-- ch10-p037 -->
Clearly, in this atmosphere the making of surplus-value by surplus labor is no secret.

<!-- ch10-p038 -->
> “If you allow me,” said a highly respectable master to me, “to work only ten minutes in the day over-time, you put one thousand a year in my pocket.”[^10.28] “Moments are the elements of profit.”[^10.29]

[^10.28]: Cited above, p. 48.

[^10.29]: Report of the Insp. &c., 30th April 1860, p. 56.

<!-- ch10-p039 -->
From this point of view nothing is more characteristic than the naming of the workers who work full time as “full-timers,” and of the children under 13, who are only allowed to work 6 hours, as “half-timers.” Here the worker is nothing more than personified labor-time. All individual differences are merged into those of “full-timers” and “half-timers.”[^10.30]

[^10.30]: This is the official expression both in the factories and in the reports.

### Section 3: Branches of English Industry Without Legal Limits to Exploitation

<!-- ch10-p040 -->
So far we have looked at the tendency to lengthen the working day, the werewolf’s hunger for surplus labor, in one department of industry. There the monstrous demands made on the workers were so extreme that, as an English bourgeois economist (bourgeois: belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it) says, not even the cruelties of the Spaniards to the Native Americans surpassed them.[^10.31] In the end, these demands caused capital to be bound by the chains of legal regulation. Now let us glance at certain branches of production in which the exploitation of labor is still free of fetters today, or was free of them until yesterday.

[^10.31]: “The cupidity of mill-owners whose cruelties in the pursuit of gain have hardly been exceeded by those perpetrated by the Spaniards on the conquest of America in the pursuit of gold.” John Wade, “History of the Middle and Working Classes,” 3rd Ed. London, 1835, p. 114. The theoretical part of this book, a kind of handbook of political economy, is original in some parts, for example on trade crises, considering the time when it was published. The historical part is, to a great extent, a shameless plagiarism of Sir F. M. Eden’s “The State of the Poor,” London, 1797.

<!-- ch10-p041 -->
> Mr. Broughton Charlton, a county magistrate, was chairman of a meeting held at the Assembly Rooms, Nottingham, on the 14th January, 1860, and in that role he declared “that there was an amount of privation and suffering among that portion of the population connected with the lace trade, unknown in other parts of the kingdom, indeed, in the civilised world .... Children of nine or ten years are dragged from their squalid beds at two, three, or four o’clock in the morning and compelled to work for a bare subsistence until ten, eleven, or twelve at night, their limbs wearing away, their frames dwindling, their faces whitening, and their humanity absolutely sinking into a stone-like torpor, utterly horrible to contemplate.... We are not surprised that Mr. Mallett, or any other manufacturer, should stand forward and protest against discussion.... The system, as the Rev. Montagu Valpy describes it, is one of unmitigated slavery, socially, physically, morally, and spiritually.... What can be thought of a town which holds a public meeting to petition that the period of labour for men shall be diminished to eighteen hours a day? .... We declaim against the Virginian and Carolinian cotton-planters. Is their black-market, their lash, and their barter of human flesh more detestable than this slow sacrifice of humanity which takes place in order that veils and collars may be fabricated for the benefit of capitalists?”[^10.32]

[^10.32]: *Daily Telegraph, 17th* January, 1860.

<!-- ch10-p042 -->
Over the last 22 years, the potteries of Staffordshire have been the subject of three parliamentary inquiries. Their results are set down in three reports. The first is Mr. Scriven’s Report of 1841 to the “Children’s Employment Commissioners.” The second is the report of Dr. Greenhow of 1860, published by order of the medical officer of the Privy Council (Public Health, 3rd Report, 112-113). Lastly, in the “First Report of the Children’s Employment Commission, of the 13th June, 1863,” there is the report of Mr. Longe of 1862. For my purpose it is enough to take some statements of the exploited children themselves from the reports of 1860 and 1863. From the children we may form an opinion about the adults, especially the girls and women. And this is in a branch of industry next to which cotton-spinning looks like a pleasant and healthy occupation.[^10.33]

[^10.33]: Compare F. Engels “Lage, etc.” pp. 249-51.

<!-- ch10-p043 -->
William Wood, 9 years old, was 7 years and 10 months old when he began to work. From the beginning he “ran moulds” (carried the newly molded articles into the drying-room, and afterwards brought back the empty mold). He came to work every day of the week at 6 a.m., and stopped about 9 p.m. “I work till 9 o’clock at night six days in the week. I have done so seven or eight weeks.”

<!-- ch10-p044 -->
> Fifteen hours of labor for a child 7 years old! J. Murray, 12 years of age, says: “I turn jigger, and run moulds. I come at 6. Sometimes I come at 4. I worked all night last night, till 6 o’clock this morning. I have not been in bed since the night before last. There were eight or nine other boys working last night. All but one have come this morning. I get 3 shillings and sixpence. I do not get any more for working at night. I worked two nights last week.”

<!-- ch10-p045 -->
Fernyhough, a boy of ten, says:

<!-- ch10-p046 -->
> “I have not always an hour (for dinner). I have only half an hour sometimes; on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday.”[^10.34]

[^10.34]: Children’s Employment Commission. First report., etc., 1863. Evidence. pp. 16, 19, 18.

<!-- ch10-p047 -->
Dr. Greenhow states that the average length of life in the pottery districts of Stoke-on-Trent and Wolstanton is extraordinarily short. In the district of Stoke, only 36.6% of the adult male population above 20 is employed in the potteries, and in Wolstanton only 30.4%. Yet among the men of that age, more than half of all deaths in the first district, and nearly 2/5 in the second, are the result of lung diseases among the potters. Dr. Boothroyd, a medical practitioner at Hanley, says:

<!-- ch10-p048 -->
“Each successive generation of potters is more dwarfed and less robust than the preceding one.”

<!-- ch10-p049 -->
In the same way another doctor, Mr. M’Bean, says:

<!-- ch10-p050 -->
> “Since he began to practice among the potters 25 years ago, he had observed a marked degeneration especially shown in diminution of stature and breadth.”

<!-- ch10-p051 -->
These statements are taken from the report of Dr. Greenhow in 1860.[^10.35]

[^10.35]: Public Health, 3rd report, etc., pp. 102, 104, 105.

<!-- ch10-p052 -->
From the report of the Commissioners in 1863, we take the following. Dr. J. T. Arledge, senior physician of the North Staffordshire Infirmary, says:

<!-- ch10-p053 -->
> “The potters as a class, both men and women, represent a degenerated population, both physically and morally. They are, as a rule, stunted in growth, ill-shaped, and frequently ill-formed in the chest; they become prematurely old, and are certainly short-lived; they are phlegmatic and bloodless, and exhibit their debility of constitution by obstinate attacks of dyspepsia [indigestion], and disorders of the liver and kidneys, and by rheumatism. But of all diseases they are especially prone to chest-disease, to pneumonia, phthisis [tuberculosis], bronchitis, and asthma. One form would appear peculiar to them, and is known as potter’s asthma, or potter’s consumption. Scrofula attacking the glands, or bones, or other parts of the body, is a disease of two-thirds or more of the potters .... That the ‘degenerescence’ of the population of this district is not even greater than it is, is due to the constant recruiting from the adjacent country, and intermarriages with more healthy races.”[^10.36]

[^10.36]: Child. Empl. Comm. I. Report, p. 24.

<!-- ch10-p054 -->
Mr. Charles Parsons, formerly house surgeon of the same institution, writes in a letter to Commissioner Longe, among other things:

<!-- ch10-p055 -->
> “I can only speak from personal observation and not from statistical data, but I do not hesitate to assert that my indignation has been aroused again and again at the sight of poor children whose health has been sacrificed to gratify the avarice of either parents or employers.” He lists the causes of the potters’ diseases, and sums them up in the phrase “long hours.” The report of the Commission trusts that “a manufacture which has assumed so prominent a place in the whole world, will not long be subject to the remark that its great success is accompanied with the physical deterioration, widespread bodily suffering, and early death of the workpeople ... by whose labour and skill such great results have been achieved.”[^10.37]

[^10.37]: Children’s Employment Commission, p. 22, and xi.

<!-- ch10-p056 -->
And everything that holds for the potteries in England is true of those in Scotland.[^10.38]

[^10.38]: cited above, p. xlviii.

<!-- ch10-p057 -->
The manufacture of lucifer matches (early friction matches) dates from 1833, when a method was discovered for putting phosphorus on the match itself. Since 1845 this manufacture has developed rapidly in England. It has spread especially in the thickly populated parts of London, and also in Manchester, Birmingham, Liverpool, Bristol, Norwich, Newcastle and Glasgow. Along with it has spread the form of lockjaw that a Vienna physician discovered in 1845 to be a disease peculiar to lucifer-match makers. Half the workers are children under thirteen and young persons under eighteen. Because it is so unhealthy and unpleasant, the manufacture has such a bad name that only the most miserable part of the working class, half-starved widows and the like, hand their children over to it, “the ragged, half-starved, untaught children.”[^10.39]

[^10.39]: cited above, p. liv.

<!-- ch10-p058 -->
Of the witnesses that Commissioner White examined (1863), 270 were under 18, 50 under 10, 10 only 8, and 5 only 6 years old. The working day ranged from 12 to 14 or 15 hours. There was night-labor, and meal-times were irregular. Meals were mostly eaten in the very workrooms that are poisoned with phosphorus. Dante would have found the worst horrors of his Inferno surpassed in this manufacture.

<!-- ch10-p059 -->
In the manufacture of paper-hangings (wallpaper), the coarser kinds are printed by machine and the finer ones by hand (block-printing). The busiest months are from the beginning of October to the end of April. During this time the work goes on fast and furious, without a break, from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. or further into the night.

<!-- ch10-p060 -->
J. Leach states in evidence:

<!-- ch10-p061 -->
> “Last winter six out of nineteen girls were away from ill-health at one time from over-work. I have to bawl at them to keep them awake.” W. Duffy: “I have seen when the children could none of them keep their eyes open for the work; indeed, none of us could.” J. Lightbourne: “Am 13 ... We worked last winter till 9 (evening), and the winter before till 10. I used to cry with sore feet every night last winter.” G. Apsden: “That boy of mine when he was 7 years old I used to carry him on my back to and fro through the snow, and he used to have 16 hours a day ... I have often knelt down to feed him as he stood by the machine, for he could not leave it or stop.” Smith, the managing partner of a Manchester factory: “We (he means his “hands” who work for “us”) work on with no stoppage for meals, so that day’s work of 10½ hours is finished by 4.30 p.m., and all after that is over-time.”[^10.40] (Does this Mr. Smith take no meals himself during 10½ hours?) “We (this same Smith) seldom leave off working before 6 p.m. (he means leave off the consumption of “our” labor-power machines), so that we (iterum Crispinus [Crispinus again]) are really working over-time the whole year round. For all these, children and adults alike (152 children and young persons and 140 adults), the average work for the last 18 months has been at the very least 7 days, 5 hours, or 78 1/2 hours a week. For the six weeks ending May 2nd this year (1862), the average was higher – 8 days or 84 hours a week.”

[^10.40]: This is not to be taken in the same sense as our surplus labor-time. These gentlemen consider 10½ hours of labor as the normal working day, which of course includes the normal surplus labor. After this begins “overtime,” which is paid a little better. We will see later that the labor spent during the so-called normal day is paid below its value. So the overtime is simply a capitalist trick to extort more surplus labor. It would still be that, even if the labor-power spent during the normal working day were properly paid.

<!-- ch10-p062 -->
This same Mr. Smith, who is so extremely devoted to the *pluralis majestatis* [the Royal “we,” i.e., speaking on behalf of his subjects], adds with a smile, “Machine-work is not great.” In the same way, the employers in block-printing say: “Hand labour is more healthy than machine work.” On the whole, the manufacturers declare themselves indignantly against the proposal “to stop the machines at least during meal-times.”

<!-- ch10-p063 -->
> “A clause,” says Mr. Otley, manager of a wall-paper factory in the Borough (Southwark, in London), “which allowed work between, say 6 a.m. and 9 p.m. would suit us (!) very well, but the factory hours, 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., are not suitable. Our machine is always stopped for dinner. (What generosity!) There is no waste of paper and colour to speak of. But,” he adds sympathetically, “I can understand the loss of time not being liked.”

<!-- ch10-p064 -->
The report of the Commission naively gives its opinion on the fear of some “leading firms” of losing time (that is, the time for taking possession of the labor of others) and so losing profit. This fear, it says, is not a good enough reason for letting children under 13, and young persons under 18, who work 12 to 16 hours a day, lose their dinner. Nor is it a good enough reason for giving them their dinner the way coal and water are supplied to the steam-engine, soap to wool, oil to the wheel – as mere auxiliary material for the instruments of labor, during the process of production itself.[^10.41]

[^10.41]: cited above, Evidence, pp. 123, 124, 125, 140, and 54.

<!-- ch10-p065 -->
No branch of industry in England has kept, up to the present day, a method of production as archaic as baking. (We leave aside the making of bread by machinery, which was introduced recently.) As we see from the poets of the Roman Empire, it is a pre-Christian method. But capital, as was said earlier, is at first indifferent to the technical character of the labor process (the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things). It begins by taking that process just as it finds it.

<!-- ch10-p066 -->
The incredible adulteration of bread, especially in London, was first exposed by the House of Commons Committee “on the adulteration of articles of food” (1855-56), and by Dr. Hassall’s work, “Adulterations detected.”[^10.42] These revelations led to the Act of August 6th, 1860, “for preventing the adulteration of articles of food and drink.” It was a law that did not work, since it naturally shows the tenderest consideration for every Free-trader who resolves, by buying or selling adulterated commodities, “to turn an honest penny.”[^10.43] The Committee itself stated, more or less naively, its conviction that Free-trade essentially meant trade in adulterated goods, or, as the English ingeniously put it, “sophisticated” goods. In fact, this kind of sophistry knows better than Protagoras how to make white black and black white. It knows better than the Eleatic philosophers how to demonstrate *ad oculos* [before your own eyes] that everything is only appearance.[^10.44]

[^10.42]: Alum, finely powdered or mixed with salt, is a normal article of trade, bearing the significant name of “bakers’ stuff.”

[^10.43]: Soot is a well-known and very energetic form of carbon. It makes a manure that capitalistic chimney-sweeps sell to English farmers. Now in 1862, in a lawsuit, a British jury had to decide this question: is soot that, without the buyer’s knowledge, has 90% of dust and sand mixed into it genuine soot in the commercial sense, or adulterated soot in the legal sense? The “amis du commerce” [friends of commerce] decided it was genuine commercial soot. They threw out the case of the plaintiff, a farmer, who in addition had to pay the costs of the suit.

[^10.44]: The French chemist Chevallier wrote a treatise on the “sophistications” of commodities. He reviews 600 or more articles, and for many of them he lists 10, 20, 30 different methods of adulteration. He adds that he does not know all the methods, and does not mention all that he knows. He gives 6 kinds of adulteration of sugar, 9 of olive oil, 10 of butter, 12 of salt, 19 of milk, 20 of bread, 23 of brandy, 24 of meal, 28 of chocolate, 30 of wine, 32 of coffee, etc. Even God Almighty does not escape this fate. See Rouard de Card, “On the Falsifications of the materials of the Sacrament.” (“De la falsification des substances sacramentelles,” Paris, 1856.)

<!-- ch10-p067 -->
At any rate, the Committee had turned the public’s attention to its “daily bread,” and so to the baking trade. At the same time, the London journeymen bakers raised their cry against their over-work, etc., in public meetings and in petitions to Parliament. The cry was so urgent that Mr. H. S. Tremenheere was appointed Royal Commissioner of Inquiry. He was also a member of the Commission of 1863 that has been mentioned several times. His report,[^10.45] together with the evidence given, stirred not the heart of the public but its stomach. Englishmen, always well up in the Bible, knew well enough that man is commanded to eat his bread in the sweat of his brow, unless, by the grace of being chosen, he is a capitalist, or a landlord, or the holder of a paid office with no duties. But they did not know that every day, in his bread, he had to eat a certain amount of human sweat mixed with pus from abscesses, cobwebs, dead black-beetles, and rotten German yeast, not counting alum, sand, and other agreeable mineral ingredients. So, without any regard for his holiness, Free-trade, the free baking-trade was placed under the supervision of State inspectors (at the close of the Parliamentary session of 1863). By the same Act of Parliament, work from 9 in the evening to 5 in the morning was forbidden for journeymen bakers under 18. This last clause speaks volumes about the over-work in this old-fashioned, homely line of business.

[^10.45]: “Report, &c., relative to the grievances complained of by the journeymen bakers, &c., London, 1862,” and “Second Report, &c., London, 1863.”

<!-- ch10-p068 -->
> “The work of a London journeyman baker begins, as a rule, at about eleven at night. At that hour he ‘makes the dough,’ – a laborious process, which lasts from half an hour to three quarters of an hour, according to the size of the batch or the labour bestowed upon it. He then lies down upon the kneading-board, which is also the covering of the trough in which the dough is ‘made’; and with a sack under him, and another rolled up as a pillow, he sleeps for about a couple of hours. He is then engaged in a rapid and continuous labour for about five hours – throwing out the dough, ‘scaling it off,’ moulding it, putting it into the oven, preparing and baking rolls and fancy bread, taking the batch bread out of the oven, and up into the shop, &c., &c. The temperature of a bakehouse ranges from about 75 to upwards of 90 degrees, and in the smaller bakehouses approximates usually to the higher rather than to the lower degree of heat. When the business of making the bread, rolls, &c., is over, that of its distribution begins, and a considerable proportion of the journeymen in the trade, after working hard in the manner described during the night, are upon their legs for many hours during the day, carrying baskets, or wheeling hand-carts, and sometimes again in the bakehouse, leaving off work at various hours between 1 and 6 p.m. according to the season of the year, or the amount and nature of their master’s business; while others are again engaged in the bakehouse in ‘bringing out’ more batches until late in the afternoon.[^10.46]... During what is called ‘the London season,’ the operatives belonging to the ‘full-priced’ bakers at the West End of the town, generally begin work at 11 p.m., and are engaged in making the bread, with one or two short (sometimes very short) intervals of rest, up to 8 o’clock the next morning. They are then engaged all day long, up to 4, 5, 6, and as late as 7 o’clock in the evening carrying out bread, or sometimes in the afternoon in the bakehouse again, assisting in the biscuit-baking. They may have, after they have done their work, sometimes five or six, sometimes only four or five hours’ sleep before they begin again. On Fridays they always begin sooner, some about ten o’clock, and continue in some cases, at work, either in making or delivering the bread up to 8 p.m. on Saturday night, but more generally up to 4 or 5 o’clock, Sunday morning. On Sundays the men must attend twice or three times during the day for an hour or two to make preparations for the next day’s bread.... The men employed by the underselling masters (who sell their bread under the ‘full price,’ and who, as already pointed out, comprise three-fourths of the London bakers) have not only to work on the average longer hours, but their work is almost entirely confined to the bakehouse. The underselling masters generally sell their bread... in the shop. If they send it out, which is not common, except as supplying chandlers’ shops, they usually employ other hands for that purpose. It is not their practice to deliver bread from house to house. Towards the end of the week ... the men begin on Thursday night at 10 o’clock, and continue on with only slight intermission until late on Saturday evening.”[^10.47]

[^10.46]: cited above, First Report, &c., p. vi.

[^10.47]: cited above, p. lxxi.

<!-- ch10-p069 -->
Even the bourgeois intellect understands the position of the “underselling” masters. “The unpaid labour of the men was made the source whereby the competition was carried on.”[^10.48] And the “full-priced” baker denounces his underselling competitors to the Commission of Inquiry as thieves of other people’s labor and as adulterators.

[^10.48]: George Read, “The History of Baking,” London, 1848, p. 16.

<!-- ch10-p070 -->
> “They only exist now by first defrauding the public, and next getting 18 hours’ work out of their men for 12 hours’ wages.”[^10.49]

[^10.49]: Report (First) &c. Evidence of the “full-priced” baker Cheeseman, p. 108.

<!-- ch10-p071 -->
The adulteration of bread, and the formation of a class of bakers who sell bread below the full price, date from the beginning of the 18th century. That was when the trade lost its corporate character (its organization as a guild), and the capitalist, in the form of the miller or flour-factor (flour merchant), rose up behind the nominal master baker.[^10.50] This laid the foundation of capitalist production in this trade, and of the unlimited lengthening of the working day and of night-labor, although night-labor gained a serious footing, even in London, only after 1824.[^10.51]

[^10.50]: George Read, cited above. At the end of the 17th and the beginning of the 18th centuries, the factors (agents) who crowded into every possible trade were still denounced as “public nuisances.” Thus the Grand Jury at the quarter session of the Justices of the Peace for the County of Somerset addressed a presentment (a formal complaint) to the Lower House. Among other things, it states “that these factors of Blackwell Hall are a Public Nuisance and Prejudice to the Clothing Trade, and ought to be put down as a Nuisance.” “The Case of our English Wool., &c.,” London, 1685, pp. 6, 7.

[^10.51]: First Report, &c.

<!-- ch10-p072 -->
After what has just been said, it will be understood that the Report of the Commission classes journeymen bakers among the short-lived workers. Having by good luck escaped the normal decimation of the children of the working class, they rarely reach the age of 42. Nevertheless, the baking trade is always flooded with applicants. London gets its supply of these labor-powers from Scotland, from the western agricultural districts of England, and from Germany.

<!-- ch10-p073 -->
In the years 1858-60, the journeymen bakers in Ireland organized great meetings at their own expense to agitate against night work and Sunday work. The public took their side with Irish warmth, for example at the Dublin meeting in May, 1860. As a result of this movement, day-labor alone was successfully established in Wexford, Kilkenny, Clonmel, Waterford, etc.

<!-- ch10-p074 -->
> “In Limerick, where the grievances of the journeymen are demonstrated to be excessive, the movement has been defeated by the opposition of the master bakers, the miller bakers being the greatest opponents. The example of Limerick led to a retrogression in Ennis and Tipperary. In Cork, where the strongest possible demonstration of feeling took place, the masters, by exercising their power of turning the men out of employment, have defeated the movement. In Dublin, the master bakers have offered the most determined opposition to the movement, and by discountenancing as much as possible the journeymen promoting it, have succeeded in leading the men into acquiescence in Sunday work and night-work, contrary to the convictions of the men.”[^10.52]

[^10.52]: Report of Committee on the Baking Trade in Ireland for 1861.

<!-- ch10-p075 -->
The Committee of the English Government (a Government that, in Ireland, is armed to the teeth and generally knows how to show it) protests in mild, though funereal, tones to the implacable master bakers of Dublin, Limerick, Cork, etc.:

<!-- ch10-p076 -->
> “The Committee believe that the hours of labour are limited by natural laws, which cannot be violated with impunity. That for master bakers to induce their workmen, by the fear of losing employment, to violate their religious convictions and their better feelings, to disobey the laws of the land, and to disregard public opinion (this all refers to Sunday labor), is calculated to provoke ill-feeling between workmen and masters, ... and affords an example dangerous to religion, morality, and social order.... The Committee believe that any constant work beyond 12 hours a-day encroaches on the domestic and private life of the working-man, and so leads to disastrous moral results, interfering with each man’s home, and the discharge of his family duties as a son, a brother, a husband, a father. That work beyond 12 hours has a tendency to undermine the health of the workingman, and so leads to premature old age and death, to the great injury of families of working-men, thus deprived of the care and support of the head of the family when most required.”[^10.53]

[^10.53]: cited above.

<!-- ch10-p077 -->
So much for Ireland. On the other side of the channel, in Scotland, the agricultural worker, the plowman, protests against his 13-14 hours’ work in the harshest climate, with 4 hours’ extra work on Sunday (in this land of strict Sabbath-keepers!).[^10.54] Meanwhile, at the same time, three railway men are standing before a London coroner’s jury: a guard, an engine-driver, and a signalman. A tremendous railway accident has hurried hundreds of passengers into another world. The negligence of the employee is the cause of the disaster. They declare with one voice before the jury that ten or twelve years earlier their labor lasted only eight hours a day. During the last five or six years it had been screwed up to 14, 18, and 20 hours. Under especially heavy pressure from holiday-makers, at times of excursion trains, it often lasted 40 or 50 hours without a break. They were ordinary men, not Cyclops. At a certain point their labor-power failed. A stupor seized them. Their brains stopped thinking, and their eyes stopped seeing. The thoroughly “respectable” British jurymen answered with a verdict that sent them for trial at the next assizes (the periodic criminal courts) on a charge of manslaughter. In a gentle “rider” added to their verdict, the jurymen expressed the pious hope that in future the capitalist magnates of the railways would be more extravagant in buying a sufficient quantity of labor-power, and more “abstemious,” more “self-denying,” more “thrifty,” in draining the labor-power they paid for.[^10.55]

[^10.54]: Public meeting of agricultural labourers at Lasswade, near Edinburgh, January 5th, 1866. (See *Workman’s Advocate*, January 13th, 1866.) The formation, since the close of 1865, of a Trades’ Union among the agricultural workers, at first in Scotland, is a historic event. In one of the most oppressed agricultural districts of England, Buckinghamshire, the workers made a great strike in March, 1867, to raise their weekly wage from 9-10 shillings to 12 shillings. (It will be seen from the preceding passage that the movement of the English agricultural proletariat — the class of wage workers, who own nothing they can live by except their labor-power — begins again in the sixties. That movement had been entirely crushed since its violent outbreaks were suppressed after 1830, and especially since the new Poor Laws were introduced. It goes on until it finally becomes epoch-making in 1872. I return to this in the 2nd volume, as well as to the Blue books on the position of the English land workers that have appeared since 1867. Addendum to the 3rd ed.)

[^10.55]: *Reynolds’ Newspaper*, January, 1866. — Every week this same paper prints, under sensational headings such as “Fearful and fatal accidents,” “Appalling tragedies,” etc., a whole list of fresh railway disasters. An employee on the North Staffordshire line comments on them: “Everyone knows the consequences that may occur if the driver and fireman of a locomotive engine are not continually on the look-out. How can that be expected from a man who has been at such work for 29 or 30 hours, exposed to the weather, and without rest. The following is an example which is of very frequent occurrence: — One fireman commenced work on the Monday morning at a very early hour. When he had finished what is called a day’s work, he had been on duty 14 hours 50 minutes. Before he had time to get his tea, he was again called on for duty.... The next time he finished he had been on duty 14 hours 25 minutes, making a total of 29 hours 15 minutes without intermission. The rest of the week’s work was made up as follows: — Wednesday, 15 hours; Thursday, 15 hours 35 minutes; Friday, 14½ hours; Saturday, 14 hours 10 minutes, making a total for the week of 88 hours 30 minutes. Now, sir, fancy his astonishment on being paid 6 1/4 days for the whole. Thinking it was a mistake, he applied to the time-keeper,... and inquired what they considered a day’s work, and was told 13 hours for a goods man (*i.e*., 78 hours).... He then asked for what he had made over and above the 78 hours per week, but was refused. However, he was at last told they would give him another quarter, *i.e*., 10d.,” cited above, 4th February. 1866.

<!-- ch10-p078 -->
A motley crowd of workers of all trades, ages, and sexes presses on us, more eagerly than the souls of the slain pressed on Ulysses. Without looking at the Blue books under their arms, we see at a glance the mark of over-work on them. From this crowd let us take two more figures, whose striking contrast proves that before capital all men are alike: a milliner and a blacksmith.

<!-- ch10-p079 -->
In the last week of June, 1863, all the London daily papers published a paragraph with the “sensational” heading, “Death from simple over-work.” It dealt with the death of the milliner Mary Anne Walkley, 20 years of age. She was employed in a highly respectable dressmaking establishment, exploited by a lady with the pleasant name of Elise. The old, often-told story[^10.56] was told once more. This girl worked, on average, 16½ hours, and during the season often 30 hours without a break, while her failing labor-power was revived now and then with sherry, port, or coffee. It was just then the height of the season. Gorgeous dresses had to be conjured up in the twinkling of an eye for the noble ladies invited to the ball in honor of the newly imported Princess of Wales. Mary Anne Walkley had worked without a break for 26½ hours, together with 60 other girls, 30 in one room, which provided only 1/3 of the cubic feet of air they needed. At night they slept in pairs in one of the stifling holes into which the bedroom was divided by board partitions.[^10.57] And this was one of the best millinery establishments in London. Mary Anne Walkley fell ill on the Friday and died on the Sunday, without, to the astonishment of Madame Elise, having first finished the work in hand. The doctor, Mr. Keys, who was called too late to her death-bed, duly bore witness before the coroner’s jury that

[^10.56]: Compare F. Engels, cited above, pp. 253, 254.

[^10.57]: Dr. Letheby, Consulting Physician of the Board of Health, declared: “The minimum of air for each adult ought to be in a sleeping room 300, and in a dwelling room 500 cubic feet.” Dr. Richardson, Senior Physician to one of the London Hospitals, says: “With needlewomen of all kinds, including milliners, dressmakers, and ordinary seamstresses, there are three miseries — over-work, deficient air, and either deficient food or deficient digestion.... Needlework, in the main, ... is infinitely better adapted to women than to men. But the mischiefs of the trade, in the metropolis especially, are that it is monopolised by some twenty-six capitalists, who, under the advantages that spring from capital, can bring in capital to force economy out of labour. This power tells throughout the whole class. If a dressmaker can get a little circle of customers, such is the competition that, in her home, she must work to the death to hold together, and this same over-work she must of necessity inflict on any who may assist her. If she fail, or do not try independently, she must join an establishment, where her labour is not less, but where her money is safe. Placed thus, she becomes a mere slave, tossed about with the variations of society. Now at home, in one room, starving, or near to it, then engaged 15, 16, aye, even 18 hours out of the 24, in an air that is scarcely tolerable, and on food which, even if it be good, cannot be digested in the absence of pure air. On these victims, consumption, which is purely a disease of bad air, feeds.” Dr. Richardson: “Work and Over-work,” in “Social Science Review,” 18th July, 1863.

<!-- ch10-p080 -->
> “Mary Anne Walkley had died from long hours of work in an over-crowded work-room, and a too small and badly ventilated bedroom.”

<!-- ch10-p081 -->
To teach the doctor some good manners, the coroner’s jury then brought in a verdict that

<!-- ch10-p082 -->
> “the deceased had died of apoplexy, but there was reason to fear that her death had been accelerated by over-work in an over-crowded workroom, &c.”

<!-- ch10-p083 -->
“Our white slaves,” cried the *Morning Star*, the paper of the Free-traders Cobden and Bright, “our white slaves, who are toiled into the grave, for the most part silently pine and die.”[^10.58]

[^10.58]: *Morning Star*, 23rd June, 1863. — *The Times* used the incident to defend the American slave-owners against Bright, etc. “Very many of us think,” says an editorial of July 2nd, 1863, “that, while we work our own young women to death, using the scourge of starvation, instead of the crack of the whip, as the instrument of compulsion, we have scarcely a right to hound on fire and slaughter against families who were born slave-owners, and who, at least, feed their slaves well, and work them lightly.” In the same way the *Standard,* a Tory paper, attacked the Rev. Newman Hall: “He excommunicated the slave-owners, but prays with the fine folk who, without remorse, make the omnibus drivers and conductors of London, &c., work 16 hours a-day for the wages of a dog.” Finally the oracle spoke: Thomas Carlyle, of whom I wrote in 1850, “Zum Teufel ist der Genius, der Kultus ist geblieben.” [“The genius has gone to the devil, the cult has remained,” paraphrasing Schiller] In a short parable, he reduces the one great event of present-day history, the American Civil War, to this level: the Peter of the North wants to break the head of the Paul of the South with all his might, because the Peter of the North hires his labor by the day, and the Paul of the South hires his by the life. (*Macmillan’s Magazine.* Ilias Americana in nuce. August, 1863.) So the bubble of Tory sympathy for the urban workers — by no means for the rural ones — has burst at last. The sum of it all is — slavery!

<!-- ch10-p084 -->
> “It is not in dressmakers’ rooms that working to death is the order of the day, but in a thousand other places; in every place I had almost said, where ‘a thriving business’ has to be done.... We will take the blacksmith as a type. If the poets were true, there is no man so hearty, so merry, as the blacksmith; he rises early and strikes his sparks before the sun; he eats and drinks and sleeps as no other man. Working in moderation, he is, in fact, in one of the best of human positions, physically speaking. But we follow him into the city or town, and we see the stress of work on that strong man, and what then is his position in the death-rate of his country. In Marylebone, blacksmiths die at the rate of 31 per thousand per annum, or 11 above the mean of the male adults of the country in its entirety. The occupation, instinctive almost as a portion of human art, unobjectionable as a branch of human industry, is made by mere excess of work, the destroyer of the man. He can strike so many blows per day, walk so many steps, breathe so many breaths, produce so much work, and live an average, say of fifty years; he is made to strike so many more blows, to walk so many more steps, to breathe so many more breaths per day, and to increase altogether a fourth of his life. He meets the effort; the result is, that producing for a limited time a fourth more work, he dies at 37 for 50.”[^10.59]

[^10.59]: Dr. Richardson, cited above.

### Section 4: Day and Night Work. The Relay System

<!-- ch10-p085 -->
Considered from the standpoint of creating surplus-value, constant capital, the means of production, exists only to absorb labor, and with every drop of labor a proportional amount of surplus labor. (Constant capital is the part of capital spent on means of production. Its value is passed on to the product but does not grow.) As long as the means of production fail to do this, their mere existence is a relative loss to the capitalist, because for as long as they lie idle they represent a useless advance of capital. And this loss becomes positive and absolute as soon as the break in their use makes extra outlay necessary when work starts again. Extending the working day beyond the limits of the natural day, into the night, is only a partial remedy. It quenches the vampire thirst for the living blood of labor only to a slight degree. So the built-in tendency of capitalist production is to appropriate labor during all the 24 hours of the day. But it is physically impossible to exploit the same individual labor-power constantly, by night as well as by day. To overcome this physical obstacle, an alternation becomes necessary between the workers whose powers are exhausted by day and those who are used up by night. This alternation can be arranged in various ways. For example, it may be arranged so that part of the workers are employed on day-work one week and on night-work the next. It is well known that this relay system, this alternation of two sets of workers, held full sway in the full-blooded youth of the English cotton industry, and that today it still flourishes, among other places, in the cotton spinning of the Moscow district. This 24-hour process of production exists today as a system in many branches of industry in Great Britain that are still “free”: in the blast-furnaces, forges, plate-rolling mills, and other metalworking establishments in England, Wales, and Scotland. Here the working time includes not only the 24 hours of the 6 working days, but also a great part of the 24 hours of Sunday. The workers are men and women, adults and children of both sexes. The ages of the children and young persons run through every grade in between, from 8 (in some cases from 6) to 18.[^10.60]

[^10.60]: Children’s Employment Commission. Third Report. London, 1864, pp. iv., v., vi.

<!-- ch10-p086 -->
In some branches of industry, the girls and women work through the night together with the male workers.[^10.61]

[^10.61]: “Both in Staffordshire and in South Wales young girls and women are employed on the pit banks and on the coke heaps, not only by day but also by night. This practice has been often noticed in Reports presented to Parliament, as being attended with great and notorious evils. These females employed with the men, hardly distinguished from them in their dress, and begrimed with dirt and smoke, are exposed to the deterioration of character, arising from the loss of self-respect, which can hardly fail to follow from their unfeminine occupation.” (cited above, 194, p. xxvi. Compare Fourth Report (1865), 61, p. xiii.) The same is true in glass-works.

<!-- ch10-p087 -->
Leaving aside the generally harmful effects of night-labor,[^10.62] a process of production that runs unbroken through the 24 hours offers very welcome opportunities to exceed the limits of the normal working day, for example in the branches of industry already mentioned, which are extremely exhausting. The official working day usually means 12 hours for each worker, by night or by day. But the overwork beyond this amount is in many cases, to use the words of the English official report, “truly fearful.”[^10.63]

[^10.62]: A steel manufacturer who employs children on night-labor remarked: “It seems but natural that boys who work at night cannot sleep and get proper rest by day, but will be running about.” (cited above, Fourth Report, 63, p. xiii.) On the importance of sunlight for keeping up and growing the body, a physician writes: “Light also acts upon the tissues of the body directly in hardening them and supporting their elasticity. The muscles of animals, when they are deprived of a proper amount of light, become soft and inelastic, the nervous power loses its tone from defective stimulation, and the elaboration of all growth seems to be perverted.... In the case of children, constant access to plenty of light during the day, and to the direct rays of the sun for a part of it, is most essential to health. Light assists in the elaboration of good plastic [tissue-forming] blood, and hardens the fibre after it has been laid down. It also acts as a stimulus upon the organs of sight, and by this means brings about more activity in the various cerebral functions.” Dr. W. Strange, Senior Physician of the Worcester General Hospital, from whose work on “Health” (1864) this passage is taken, writes in a letter to Mr. White, one of the commissioners: “I have had opportunities formerly, when in Lancashire, of observing the effects of nightwork upon children, and I have no hesitation in saying, contrary to what some employers were fond of asserting, those children who were subjected to it soon suffered in their health.” (cited above, 284., p. 55.) That such a question should become the material of serious controversy shows plainly how capitalist production acts on the brain-functions of capitalists and their retainers.

[^10.63]: cited above, 57, p. xii.

<!-- ch10-p088 -->
> “It is impossible,” the report continues, “for any mind to realise the amount of work described in the following passages as being performed by boys of from 9 to 12 years of age ... without coming irresistibly to the conclusion that such abuses of the power of parents and of employers can no longer be allowed to exist.”[^10.64]

[^10.64]: cited above, Fourth Report (1865). 58. p. xii.

<!-- ch10-p089 -->
> “The practice of boys working at all by day and night turns either in the usual course of things, or at pressing times, seems inevitably to open the door to their not unfrequently working unduly long hours. These hours are, indeed, in some cases, not only cruelly but even incredibly long for children. Amongst a number of boys it will, of course, not unfrequently happen that one or more are from some cause absent. When this happens, their place is made up by one or more boys, who work in the other turn. That this is a well understood system is plain ... from the answer of the manager of some large rolling-mills, who, when I asked him how the place of the boys absent from their turn was made up, ‘I daresay, sir, you know that as well as I do,’ and admitted the fact.”[^10.65]

[^10.65]: cited above.

<!-- ch10-p090 -->
> “At a rolling-mill where the proper hours were from 6 a.m. to 5½ p.m., a boy worked about four nights every week till 8½ p.m. at least ... and this for six months. Another, at 9 years old, sometimes made three 12-hour shifts running, and, when 10, has made two days and two nights running.” A third, “now 10 ... worked from 6 a.m. till 12 p.m. three nights, and till 9 p.m. the other nights.” “Another, now 13, ... worked from 6 p.m. till 12 noon next day, for a week together, and sometimes for three shifts together, e.g., from Monday morning till Tuesday night.” “Another, now 12, has worked in an iron foundry at Stavely from 6 a.m. till 12 p.m. for a fortnight on end; could not do it any more.” “George Allinsworth, age 9, came here as cellar-boy last Friday; next morning we had to begin at 3, so I stopped here all night. Live five miles off. Slept on the floor of the furnace, over head, with an apron under me, and a bit of a jacket over me. The two other days I have been here at 6 a.m. Aye! it *is* hot in here. Before I came here I was nearly a year at the same work at some works in the country. Began there, too, at 3 on Saturday morning – always did, but was very gain [near] home, and could sleep at home. Other days I began at 6 in the morning, and gi’en [given] over at 6 or 7 in the evening,” etc.[^10.66]

[^10.66]: cited above, p. xiii. The level of culture of these “labor-powers” must naturally be what appears in the following dialogues with one of the commissioners: Jeremiah Haynes, age 12 — “Four times four is 8; 4 fours are 16. A king is him that has all the money and gold. We have a king (told it is a Queen), they call her the Princess Alexandra. Told that she married the Queen’s son. The Queen’s son is the Princess Alexandra. A Princess is a man.” William Turner, age 12 — “Don’t live in England. Think it is a country, but didn’t know before.” John Morris, age 14 — “Have heard say that God made the world, and that all the people was drownded but one, heard say that one was a little bird.” William Smith age 15 — “God made man, man made woman.” Edward Taylor, age 15 — “Do not know of London.” Henry Matthewman, age 17 — “Had been to chapel, but missed a good many times lately. One name that they preached about was Jesus Christ, but I cannot say any others, and I cannot tell anything about him. He was not killed, but died like other people. He was not the same as other people in some ways, because he was religious in some ways and others isn’t.” (cited above, p. xv.) “The devil is a good person. I don’t know where he lives.” “Christ was a wicked man.” “This girl spelt God as dog, and did not know the name of the queen.” (“Ch. Employment Comm. V. Report, 1866” p. 55, n. 278.) The same system prevails in the glass and paper works as in the metal works already cited. In the paper factories, where the paper is made by machinery, night-work is the rule for all processes except rag-sorting. In some cases night-work, by relays, goes on without a break through the whole week, usually from Sunday night until midnight of the following Saturday. Each week, those on day-work work 5 days of 12 hours and 1 day of 18 hours; those on night-work, 5 nights of 12 hours and 1 of 6 hours. In other cases each set works 24 hours in a row on alternate days, one set working 6 hours on Monday and 18 on Saturday to make up the 24 hours. In still other cases an in-between system prevails, under which everyone employed on the paper-making machinery works 15 or 16 hours every day of the week. This system, says Commissioner Lord, “seems to combine all the evils of both the 12 hours’ and the 24 hours’ relays.” Children under 13, young persons under 18, and women work under this night system. Sometimes, under the 12-hour system, they are forced to work a double turn of 24 hours, because those who ought to relieve them fail to turn up. The evidence proves that boys and girls very often work overtime, which not infrequently stretches to 24 or even 36 hours of unbroken toil. In the continuous and unvarying process of glazing there are girls of 12 who work 14 hours a day for the whole month, “without any regular relief or cessation beyond 2 or, at most, 3 breaks of half an hour each for meals.” In some mills where regular night-work has been entirely given up, overwork goes on to a terrible extent, “and that often in the dirtiest, and in the hottest, and in the most monotonous of the various processes.” (“Ch. Employment Comm. Report IV., 1865,” p. xxxviii, and xxxix.)

<!-- ch10-p091 -->
Let us now hear how capital itself regards this 24-hour system. The extreme forms of the system, its abuse in the “cruel and incredible” extension of the working day, are naturally passed over in silence. Capital speaks of the system only in its “normal” form.

<!-- ch10-p092 -->
Messrs. Naylor & Vickers are steel manufacturers who employ between 600 and 700 persons. Only 10 percent of these are under 18, and of those, only 20 boys under 18 work in night sets. The firm expresses itself as follows:

<!-- ch10-p093 -->
> “The boys do not suffer from the heat. The temperature is probably from 86° to 90°.... At the forges and in the rolling mills the hands work night and day, in relays, but all the other parts of the work are day-work, i.e.*,* from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. In the forge the hours are from 12 to 12. Some of the hands always work in the night, without any alternation of day and night work.... We do not find any difference in the health of those who work regularly by night and those who work by day, and probably people can sleep better if they have the same period of rest than if it is changed.... About 20 of the boys under the age of 18 work in the night sets.... We could not well do without lads under 18 working by night. The objection would be the increase in the cost of production.... Skilled hands and the heads in every department are difficult to get, but of lads we could get any number.... But from the small proportion of boys that we employ, the subject *(i.e*., of restrictions on night-work) is of little importance or interest to us.”[^10.67]

[^10.67]: Fourth Report, &c., 1865, 79, p. xvi.

<!-- ch10-p094 -->
Mr. J. Ellis belongs to the firm of Messrs. John Brown & Co., steel and iron works, which employs about 3,000 men and boys. Part of the firm’s operations, namely iron and heavier steel work, goes on night and day by relays. Mr. Ellis states “that in the heavier steel work one or two boys are employed to a score or two men.” Their concern employs more than 500 boys under 18, of whom about 1/3, or 170, are under the age of 13. On the proposed change in the law, Mr. Ellis says:

<!-- ch10-p095 -->
> “I do not think it would be very objectionable to require that no person under the age of 18 should work more than 12 hours in the 24. But we do not think that any line could be drawn over the age of 12, at which boys could be dispensed with for night-work. But we would sooner be prevented from employing boys under the age of 13, or even so high as 14, at all, than not be allowed to employ boys that we do have at night. Those boys who work in the day sets must take their turn in the night sets also, because the men could not work in the night sets only; it would ruin their health.... We think, however, that night-work in alternate weeks is no harm.”

<!-- ch10-p096 -->
(Messrs. Naylor & Vickers, on the other hand, in keeping with the interest of their business, thought that night-labor changed at regular intervals might possibly do more harm than continual night-labor.)

<!-- ch10-p097 -->
> “We find the men who do it, as well as the others who do other work only by day.... Our objections to not allowing boys under 18 to work at night, would be on account of the increase of expense, but this is the only reason.”

<!-- ch10-p098 -->
> (What cynical naïveté!) “We think that the increase would be more than the trade, with due regard to its being successfully carried out, could fairly bear. (What mealy-mouthed wording!)
