Labour is scarce here, and might fall short if there were such a regulation.” (that is, Ellis Brown & Co. might fall into the fatal predicament of having to pay labor-power its full value.)[^10.68]

[^10.68]: cited above, 80. p. xvi.

<!-- ch10-p099 -->
The “Cyclops Steel and Iron Works” of Messrs. Cammell & Co. are set up on the same large scale as those of John Brown & Co., mentioned above. The managing director had handed in his evidence to the Government Commissioner, Mr. White, in writing. Later, when the manuscript had been returned to him for revision, he found it convenient to suppress it. Mr. White, however, has a good memory. He remembered quite clearly that, for the Messrs. Cyclops, forbidding the night-labor of children and young persons “would be impossible, it would be tantamount to stopping their works.” And yet their business employs little more than 6% of boys under 18, and less than 1% under 13.[^10.69]

[^10.69]: cited above, 82. p. xvii.

<!-- ch10-p100 -->
On the same subject Mr. E. F. Sanderson, of the firm of Sanderson, Bros., & Co., steel rolling-mills and forges, Attercliffe, says:

<!-- ch10-p101 -->
> “Great difficulty would be caused by preventing boys under 18 from working at night. The chief would be the increase of cost from employing men instead of boys. I cannot say what this would be, but probably it would not be enough to enable the manufacturers to raise the price of steel, and consequently it would fall on them, as of course the men (what odd-headed folk!) would refuse to pay it.”

<!-- ch10-p102 -->
Mr. Sanderson does not know how much he pays the children, but

<!-- ch10-p103 -->
> “perhaps the younger boys get from 4s. to 5s. a week.... The boys’ work is of a kind for which the strength of the boys is generally (‘generally,’ of course not always) quite sufficient, and consequently there would be no gain in the greater strength of the men to counterbalance the loss, or it would be only in the few cases in which the metal is heavy. The men would not like so well not to have boys under them, as men would be less obedient. Besides, boys must begin young to learn the trade. Leaving day-work alone open to boys would not answer this purpose.”

<!-- ch10-p104 -->
And why not? Why could boys not learn their handicraft in the daytime? Your reason?

<!-- ch10-p105 -->
> “Owing to the men working days and nights in alternate weeks, the men would be separated half the time from their boys, and would lose half the profit which they make from them. The training which they give to an apprentice is considered as part of the return for the boys’ labour, and thus enables the man to get it at a cheaper rate. Each man would want half of this profit.”

<!-- ch10-p106 -->
In other words, Messrs. Sanderson would have to pay part of the adult men’s wages out of their own pockets, instead of paying it with the night-work of the boys. Messrs. Sanderson’s profit would then fall to some extent, and this is the good Sandersonian reason why boys cannot learn their handicraft in the day.[^10.70] Besides this, it would throw night-labor on those who worked in place of the boys, and they would not be able to stand it. In fact the difficulties would be so great that they would very likely lead to night-work being given up altogether, and “as far as the work itself is concerned,” says E. F. Sanderson, “this would suit as well, but –” But Messrs. Sanderson have something else to make besides steel. Steel-making is simply a pretext for surplus-value making. The smelting furnaces, rolling-mills, etc., the buildings, machinery, iron, coal, etc., have something more to do than turn themselves into steel. They are there to absorb surplus labor, and naturally they absorb more in 24 hours than in 12. In fact, by the grace of God and the law, they give the Sandersons a check drawn on the working time of a certain number of workers for all the 24 hours of the day. And as soon as their function of absorbing labor is interrupted, they lose their character as capital, and so are a pure loss for the Sandersons.

[^10.70]: In our reflecting and reasoning age a man is not worth much who cannot give a good reason for everything, no matter how bad or how crazy. Everything in the world that has been done wrong has been done wrong for the very best of reasons. (Hegel, cited above, p. 249)

<!-- ch10-p107 -->
> “But then there would be the loss from so much expensive machinery, lying idle half the time, and to get through the amount of work which we are able to do on the present system, we should have to double our premises and plant, which would double the outlay.”

<!-- ch10-p108 -->
But why should these Sandersons claim a privilege not enjoyed by the other capitalists, who work only during the day, and whose buildings, machinery, and raw material therefore lie “idle” during the night? E. F. Sanderson answers in the name of all the Sandersons:

<!-- ch10-p109 -->
> “It is true that there is this loss from machinery lying idle in those manufactories in which work only goes on by day. But the use of furnaces would involve a further loss in our case. If they were kept up there would be a waste of fuel (instead of, as now, a waste of the living substance of the workers), and if they were not, there would be loss of time in laying the fires and getting the heat up (while the loss of sleeping time, even to children of 8, is a gain of working time for the Sanderson tribe), and the furnaces themselves would suffer from the changes of temperature.” (While those same furnaces suffer nothing from the day and night change of labor.)[^10.71]

[^10.71]: cited above, 85, p. xvii. The glass manufacturers have similar tender scruples: regular meal-times for the children are impossible, they say, because then a certain quantity of heat radiated by the furnaces would be “a pure loss” or “wasted.” Commissioner White answers them. His answer is unlike that of Ure, Senior, etc., and of their puny German plagiarists in Roscher’s style, who are touched by the “abstinence,” “self-denial,” and “saving” of the capitalists in spending their gold, and by their Timur-Tamerlanish lavishness with human life! “A certain amount of heat beyond what is usual at present might also be going to waste, if meal-times were secured in these cases, but it seems likely not equal in money-value to the waste of animal power now going on in glass-houses throughout the kingdom from growing boys not having enough quiet time to eat their meals at ease, with a little rest afterwards for digestion.” (cited above, p. xiv.) And this in the year of progress 1865! Leaving aside the strength spent in lifting and carrying, such a child, in the sheds where bottle and flint glass are made, walks 15-20 miles in every 6 hours while doing his work! And the work often lasts 14 or 15 hours! In many of these glass works, as in the Moscow spinning mills, the system of 6 hours’ relays is in force. “During the working part of the week six hours is the utmost unbroken period ever attained at any one time for rest, and out of this has to come the time spent in coming and going to and from work, washing, dressing, and meals, leaving a very short period indeed for rest, and none for fresh air and play, unless at the expense of the sleep necessary for young boys, especially at such hot and fatiguing work.... Even the short sleep is obviously liable to be broken by a boy having to wake himself if it is night, or by the noise, if it is day.” Mr. White gives cases where a boy worked 36 hours in a row; others where boys of 12 drudged on until 2 in the morning, and then slept in the works till 5 a.m. (3 hours!) only to start work again. “The amount of work,” say Tremenheere and Tufnell, who drafted the general report, “done by boys, youths, girls, and women, in the course of their daily or nightly spell of labour, is certainly extraordinary.” (cited above, xliii. and xliv.) Meanwhile, late at night, self-denying Mr. Glass-Capital, primed with port-wine, reels out of his club on his way home, droning idiotically: “Britons never, never shall be slaves!”

### Section 5: The Struggle for a Normal Working Day. Compulsory Laws for the Extension of the Working Day from the Middle of the 14th to the End of the 17th Century

<!-- ch10-p110 -->
“What is a working day? What is the length of time during which capital may consume the labour-power whose daily value it buys? How far may the working day be extended beyond the working-time necessary for the reproduction of labour-power itself?” We have seen how capital answers these questions: the working day contains the full 24 hours, minus the few hours of rest without which labor-power absolutely refuses to serve again. So it goes without saying that the worker, his whole life long, is nothing but labor-power. It follows that all his disposable time is, by nature and by law, labor-time, to be devoted to the self-expansion of capital. Time for education, for intellectual development, for carrying out social functions and for social dealings, for the free play of his bodily and mental activity, even the rest time of Sunday (and that in a country of strict Sabbath-keepers!)[^10.72] – moonshine! But in its blind, unrestrainable passion, its werewolf hunger for surplus labor, capital oversteps not only the moral but even the merely physical maximum limits of the working day. It seizes the time needed for the growth, development, and healthy upkeep of the body. It steals the time required for taking in fresh air and sunlight. It haggles over a meal-time, and where possible it makes the meal part of the production process itself, so that food is given to the worker as to a mere means of production, as coal is fed to the boiler and grease and oil to the machinery. It cuts down the sound sleep needed to restore, repair, and refresh the bodily powers to just as many hours of stupor as an organism that is absolutely exhausted needs in order to revive. It is not the normal upkeep of labor-power that is to set the limits of the working day. It is the greatest possible daily expenditure of labor-power, no matter how diseased, forced, and painful it may be, that is to set the limits of the workers’ period of rest. Capital cares nothing for how long labor-power lives. All that concerns it is simply and solely the maximum of labor-power that can be set flowing in one working day. It reaches this goal by shortening the worker’s life, just as a greedy farmer snatches bigger harvests from the soil by robbing it of its fertility.

[^10.72]: In England, even now, a worker in a rural district is occasionally sentenced to prison for desecrating the Sabbath by working in his front garden. The same worker is punished for breach of contract if he stays away from his metal, paper, or glass works on a Sunday, even if he does so out of a religious whim. The orthodox Parliament will hear nothing of Sabbath-breaking if it happens in the process of expanding capital. A memorial (August 1863), in which the London day-laborers in fish and poultry shops asked for Sunday labor to be abolished, states that for the first 6 days of the week their work lasts 15 hours a day on average, and on Sunday 8-10 hours. From this same memorial we also learn that the delicate gourmets among the aristocratic hypocrites of Exeter Hall especially encourage this “Sunday labour.” These “holy ones,” so zealous *in cute curanda* [in caring for their own skin, that is, their bodily pleasures], show their Christianity by the humility with which they bear the overwork, the hardships, and the hunger of others. *Obsequium ventris istis (the labourers) perniciosius est* [Serving the belly is more ruinous to them (the workers) – paraphrase of Horace].

<!-- ch10-p111 -->
Thus, by extending the working day, the capitalist mode of production (essentially the production of surplus-value, the absorption of surplus labor) produces not only the deterioration of human labor-power, by robbing it of its normal moral and physical conditions of development and activity. It also produces the premature exhaustion and death of this labor-power itself.[^10.73] It extends the worker’s production time within a given period by shortening his actual lifetime.

[^10.73]: “We have given in our previous reports the statements of several experienced manufacturers to the effect that over-hours ... certainly tend prematurely to exhaust the working power of the men.” (cited above, 64. p. xiii.)

<!-- ch10-p112 -->
But the value of labor-power includes the value of the commodities needed to reproduce the worker, that is, to keep the working class going. Capital, in its boundless passion for self-expansion, necessarily strives for an unnatural extension of the working day. If this extension shortens the life of the individual worker, and so the length of time his labor-power lasts, then the forces used up have to be replaced more quickly, and the total cost of reproducing labor-power will be greater. It is just as with a machine: the faster the machine wears out, the greater the part of its value that has to be reproduced every day. So it would seem that capital’s own interest points toward a normal working day.

<!-- ch10-p113 -->
The slave-owner buys his worker as he buys his horse. If he loses his slave, he loses capital that he can only replace by spending money again in the slave market.

<!-- ch10-p114 -->
> But “the rice-grounds of Georgia, or the swamps of the Mississippi may be fatally injurious to the human constitution; but the waste of human life which the cultivation of these districts necessitates, is not so great that it cannot be repaired from the teeming preserves of Virginia and Kentucky. Considerations of economy, moreover, which, under a natural system, afford some security for humane treatment by identifying the master’s interest with the slave’s preservation, when once trading in slaves is practiced, become reasons for racking to the uttermost the toil of the slave; for, when his place can at once be supplied from foreign preserves, the duration of his life becomes a matter of less moment [importance] than its productiveness while it lasts. It is accordingly a maxim of slave management, in slave-importing countries, that the most effective economy is that which takes out of the human chattel in the shortest space of time the utmost amount of exertion it is capable of putting forth. It is in tropical culture, where annual profits often equal the whole capital of plantations, that negro life is most recklessly sacrificed. It is the agriculture of the West Indies, which has been for centuries prolific of fabulous wealth, that has engulfed millions of the African race. It is in Cuba, at this day, whose revenues are reckoned by millions, and whose planters are princes, that we see in the servile class, the coarsest fare, the most exhausting and unremitting toil, and even the absolute destruction of a portion of its numbers every year.”[^10.74]

[^10.74]: Cairnes, “The Slave Power,” pp. 110. 111.

<!-- ch10-p115 -->
*Mutato nomine de te fabula narratur* [Change the name, and the story is told about you – Horace]. For slave trade read labor market; for Kentucky and Virginia read Ireland and the agricultural districts of England, Scotland, and Wales; for Africa read Germany. We heard how overwork thinned the ranks of the bakers in London. Even so, the London labor market is always overstocked with German and other candidates for death in the bakeries. Pottery, as we saw, is one of the industries whose workers live the shortest lives. So is there any shortage of potters? Josiah Wedgwood, the inventor of modern pottery, who was himself originally an ordinary worker, told the House of Commons in 1785 that the whole trade employed from 15,000 to 20,000 people.[^10.75] In the year 1861 the population of just the town centers of this industry in Great Britain numbered 101,302.

[^10.75]: John Ward: “The Borough of Stoke-upon-Trent,” London, 1843, p. 42.

<!-- ch10-p116 -->
> “The cotton trade has existed for ninety years.... It has existed for three generations of the English race, and I believe I may safely say that during that period it has destroyed nine generations of factory operatives.”[^10.76]

[^10.76]: Ferrand’s Speech in the House of Commons, 27th April, 1863.

<!-- ch10-p117 -->
No doubt in certain periods of feverish activity the labor market shows significant gaps. In 1834, for example. But then the manufacturers proposed to the Poor Law Commissioners that they should send the “surplus-population” of the agricultural districts to the north, explaining “that the manufacturers would absorb and use it up.”[^10.77]

[^10.77]: “Those were the very words used by the cotton manufacturers.” Cited above.

<!-- ch10-p118 -->
> Agents were appointed with the consent of the Poor Law Commissioners. ... An office was set up in Manchester, to which lists were sent of those workpeople in the agricultural districts wanting employment, and their names were registered in books. The manufacturers attended at these offices, and selected such persons as they chose; when they had selected such persons as their ‘wants required’, they gave instructions to have them forwarded to Manchester, and they were sent, ticketed like bales of goods, by canals, or with carriers, others tramping on the road, and many of them were found on the way lost and half-starved. This system had grown up unto a regular trade. This House will hardly believe it, but I tell them, that this traffic in human flesh was as well kept up, they were in effect as regularly sold to these [Manchester] manufacturers as slaves are sold to the cotton-grower in the United States.... In 1860, ‘the cotton trade was at its zenith.’ ... The manufacturers again found that they were short of hands.... They applied to the ‘flesh agents, as they are called. Those agents sent to the southern downs of England, to the pastures of Dorsetshire, to the glades of Devonshire, to the people tending kine [cattle] in Wiltshire, but they sought in vain. The surplus-population was ‘absorbed.’”

<!-- ch10-p119 -->
When the French treaty was concluded, the *Bury Guardian* said that “10,000 additional hands could be absorbed by Lancashire, and that 30,000 or 40,000 will be needed.” After the “flesh agents and sub-agents” had searched the agricultural districts in vain,

<!-- ch10-p120 -->
> “a deputation came up to London, and waited on the right hon. gentleman [Mr. Villiers, President of the Poor Law Board] with a view of obtaining poor children from certain union houses [workhouses] for the mills of Lancashire.”[^10.78]

[^10.78]: Cited above. Mr. Villiers, despite the best of intentions on his part, was “legally” obliged to refuse the manufacturers’ requests. These gentlemen, however, got what they wanted through the obliging nature of the local poor law boards. Mr. A. Redgrave, Inspector of Factories, asserts that this time the system under which orphans and pauper children were treated “legally” as apprentices “was not accompanied with the old abuses” (on these “abuses” see Engels, cited above). He grants, though, that in one case there certainly was “abuse of this system in respect to a number of girls and young women brought from the agricultural districts of Scotland into Lancashire and Cheshire.” Under this system the manufacturer made a contract with the workhouse authorities for a certain period. He fed, clothed, and housed the children, and gave them a small allowance of money. A remark of Mr. Redgrave’s, which I will quote in a moment, seems strange. This is especially so if we consider that even among the years of prosperity of the English cotton trade, the year 1860 stands without equal, and that, besides, wages were exceptionally high. For this extraordinary demand for work had to contend with the depopulation of Ireland; with unexampled emigration from the English and Scottish agricultural districts to Australia and America; and with an actual fall in the population in some of the English agricultural districts. This fall was due partly to an actual breakdown of the workers’ vital force, and partly to the dispersal of the available population that the dealers in human flesh had already carried out. Despite all this Mr. Redgrave says: “This kind of labour, however, would only be sought after when none other could be procured, for it is a high-priced labour. The ordinary wages of a boy of 13 would be about 4s. per week, but to lodge, to clothe, to feed, and to provide medical attendance and proper superintendence for 50 or 100 of these boys, and to set aside some remuneration for them, could not be accomplished for 4s. a-head per week.” (Report of the Inspector of Factories for 30th April, 1860, p. 27.) Mr. Redgrave forgets to tell us how the worker himself can do all this for his children out of their 4s. a week in wages, when the manufacturer cannot do it for the 50 or 100 children who are housed, fed, and supervised all together. To guard against drawing false conclusions from the text, I should remark here that the English cotton industry, ever since it was placed under the Factory Act of 1850 with its regulation of labor-time, etc., must be regarded as the model industry of England. The English cotton factory worker is in every respect better off than his companion in misery on the Continent. “The Prussian factory operative labours at least ten hours per week more than his English competitor, and if employed at his own loom in his own house, his labour is not restricted to even those additional hours. (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact.,” 31st October, 1855, p. 103.) Redgrave, the Factory Inspector mentioned above, traveled on the Continent after the Industrial Exhibition in 1851, especially in France and Germany, to inquire into the conditions of the factories. Of the Prussian factory worker he says: “He receives a remuneration sufficient to procure the simple fare, and to supply the slender comforts to which he has been accustomed ... he lives upon his coarse fare, and works hard, wherein his position is subordinate to that of the English operative.” (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact.” 31st Oct., 1855, p. 85.)

<!-- ch10-p121 -->
What experience generally shows the capitalist is a constant excess of population, that is, an excess in relation to the needs of the moment of capital that absorbs surplus labor. This is so although the excess is made up of generations of human beings who are stunted, short-lived, and swiftly replacing each other, plucked, so to speak, before they are ripe.[^10.79] And indeed, experience shows the intelligent observer how swiftly and how firmly the capitalist mode of production, which historically speaking dates only from yesterday, has seized the vital power of the people by the very root. It shows how the degeneration of the industrial population is only slowed down by the constant absorption of primitive and physically uncorrupted elements from the country. It shows how even the country workers, in spite of fresh air and the principle of natural selection that works so powerfully among them and lets only the strongest survive, are already beginning to die off.[^10.80] Capital, which has such good reasons for denying the sufferings of the legions of workers that surround it, is in practice moved as much and as little by the prospect of the coming degradation and final depopulation of the human race as by the probable fall of the earth into the sun. In every stock-market swindle everyone knows that some time or other the crash must come. But everyone hopes that it will fall on the head of his neighbor, after he himself has caught the shower of gold and put it in a safe place. *Après moi le déluge!* [After me, the flood!] is the watchword of every capitalist and of every capitalist nation. Hence capital is reckless of the health or length of life of the worker, unless society compels it to care.[^10.81] To the outcry about physical and mental degradation, premature death, and the torture of overwork, it answers: Why should these trouble us, since they increase our profits? But taking things as a whole, all this does not, indeed, depend on the good or ill will of the individual capitalist. Free competition brings out the built-in laws of capitalist production in the form of external, coercive laws that have power over every individual capitalist.[^10.82]

[^10.79]: The overworked “die off with strange rapidity; but the places of those who perish are instantly filled, and a frequent change of persons makes no alteration in the scene.” (“England and America.” London, 1833, vol. I, p. 55. By E. G. Wakefield.)

[^10.80]: See “Public Health. Sixth Report of the Medical Officer of the Privy Council, 1863.” Published in London 1864. This report deals especially with the agricultural workers. “Sutherland ... is commonly represented as a highly improved county ... but ... recent inquiry has discovered that even there, in districts once famous for fine men and gallant soldiers, the inhabitants have degenerated into a meagre and stunted race. In the healthiest situations, on hill sides fronting the sea, the faces of their famished children are as pale as they could be in the foul atmosphere of a London alley.” (W. Th. Thornton. “Overpopulation and its Remedy.” cited above, pp. 74, 75.) In fact they resemble the 30,000 “gallant Highlanders” whom Glasgow packs together like pigs in its wynds and closes (narrow lanes and alleys), along with prostitutes and thieves.

[^10.81]: “But though the health of a population is so important a fact of the national capital, we are afraid it must be said that the class of employers of labour have not been the most forward to guard and cherish this treasure.... The consideration of the health of the operatives was forced upon the mill-owners.” (*Times*, November 5th, 1861.) “The men of the West Riding became the clothiers of mankind ... the health of the workpeople was sacrificed, and the race in a few generations must have degenerated. But a reaction set in. Lord Shaftesbury’s Bill limited the hours of children’s labour,” etc. (“Report of the Registrar-General,” for October 1861.)

[^10.82]: So we find, for example, that at the beginning of 1863, 26 firms owning large potteries in Staffordshire, among them Josiah Wedgwood, & Sons, petition in a memorial for “some legislative enactment.” Competition with other capitalists does not allow them to limit working time for children, etc., of their own free will. “Much as we deplore the evils before mentioned, it would not be possible to prevent them by any scheme of agreement between the manufacturers. ... Taking all these points into consideration, we have come to the conviction that some legislative enactment is wanted.” (“Children’s Employment Comm.” Rep. I, 1863, p. 322.) Most recently a much more striking example has turned up. During a period of feverish activity, the rise in the price of cotton had led the manufacturers in Blackburn to agree among themselves to shorten the working time in their mills for a certain fixed period. This period ended about the end of November, 1871. Meanwhile, the wealthier manufacturers, who combined spinning with weaving, used the fall in production that resulted from this agreement to expand their own business, and so made great profits at the expense of the small employers. The small employers, in their desperate straits, then turned to the factory workers, urged them earnestly to agitate for the 9 hours’ system, and promised money contributions to this end.

<!-- ch10-p122 -->
Setting up a normal working day is the result of centuries of struggle between capitalist and worker. The history of this struggle shows two opposed tendencies. Compare, for example, the English factory legislation of our time with the English labor Statutes from the 14th century until well into the middle of the 18th.[^10.83] While the modern Factory Acts shortened the working day by compulsion, the earlier statutes tried to lengthen it by compulsion. Of course, the claims of capital in embryo – when, just beginning to grow, it secures the right to absorb a *quantum sufficit* [sufficient amount] of surplus labor, not merely by the force of economic relations but with the help of the State – look very modest next to the concessions that it has to make, growling and struggling, once it is grown up. It takes centuries before the “free” worker, thanks to the development of capitalist production, agrees, that is, *is* compelled by social conditions, to sell the whole of his active life, his very capacity for work, for the price of the necessaries of life: to sell his birthright for a mess of pottage. Hence it is natural that two things roughly coincide. One is the lengthening of the working day that capital, from the middle of the 14th to the end of the 17th century, tries to impose on adult workers by State measures. The other is the shortening of the working day that the State has carried out here and there, in the second half of the 19th century, to prevent the coining of children’s blood into capital. What has been proclaimed today, for example in the State of Massachusetts, until recently the freest State of the North-American Republic, as the legal limit on the labor of children under 12, was in England, even in the middle of the 17th century, the normal working day of able-bodied craftsmen, robust laborers, and athletic blacksmiths.[^10.84]

[^10.83]: The labor Statutes, similar ones to which were passed at the same time in France, the Netherlands, and elsewhere, were first formally repealed in England in 1813, long after changes in the methods of production had made them obsolete.

[^10.84]: “No child under 12 years of age shall be employed in any manufacturing establishment more than 10 hours in one day.” General Statutes of Massachusetts, 63, ch. 12. (The various Statutes were passed between 1836 and 1858.) “Labour performed during a period of 10 hours on any day in all cotton, woollen, silk, paper, glass, and flax factories, or in manufactories of iron and brass, shall be considered a legal day’s labour. And be it enacted, that hereafter no minor engaged in any factory shall be holden [held] or required to work more than 10 hours in any day, or 60 hours in any week; and that hereafter no minor shall be admitted as a worker under the age of 10 years in any factory within this State.” State of New Jersey. An Act to limit the hours of labour, &c., § 1 and 2. (Law of 18th March, 1851.) “No minor who has attained the age of 12 years, and is under the age of 15 years, shall be employed in any manufacturing establishment more than 11 hours in any one day, nor before 5 o’clock in the morning, nor after 7.30 in the evening.” (“Revised Statutes of the State of Rhode Island,” etc., ch. 139, § 23, 1st July, 1857.)

<!-- ch10-p123 -->
The first “Statute of Labourers” (23 Edward III., 1349) found its immediate pretext (not its cause, for legislation of this kind lasts for centuries after its pretext has disappeared) in the great plague that decimated the people, so that, as a Tory writer says, “The difficulty of getting men to work on reasonable terms (that is, at a price that left their employers a reasonable quantity of surplus labor) grew to such a height as to be quite intolerable.”[^10.85] Reasonable wages were therefore fixed by law, and so were the limits of the working day. This second point, the only one that interests us here, is repeated in the Statute of 1496 (Henry VII.). According to this statute (which, however, could not be enforced), the working day for all craftsmen and field laborers from March to September ought to last from 5 in the morning to between 7 and 8 in the evening. But the meal-times consist of 1 hour for breakfast, 1½ hours for dinner, and ½ an hour for “noon-meate,” that is, exactly twice as much as under the Factory Acts now in force.[^10.86] In winter, work was to last from 5 in the morning until dark, with the same breaks. A statute of Elizabeth of 1562 leaves the length of the working day untouched for all workers “hired for daily or weekly wage,” but it aims at limiting the breaks to 2½ hours in the summer, or to 2 in the winter. Dinner is to last only 1 hour, and the “afternoon-sleep of half an hour” is allowed only between the middle of May and the middle of August. For every hour of absence, 1d. is to be deducted from the wage. In practice, however, conditions were much more favorable to the workers than the statute-book says. William Petty, the father of political economy, and to some extent the founder of statistics, says in a work that he published in the last third of the 17th century:

[^10.85]: “Sophisms of Free Trade.” 7th Ed. London, 1850, p. 205, 9th Ed., p. 253. This same Tory, moreover, admits that “Acts of Parliament regulating wages, but against the labourer and in favour of the master, lasted for the long period of 464 years. Population grew. These laws were then found, and really became, unnecessary and burdensome.” (cited above, p. 206.)

[^10.86]: J. Wade rightly remarks about this statute: “From the statement above (i.e., with regard to the statute) it appears that in 1496 the diet was considered equivalent to one-third of the income of an artificer and one-half the income of a labourer, which indicates a greater degree of independence among the working-classes than prevails at present; for the board, both of labourers and artificers, would now be reckoned at a much higher proportion of their wages.” (J. Wade, “History of the Middle and Working Classes,” pp. 24, 25, and 577.) The opinion that this difference comes from the difference in the price relations between food and clothing then and now is refuted by even the most cursory glance at “Chronicon Preciosum, &c.” By Bishop Fleetwood. 1st Ed., London, 1707; 2nd Ed., London, 1745.

<!-- ch10-p124 -->
> “Labouring-men (at that time this meant field laborers) work 10 hours per diem [a day], and make 20 meals per week, viz., 3 a day for working days, and 2 on Sundays; whereby it is plain, that if they could fast on Friday nights, and dine in one hour and an half, whereas they take two, from eleven to one; thereby thus working 1/20 more, and spending 1/20 less, the above-mentioned (tax) might be raised.”[^10.87]

[^10.87]: W. Petty. “Political Anatomy of Ireland, Verbum Sapienti,” 1672, Ed. 1691, p. 10.

<!-- ch10-p125 -->
Was Dr. Andrew Ure not right to denounce the 12 hours’ bill of 1833 as a step back to the times of the dark ages? It is true that these regulations, contained in the statute Petty mentions, also apply to apprentices. But the following complaint shows what the condition of child labor was, even at the end of the 17th century:

<!-- ch10-p126 -->
> “’Tis not their practice (in Germany) as with us in this kingdom, to bind an apprentice for seven years; three or four is their common standard: and the reason is, because they are educated from their cradle to something of employment, which renders them the more apt and docile, and consequently the more capable of attaining to a ripeness and quicker proficiency in business. Whereas our youth, here in England, being bred to nothing before they come to be apprentices, make a very slow progress and require much longer time wherein to reach the perfection of accomplished artists [skilled craftsmen].”[^10.88]

[^10.88]: “A Discourse on the necessity of encouraging Mechanick Industry,” London, 1690, p. 13. Macaulay, who has falsified English history in the interests of the Whigs and the bourgeoisie, declares as follows: “The practice of setting children prematurely to work ... prevailed in the 17th century to an extent which, when compared with the extent of the manufacturing system, seems almost incredible. At Norwich, the chief seat of the clothing trade, a little creature of six years old was thought fit for labour. Several writers of that time, and among them some who were considered as eminently benevolent, mention with exultation the fact that in that single city, boys and girls of very tender age create wealth exceeding what was necessary for their own subsistence by twelve thousand pounds a year. The more carefully we examine the history of the past, the more reason shall we find to dissent from those who imagine that our age has been fruitful of new social evils.... That which is new is the intelligence and the humanity which remedies them.” (“History of England,” vol. 1., p. 417.) Macaulay might have reported further that “extremely well-disposed” *amis du commerce* [friends of trade] in the 17th century tell “with exultation” how a child of four was employed in a poorhouse in Holland. He might also have reported that this example of “*vertu mise en pratique*” [virtue put into practice] passes muster in all the humanitarian works in Macaulay’s style, right up to the time of Adam Smith. It is true that when manufacture (the stage and form of capitalist production, roughly from the mid-16th to the late 18th century, based on handicraft work divided among many workers in one workshop) replaces handicrafts, traces of the exploitation of children begin to appear. This exploitation had always existed to a certain extent among peasants, and it was the more developed, the heavier the yoke pressing on the farmer. The tendency of capital is unmistakably there; but the facts themselves are still as isolated as the appearance of two-headed children. Hence the far-seeing “*amis du commerce*” noted them “with exultation” as especially remarkable and as wonders, and recommended them as models for their own time and for posterity. This same Scottish sycophant and smooth talker, Macaulay, says: “We hear to-day only of retrogression and see only progress.” What eyes, and especially what ears!

<!-- ch10-p127 -->
Still, during the greater part of the 18th century, up to the era of modern industry and the machine system, capital in England had not succeeded in seizing for itself the whole week of the worker by paying the weekly value of labor-power. The agricultural laborers, however, were an exception. The workers could live for a whole week on the wage of four days, and to them this did not seem a sufficient reason to work the other two days for the capitalist. One party of English economists, in the interest of capital, denounces this obstinacy in the most violent terms; another party defends the workers. Let us listen, for example, to the contest between Postlethwayt, whose Dictionary of Trade then had the same reputation as the similar works of MacCulloch and MacGregor have today, and the author (already quoted) of the “Essay on Trade and Commerce.”[^10.89]

[^10.89]: Among the accusers of the workers, the angriest is the anonymous author, quoted in the text, of “An Essay on Trade and Commerce, containing Observations on Taxes, &c.,” London, 1770. He had already dealt with this subject in his earlier work: “Considerations on Taxes.” London, 1765. On the same side follows that Polonius, Arthur Young, the unspeakable statistical babbler. Among the defenders of the working class the foremost are: Jacob Vanderlint, in: “Money Answers all Things.” London, 1734; the Rev. Nathaniel Forster, D. D., in “An Enquiry into the Causes of the Present High Price of Provisions,” London, 1767; Dr. Price; and especially Postlethwayt, both in the supplement to his “Universal Dictionary of Trade and Commerce” and in his “Great Britain’s Commercial Interest explained and improved.” 2nd Edition, 1755. The facts themselves are confirmed by many other writers of the time, among others by Josiah Tucker.

<!-- ch10-p128 -->
Postlethwayt says, among other things:

<!-- ch10-p129 -->
> “We cannot put an end to those few observations, without noticing that trite remark in the mouth of too many; that if the industrious poor can obtain enough to maintain themselves in five days, they will not work the whole six. Whence they infer the necessity of even the necessaries of life being made dear by taxes, or any other means, to compel the working artisan and manufacturer [manufacturing worker] to labour the whole six days in the week, without ceasing. I must beg leave to differ in sentiment from those great politicians, who contend for the perpetual slavery of the working people of this kingdom; they forget the vulgar adage, all work and no play. Have not the English boasted of the ingenuity and dexterity of her working artists and manufacturers which have heretofore [until now] given credit and reputation to British wares in general? What has this been owing to? To nothing more probably than the relaxation of the working people in their own way. Were they obliged to toil the year round, the whole six days in the week, in a repetition of the same work, might it not blunt their ingenuity, and render them stupid instead of alert and dexterous; and might not our workmen lose their reputation instead of maintaining it by such eternal slavery? ... And what sort of workmanship could we expect from such hard-driven animals? ... Many of them will execute as much work in four days as a Frenchman will in five or six. But if Englishmen are to be eternal drudges, ’tis to be feared they will degenerate below the Frenchmen. As our people are famed for bravery in war, do we not say that it is owing to good English roast beef and pudding in their bellies, as well as their constitutional spirit of liberty? And why may not the superior ingenuity and dexterity of our artists and manufacturers, be owing to that freedom and liberty to direct themselves in their own way, and I hope we shall never have them deprived of such privileges and that good living from whence their ingenuity no less than their courage may proceed.”[^10.90]

[^10.90]: Postlethwayt, cited above, “First Preliminary Discourse,” p. 14.

<!-- ch10-p130 -->
The author of the “Essay on Trade and Commerce” replies to this:

<!-- ch10-p131 -->
> “If the making of every seventh day an holiday is supposed to be of divine institution, as it implies the appropriating the other six days to labour” (he means capital, as we shall soon see) “surely it will not be thought cruel to enforce it .... That mankind in general, are naturally inclined to ease and indolence, we fatally experience to be true, from the conduct of our manufacturing populace, who do not labour, upon an average, above four days in a week, unless provisions happen to be very dear.... Put all the necessaries of the poor under one denomination; for instance, call them all wheat, or suppose that ... the bushel of wheat shall cost five shillings and that he (a manufacturer [manufacturing worker]) earns a shilling by his labour, he then would be obliged to work five days only in a week. If the bushel of wheat should cost but four shillings, he would be obliged to work but four days; but as wages in this kingdom are much higher in proportion to the price of necessaries ... the manufacturer, who labours four days, has a surplus of money to live idle with the rest of the week. ... I hope I have said enough to make it appear that the moderate labour of six days in a week is no slavery. Our labouring people do this, and to all appearance are the happiest of all our labouring poor,[^10.91] but the Dutch do this in manufactures, and appear to be a very happy people. The French do so, when holidays do not intervene.[^10.92] But our populace have adopted a notion, that as Englishmen they enjoy a birthright privilege of being more free and independent than in any country in Europe. Now this idea, as far as it may affect the bravery of our troops, may be of some use; but the less the manufacturing poor have of it, certainly the better for themselves and for the State. The labouring people should never think themselves independent of their superiors.... It is extremely dangerous to encourage mobs in a commercial state like ours, where, perhaps, seven parts out of eight of the whole, are people with little or no property. The cure will not be perfect, till our manufacturing poor are contented to labour six days for the same sum which they now earn in four days.”[^10.93]

[^10.91]: “An Essay,” etc. He himself tells us on p. 96 what the “happiness” of the English agricultural laborer consisted of, already in 1770. “Their powers are always upon the stretch, they cannot live cheaper than they do, nor work harder.”

[^10.92]: Protestantism, by turning almost all the traditional holidays into workdays, plays an important part in the genesis of capital.

[^10.93]: “An Essay,” etc., pp. 15, 41, 96, 97, 55, 57, 69. — As early as 1734, Jacob Vanderlint declared that the secret behind the capitalists’ outcry about the laziness of the working people was simply this: they demanded 6 days’ labor instead of 4 for the same wages.

<!-- ch10-p132 -->
To this end, and for “extirpating idleness debauchery and excess,” for promoting a spirit of industry, for “lowering the price of labour in our manufactories, and easing the lands of the heavy burden of poor’s rates,” our “faithful Eckart” of capital proposes this well-tried device: to shut up such workers as become dependent on public support, in a word, paupers, in “an *ideal workhouse.”* Such an ideal workhouse must be made a “House of Terror,” and not an asylum for the poor, “where they are to be plentifully fed, warmly and decently clothed, and where they do but little work.”[^10.94] In this “House of Terror,” this “ideal workhouse, the poor shall work 14 hours in a day, allowing proper time for meals, in such manner that there shall remain 12 hours of neat-labour [net labor].”[^10.95]

[^10.94]: Cited above, p. 242.

[^10.95]: Cited above. “The French,” he says, “laugh at our enthusiastic ideas of liberty.” Cited above, p. 78.

<!-- ch10-p133 -->
Twelve working hours a day in the Ideal Workhouse, in the “House of Terror” of 1770! 63 years later, in 1833, when the English Parliament reduced the working day for children of 13 to 18, in four branches of industry, to 12 full hours, the judgment day of English industry had dawned! In 1852, when Louis Bonaparte sought to secure his position with the bourgeoisie by tampering with the legal working day, the French working people cried out with one voice: “the law that limits the working day to 12 hours is the one good that has remained to us of the legislation of the Republic!”[^10.96] At Zürich the work of children over 10 is limited to 12 hours; in Aargau in 1862, the work of children between 13 and 16 was reduced from 12½ to 12 hours; in Austria in 1860, the same reduction was made for children between 14 and 16.[^10.97] “What a progress,” since 1770! Macaulay would shout with exultation!

[^10.96]: “They especially objected to work beyond the 12 hours per day, because the law which fixed those hours, is the only good which remains to them of the legislation of the Republic.” (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact.”, 31st October, 1856, p. 80.) The French Twelve Hours’ Bill of September 5th, 1850, a bourgeois edition of the decree of the Provisional Government of March 2nd, 1848, applies in all workshops without exception. Before this law, the working day in France had no definite limit. In the factories it lasted 14, 15, or more hours. See “Des classes ouvrières en France, pendant l’année 1848. Par M. Blanqui.” M. Blanqui the economist, not the revolutionary, had been entrusted by the Government with an inquiry into the condition of the working class.

[^10.97]: Belgium is the model bourgeois state as regards the regulation of the working day. Lord Howard of Welden, English Plenipotentiary at Brussels, reports to the Foreign Office on May 12th, 1862: “M. Rogier, the minister, informed me that children’s labour is limited neither by a general law nor by any local regulations; that the Government, during the last three years, intended in every session to propose a bill on the subject, but always found an insuperable obstacle in the jealous opposition to any legislation in contradiction with the principle of perfect freedom of labour.”

<!-- ch10-p134 -->
The “House of Terror” for paupers, which the capitalist soul of 1770 only dreamed of, was made real a few years later in the shape of a gigantic “Workhouse” for the industrial worker himself. It is called the Factory. And this time the ideal pales before the reality.

### Section 6: The Struggle for a Normal Working Day. Compulsory Limitation by Law of the Working-Time. English Factory Acts, 1833

<!-- ch10-p135 -->
After capital had taken centuries to extend the working day to its normal maximum limit, and then beyond this to the limit of the natural day of 12 hours,[^10.98] the birth of machinery and modern industry in the last third of the 18th century was followed by a violent encroachment, like an avalanche in its intensity and extent. Every bound set by morals and nature, by age and sex, by day and night, was broken down. Even the ideas of day and night, which in the old statutes had a rustic simplicity, became so confused that as late as 1860 an English judge needed a truly Talmudic subtlety to explain “judicially” what was day and what was night.[^10.99] Capital celebrated its orgies.

[^10.98]: “It is certainly much to be regretted that any class of persons should toil 12 hours a day, which, including the time for their meals and for going to and returning from their work, amounts, in fact, to 14 of the 24 hours.... Without entering into the question of health, no one will hesitate, I think, to admit that, *in a moral point of view*, so entire an absorption of the time of the working-classes, without intermission, from the early age of 13, and in trades not subject to restriction, much younger, must be extremely prejudicial, and is an evil greatly to be deplored.... For the sake, therefore, of public morals, of bringing up an orderly population, and of giving the great body of the people a reasonable enjoyment of life, it is much to be desired that in all trades some portion of every working day should be reserved for rest and leisure.” (Leonard Horner in “Reports of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Dec., 1841.”)

[^10.99]: See “Judgment of Mr. J. H. Otway, Belfast. Hilary Sessions, County Antrim, 1860.”

<!-- ch10-p136 -->
At first the working class was stunned by the noise and turmoil of the new system of production. As soon as it had recovered its senses to some extent, its resistance began, and it began first in England, the homeland of machinery. For 30 years, however, the concessions the workers won were purely nominal. Parliament passed 5 labor laws between 1802 and 1833, but it was shrewd enough not to vote a penny for carrying them out, for the officials needed, etc.[^10.100]

[^10.100]: It is very characteristic of the regime of Louis Philippe, the bourgeois king, that the one Factory Act passed during his reign, that of March 22nd, 1841, was never put into force. And this law dealt only with child labor. It fixed 8 hours a day for children between 8 and 12, 12 hours for children between 12 and 16, etc., with many exceptions that allow night-work even for children 8 years old. In a country where every mouse is under police administration, the supervision and enforcement of this law are left to the good will of the *amis du commerce* [friends of trade]. Only since 1853 has a paid government inspector been appointed, and that in one single department, the Departement du Nord. No less characteristic of the development of French society in general is the fact that Louis Philippe’s law stood alone among the all-embracing mass of French laws until the Revolution of 1848.

<!-- ch10-p137 -->
> These laws remained a dead letter. “The fact is, that prior to the Act of 1833, young persons and children were worked all night, all day, or both *ad libitum* [at will].”[^10.101]

[^10.101]: “Report of Insp. of Fact.” 30th April, 1860, p. 50.

<!-- ch10-p138 -->
A normal working day for modern industry dates only from the Factory Act of 1833, which covered cotton, wool, flax, and silk factories. Nothing is more characteristic of the spirit of capital than the history of the English Factory Acts from 1833 to 1864.

<!-- ch10-p139 -->
The Act of 1833 declares that the ordinary factory working day runs from half-past five in the morning to half-past eight in the evening. Within these limits, a period of 15 hours, it is lawful to employ young persons (that is, persons between 13 and 18 years of age) at any time of the day, provided that no individual young person works more than 12 hours in any one day, except in certain cases specially provided for. The 6th section of the Act provided: “That there shall be allowed in the course of every day not less than one and a half hours for meals to every such person restricted as hereinbefore provided.” The employment of children under 9 was forbidden, with exceptions mentioned later. The work of children between 9 and 13 was limited to 8 hours a day. Night-work, that is, according to this Act, work between 8:30 p.m. and 5:30 a.m., was forbidden for all persons between 9 and 18.

<!-- ch10-p140 -->
The law-makers were so far from wishing to infringe on the freedom of capital to exploit adult labor-power, or, as they called it, “the freedom of labour,” that they created a special system to prevent the Factory Acts from having so outrageous a consequence.

<!-- ch10-p141 -->
> “The great evil of the factory system [production in which a system of machines, driven by a central power source, does the work and workers attend the machines] as at present conducted,” says the first report of the Central Board of the Commission of June 28th 1833, “has appeared to us to be that it entails the necessity of continuing the labour of children to the utmost length of that of the adults. The only remedy for this evil, short of the limitation of the labour of adults which would, in our opinion, create an evil greater than that which is sought to be remedied, appears to be the plan of working double sets of children.”

<!-- ch10-p142 -->
... Under the name of System of Relays, this “plan” was therefore carried out. For example, from 5.30 a.m. until 1.30 in the afternoon one set of children between 9 and 13 was “put to” [set to work], and from 1.30 p.m. to 8.30 in the evening another set, etc.

<!-- ch10-p143 -->
To reward the manufacturers for having ignored, in the most barefaced way, all the Acts on children’s labor passed during the last twenty-two years, the pill was gilded for them still further. Parliament decreed that after March 1st, 1834, no child under 11, after March 1st 1835, no child under 12, and after March 1st, 1836, no child under 13 was to work more than eight hours in a factory. This “liberalism,” so full of consideration for “capital,” was all the more remarkable because Dr. Farre, Sir A. Carlisle, Sir B. Brodie, Sir C. Bell, Mr. Guthrie, etc., in a word, the most distinguished physicians and surgeons in London, had declared in their evidence before the House of Commons that delay was dangerous. Dr. Farre put it still more bluntly.

<!-- ch10-p144 -->
> “Legislation is necessary for the prevention of death, in any form in which it can be prematurely inflicted, and certainly this (i.e., the factory method) must be viewed as a most cruel mode of inflicting it.”

<!-- ch10-p145 -->
That same “reformed” Parliament, in its delicate consideration for the manufacturers, condemned children under 13, for years to come, to 72 hours of work per week in the Factory Hell. On the other hand, in the Emancipation Act, which also handed out freedom drop by drop, it forbade the planters, from the very start, to work any Black slave more than 45 hours a week.

<!-- ch10-p146 -->
But capital was in no way reconciled, and it now began a noisy agitation that went on for several years. The agitation turned mainly on the age of those who, under the name of children, were limited to 8 hours’ work and were subject to a certain amount of compulsory education. According to capitalistic anthropology, the age of childhood ended at 10, or at the very most at 11. The nearer the time came for the Factory Act to come into full force, the fatal year 1836, the more wildly the mob of manufacturers raged. In fact, they managed to intimidate the government so much that in 1835 it proposed to lower the limit of the age of childhood from 13 to 12. In the meantime the pressure from outside grew more threatening. The House of Commons lost its courage. It refused to throw children of 13 under the Juggernaut Car of capital for more than 8 hours a day, and the Act of 1833 came into full operation. It remained unchanged until June, 1844.

<!-- ch10-p147 -->
In the ten years during which the Act regulated factory work, first in part and then entirely, the official reports of the factory inspectors are full of complaints that it was impossible to put the Act into force. The law of 1833 left the lords of capital free, during the 15 hours from 5.30 a.m. to 8.30 p.m., to make every “young person” and every “child” begin, break off, resume, or end his 12 or 8 hours at any moment they liked. It also allowed them to give different persons different times for meals. So these gentlemen soon discovered a new “system of relays,” in which the labor-horses were not changed at fixed stations but were constantly re-harnessed at changing stations. We will not dwell longer on the beauty of this system, since we shall have to return to it later. But this much is clear at first glance: this system canceled the whole Factory Act, not only in its spirit but in its letter. With this complex bookkeeping for each individual child or young person, how could factory inspectors enforce the legally fixed work-time and the granting of the legal mealtimes? In a great many of the factories the old brutalities soon blossomed out again unpunished. In an interview with the Home Secretary (1844), the factory inspectors demonstrated that any control was impossible under the newly invented relay system.[^10.102] In the meantime, however, circumstances had greatly changed. The factory workers, especially since 1838, had made the Ten Hours’ Bill their economic election-cry, as they had made the Charter their political one. Even some of the manufacturers who had run their factories in line with the Act of 1833 flooded Parliament with written petitions about the immoral competition of their false brethren, whom greater impudence or luckier local circumstances enabled to break the law. Moreover, however much the individual manufacturer might give free rein to his old lust for gain, the spokesmen and political leaders of the manufacturing class ordered a change of front and of language toward the workers. They had entered the contest for the repeal of the Corn Laws (the tariffs on imported grain), and needed the workers to help them to victory. So they promised not only a double-sized loaf of bread but also the enactment of the Ten Hours’ Bill in the Free-trade millennium.[^10.103] All the less, then, did they dare to oppose a measure meant only to make the law of 1833 a reality. Threatened in their holiest interest, the rent of land, the Tories thundered with philanthropic indignation against the “nefarious practices”[^10.104] of their foes.

[^10.102]: “Rept. of Insp. of Fact.,” 31st October, 1849, p. 6

[^10.103]: “Rept. of Insp. of Fact.,” 31st October, 1848, p. 98.

[^10.104]: Leonard Horner uses the expression “nefarious practices” in his official reports. (“Report of Insp. of Fact.,” 31st October, 1859, p. 7.)

<!-- ch10-p148 -->
This was the origin of the additional Factory Act of June 7th, 1844. It came into effect on September 10th, 1844. It places a new category of workers under protection, namely women over 18. They were placed in every respect on the same footing as the young persons: their work time was limited to twelve hours, their night-labor was forbidden, etc. For the first time, legislation found itself compelled to control the labor of adults directly and officially. The Factory Report of 1844-1845 says with irony:

<!-- ch10-p149 -->
> “No instances have come to my knowledge of adult women having expressed any regret at their *rights* being thus far interfered with.”[^10.105] The working time of children under 13 was reduced to 6½ hours a day, and in certain circumstances to 7 hours.[^10.106]

[^10.105]: “Rept.,” etc., 30th Sept., 1844, p. 15.

[^10.106]: The Act allows children to be employed for 10 hours if they do not work day after day, but only on alternate days. On the whole, this clause remained a dead letter.

<!-- ch10-p150 -->
To get rid of the abuses of the “spurious relay system,” the law laid down, among others, the following important regulations: –

<!-- ch10-p151 -->
> “That the hours of work of children and young persons shall be reckoned from the time when any child or young person shall begin to work in the morning.”

<!-- ch10-p152 -->
So if A, for example, begins work at 8 in the morning and B at 10, B’s work-day must still end at the same hour as A’s. “The time shall be regulated by a public clock,” for example the nearest railway clock, by which the factory clock is to be set. The occupier is to hang up a “legible” printed notice stating the hours for the beginning and ending of work and the times allowed for the various meals. Children who begin work before 12 noon may not be employed again after 1 p.m. So the afternoon shift must consist of children other than those employed in the morning. Of the hour and a half for meal-times,

<!-- ch10-p153 -->
> “one hour thereof at the least shall be given before three of the clock in the afternoon ... and at the same period of the day. No child or young person shall be employed more than five hours before 1 p.m. without an interval for meal-time of at least 30 minutes. No child or young person [or female] shall be employed or allowed to remain in any room in which any manufacturing process is then [that is, at mealtimes] carried on,” etc.

<!-- ch10-p154 -->
We have seen that these minute details, which regulate with military uniformity, by the stroke of the clock, the times, limits, and pauses of work, were not at all the products of Parliamentary fancy. They developed gradually out of circumstances, as natural laws of the modern mode of production. Their formulation, official recognition, and proclamation by the State were the result of a long struggle between classes. One of their first consequences was that in practice the working day of the adult males in factories became subject to the same limits, since in most processes of production the cooperation of the children, young persons, and women is indispensable. On the whole, therefore, during the period from 1844 to 1847, the 12 hours’ working day became general and uniform in all branches of industry under the Factory Act.

<!-- ch10-p155 -->
The manufacturers, however, did not allow this “progress” without a compensating “retrogression.” At their instigation the House of Commons lowered the minimum age of exploitable children from 9 to 8. This was to ensure the additional supply of factory children that is due to capitalists according to divine and human law.[^10.107]

[^10.107]: “As a reduction in their hours of work would cause a larger number (of children) to be employed, it was thought that the additional supply of children from 8 to 9 years of age would meet the increased demand” (cited above, p. 13).

<!-- ch10-p156 -->
The years 1846-47 opened a new era in the economic history of England. In those years the Corn Laws were repealed, along with the duties on cotton and other raw materials. Free trade was proclaimed the guiding star of legislation. In a word, the millennium had arrived. On the other hand, in those same years the Chartist movement and the agitation for 10 hours reached their highest point. They found allies in the Tories, who were hungry for revenge. The army of Free-traders, oath-breakers with Bright and Cobden at their head, opposed the bill fanatically. Despite them, the Ten Hours’ Bill, fought for over so long, passed through Parliament.

<!-- ch10-p157 -->
The new Factory Act of June 8th, 1847, laid down that on July 1st, 1847, the working day of “young persons” (from 13 to 18) and of all females should be shortened, as a first step, to 11 hours, and that on May 1st, 1848, it should be limited once and for all to 10 hours. In other respects, the Act only amended and completed the Acts of 1833 and 1844.

<!-- ch10-p158 -->
Capital now launched a preliminary campaign to prevent the Act from coming into full force on May 1st, 1848. And the workers themselves, under the pretense that experience had taught them, were to help destroy their own work. The moment was cleverly chosen.

<!-- ch10-p159 -->
> “It must be remembered, too, that there has been more than two years of great suffering (in consequence of the terrible crisis of 1846-47) among the factory operatives, from many mills having worked short time, and many being altogether closed. A considerable number of the operatives must therefore be in very narrow circumstances; many, it is to be feared, in debt; so that it might fairly have been presumed that at the present time they would prefer working the longer time, in order to make up for past losses, perhaps to pay off debts, or get their furniture out of pawn, or replace that sold, or to get a new supply of clothes for themselves and their families.”[^10.108]

[^10.108]: Rep. of Insp. of Fact.,” 31st Oct., 1848, p. 16.

<!-- ch10-p160 -->
The manufacturers tried to make the natural effect of these circumstances worse by a general wage cut of 10%. This was done, so to speak, to celebrate the opening of the new Free-trade era. Then came a further cut of 8 1/3% as soon as the working day was shortened to 11 hours, and a cut of double that amount as soon as it was finally shortened to 10 hours. So wherever circumstances allowed it, wages were cut by at least 25%.[^10.109] Under conditions so favorably prepared, the agitation among the factory workers for the repeal of the Act of 1847 was begun. Neither lies, bribery, nor threats were spared in this attempt. But it was all in vain. As for the half-dozen petitions in which workers were made to complain of “their oppression by the Act,” the petitioners themselves declared under oral examination that their signatures had been extorted from them. “They felt themselves oppressed, but not exactly by the Factory Act.”[^10.110] But if the manufacturers did not succeed in making the workers speak as they wished, they themselves shrieked all the louder, in the press and in Parliament, in the name of the workers. They denounced the Factory Inspectors as a kind of revolutionary commissioners, like those of the French National Convention, ruthlessly sacrificing the unhappy factory workers to their humanitarian whim. This maneuver also failed. Factory Inspector Leonard Horner, in person and through his sub-inspectors, examined many witnesses in the factories of Lancashire. About 70% of the workers examined declared in favor of 10 hours, a much smaller percentage in favor of 11, and an altogether insignificant minority for the old 12 hours.[^10.111]

[^10.109]: “I found that men who had been getting 10s. a week, had had 1s. taken off for a reduction in the rate of 10 per cent, and 1s. 6d. off the remaining 9s. for the reduction in time, together 2s. 6d., and notwithstanding this, many of them said they would rather work 10 hours.” Cited above.

[^10.110]: “‘Though I signed it [the petition], I said at the time I was putting my hand to a wrong thing.’ ‘Then why did you put your hand to it?’ ‘Because I should have been turned off [dismissed] if I had refused.’ Whence it would appear that this petitioner felt himself ‘oppressed,’ but not exactly by the Factory Act.” Cited above, p. 102.

[^10.111]: p. 17, cited above. In Mr. Horner’s district 10,270 adult male workers were examined in this way in 181 factories. Their evidence is in the appendix to the Factory Reports for the half-year ending October 1848. These examinations also provide valuable material in other connections.

<!-- ch10-p161 -->
Another “friendly” dodge was to make the adult males work 12 to 15 hours, and then to trumpet this fact abroad as the best proof of what the proletariat desired in its heart of hearts. But the “ruthless” Factory Inspector Leonard Horner was again on the spot. The majority of the “over-times” (the men working the longer hours) declared:

<!-- ch10-p162 -->
> “They would much prefer working ten hours for less wages, but that they had no choice; that so many were out of employment (so many spinners getting very low wages by having to work as piecers, being unable to do better), that if they refused to work the longer time, others would immediately get their places, so that it was a question with them of agreeing to work the longer time, or of being thrown out of employment altogether.”[^10.112]

[^10.112]: Cited above. See the evidence collected by Leonard Horner himself, Nos. 69, 70, 71, 72, 92, 93, and that collected by Sub-Inspector A., Nos. 51, 52, 58, 59, 62, 70, of the Appendix. One manufacturer, too, tells the plain truth. See No. 14, and No. 265, cited above.

<!-- ch10-p163 -->
So the preliminary campaign of capital came to grief, and the Ten Hours’ Act came into force on May 1st, 1848. But meanwhile the fiasco of the Chartist party, whose leaders were imprisoned and whose organization was broken up, had shaken the English working class’s confidence in its own strength. Soon after this, the June insurrection in Paris and its bloody suppression united all factions of the ruling classes, in England as on the Continent: landlords and capitalists, stock-exchange wolves and shop-keepers, Protectionists and Free-traders, government and opposition, priests and freethinkers, young whores and old nuns. They united under the common cry for the salvation of Property, Religion, the Family and Society. Everywhere the working class was outlawed, placed under a ban, under a virtual law of suspects. The manufacturers no longer had any need to restrain themselves. They broke out in open revolt, not only against the Ten Hours’ Act, but against the whole of the legislation that since 1833 had aimed at restricting to some extent the “free” exploitation of labor-power. It was a pro-slavery rebellion in miniature, carried on for over two years with a cynical recklessness and a terrorist energy that came all the cheaper because the rebel capitalist risked nothing except the skin of his “hands.”

<!-- ch10-p164 -->
To understand what comes next, we must keep the following in mind. The Factory Acts of 1833, 1844, and 1847 were all three in force, insofar as one did not amend another. Not one of them limited the working day of the male worker over 18. And since 1833 the 15 hours from 5.30 a.m. to 8.30 p.m. had remained the legal “day,” within whose limits first the 12, and later the 10 hours’ labor of young persons and women had to be performed under the prescribed conditions.

<!-- ch10-p165 -->
The manufacturers began by dismissing, here and there, part of the young persons and women they employed, in many cases half of them, and then by bringing back the almost obsolete night-work for the adult males. The Ten Hours’ Act, they cried, leaves no other alternative.[^10.113]

[^10.113]: Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1848, pp. 133, 134.

<!-- ch10-p166 -->
Their second step concerned the legal pauses for meals. Let us hear the Factory Inspectors.

<!-- ch10-p167 -->
> “Since the restriction of the hours of work to ten, the factory occupiers maintain, although they have not yet practically gone the whole length, that supposing the hours of work to be from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. they fulfil the provisions of the statutes by allowing an hour before 9 a.m. and half an hour after 7 p.m. [for meals]. In some cases they now allow an hour, or half an hour for dinner, insisting at the same time, that they are not bound to allow any part of the hour and a half in the course of the factory working day.”[^10.114] So the manufacturers maintained that the scrupulously strict provisions of the Act of 1844 on meal-times only gave the factory workers permission to eat and drink before coming into the factory and after leaving it, that is, at home. And why should the workers not eat their dinner before 9 in the morning? The crown lawyers, however, decided that the prescribed meal-times

[^10.114]: Reports, &c., for 30th April, 1848, p. 47.

<!-- ch10-p168 -->
> “must be in the interval during the working-hours, and that it will not be lawful to work for 10 hours continuously, from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m., without any interval.”[^10.115]

[^10.115]: Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1848, p. 130.

<!-- ch10-p169 -->
After these pleasant demonstrations, Capital opened its revolt with a step that agreed with the letter of the law of 1844, and was therefore legal.

<!-- ch10-p170 -->
The Act of 1844 certainly prohibited employing after 1 p.m. those children, from 8 to 13, who had been employed before noon. But it did not regulate in any way the 6½ hours’ work of the children whose work-time began at 12 midday or later. Children of 8, if they began work at noon, might be employed from 12 to 1, 1 hour; from 2 to 4 in the afternoon, 2 hours; from 5 to 8.30 in the evening, 3½ hours; in all, the legal 6½ hours. Or better still. To make their work coincide with that of the adult male workers up to 8.30 p.m., the manufacturers only had to give them no work till 2 in the afternoon; they could then keep them in the factory without a break till 8.30 in the evening.

<!-- ch10-p171 -->
> “And it is now expressly admitted that the practice exists in England from the desire of mill-owners to have their machinery at work for more than 10 hours a-day, to keep the children at work with male adults after all the young persons and women have left, and until 8.30 p.m. if the factory-owners choose.”[^10.116]

[^10.116]: Reports, &c., cited above, p. 142.

<!-- ch10-p172 -->
Workers and factory inspectors protested on grounds of health and morals, but Capital answered:

<!-- ch10-p173 -->
> “My deeds upon my head! I crave the law,\
> The penalty and forfeit of my bond.”

<!-- ch10-p174 -->
In fact, according to statistics laid before the House of Commons on July 26th, 1850, in spite of all protests, on July 15th, 1850, 3,742 children in 257 factories were subjected to this “practice.”[^10.117] Still, this was not enough. The lynx eye of Capital discovered that the Act of 1844 did not allow 5 hours’ work before mid-day without a pause of at least 30 minutes for refreshment, but prescribed nothing of the kind for work after mid-day. So it demanded and obtained the enjoyment not only of making children of 8 drudge without a break from 2 to 8.30 p.m., but also of making them go hungry during that time.

[^10.117]: Reports &c., for 31st October, 1850, pp. 5, 6.

<!-- ch10-p175 -->
> “Ay, his breast.\
> So says the bond.”

<!-- ch10-p176 -->
This Shylock-like clinging[^10.118] to the letter of the law of 1844, insofar as it regulated children’s labor, was only the lead-up to an open revolt against the same law, insofar as it regulated the labor of “young persons and women.” The reader will remember that the chief aim and object of that law was to abolish the “false relay system.” The employers began their revolt with a simple declaration. The sections of the Act of 1844 that prohibited using young persons and women at will, in whatever short fractions of the 15-hour day the employer chose, had been “comparatively harmless,” they said, so long as the work-time was fixed at 12 hours. But under the Ten Hours’ Act they were a “grievous hardship.”[^10.119] In the coolest manner, they informed the inspectors that they would place themselves above the letter of the law and bring back the old system on their own account.[^10.120] They were doing this, they said, in the interests of the ill-advised factory workers themselves, “in order to be able to pay them higher wages.”

[^10.118]: The nature of capital stays the same in its developed form as in its undeveloped form. The code that the influence of the slave-owners imposed on the territory of New Mexico, shortly before the outbreak of the American Civil War, says that the worker, insofar as the capitalist has bought his labor-power, “is his (the capitalist’s) money.” The same view was current among the Roman patricians. The money they had advanced to the plebeian debtor had been transformed, by way of the means of subsistence, into the flesh and blood of the debtor. This “flesh and blood” was therefore “their money.” Hence the Shylock-law of the Ten Tables. Linguet’s hypothesis that the patrician creditors from time to time held banquets of debtors’ flesh beyond the Tiber may remain as undecided as Daumer’s hypothesis about the Christian Eucharist.

[^10.119]: Reports, &c., for 30th April, 1848, p. 28.

[^10.120]: So, among others, did Philanthropist Ashworth, writing to Leonard Horner in a disgusting Quaker letter. (Reports, &c., April, 1849, p. 4.)

<!-- ch10-p177 -->
> “This was the only possible plan by which to maintain, under the Ten Hours’ Act, the industrial supremacy of Great Britain.” “Perhaps it may be a little difficult to detect irregularities under the relay system; but what of that? Is the great manufacturing interest of this country to be treated as a secondary matter in order to save some little trouble to Inspectors and Sub-Inspectors of Factories?”[^10.121]

[^10.121]: Cited above, p. 140.

<!-- ch10-p178 -->
All these tricks were, naturally, of no use. The Factory Inspectors went to the courts of law. But soon the Home Secretary, Sir George Grey, was overwhelmed by such a cloud of dust of petitions from the employers that in a circular of August 5th, 1848, he recommends the inspectors not

<!-- ch10-p179 -->
> “to lay informations [bring charges] against mill-owners for a breach of the letter of the Act, or for employment of young persons by relays in cases in which there is no reason to believe that such young persons have been actually employed for a longer period than that sanctioned by law.” After this, Factory Inspector J. Stuart allowed the so-called relay system during the 15 hours of the factory day throughout Scotland, where it soon flourished again as in the old days. The English Factory Inspectors, on the other hand, declared that the Home Secretary had no power to suspend the law like a dictator, and they went on with their legal proceedings against the pro-slavery rebellion.

<!-- ch10-p180 -->
But what was the good of summoning the capitalists when the courts – in this case the country magistrates, Cobbett’s “Great Unpaid” – acquitted them? In these courts, the employers sat in judgment on themselves. An example. One Eskrigge, a cotton-spinner of the firm of Kershaw, Leese, & Co., had laid before the Factory Inspector of his district the plan of a relay system intended for his mill. When he was refused, he at first kept quiet. A few months later, an individual named Robinson, also a cotton-spinner, and if not Eskrigge’s Man Friday, at any rate related to him, appeared before the borough magistrates of Stockport. He was charged with introducing the identical plan of relays that Eskrigge had invented. Four Justices sat on the bench. Three of them were cotton-spinners, and at their head was this same inevitable Eskrigge. Eskrigge acquitted Robinson, and then took the view that what was right for Robinson was fair for Eskrigge. Backed by his own legal decision, he introduced the system into his own factory at once.[^10.122] Of course, the very makeup of this court was in itself a violation of the law.[^10.123]
