[^10.122]: Reports, &c., for 30th April, 1849, pp. 21, 22. Compare similar examples, same source, pp. 4, 5.

[^10.123]: By I. and II. Will. IV., ch. 24, s. 10, known as Sir John Hobhouse’s Factory Act, any owner of a cotton-spinning or weaving mill, or the father, son, or brother of such an owner, was forbidden to act as Justice of the Peace in any inquiries that concerned the Factory Act.

<!-- ch10-p181 -->
> These judicial farces, exclaims Inspector Howell, “urgently call for a remedy – either that the law should be so altered as to be made to conform to these decisions, or that it should be administered by a less fallible tribunal, whose decisions would conform to the law ... when these cases are brought forward. I long for a stipendiary magistrate [a paid, professional magistrate].”[^10.124]

[^10.124]: Cited above.

<!-- ch10-p182 -->
The crown lawyers declared the employers’ interpretation of the Act of 1848 absurd. But the Saviors of Society would not let themselves be turned from their purpose. Leonard Horner reports:

<!-- ch10-p183 -->
> “Having endeavoured to enforce the Act ... by ten prosecutions in seven magisterial divisions, and having been supported by the magistrates in one case only ... I considered it useless to prosecute more for this evasion of the law. That part of the Act of 1848 which was framed for securing uniformity in the hours of work, ... is thus no longer in force in my district (Lancashire). Neither have the sub-inspectors or myself any means of satisfying ourselves, when we inspect a mill working by shifts, that the young persons and women are not working more than 10 hours a-day.... In a return of the 30th April, ... of millowners working by shifts, the number amounts to 114, and has been for some time rapidly increasing. In general, the time of working the mill is extended to 13½ hours’ from 6 a.m. to 7½ p.m., .... in some instances it amounts to 15 hours, from 5½ a.m. to 8½ p.m.”[^10.125]

[^10.125]: Reports, &c., for 30th April, 1849, p. 5.

<!-- ch10-p184 -->
As early as December, 1848, Leonard Horner had a list of 65 manufacturers and 29 overseers who unanimously declared that, under this relay system, no system of supervision could prevent enormous overwork.[^10.126] The same children and young persons were shifted now from the spinning-room to the weaving-room, now, during 15 hours, from one factory to another.[^10.127] How was it possible to control a system which,

[^10.126]: Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1849, p. 6.

[^10.127]: Reports, &c., for 30th April, 1849, p. 21.

<!-- ch10-p185 -->
> “under the guise of relays, is some one of the many plans for shuffling ‘the hands’ about in endless variety, and shifting the hours of work and of rest for different individuals throughout the day, so that you may never have one complete set of hands working together in the same room at the same time.”[^10.128]

[^10.128]: Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1848, p. 95.

<!-- ch10-p186 -->
But quite apart from actual overwork, this so-called relay system was a product of capitalist fantasy that Fourier, in his humorous sketches of “Courses Seances” [short sessions], never outdid, except that the “attraction of labour” was turned into the attraction of capital. Look, for example, at those schemes of the employers that the “respectable” press praised as models of “what a reasonable degree of care and method can accomplish.” The *personnel* of the workers was sometimes divided into anywhere from 12 to 14 categories, and these categories themselves kept changing and rearranging their members. During the 15 hours of the factory day, capital dragged the worker in now for 30 minutes, now for an hour, and then pushed him out again, only to drag him into the factory and thrust him out once more. It hounded him this way and that, in scattered shreds of time, without ever losing its grip on him until the full 10 hours’ work was done. As on the stage, the same persons had to appear in turn in the different scenes of the different acts. But just as an actor belongs to the stage during the whole course of the play, so the factory workers belonged to the factory during 15 hours, not counting the time for going and coming. So the hours of rest were turned into hours of forced idleness, which drove the young men to the tavern and the girls to the brothel. Day after day the capitalist hit upon new tricks for keeping his machinery going 12 or 15 hours without increasing the number of his workers, and at every new trick the worker had to gulp down his meals now in this fragment of time, now in that. At the time of the 10 hours’ agitation, the employers had cried out that the working mob was petitioning in the hope of getting 12 hours’ wages for 10 hours’ work. Now they turned the medal around. They paid 10 hours’ wages for 12 or 15 hours’ lordship over labor-power.[^10.129] This was the heart of the matter. This was the employers’ interpretation of the 10 hours’ law! These were the same oily Free-traders, sweating with the love of humanity, who for a full 10 years, during the Anti-Corn Law agitation, had preached to the factory workers, with calculations in pounds, shillings, and pence, that with free importation of grain, and with the means English industry possessed, 10 hours’ labor would be quite enough to make the capitalists rich.[^10.130] After two years, this revolt of capital was at last crowned with victory by a decision of one of the four highest Courts of Justice in England, the Court of Exchequer. In a case brought before it on February 8th, 1850, this court decided that the manufacturers were certainly acting against the sense of the Act of 1844, but that this Act itself contained certain words that made it meaningless. “By this decision, the Ten Hours’ Act was abolished.”[^10.131] A crowd of employers who until then had been afraid of using the relay system for young persons and women now took it up heart and soul.[^10.132]

[^10.129]: See Reports, &c., for 30th April, 1849, p. 6, and the detailed explanation of the “shifting system” by Factory Inspectors Howell and Saunders, in “Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1848.” See also the petition to the Queen from the clergy of Ashton and the surrounding area, in the spring of 1849, against the “shift system.”

[^10.130]: Compare, for example, “The Factory Question and the Ten Hours’ Bill.”, By R. H. Greg, 1837.

[^10.131]: F. Engels: “The English Ten Hours’ Bill.” (In the “*Neue Rheinische Zeitung. Politisch-oekonomische Revue.*” Edited by K. Marx. April number, 1850, p. 13.) During the American Civil War, the same “high” Court of Justice discovered a verbal ambiguity that exactly reversed the meaning of the law against the arming of pirate ships.

[^10.132]: Rep., &c., for 30th April, 1850.

<!-- ch10-p187 -->
But this apparently decisive victory of capital was followed at once by a sharp backlash. Until now the workers had offered a passive resistance, although an unbending and unceasing one. Now they protested at threatening meetings in Lancashire and Yorkshire. So the supposed Ten Hours’ Act was simply humbug, parliamentary cheating, and had never existed! The Factory Inspectors urgently warned the Government that class antagonism had reached an incredible pitch of tension. Some of the employers themselves grumbled:

<!-- ch10-p188 -->
> “On account of the contradictory decisions of the magistrates, a condition of things altogether abnormal and anarchical obtains [prevails]. One law holds in Yorkshire, another in Lancashire, one law in one parish of Lancashire, another in its immediate neighbourhood. The manufacturer in large towns could evade the law, the manufacturer in country districts could not find the people necessary for the relay system, still less for the shifting of hands from one factory to another,” etc.

<!-- ch10-p189 -->
And the first birthright of capital is equal exploitation of labor-power by all capitalists.

<!-- ch10-p190 -->
Under these circumstances a compromise between employers and workers was reached, and it received the seal of Parliament in the additional Factory Act of August 5th, 1850. The working day for “young persons and women” was raised from 10 to 10½ hours for the first five days of the week, and shortened to 7½ on the Saturday. The work was to go on between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m.[^10.133], with pauses of not less than 1½ hours for meal-times. These meal-times were to be given at one and the same time for all, and in line with the conditions of 1844. This put an end to the relay system once and for all.[^10.134] For children’s labor, the Act of 1844 remained in force.

[^10.133]: In winter, the hours from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. may be used instead.

[^10.134]: “The present law (of 1850) was a compromise whereby the employed surrendered the benefit of the Ten Hours’ Act for the advantage of one uniform period for the commencement and termination of the labour of those whose labour is restricted.” (Reports, &c., for 30th April, 1852, p. 14.)

<!-- ch10-p191 -->
One set of employers, this time as before, secured for itself special seigneurial rights (the rights of a feudal lord) over the children of the proletariat. These were the silk manufacturers. In 1833 they had howled out threateningly that “if the liberty of working children of any age for 10 hours a day were taken away, it would stop their works.”[^10.135] It would be impossible for them, they said, to buy enough children over 13. They extorted the privilege they wanted. Later investigation showed that the pretext was a deliberate lie.[^10.136] That did not, however, prevent them, for 10 years, from spinning silk 10 hours a day out of the blood of little children who had to be placed on stools to do their work.[^10.137] The Act of 1844 certainly “robbed” them of the “liberty” of employing children under 11 for longer than 6½ hours a day. But on the other hand it secured them the privilege of working children between 11 and 13 for 10 hours a day, and of canceling, in these children’s case, the schooling made compulsory for all other factory children. This time the pretext was

[^10.135]: Reports, &c., for Sept., 1844, p. 13.

[^10.136]: Cited above.

[^10.137]: Cited above.

<!-- ch10-p192 -->
> “the delicate texture of the fabric in which they were employed, requiring a lightness of touch, only to be acquired by their early introduction to these factories.”[^10.138]

[^10.138]: “Reports, &c., for 31st Oct., 1846,” p. 20.

<!-- ch10-p193 -->
The children were slaughtered outright for the sake of their delicate fingers, as the horned cattle in Southern Russia are slaughtered for the sake of their hide and tallow. At length, in 1850, the privilege granted in 1844 was limited to the departments of silk-twisting and silk-winding. But here, to make up to capital for the loss of its “freedom,” the work-time for children from 11 to 13 was raised from 10 to 10½ hours. Pretext: “Labour in silk mills was lighter than in mills for other fabrics, and less likely in other respects also to be prejudicial to health.”[^10.139] Official medical inquiries proved afterwards that, on the contrary,

[^10.139]: Reports, &c., for 31st Oct., 1861, p. 26.

<!-- ch10-p194 -->
> “the average death-rate is exceedingly high in the silk districts and amongst the female part of the population is higher even than it is in the cotton districts of Lancashire.”[^10.140]

[^10.140]: Cited above, p. 27. On the whole, the working population that is subject to the Factory Act has greatly improved physically. All medical testimony agrees on this point, and my own observation at different times has convinced me of it. Nevertheless, even leaving aside the terrible death-rate of children in the first years of their life, the official reports of Dr. Greenhow show the unfavorable health conditions of the manufacturing districts compared with “agricultural districts of normal health.” As evidence, take the following table from his 1861 report: —

    ```text
    Pecentage of Adult Males    14.9    42.6    37.3    41.9    31.0   14.9    36.6    30.4           —
    Engaged in Manufactures
    Death-rate from             598     708     547     611     691     588     721     726          305
    Pulmonary Affections per
    100,000 Males
    Name of District           Wigan   Black   Halifax  Brad   Maccle  Leek   Stoke-  Woolst    8 healthy
                                        burn            ford   sfield          upon-   anton  agricultural
                                                                               Trent             districts
    Death-rate from             644     734     564     603     804     705     665     727          340
    Pulmonary Affections per
    100,000 Females
    Pecentage of Adult          18.0    34.9    20.4    30.0    26.0   17.2    19.3    13.9           —
    Females Engaged in
    Manufactures
    Kind of  Female            Cotton   Do.     Wors    Do.     Silk    Do.   Earthen   Do.           —
    Occupation                                   ted                           ware
    ```

<!-- ch10-p195 -->
Despite the protests of the Factory Inspector, renewed every 6 months, the abuse continues to this day.[^10.141]

[^10.141]: It is well known how reluctantly the English “Free-traders” gave up the protective duty on the silk manufacture. In place of protection against French imports, the lack of protection for English factory children now serves their turn.

<!-- ch10-p196 -->
The Act of 1850 changed the 15 hours’ time from 6 a.m. to 8.30 p.m. into the 12 hours from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., but for “young persons and women” only. So it did not affect children, who could always be employed for half an hour before this period and 2½ hours after it, provided their labor as a whole did not exceed 6½ hours. While the bill was under discussion, the Factory Inspectors laid before Parliament statistics of the infamous abuses caused by this anomaly. It was no use. In the background lurked the intention of using the children to screw up the working day of adult males to 15 hours in prosperous years. The experience of the three following years showed that such an attempt was bound to come to grief against the resistance of the adult male factory workers. So the Act of 1850 was finally completed in 1853 by forbidding the “employment of children in the morning before and in the evening after young persons and women.” From then on, with a few exceptions, the Factory Act of 1850 regulated the working day of all workers in the branches of industry that come under it.[^10.142] Half a century had passed since the first Factory Act.[^10.143]

[^10.142]: During 1859 and 1860, the peak years of the English cotton industry, some manufacturers tried to win the adult male factory workers over to a longer working day with the decoy bait of higher wages for overtime. The hand-mule spinners and self-actor minders put an end to the experiment with a petition to their employers, in which they say: “Plainly speaking, our lives are to us a burthen [burden]; and, while we are confined to the mills *nearly two days a week more* than the other operatives of the country, we feel like helots [state serfs of ancient Sparta] in the land, and that we are perpetuating a system injurious to ourselves and future generations.... This, therefore, is to give you most respectful notice that when we commence work again after the Christmas and New Year’s holidays, we shall work 60 hours per week, and no more, or from six to six, with one hour and a half out.” (Reports, &c., for 30th April, 1860, p. 30.)

[^10.143]: On the means that the wording of this Act offered for its own violation: the Parliamentary Return “Factories Regulation Act” (6th August, 1859), and in it Leonard Horner’s “Suggestions for amending the Factory Acts to enable the Inspectors to prevent illegal working, now becoming very prevalent.”

<!-- ch10-p197 -->
For the first time, factory legislation went beyond its original sphere with the “Printworks’ Act of 1845.” The displeasure with which capital received this new “extravagance” speaks through every line of the Act. It limits the working day for children from 8 to 13, and for women, to 16 hours, between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m., without any legal pause for meal-times. It allows males over 13 to be worked at will, day and night.[^10.144] It is a Parliamentary abortion.[^10.145]

[^10.144]: Children of the age of 8 years and upwards, have, indeed, been employed from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m. during the last half year in my district.” (Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1857, p. 39.)

[^10.145]: “The Printworks’ Act is admitted to be a failure both with reference to its educational and protective provisions.” (Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1862, p. 52.)

<!-- ch10-p198 -->
However, the principle had triumphed with its victory in those great branches of industry that are the most characteristic creation of the modern mode of production. Their wonderful development from 1853 to 1860, hand in hand with the physical and moral rebirth of the factory workers, was plain to see even for the most half-blind. The employers, from whom the legal limitation and regulation had been wrung step by step in a civil war lasting half a century, themselves now pointed showily to the contrast with the branches of exploitation that were still “free.”[^10.146] The Pharisees of “Political Economy” now proclaimed the insight that a legally fixed working day is necessary as a characteristic new discovery of their “science.”[^10.147] It is easy to understand that after the factory magnates had resigned themselves and become reconciled to the inevitable, capital’s power of resistance gradually weakened. At the same time, the working class’s power of attack grew with the number of its allies in the classes of society that had no direct interest in the question. Hence the comparatively rapid advance since 1860.

[^10.146]: So, for example, E. Potter in a letter to the *Times* of March 24th, 1863. The *Times* reminded him of the manufacturers’ revolt against the Ten Hours’ Bill.

[^10.147]: So, among others, did Mr. W. Newmarch, collaborator and editor of Tooke’s “History of Prices.” Is it a scientific advance to make cowardly concessions to public opinion?

<!-- ch10-p199 -->
In 1860 the dye-works and bleach-works all came under the Factory Act of 1850;[^10.148] the lace and stocking branches of manufacture followed in 1861.

[^10.148]: The Act passed in 1860 laid down that for dye-works and bleach-works the working day should be fixed provisionally at 12 hours on August 1st, 1861, and finally at 10 hours on August 1st, 1862, that is, at 10½ hours for ordinary days and 7½ for Saturday. Now, when the fatal year 1862 came, the old farce was repeated. Besides this, the manufacturers petitioned Parliament to allow the employment of young persons and women for 12 hours for one year longer. “In the existing condition of the trade (the time of the cotton famine), it was greatly to the advantage of the operatives to work 12 hours per day, and make wages when they could.” A bill to this effect had been brought in, “and it was mainly due to the action of the operative bleachers in Scotland that the bill was abandoned.” (Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1862, pp. 14-15.) Defeated in this way by the very workers in whose name it claimed to speak, Capital discovered, with the help of lawyer’s spectacles, that the Act of 1860, drawn up in double-edged phrases like all the Acts of Parliament for the “protection of labour,” gave it a pretext for excluding the calenderers (who pressed cloth between rollers) and the finishers from the Act’s coverage. English jurisprudence, always the faithful servant of capital, gave this piece of legal pettifogging its approval in the Court of Common Pleas. “The operatives have been greatly disappointed ... they have complained of over-work, and it is greatly to be regretted that the clear intention of the legislature should have failed by reason of a faulty definition.” (Cited above, p. 18.)

<!-- ch10-p200 -->
As a result of the first report of the Commission on the employment of children (1863), the same fate was shared by the manufacturers of all earthenwares (not merely pottery), Lucifer-matches, percussion caps, cartridges, carpets, fustian-cutting, and many processes included under the name of “finishing.” In the year 1863 bleaching in the open air[^10.149] and baking were placed under special Acts. In open-air bleaching, these Acts forbade the labor of young persons and women during the night-time (from 8 in the evening to 6 in the morning); in baking, they forbade the employment of journeymen bakers under 18 between 9 in the evening and 5 in the morning. We shall return to the later proposals of the same Commission, which threatened to deprive all the important branches of English industry of their “freedom,” with the exception of agriculture, mines, and the means of transport.[^10.150]

[^10.149]: The “open-air bleachers” had evaded the law of 1860 by means of the lie that no women worked at it at night. The Factory Inspectors exposed the lie, and at the same time petitions from the factory workers robbed Parliament of its notions about the cool meadow-fragrance in which open-air bleaching was reported to take place. In this airy bleaching, drying-rooms were used at temperatures of 90° to 100° Fahrenheit, and the work in them was done mostly by girls. “Cooling” is the technical expression for their occasional escape from the drying-rooms into the fresh air. “Fifteen girls in stoves. Heat from 80° to 90° for linens, and 100° and upwards for cambrics [fine linens]. Twelve girls ironing and doing-up in a small room about 10 feet square, in the centre of which is a close stove. The girls stand round the stove, which throws out a terrific heat, and dries the cambrics rapidly for the ironers. The hours of work for these hands are unlimited. If busy, they work till 9 or 12 at night for successive nights.” (Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1862, p. 56.) A medical man states: “No special hours are allowed for cooling, but if the temperature gets too high, or the workers’ hands get soiled from perspiration, they are allowed to go out for a few minutes.... My experience, which is considerable, in treating the diseases of stove workers, compels me to express the opinion that their sanitary condition is by no means so high as that of the operatives in a spinning factory (and Capital, in its petitions to Parliament, had painted them as glowing with health in the style of Rubens.) The diseases most observable amongst them are phthisis [tuberculosis], bronchitis, irregularity of uterine functions, hysteria in its most aggravated forms, and rheumatism. All of these, I believe, are either directly or indirectly induced by the impure, overheated air of the apartments in which the hands are employed and the want of sufficient comfortable clothing to protect them from the cold, damp atmosphere, in winter, when going to their homes.” (Cited above, pp. 56-57.) On the supplementary law of 1860, wrung from these open-air bleachers, the Factory Inspectors remarked: “The Act has not only failed to afford that protection to the workers which it appears to offer, but contains a clause ... apparently so worded that, unless persons are detected working after 8 o’clock at night they appear to come under no protective provisions at all, and if they do so work the mode of proof is so doubtful that a conviction can scarcely follow.” (Cited above, p. 52.) “To all intents and purposes, therefore, as an Act for any benevolent or educational purpose, it is a failure; since it can scarcely be called benevolent to permit, which is tantamount to compelling, women and children to work 14 hours a day with or without meals, as the case may be, and perhaps for longer hours than these, without limit as to age, without reference to sex, and without regard to the social habits of the families of the neighbourhood, in which such works (bleaching and dyeing) are situated.” (Reports, &c., for 30th April, 1863, p. 40.)

[^10.150]: *Note to the 2nd Ed.* Since 1866, when I wrote the above passages, a reaction has set in again.

### Section 7: The Struggle for a Normal Working Day. Reaction of the English Factory Acts on Other Countries

<!-- ch10-p201 -->
The reader will bear in mind that the production of surplus-value, or the extraction of surplus labor, is the specific end and aim, the sum and substance, of capitalist production. This is so quite apart from any changes in the mode of production that may arise from the subordination of labor to capital. The reader will remember that, as far as we have gone so far, only the independent worker, and therefore only the worker legally entitled to act for himself, enters into a contract with the capitalist as a seller of a commodity. So if, in our historical sketch, modern industry on the one hand, and on the other the labor of those who are minors physically and legally, play important parts, modern industry was for us only a special department, and the labor of minors only a specially striking example, of the exploitation of labor. Without, however, anticipating the later development of our inquiry, the following points follow from the mere connection of the historical facts before us:

<!-- ch10-p202 -->
*First*. Capital's passion for an unlimited and reckless extension of the working day is first satisfied in the industries that were the first to be revolutionized by water-power, steam, and machinery. These were the first creations of the modern mode of production: cotton, wool, flax, and silk spinning, and weaving. The changes in the material mode of production, and the corresponding changes in the social relations of the producers,[^10.151] first gave rise to an excess beyond all bounds. Then, in opposition to this, they called forth a control by Society that legally limits, regulates, and makes uniform the working day and its breaks. During the first half of the nineteenth century, therefore, this control appears simply as exceptional legislation.[^10.152] As soon as this original domain of the new mode of production had been conquered, it was found that a great deal had happened in the meantime. Not only had many other branches of production been made to adopt the same factory system (production in which a system of machines, driven by a central power source, does the work and workers attend the machines). Branches of manufacture with more or less obsolete methods, such as potteries, glass-making, etc., old-fashioned handicrafts like baking, and finally even the so-called domestic industries, such as nail-making,[^10.153] had also long since fallen as completely under capitalist exploitation as the factories themselves. So legislation was compelled gradually to get rid of its exceptional character. Or, where it proceeds after the manner of the Roman Casuists, as it does in England, it was compelled to declare any house in which work was done to be a factory.[^10.154]

[^10.151]: “The conduct of each of these classes (capitalists and workmen) has been the result of the relative situation in which they have been placed.” (Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1848, p. 113.)

[^10.152]: “The employments, placed under restriction, were connected with the manufacture of textile fabrics by the aid of steam or water-power. There were two conditions to which an employment must be subject to cause it to be inspected, viz., the use of steam or waterpower, and the manufacture of certain specified fibre.” (Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1864, p. 8.)

[^10.153]: Specially valuable material on the condition of the so-called domestic industries can be found in the latest reports of the Children’s Employment Commission.

[^10.154]: “The Acts of last Session (1864) ... embrace a diversity of occupations, the customs in which differ greatly, and the use of mechanical power to give motion to machinery is no longer one of the elements necessary, as formerly, to constitute, in legal phrase, a ‘Factory.’” (Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1864, p. 8.)

<!-- ch10-p203 -->
*Second*. The history of the regulation of the working day in certain branches of production, and the struggle still going on in others over this regulation, prove conclusively one thing. Once capitalist production has reached a certain stage, the isolated worker, the worker as “free” seller of his labor-power, gives in without any power of resistance. The creation of a normal working day is, therefore, the product of a long civil war, more or less disguised, between the capitalist class and the working class. As the contest takes place in the arena of modern industry, it first breaks out in the home of that industry, England.[^10.155] The English factory workers were the champions not only of the English working class but of the modern working class in general, as their theorists were the first to throw down the gauntlet to the theory of capital.[^10.156] Hence the philosopher of the Factory, Ure, denounces it as an unspeakable disgrace to the English working class that they wrote “the slavery of the Factory Acts” on the banner which they carried against capital, manfully striving for “perfect freedom of labour.”[^10.157]

[^10.155]: Belgium, the paradise of Continental Liberalism, shows no trace of this movement. Even in the coal and metal mines, workers of both sexes and of all ages are consumed in perfect “freedom”, at any time and for any length of time. Of every 1,000 persons employed there, 733 are men, 88 women, 135 boys, and 44 girls under 16. In the blast furnaces, etc., of every 1,000, 668 are men, 149 women, 98 boys, and 85 girls under 16. Add to this the low wages paid for the enormous exploitation of mature and immature labor-power. The average daily pay for a man is 2s. 8d., for a woman 1s. 8d., for a boy 1s. 2½d. As a result, Belgium in 1863 had nearly doubled both the amount and the value of its exports of coal, iron, etc., compared with 1850.

[^10.156]: Soon after 1810, Robert Owen not only argued in theory that the working day must be limited, but actually introduced the 10 hours’ day in his factory at New Lanark. This was laughed at as a communistic Utopia. So were his “Combination of children’s education with productive labour and the Co-operative Societies of Workingmen”, which he was the first to call into being. Today the first Utopia is a Factory Act, the second appears as an official phrase in all Factory Acts, and the third is already being used as a cloak for reactionary humbug.

[^10.157]: Ure: “French translation, Philosophie des Manufactures.” Paris, 1836, Vol. II, pp. 39, 40, 67, 77, etc.

<!-- ch10-p204 -->
France limps slowly behind England. It took the February revolution to bring into the world the 12 hours’ law,[^10.158] which is much more defective than its English original. For all that, the French revolutionary method has its special advantages. It commands, once and for all, the same limit to the working day in all workshops and factories without distinction. English legislation, meanwhile, reluctantly gives way to the pressure of circumstances, now on this point, now on that, and is getting lost in a hopelessly bewildering tangle of contradictory laws.[^10.159] On the other hand, the French law proclaims as a principle what in England was won only in the name of children, minors, and women, and has only recently been claimed for the first time as a general right.[^10.160]

[^10.158]: The Compte Rendu of the International Statistical Congress at Paris, 1855, states: “The French law, which limits the length of daily labour in factories and workshops to 12 hours, does not confine this work to definite fixed hours. For children’s labour only the work-time is prescribed as between 5 a.m. and 9 p.m. Therefore, some of the masters use the right which this fatal silence gives them to keep their works going, without intermission, day in, day out, possibly with the exception of Sunday. For this purpose they use two different sets of workers, of whom neither is in the workshop more than 12 hours at a time, but the work of the establishment lasts day and night. The law is satisfied, but is humanity?” Besides “the destructive influence of night-labour on the human organism,” stress is also laid on “the fatal influence of the association of the two sexes by night in the same badly-lighted workshops.”

[^10.159]: “For instance, there is within my district one occupier who, within the same curtilage [enclosed premises], is at the same time a bleacher and dyer under the Bleaching and Dyeing Works Act, a printer under the Print Works Act, and a finisher under the Factory Act.” (Report of Mr. Baker, in Reports, lic., for October 31st, 1861, p. 20.) After listing the different provisions of these Acts, and the complications that arise from them, Mr. Baker says: “It will hence appear that it must be very difficult to secure the execution of these three Acts of Parliament where the occupier chooses to evade the law.” But what this does assure to the lawyers is lawsuits.

[^10.160]: So the Factory Inspectors at last venture to say: “These objections (of capital to the legal limitation of the working day) must succumb before the broad principle of the rights of labour.... There is a time when the master’s right in his workman’s labour ceases, and his time becomes his own, even if there were no exhaustion in the question.” (Reports, &c., for 31st Oct., 1862, p. 54.)

<!-- ch10-p205 -->
In the United States of North America, every independent movement of the workers was paralyzed as long as slavery disfigured a part of the Republic. Labor cannot set itself free in the white skin where in the black it is branded. But out of the death of slavery a new life at once arose. The first fruit of the Civil War was the eight hours’ agitation, which ran with the seven-leagued boots of the locomotive from the Atlantic to the Pacific, from New England to California. The General Congress of Labor at Baltimore (August 16th, 1866) declared:

<!-- ch10-p206 -->
> “The first and great necessity of the present, to free the labour of this country from capitalistic slavery, is the passing of a law by which eight hours shall be the normal working day in all States of the American Union. We are resolved to put forth all our strength until this glorious result is attained.”[^10.161]

[^10.161]: “We, the workers of Dunkirk, declare that the length of time of labour required under the present system is too great, and that, far from leaving the worker time for rest and education, it plunges him into a condition of servitude but little better than slavery. That is why we decide that 8 hours are enough for a working day, and ought to be legally recognised as enough; why we call to our help that powerful lever, the press; ... and why we shall consider all those that refuse us this help as enemies of the reform of labour and of the rights of the labourer.” (Resolution of the Working Men of Dunkirk, New York State, 1866.)

<!-- ch10-p207 -->
At the same time, the Congress of the International Working Men’s Association at Geneva, on the proposal of the London General Council, resolved that “the limitation of the working day is a preliminary condition without which all further attempts at improvement and emancipation must prove abortive... the Congress proposes eight hours as the legal limit of the working day.”

<!-- ch10-p208 -->
Thus the movement of the working class on both sides of the Atlantic, which had grown instinctively out of the conditions of production themselves, endorsed the words of the English Factory Inspector R. J. Saunders:

<!-- ch10-p209 -->
> “Further steps towards a reformation of society can never be carried out with any hope of success, unless the hours of labour be limited, and the prescribed limit strictly enforced.”[^10.162]

[^10.162]: Reports, &c., for Oct., 1848, p. 112.

<!-- ch10-p210 -->
It must be admitted that our worker comes out of the process of production different from how he went in. In the market he stood as the owner of the commodity “labor-power”, face to face with other owners of commodities, dealer against dealer. The contract by which he sold his labor-power to the capitalist proved, so to speak, in black and white that he was free to dispose of himself. Once the bargain is concluded, it is discovered that he was no “free agent”; that the time for which he is free to sell his labor-power is the time for which he is forced to sell it;[^10.163] that in fact the vampire will not lose its hold on him “so long as there is a muscle, a nerve, a drop of blood to be exploited.”[^10.164] For “protection” against “the serpent of their agonies,” the workers must put their heads together. As a class, they must force the passing of a law, an all-powerful social barrier that shall prevent the very workers from selling themselves and their families into slavery and death by voluntary contract with capital.[^10.165] In place of the pompous catalogue of the “inalienable rights of man” comes the modest Magna Charta of a legally limited working day, which shall make clear “when the time which the worker sells is ended, and when his own begins.” Quantum mutatus ab illo! [How greatly changed from that! – Virgil][^10.166]

[^10.163]: “The proceedings (the manoeuvres of capital, e.g., from 1848-50) have afforded, moreover, incontrovertible proof of the fallacy of the assertion so often advanced, that operatives need no protection, but may be considered as free agents in the disposal of the only property which they possess — the labour of their hands and the sweat of their brows.” (Reports, &c., for April 30th, 1850, p. 45.) “Free labour (if so it may be termed) even in a free country, requires the strong arm of the law to protect it.” (Reports, &c., for October 31st, 1864, p. 34.) “To permit, which is tantamount to compelling ... to work 14 hours a day with or without meals,” etc. (Repts., &c., for April 30th, 1863, p. 40.)

[^10.164]: Friedrich Engels, cited above, p. 5.

[^10.165]: In the branches of industry that come under it, the 10 Hours’ Act has “put an end to the premature decrepitude of the former long-hour workers.” (Reports, &c., for 31st Oct., 1859, p. 47.) “Capital (in factories) can never be employed in keeping the machinery in motion beyond a limited time, without certain injury to the health and morals of the labourers employed; and they are not in a position to protect themselves.” (cited above, p. 8)

[^10.166]: “A still greater boon is the distinction at last made clear between the worker’s own time and his master’s. The worker knows now when that which he sells is ended, and when his own begins; and by possessing a sure foreknowledge of this, is enabled to prearrange his own minutes for his own purposes.” (cited above, p. 52.) “By making them masters of their own time (the Factory Acts) have given them a moral energy which is directing them to the eventual possession of political power” (cited above, p. 47). With suppressed irony, and in very carefully weighed words, the Factory Inspectors hint that the actual law also frees the capitalist from some of the brutality natural to a man who is a mere embodiment of capital, and that it has given him time for a little “culture.” “Formerly the master had no time for anything but money; the servant had no time for anything but labour” (cited above, p. 48).

## Chapter 11: Rate and Mass of Surplus-Value

<!-- ch11-p001 -->
In this chapter, as up to now, the value of labor-power, and therefore the part of the working day needed to reproduce or maintain that labor-power, are assumed to be given, constant quantities. (Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist. The value of labor-power is the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker, and to raise the next generation of workers, able to work. Value is what commodities, things produced in order to be exchanged and not for the producer's own use, have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time. The working day is the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor.)

<!-- ch11-p002 -->
With this as our premise, once the rate of surplus-value is given, the mass of surplus-value that the individual worker supplies to the capitalist in a definite period of time is given at the same time. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it. The rate of surplus-value is the ratio of surplus-value to variable capital (s/v), that is, of surplus labor to necessary labor; it is also called the degree of exploitation of labor-power.) For example, suppose the necessary labor amounts to 6 hours daily, expressed in an amount of gold = 3 shillings. (Necessary labor is the part of the working day in which the worker produces the equivalent of the value of their own labor-power, that is, of their wages.) Then 3s. is the daily value of one labor-power, or the value of the capital advanced in buying one labor-power. (Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger.) Suppose, further, that the rate of surplus-value is 100%. Then this variable capital of 3s. (variable capital being the part of capital spent on labor-power, which reproduces its own value and also produces surplus-value, so that its size varies) produces a mass of surplus-value of 3s. In other words, the worker supplies daily a mass of surplus labor equal to 6 hours (surplus labor being the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist).

<!-- ch11-p003 -->
But the variable capital of a capitalist is the money expression of the total value of all the labor-powers that he employs at the same time. Its value is therefore equal to the average value of one labor-power multiplied by the number of labor-powers employed. So, with a given value of labor-power, the size of the variable capital varies directly with the number of workers employed at the same time. If the daily value of one labor-power = 3s., then a capital of 300s. must be advanced in order to exploit 100 labor-powers daily, or n times 3s. in order to exploit n labor-powers daily.

<!-- ch11-p004 -->
In the same way, if a variable capital of 3s., the daily value of one labor-power, produces a daily surplus-value of 3s., then a variable capital of 300s. will produce a daily surplus-value of 300s., and one of n times 3s. a daily surplus-value of n × 3s. The mass of surplus-value produced is therefore equal to the surplus-value that the working day of one worker supplies, multiplied by the number of workers employed. But further, the value of labor-power being given, the mass of surplus-value that a single worker produces is determined by the rate of surplus-value. So this law follows: the mass of surplus-value produced is equal to the amount of variable capital advanced, multiplied by the rate of surplus-value. In other words, it is determined by the compound ratio between the number of labor-powers exploited at the same time by the same capitalist and the degree of exploitation of each individual labor-power.

<!-- ch11-p005 -->
Let the mass of surplus-value be S; the surplus-value supplied by the individual worker in the average day, s; the variable capital advanced daily to buy one individual labor-power, v; the sum total of the variable capital, V; the value of an average labor-power, P; its degree of exploitation, (a'/a) (surplus labor/necessary labor); and the number of workers employed, n. We would then have:

<!-- ch11-p006 -->
(s/v) × V\
S =\
{\
P × (a'/a) × n

<!-- ch11-p007 -->
It is always assumed not only that the value of an average labor-power is constant, but also that the workers employed by a capitalist are reduced to average workers. There are exceptional cases in which the surplus-value produced does not increase in proportion to the number of workers exploited; but then the value of labor-power does not remain constant.

<!-- ch11-p008 -->
In producing a definite mass of surplus-value, therefore, a decrease in one factor may be made up for by an increase in the other. If the variable capital shrinks, and at the same time the rate of surplus-value rises in the same ratio, the mass of surplus-value produced stays unchanged. Suppose, on our earlier assumption, that the capitalist must advance 300s. in order to exploit 100 workers a day, and that the rate of surplus-value amounts to 50%. Then this variable capital of 300s. yields a surplus-value of 150s., or of 100 × 3 working hours. Now suppose the rate of surplus-value doubles, or the working day is extended from 6 to 12 hours instead of from 6 to 9, and at the same time the variable capital is cut by half, to 150s. It too yields a surplus-value of 150s., or 50 × 6 working hours. A reduction of the variable capital may therefore be made up for by a proportionate rise in the degree of exploitation of labor-power; or a decrease in the number of workers employed, by a proportionate extension of the working day. Within certain limits, therefore, the supply of labor that capital can exploit is independent of the supply of workers.[^11.1] On the other hand, a fall in the rate of surplus-value leaves the mass of surplus-value produced unchanged if the amount of variable capital, or the number of workers employed, increases in the same proportion.

[^11.1]: This elementary law appears to be unknown to the vulgar economists (economists who only describe and defend the surface appearances of the system, without investigating its real relations). Like upside-down Archimedes, they imagine that in the fixing of the market-price of labor by supply and demand they have found the fulcrum by means of which, not to move the world, but to stop its motion.

<!-- ch11-p009 -->
Nevertheless, making up for a decrease in the number of workers employed, or in the amount of variable capital advanced, by a rise in the rate of surplus-value or by lengthening the working day has limits that cannot be crossed. Whatever the value of labor-power may be, whether the working time necessary to maintain the worker is 2 or 10 hours, the total value that a worker can produce, day in, day out, is always less than the value in which 24 hours of labor are embodied. It is less than 12s., if 12s. is the money expression for 24 hours of realized labor. On our former assumption, 6 working hours are needed daily to reproduce the labor-power itself, or to replace the value of the capital advanced to buy it. On that assumption, a variable capital of 1,500s. that employs 500 workers at a rate of surplus-value of 100%, with a 12 hours' working day, produces a surplus-value of 1,500s. daily, or 6 × 500 working hours. A capital of 300s. that employs 100 workers a day with a rate of surplus-value of 200%, or with a working day of 18 hours, produces a mass of surplus-value of only 600s., or 12 × 100 working hours. And its total value-product, the equivalent of the variable capital advanced plus the surplus-value, can never, day in, day out, reach the sum of 1,200s., or 24 × 100 working hours. The average working day is by nature always less than 24 hours, and this absolute limit sets an absolute limit to making up for a reduction of variable capital by a higher rate of surplus-value, or for a decrease in the number of workers exploited by a higher degree of exploitation of labor-power. This obvious law is important for clearing up many phenomena. They arise from a tendency of capital (to be worked out later on) to reduce as much as possible the number of workers it employs, or its variable part, the part turned into labor-power. This tendency contradicts its other tendency, to produce the greatest possible mass of surplus-value. On the other hand, if the mass of labor-power employed, or the amount of variable capital, increases, but not in proportion to the fall in the rate of surplus-value, the mass of surplus-value produced falls.

<!-- ch11-p010 -->
A third law follows from the fact that the mass of surplus-value produced is determined by two factors: the rate of surplus-value and the amount of variable capital advanced. Given the rate of surplus-value, or the degree of exploitation of labor-power, and given the value of labor-power, or the amount of necessary working time, it is self-evident that the greater the variable capital, the greater would be the mass of value and of surplus-value produced. If the limit of the working day is given, and also the limit of its necessary part, the mass of value and surplus-value that an individual capitalist produces clearly depends exclusively on the mass of labor that he sets in motion. But under the conditions assumed above, this depends on the mass of labor-power, or the number of workers, that he exploits; and this number in turn is determined by the amount of variable capital advanced. So, with a given rate of surplus-value and a given value of labor-power, the masses of surplus-value produced vary directly with the amounts of the variable capitals advanced. Now we know that the capitalist divides his capital into two parts. One part he lays out on means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things). This is the constant part of his capital. The other part he lays out on living labor-power. This part forms his variable capital. On the basis of the same mode of social production, the division of capital into constant and variable differs in different branches of production. Within the same branch of production, too, this relation changes with changes in the technical conditions and in the social combinations of the processes of production. But whatever the proportion in which a given capital breaks up into a constant and a variable part, whether the variable part is to the constant part as 1:2 or 1:10 or 1:x, this does not affect the law just laid down. For, according to our earlier analysis, the value of the constant capital reappears in the value of the product, but does not enter into the newly produced value, the newly created value-product. To employ 1,000 spinners, more raw material, spindles, etc., are of course required than to employ 100. But the value of these additional means of production may rise, fall, stay the same, be large or small; it has no influence on the process by which surplus-value is created by means of the labor-powers that set them in motion. The law shown above therefore now takes this form: the masses of value and of surplus-value produced by different capitals – the value of labor-power being given and its degree of exploitation being equal – vary directly with the amounts of the variable parts of these capitals, that is, of their parts turned into living labor-power.

<!-- ch11-p011 -->
This law clearly contradicts all experience based on appearance. Everyone knows that a cotton spinner who, reckoning the percentage on the whole of the capital he applies, employs much constant and little variable capital, does not on that account pocket less profit or surplus-value than a baker, who sets in motion relatively much variable and little constant capital. To solve this apparent contradiction, many intermediate terms are still needed, just as, from the standpoint of elementary algebra, many intermediate terms are needed to understand that 0/0 may represent an actual magnitude. Classical economics (that is, the economists from Petty to Ricardo who investigated the real relations of production), although it does not formulate the law, holds to it by instinct, because the law is a necessary consequence of the general law of value. Classical economics tries to rescue the law from collision with contradictory phenomena by a violent abstraction. It will be seen later[^11.2] how the school of Ricardo has come to grief over this stumbling block. Vulgar economics, which indeed “has really learnt nothing,” here as everywhere sticks to appearances against the law that regulates and explains them. In opposition to Spinoza, it believes that “ignorance is a sufficient reason.”

[^11.2]: Further details will be given in Book IV.

<!-- ch11-p012 -->
The labor set in motion by the total capital of a society, day in, day out, may be regarded as a single collective working day. If, for example, the number of workers is a million, and the average working day of a worker is 10 hours, the social working day consists of ten million hours. With a given length of this working day, whether its limits are fixed physically or socially, the mass of surplus-value can only be increased by increasing the number of workers, that is, the working population. Here the growth of population forms the mathematical limit to the production of surplus-value by the total social capital. On the other hand, with a given size of population, this limit is formed by the possible lengthening of the working day.[^11.3] It will be seen in the following chapter, however, that this law holds only for the form of surplus-value dealt with so far.

[^11.3]: “The Labour, that is the economic time, of society, is a given portion, say ten hours a day of a million of people, or ten million hours.... Capital has its boundary of increase. This boundary may, at any given period, be attained in the actual extent of economic time employed.” (“An Essay on the Political Economy of Nations.” London, 1821, pp. 47, 49.)

<!-- ch11-p013 -->
From the treatment of the production of surplus-value so far, it follows that not every sum of money, or of value, can be turned into capital at will. To make this transformation, in fact, a certain minimum of money or of exchange-value (the proportion in which one commodity trades for others) must be presupposed in the hands of the individual owner of money or commodities. The minimum of variable capital is the cost price of a single labor-power, employed the whole year through, day in, day out, for the production of surplus-value. (Price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity.) If this worker owned his own means of production, and were satisfied to live as a worker, he would not need to work beyond the time necessary to reproduce his means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live), say 8 hours a day. Besides, he would need only enough means of production for 8 working hours. The capitalist, on the other hand, who makes him do, say, 4 hours' surplus labor besides these 8 hours, needs an additional sum of money to supply the additional means of production. On our assumption, however, the capitalist would have to employ two workers in order to live on the surplus-value he appropriates daily as well as a worker, and no better, that is, to be able to satisfy his necessary wants. In this case the mere maintenance of life would be the end of his production, not the increase of wealth; but the increase of wealth is implied in capitalist production. For him to live only twice as well as an ordinary worker, and also turn half of the surplus-value produced into capital, he would have to raise the minimum of capital advanced 8 times, along with the number of workers. Of course he can, like his worker, set to work himself and take a direct part in the process of production. But then he is only a hybrid between capitalist and worker, a “small master.” A certain stage of capitalist production requires that the capitalist be able to devote the whole of the time during which he functions as a capitalist, that is, as personified capital, to appropriating and therefore controlling the labor of others, and to selling the products of this labor.[^11.4] The guilds of the middle ages therefore tried to prevent by force the master of a trade from turning into a capitalist, by limiting the number of workers one master could employ to a very small maximum. The owner of money or commodities actually turns into a capitalist only in cases where the minimum sum advanced for production greatly exceeds the maximum of the middle ages. Here, as in natural science, we see the correctness of the law discovered by Hegel (in his “Logic”), that merely quantitative differences beyond a certain point pass into qualitative changes.[^11.5]

[^11.4]: “The farmer cannot rely on his own labour, and if he does, I will maintain that he is a loser by it. His employment should be a general attention to the whole: his thresher must be watched, or he will soon lose his wages in corn not threshed out, his mowers, reapers, &c., must be looked after; he must constantly go round his fences; he must see there is no neglect; which would be the case if he was confined to any one spot.” (“An Inquiry into the Connexion between the Present Price of Provisions and the Size of Farms, &c. By a Farmer.” London, 1773, p. 12.) This book is very interesting. In it one may study the origin of the “capitalist farmer” or “merchant farmer,” as he is explicitly called, and note his self-glorification at the expense of the small farmer, who is concerned only with bare subsistence. “The class of capitalists are from the first partially, and they become ultimately completely, discharged from the necessity of the manual labour.” (“Textbook of Lectures on the Political Economy of Nations. By the Rev. Richard Jones.” Hertford 1852. Lecture III., p. 39.)

[^11.5]: The molecular theory of modern chemistry, first worked out scientifically by Laurent and Gerhardt, rests on no other law. (Addition to 3rd Edition.) To explain this statement, which is not very clear to non-chemists, we note that the author is speaking here of the homologous series of carbon compounds, first so named by C. Gerhardt in 1843. Each of these series has its own general algebraic formula. Thus the series of paraffins: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, that of the normal alcohols: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>O; of the normal fatty acids: CnH<sub>2n</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, and many others. In the above examples, each time CH<sub>2</sub> is simply added in quantity to the molecular formula, a qualitatively different body is formed. On the share of Laurent and Gerhardt (overestimated by Marx) in establishing this important fact, see Kopp, “Entwicklung der Chemie.” Munchen, 1873, pp. 709, 716, and Schorkmmer, “The Rise and Development of Organic Chemistry.” London, 1879, p. 54. — *F. E.*. See Letter from Marx to Engels, 22 June 1867

    For Hegel’s formulation of the idea in the *Logic*, see Remark: Examples of Such Nodal Lines; the Maxim, ‘Nature Does Not Make Leaps’.

<!-- ch11-p014 -->
The minimum sum of value that the individual owner of money or commodities must command in order to metamorphose himself into a capitalist changes with the different stages of development of capitalist production. At given stages it also differs in different spheres of production, according to their special and technical conditions. Certain spheres of production demand, even at the very start of capitalist production, a minimum of capital that is not yet found in the hands of single individuals. This gives rise partly to state subsidies to private persons, as in France in the time of Colbert, and as in many German states up to our own time; and partly to the formation of societies with a legal monopoly for exploiting certain branches of industry and trade, the forerunners of our modern joint-stock companies.[^11.6]

[^11.6]: Martin Luther calls institutions of this kind “The Company Monopolia.”

<!-- ch11-p015 -->
Within the process of production, as we have seen, capital acquired command over labor, that is, over functioning labor-power, or the worker himself. The capitalist, as personified capital, takes care that the worker does his work regularly and with the proper degree of intensity.

<!-- ch11-p016 -->
Capital further developed into a coercive relation, which compels the working class to do more work than the narrow round of its own needs prescribes. As a producer of the activity of others, as a pumper-out of surplus labor and exploiter of labor-power, it surpasses all earlier systems of production based on directly forced labor in energy, disregard of limits, recklessness, and efficiency.

<!-- ch11-p017 -->
At first, capital subordinates labor on the basis of the technical conditions in which it historically finds it. It does not, therefore, change the mode of production immediately. So the production of surplus-value in the form we have considered so far, by simply extending the working day, proved to be independent of any change in the mode of production itself. It was no less active in the old-fashioned bakeries than in the modern cotton factories.

<!-- ch11-p018 -->
If we consider the process of production from the point of view of the simple labor process (the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things), the worker relates to the means of production not as capital, but as the mere means and material of his own intelligent productive activity. In tanning, for example, he deals with the skins simply as his object of labor. It is not the capitalist whose skin he tans. But it is different as soon as we look at the process of production from the point of view of the process of creating surplus-value. The means of production are at once changed into means for absorbing the labor of others. It is now no longer the worker who employs the means of production, but the means of production that employ the worker. Instead of being consumed by him as material elements of his productive activity, they consume him as the ferment necessary to their own life-process; and the life-process of capital consists only in its movement as value that constantly expands, constantly multiplies itself. Furnaces and workshops that stand idle at night, and absorb no living labor, are “a mere loss” to the capitalist. Hence furnaces and workshops constitute lawful claims on the night-labor of the workers. The simple transformation of money into the material factors of the process of production, into means of production, turns these means of production into a title and a right to the labor and surplus labor of others. One example will show, in conclusion, how this distortion, peculiar to and characteristic of capitalist production, this complete inversion of the relation between dead and living labor (labor already embodied in means of production, and the labor of workers now at work), between value and the force that creates value, is mirrored in the consciousness of capitalists. During the revolt of the English factory lords between 1848 and 1850, “the head of one of the oldest and most respectable houses in the West of Scotland, Messrs. Carlile Sons & Co., of the linen and cotton thread factory at Paisley, a company which has now existed for about a century, which was in operation in 1752, and four generations of the same family have conducted it” ... this “very intelligent gentleman” then wrote a letter[^11.7] in the *Glasgow Daily Mail* of April 25th, 1849, with the title “The relay system” (a system of shifts in which workers, especially children, were switched in and out at different times, which made the legal hours hard to check). Among other things, the letter contains the following grotesquely naive passage: “Let us now ... see what evils will attend the limiting to 10 hours the working of the factory.... They amount to the most serious damage to the millowner’s prospects and property. If he (that is, his “hands”) worked 12 hours before, and is limited to 10, then every 12 machines or spindles in his establishment shrink to 10, and should the works be disposed of, they will be valued only as 10, so that a sixth part would thus be deducted from the value of every factory in the country.”[^11.8]

[^11.7]: Reports of Insp. of Fact., April 30th, 1849, p. 59.

[^11.8]: Cited above, p. 60. Factory Inspector Stuart, himself a Scot, and, unlike the English Factory Inspectors, wholly taken captive by the capitalist way of thinking, expressly remarks on this letter, which he includes in his report, that it is “the most useful of the communications which any of the factory-owners working with relays have given to those engaged in the same trade, and which is the most calculated to remove the prejudices of such of them as have scruples respecting any change of the arrangement of the hours of work.”

<!-- ch11-p019 -->
To this West of Scotland bourgeois brain (bourgeois: belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it), heir to the accumulated capitalist qualities of “four generations,” the value of the means of production, spindles, etc., is so inseparably mixed up with their property, as capital, of expanding their own value and swallowing up daily a definite quantity of the unpaid labor of others, that the head of the firm of Carlile & Co. actually imagines the following. If he sells his factory, so he imagines, not only will the value of the spindles be paid to him, but in addition their power of annexing surplus-value: not only the labor that is embodied in them and is necessary to produce spindles of this kind, but also the surplus labor that they help to pump out daily from the brave Scots of Paisley. And for that very reason he thinks that with the shortening of the working day by 2 hours, the selling-price of 12 spinning machines dwindles to that of 10!

# Part 4: Production of Relative Surplus-Value

## Chapter 12: The Concept of Relative Surplus-Value

<!-- ch12-p001 -->
Up to this point we have treated the part of the working day that merely produces an equivalent for the value paid by the capitalist for the worker's labor-power as a constant quantity. And that is in fact what it is, under given conditions of production and at a given stage in the economic development of society. (The working day is the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor. Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time. Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist.) Beyond this time, his necessary labor-time, the worker, as we saw, could go on working for 2, 3, 4, 6, etc., hours. The rate of surplus-value and the length of the working day depended on how far this extension went. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it. The rate of surplus-value is the ratio of surplus-value to variable capital, s/v, that is, of surplus labor to necessary labor; it is also called the degree of exploitation of labor-power.) Although the necessary labor-time was constant, we saw, on the other hand, that the total working day was variable. Now suppose we have a working day whose length is given, and whose division between necessary labor and surplus labor is given too. (Surplus labor is the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist.) Let the whole line a c, a–b–c, represent, for example, a working day of 12 hours; the part a b, 10 hours of necessary labor; and the part b c, 2 hours of surplus labor. How, then, can the production of surplus-value be increased, that is, how can the surplus labor be extended, without any extension of a c, or independently of any such extension?

<!-- ch12-p002 -->
The length of a c is given. Even so, b c seems capable of being extended, if not by stretching it past its end c, which is also the end of the working day a c, then at any rate by pushing its starting-point b back in the direction of a. Assume that b'–b in the line ab'bc is equal to half of b c

<!-- ch12-p003 -->
a–––b'–b––c

<!-- ch12-p004 -->
or to one hour's labor-time. If we now move the point b to b' in a c, the working day of 12 hours, then b c becomes b' c. The surplus labor increases by one half, from 2 hours to 3 hours, although the working day stays at 12 hours as before. But this extension of the surplus labor-time from b c to b' c, from 2 hours to 3 hours, is clearly impossible unless the necessary labor-time shrinks at the same time from a b to a b', from 10 hours to 9 hours. The extension of the surplus labor would correspond to a shortening of the necessary labor. In other words, part of the labor-time that was previously in reality spent for the worker's own benefit would be turned into labor-time for the benefit of the capitalist. What would change is not the length of the working day, but its division into necessary labor-time and surplus labor-time.

<!-- ch12-p005 -->
On the other hand, clearly the length of the surplus labor is given when the length of the working day and the value of labor-power are given. The value of labor-power, that is, the labor-time needed to produce labor-power, determines the labor-time needed to reproduce that value. If one working-hour is embodied in sixpence, and the value of a day's labor-power is five shillings, the worker must work 10 hours a day to replace the value that capital has paid for his labor-power, or to produce an equivalent for the value of the means of subsistence he needs each day. (Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger. Means of subsistence are the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live.) Given the value of these means of subsistence, the value of his labor-power is given;[^12.1] and given the value of his labor-power, the length of his necessary labor-time is given. The length of the surplus labor, however, is found by subtracting the necessary labor-time from the total working day. Ten hours subtracted from twelve leave two, and it is not easy to see how, under the given conditions, the surplus labor can possibly be extended beyond two hours. No doubt the capitalist can pay the worker four shillings and sixpence, or even less, instead of five shillings. Nine hours' labor-time would be enough to reproduce this value of four shillings and sixpence. So three hours of surplus labor instead of two would go to the capitalist, and the surplus-value would rise from one shilling to eighteen-pence. But this result would be obtained only by pushing the worker's wages below the value of his labor-power. (Wages are the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself.) With the four shillings and sixpence that he produces in nine hours, he can get one-tenth less of the necessaries of life than before, and so the proper reproduction of his labor-power is crippled. In this case the surplus labor would be extended only by overstepping its normal limits; its territory would be enlarged only by seizing part of the territory of necessary labor-time. This method plays an important part in actual practice. Despite that, we cannot consider it here, because we have assumed that all commodities, including labor-power, are bought and sold at their full value. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, that is, sold, not for the producer's own use.) Granted this, it follows that the labor-time needed to produce labor-power, or to reproduce its value, cannot be reduced by a fall in the worker's wages below the value of his labor-power, but only by a fall in this value itself. Given the length of the working day, the extension of the surplus labor must necessarily come from cutting the necessary labor-time; the cut cannot come from the extension. In the example we have taken, the value of labor-power must actually fall by one-tenth so that the necessary labor-time can be reduced by one-tenth, that is, from ten hours to nine, and so that the surplus labor can consequently be extended from two hours to three.

[^12.1]: The value of his average daily wages is determined by what the worker needs “so as to live, labour, and generate.” (Wm. Petty: “Political Anatomy of Ireland,” 1672, p. 64.) “The price of Labour is always constituted of the price of necessaries ... whenever ... the labouring man’s wages will not, suitably to his low rank and station, as a labouring man, support such a family as is often the lot of many of them to have,” he does not receive proper wages. (J. Vanderlint, cited above, p. 15.) “Le simple ouvrier, qui n’a que ses bras et son industrie, n’a rien qu’autant qu’il parvient à vendre à d’autres sa peine... En tout genre de travail il doit arriver, et il arrive en effet, que le salaire de l’ouvrier se borne à ce qui lui est nécessaire pour lui procurer sa subsistance.” [The ordinary worker, who has nothing but his arms and his industriousness, has nothing unless he manages to sell his toil to others ... In every kind of work it must happen, and it does in fact happen, that the worker's wage is limited to what he needs to obtain his subsistence.] (Turgot, “Réflexions, &c.,” *Oeuvres*, éd. Daire t. I, p. 10.) “The price of the necessaries of life is, in fact, the cost of producing labour.” (Malthus, “Inquiry into, &c., Rent,” London, 1815, p. 48, note.)

<!-- ch12-p006 -->
Such a fall in the value of labor-power implies, however, that the same necessaries of life that used to be produced in ten hours can now be produced in nine hours. But this is impossible without an increase in the productivity of labor. For example, suppose a shoemaker with given tools makes one pair of boots in one working day of twelve hours. If he has to make two pairs in the same time, the productivity of his labor must be doubled. This cannot be done except by a change in his tools, or in his way of working, or in both. So the conditions of production, that is, his mode of production, and the labor process itself, must be revolutionized. (The labor process is the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things.) By an increase in the productivity of labor, we mean, in general, a change in the labor process of such a kind that it shortens the labor-time socially necessary to produce a commodity (the time needed to produce an article under the normal conditions of production of the day, with the average skill and intensity of labor), and gives a given quantity of labor the power to produce a greater quantity of use-value (the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties).[^12.2] Until now, in dealing with surplus-value that arises from simply extending the working day, we have assumed the mode of production to be given and unchanging. But when surplus-value has to be produced by turning necessary labor into surplus labor, it is by no means enough for capital to take over the labor process in the form in which history has handed it down, and then simply to make that process last longer. The technical and social conditions of the process, and so the very mode of production, must be revolutionized before the productivity of labor can be increased. Only by that means can the value of labor-power be made to sink, and the part of the working day needed to reproduce that value be shortened.

[^12.2]: Quando si perfezionano le arti, che non è altro che la scoperta di nuove vie, onde si possa compiere una manufattura con meno gente o (che è lo stesso) in minor tempo di prima.” [When the crafts are perfected, which is nothing other than the discovery of new ways by which a product can be made with fewer people or (which is the same thing) in less time than before] (Galiani, cited above, p. 159.) “L’économie sur les frais de production ne peut donc être autre chose que l’économie sur la quantité de travail employé pour produire.” [So saving on the costs of production can be nothing other than saving on the quantity of labor employed to produce] (Sismondi, “Études,” t. I. p. 22.)

<!-- ch12-p007 -->
I call the surplus-value produced by lengthening the working day *absolute surplus-value*. On the other hand, I call the surplus-value that arises from cutting the necessary labor-time, and from the corresponding change in the relative lengths of the two parts of the working day, *relative surplus-value*.

<!-- ch12-p008 -->
To bring about a fall in the value of labor-power, the increase in the productivity of labor must take hold of those branches of industry whose products determine the value of labor-power, and so either belong to the class of customary means of subsistence, or can take the place of those means. But the value of a commodity is determined not only by the quantity of labor that the worker directly spends on that commodity, but also by the labor contained in the means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things). For instance, the value of a pair of boots depends not only on the cobbler's labor, but also on the value of the leather, wax, thread, etc. So a fall in the value of labor-power is also brought about by an increase in the productivity of labor, and by a corresponding cheapening of commodities, in those industries that supply the instruments of labor and the raw material which form the material elements of the constant capital needed to produce the necessaries of life. (Constant capital is the part of capital spent on means of production; its value is passed on to the product but does not grow.) But an increase in the productivity of labor in those branches of industry that supply neither the necessaries of life nor the means of production for such necessaries leaves the value of labor-power undisturbed.

<!-- ch12-p009 -->
Of course, the cheapened commodity causes only a fall in the value of labor-power to that extent, that is, a fall proportional to how far that commodity is used in reproducing labor-power. Shirts, for instance, are a necessary means of subsistence, but they are only one out of many. The whole of the necessaries of life, however, consists of various commodities, each the product of a separate industry, and the value of each of those commodities enters as a component part into the value of labor-power. The value of labor-power decreases as the labor-time needed to reproduce it decreases. The total decrease is the sum of all the different cuts in labor-time made in those various separate industries. Here we treat this general result as if it were the immediate result directly aimed at in each individual case. When an individual capitalist cheapens shirts, for instance, by increasing the productivity of labor, he by no means necessarily aims at reducing the value of labor-power and shortening the necessary labor-time to that extent. But only insofar as he ultimately contributes to this result does he help to raise the general rate of surplus-value.[^12.3] The general and necessary tendencies of capital must be distinguished from their forms of appearance.

[^12.3]: “Let us suppose ... the products ... of the manufacturer are doubled by improvement in machinery ... he will be able to clothe his workmen by means of a smaller proportion of the entire return ... and thus his profit will be raised. But in no other way will it be influenced.” (Ramsay, cited above, pp. 168, 169.)

<!-- ch12-p010 -->
We do not intend to consider here how the built-in laws of capitalist production show themselves in the movements of individual masses of capital.
