There they assert themselves as coercive laws of competition, and they are brought home to the mind and consciousness of the individual capitalist as the motives that direct his operations. But this much is clear: a scientific analysis of competition is not possible until we have a grasp of the inner nature of capital. In the same way, the apparent motions of the heavenly bodies can be understood only by someone who knows their real motions, which the senses cannot directly perceive. Nevertheless, to help understand the production of relative surplus-value better, we may add the following remarks, in which we assume nothing more than the results we have already reached.

<!-- ch12-p011 -->
If one hour's labor is embodied in sixpence, a value of six shillings will be produced in a working day of 12 hours. Suppose that, with the prevailing productivity of labor, 12 articles are produced in these 12 hours. Let the value of the means of production used up in each article be sixpence. Under these circumstances each article costs one shilling: sixpence for the value of the means of production, and sixpence for the value newly added in working with those means. Now let some one capitalist manage to double the productivity of labor, and to produce 24 such articles instead of 12 in the working day of 12 hours. If the value of the means of production stays the same, the value of each article will fall to ninepence: sixpence for the value of the means of production and threepence for the value newly added by the labor. Despite the doubled productivity of labor, the day's labor creates, as before, a new value of six shillings and no more, but this value is now spread over twice as many articles. Each article now has 1/24th of this value embodied in it instead of 1/12th, threepence instead of sixpence. Or, what comes to the same thing, only half an hour's labor-time, instead of a whole hour's, is now added to the means of production while they are being turned into each article. The individual value of these articles is now below their social value. In other words, they have cost less labor-time than the great bulk of the same article produced under the average social conditions. On average, each article costs one shilling and represents 2 hours of social labor; but under the changed mode of production it costs only ninepence, or contains only 1½ hours' labor. The real value of a commodity, however, is not its individual value but its social value. That is to say, its real value is measured not by the labor-time the article costs the producer in each individual case, but by the labor-time socially required to produce it. So if the capitalist who applies the new method sells his commodity at its social value of one shilling, he sells it for threepence above its individual value, and so realizes an extra surplus-value of threepence. On the other hand, for him the working day of 12 hours is now represented by 24 articles instead of 12. So, to get rid of the product of one working day, the demand must be double what it was, that is, the market must become twice as large. Other things being equal, his commodities can command a larger market only if their prices are lowered. (Price is the money name of the value, that is, of the labor, embodied in a commodity.) He will therefore sell them above their individual value but below their social value, say at tenpence each. In this way he still squeezes an extra surplus-value of one penny out of each. He pockets this increase in surplus-value whether or not his commodities belong to the class of necessary means of subsistence that help to determine the general value of labor-power. So, independently of this last circumstance, each individual capitalist has a motive to cheapen his commodities by increasing the productivity of labor.

<!-- ch12-p012 -->
Nevertheless, even in this case, the increased production of surplus-value arises from cutting the necessary labor-time and from the corresponding extension of the surplus labor.[^12.4] Let the necessary labor-time amount to 10 hours, the value of a day's labor-power to five shillings, the surplus labor-time to 2 hours, and the daily surplus-value to one shilling. But the capitalist now produces 24 articles, which he sells at tenpence apiece, making twenty shillings in all. Since the value of the means of production is twelve shillings, 14 2/5 of these articles merely replace the constant capital advanced. The labor of the 12 hours' working day is represented by the remaining 9 3/5 articles. Since the price of the labor-power is five shillings, 6 articles represent the necessary labor-time, and 3 3/5 articles the surplus labor. The ratio of the necessary labor to the surplus labor, which under average social conditions was 5:1, is now only 5:3. We can reach the same result in the following way. The value of the product of the working day of 12 hours is twenty shillings. Of this sum, twelve shillings belong to the value of the means of production, a value that merely reappears. That leaves eight shillings, which are the expression in money of the value newly created during the working day. This sum is greater than the sum that expresses average social labor of the same kind: twelve hours of that labor are expressed by only six shillings. The exceptionally productive labor acts as intensified labor; in equal periods of time it creates greater values than average social labor of the same kind. (See Ch. I. Sect 2. p. 44.) But our capitalist still goes on paying only five shillings, as before, as the value of a day's labor-power. So the worker now needs to work only 7½ hours instead of 10 to reproduce this value. His surplus labor is therefore increased by 2½ hours, and the surplus-value he produces grows from one shilling into three. So the capitalist who applies the improved method of production takes a greater part of the working day for surplus labor than the other capitalists in the same trade do. He does individually what the whole body of capitalists engaged in producing relative surplus-value do collectively. On the other hand, however, this extra surplus-value vanishes as soon as the new method of production has become general, and has thus made the difference between the individual value of the cheapened commodity and its social value vanish. The law that value is determined by labor-time brings the individual capitalist who applies the new method of production under its rule, by compelling him to sell his goods below their social value. This same law, acting as a coercive law of competition, forces his competitors to adopt the new method.[^12.5] So the general rate of surplus-value is ultimately affected by the whole process only when the increase in the productivity of labor has taken hold of the branches of production that are connected with the necessary means of subsistence, and has cheapened the commodities that form part of them and are therefore elements of the value of labor-power.

[^12.4]: “A man’s profit does not depend upon his command of the produce of other men’s labour, but upon his command of labour itself. If he can sell his goods at a higher price, while his workmen’s wages remain unaltered, he is clearly benefited.... A smaller proportion of what he produces is sufficient to put that labour into motion, and a larger proportion consequently remains for himself.” (“Outlines of Pol. Econ.” London, 1832, pp. 49, 50.)

[^12.5]: “If my neighbour by doing much with little labour, can sell cheap, I must contrive to sell as cheap as he. So that every art, trade, or engine, doing work with labour of fewer hands, and consequently cheaper, begets in others a kind of necessity and emulation, either of using the same art, trade, or engine, or of inventing something like it, that every man may be upon the square, that no man may be able to undersell his neighbour.” (“The Advantages of the East India Trade to England,” London, 1720, p. 67.)

<!-- ch12-p013 -->
The value of commodities is in inverse ratio to the productivity of labor. So too is the value of labor-power, because it depends on the values of commodities. Relative surplus-value, on the contrary, is directly proportional to that productivity. It rises when productivity rises and falls when productivity falls. Assuming the value of money to be constant, an average social working day of 12 hours always produces the same new value, six shillings, however this sum may be divided between surplus-value and wages. But suppose that increased productivity makes the value of the necessaries of life fall, and so reduces the value of a day's labor-power from five shillings to three. Then the surplus-value increases from one shilling to three. Ten hours were needed to reproduce the value of the labor-power; now only six are needed. Four hours have been set free, and can be annexed to the territory of surplus labor. So there is a built-in inclination and constant tendency in capital to raise the productivity of labor, in order to cheapen commodities, and by cheapening commodities to cheapen the worker himself.[^12.6]

[^12.6]: “In whatever proportion the expenses of a labourer are diminished, in the same proportion will his wages be diminished, if the restraints upon industry are at the same time taken off.” (“Considerations Concerning Taking off the Bounty on Corn Exported,” etc., London, 1753, p. 7.) “The interest of trade requires, that corn and all provisions should be as cheap as possible; for whatever makes them dear, must make labour dear also ... in all countries, where industry is not restrained, the price of provisions must affect the price of labour. This will always be diminished when the necessaries of life grow cheaper.” (cited above, p. 3.) “Wages are decreased in the same proportion as the powers of production increase. Machinery, it is true, cheapens the necessaries of life, but it also cheapens the labourer.” (“A Prize Essay on the Comparative Merits of Competition and Co-operation.” London, 1834, p. 27.)

<!-- ch12-p014 -->
The value of a commodity is, in itself, of no interest to the capitalist. What alone interests him is the surplus-value that lives in it and can be realized by sale. Realizing the surplus-value necessarily brings with it the refunding of the value that was advanced. Now, relative surplus-value increases in direct proportion to the development of the productivity of labor, while, on the other hand, the value of commodities falls in the same proportion. One and the same process cheapens commodities and increases the surplus-value contained in them. So here we have the solution of the riddle: why does the capitalist, whose sole concern is the production of exchange-value, constantly try to push down the exchange-value of commodities? (Exchange-value is the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for.) With this riddle Quesnay, one of the founders of political economy (the science of economics as it was then called), tormented his opponents, and they could give him no answer.

<!-- ch12-p015 -->
“You acknowledge,” he says, “that the more expenses and the cost of labour can, in the manufacture of industrial products, be reduced without injury to production, the more advantageous is such reduction, because it diminishes the price of the finished article. And yet, you believe that the production of wealth, which arises from the labour of the workpeople, consists in the augmentation of the exchange-value of their products.”[^12.7]

[^12.7]: “Ils conviennent que plus on peut, sans préjudice, épargner de frais ou de travaux dispendieux dans la fabrication des ouvrages des artisans, plus cette épargne est profitable par la diminution des prix de ces ouvrages. Cependant ils croient que la production de richesse qui résulte des travaux des artisans consiste dans l’augmentation de la valeur vénale de leurs ouvrages.” (Quesnay: “Dialogues sur le Commerce et les Travaux des Artisans.” pp. 188, 189.)

<!-- ch12-p016 -->
So the shortening of the working day is by no means the aim of capitalist production when labor is economized by increasing its productivity.[^12.8] The only aim is to shorten the labor-time needed to produce a definite quantity of commodities. When the productivity of his labor has been increased, the worker produces, say, 10 times as many commodities as before, and so spends one-tenth as much labor-time on each. This fact by no means prevents him from going on working 12 hours as before, or from producing 1,200 articles in those 12 hours instead of 120. Indeed, more than that, his working day may be lengthened at the same time, so that he produces, say, 1,400 articles in 14 hours. So in the treatises of economists of the type of MacCulloch, Ure, Senior, and *tutti quanti* [all the rest of them], we may read on one page that the worker owes capital a debt of gratitude for developing his productivity, because this shortens the necessary labor-time, and on the next page that he must prove his gratitude by working 15 hours in future instead of 10. Within the limits of capitalist production, the object of all development of the productivity of labor is to shorten the part of the working day in which the worker must labor for his own benefit, and, by that very shortening, to lengthen the other part of the day, in which he is at liberty to work for the capitalist free of charge. How far this result can also be reached without cheapening commodities will appear when we examine the particular methods of producing relative surplus-value. We now go on to that examination.

[^12.8]: “Ces spéculateurs si économes du travail des ouvriers qu’il faudrait qu’ils payassent.” [These speculators, so sparing with the labor of the workers they would have to pay] (J. N. Bidaut: “Du Monopole qui s’établit dans les arts industriels et le commerce.” Paris, 1828, p. 13.) “The employer will be always on the stretch to economise time and labour.” (Dugald Stewart: Works ed. by Sir W. Hamilton, Edinburgh, v., viii., 1855. “Lectures on Polit. Econ.,” p. 318.) “Their (the capitalists’) interest is that the productive powers of the labourers they employ should be the greatest possible. On promoting that power their attention is fixed and almost exclusively fixed.” (R. Jones: cited above, Lecture III.)

## Chapter 13: Cooperation

<!-- ch13-p001 -->
As we have already seen, capitalist production really begins only when each individual capital employs a comparatively large number of workers at the same time, and when, as a result, the labor process is carried on on a large scale and yields relatively large quantities of products. (Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger. The labor process is the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things.) A larger number of workers working together, at the same time, in one place (or, if you like, in the same field of labor), to produce the same sort of commodity under the mastery of one capitalist, is the starting-point of capitalist production, both historically and logically. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer’s own use.) As far as the mode of production itself is concerned, manufacture in the strict sense of the word can hardly be told apart, in its earliest stages, from the handicraft trades of the guilds, except by the greater number of workers employed at the same time by one and the same individual capital. (Manufacture is the stage and form of capitalist production, roughly from the mid-16th to the late 18th century, based on handicraft work divided among many workers in one workshop.) The workshop of the medieval master craftsman is simply made larger.

<!-- ch13-p002 -->
So at first the difference is purely quantitative. We have shown that the surplus-value produced by a given capital is equal to the surplus-value produced by each worker multiplied by the number of workers employed at the same time. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it. Labor-power is a person’s capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist.) The number of workers does not in itself affect either the rate of surplus-value or the degree of exploitation of labor-power. (The rate of surplus-value is the ratio of surplus-value to variable capital, that is, of surplus labor to necessary labor.) If a working day of 12 hours is embodied in six shillings, 1,200 such days will be embodied in 1,200 times 6 shillings. (The working day is the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor.) In one case 12 × 1,200 working hours are incorporated in the product, and in the other 12 such hours. In the production of value, a number of workers count merely as so many individual workers. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) So it makes no difference to the value produced whether the 1,200 men work separately or are united under the control of one capitalist.

<!-- ch13-p003 -->
Nevertheless, within certain limits, a change does take place. The labor realized in value is labor of an average social quality, and so it is the expenditure of average labor-power. Any average magnitude, however, is merely the average of a number of separate magnitudes, all of one kind but differing in quantity. In every industry, each individual worker, be he Peter or Paul, differs from the average worker. These individual differences, or “errors” as they are called in mathematics, cancel one another out and vanish whenever a certain minimum number of workers are employed together. The celebrated sophist and sycophant Edmund Burke goes so far as to make the following assertion, based on his practical observations as a farmer: namely, that “in so small a platoon” as that of five farm laborers, all individual differences in the labor vanish, and that therefore any five adult farm laborers taken together will do as much work in the same time as any other five.[^13.1] But however that may be, it is clear that the collective working day of a large number of workers employed at the same time, divided by the number of these workers, gives one day of average social labor. For example, let the working day of each individual be 12 hours. Then the collective working day of 12 men employed at the same time consists of 144 hours. The labor of each of the dozen men may deviate more or less from average social labor, each of them needing a different time for the same operation. Yet since the working day of each is one-twelfth of the collective working day of 144 hours, it has the qualities of an average social working day. From the point of view of the capitalist who employs these 12 men, however, the working day is that of the whole dozen. Each individual man’s day is an equal fraction of the collective working day. It makes no difference whether the 12 men help one another in their work, or whether the only connection between their operations is the fact that they are all working for the same capitalist. But if the 12 men are employed in six pairs, by as many different small employers, it will be quite a matter of chance whether each of these employers produces the same value, and so whether he realizes the general rate of surplus-value. Deviations would occur in individual cases. Suppose one worker needed considerably more time to produce a commodity than is socially necessary. Then in his case the length of the necessary labor-time would noticeably deviate from the labor-time socially necessary on average. (Socially necessary labor-time is the time needed to produce an article under the normal conditions of production of the day, with the average skill and intensity of labor.) So his labor would not count as average labor, nor his labor-power as average labor-power. It would either not be saleable at all, or only for something below the average value of labor-power, that is, below the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker (and to raise the next generation of workers) able to work. A fixed minimum of efficiency in all labor is therefore assumed, and we shall see later on that capitalist production provides the means of fixing this minimum. Nevertheless, this minimum deviates from the average, although on the other hand the capitalist has to pay the average value of labor-power. So of the six small employers, one would squeeze out more than the average rate of surplus-value, another less. The inequalities would balance out for society at large, but not for the individual employers. Thus the laws of the production of value are only fully realized for the individual producer when he produces as a capitalist and employs a number of workers together, whose labor, by its collective nature, is at once stamped as average social labor.[^13.2]

[^13.1]: “Unquestionably, there is a good deal of difference between the value of one man’s labour and that of another from strength, dexterity, and honest application. But I am quite sure, from my best observation, that any given five men will, in their total, afford a proportion of labour equal to any other five within the periods of life I have stated; that is, that among such five men there will be one possessing all the qualifications of a good workman, one bad, and the other three middling, and approximating to the first, and the last. So that in so small a platoon as that of even five, you will find the full complement of all that five men can earn.” (E. Burke, cited above, pp. 15, 16.) Compare Quételet on the average individual.

[^13.2]: Professor Roscher claims to have discovered that one needlewoman employed by Mrs. Roscher for two days does more work than two needlewomen employed together for one day. The learned professor should not study the capitalist process of production in the nursery, nor in circumstances where the principal character, the capitalist, is missing.

<!-- ch13-p004 -->
Even without any change in the method of working, employing a large number of workers at the same time brings about a revolution in the material conditions of the labor process. The buildings in which they work, the storehouses for the raw material, the implements and utensils used by the workers at the same time or in turns, in short, a portion of the means of production, are now consumed in common. (The means of production are the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things.) On the one hand, the exchange-value of these means of production is not increased, for the exchange-value of a commodity is not raised by its use-value being consumed more thoroughly and to greater advantage. (Exchange-value is the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for. Use-value is the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties.) On the other hand, they are used in common, and therefore on a larger scale than before. A room where twenty weavers work at twenty looms must be larger than the room of a single weaver with two assistants. But it costs less labor to build one workshop for twenty persons than to build ten workshops for two weavers each. So the value of the means of production that are concentrated for use in common on a large scale does not increase in direct proportion to their expansion and to their increased useful effect. When consumed in common, they give up a smaller part of their value to each single product. This is partly because the total value they part with is spread over a greater quantity of products. It is partly because their value, though greater in absolute terms, is relatively less than the value of isolated means of production, when we consider their sphere of action in the process. Because of this, the value of a part of the constant capital falls, and the total value of the commodity falls in proportion to the size of that fall. (Constant capital is the part of capital spent on means of production. Its value is passed on to the product but does not grow.) The effect is the same as if the means of production had cost less. The saving in their use is due entirely to their being consumed in common by a large number of workers. Moreover, they acquire this character of being necessary conditions of social labor even when the many workers gathered together do not help one another, but merely work side by side. It is a character that distinguishes them from the scattered and relatively more costly means of production of isolated, independent workers, or of small employers. A portion of the instruments of labor acquires this social character before the labor process itself does.

<!-- ch13-p005 -->
Saving in the use of the means of production has to be looked at from two sides. First, as cheapening commodities, and thereby bringing about a fall in the value of labor-power. Second, as changing the ratio of the surplus-value to the total capital advanced, that is, to the sum of the values of the constant and variable capital. (Variable capital is the part of capital spent on labor-power. It reproduces its own value and also produces surplus-value, so its size varies.) The second side will not be considered until we come to the third book. To that book we also put off many other points relating to the present question, so as to treat them in their proper connection. The course of our analysis forces us to split up the subject-matter in this way, and this splitting up is quite in keeping with the spirit of capitalist production. For in this mode of production the worker finds the instruments of labor existing independently of him, as another man’s property. So, as far as he is concerned, saving in their use appears to be a separate operation, one that does not concern him, and which therefore has no connection with the methods by which his own personal productivity is increased.

<!-- ch13-p006 -->
When many workers work together side by side, whether in one and the same process, or in different but connected processes, they are said to cooperate, or to work in cooperation.[^13.3]

[^13.3]: “Concours de forces.” [Combination of forces] (Destutt de Tracy, cited above, p. 80.)

<!-- ch13-p007 -->
The attacking power of a squadron of cavalry, or the defensive power of a regiment of infantry, is essentially different from the sum of the attacking or defensive powers of the individual cavalry or infantry soldiers taken separately. In just the same way, the sum total of the mechanical forces exerted by isolated workers differs from the social force that is developed when many hands take part at the same time in one and the same undivided operation, such as raising a heavy weight, turning a winch, or removing an obstacle.[^13.4] In such cases the effect of the combined labor either could not be produced at all by isolated individual labor, or could be produced only by a great expenditure of time, or only on a very stunted scale. Here we have not only an increase, by means of cooperation, in the productive power of the individual, but the creation of a new power, namely, the collective power of masses.[^13.5]

[^13.4]: “There are numerous operations of so simple a kind as not to admit a division into parts, which cannot be performed without the co-operation of many pairs of hands. I would instance the lifting of a large tree on to a wain [wagon] ... everything, in short, which cannot be done unless a great many pairs of hands help each other in the same undivided employment and at the same time.” (E. G. Wakefield: “A View of the Art of Colonisation.” London, 1849, p. 168.)

[^13.5]: “As one man cannot, and ten men must strain to lift a ton of weight, yet 100 men can do it only by the strength of a finger of each of them.” (John Betters: “Proposals for Raising a Colledge of Industry.” London, 1696, p. 21.)

<!-- ch13-p008 -->
Apart from the new power that arises from the fusion of many forces into one single force, in most industries mere social contact gives rise to rivalry and a stirring of the animal spirits that raise the efficiency of each individual worker. That is why a dozen persons working together will, in their collective working day of 144 hours, produce far more than twelve isolated men each working 12 hours, or than one man who works twelve days in a row.[^13.6] The reason for this is that man is, if not a political animal,[^13.7] as Aristotle contends, at any rate a social animal.

[^13.6]: “There is also” (when the same number of men are employed by one farmer on 300 acres, instead of by ten farmers with 30 acres a piece) “an advantage in the proportion of servants, which will not so easily be understood but by practical men; for it is natural to say, as 1 is to 4, so are 3 to 12; but this will not hold good in practice; for in harvest time and many other operations which require that kind of despatch by the throwing many hands together, the work is better and more expeditiously done: f i. [for instance] in harvest, 2 drivers, 2 loaders, 2 pitchers, 2 rakers, and the rest at the rick [haystack], or in the barn, will despatch double the work that the same number of hands would do if divided into different gangs on different farms.” (“An Inquiry into the Connexion between the Present Price of Provisions and the Size of Farms.” By a Farmer. London, 1773, pp. 7, 8.)

[^13.7]: Strictly, Aristotle’s definition is that man is by nature a town-citizen. This is quite as characteristic of ancient classical society as Franklin’s definition of man as a tool-making animal is characteristic of Yankeedom.

<!-- ch13-p009 -->
A number of men may be occupied together at the same time on the same work, or the same kind of work. Yet the labor of each, as a part of the collective labor, may correspond to a distinct phase of the labor process. Because of cooperation, the object of their labor passes more quickly through all these phases. For instance, suppose a dozen masons place themselves in a row, so as to pass stones from the foot of a ladder to its top. Each of them does the same thing. Nevertheless, their separate acts form connected parts of one total operation. They are particular phases that each stone must go through, and so the stones are carried up more quickly by the 24 hands of the row of men than they could be if each man went up and down the ladder separately with his load.[^13.8] The object is carried over the same distance in a shorter time. Again, labor is combined whenever a building, for instance, is worked on from different sides at the same time, although here too the cooperating masons are doing the same work, or the same kind of work. The 12 masons, in their collective working day of 144 hours, make much more progress with the building than one mason could make working for 12 days, or 144 hours. The reason is that a body of men working in concert has hands and eyes both in front and behind, and is, to a certain degree, everywhere at once. The various parts of the work progress at the same time.

[^13.8]: “On doit encore remarquer que cette division partielle de travail peut se faire quand même les ouvriers sont occupés d’une même besogne. Des maçons par exemple, occupés à faire passer de mains en mains des briques à un échafaudage supérieur, font tous la même besogne, et pourtant il existe parmi eux une espèce de division de travail, qui consiste en ce que chacun d’eux fait passer la brique par un espace donné, et que tous ensemble la font parvenir beaucoup plus promptement à l’endroit marqué qu’ils ne le feraient si chacun d’eux portait sa brique séparément jusqu’à l’échafaudage supérieur.” [It should also be noted that this partial division of labor can happen even when the workers are busy with one and the same task. Masons, for example, who are busy passing bricks from hand to hand up to a higher scaffold, are all doing the same task, and yet there is a kind of division of labor among them. It consists in this: each of them passes the brick through a given space, and all of them together make it reach the marked spot much more quickly than they would if each of them carried his brick separately up to the higher scaffold.] (F. Skarbek: “Théorie des richesses sociales.” Paris, 1839, t. I, pp. 97, 98.)

<!-- ch13-p010 -->
In the examples above we have stressed that the men do the same work, or the same kind of work. We did so because this, the simplest form of labor in common, plays a great part in cooperation, even in its most fully developed stage. If the work is complicated, then the mere number of men who cooperate allows the various operations to be shared out among different workers, and so to be carried on at the same time. The time needed to complete the whole work is shortened in this way.[^13.9]

[^13.9]: “Est-il question d’exécuter un travail compliqué, plusieurs choses doivent être faites simultanément. L’un en fait une pendant que l’autre en fait une autre, et tous contribuent à l’effet qu’un seul homme n’aurait pu produire. L’un rame pendant que l’autre tient le gouvernail, et qu’un troisième jette le filet on harponne le poisson, et la pêche a un succès impossible sans ce concours.” [Is it a matter of carrying out a complicated piece of work? Then several things must be done at the same time. One person does one thing while another does something else, and they all contribute to an effect that a single man could not have produced. One rows while another holds the rudder, and a third casts the net or harpoons the fish, and the fishing has a success that would be impossible without this combined effort.] (Destutt de Tracy, cited above.)

<!-- ch13-p011 -->
In many industries there are critical periods, set by the nature of the process, during which certain definite results must be obtained. For instance, if a flock of sheep has to be shorn, or a field of wheat cut and harvested, the quantity and quality of the product depend on the work being begun and finished within a certain time. In these cases the time the process ought to take is fixed in advance, just as it is in herring fishing. A single person cannot carve a working day of more than, say, 12 hours out of the natural day, but 100 men cooperating extend the working day to 1,200 hours. The shortness of the time allowed for the work is made up for by the large mass of labor thrown onto the field of production at the decisive moment. Finishing the task in the proper time depends on applying many combined working days at the same time. The amount of useful effect depends on the number of workers. This number, however, is always smaller than the number of isolated workers needed to do the same amount of work in the same period.[^13.10] It is because this kind of cooperation is missing that every year quantities of grain are wasted in the western part of the United States, and quantities of cotton in those parts of East India where English rule has destroyed the old communities.[^13.11]

[^13.10]: “The doing of it (agricultural work) at the critical juncture is of so much the greater consequence.” (“An Inquiry into the Connexion between the Present Price,” etc., p. 9.) “In agriculture, there is no more important factor than that of time.” (Liebig: “Ueber Theorie und Praxis in der Landwirtschaft.” 1856, p. 23.)

[^13.11]: “The next evil is one which one would scarcely expect to find in a country which exports more labour than any other in the world, with the exception, perhaps, of China and England ‒ the impossibility of procuring a sufficient number of hands to clean the cotton. The consequence of this is that large quantities of the crop are left unpicked, while another portion is gathered from the ground when it has fallen, and is of course discoloured and partially rotted, so that for want of labour at the proper season the cultivator is actually forced to submit to the loss of a large part of that crop for which England is so anxiously looking.” (“Bengal Hurkaru.” Bi-Monthly Overland Summary of News, 22nd July, 1861.)

<!-- ch13-p012 -->
On the one hand, cooperation allows the work to be carried on over a wide area. So it is absolutely required in certain undertakings, such as draining land, building dikes, irrigation works, and making canals, roads, and railways. On the other hand, while it extends the scale of production, it makes possible a relative shrinking of the area in which production takes place. This shrinking of the area happens at the same time as the extension of scale, and arises from it, and it cuts out a number of useless expenses. It is due to the gathering together of workers, to the bringing together of various processes, and to the concentration of the means of production.[^13.12]

[^13.12]: As cultivation progresses, “all, and perhaps more than all, the capital and labour which once loosely occupied 500 acres, are now concentrated for the more complete tillage of 100.” Although “relatively to the amount of capital and labour employed, space is concentrated, it is an enlarged sphere of production, as compared to the sphere of production formerly occupied or worked upon by one single independent agent of production.” (R. Jones: “An Essay on the Distribution of Wealth,” part I. On Rent. London, 1831. p. 191.)

<!-- ch13-p013 -->
Compared with an equal sum of isolated working days, the combined working day produces a greater quantity of use-values, and so it reduces the labor-time needed to produce a given useful effect. In a given case, the combined working day may gain this increased productive power for any of several reasons. It may raise the mechanical force of labor. It may extend labor's sphere of action over a greater space. It may shrink the field of production relative to the scale of production. It may set large masses of labor to work at the critical moment. It may stir up rivalry between individuals and raise their animal spirits. It may stamp the similar operations carried on by a number of people with continuity and many-sidedness. It may carry out different operations at the same time. It may save on means of production by using them in common. Or it may give individual labor the character of average social labor. Whichever of these is the cause of the increase, the special productive power of the combined working day is, under all circumstances, the social productive power of labor, or the productive power of social labor. This power comes from cooperation itself. When the worker cooperates with others in a planned way, he strips off the chains of his individuality and develops the capabilities of his species.[^13.13]

[^13.13]: “La forza di ciascuno uomo è minima, ma la riunione delle minime forze forma una forza totale maggiore anche della somma delle forze medesime fino a che le forze per essere riunite possono diminuere il tempo ed accrescere lo spazio della loro azione.” [“The strength of each man is very small, but the union of very small strengths forms a total strength greater even than the sum of those same strengths, to the point that the strengths, by being united, can reduce the time and enlarge the space of their action.”] (G. R. Carli, Note to P. Verri, cited above, t. xv., p. 196.)

<!-- ch13-p014 -->
As a general rule, workers cannot cooperate without being brought together: being gathered in one place is a necessary condition of their cooperation. So wage workers cannot cooperate unless the same capital, the same capitalist, employs them at the same time, and therefore unless he buys their labor-powers at the same time. The total value of these labor-powers, or the amount of these workers' wages for a day or a week, as the case may be, must be ready in the capitalist's pocket before the workers are assembled for the process of production. (Wages are the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself.) Paying 300 workers at once, even for only one day, requires a greater outlay of capital than paying a smaller number of men, week by week, for a whole year. So the number of workers who cooperate, or the scale of cooperation, depends in the first place on the amount of capital that the individual capitalist can spare for buying labor-power. In other words, it depends on how far a single capitalist has command over the means of subsistence of a number of workers, that is, over the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities they need to live.

<!-- ch13-p015 -->
And what holds for the variable capital holds for the constant capital too. For example, the capitalist who employs 300 men spends 30 times as much on raw material as each of 30 capitalists who employ 10 men each. It is true that the value and quantity of the instruments of labor used in common do not increase at the same rate as the number of workers, but they do increase very considerably. So the concentration of large masses of the means of production in the hands of individual capitalists is a material condition for the cooperation of wage workers. And the extent of the cooperation, or the scale of production, depends on the extent of this concentration.

<!-- ch13-p016 -->
We saw in an earlier chapter that a certain minimum amount of capital was necessary so that the number of workers employed at the same time, and so the amount of surplus-value produced, might be large enough to free the employer himself from manual labor, to turn him from a small employer into a capitalist, and in this way formally to establish capitalist production. We now see that a certain minimum amount is a necessary condition for turning numerous isolated and independent processes into one combined social process.

<!-- ch13-p017 -->
We also saw that at first, the subjection of labor to capital was only a formal result of the fact that the worker works for the capitalist, and so under him, instead of working for himself. Through the cooperation of numerous wage workers, the rule of capital develops into a requirement for carrying on the labor process itself, into a real requirement of production. It is now as indispensable for a capitalist to command on the field of production as it is for a general to command on the field of battle.

<!-- ch13-p018 -->
All combined labor on a large scale needs, more or less, a directing authority, to secure the harmonious working of the individual activities and to perform the general functions that arise from the action of the combined organism as a whole, as distinct from the action of its separate organs. A single violin player is his own conductor; an orchestra needs a separate one. The work of directing, supervising, and adjusting becomes one of the functions of capital from the moment that the labor under capital's control becomes cooperative. Once it is a function of capital, it takes on special characteristics.

<!-- ch13-p019 -->
The driving motive, the end and aim of capitalist production, is to extract the greatest possible amount of surplus-value,[^13.14] and so to exploit labor-power to the greatest possible extent. As the number of cooperating workers grows, so does their resistance to the rule of capital, and with it the need for capital to overcome this resistance by pressing back. The control the capitalist exercises is not only a special function that arises from the nature of the social labor process and is specific to that process. It is at the same time a function of exploiting a social labor process. So it is rooted in the unavoidable antagonism between the exploiter and the living and laboring raw material he exploits.

[^13.14]: “Profits ... is the sole end of trade.” (J. Vanderlint, cited above, p. 11.)

<!-- ch13-p020 -->
Again, as the mass of the means of production grows, means that now belong no longer to the worker but to the capitalist, so does the need for some effective control over their proper use.[^13.15] Moreover, the cooperation of wage workers is brought about entirely by the capital that employs them. Their union into one single productive body, and the linking of their individual functions, are things foreign and external to them. They are not the workers' own act, but the act of the capital that brings them together and keeps them together. So the connection between their various kinds of labor appears to them, in idea, as a plan drawn up in advance by the capitalist. In practice it appears to them as the authority of that same capitalist, as the powerful will of another, who subjects their activity to his aims. The process of production itself has a two-fold nature: on the one hand, it is a social process for producing use-values; on the other, it is a process for creating surplus-value. If, then, the capitalist's control is two-fold in substance because of this, in form that control is despotic. As cooperation extends its scale, this despotism takes on forms of its own. At first the capitalist is freed from actual labor as soon as his capital has reached the minimum amount with which capitalist production as such begins. In the same way, he now hands over the work of direct and constant supervision of individual workers and groups of workers to a special kind of wage worker. An industrial army of workers under the command of a capitalist needs, like a real army, officers (managers) and sergeants (foremen, overseers), who command in the capitalist's name while the work is being done. The work of supervision becomes their established and exclusive function. When the political economist compares the mode of production of isolated peasants and craftsmen with production by slave labor, he counts this labor of supervision among the overhead costs of production.[^13.16] But when he considers the capitalist mode of production, he does the opposite. He treats the work of control that the cooperative character of the labor process makes necessary as identical with the different work of control that the capitalist character of that process, and the antagonism of interests between capitalist and worker, make necessary.[^13.17] A man is not a capitalist because he is a leader of industry; on the contrary, he is a leader of industry because he is a capitalist. The leadership of industry is an attribute of capital, just as in feudal times the functions of general and judge were attributes of landed property.[^13.18]

[^13.15]: That Philistine paper, the *Spectator*, states that after a sort of partnership between capitalist and workers was introduced in the “Wirework Company of Manchester,” “the first result was a sudden decrease in waste, the men not seeing why they should waste their own property any more than any other master’s, and waste is, perhaps, next to bad debts, the greatest source of manufacturing loss.” The same paper finds that the main defect in the Rochdale cooperative experiments is this: “They showed that associations of workmen could manage shops, mills, and almost all forms of industry with success, and they immediately improved the condition of the men; but then they did not leave a clear place for masters.” Quelle horreur! [How horrible!]

[^13.16]: Professor Cairnes first states that the supervision of labor is a leading feature of production by slaves in the Southern States of North America. He then continues: “The peasant proprietor (of the North), appropriating the whole produce of his toil, needs no other stimulus to exertion. Superintendence is here completely dispensed with.” (Cairnes, cited above, pp. 48, 49.)

[^13.17]: Sir James Steuart, a writer altogether remarkable for his quick eye for the typical social differences between different modes of production, says: “Why do large undertakings in the manufacturing way ruin private industry, but by coming nearer to the simplicity of slaves?” (“Prin. of Pol. Econ.,” London, 1767, v. I., pp. 167, 168.)

[^13.18]: So Auguste Comte and his school might have shown that feudal lords are an eternal necessity, in the same way that they have done for the lords of capital.

<!-- ch13-p021 -->
The worker owns his labor-power until he has finished bargaining over its sale with the capitalist. And he can sell no more than what he has, that is, his individual, isolated labor-power. This state of things is in no way changed by the fact that the capitalist buys the labor-power of 100 men instead of one, and makes separate contracts with 100 unconnected men instead of with one. He is free to set the 100 men to work without letting them cooperate. He pays them the value of 100 independent labor-powers, but he does not pay for the combined labor-power of the hundred. Since they are independent of each other, the workers are isolated persons, who enter into relations with the capitalist, but not with one another. Their cooperation begins only with the labor process, but by then they have ceased to belong to themselves. On entering that process, they become part of capital. As cooperators, as members of a working organism, they are merely particular forms in which capital exists. So the productive power the worker develops when working in cooperation is the productive power of capital. This power is developed free of charge whenever the workers are placed under certain conditions, and it is capital that places them under those conditions. This power costs capital nothing. On the other hand, the worker himself does not develop it before his labor belongs to capital. For both reasons, it appears as a power with which Nature has endowed capital ‒ a productive power built into capital.

<!-- ch13-p022 -->
The colossal effects of simple cooperation can be seen in the gigantic structures of the ancient Asian peoples, the Egyptians, the Etruscans, etc.

<!-- ch13-p023 -->
> “It has happened in times past that these Oriental States, after supplying the expenses of their civil and military establishments, have found themselves in possession of a surplus which they could apply to works of magnificence or utility. And in the construction of these, their command over the hands and arms of almost the entire non-agricultural population has produced stupendous monuments which still indicate their power. The teeming valley of the Nile ... produced food for a swarming non-agricultural population, and this food, belonging to the monarch and the priesthood, afforded the means of erecting the mighty monuments which filled the land.... In moving the colossal statues and vast masses of which the transport creates wonder, human labour almost alone, was prodigally [lavishly] used.... The number of the labourers and the concentration of their efforts sufficed. We see mighty coral reefs rising from the depths of the ocean into islands and firm land, yet each individual depositor is puny, weak, and contemptible. The non-agricultural labourers of an Asiatic monarchy have little but their individual bodily exertions to bring to the task, but their number is their strength, and the power of directing these masses gave rise to the palaces and temples, the pyramids, and the armies of gigantic statues of which the remains astonish and perplex us. It is that confinement of the revenues which feed them, to one or a few hands, which makes such undertakings possible.”[^13.19]

[^13.19]: R. Jones. “Textbook of Lectures,” etc., pp. 77, 78. The ancient Assyrian, Egyptian, and other collections in London and in other European capitals make us eye-witnesses of the ways that cooperative labor was carried on.

<!-- ch13-p024 -->
In modern society, this power of the Asiatic and Egyptian kings, the Etruscan priest-rulers, etc., has been transferred to the capitalist, whether he is an isolated capitalist or, as in joint-stock companies, a collective one.

<!-- ch13-p025 -->
Cooperation as we find it at the dawn of human development, among peoples who live by hunting,[^13.20] or, say, in the agriculture of Indian communities, rests on two things. On the one hand, it rests on common ownership of the means of production. On the other hand, it rests on the fact that in those cases each individual has no more torn himself loose from the umbilical cord of his tribe or community than each bee has freed itself from its connection with the hive. Both of these features distinguish such cooperation from capitalist cooperation. The occasional use of cooperation on a large scale in ancient times, in the middle ages, and in modern colonies rests on relations of domination and servitude, mainly on slavery. The capitalist form, on the contrary, presupposes from first to last the free wage worker, who sells his labor-power to capital. Historically, however, this form develops in opposition to peasant agriculture and to the carrying on of independent handicrafts, whether in guilds or not.[^13.21] From the standpoint of these, capitalist cooperation does not show itself as one particular historical form of cooperation. Instead, cooperation itself appears to be a historical form peculiar to the capitalist process of production, one that specifically distinguishes it.

[^13.20]: Linguet is improbably right when, in his “Théorie des Lois Civiles”, he declares hunting to be the first form of cooperation, and man-hunting (war) one of the earliest forms of hunting.

[^13.21]: Small-scale peasant agriculture and the carrying on of independent handicrafts together form the basis of the feudal mode of production, and after that system dissolves, they continue side by side with the capitalist mode. They also form the economic foundation of the classical communities at their best, after the primitive form of common ownership of land had disappeared, and before slavery had seized on production in earnest.

<!-- ch13-p026 -->
The social productive power of labor that cooperation develops appears to be the productive power of capital. In just the same way, cooperation itself, contrasted with the process of production carried on by isolated independent workers, or even by small employers, appears to be a specific form of the capitalist process of production. It is the first change that the actual labor process undergoes when it is subjected to capital. This change takes place spontaneously. Its necessary condition, the employment of a large number of wage workers at the same time in one and the same process, is also the starting-point of capitalist production. This point coincides with the birth of capital itself. So if, on the one hand, the capitalist mode of production presents itself to us historically as a necessary condition for turning the labor process into a social process, then, on the other hand, this social form of the labor process presents itself as a method capital uses to exploit labor more profitably, by increasing that labor's productivity.

<!-- ch13-p027 -->
In the elementary form in which we have looked at it so far, cooperation necessarily goes hand in hand with all production on a large scale. But in itself it does not represent a fixed form typical of a particular epoch in the development of the capitalist mode of production. At most it appears to do so, and then only roughly, in the handicraft-like beginnings of manufacture,[^13.22] and in the kind of large-scale agriculture that corresponds to the epoch of manufacture. That agriculture differs from peasant agriculture mainly in the number of workers employed at the same time and in the mass of means of production concentrated for their use. Simple cooperation is always the prevailing form in those branches of production in which capital operates on a large scale and division of labor and machinery play only a minor part.

[^13.22]: “Whether the united skill, industry, and emulation of many together on the same work be not the way to advance it? And whether it had been otherwise possible for England, to have carried on her Woollen Manufacture to so great a perfection?” (Berkeley. “The Querist.” London, 1751, p. 56, par. 521.)

<!-- ch13-p028 -->
Cooperation always remains the fundamental form of the capitalist mode of production. Nevertheless, the elementary form of cooperation continues to exist as a particular form of capitalist production, side by side with the more developed forms of that mode of production.

## Chapter 14: Division of Labor and Manufacture

### Section 1: Two-Fold Origin of Manufacture

<!-- ch14-p001 -->
The kind of cooperation that is based on division of labor takes its typical form in manufacture. (Cooperation means many workers working together, side by side, in the same or connected processes, under one capitalist's command. Division of labor, here, means the splitting of the making of one product into many separate tasks, each done by a specialized worker. Manufacture means the stage and form of capitalist production based on handicraft work divided among many workers in one workshop.) Throughout the manufacturing period properly so called, this cooperation is the prevailing, characteristic form of the capitalist process of production. That period, roughly speaking, runs from the middle of the 16th to the last third of the 18th century.

<!-- ch14-p002 -->
Manufacture arises in two ways:

<!-- ch14-p003 -->
(1.) By bringing together, in one workshop under the control of a single capitalist, workers who belong to various independent handicrafts, but through whose hands a given article must pass on its way to completion. A carriage, for example, used to be the product of the labor of a great number of independent craftsmen, such as wheelwrights, harness-makers, tailors, locksmiths, upholsterers, turners, fringe-makers, glaziers, painters, polishers, gilders, etc. In the manufacture of carriages, however, all these different craftsmen are brought together in one building, where they work into one another's hands. It is true that a carriage cannot be gilded before it has been made. But if a number of carriages are being made at the same time, some may be in the hands of the gilders while others are going through an earlier process. So far, we are still in the domain of simple cooperation, which finds its materials ready to hand in the shape of men and things. But very soon an important change takes place. The tailor, the locksmith, and the other craftsmen are now occupied only in carriage-making, and each of them gradually loses, through lack of practice, the ability to carry on his old handicraft to its full extent. But, on the other hand, his activity, now confined to one groove, takes the form best suited to its narrowed sphere of action. At first, carriage manufacture is a combination of various independent handicrafts. Little by little, it becomes the splitting up of carriage-making into its various detail processes. Each of these processes crystallizes into the exclusive function of a particular worker, while the manufacture as a whole is carried on by these men together. In the same way, cloth manufacture, and a whole series of other branches of manufacture too, arose by combining different handicrafts under the control of a single capitalist.[^14.1]

[^14.1]: To give a more modern example: The silk spinning and weaving of Lyon and Nîmes “est toute patriarcale; elle emploie beaucoup de femmes et d’enfants, mais sans les épuiser ni les corrompre; elle les laisse dans leur belles valises de la Drôme, du Var, de l’Isère, de Vaucluse, pour y élever des vers et dévider leurs cocons; jamais elle n’entre dans une véritable fabrique. Pour être aussi bien observé ... le principe de la division du travail s’y revêt d’un caractère spécial. Il y a bien des dévideuses, des moulineurs, des teinturiers, des encolleurs, puis des tisserands; mais ils ne sont pas réunis dans un même établissement, ne dépendent pas d’un même maître, tous ils sont indépendants” [... is entirely patriarchal. It employs many women and children, but without exhausting or corrupting them. It leaves them in their beautiful valleys of the Drôme, the Var, the Isère, the Vaucluse, to raise silkworms there and unwind their cocoons. It never enters a real factory. Though it is observed just as well ... the principle of the division of labor takes on a special character here. There are indeed winders, throwsters (silk twisters), dyers, sizers (yarn stiffeners), and then weavers; but they are not brought together in the same establishment, and they do not depend on the same master; they are all independent] (A. Blanqui: “Cours, d’Econ. Industrielle.” Recueilli par A. Blaise. Paris, 1838-39, p. 79.) Since Blanqui wrote this, the various independent workers have, to some extent, been united in factories. [And since Marx wrote the above, the power-loom has invaded these factories, and now, in 1886, it is rapidly replacing the hand-loom. (*Added in the 4th German edition*. The Krefeld silk industry also has its own tale to tell about this.) F. E.]

<!-- ch14-p004 -->
(2.) Manufacture also arises in a way that is exactly the reverse of this ‒ namely, when one capitalist employs at the same time, in one workshop, a number of craftsmen who all do the same work, or the same kind of work, such as making paper, type, or needles. This is cooperation in its most elementary form. Each of these craftsmen (with the help, perhaps, of one or two apprentices) makes the entire commodity, and so he performs, one after another, all the operations needed to produce it. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, that is, sold, not for the producer's own use.) He still works in his old handicraft way. But very soon external circumstances cause a different use to be made of the concentration of the workers on one spot, and of the fact that they work at the same time. Perhaps an increased quantity of the article has to be delivered within a given time. The work is therefore redistributed. Instead of each man being allowed to perform all the various operations one after another, these operations are changed into disconnected, isolated ones, carried on side by side. Each is assigned to a different craftsman, and all of them together are performed at the same time by the cooperating workers. This chance division of the work gets repeated, develops advantages of its own, and gradually hardens into a systematic division of labor. The commodity, from being the individual product of an independent craftsman, becomes the social product of a union of craftsmen, each of whom performs one, and only one, of the partial operations that make it up. In the case of a papermaker belonging to a German Guild, certain operations merged one into the other as the successive acts of one craftsman. In the Dutch paper manufacture, the same operations became so many partial operations carried on side by side by numerous cooperating workers. The needlemaker of the Nuremberg Guild was the cornerstone on which the English needle manufacture was built. But in Nuremberg that single craftsman performed a series of perhaps 20 operations one after another, while in England it was not long before there were 20 needlemakers side by side, each performing just one of those 20 operations. And as a result of further experience, each of those 20 operations was split up again, isolated, and made the exclusive function of a separate worker.

<!-- ch14-p005 -->
So the way in which manufacture arises, its growth out of handicrafts, is two-fold. On the one hand, it arises from the union of various independent handicrafts. These are stripped of their independence and specialized to such an extent that they are reduced to mere supplementary partial processes in the production of one particular commodity. On the other hand, it arises from the cooperation of craftsmen of one handicraft. It splits that particular handicraft up into its various detail operations, isolating them and making them independent of one another, up to the point where each becomes the exclusive function of a particular worker. On the one hand, therefore, manufacture either introduces division of labor into a process of production, or develops that division further; on the other hand, it unites handicrafts that were formerly separate. But whatever its particular starting-point may have been, its final form is always the same ‒ a productive mechanism whose parts are human beings.

<!-- ch14-p006 -->
To understand the division of labor in manufacture properly, it is essential to grasp the following points firmly. First, here the breaking down of a process of production into its various successive steps coincides strictly with the breaking down of a handicraft into its successive manual operations. Whether complex or simple, each operation has to be done by hand. It keeps the character of a handicraft, and so it depends on the strength, skill, quickness, and sureness of the individual worker in handling his tools. The handicraft remains the basis. This narrow technical basis rules out a really scientific analysis of any definite process of industrial production, since it is still a condition that each detail process the product goes through must be capable of being done by hand and of forming, in its way, a separate handicraft. It is just because handicraft skill remains, in this way, the foundation of the process of production, that each worker is assigned exclusively to a partial function, and that for the rest of his life his labor-power is turned into the organ of this detail function. (Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist.)

<!-- ch14-p007 -->
Secondly, this division of labor is a particular sort of cooperation, and many of its disadvantages spring from the general character of cooperation, and not from this particular form of it.

### Section 2: The Detail Laborer and his Implements

<!-- ch14-p008 -->
If we now look more closely at the details, it is clear, in the first place, that a worker who performs one and the same simple operation all his life turns his whole body into the automatic, specialized tool of that operation. As a result, he takes less time to do it than the craftsman who performs a whole series of operations one after another. But the collective worker, who makes up the living mechanism of manufacture, consists solely of such specialized detail workers. Hence, compared with independent handicraft, more is produced in a given time, or the productive power of labor is increased.[^14.2] Moreover, once this fractional work has been established as the exclusive function of one person, the methods it uses become perfected. The worker’s constant repetition of the same simple act, and the concentration of his attention on it, teach him by experience how to get the desired result with the least possible effort. But since there are always several generations of workers living at the same time and working together at making a given article, the technical skill and the tricks of the trade acquired in this way become established, and are accumulated and handed down.[^14.3]

[^14.2]: “The more any manufacture of much variety shall be distributed and assigned to different artists [craftsmen], the same must needs be better done and with greater expedition, with less loss of time and labour.” (“The Advantages of the East India Trade,” London, 1720, p. 71.)

[^14.3]: “Easy labour is transmitted skill.” (Th. Hodgskin, “Popular Political Economy,” p. 48.)

<!-- ch14-p009 -->
In fact, manufacture produces the skill of the detail worker. It does so by reproducing within the workshop the naturally developed differentiation of trades that it found ready to hand in society at large, and by systematically driving that differentiation to an extreme. On the other hand, turning fractional work into one man’s lifelong calling corresponds to the tendency shown by earlier societies to make trades hereditary: either to petrify them into castes, or, whenever definite historical conditions produced in the individual a tendency to vary in a way that did not fit the nature of castes, to harden them into guilds. Castes and guilds arise from the action of the same natural law that governs the differentiation of plants and animals into species and varieties. The only difference is that, once a certain degree of development has been reached, the heredity of castes and the exclusiveness of guilds are decreed as a law of society.[^14.4]

[^14.4]: “The arts also have ... in Egypt reached the requisite degree of perfection. For it is the only country where artificers [craftsmen] may not in any way meddle with the affairs of another class of citizens, but must follow that calling alone which by law is hereditary in their clan.... In other countries it is found that tradesmen divide their attention between too many objects. At one time they try agriculture, at another they take to commerce, at another they busy themselves with two or three occupations at once. In free countries, they mostly frequent the assemblies of the people.... In Egypt, on the contrary, every artificer is severely punished if he meddles with affairs of State, or carries on several trades at once. Thus there is nothing to disturb their application to their calling.... Moreover, since they inherit from their forefathers numerous rules, they are eager to discover fresh advantages” (Diodorus Siculus: Bibl. Hist. I. 1. c., 74.)

<!-- ch14-p010 -->
> “The muslins of Dakka in fineness, the calicoes and other piece goods of Coromandel in brilliant and durable colours, have never been surpassed. Yet they are produced without capital, machinery, division of labour, or any of those means which give such facilities to the manufacturing interest of Europe. The weaver is merely a detached individual, working a web when ordered of a customer, and with a loom of the rudest construction, consisting sometimes of a few branches or bars of wood, put roughly together. There is even no expedient for rolling up the warp [the lengthwise threads of the cloth]; the loom must therefore be kept stretched to its full length, and becomes so inconveniently large that it cannot be contained within the hut of the manufacturer, who is therefore compelled to ply his trade in the open air, where it is interrupted by every vicissitude [change] of the weather.”[^14.5]

[^14.5]: “Historical and descriptive account of Brit. India, &c.,” by Hugh Murray and James Wilson, etc., Edinburgh 1832, v. II., p. 449. The Indian loom is upright, that is, the warp is stretched vertically.

<!-- ch14-p011 -->
It is only the special skill accumulated from generation to generation, and passed down from father to son, that gives the Hindu this proficiency, as it gives it to the spider. And yet the work of such a Hindu weaver is very complicated compared with that of a worker in manufacture.

<!-- ch14-p012 -->
A craftsman who performs, one after another, the various fractional operations involved in producing a finished article must sometimes change his place and sometimes his tools. Passing from one operation to another interrupts the flow of his labor and creates, so to speak, gaps in his working day. These gaps close up as soon as he is tied to one and the same operation all day long; they vanish in proportion as the changes in his work decrease. The resulting increase in productive power is due either to more labor-power being spent in a given time, that is, to increased intensity of labor, or to a decrease in the amount of labor-power consumed unproductively. Every transition from rest to motion demands an extra expenditure of power, and this is made up for by keeping up the normal speed for longer once it has been reached. On the other hand, constant labor of one uniform kind disturbs the intensity and flow of a man’s animal spirits, which find refreshment and delight in mere change of activity.

<!-- ch14-p013 -->
The productivity of labor, that is, how much a given amount of labor produces in a given time, depends not only on the skill of the worker but also on how perfect his tools are. Tools of the same kind, such as knives, drills, gimlets, hammers, etc., may be used in different processes, and the same tool may serve various purposes in a single process. But as soon as the different operations of a labor process (the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things) are separated from one another, and each fractional operation takes on, in the hands of the detail worker, a suitable form of its own, the tools that previously served more than one purpose have to be altered. The direction this change takes is determined by the difficulties caused by the tool’s unchanged form. Manufacture is marked by the differentiation of the instruments of labor, a differentiation by which tools of a given sort take on fixed shapes, adapted to each particular use. It is also marked by the specialization of those instruments, so that each special tool shows its full effect only in the hands of a specific detail worker. In Birmingham alone 500 varieties of hammers are produced. Not only is each adapted to one particular process, but several varieties often serve exclusively for the different operations in one and the same process. The manufacturing period simplifies, improves, and multiplies the implements of labor by adapting them to the exclusively special functions of each detail worker.[^14.6] In this way it creates, at the same time, one of the material conditions for the existence of machinery, which consists of a combination of simple instruments.

[^14.6]: Darwin, in his epoch-making work on the origin of species, remarks with reference to the natural organs of plants and animals: “So long as one and the same organ has different kinds of work to perform, a ground for its changeability may possibly be found in this, that natural selection preserves or suppresses each small variation of form less carefully than if that organ were destined for one special purpose alone. Thus, knives that are adapted to cut all sorts of things, may, on the whole, be of one shape; but an implement destined to be used exclusively in one way must have a different shape for every different use.”

<!-- ch14-p014 -->
The detail worker and his tools are the simplest elements of manufacture. Let us now turn to manufacture as a whole.

### Section 3: The Two Fundamental Forms of Manufacture: Heterogeneous Manufacture, Serial Manufacture

<!-- ch14-p015 -->
The organization of manufacture has two fundamental forms. Although they sometimes blend, they are essentially different in kind. Moreover, they play very different parts later on, when manufacture is transformed into modern industry carried on by machinery. (Modern industry is large-scale production based on machinery and the factory system.) This double character comes from the nature of the article produced. Either the article results from the mere mechanical fitting together of partial products made independently, or it owes its completed shape to a series of connected processes and manual operations.

<!-- ch14-p016 -->
A locomotive, for instance, consists of more than 5,000 independent parts. It cannot, however, serve as an example of the first kind of genuine manufacture, because it is a structure produced by modern mechanical industry. But a watch can, and William Petty used it to illustrate the division of labor in manufacture. The watch was once the individual work of a Nuremberg craftsman. It has been transformed into the social product of an immense number of detail workers, such as mainspring makers, dial makers, spiral spring makers, jeweled hole makers, ruby lever makers, hand makers, case makers, screw makers, gilders, with numerous subdivisions, such as wheel makers (brass and steel separate), pin makers, movement makers, acheveur de pignon [pinion finisher] (fixes the wheels on the axles, polishes the facets, etc.), pivot makers, planteur de finissage [finishing setter] (puts the wheels and springs in the works), finisseur de barillet [barrel finisher] (cuts teeth in the wheels, makes the holes of the right size, etc.), escapement makers, cylinder makers for cylinder escapements, escapement wheel makers, balance wheel makers, raquette makers (apparatus for regulating the watch), the planteur d’échappement [escapement setter] (escapement maker proper); then the repasseur de barillet [barrel re-finisher] (finishes the box for the spring, etc.), steel polishers, wheel polishers, screw polishers, figure painters, dial enamelers (melt the enamel on the copper), fabricant de pendants [pendant maker] (makes the ring by which the case is hung), finisseur de charnière [hinge finisher] (puts the brass hinge in the cover, etc.), faiseur de secret [secret maker] (puts in the springs that open the case), graveur [engraver], ciseleur [chaser], polisseur de boîte [case polisher], etc., etc., and last of all the repasseur [re-finisher], who fits together the whole watch and hands it over in going order. Only a few parts of the watch pass through several hands. All these membra disjecta [scattered limbs] come together for the first time in the hand that binds them into one mechanical whole. The finished product has only an external relation to its various and diverse elements. This makes it a matter of chance, in this case as in the case of all similar finished articles, whether the detail workers are brought together in one workshop or not. The detail operations may further be carried on like so many independent handicrafts, as they are in the Cantons of Vaud and Neufchâtel. In Geneva, on the other hand, there are large watch manufacturing workshops where the detail workers cooperate directly under the control of a single capitalist. And even in these workshops the dial, the springs, and the case are seldom made in the factory itself. In the watch trade, carrying on the trade as a manufacture, with the workers concentrated in one place, is profitable only under exceptional conditions. This is because competition is greater among the workers who want to work at home, and because splitting the work into a number of heterogeneous processes allows only little use of the instruments of labor in common, and the capitalist, by scattering the work, saves the outlay on workshops, etc.[^14.7] Nevertheless, the position of this detail worker, who works at home but does so for a capitalist (manufacturer, établisseur [establisher]), is very different from that of the independent craftsman, who works for his own customers.[^14.8]

[^14.7]: In the year 1854 Geneva produced 80,000 watches, which is not one-fifth of the production in the Canton of Neufchâtel. La Chaux-de-Fond alone, which we may regard as one huge watch manufacturing workshop, produces twice as many watches each year as Geneva. From 1850-61 Geneva produced 720,000 watches. See “Report from Geneva on the Watch Trade” in “Reports by H. M.’s Secretaries of Embassy and Legation on the Manufactures, Commerce, &c., No. 6, 1863.” Some articles merely consist of parts fitted together, and their production is split up into processes that have no connection with each other. This lack of connection alone makes it very difficult to convert such a manufacture into a branch of modern industry carried on by machinery. But in the case of a watch there are two further obstacles in addition: the minuteness and delicacy of its parts, and its character as a luxury article.
