Hence their variety, which is so great that in the best London houses scarcely a dozen watches are made alike in the course of a year. The watch manufacturing workshop of Messrs. Vacheron & Constantin, which has used machinery with success, produces at most three or four different varieties of size and form.

[^14.8]: In watchmaking, that classic example of heterogeneous manufacture, we can study with great accuracy the differentiation and specialization of the instruments of labor, mentioned above, that the subdivision of handicrafts brings about.

<!-- ch14-p017 -->
The second kind of manufacture, its perfected form, produces articles that go through connected phases of development, through a series of processes step by step. An example is the wire in the manufacture of needles, which passes through the hands of 72, and sometimes even 92, different detail workers.

<!-- ch14-p018 -->
Insofar as such a manufacture, when first started, combines scattered handicrafts, it reduces the distance between the various phases of production. The time taken in passing from one stage to another is shortened, and so is the labor that carries out this passage.[^14.9] Compared with a handicraft, productive power is gained, and this gain is due to the general cooperative character of manufacture. On the other hand, division of labor, which is the distinguishing principle of manufacture, requires the various stages of production to be isolated and independent of each other. To set up and maintain a connection between the isolated functions, the article must be carried constantly from one hand to another, and from one process to another. From the standpoint of modern mechanical industry, this necessity stands out as a characteristic and costly disadvantage, and one that is built into the principle of manufacture.[^14.10]

[^14.9]: “In so close a cohabitation of the people, the carriage [transport] must needs be less.” (“The Advantages of the East India Trade,” p. 106.)

[^14.10]: “The isolation of the different stages of manufacture, consequent upon the employment of manual labour, adds immensely to the cost of production, the loss mainly arising from the mere removals from one process to another.” (“The Industry of Nations.” London, 1855, Part II, p. 200.)

<!-- ch14-p019 -->
If we focus on some particular batch of raw material (of rags, for instance, in paper manufacture, or of wire in needle manufacture), we see that it passes in succession through a series of stages in the hands of the various detail workers until it is complete. On the other hand, if we look at the workshop as a whole, we see the raw material in all the stages of its production at the same time. The collective worker draws the wire with one set of his many hands, armed with one kind of tool. At the same time, with another set, armed with different tools, he straightens it; with another, he cuts it; with another, he points it; and so on. The different detail processes, which were successive in time, have become simultaneous: they go on side by side in space. Hence a greater amount of finished commodities is produced in a given time.[^14.11] This simultaneity, it is true, is due to the general cooperative form of the process as a whole. But manufacture not only finds the conditions for cooperation ready to hand; it also, to some extent, creates them by subdividing handicraft labor. On the other hand, it achieves this social organization of the labor process only by riveting each worker to a single fractional detail.

[^14.11]: “It (the division of labour) produces also an economy of time by separating the work into its different branches, all of which may be carried on into execution at the same moment.... By carrying on all the different processes at once, which an individual must have executed separately, it becomes possible to produce a multitude of pins completely finished in the same time as a single pin might have been either cut or pointed.” (Dugald Stewart, cited above, p. 319.)

<!-- ch14-p020 -->
The fractional product of each detail worker is, at the same time, only a particular stage in the development of one and the same finished article. So each worker, or each group of workers, prepares the raw material for another worker or group. The result of the labor of the one is the starting-point for the labor of the other. The one worker therefore directly gives work to the other. The labor-time needed in each partial process to attain the desired effect is learned by experience. The mechanism of manufacture as a whole is based on the assumption that a given result will be obtained in a given time. Only on this assumption can the various supplementary labor processes go on without interruption, simultaneously, and side by side. Clearly, this direct dependence of the operations, and therefore of the workers, on each other forces each one of them to spend no more than the necessary time on his work. In this way a continuity, uniformity, regularity, order,[^14.12] and even intensity of labor arise that are of quite a different kind from those found in an independent handicraft or even in simple cooperation. In the production of commodities generally, the rule that the labor-time spent on a commodity should not exceed the socially necessary labor-time for its production (the time needed to produce an article under the normal conditions of production of the day, with the average skill and intensity of labor) appears to be established by the mere effect of competition. For, to put it superficially, each single producer is obliged to sell his commodity at its market price. In manufacture, on the contrary, turning out a given amount of product in a given time is a technical law of the process of production itself.[^14.13]

[^14.12]: “The more variety of artists [craftsmen] to every manufacture... the greater the order and regularity of every work, the same must needs be done in less time, the labour must be less.” (“The Advantages,” etc., p. 68.)

[^14.13]: Nevertheless, in many branches of industry the manufacturing system achieves this result only very imperfectly, because it does not know how to control with certainty the general chemical and physical conditions of the process of production.

<!-- ch14-p021 -->
Different operations, however, take unequal lengths of time, and therefore yield unequal quantities of fractional products in equal times. If, therefore, the same worker has to perform the same operation day after day, there must be a different number of workers for each operation. In type manufacture, for instance, there are four founders and two breakers to one rubber: the founder casts 2,000 type an hour, the breaker breaks up 4,000, and the rubber polishes 8,000. Here we have again the principle of cooperation in its simplest form, the simultaneous employment of many people doing the same thing; only now this principle is the expression of an organic relation. The division of labor, as carried out in manufacture, not only simplifies and multiplies the qualitatively different parts of the social collective worker. It also creates a fixed mathematical relation or ratio that regulates the quantitative extent of those parts, that is, the relative number of workers, or the relative size of the group of workers, for each detail operation. Along with the qualitative subdivision of the social labor process, it develops a quantitative rule and proportionality for that process.

<!-- ch14-p022 -->
Once the most fitting proportion between the numbers of detail workers in the various groups has been established by experiment, for production on a given scale, that scale can be extended only by employing a multiple of each particular group.[^14.14] There is this in addition: the same individual can do certain kinds of work just as well on a large scale as on a small one; for instance, the labor of supervision, the carrying of the fractional product from one stage to the next, etc. Isolating such functions and assigning them to a particular worker does not become advantageous until the number of workers employed has increased; but this increase must affect every group in proportion.

[^14.14]: “When (from the peculiar nature of the produce of each manufactory), the number of processes into which it is most advantageous to divide it is ascertained, as well as the number of individuals to be employed, then all other manufactories which do not employ a direct multiple of this number will produce the article at a greater cost.... Hence arises one of the causes of the great size of manufacturing establishments.” (C. Babbage. “On the Economy of Machinery,” 1st ed. London. 1832. Ch. xxi, pp. 172-73.)

<!-- ch14-p023 -->
The isolated group of workers to whom any particular detail function is assigned is made up of elements of the same kind, and is one of the component parts of the total mechanism. In many branches of manufacture, however, the group itself is an organized body of labor, and the total mechanism is a repetition or multiplication of these elementary organisms. Take, for instance, the manufacture of glass bottles. It can be broken down into three essentially different stages. First comes the preliminary stage: preparing the components of the glass, mixing the sand and lime, etc., and melting them into a fluid mass of glass.[^14.15] Various detail workers are employed in this first stage, as also in the final one of removing the bottles from the drying furnace, sorting and packing them, etc. In the middle, between these two stages, comes the glass melting proper, the working of the fluid mass. At each mouth of the furnace there works a group, called “the hole,” made up of one bottlemaker or finisher, one blower, one gatherer, one putter-up or whetter-off, and one taker-in. These five detail workers are so many special organs of a single working organism that acts only as a whole, and so can operate only through the direct cooperation of all five. The whole body is paralyzed if even one of its members is missing. But a glass furnace has several openings (in England from 4 to 6). Each of them holds an earthenware melting-pot full of molten glass, and employs a similar five-member group of workers. The organization of each group is based on division of labor, but the bond between the different groups is simple cooperation. This cooperation uses one of the means of production, the furnace, in common, and so makes it be used up more economically. (Means of production are the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things.) Such a furnace, with its 4-6 groups, makes up a glass house; and a glass manufacturing workshop includes a number of such glass houses, together with the apparatus and workers needed for the preparatory and final stages.

[^14.15]: In England, the melting-furnace is separate from the glass-furnace in which the glass is worked. In Belgium, one and the same furnace serves for both processes.

<!-- ch14-p024 -->
Finally, just as manufacture arises in part from combining various handicrafts, so too it develops into a combination of various branches of manufacture. The larger English glass manufacturers, for instance, make their own earthenware melting-pots, because the success or failure of the process depends to a great extent on the quality of these pots. Here the manufacture of one of the means of production is united with that of the product. On the other hand, the manufacture of the product may be united with other branches of manufacture for which that product is the raw material, or with branches of manufacture whose products it is itself later mixed with. Thus we find the manufacture of flint glass combined with glass cutting and brass founding, the brass founding being for the metal settings of various glass articles. The various branches of manufacture combined in this way form more or less separate departments of a larger manufacture, but they are at the same time independent processes, each with its own division of labor. In spite of the many advantages this combination of branches of manufacture offers, it never grows into a complete technical system on its own foundation. That happens only when it is transformed into an industry carried on by machinery.

<!-- ch14-p025 -->
Early in the manufacturing period, the principle of lessening the necessary labor-time in the production of commodities[^14.16] was accepted and formulated. And the use of machines sprang up here and there, especially for certain simple first processes that have to be carried out on a very large scale and with the application of great force. Thus, at an early period in paper manufacture, the rags were torn up by paper-mills; and in metal works, the ores were pounded by stamping mills.[^14.17] The Roman Empire had handed down the elementary form of all machinery in the water-wheel.[^14.18]

[^14.16]: This can be seen from W. Petty, John Bellers, Andrew Yarranton, “The Advantages of the East India Trade,” and J. Vanderlint, not to mention others.

[^14.17]: Toward the end of the 16th century, mortars and sieves were still used in France for pounding and washing ores.

[^14.18]: The whole history of the development of machinery can be traced in the history of the grain mill. In England the factory is still a “mill.” In German technological works of the first decade of this century, the term “Mühle” [mill] is still in use, not only for all machinery driven by the forces of Nature, but also for all manufacturing workshops where apparatus of the nature of machinery is applied.

<!-- ch14-p026 -->
The handicraft period handed down to us the great inventions of the compass, of gunpowder, of type-printing, and of the automatic clock. But on the whole, machinery played the subordinate part that Adam Smith assigns to it in comparison with division of labor.[^14.19] The sporadic use of machinery in the 17th century was of the greatest importance, because it gave the great mathematicians of that time a practical basis and a stimulus for creating the science of mechanics.

[^14.19]: As will be seen in more detail in the fourth book of this work, Adam Smith has not established a single new proposition about division of labor. What marks him out, however, as the political economist above all others of the period of manufacture is the stress he lays on division of labor. The subordinate part he assigns to machinery gave rise, in the early days of modern mechanical industry, to the polemic of Lauderdale and, at a later period, to that of Ure. A. Smith also confuses the differentiation of the instruments of labor, in which the detail workers themselves took an active part, with the invention of machinery. In the invention of machinery, it is not the workers in manufacturing workshops who play a part, but learned men, craftsmen, and even peasants (Brindley).

<!-- ch14-p027 -->
The collective worker, formed by combining a number of detail workers, is the machinery specially characteristic of the manufacturing period. The producer of a commodity performs various operations in turn, and these merge into one another as production goes on. They make different demands on him. In one operation he must exert more strength, in another more skill, in another more attention; and the same individual does not possess all these qualities in an equal degree. Once manufacture has separated the various operations, made them independent, and isolated them, the workers are divided, classified, and grouped according to their dominant qualities. If their natural gifts are, on the one hand, the foundation on which the division of labor is built, on the other hand manufacture, once introduced, develops in them new powers that are by nature fitted only for limited and special functions. The collective worker now possesses all the qualities needed for production in an equal degree of excellence. He spends them in the most economical way, by using all his organs, which consist of particular workers or groups of workers, exclusively in performing their special functions.[^14.20] The one-sidedness and the deficiencies of the detail worker become perfections when he is part of the collective worker.[^14.21] The habit of doing only one thing turns him into a never-failing instrument, while his connection with the whole mechanism forces him to work with the regularity of the parts of a machine.[^14.22]

[^14.20]: “The master manufacturer, by dividing the work to be executed into different processes, each requiring different degrees of skill or of force, can purchase exactly that precise quantity of both which is necessary for each process; whereas, if the whole work were executed by one workman, that person must possess sufficient skill to perform the most difficult, and sufficient strength to execute the most laborious of the operations into which the article is divided.” (Ch. Babbage, cited above, ch. xix.)

[^14.21]: For instance, abnormal development of some muscles, curvature of bones, etc.

[^14.22]: One of the Inquiry Commissioners asked how the young persons are kept steadily at their work. Mr. Wm. Marshall, the general manager of a glass manufacturing workshop, answered the question very correctly: “They cannot well neglect their work; when they once begin, they must go on; they are just the same as parts of a machine.” (“Children’s Empl. Comm.,” 4th Rep., 1865, p. 247.)

<!-- ch14-p028 -->
The collective worker has functions both simple and complex, both high and low. So his members, the individual labor-powers, need different degrees of training, and must therefore have different values. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) Manufacture therefore develops a hierarchy of labor-powers, and a scale of wages corresponds to it. (Wages are the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself.) If, on the one hand, the individual workers are appropriated and annexed for life by a limited function, on the other hand the various operations of the hierarchy are parceled out among the workers according to both their natural and their acquired abilities.[^14.23] Every process of production, however, requires certain simple manipulations that every man is capable of doing. These too are now cut off from their connection with the weightier elements of activity, and hardened into exclusive functions of specially appointed workers. Hence, in every handicraft it seizes on, manufacture gives rise to a class of so-called unskilled workers, a class that handicraft industry strictly excluded. If it develops a one-sided specialty into a perfection, at the expense of a man's whole working capacity, it also begins to make a specialty of the absence of all development. Alongside the hierarchical grading there appears the simple separation of the workers into skilled and unskilled. For the unskilled, the cost of apprenticeship disappears. For the skilled, it diminishes compared with that of craftsmen, because the functions have been simplified. In both cases the value of labor-power falls.[^14.24] (The value of labor-power is the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker, and to raise the next generation of workers, able to work.) An exception to this law holds whenever the breaking up of the labor process gives rise to new and comprehensive functions that had either no place at all, or only a very modest one, in handicrafts. The fall in the value of labor-power, caused by the disappearance or reduction of the costs of apprenticeship, means a direct increase of surplus-value for the benefit of capital. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it. Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger.) For everything that shortens the necessary labor-time required for reproducing labor-power extends the domain of surplus labor. (Necessary labor-time is the part of the working day in which the worker produces the equivalent of the value of their own labor-power, that is, of their wages; surplus labor is the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist.)

[^14.23]: Dr. Ure, in his glorification of Modern Mechanical Industry, brings out the peculiar character of manufacture more sharply than earlier economists, who did not have his polemical interest in the matter. He brings it out more sharply even than his contemporaries, Babbage for example, who, though much his superior as a mathematician and expert in mechanics, treated mechanical industry from the standpoint of manufacture alone. Ure says, “This appropriation ... to each, a workman of appropriate value and cost was naturally assigned, forms the very essence of division of labour.” On the other hand, he describes this division as “adaptation of labour to the different talents of men,” and lastly, he characterizes the whole manufacturing system as “a system for the division or gradation of labour,” as “the division of labour into degrees of skill,” etc. (Ure, cited above, pp. 19-23 passim.)

[^14.24]: “Each handicraftsman being ... enabled to perfect himself by practice in one point, became ... a cheaper workman.” (Ure, cited above, p. 19.)

### Section 4: Division of Labor in Manufacture, and Division of Labor in Society

<!-- ch14-p029 -->
We first looked at the origin of manufacture, then at its simple elements, then at the detail worker and his tools, and finally at the mechanism as a whole. We will now touch briefly on the relation between the division of labor in manufacture and the social division of labor, which forms the foundation of all production of commodities.

<!-- ch14-p030 -->
If we keep only labor in view, we may call the separation of social production into its main divisions or *genera* [kinds] – namely agriculture, industries, etc. – division of labor in general. We may call the splitting up of these families into species and sub-species division of labor in particular. And we may call the division of labor within the workshop division of labor in singular, or in detail.[^14.25]

[^14.25]: “Division of labour proceeds from the separation of professions the most widely different to that division, where several labourers divide between them the preparation of one and the same product, as in manufacture.” (Storch: “Cours d’Econ. Pol.,” Paris Edn. t. I., p. 173.) “Nous rencontrons chez les peuples parvenus à un certain degré de civilisation trois genres de divisions d’industrie: la première, que nous nommerons générale, amène la distinction des producteurs en agriculteurs, manufacturiers et commerçants, elle se rapporte aux trois principales branches d’industrie nationale; la seconde qu’on pourrait appeler spéciale, est la division de chaque genre d’industrie en espèces ... la troisième division d’industrie, celle enfin qu’on devrait qualifier de division de la besogne on de travail proprement dit, est celle qui s’établit dans les arts et les métiers séparés ... qui s’établit dans la plupart des manufactures et des ateliers.” [Among peoples who have reached a certain level of civilization, we find three kinds of division of labor. The first, which we will call general, divides the producers into farmers, manufacturers, and traders; it corresponds to the three main branches of the nation's labor. The second, which one could call particular, is the division of each branch of labor into species. ... The third division of labor, which one should call a division of tasks, or of labor in the strict sense, is the one that grows up in the individual crafts and trades ... which is established in most manufacturing establishments and workshops.] (Skarbek, cited above, pp. 84, 85.)

<!-- ch14-p031 -->
Division of labor in a society, and the tying down of individuals to a particular occupation that goes with it, develops from opposite starting-points, just as the division of labor in manufacture does. Within a family,[^14.26] and after further development within a tribe, a division of labor springs up naturally. It is caused by differences of sex and age, and so rests on a purely physiological foundation. This division widens its material as the community expands and the population grows, and above all through conflicts between different tribes and the conquest of one tribe by another. On the other hand, as I have remarked before, the exchange of products springs up at the points where different families, tribes, and communities come into contact. For at the beginning of civilization it is not private individuals but families, tribes, etc., that meet on an independent footing. Different communities find different means of production and different means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live) in their natural surroundings. So their modes of production and of living, and their products, are different. It is this spontaneously developed difference that, when different communities come into contact, calls forth the mutual exchange of products, and so the gradual conversion of those products into commodities. Exchange does not create the differences between the spheres of production. It brings spheres that are already different into relation with each other, and so turns them into more or less interdependent branches of the collective production of an enlarged society. In this second case, the social division of labor arises from exchange between spheres of production that were originally distinct and independent of one another. In the first case, where the physiological division of labor is the starting-point, the particular organs of a compact whole grow loose and break off, mainly because of the exchange of commodities with foreign communities. They then become so isolated from one another that the only bond still connecting the various kinds of work is the exchange of the products as commodities. In the one case, what was independent before is made dependent; in the other, what was dependent before is made independent.

[^14.26]: *Note to the third edition.* Later, very searching study of the primitive condition of humanity led the author to the conclusion that it was not the family that originally developed into the tribe. On the contrary, the tribe was the primitive and spontaneously developed form of human association, based on blood relationship. The many and various forms of the family developed afterwards, out of the first beginnings of the loosening of tribal bonds. [F. E.]

<!-- ch14-p032 -->
The foundation of every division of labor that is well developed and brought about by the exchange of commodities is the separation between town and country.[^14.27] It may be said that the whole economic history of society is summed up in the movement of this opposition. For the present, however, we pass it over.

[^14.27]: Sir James Steuart is the economist who has handled this subject best. His book appeared ten years before the “Wealth of Nations.” How little it is known, even today, can be judged from this fact: the admirers of Malthus do not even know that the first edition of Malthus's work on population contains, apart from its purely declamatory part, very little but extracts from Steuart, and to a lesser degree from Wallace and Townsend.

<!-- ch14-p033 -->
A certain number of workers employed at the same time are the material precondition for division of labor in manufacture. In the same way, the number and density of the population, which here correspond to the crowding together in one workshop, are a necessary condition for the division of labor in society.[^14.28] This density, however, is more or less relative. A relatively thinly populated country with well-developed means of communication has a denser population than a more numerously populated country with badly developed means of communication. In this sense the Northern States of the American Union, for instance, are more thickly populated than India.[^14.29]

[^14.28]: “There is a certain density of population which is convenient, both for social intercourse, and for that combination of powers by which the produce of labour is increased.” (James Mill, cited above, p. 50.) “As the number of labourers increases, the productive power of society augments in the compound ratio of that increase, multiplied by the effects of the division of labour.” (Th. Hodgskin, cited above, pp. 125, 126.)

[^14.29]: Because of the great demand for cotton after 1861, cotton production in some thickly populated districts of India was extended at the expense of rice growing. Local famines followed, because the poor means of communication did not allow a failure of rice in one district to be made up by bringing rice in from another.

<!-- ch14-p034 -->
The production and the circulation of commodities (the exchange of commodities through money: selling and buying) are the general preconditions of the capitalist mode of production. So division of labor in manufacture requires that division of labor in society at large should already have reached a certain degree of development. The other way round, division of labor in manufacture reacts on division of labor in society, and develops and multiplies it. As the instruments of labor become more differentiated, so, at the same time, do the industries that produce these instruments.[^14.30] Suppose the manufacturing system seizes on an industry that was previously carried on by one producer together with other industries, either as the chief or as a subordinate industry. These industries then immediately break their connection and become independent. If it seizes on a particular stage in the production of a commodity, the other stages of its production become so many independent industries. It has already been stated that where the finished article is merely a number of parts fitted together, the detail operations may re-establish themselves as genuine and separate handicrafts. To carry out the division of labor in manufacture more perfectly, a single branch of production is split up into numerous, and to some extent entirely new, branches of manufacture. The split follows the varieties of its raw material, or the various forms that one and the same raw material may take. So in France alone, in the first half of the 18th century, over 100 different kinds of silk fabrics were woven, and in Avignon it was law that “every apprentice should devote himself to only one sort of fabrication, and should not learn the preparation of several kinds of stuff at once.” The territorial division of labor, which confines special branches of production to special districts of a country, gets a fresh stimulus from the manufacturing system, which exploits every special advantage.[^14.31] The colonial system and the opening up of the world's markets, both of which belong to the general conditions of existence of the manufacturing period, supply rich material for developing the division of labor in society. This is not the place to go on to show how division of labor seizes not only the economic sphere but every other sphere of society. Everywhere it lays the foundation of that all-absorbing system of specializing and sorting people, that development in a person of one single ability at the expense of all the others, which made A. Ferguson, Adam Smith's teacher, exclaim: “We make a nation of Helots [state serfs of ancient Sparta], and have no free citizens.”[^14.32]

[^14.30]: So as early as the 17th century, the making of shuttles formed a special branch of industry in Holland.

[^14.31]: Whether the woollen manufacture of England is not divided into several parts or branches appropriated to particular places, where they are only or principally manufactured; fine cloths in Somersetshire, coarse in Yorkshire, long ells at Exeter, soies at Sudbury, crapes at Norwich, linseys at Kendal, blankets at Whitney, and so forth.” (Berkeley: “The Querist,” 1751, § 520.)

[^14.32]: A. Ferguson: “History of Civil Society.” Edinburgh, 1767; Part iv, sect. ii., p. 285.

<!-- ch14-p035 -->
But in spite of the many analogies and links between them, division of labor inside a society and division of labor inside a workshop differ not only in degree but also in kind. The analogy seems most beyond dispute where an invisible bond unites the various branches of trade. For instance, the cattle-breeder produces hides, the tanner makes the hides into leather, and the shoemaker makes the leather into boots. Here what each of them produces is only a step toward the final form, which is the product of all their labors combined. Besides these, there are all the various industries that supply the cattle-breeder, the tanner, and the shoemaker with means of production. Now it is quite possible to imagine, with Adam Smith, that the difference between this social division of labor and the division in manufacture is merely subjective. On this view it exists only for the observer: in a manufacturing workshop he can see at one glance all the many operations being carried out in one place, while in the example above, the spreading of the work over great areas and the great number of people employed in each branch of labor hide the connection.[^14.33] But what forms the bond between the independent labors of the cattle-breeder, the tanner, and the shoemaker? The fact that their products are commodities. What, on the other hand, is characteristic of division of labor in manufacture? The fact that the detail worker produces no commodities.[^14.34] Only the common product of all the detail workers becomes a commodity.[^14.35] Division of labor in society comes about through the purchase and sale of the products of different branches of industry. The connection between the detail operations in a workshop, by contrast, comes from the sale of the labor-power of several workers to one capitalist, who applies it as combined labor-power. The division of labor in the workshop implies that the means of production are concentrated in the hands of one capitalist. The division of labor in society implies that they are dispersed among many independent producers of commodities. Inside the workshop, the iron law of proportionality subjects definite numbers of workers to definite functions. In the society outside the workshop, chance and whim have full play in distributing the producers and their means of production among the various branches of industry. It is true that the different spheres of production constantly tend toward an equilibrium. On the one hand, each producer of a commodity is bound to produce a use-value (the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties), to satisfy a particular social want; and while the extent of these wants differs in quantity, there is still an inner relation that settles their proportions into a regular system, and a system of spontaneous growth at that. On the other hand, the law of the value of commodities ultimately determines how much of its available working time society can spend on each particular class of commodities. But this constant tendency of the various spheres of production toward equilibrium works only as a reaction against the constant upsetting of that equilibrium. Within the workshop, the division of labor is carried out regularly according to a plan fixed in advance. Within society, this becomes a necessity imposed by nature after the fact, which controls the lawless whims of the producers and can be seen in the barometer-like fluctuations of market prices. Division of labor within the workshop implies the undisputed authority of the capitalist over people who are only parts of a mechanism that belongs to him. The division of labor within society brings into contact independent commodity producers who acknowledge no authority but that of competition, the coercion exerted by the pressure of their mutual interests – just as in the animal kingdom the *bellum omnium contra omnes* [war of all against all – Hobbes] more or less preserves the conditions of existence of every species. The same bourgeois mind (bourgeois means belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it) praises division of labor in the workshop, the life-long annexation of the worker to a partial operation, and his complete subjection to capital, as an organization of labor that increases its productivity. That same bourgeois mind denounces just as vigorously every conscious attempt to control and regulate the process of production socially, as an attack on such sacred things as the rights of property, freedom, and unrestricted play for the inclinations of the individual capitalist. It is very characteristic that the enthusiastic apologists of the factory system – production in which a system of machines, driven by a central power source, does the work and workers attend the machines – have nothing more damning to say against a general organization of the labor of society than that it would turn all society into one immense factory.

[^14.33]: In manufacture proper, he says, the division of labor appears to be greater, because “those employed in every different branch of the work can often be collected into the same workhouse, and placed at once under the view of the spectator. In those great manufactures, (!) on the contrary, which are destined to supply the great wants of the great body of the people, every different branch of the work employs so great a number of workmen, that it is impossible to collect them all into the same workhouse ... the division is not near so obvious.” (A. Smith: “Wealth of Nations,” bk. i, ch. i.) The famous passage in the same chapter that begins with the words “Observe the accommodation of the most common artificer or day-labourer in a civilised and thriving country,” etc., and then goes on to describe what an enormous number and variety of industries contribute to satisfying the wants of an ordinary worker, is copied almost word for word from B. de Mandeville's Remarks to his “Fable of the Bees, or Private Vices, Publick Benefits.” (First ed., without the remarks, 1706; with the remarks, 1714.)

[^14.34]: “There is no longer anything which we can call the natural reward of individual labour. Each labourer produces only some part of a whole, and each part, having no value or utility in itself, there is nothing on which the labourer can seize, and say: It is my product, this I will keep to myself.” (“Labour Defended against the Claims of Capital.” London, 1825, p. 25.) The author of this admirable work is the Th. Hodgskin I have already cited.

[^14.35]: This distinction between division of labor in society and in manufacture was illustrated in practice to the Yankees. One of the new taxes devised in Washington during the civil war was a duty of 6% “on all industrial products.” Question: What is an industrial product? Answer of the legislature: A thing is produced “when it is made,” and it is made when it is ready for sale. Now, one example out of many. The New York and Philadelphia manufacturers had previously been in the habit of “making” umbrellas with all their accessories. But since an umbrella is a hodgepodge of very different parts, these parts gradually became the products of various separate industries, carried on independently in different places. They entered the umbrella manufacturing workshop as separate commodities, and were fitted together there. The Yankees have given articles fitted together in this way the name of “assembled articles,” a name they deserve, since they are an assemblage of taxes. So the umbrella “assembles,” first, 6% on the price of each of its elements, and then a further 6% on its own total price.

<!-- ch14-p036 -->
If, in a society with capitalist production, anarchy in the social division of labor and despotism in the division of labor in the workshop are each a condition of the other, we find the opposite in those earlier forms of society in which the separation of trades developed spontaneously, then hardened, and was finally made permanent by law. There we find, on the one hand, an example of the labor of society organized according to an approved and authoritative plan, and on the other, the complete exclusion of division of labor in the workshop, or at any rate only a stunted, or sporadic and accidental, development of it.[^14.36]

[^14.36]: “On peut... établir en règle générale, que moins l’autorité préside à la division du travail dans l’intérieur de la société, plus la division du travail se développe dans l’intérieur de l’atelier, et plus elle y est soumise à l’autorité d’un seul. Ainsi l’autorité dans l’atelier et celle dans la société, par rapport à la division du travail, sont en raison inverse l’une de l’autre.” [It can ... be laid down as a general rule that the less authority presides over the division of labor inside society, the more the division of labor develops inside the workshop, and the more it is subject there to the authority of a single person. So authority in the workshop and authority in society, in relation to the division of labor, are in inverse ratio to each other.] (Karl Marx, “Misère,” etc., pp. 130-131.)

<!-- ch14-p037 -->
Those small and extremely ancient Indian communities, some of which have lasted down to this day, are based on holding the land in common, on combining agriculture and handicrafts, and on an unalterable division of labor, which serves as a ready-made plan and scheme whenever a new community is started. Each one covers an area of from 100 up to several thousand acres and forms a compact whole that produces everything it needs. Most of the products are meant for direct use by the community itself and do not take the form of a commodity. So production here is independent of the division of labor that is brought about in Indian society as a whole by the exchange of commodities. Only the surplus becomes a commodity, and even a part of that only once it has reached the hands of the State. From time immemorial a certain quantity of these products has found its way into the State's hands as rent paid in kind. The constitution of these communities varies in different parts of India. In those of the simplest form, the land is farmed in common and the produce is divided among the members. At the same time, spinning and weaving are carried on in each family as side industries. Side by side with the masses all occupied with this same work, we find the “chief inhabitant,” who is judge, police, and tax-collector in one; the bookkeeper, who keeps the accounts of the farming and records everything connected with it; another official, who prosecutes criminals, protects strangers traveling through, and escorts them to the next village; the boundary man, who guards the boundaries against neighboring communities; the water-overseer, who distributes water for irrigation from the common tanks; the Brahmin, who conducts the religious services; the schoolmaster, who teaches the children reading and writing in the sand; the calendar-Brahmin, or astrologer, who announces the lucky or unlucky days for sowing and harvest and for every other kind of farm work; a smith and a carpenter, who make and repair all the farm implements; the potter, who makes all the pottery of the village; the barber; the washerman, who washes clothes; the silversmith; and here and there the poet, who in some communities replaces the silversmith and in others the schoolmaster. This dozen individuals is kept at the expense of the whole community. If the population increases, a new community is founded on unoccupied land, on the pattern of the old one. The whole mechanism shows a systematic division of labor. But a division like that in manufacture is impossible, since the smith, the carpenter, etc., find an unchanging market, and at most there are, depending on the size of the villages, two or three of each instead of one.[^14.37] The law that regulates the division of labor in the community acts with the irresistible authority of a law of Nature. At the same time, each individual craftsman, the smith, the carpenter, and so on, carries out all the operations of his handicraft in his workshop in the traditional way, but independently, and without recognizing any authority over him. Take the simplicity of the organization for production in these self-sufficient communities, which constantly reproduce themselves in the same form and, when accidentally destroyed, spring up again on the same spot and with the same name[^14.38] – this simplicity supplies the key to the secret of the unchangeableness of Asiatic societies. That unchangeableness stands in striking contrast with the constant breaking up and refounding of Asiatic States and the never-ending changes of dynasty. The structure of the economic elements of society remains untouched by the storm-clouds of the political sky.

[^14.37]: Lieut.-Col. Mark Wilks: “Historical Sketches of the South of India.” London, 1810-17, v. I., pp. 118-20. A good description of the various forms of the Indian communities can be found in George Campbell's “Modern India.” London, 1852.

[^14.38]: “Under this simple form ... the inhabitants of the country have lived from time immemorial. The boundaries of the villages have been but seldom altered; and though the villages themselves have been sometimes injured, and even desolated by war, famine, and disease, the same name, the same limits, the same interests, and even the same families, have continued for ages. The inhabitants give themselves no trouble about the breaking up and division of kingdoms; while the village remains entire, they care not to what power it is transferred, or to what sovereign it devolves; its internal economy remains unchanged.” (Th. Stamford Raffles, late Lieut. Gov. of Java: “The History of Java.” London, 1817, Vol. I., p. 285.)

<!-- ch14-p038 -->
The rules of the guilds, as I have said before, strictly limited the number of apprentices and journeymen that a single master could employ, and so prevented him from becoming a capitalist. Besides, he could not employ his journeymen in many handicrafts other than the one in which he was a master. The guilds eagerly fought off every encroachment by merchants' capital, the only form of free capital they came into contact with. A merchant could buy every kind of commodity, but he could not buy labor as a commodity. He was only tolerated, as a dealer in the products of the handicrafts. If circumstances called for a further division of labor, the existing guilds split into varieties, or founded new guilds alongside the old ones; but they did all this without concentrating various handicrafts in a single workshop. So the guild organization, however much it may have helped to create the material conditions for the existence of manufacture by separating, isolating, and perfecting the handicrafts, excluded division of labor in the workshop. On the whole, the worker and his means of production stayed closely united, like the snail and its shell. So the principal basis of manufacture was missing: the separation of the worker from his means of production, and the conversion of these means into capital.

<!-- ch14-p039 -->
Division of labor in society at large, whether or not it is brought about by the exchange of commodities, is common to the most diverse economic formations of society. But division of labor in the workshop, as practiced by manufacture, is a special creation of the capitalist mode of production alone.

### Section 5: The Capitalistic Character of Manufacture

<!-- ch14-p040 -->
An increased number of workers under the control of one capitalist is the natural starting-point both of cooperation in general and of manufacture in particular. But the division of labor in manufacture makes this increase in the number of workers a technical necessity. Here the minimum number of workers that any given capitalist is bound to employ is prescribed by the division of labor already established. On the other hand, the advantages of further division can be gained only by adding to the number of workers, and this can be done only by adding multiples of the various detail groups. But an increase in the variable component of the capital employed (the part spent on labor-power) requires an increase in its constant component (the part spent on means of production) as well: in the workshops, implements, etc., and above all in the raw material, the demand for which grows faster than the number of workers. The quantity of raw material that a given amount of labor consumes in a given time increases in the same ratio as the productive power of that labor increases as a result of its division. Hence it is a law, based on the very nature of manufacture, that the minimum amount of capital that each capitalist is bound to have in hand must keep increasing. In other words, the transformation of the social means of production and means of subsistence into capital must keep extending.[^14.39]

[^14.39]: “It is not sufficient that the capital” (the writer should have said the necessary means of subsistence and of production) “required for the subdivision of handicrafts should be in readiness in the society: it must also be accumulated in the hands of the employers in sufficiently large quantities to enable them to conduct their operations on a large scale.... The more the division increases, the more does the constant employment of a given number of labourers require a greater outlay of capital in tools, raw material, &c.” (Storch: “Cours d’Econ. Polit.” Paris Ed., t. I., pp. 250, 251.) “La concentration des instruments de production et la division du travail sont aussi inséparables l’une de l’autre que le sont, dans le régime politique, la concentration des pouvoirs publics et la division des intérêts privés.” [The concentration of the instruments of production and the division of labor are as inseparable from each other as, in politics, the concentration of public powers and the division of private interests are.] (Karl Marx, cited above, p. 134.)

<!-- ch14-p041 -->
In manufacture, as in simple cooperation, the collective working organism is a form in which capital exists. The mechanism made up of many individual detail workers belongs to the capitalist. Hence the productive power that results from combining labors appears to be the productive power of capital. Manufacture proper not only subjects the previously independent worker to the discipline and command of capital. It also creates a hierarchy of ranks among the workers themselves. Simple cooperation leaves the individual's way of working mostly unchanged, while manufacture revolutionizes it thoroughly and seizes labor-power by its very roots. It turns the worker into a crippled monstrosity, by forcing on his skill in one detail at the expense of a whole world of productive abilities and instincts; just as in the States of La Plata they butcher a whole beast for the sake of its hide or its tallow. Not only are the detail tasks distributed among different individuals; the individual himself is made into the automatic motor of a fractional operation,[^14.40] and the absurd fable of Menenius Agrippa, which makes a man a mere fragment of his own body, comes true.[^14.41] If at first the worker sells his labor-power to capital because he lacks the material means of producing a commodity, now his very labor-power refuses its services unless it has been sold to capital. Its functions can be carried out only in an environment that exists in the capitalist's workshop after the sale. Unfitted by nature to make anything independently, the manufacturing worker develops productive activity as a mere appendage of the capitalist's workshop.[^14.42] Just as the chosen people bore Jehovah's own signature on their faces, so the division of labor brands the manufacturing worker as the property of capital.

[^14.40]: Dugald Stewart calls manufacturing workers “living automatons ... employed in the details of the work.” (Cited above, p. 318.)

[^14.41]: In corals, each individual is in fact the stomach of the whole group. But it supplies the group with nourishment, instead of withdrawing it, as the Roman patrician did.

[^14.42]: “L’ouvrier qui porte dans ses bras tout un métier, peut aller partout exercer son industrie et trouver des moyens de subsister: l’autre (the manufacturing labourer) n’est qu’un accessoire qui, séparé de ses confrères, n’a plus ni capacité, ni indépendance, et qui se trouve force d’accepter la loi qu’on juge à propos de lui imposer.” [The worker who carries a whole craft in his arms can go anywhere to practice his trade and find the means of subsistence. The other (the manufacturing worker) is only an accessory who, once separated from his fellows, no longer has either ability or independence, and finds himself forced to accept whatever law it is thought fit to impose on him.] (Storch, cited above, Petersb. edit., 1815, t. I., p. 204.)

<!-- ch14-p042 -->
The independent peasant or craftsman exercises knowledge, judgment, and will, even if only to a very small degree, in the same way that the savage makes the whole art of war consist in the exercise of his own personal cunning. These faculties are now required only for the workshop as a whole. Intelligence in production expands in one direction because it vanishes in many others. What the detail workers lose is concentrated in the capital that employs them.[^14.43] It is a result of the division of labor in manufacture that the worker is brought face to face with the intellectual powers of the material process of production as the property of another, and as a ruling power. This separation begins in simple cooperation, where the capitalist represents to the individual worker the unity and the will of the combined labor. It develops in manufacture, which cuts the worker down into a detail worker. It is completed in modern industry, which makes science a productive force separate from labor and presses it into the service of capital.[^14.44]

[^14.43]: A. Ferguson, cited above, p. 281: “The former may have gained what the other has lost.”

[^14.44]: “The man of knowledge and the productive labourer come to be widely divided from each other, and knowledge, instead of remaining the handmaid of labour in the hand of the labourer to increase his productive powers ... has almost everywhere arrayed itself against labour ... systematically deluding and leading them (the labourers) astray in order to render their muscular powers entirely mechanical and obedient.” (W. Thompson: “An Inquiry into the Principles of the Distribution of Wealth.” London, 1824, p. 274.)

<!-- ch14-p043 -->
In manufacture, if the collective worker, and through him capital, is to be made rich in social productive power, each worker must be made poor in individual productive powers.

<!-- ch14-p044 -->
> “Ignorance is the mother of industry as well as of superstition. Reflection and fancy are subject to err; but a habit of moving the hand or the foot is independent of either. Manufactures, accordingly, prosper most where the mind is least consulted, and where the workshop may ... be considered as an engine, the parts of which are men.”[^14.45]

[^14.45]: A. Ferguson, cited above, p. 280.

<!-- ch14-p045 -->
In fact, in the middle of the 18th century, a few manufacturers preferred to employ half-idiotic persons for certain operations that were trade secrets.[^14.46]

[^14.46]: J. D. Tuckett: “A History of the Past and Present State of the Labouring Population.” London, 1846.

<!-- ch14-p046 -->
> “The understandings of the greater part of men,” says Adam Smith, “are necessarily formed by their ordinary employments. The man whose whole life is spent in performing a few simple operations ... has no occasion to exert his understanding... He generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become.”

<!-- ch14-p047 -->
After describing the stupidity of the detail worker, he goes on:

<!-- ch14-p048 -->
> “The uniformity of his stationary life naturally corrupts the courage of his mind... It corrupts even the activity of his body and renders him incapable of exerting his strength with vigour and perseverance in any other employments than that to which he has been bred. His dexterity at his own particular trade seems in this manner to be acquired at the expense of his intellectual, social, and martial virtues. But in every improved and civilised society, this is the state into which the labouring poor, that is, the great body of the people, must necessarily fall.”[^14.47]

[^14.47]: A. Smith: “Wealth of Nations,” Bk. v., ch. i, art. ii. As a pupil of A. Ferguson, who had shown the harmful effects of the division of labor, Adam Smith was perfectly clear on this point. In the introduction to his work, where he expressly sets out to praise the division of labor, he mentions only in passing that it is the source of social inequalities. Not until the 5th Book, on the Revenue of the State, does he reproduce Ferguson. In my “Misère de la Philosophie,” I have sufficiently explained the historical connection between Ferguson, A. Smith, Lemontey, and Say, as regards their criticisms of the division of labor. There I have also shown, for the first time, that the division of labor as practiced in manufacture is a specific form of the capitalist mode of production.

<!-- ch14-p049 -->
To prevent the division of labor from completely degrading the great mass of the people, A. Smith recommends that the State educate the people, but prudently, and in homeopathic doses. G. Garnier, his French translator and commentator, who under the first French Empire quite naturally developed into a senator, quite as naturally opposes him on this point. Education of the masses, Garnier urges, violates the first law of the division of labor, and with it

<!-- ch14-p050 -->
> “our whole social system would be proscribed [outlawed].” “Like all other divisions of labour,” he says, “that between hand labour and head labour[^14.48] is more pronounced and decided in proportion as society (he rightly uses this word, for capital, landed property, and their State) becomes richer. This division of labour, like every other, is an effect of past, and a cause of future progress... ought the government then to work in opposition to this division of labour, and to hinder its natural course? Ought it to expend a part of the public money in the attempt to confound and blend together two classes of labour, which are striving after division and separation?”[^14.49]

[^14.48]: Ferguson had already said, cited above, p. 281: “And thinking itself, in this age of separations, may become a peculiar craft.”

[^14.49]: G. Garnier, vol. V. of his translation of A. Smith, pp. 4-5.

<!-- ch14-p051 -->
Some crippling of body and mind is inseparable even from the division of labor in society as a whole. However, because manufacture carries this social separation of branches of labor much further, and also, by its own peculiar kind of division, attacks the individual at the very roots of his life[^14.50], it is the first to supply the materials for industrial pathology, and to give it a start.

[^14.50]: Ramazzini, professor of practical medicine at Padua, published his work “De morbis artificum” in 1713. It was translated into French in 1781, and reprinted in 1841 in the “Encyclopédie des Sciences Médicales. 7me Dis. Auteurs Classiques.” The period of modern mechanical industry has, of course, greatly enlarged his catalogue of the diseases of labor. See “Hygiène physique et morale de l’ouvrier dans les grandes villes en général et dans la ville de Lyon en particulier. Par le Dr. A. L. Fonteret, Paris, 1858,” and “Die Krankheiten, welche verschiednen Ständen, Altern und Geschlechtern eigenthümlich sind. 6 Vols. Ulm, 1860,” and others. In 1854 the Society of Arts appointed a Commission of Inquiry into industrial pathology. The list of documents this commission collected can be seen in the catalogue of the “Twickenham Economic Museum.” The official “Reports on Public Health” are very important. See also Eduard Reich, M. D. “Ueber die Entartung des Menschen,” Erlangen, 1868.

<!-- ch14-p052 -->
> “To subdivide a man is to execute him, if he deserves the sentence, to assassinate him if he does not... The subdivision of labour is the assassination of a people.”[^14.51]

[^14.51]: (D. Urquhart: “Familiar Words.” London, 1855, p. 119.) Hegel held very heretical views on the division of labor. In his “Rechtsphilosophie” he says: “By well educated men we understand in the first instance, those who can do everything that others do.”

<!-- ch14-p053 -->
Cooperation based on the division of labor, in other words manufacture, begins as a formation that arises spontaneously. As soon as it gains some solidity and scope, it becomes the recognized, methodical, and systematic form of capitalist production. History shows how the division of labor peculiar to manufacture in the strict sense first finds its best-suited form by experience, as it were behind the backs of the actors. Then, like the guild handicrafts, it strives to hold fast to that form once it has been found, and here and there it succeeds in keeping it for centuries. Any change in this form, except in trivial matters, is due solely to a revolution in the instruments of labor. Wherever modern manufacture arises (I am not referring here to modern industry based on machinery), it either finds the disjecta membra poetae [the scattered limbs of the poet] ready to hand, only waiting to be collected together, as in the manufacture of clothes in large towns; or it can easily apply the principle of division simply by assigning the various operations of a handicraft (such as book-binding) exclusively to particular men. In such cases, a week's experience is enough to fix the proportion between the numbers of workers needed for the various functions.[^14.52]

[^14.52]: The simple belief in the inventive genius that the individual capitalist exercises in advance in the division of labor exists nowadays only among German professors of the stamp of Herr Roscher. To reward the capitalist, from whose Jovian head the division of labor sprang ready-made, Roscher dedicates to him “various wages” (diverse *Arbeitslöhne*). How far the division of labor is applied depends on the length of the purse, not on the greatness of the genius.

<!-- ch14-p054 -->
By breaking handicrafts down, by specializing the instruments of labor, by forming detail workers, and by grouping and combining them into a single mechanism, the division of labor in manufacture creates a qualitative gradation and a quantitative proportion in the social process of production. It therefore creates a definite organization of the labor of society, and so at the same time develops new productive forces in society. In its specific capitalist form (and under the given conditions it could take no form other than a capitalist one), manufacture is only a particular method of producing relative surplus-value, or of increasing, at the worker's expense, the self-expansion of capital, which is usually called social wealth, “Wealth of Nations,” etc. (Relative surplus-value is surplus-value obtained by shortening necessary labor-time, by making workers' necessities cheaper through higher productivity, so that more of a working day of given length is surplus labor.) Manufacture increases the social productive power of labor not only for the benefit of the capitalist instead of the worker, but it does this by crippling the individual workers. It creates new conditions for the rule of capital over labor. So if, on the one hand, it appears historically as progress and as a necessary phase in the economic development of society, on the other hand it is a refined and civilized method of exploitation.

<!-- ch14-p055 -->
Political economy (the science of economics as it was then called), which first arose as an independent science during the period of manufacture, views the social division of labor only from the standpoint of manufacture,[^14.53] and sees in it only a means of producing more commodities with a given quantity of labor, and so of cheapening commodities and speeding up the accumulation of capital (the turning of surplus-value back into capital, so that capital grows). In the sharpest contrast with this stress on quantity and exchange-value (the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for) stands the attitude of the writers of classical antiquity, who hold exclusively to quality and use-value.[^14.54] For them, as a result of the separation of the social branches of production, commodities are better made, people's various inclinations and talents choose a field that suits them,[^14.55] and without some restraint no important results can be achieved anywhere.[^14.56] Hence both product and producer are improved by the division of labor. If the growth of the quantity produced is occasionally mentioned, this is only with reference to a greater abundance of use-values. There is not a word about exchange-value or about the cheapening of commodities. This view, from the standpoint of use-value alone, is taken both by Plato,[^14.57] who treats the division of labor as the foundation of the division of society into classes, and by Xenophon[^14.58], who, with a characteristically bourgeois instinct, comes closer to the division of labor within the workshop. Plato's Republic, insofar as it treats the division of labor as the formative principle of the State, is merely the Athenian idealization of the Egyptian caste system. Egypt served as the model of an industrial country to many of his contemporaries too, among them Isocrates,[^14.59] and it kept this importance for the Greeks of the Roman Empire.[^14.60]

[^14.53]: The older writers, such as Petty and the anonymous author of “Advantages of the East India Trade,” bring out the capitalist character of the division of labor as applied in manufacture more than A. Smith does.

[^14.54]: Among the moderns, a few 18th-century writers may be excepted, such as Beccaria and James Harris, who almost entirely follow the ancients on the division of labor. Thus Beccaria: “Ciascuno prova coll’esperienza, che applicando la mano e l’ingegno sempre allo stesso genere di opere e di produtte, egli più facili, più abbondanti e migliori ne traca risultati, di quello che se ciascuno isolatamente le cose tutte a se necessarie soltanto facesse.... Dividendosi in tal maniera per la comune e privata utilità gli uomini in varie classi e condizioni.” [Everyone knows from experience that if he always applies his hand and his intelligence to the same kind of work and products, he gets results that come more easily, more abundantly, and better than if each person made, on his own, all the things he needs ... In this way men divide themselves into various classes and conditions, for the common and the private benefit.](Cesare Beccaria: “Elementi di Econ: Pubblica,” ed. Custodi, Parte Moderna, t. xi, p. 29.) James Harris, later Earl of Malmesbury, famous for the “Diaries” of his embassy at St. Petersburg, says in a note to his “Dialogue Concerning Happiness,” London, 1741, reprinted later in “Three Treatises, 3 Ed., Lond., 1772: “The whole argument to prove society natural (i.e., by division of employments) ... is taken from the second book of Plato’s Republic.”

[^14.55]: Thus in the Odyssey xiv., 228, [“Αλλος γαρ ταλλοισιν ανερ επιτερπεται εργοις” For different men take delight in different works] and Archilochus in Sextus Empiricus, [“αλλος αλλω επ εργο καρδιην ιαινεται.” each man has his heart cheered by a different work]

[^14.56]: [“Πολλ ηπισταιο εργα, χαχως δ ηπιστανο παντα.” He knew how to do many works, but did them all badly – Homer] Every Athenian considered himself superior to a Spartan as a producer of commodities; for in time of war the Spartan had men enough at his disposal but could not command money, as Thucydides makes Pericles say in the speech urging the Athenians into the Peloponnesian war: [“σωμασι τε ετοιμοτεροι οι αυτονργοι των αντηρωπων η χρημασι πολεμειν” people who produce for their own needs are readier to wage war with their bodies than with their money] (Thuc.: 1, I. c. 41.) Nevertheless, even in material production, [autarceia self-sufficiency], as opposed to the division of labor, remained their ideal, [“παρων γαρ το, ευ, παρα τουτων χαι το αυταρεσς.” For with the latter there is well-being, but with the former there is independence.] It should be mentioned here that at the time of the fall of the 30 Tyrants there were still not 5,000 Athenians without landed property.

[^14.57]: With Plato, the division of labor within the community develops out of the many-sided needs and the limited abilities of individuals. His main point is that the worker must adapt himself to the work, not the work to the worker. Adapting the work to the worker is unavoidable if he carries on several trades at once, which makes one or another of them secondary. [“Ου γαρ ετηελει το πραττομενον τεν του πραττονιος σχηολεν περιμενειν, αλλ αναγκε το ν πραττοντα το πραττομενο επακολοοτηειν με εν παρεργου μερει. Αναγκε. Εκ δε τουτον πλειο τε εκαστα γιγνεται και καλλιον και ραον, οταν εις εν καια πηψσιν και εν καιρο σχ ηολεν τον αλλον αγον, πραττε.”] [For the worker must wait on the work; the work will not wait on his leisure and let itself be done in a spare moment. — Yes, he must. — So the conclusion is that more of everything will be produced, and the work will be done more easily and better, when each man is freed from all other occupations to do, at the right time, the one thing he is naturally fitted for.] (Rep. 1. 2. Ed. Baiter, Orelli, etc.) Similarly in Thucydides, cited above, c. 142: “Seafaring is an art like any other, and cannot, as circumstances require, be carried on as a subsidiary occupation; nay, other subsidiary occupations cannot be carried on alongside of this one.” If the work, says Plato, has to wait for the worker, the critical point in the process is missed and the article is spoiled, “εργου χαιρον διολλυται.” [the right moment for the work is lost] The same Platonic idea turns up again in the protest of the English bleachers against the clause in the Factory Act that fixes mealtimes for all factory workers. Their business cannot wait on the convenience of the workers, for “in the various operations of singeing, washing, bleaching, mangling, calendering, and dyeing, none of them can be stopped at a given moment without risk of damage ... to enforce the same dinner hour for all the workpeople might occasionally subject valuable goods to the risk of danger by incomplete operations.” *Le platonisme où va-t-il se nicher!* [Where will Platonism turn up next!]

[^14.58]: Xenophon says that it is not only an honor to receive food from the table of the King of Persia, but that such food is also much tastier than other food. “And there is nothing wonderful in this, for as the other arts are brought to special perfection in the great towns, so the royal food is prepared in a special way. For in the small towns the same man makes bedsteads, doors, ploughs, and tables: often, too, he builds houses into the bargain, and is quite content if he finds custom [customers] sufficient for his sustenance. It is altogether impossible for a man who does so many things to do them all well. But in the great towns, where each can find many buyers, one trade is sufficient to maintain the man who carries it on. Nay, there is often not even need of one complete trade, but one man makes shoes for men, another for women. Here and there one man gets a living by sewing, another by cutting out shoes; one does nothing but cut out clothes, another nothing but sew the pieces together. It follows necessarily then, that he who does the simplest kind of work, undoubtedly does it better than anyone else. So it is with the art of cooking.” (Xen. Cyrop. I. viii., c. 2.) Here Xenophon stresses only the excellence to be achieved in use-value, although he knows well that the gradations of the division of labor depend on the extent of the market.

[^14.59]: He (Busiris) divided them all into special castes ... commanded that the same individuals should always carry on the same trade, for he knew that they who change their occupations become skilled in none; but that those who constantly stick to one occupation bring it to the highest perfection. In truth, we shall also find that in relation to the arts and handicrafts, they have outstripped their rivals more than a master does a bungler; and the contrivances for maintaining the monarchy and the other institutions of their State are so admirable that the most celebrated philosophers who treat of this subject praise the constitution of the Egyptian State above all others. (Isocrates, Busiris, c. 8.)

[^14.60]: Compare Diodorus Siculus.

<!-- ch14-p056 -->
During the manufacturing period proper, that is, the period in which manufacture is the predominant form taken by capitalist production, many obstacles stand in the way of the full development of manufacture's own peculiar tendencies. As we have already seen, manufacture creates a simple separation of the workers into skilled and unskilled, at the same time as it arranges them in a hierarchy of classes. Even so, the number of unskilled workers remains very limited, because of the predominant influence of the skilled. Manufacture adapts the detail operations to the different degrees of maturity, strength, and development of the living instruments of labor, and so tends toward the exploitation of women and children. Yet this tendency as a whole is wrecked on the habits and the resistance of the male workers. The splitting up of handicrafts lowers the cost of training the worker, and so lowers his value. Yet the more difficult detail work still needs a longer apprenticeship, and even where apprenticeship would be unnecessary, the workers jealously insist on it. In England, for example, we find the laws of apprenticeship, with their seven years' probation, in full force right down to the end of the manufacturing period; they are not thrown aside until modern industry arrives. Since handicraft skill is the foundation of manufacture, and since the mechanism of manufacture as a whole has no framework apart from the workers themselves, capital is constantly forced to wrestle with the insubordination of the workers.

<!-- ch14-p057 -->
> “By the infirmity of human nature,” says friend Ure, “it happens that the more skilful the workman, the more self-willed and intractable he is apt to become, and of course the less fit a component of a mechanical system in which ... he may do great damage to the whole”[^14.61]

[^14.61]: Ure, cited above, p. 20.

<!-- ch14-p058 -->
Hence, throughout the whole manufacturing period, there runs the complaint that the workers lack discipline[^14.62]. And even if we did not have the testimony of contemporary writers, the simple facts would speak volumes: that between the 16th century and the epoch of modern industry, capital failed to become master of all the working time the manufacturing workers had available; that manufacturing workshops are short-lived; and that they change their location from one country to another as the workers emigrate or immigrate. “Order must in one way or another be established,” exclaims the often-cited author of the “Essay on Trade and Commerce” in 1770. “Order,” echoes Dr. Andrew Ure 66 years later, “Order” was lacking in manufacture based on “the scholastic dogma of division of labour,” and “Arkwright created order.”

[^14.62]: This is more the case in England than in France, and more in France than in Holland.

<!-- ch14-p059 -->
At the same time, manufacture was unable either to take hold of the production of society in its full extent or to revolutionize that production to its very core. It towered up as an economic work of art on the broad foundation of the town handicrafts and the rural domestic industries. At a certain stage of its development, the narrow technical basis on which manufacture rested came into conflict with requirements of production that manufacture itself had created.

<!-- ch14-p060 -->
One of its most finished creations was the workshop for producing the instruments of labor themselves, including above all the complicated mechanical apparatus already in use at the time.

<!-- ch14-p061 -->
> A machine-factory, says Ure, “displayed the division of labour in manifold gradations ‒ the file, the drill, the lathe, having each its different workman in the order of skill.” (P. 21.)

<!-- ch14-p062 -->
This workshop, the product of the division of labor in manufacture, produced in its turn ‒ machines. It is machines that sweep away the craftsman's work as the regulating principle of social production. Thus, on the one hand, the technical reason for tying the worker for life to one detail function is removed. On the other hand, the fetters that this same principle laid on the rule of capital fall away.

## Chapter 15: Machinery and Modern Industry

### Section 1 : The Development of Machinery

<!-- ch15-p001 -->
John Stuart Mill says in his “Principles of Political Economy” (political economy is the science of economics as it was then called):

<!-- ch15-p002 -->
> “It is questionable if all the mechanical inventions yet made have lightened the day’s toil of any human being.”[^15.1]

[^15.1]: Mill should have said “of any human being not fed by other people’s labor,” for machinery has, without doubt, greatly increased the number of well-to-do idlers.

<!-- ch15-p003 -->
But that is by no means the aim of the capitalist use of machinery. Like every other increase in the productivity of labor, machinery is meant to make commodities cheaper and, by shortening the part of the working day in which the worker works for himself, to lengthen the other part, the part that he gives to the capitalist without an equivalent. In short, it is a means of producing surplus-value. (The productivity of labor is how much a given amount of labor produces in a given time. A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, that is, sold, not for the producer's own use. The working day is the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor. Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it.)

<!-- ch15-p004 -->
In manufacture, the revolution in the mode of production begins with labor-power; in modern industry, it begins with the instruments of labor. (Manufacture is the stage and form of capitalist production, roughly from the mid-16th to the late 18th century, based on handicraft work divided among many workers in one workshop. Modern industry is large-scale production based on machinery and the factory system. Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist.) So our first question is: how are the instruments of labor turned from tools into machines? Or, what is the difference between a machine and the implements of a handicraft? We are concerned here only with striking and general characteristics. For epochs in the history of society are no more separated from each other by hard and fast dividing lines than geological epochs are.

<!-- ch15-p005 -->
