Mathematicians and specialists in mechanics, followed in this by a few English economists, call a tool a simple machine and a machine a complex tool. They see no essential difference between them. They even give the name of machine to the simple mechanical powers: the lever, the inclined plane, the screw, the wedge, etc.[^15.2] In fact, every machine is a combination of those simple powers, however they may be disguised. From the economic point of view this explanation is worth nothing, because it lacks the historical element. Another explanation of the difference between tool and machine is this: with a tool, man is the motive power, while the motive power of a machine is something other than man, for example an animal, water, wind, and so on.[^15.3] On this view, a plow drawn by oxen, a device common to the most different epochs, would be a machine. Claussen's circular loom, on the other hand, which is worked by a single worker and weaves 96,000 picks per minute, would be a mere tool. Indeed, this very loom would be a tool when worked by hand, but a machine if worked by steam. And since the use of animal power is one of man's earliest inventions, production by machinery would have come before production by handicrafts. When John Wyatt brought out his spinning machine in 1735, and began the industrial revolution of the 18th century, he did not say a word about a donkey driving it instead of a man. And yet this part fell to the donkey. He described it as a machine “to spin without fingers.”[^15.4]

[^15.2]: See, for example, Hutton: “Course of Mathematics.”

[^15.3]: “From this point of view we may draw a sharp line of distinction between a tool and a machine: spades, hammers, chisels, &c., combinations of levers and of screws, in all of which, no matter how complicated they may be in other respects, man is the motive power, ... all this falls under the idea of a tool; but the plough, which is drawn by animal power, and wind-mills, &c., must be classed among machines.” (Wilhelm Schulz: “Die Bewegung der Produktion.” Zürich, 1843, p. 38.) In many respects a book worth recommending.

[^15.4]: Spinning machines, though very imperfect ones, had already been used before his time, and Italy was probably the country where they first appeared. A critical history of technology would show how little any of the inventions of the 18th century is the work of a single individual. So far there is no such book. Darwin has interested us in the history of Nature's Technology, that is, in the formation of the organs of plants and animals, organs that serve as instruments of production for sustaining life. Does not the history of the productive organs of man, organs that are the material basis of all social organization, deserve equal attention? And would not such a history be easier to compile, since, as Vico says, human history differs from natural history in this: we have made the former, but not the latter? Technology reveals how man deals with Nature, the process of production by which he sustains his life. In doing so it also lays bare how his social relations are formed, and how the mental conceptions that flow from them are formed. Even every history of religion that fails to take account of this material basis is uncritical. It is, in reality, much easier to discover by analysis the earthly core of the misty creations of religion than to do the reverse: to develop, from the actual relations of life, the heavenly forms that correspond to those relations. This second method is the only materialist, and therefore the only scientific, one. The weak points in the abstract materialism of natural science, a materialism that leaves out history and its process, show at once in the abstract and ideological conceptions of its spokesmen whenever they venture beyond the bounds of their own specialty.

<!-- ch15-p006 -->
All fully developed machinery consists of three essentially different parts: the motor mechanism, the transmitting mechanism, and finally the tool or working machine. The motor mechanism is what sets the whole in motion. Either it generates its own motive power, like the steam-engine, the caloric (hot-air) engine, the electromagnetic machine, etc., or it is driven by some natural force that already exists, as the water-wheel is by a head of water, the wind-mill by wind, etc. The transmitting mechanism is made up of fly-wheels, shafting, toothed wheels, pulleys, straps, ropes, bands, pinions, and gearing of the most varied kinds. It regulates the motion, changes its form where necessary, for example from straight-line to circular, and divides and distributes it among the working machines. These first two parts of the whole mechanism are there only to set the working machines in motion, and by means of this motion the object of labor is seized and changed as desired. The tool or working machine is the part of the machinery with which the industrial revolution of the 18th century started. And to this day it constantly serves as such a starting-point whenever a handicraft, or a manufacture, is turned into an industry carried on by machinery.

<!-- ch15-p007 -->
If we look more closely at the working machine proper, we find in it, as a general rule, though often, no doubt, in very altered forms, the apparatus and tools used by the craftsman or by the worker in manufacture. The difference is that instead of being human implements, they are the implements of a mechanism, or mechanical implements. Either the entire machine is only a more or less altered mechanical edition of the old handicraft tool, as with the power-loom,[^15.5] or the working parts fitted into the frame of the machine are old acquaintances, as spindles are in a mule, needles in a stocking-loom, saws in a sawing-machine, and knives in a chopping machine. The distinction between these tools and the body proper of the machine exists from their very birth. For the tools mostly continue to be produced by handicraft or by manufacture, and are fitted afterwards into the body of the machine, which is the product of machinery.[^15.6] The machine proper is therefore a mechanism that, once set in motion, performs with its tools the same operations that the worker formerly performed with similar tools. Whether the motive power comes from man or from some other machine makes no difference in this respect. From the moment the tool proper is taken from man and fitted into a mechanism, a machine takes the place of a mere implement. The difference strikes one at once, even in cases where man himself remains the prime mover. The number of implements that he himself can use at the same time is limited by the number of his own natural instruments of production, by the number of his bodily organs. In Germany they tried at first to make one spinner work two spinning-wheels, that is, to work with both hands and both feet at the same time. This was too difficult. Later a treadle spinning-wheel with two spindles was invented, but skilled spinners who could spin two threads at once were almost as rare as two-headed men. The Jenny, on the other hand, spun with 12-18 spindles even at its very birth, and the stocking-loom knits with many thousand needles at once. From the very first, the number of tools that a machine can bring into play at the same time is freed from the organic limits that hem in the tools of a craftsman.

[^15.5]: Especially in the original form of the power-loom, we recognize the ancient loom at first glance. In its modern form, the power-loom has undergone essential changes.

[^15.6]: Only during the last 15 years (that is, since about 1850) has a constantly growing share of these machine tools been made in England by machinery, and not by the same manufacturers who make the machines. Examples of machines for making these mechanical tools are the automatic bobbin-making engine, the cardsetting engine, shuttle-making machines, and machines for forging mule and throstle spindles.

<!-- ch15-p008 -->
In many hand implements the distinction between man as mere motive power and man as the worker or operator properly so called stands out in striking contrast. For example, the foot is merely the prime mover of the spinning-wheel, while the hand, working with the spindle, drawing and twisting, performs the real operation of spinning. It is this last part of the craftsman's implement that the industrial revolution seizes first. It leaves the worker, in addition to his new labor of watching the machine with his eyes and correcting its mistakes with his hands, the merely mechanical part of being the moving power. On the other hand, there are implements for which man has always acted as a simple motive power, for example by turning the crank of a mill,[^15.7] by pumping, by moving the arm of a bellows up and down, by pounding with a mortar, etc. Such implements soon call for the use of animals, water[^15.8] and wind as motive powers. Here and there, long before the period of manufacture, and also to some extent during that period, these implements pass over into machines, but without causing any revolution in the mode of production. In the period of modern industry it becomes clear that these implements, even in their form as hand tools, are already machines. For example, the pumps with which the Dutch emptied the Lake of Harlem in 1836-7 were built on the principle of ordinary pumps. The only difference was that their pistons were driven by giant, Cyclops-like steam-engines instead of by men. In England the blacksmith's common and very imperfect bellows is occasionally turned into a blowing-engine by connecting its arm to a steam-engine. The steam-engine itself, as it was when it was invented during the manufacturing period at the close of the 17th century, and as it remained down to 1780,[^15.9] did not give rise to any industrial revolution. On the contrary, it was the invention of machines that made a revolution in the form of steam-engines necessary. As soon as man, instead of working with an implement on the object of his labor, becomes merely the motive power of an implement-machine, it is a mere accident that the motive power is disguised as human muscle; it may equally well take the form of wind, water or steam. Of course, this does not prevent such a change of form from producing great technical changes in a mechanism that was originally built to be driven by man alone. Nowadays all machines that still have their way to make, such as sewing-machines, bread-making machines, etc., are built to be driven both by human and by purely mechanical motive power, unless their very nature rules out their use on a small scale.

[^15.7]: Moses says: “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treads the corn.” The Christian philanthropists of Germany, on the contrary, fastened a wooden board around the necks of the serfs whom they used as a motive power for grinding, to keep them from putting flour into their mouths with their hands.

[^15.8]: It was partly the lack of streams with a good fall, and partly their battles with too much water in other respects, that forced the Dutch to turn to wind as a motive power. They got the wind-mill itself from Germany. There its invention started a pretty squabble among the nobles, the priests, and the emperor over which of the three the wind “belonged” to. The air makes bondage, was the cry in Germany, at the same time as the wind was making Holland free. What it reduced to bondage in this case was not the Dutchman, but the land for the Dutchman. In 1836, 12,000 windmills of 6,000 horse-power were still used in Holland to keep two-thirds of the land from turning back into swamps.

[^15.9]: It was, indeed, greatly improved by Watt's first, so-called single-acting engine. But in this form it remained a mere machine for raising water, and brine from salt mines.

<!-- ch15-p009 -->
The machine that is the starting-point of the industrial revolution replaces the worker who handles a single tool with a mechanism that operates with a number of similar tools and is set in motion by a single motive power, whatever form that power may take.[^15.10] Here we have the machine, but only as an elementary factor of production by machinery.

[^15.10]: “The union of all these simple instruments, set in motion by a single motor, constitutes a machine.” (Babbage, cited above.)

<!-- ch15-p010 -->
An increase in the size of the machine and in the number of its working tools calls for a more massive mechanism to drive it. To overcome its resistance, this mechanism needs a mightier moving power than man's, quite apart from the fact that man is a very imperfect instrument for producing uniform, continuous motion. But assume that he is acting simply as a motor, that a machine has taken the place of his tool: then clearly natural forces can replace him. Of all the great motors handed down from the manufacturing period, horse-power is the worst, partly because a horse has a head of his own, partly because he is costly, and the extent to which he can be used in factories is very limited.[^15.11] Nevertheless the horse was widely used in the infancy of modern industry. This is proved both by the complaints of agriculturists of the time and by the term “horse-power,” which has survived to this day as an expression for mechanical force.

[^15.11]: In January, 1861, John C. Morton read a paper before the Society of Arts on “The forces employed in agriculture.” In it he says: “Every improvement that furthers the uniformity of the land makes the steam-engine more and more applicable to the production of pure mechanical force.... Horse-power is requisite wherever crooked fences and other obstructions prevent uniform action. These obstructions are vanishing day by day. For operations that demand more exercise of will than actual force, the only power applicable is that controlled every instant by the human mind – in other words, man-power.” Mr. Morton then reduces steam-power, horse-power, and man-power to the unit generally used for steam-engines, namely the force needed to raise 33,000 lbs. one foot in one minute. He reckons the cost of one horse-power from a steam-engine at 3d. per hour, and from a horse at 5½d. per hour. Further, if a horse is to stay fully healthy, it can work no more than 8 hours a day. By using steam-power, at least three out of every seven horses used on tillage land during the year can be done without, at a cost no greater than what the horses done without would cost during the 3 or 4 months in which alone they can be used effectively. Lastly, in those farming operations in which steam-power can be used, it improves the quality of the work compared with horse-power. To do the work of a steam-engine would take 66 men, at a total cost of 15s. an hour, and to do the work of a horse, 32 men, at a total cost of 8s. an hour.

<!-- ch15-p011 -->
Wind was too unsteady and uncontrollable. Besides, in England, the birthplace of modern industry, the use of water power predominated even during the manufacturing period. In the 17th century attempts had already been made to turn two pairs of millstones with a single water-wheel. But the larger gearing was too much for the water power, which had now become insufficient, and this was one of the circumstances that led to a more exact investigation of the laws of friction. In the same way, in mills set in motion by pushing and pulling a lever, the irregularity caused by the motive power led to the theory and the application of the fly-wheel, which later plays so important a part in modern industry.[^15.12] In this way the first scientific and technical elements of modern mechanical industry were developed during the manufacturing period. Arkwright's throstle spinning mill was turned by water from the very first. But for all that, the use of water as the predominant motive power was beset with difficulties. It could not be increased at will, it failed at certain seasons of the year, and, above all, it was essentially local.[^15.13] Not until the invention of Watt's second, so-called double-acting steam-engine was a prime mover found that produced its own force by consuming coal and water, and whose power was entirely under man's control. It was mobile and a means of locomotion. It was urban and not, like the water-wheel, rural. It allowed production to be concentrated in towns, instead of being scattered up and down the country as with the water-wheels.[^15.14] It could be applied to every kind of technical use, and, relatively speaking, local circumstances had little effect on its choice of location. The greatness of Watt's genius showed itself in the specification of the patent that he took out in April, 1784. In that specification his steam-engine is described, not as an invention for a specific purpose, but as an agent that can be applied universally in mechanical industry. In it he points out uses, many of which, such as the steam-hammer, were not introduced until half a century later. Nevertheless he doubted that steam-engines could be used in navigation. His successors, Boulton and Watt, sent steam-engines of colossal size for ocean steamers to the exhibition of 1851.

[^15.12]: Faulhaber, 1625; De Caus, 1688.

[^15.13]: The modern turbine frees the industrial exploitation of water-power from many of its former fetters.

[^15.14]: “In the early days of textile manufactures, the locality of the factory depended upon the existence of a stream having a sufficient fall to turn a water-wheel; and, although the establishment of the water-mills was the commencement of the breaking up of the domestic system of manufacture, yet the mills necessarily situated upon streams, and frequently at considerable distances the one from the other, formed part of a rural, rather than an urban system; and it was not until the introduction of the steam-power as a substitute for the stream that factories were congregated in towns, and localities where the coal and water required for the production of steam were found in sufficient quantities. The steam-engine is the parent of manufacturing towns.” (A. Redgrave in “Reports of the Insp. of Fact., 30th April, 1860,” p. 36.)

<!-- ch15-p012 -->
As soon as tools had been turned from hand implements of man into implements of a mechanical apparatus, of a machine, the motive mechanism also took on an independent form, entirely freed from the limits of human strength. With that, the individual machine that we have been considering so far sinks into a mere factor in production by machinery. One motive mechanism could now drive many machines at once. The motive mechanism grows with the number of machines that are turned at the same time, and the transmitting mechanism becomes a wide-spreading apparatus.

<!-- ch15-p013 -->
We now go on to distinguish the cooperation of a number of machines of one kind from a complex system of machinery.

<!-- ch15-p014 -->
In the first case, a single machine makes the whole product. It performs all the different operations that were previously done by one craftsman with his tool (for instance, by a weaver with his loom), or by several craftsmen one after another, either separately or as members of a system of manufacture.[^15.15] For example, in the manufacture of envelopes, one man folded the paper with the folder, another put on the gum, a third turned over the flap on which the emblem is stamped, a fourth embossed the emblem, and so on; and for each of these operations the envelope had to change hands. Now one single envelope machine performs all these operations at once, and makes more than 3,000 envelopes in an hour. At the London exhibition of 1862 there was an American machine for making paper cones. It cut the paper, pasted, folded, and finished 300 of them a minute. Here the whole process, which was split up into a series of operations and carried out by them when it was carried on as manufacture, is completed by a single machine working a combination of various tools. Now, such a machine may be merely a reproduction of a complicated hand tool, or it may be a combination of various simple tools that manufacture had specialized. In either case, in the factory, that is, in the workshop in which only machinery is used, we meet simple cooperation again. Leaving the worker out of consideration for the moment, this cooperation appears to us, at first, as the bringing together in one place of similar machines working at the same time. Thus a weaving factory is made up of a number of power-looms working side by side, and a sewing factory of a number of sewing-machines all in the same building. But here the whole system has a technical unity, because all the machines receive their impulse at the same time, and to an equal degree, from the beats of the common prime mover, through the transmitting mechanism. And this mechanism is also, to a certain extent, common to them all, since only particular branches of it branch off to each machine. So, just as a number of tools form the organs of a machine, a number of machines of one kind form the organs of the motive mechanism.

[^15.15]: From the standpoint of the division of labor in manufacture (the splitting of the making of one product into many separate tasks, each done by a specialized worker), weaving was not simple manual labor. On the contrary, it was complicated manual labor, and so the power-loom is a machine that does very complicated work. It is completely wrong to suppose that modern machinery at first took over only those operations that division of labor had simplified. During the manufacturing period, spinning and weaving were split up into new varieties, and their tools were modified and improved; but the labor itself was in no way divided, and it kept its handicraft character. It is not the labor, but the instrument of labor, that serves as the starting-point of the machine.

<!-- ch15-p015 -->
A real system of machinery, however, does not take the place of these independent machines until the object of labor goes through a connected series of detail processes, carried out by a chain of machines of different kinds, each one supplementing the other. Here we have once more the cooperation by division of labor that is typical of manufacture; only now it is a combination of detail machines. The special tools of the various detail workers (workers who each spend their whole working life performing one small part of a larger process), such as those of the beaters, combers, spinners, etc., in the wool manufacture, are now turned into the tools of specialized machines. Each machine forms a special organ, with a special function, in the system. In those branches of industry where the machinery system is first introduced, manufacture itself provides, in a general way, the natural basis for the division of the process of production, and so for its organization.[^15.16] Nevertheless an essential difference shows itself at once. In manufacture, it is the workers who, with their hand tools, must carry on each particular detail process, either singly or in groups. If, on the one hand, the worker becomes adapted to the process, on the other hand the process was first made to suit the worker. This subjective principle of the division of labor no longer exists in production by machinery. Here the process as a whole is examined objectively, in itself, that is, without regard to the question of how human hands would carry it out, and it is analyzed into its component phases. The problem of how to carry out each detail process, and how to bind them all into a whole, is solved with the help of machines, chemistry, etc.[^15.17] But of course here too the theory must be perfected by experience accumulated on a large scale. Each detail machine supplies raw material to the next machine in line. Since they are all working at the same time, the product is always going through the various stages of its making, and is also constantly passing from one phase to another. In manufacture, the direct cooperation of the detail workers sets up a numerical proportion between the special groups. In the same way, in an organized system of machinery, where one detail machine constantly keeps another busy, a fixed relation is set up between their numbers, their size, and their speed. The collective machine is now an organized system of various kinds of single machines, and of groups of single machines. It becomes more and more perfect the more the process as a whole becomes a continuous one, that is, the less the raw material is interrupted on its way from its first phase to its last; in other words, the more its passage from one phase to another is carried out, not by the hand of man, but by the machinery itself. In manufacture, the isolation of each detail process is a condition imposed by the nature of division of labor; in the fully developed factory, on the contrary, the continuity of those processes is essential.

[^15.16]: Before the era of mechanical industry, the wool manufacture was the leading manufacture in England. Hence it was in this industry that most of the experiments were made, in the first half of the 18th century. Cotton, which needed less careful preparation before machines could work it, benefited from the experience gained on wool; just as, later, the processing of wool by machinery was developed along the lines of cotton-spinning and weaving by machinery. It was only in the 10 years immediately before 1866 that isolated parts of the wool manufacture, such as wool-combing, were brought into the factory system (production in which a system of machines, driven by a central power source, does the work and workers attend the machines). “The application of power to the process of combing wool ... extensively in operation since the introduction of the combingmachine, especially Lister’s ... undoubtedly had the effect of throwing a very large number of men out of work. Wool was formerly combed by hand, most frequently in the cottage of the comber. It is now very generally combed in the factory, and hand-labour is superseded, except in some particular kinds of work, in which hand-combed wool is still preferred. Many of the hand-combers found employment in the factories, but the produce of the hand-combers bears so small a proportion to that of the machine, that the employment of a very large number of combers has passed away.” (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct., 1856,” p. 16.)

[^15.17]: “The principle of the factory system, then, is to substitute ... the partition of a process into its essential constituents, for the division or graduation of labour among artisans.” (Andrew Ure: “The Philosophy of Manufactures,” London, 1835, p. 20.)

<!-- ch15-p016 -->
A system of machinery may rest on the mere cooperation of similar machines, as in weaving, or on a combination of different machines, as in spinning. Either way, it forms in itself one huge automaton whenever it is driven by a self-acting prime mover. But although the factory as a whole may be driven by its steam-engine, some of the individual machines may still need the worker's help for some of their movements. (Such help was needed for running in the mule carriage before the invention of the self-acting mule, and is still needed in fine-spinning mills.) Or else, to let a machine do its work, certain parts of it may have to be handled by the worker like a hand tool; this was the case in machine-makers' workshops before the slide rest was turned into a self-actor. As soon as a machine carries out, without man's help, all the movements needed to work up the raw material, and needs only his attendance, we have an automatic system of machinery, and one that can be constantly improved in its details. Such improvements as the device that stops a drawing frame whenever a sliver breaks, and the self-acting stop that halts the power-loom as soon as the shuttle bobbin runs out of weft, are quite modern inventions. As an example both of continuous production and of the carrying out of the automatic principle, we may take a modern paper mill. In the paper industry generally, we can usefully study in detail not only the differences between modes of production based on different means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things), but also the connection between the social conditions of production and those modes. For the old German paper-making gives us a sample of handicraft production; that of Holland in the 17th and of France in the 18th century, a sample of manufacture in the strict sense; and that of modern England, a sample of the automatic making of this article. Besides these, there still exist in India and China two distinct ancient Asiatic forms of the same industry.

<!-- ch15-p017 -->
An organized system of machines, which receives its motion through the transmitting mechanism from a central automaton, is the most developed form of production by machinery. Here, in place of the isolated machine, we have a mechanical monster whose body fills whole factories. His demon power, at first veiled under the slow and measured motions of his giant limbs, at last breaks out into the fast and furious whirl of his countless working organs.

<!-- ch15-p018 -->
There were mules and steam-engines before there were any workers whose only occupation was to make mules and steam-engines, just as men wore clothes before there were such people as tailors. The inventions of Vaucanson, Arkwright, Watt, and others were, however, workable only because these inventors found ready to hand a considerable number of skilled mechanical workers, placed at their disposal by the manufacturing period. Some of these workers were independent craftsmen of various trades; others were grouped together in manufacturing workshops, in which, as mentioned before, division of labor was strictly carried out. As inventions grew in number, and the demand for the newly discovered machines grew larger, the machine-making industry split up more and more into numerous independent branches, and division of labor in these manufacturing workshops developed further and further. Here, then, we see in manufacture the immediate technical foundation of modern industry. Manufacture produced the machinery by means of which modern industry abolished the handicraft and manufacturing systems in those spheres of production that it first seized upon. So the factory system was raised, in the natural course of things, on an inadequate foundation. When the system reached a certain degree of development, it had to root up this ready-made foundation, which in the meantime had been worked out further along the old lines, and to build up for itself a basis that would correspond to its own methods of production. The individual machine stays dwarfish as long as it is worked by human power alone, and no system of machinery could be properly developed before the steam-engine took the place of the earlier motive powers: animals, wind, and even water. In just the same way, modern industry was crippled in its full development as long as its characteristic instrument of production, the machine, owed its existence to personal strength and personal skill, and depended on the muscular development, the keenness of sight, and the cunning of hand with which the detail workers in manufacturing workshops, and the manual workers in handicrafts, wielded their dwarfish tools. Thus, apart from the expense of machines made in this way (a circumstance that is always present to the mind of the capitalist), the expansion of industries carried on by machinery, and the invasion of new branches of production by machinery, depended on the growth of a class of workers who, because their work was almost an art, could increase their numbers only gradually, and not by leaps and bounds. But besides this, at a certain stage of its development, modern industry became technically incompatible with the basis that handicraft and manufacture had provided for it. The prime movers, the transmitting mechanism, and the machines proper kept growing in size. The details of these machines became more complicated, more varied, and more regular, as they departed more and more from the model of the machines originally made by hand labor, and took on a form restricted by nothing except the conditions under which they worked.[^15.18] The automatic system had to be perfected. And a more stubborn material, such as iron instead of wood, had to be used, which became more unavoidable every day. These problems sprang up by force of circumstances, and the solution of all of them everywhere met with a stumbling-block in personal limitations, which even the collective worker (the whole body of workers, combined, treated as one productive mechanism) of manufacture could break through only to a limited extent. Machines such as the modern hydraulic press, the modern power-loom, and the modern carding engine could never have been supplied by manufacture.

[^15.18]: The power-loom was at first made mainly of wood; in its improved modern form it is made of iron. How far the old forms of the instruments of production influenced their new forms at the start is shown, among other things, by even the most superficial comparison of the present power-loom with the old one, and of the modern blowing apparatus of a blast-furnace with the first, inefficient mechanical copy of the ordinary bellows. It is shown perhaps more strikingly than in any other way by the attempts, before the present locomotive was invented, to build a locomotive that actually had two feet, which it raised from the ground one after the other, like a horse. Only after considerable development of the science of mechanics, and accumulated practical experience, does the form of a machine become settled entirely in accordance with mechanical principles, and freed from the traditional form of the tool that gave rise to it.

<!-- ch15-p019 -->
A radical change in the mode of production in one sphere of industry brings with it a similar change in other spheres. This happens at first in those branches of industry that are linked together as separate phases of one process, and yet are isolated by the social division of labor in such a way that each of them produces an independent commodity. Thus spinning by machinery made weaving by machinery a necessity, and both together made imperative the mechanical and chemical revolution that took place in bleaching, printing, and dyeing. So too, on the other hand, the revolution in cotton-spinning called forth the invention of the gin, for separating the seeds from the cotton fiber. Only by means of this invention did it become possible to produce cotton on the enormous scale now required.[^15.19] But above all, the revolution in the modes of production of industry and agriculture made necessary a revolution in the general conditions of the social process of production, that is, in the means of communication and transport. In a society whose pivot, to use an expression of Fourier's, was small-scale agriculture, with its subsidiary domestic industries, and the urban handicrafts, the means of communication and transport were so utterly inadequate to the productive needs of the manufacturing period, with its extended division of social labor, its concentration of the instruments of labor and of the workers, and its colonial markets, that they were in fact revolutionized. In the same way, the means of communication and transport handed down from the manufacturing period soon became unbearable fetters on modern industry, with its feverish haste of production, its enormous extent, its constant flinging of capital (value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger) and labor from one sphere of production into another, and its newly created connections with the markets of the whole world. Hence, apart from the radical changes made in the construction of sailing ships, the means of communication and transport were gradually adapted to the modes of production of mechanical industry, by the creation of a system of river steamers, railways, ocean steamers, and telegraphs. But the huge masses of iron that now had to be forged, welded, cut, bored, and shaped demanded, for their part, giant, Cyclops-like machines, and the methods of the manufacturing period were utterly inadequate for building them.

[^15.19]: Eli Whitney's cotton gin had, until very recently, undergone fewer essential changes than any other machine of the 18th century. Only in the last decade (that is, since 1856) has another American, Mr. Emery, of Albany, New York, made Whitney's gin out of date by an improvement as simple as it is effective.

<!-- ch15-p020 -->
So modern industry had to take the machine, its characteristic instrument of production, into its own hands, and to build machines by machines. Only when it did this did it build up a fitting technical foundation for itself and stand on its own feet. In the first decades of this century, as the use of machinery increased, machinery by degrees took over the making of machines proper. But it was only in the decade before 1866 that the building of railways and ocean steamers on a stupendous scale called into existence the Cyclops-like machines now used in building prime movers.

<!-- ch15-p021 -->
The most essential condition for producing machines by machines was a prime mover capable of exerting any amount of force, and yet under perfect control. The steam-engine already met this condition. But at the same time it was necessary to produce the geometrically exact straight lines, planes, circles, cylinders, cones, and spheres that the detail parts of the machines required. Henry Maudsley solved this problem in the first decade of this century by inventing the slide rest. This tool was soon made automatic, and in a modified form it was applied to other construction machines besides the lathe, for which it was originally intended. This mechanical device replaces, not some particular tool, but the hand itself, which produces a given form by holding and guiding the cutting tool along the iron or other material being worked on. Thus it became possible to produce the forms of the individual parts of machinery

<!-- ch15-p022 -->
> “with a degree of ease, accuracy, and speed, that no accumulated experience of the hand of the most skilled workman could give.”[^15.20]

[^15.20]: “The Industry of Nations,” London, 1855, Part II., p. 239. This work also remarks: ‘Simple and outwardly unimportant as this appendage to lathes may appear, it is not, we believe, averring [claiming] too much to state, that its influence in improving and extending the use of machinery has been as great as that produced by Watt’s improvements of the steam-engine itself. Its introduction went at once to perfect all machinery, to cheapen it, and to stimulate invention and improvement.”

<!-- ch15-p023 -->
If we now turn our attention to that part of the machinery used in building machines which forms the operating tool, we find the hand tools reappearing, but on a Cyclops-like scale. The operating part of the boring machine is an immense drill driven by a steam-engine; and without this machine, on the other hand, the cylinders of large steam-engines and of hydraulic presses could not be made. The mechanical lathe is only a Cyclops-like reproduction of the ordinary foot-lathe. The planing machine is an iron carpenter that works on iron with the same tools that the human carpenter uses on wood. The instrument that cuts the veneers on the London wharves is a gigantic razor. The tool of the shearing machine, which shears iron as easily as a tailor's scissors cut cloth, is a monster pair of scissors. And the steam-hammer works with an ordinary hammer head, but one so heavy that not Thor himself could wield it.[^15.21] These steam-hammers are an invention of Nasmyth. There is one that weighs over 6 tons and strikes with a vertical fall of 7 feet onto an anvil weighing 36 tons. It is mere child's play for it to crush a block of granite to powder, yet it is just as capable of driving a nail into a piece of soft wood with a series of light taps.[^15.22]

[^15.21]: One of these machines, used in London for forging paddle-wheel shafts, is called “Thor.” It forges a shaft of 16½ tons as easily as a blacksmith forges a horseshoe.

[^15.22]: Woodworking machines that can also be used on a small scale are mostly American inventions.

<!-- ch15-p024 -->
The instruments of labor, in the form of machinery, make it necessary to replace human force with natural forces, and rule of thumb with the conscious application of science. In manufacture, the organization of the social labor process (the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things) is purely subjective: it is a combination of detail workers. In its machinery system, modern industry has a productive organism that is purely objective, in which the worker becomes a mere appendage to an already existing material condition of production. In simple cooperation, and even in cooperation based on division of labor, the suppression of the isolated worker by the collective worker still appears to be more or less accidental. Machinery, with a few exceptions to be mentioned later, operates only by means of associated labor, or labor in common. Hence the cooperative character of the labor process is, in the case of machinery, a technical necessity dictated by the instrument of labor itself.

### Section 2: The Value Transferred by Machinery to the Product

<!-- ch15-p025 -->
We saw that the productive forces that come from cooperation and division of labor cost capital nothing. They are natural forces of social labor. In the same way, physical forces like steam, water, etc., cost nothing when they are taken over for productive processes. But just as a man needs lungs to breathe with, he needs something made by human hands in order to consume physical forces productively. A water-wheel is needed to exploit the force of water, and a steam-engine to exploit the elasticity of steam. Once discovered, the law of the deviation of the magnetic needle in the field of an electric current, or the law of the magnetization of iron around which an electric current circulates, never costs a penny.[^15.23] But exploiting these laws for telegraphy, etc., requires a costly and extensive apparatus. The tool, as we have seen, is not wiped out by the machine. From being a dwarf implement of the human organism, it expands and multiplies into the implement of a mechanism created by man. Capital now sets the worker to work, not with a hand tool, but with a machine that itself handles the tools. So it is clear at first glance that modern industry, by bringing both enormous physical forces and the natural sciences into the process of production, raises the productivity of labor to an extraordinary degree. But it is by no means equally clear that this increased productive force is not, on the other hand, bought with an increased expenditure of labor. Machinery, like every other component of constant capital (the part of capital spent on means of production; its value is passed on to the product but does not grow), creates no new value, but gives up its own value to the product that it helps to produce. Insofar as the machine has value, and so passes value on to the product, it forms an element in the value of that product. Instead of being made cheaper, the product is made dearer in proportion to the value of the machine. And it is as clear as noonday that machines and systems of machinery, the characteristic instruments of labor of modern industry, are incomparably more loaded with value than the implements used in handicrafts and in manufacture.

[^15.23]: Science, generally speaking, costs the capitalist nothing, a fact that by no means stops him from exploiting it. Capital annexes the science of others just as it annexes the labor of others. However, capitalist appropriation and personal appropriation, whether of science or of material wealth, are totally different things. Dr. Ure himself laments the gross ignorance of mechanical science among his dear machinery-exploiting manufacturers, and Liebig has a tale to tell about the astounding ignorance of chemistry shown by English chemical manufacturers.

<!-- ch15-p026 -->
In the first place, we must note that the machinery always enters the labor process as a whole, but enters the value-creating process only bit by bit. It never adds more value than it loses, on average, by wear and tear. So there is a great difference between the value of a machine and the value that machine transfers to the product in a given time. The longer the machine's life in the labor process, the greater that difference. It is true, no doubt, as we have already seen, that every instrument of labor enters the labor process as a whole, and enters the value-creating process only piecemeal, in proportion to its average daily loss by wear and tear. But this difference between the instrument as a whole and its daily wear and tear is much greater in a machine than in a tool. There are three reasons. First, the machine is made of more durable material, so it lasts longer. Second, its use is regulated by strictly scientific laws, which allows greater economy in the wear and tear of its parts and in the materials it consumes. And lastly, its field of production is incomparably larger than that of a tool. Once we allow, for both the machine and the tool, for their average daily cost, that is, for the value they pass on to the product through their average daily wear and tear, and also for their consumption of auxiliary substances such as oil, coal, and so on, each of them does its work free of charge, just like the forces that Nature supplies without the help of man. The greater the productive power of the machinery compared with that of the tool, the greater the extent of its free service compared with that of the tool. In modern industry, human beings succeeded for the first time in making the product of their past labor work on a large scale free of charge, like the forces of Nature.[^15.24]

[^15.24]: Ricardo puts such stress on this effect of machinery that he sometimes loses sight of the value that machines give up to the product, and puts machines on the same footing as natural forces. (In other connections he takes no more notice of this effect than he does of the general distinction between the labor process and the process of creating surplus-value.) Thus: “Adam Smith nowhere undervalues the services which the natural agents and machinery perform for us, but he very justly distinguishes the nature of the value which they add to commodities... as they perform their work gratuitously, the assistance which they afford us, adds nothing to value in exchange.” (Ric., cited above, pp. 336, 337.) This remark of Ricardo's is of course correct insofar as it is aimed at J. B. Say, who imagines that machines render the “service” of creating value, which forms a part of “profits.”

<!-- ch15-p027 -->
When we discussed cooperation and manufacture, we showed that certain general factors of production, such as buildings, are economized by being consumed in common, compared with the scattered means of production of the isolated worker, and that they therefore make the product cheaper. In a system of machinery, not only is the framework of the machine consumed in common by its many operating implements, but the prime mover, together with part of the transmitting mechanism, is consumed in common by the many working machines.

<!-- ch15-p028 -->
Take as given the difference between the value of the machinery and the value it transfers to the product in a day. Then how far this transferred value makes the product dearer depends, in the first place, on the size of the product, on its area, so to speak. Mr. Baynes, of Blackburn, in a lecture published in 1858, estimates that

<!-- ch15-p029 -->
> “each real mechanical horse-power[^15.25] will drive 450 self-acting mule spindles, with preparation, or 200 throstle spindles, or 15 looms for 40 inch cloth with the appliances for warping, sizing, &c.”

[^15.25]: A horse-power equals a force of 33,000 foot-pounds per minute, that is, a force that raises 33,000 pounds one foot in a minute, or one pound 33,000 feet. This is the horse-power meant in the text. In ordinary language, and also here and there in quotations in this work, a distinction is drawn between the “nominal” and the “commercial” or “indicated” horse-power of the same engine. The old or nominal horse-power is calculated only from the length of the piston-stroke and the diameter of the cylinder, and leaves steam pressure and piston speed out of account. In practice it says this: This engine would be one of 50 horse-power if it were driven with the same low steam pressure and the same slow piston speed as in the days of Boulton and Watt. But these two factors have increased enormously since those days. To measure the mechanical force an engine exerts today, an indicator has been invented which shows the pressure of the steam in the cylinder. The piston speed is easy to find out. So the “indicated” or “commercial” horse-power of an engine is expressed by a mathematical formula that takes in the diameter of the cylinder, the length of the stroke, the piston speed, and the steam pressure all at once, and shows what multiple of 33,000 pounds the engine really raises in a minute. Hence one “nominal” horse-power may exert three, four, or even five “indicated” or “real” horse-powers. This remark is made to explain various quotations in the following pages. — *F. E*.

<!-- ch15-p030 -->
In the first case, the daily cost of one horse-power, and the wear and tear of the machinery that power sets in motion, are spread over the day's output of 450 mule spindles; in the second, of 200 throstle spindles; in the third, of 15 power-looms. So only a very tiny value is transferred by such wear and tear to a pound of yarn or a yard of cloth. The same is true of the steam-hammer mentioned above. Its daily wear and tear, its coal consumption, etc., are spread over the enormous masses of iron it hammers in a day, so only a small value is added to a hundred weight of iron. But that value would be very great if this giant instrument were used for driving in nails.

<!-- ch15-p031 -->
Take as given a machine's capacity for work, that is, the number of its operating tools, or, where force is in question, their mass. Then the amount of its product will depend on the speed of its working parts: for instance, on the speed of the spindles, or on the number of blows the hammer gives in a minute. Many of these colossal hammers strike seventy times a minute, and Ryder's patent machine for forging spindles with small hammers gives as many as 700 strokes per minute.

<!-- ch15-p032 -->
Take as given the rate at which machinery transfers its value to the product. Then the amount of value so transferred depends on the total value of the machinery.[^15.26] The less labor it contains, the less value it passes on to the product. The less value it gives up, the more productive it is, and the more its services come close to those of natural forces. But the production of machinery by machinery lowers its value in relation to its extent and its effectiveness.

[^15.26]: The reader steeped in capitalist notions will naturally miss here the “interest” that the machine adds to the product in proportion to its capital value. But it is easy to see that a machine no more creates new value than any other part of constant capital does, so it cannot add any value under the name of “interest.” It is also clear that here, where we are dealing with the production of surplus-value, we cannot assume in advance that any part of that value exists under the name of interest. The capitalist way of calculating, which at first sight seems absurd and contrary to the laws of the creation of value, will be explained in the third book of this work.

<!-- ch15-p033 -->
If we analyze and compare the prices (a price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity) of commodities produced by handicrafts or manufacture with the prices of the same commodities produced by machinery, this generally shows that in the product of machinery, the value due to the instruments of labor increases relatively but decreases absolutely. In other words, its absolute amount decreases, but its amount relative to the total value of the product, of a pound of yarn, for instance, increases.[^15.27]

[^15.27]: This portion of value added by the machinery decreases both absolutely and relatively when the machinery does away with horses and other animals that are used as mere moving forces, and not as machines for changing the form of matter. We may remark here in passing that Descartes, in defining animals as mere machines, saw with the eyes of the manufacturing period, while to the eyes of the middle ages animals were man's assistants, as they were later to Von Haller in his “Restauration der Staatswissenschaften.” Descartes, like Bacon, expected that the altered methods of thought would bring about a change in the form of production and the practical mastery of Nature by Man. His “Discours de la Méthode” makes this plain. He says there: “Il est possible (by the methods he introduced in philosophy) de parvenir à des connaissances fort utiles à la vie, et qu’au lieu de cette philosophie spéculative qu’on enseigne dans les écoles, on en peut trouver une pratique, par laquelle, connaissant la force et les actions du feu, de l’eau, de l’air, des astres, et de tous les autres corps qui nous environnent, aussi distinctement que nous connaissons les divers métiers de nos artisans, nous les pourrions employer en même façon à tous les usages auxquels ils sont propres, et ainsi nous rendre comme maîtres et possesseurs de la nature” and thus “contribuer au perfectionnement de la vie humaine.” [It is possible to arrive at knowledge that is very useful in life. In place of the speculative philosophy taught in the schools, we can find a practical one. Through it, knowing the force and the actions of fire, water, air, the stars, and all the other bodies around us as clearly as we know the various trades of our craftsmen, we could use them in the same way for all the purposes they are suited to, and so make ourselves, as it were, masters and owners of nature; and thus “contribute to the perfecting of human life.”] The preface to Sir Dudley North's “Discourses upon Trade” (1691) states that Descartes' method had begun to free political economy from the old fables and superstitious notions about gold, trade, etc. On the whole, however, the early English economists sided with Bacon and Hobbes as their philosophers, while at a later period the philosopher [...] of political economy in England, France, and Italy was Locke.

<!-- ch15-p034 -->
Clearly, whenever it costs as much labor to produce a machine as is saved by using that machine, there is nothing but a shifting of labor from one place to another. So the total labor needed to produce a commodity is not reduced, and the productivity of labor is not increased. It is clear, however, that the difference between the labor a machine costs and the labor it saves, in other words, the degree of its productivity, does not depend on the difference between its own value and the value of the implement it replaces. As long as the labor spent on a machine, and so the portion of its value added to the product, stays smaller than the value the worker adds to the product with his tool, there is always a difference of labor saved in favor of the machine. The productivity of a machine is therefore measured by the human labor-power it replaces. According to Mr. Baynes, 2 factory workers are needed for the 450 mule spindles, including the preparation machinery,[^15.28] that are driven by one-horse power. Each self-acting mule spindle, working ten hours, produces 13 ounces of yarn (average number of thickness). So 2½ factory workers spin 365 5/8 lbs. of yarn a week. Hence, leaving waste aside, 366 lbs. of cotton absorb only 150 hours' labor, or fifteen days' labor of ten hours each, while being turned into yarn. But with a spinning-wheel, supposing the hand-spinner produces thirteen ounces of yarn in sixty hours, the same weight of cotton would absorb 2,700 days' labor of ten hours each, or 27,000 hours' labor.[^15.29] Where block-printing, the old method of printing calico by hand, has been replaced by machine printing, a single machine, with the help of one man or boy, prints as much four-color calico in one hour as it used to take 200 men to print.[^15.30] Before Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin in 1793, separating the seed from a pound of cotton cost an average day's labor. With his invention, one Black woman was able to clean 100 lbs. a day, and since then the effectiveness of the gin has increased considerably. A pound of cotton wool, which had previously cost 50 cents to produce, contained more unpaid labor after that invention, and so was sold at 10 cents with greater profit. In India they use an instrument, half machine, half tool, called a churka, for separating the wool from the seed. With it, one man and a woman can clean 28 lbs. a day. With the churka invented some years ago by Dr. Forbes, one man and a boy produce 250 lbs. a day. If oxen, steam, or water are used to drive it, only a few boys and girls are needed as feeders. Sixteen of these machines driven by oxen do as much work in a day as 750 people used to do on average.[^15.31]

[^15.28]: According to the annual report (1863) of the Essen chamber of commerce, the Krupp cast-steel works produced thirteen million pounds of cast steel in 1862. The works had 161 furnaces, thirty-two steam-engines (in the year 1800 this was about the number of all the steam-engines working in Manchester), and fourteen steam-hammers (representing in all 1,236 horse-power), forty-nine forges, 203 tool-machines, and about 2,400 workers. Here there are not two workers to each horse-power.

[^15.29]: Babbage estimates that in Java the spinning labor alone adds 117% to the value of the cotton. At the same period (1832), the total value added to the cotton by machinery and labor in the fine-spinning industry came to about 33% of the value of the cotton. (“On the Economy of Machinery,” pp. 165, 166.)

[^15.30]: Machine printing also saves color.

[^15.31]: See the paper read by Dr. Watson, Reporter on Products to the Government of India, before the Society of Arts, 17th April, 1860.

<!-- ch15-p035 -->
As already stated, a steam-plough does as much work in one hour, at a cost of three-pence, as 66 men at a cost of 15 shillings. I come back to this example to clear up a mistaken notion. The 15 shillings are by no means the expression in money of all the labor the 66 men spend in one hour. Suppose the ratio of surplus labor (the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist) to necessary labor (the part of the working day in which the worker produces the equivalent of the value of their own labor-power, that is, of their wages) were 100%. Then these 66 men would produce a value of 30 shillings in one hour, although their wages (the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself), 15 shillings, represent only their labor for half an hour. Suppose, then, that a machine costs as much as a year's wages of the 150 men it displaces, say £3,000. This £3,000 is by no means the expression in money of the labor these 150 men added to the object produced before the machine was introduced. It expresses only the portion of their year's labor that they spent for themselves, which their wages represented. On the other hand, the £3,000, the money-value of the machine, expresses all the labor spent on producing it, no matter in what proportion this labor forms wages for the worker and surplus-value for the capitalist. Therefore, even if a machine costs as much as the labor-power it displaces, the labor materialized in it is even then much less than the living labor (the labor of workers now at work) it replaces.[^15.32]

[^15.32]: “These mute agents (machines) are always the produce of much less labour than that which they displace, even when they are of the same money-value.” (Ricardo, cited above, p. 40.)

<!-- ch15-p036 -->
Using machinery for the sole purpose of making the product cheaper is limited in this way: less labor must be spent in producing the machinery than is displaced by using it. For the capitalist, however, this use is still more limited. He does not pay for the labor; he pays only the value of the labor-power employed (the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker, and to raise the next generation of workers, able to work). So the limit to his using a machine is fixed by the difference between the value of the machine and the value of the labor-power it replaces. The division of the day's work into necessary and surplus labor differs in different countries, and even in the same country at different periods, or in different branches of industry. Further, the worker's actual wage sometimes sinks below the value of his labor-power and sometimes rises above it. So the difference between the price of the machinery and the price of the labor-power it replaces may vary a great deal, even if the difference between the quantity of labor needed to produce the machine and the total quantity of labor it replaces stays constant.[^15.33] But it is the first difference alone that determines what it costs the capitalist to produce a commodity, and, through the pressure of competition, influences what he does. Hence machines are invented in England nowadays that are used only in North America; just as in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries machines were invented in Germany to be used only in Holland, and just as many a French invention of the eighteenth century was exploited in England alone. In the older countries, when machinery is used in some branches of industry, it creates such an excess of labor in other branches that in these other branches wages fall below the value of labor-power. This fall hinders the use of machinery there. From the standpoint of the capitalist, whose profit comes not from reducing the labor employed but from reducing the labor paid for, it makes that use unnecessary and often impossible. In some branches of the English woolen manufacture, the employment of children has been considerably reduced in recent years, and in some cases entirely abolished. Why? Because the Factory Acts made two sets of children necessary, one working six hours and the other four, or each working five hours. But the parents refused to sell the “half-timers” cheaper than the “full-timers.” Hence the replacement of the “half-timers” by machinery.[^15.34] Before the labor of women and of children under 10 years of age was forbidden in mines, capitalists considered that employing naked women and girls, often together with men, was so far sanctioned by their moral code, and especially by their ledgers, that they turned to machinery only after the Act was passed. The Yankees have invented a stone-breaking machine. The English do not use it, because the “wretch”[^15.35] who does this work gets paid for such a small portion of his labor that machinery would increase the capitalist's cost of production.[^15.36] In England women are still sometimes used instead of horses for hauling canal boats,[^15.37] because the labor needed to produce horses and machines is an accurately known quantity, while the labor needed to maintain the women of the surplus population (the workers made “surplus” to capital's needs for the time being, who serve as a reserve of available labor and press down on the employed) is below all calculation. Hence nowhere do we find a more shameful squandering of human labor-power for the most despicable purposes than in England, the land of machinery.

[^15.33]: Hence in a communist society there would be a very different scope for using machinery than there can be in a bourgeois society (one shaped by the capitalist class).

[^15.34]: “Employers of labour would not unnecessarily retain two sets of children under thirteen.... In fact one class of manufacturers, the spinners of woollen yarn, now rarely employ children under thirteen years of age, i.e., half-timers. They have introduced improved and new machinery of various kinds, which altogether supersedes the employment of children (i.e., under 13 years); f. i. [for instance], I will mention one process as an illustration of this diminution in the number of children, wherein by the addition of an apparatus, called a piecing machine, to existing machines, the work of six or four half-timers, according to the peculiarity of each machine, can be performed by one young person (over 13 years)... the half-time system ‘stimulated’ the invention of the piecing machine.” (Reports of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct., 1858.)

[^15.35]: “Wretch” is the recognized term in English political economy for the agricultural laborer.

[^15.36]: “Machinery ... can frequently not be employed until labour (he means wages) rises.” (Ricardo, cited above, p. 479.)

[^15.37]: See “Report of the Social Science Congress, at Edinburgh.” Oct., 1863.

### Section 3: The Proximate Effects of Machinery on the Workman

<!-- ch15-p037 -->
As we have shown, the starting-point of modern industry is the revolution in the instruments of labor, and this revolution reaches its most highly developed form in the organized system of machinery in a factory. Before we ask how human material is built into this objective organism, let us look at some general effects of this revolution on the worker himself.

#### A. Appropriation of Supplementary Labor-Power by Capital. The Employment of Women and Children

<!-- ch15-p038 -->
To the extent that machinery makes muscular power unnecessary, it becomes a means of employing workers who have little muscular strength, and workers whose bodies are not yet fully developed but whose limbs are all the more supple. So the labor of women and children was the first thing that capitalists who used machinery went looking for. That mighty substitute for labor and for workers was at once turned into a means of increasing the number of wage workers. It did this by enrolling every member of the worker’s family, without distinction of age or sex, under the direct rule of capital. Forced work for the capitalist took the place not only of children’s play, but also of free labor at home, within moderate limits, for the family’s own support.[^15.38]

[^15.38]: During the cotton crisis caused by the American Civil War, the English Government sent Dr. Edward Smith to Lancashire, Cheshire, and other places to report on the sanitary condition of the cotton factory workers. He reported that from a health point of view, and apart from the workers’ banishment from the factory atmosphere, the crisis had several advantages. The women now had enough free time to breastfeed their infants, instead of poisoning them with “Godfrey’s cordial.” They had time to learn to cook. Unfortunately, they acquired this art at a time when they had nothing to cook. But from this we see how capital, for the purposes of its self-expansion, has seized for itself the labor that the family needs at home. The crisis was also used to teach sewing to the workers’ daughters in sewing schools. An American revolution and a worldwide crisis, so that the working girls who spin for the whole world might learn to sew!

<!-- ch15-p039 -->
The value of labor-power was determined not only by the labor-time needed to keep the individual adult worker alive, but also by the labor-time needed to keep his family alive. Machinery throws every member of that family onto the labor market, and so it spreads the value of the man’s labor-power over his whole family. In this way it lowers the value of his labor-power. Buying the labor-power of a family of four workers may perhaps cost more than buying the labor-power of the head of the family used to cost. But in return, four days’ labor takes the place of one, and their price falls in proportion to the excess of the surplus labor of four over the surplus labor of one. For the family to live, four people must now not only labor, but also perform surplus labor for the capitalist. So we see that machinery, while it increases the human material that is the main object of capital’s power to exploit,[^15.39] at the same time raises the degree of exploitation.

[^15.39]: “The numerical increase of labourers has been great, through the growing substitution of female for male, and above all, of childish for adult labour. Three girls of 13, at wages of from 6 shillings to 8 shillings a week, have replaced the one man of mature age, of wages varying from 18 shillings to 45 shillings.” (Th. de Quincey: “The Logic of Political Econ.,” London, 1844. Note to p. 147.) Some family functions, such as nursing and breastfeeding children, cannot be suppressed entirely, so the mothers whom capital has confiscated must try substitutes of some sort. Domestic work, such as sewing and mending, has to be replaced by buying ready-made articles. So the smaller amount of labor spent in the house goes together with a larger amount of money spent. The cost of keeping the family rises and cancels out the greater income. On top of this, thrift and good judgment in using and preparing the means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live) become impossible. Plenty of material on these facts, which official political economy hides, can be found in the Reports of the Inspectors of Factories, in those of the Children’s Employment Commission, and above all in the Reports on Public Health.

<!-- ch15-p040 -->
Machinery also completely revolutionizes the contract between the worker and the capitalist, the contract that formally fixes their relations to each other. Taking the exchange of commodities as our basis, we first assumed that capitalist and worker met as free persons, as independent owners of commodities: the one owning money and means of production, the other owning labor-power. But now the capitalist buys children and young persons who are under age. Before, the worker sold his own labor-power, which he disposed of, in name at least, as a free agent. Now he sells his wife and child. He has become a slave-dealer.[^15.40] The demand for children’s labor often looks, in its form, like the inquiries for Black slaves that used to be read among the advertisements in American newspapers.

[^15.40]: The great fact is that the male factory workers forced capital to shorten the hours of labor of women and children in English factories. In striking contrast with this, the latest reports of the Children’s Employment Commission show traits of the working parents, in their traffic in children, that are truly revolting and thoroughly like slave-dealing. But the Pharisee of a capitalist, as the same reports show, denounces this brutality, which he himself creates, keeps going, and exploits, and which he moreover baptizes “freedom of labour.” “Infant labour has been called into aid ... even to work for their own daily bread. Without strength to endure such disproportionate toil, without instruction to guide their future life, they have been thrown into a situation physically and morally polluted. The Jewish historian has remarked upon the overthrow of Jerusalem by Titus that it was no wonder it should have been destroyed, with such a signal destruction, when an inhuman mother sacrificed her own offspring to satisfy the cravings of absolute hunger.” (“Public Economy Concentrated.” Carlisle, 1833, p. 66.)

<!-- ch15-p041 -->
> “My attention,” says an English factory inspector, “was drawn to an advertisement in the local paper of one of the most important manufacturing towns of my district, of which the following is a copy: Wanted, 12 to 20 young persons, not younger than what can pass for 13 years. Wages, 4 shillings a week. Apply &c.”[^15.41]

[^15.41]: A. Redgrave in “Reports of Insp. of Fact. for 31st October, 1858,” pp. 40, 41.

<!-- ch15-p042 -->
The phrase “what can pass for 13 years,” refers to the fact that under the Factory Act, children under 13 years may work only 6 hours. An officially appointed surgeon must certify their age. So the manufacturer asks for children who look as if they were already 13 years old. The English statistics of the last 20 years show, in an astonishing way, a decrease, often by leaps and bounds, in the number of children under 13 years employed in factories. According to the evidence of the factory inspectors themselves, this decrease was for the most part the work of the certifying surgeons. They overstated the children’s age, to suit the capitalist’s greed for exploitation and the parents’ sordid need to traffic in their children. In the notorious district of Bethnal Green, a public market is held every Monday and Tuesday morning, where children of both sexes from 9 years of age upwards hire themselves out to the silk manufacturers. “The usual terms are 1s. 8d. a week (this belongs to the parents) and ‘2d. for myself and tea.’ The contract is binding only for the week. The scene and language while this market is going on are quite disgraceful.”[^15.42] It has also happened in England that women have taken “children from the workhouse and let any one have them out for 2s. 6d. a week.”[^15.43] In spite of legislation, more than 2,000 boys in Great Britain are sold by their parents to serve as live chimney-sweeping machines (although plenty of machines exist to replace them).[^15.44] Machinery revolutionized the legal relations between the buyer and the seller of labor-power, so that the transaction as a whole lost the appearance of a contract between free persons. This gave the English Parliament an excuse, based on legal principles, for the state to interfere with factories. Whenever the law limits children’s labor to 6 hours in industries that were not regulated before, the manufacturers always renew their complaints. They claim that many parents take their children out of the industry brought under the Act, in order to sell them where “freedom of labour” still rules, that is, where children under 13 years are forced to work like grown-ups and so can be sold off at a higher price. But capital is by nature a leveler: in every sphere of production it demands equal conditions for exploiting labor. So the legal limitation of children’s labor in one branch of industry becomes the cause of its limitation in others.

[^15.42]: “Children’s Employment Commission, Fifth Report,” London, 1866, p. 81, n. 31. *[Added in the 4th German edition. — The Bethnal Green silk industry is now almost destroyed. — F. E.*]

[^15.43]: “Children’s Employment Commission, Third Report,” London, 1864, p. 53, n. 15.

[^15.44]: Cited above, Fifth Report, p. 22, n. 137.

<!-- ch15-p043 -->
We have already referred to the physical decline of the children and young persons, and also of the women, whom machinery subjects to the exploitation of capital: first directly, in the factories that shoot up on its basis, and then indirectly, in all the other branches of industry. Here, therefore, we dwell on only one point: the enormous death rate of the factory workers’ children during the first few years of their life. England is divided into registration districts. In sixteen of them, for every 100,000 children alive under the age of one year, there are on average only 9,000 deaths a year (in one district only 7,047). In 24 districts the deaths are over 10,000, but under 11,000; in 39 districts, over 11,000, but under 12,000; in 48 districts over 12,000, but under 13,000; in 22 districts over 20,000; in 25 districts over 21,000; in 17 over 22,000; in 11 over 23,000; in Hoo, Wolverhampton, Ashton-under-Lyne, and Preston, over 24,000; in Nottingham, Stockport, and Bradford, over 25,000; in Wisbeach, 16,000; and in Manchester, 26,125.[^15.45] An official medical inquiry in the year 1861 showed that, apart from local causes, the high death-rates are mainly due to the mothers being employed away from their homes. They are also mainly due to the neglect and mistreatment that follow from the mother’s absence, such as, among other things, too little nourishment, unsuitable food, and dosing with opiates. Besides this, an unnatural estrangement arises between mother and child, and as a result children are deliberately starved and poisoned.[^15.46] In those agricultural districts “where a minimum in the employment of women exists, the death-rate is on the other hand very low.”[^15.47] The Inquiry Commission of 1861, however, led to an unexpected result: in some purely agricultural districts bordering on the North Sea, the death-rate of children under one year old almost equaled that of the worst factory districts. So Dr. Julian Hunter was commissioned to investigate this phenomenon on the spot. His report is included in the “Sixth Report on Public Health.”[^15.48] Until then it had been supposed that the children were being decimated by malaria and other diseases typical of low-lying, marshy districts. But the inquiry showed the very opposite. The same cause that drove away malaria, namely, turning the land from a swamp in winter and a thin pasture in summer into fruitful grain land, created the exceptional death-rate of the infants.[^15.49] The 70 doctors whom Dr. Hunter questioned in that district were “wonderfully in accord” on this point. In fact, the revolution in the way of cultivating the land had brought in the industrial system.

[^15.45]: “Sixth Report on Public Health,” London, 1864, p. 34.

[^15.46]: “It (the inquiry of 1861)... showed, moreover, that while, with the described circumstances, infants perish under the neglect and mismanagement which their mothers’ occupations imply, the mothers become to a grievous extent denaturalised towards their offspring ‒ commonly not troubling themselves much at the death, and even sometimes... taking direct measures to insure it.” (cited above)

[^15.47]: Cited above, p. 454.

[^15.48]: Cited above, pp. 454-463. “Report by Dr. Henry Julian Hunter on the excessive mortality of infants in some rural districts of England.”

[^15.49]: Cited above, p. 35 and pp. 455, 456.

<!-- ch15-p044 -->
Married women, who work in gangs along with boys and girls, are placed at the farmer’s disposal for an agreed sum of money by a man called the “undertaker,” who contracts for the whole gang. “These gangs will sometimes travel many miles from their own village; they are to be met morning and evening on the roads, dressed in short petticoats, with suitable coats and boots, and sometimes trousers, looking wonderfully strong and healthy, but tainted with a customary immorality and heedless of the fatal results which their love of this busy and independent life is bringing on their unfortunate offspring who are pining at home.”[^15.50]

[^15.50]: Cited above, p. 456.

<!-- ch15-p045 -->
Every phenomenon of the factory districts is reproduced here, including, but to a greater extent, barely disguised infanticide and dosing children with opiates.[^15.51]

[^15.51]: In the agricultural districts, as in the factory districts, the use of opium among the grown-up workers, both male and female, is spreading daily. “To push the sale of opiate... is the great aim of some enterprising wholesale merchants.
