By druggists it is considered the leading article.” (Cited above, p. 459.) Infants that take opiates “shrank up into little old men,” or “wizened like little monkeys.” (Cited above, p. 460.) Here we see how India and China took their revenge on England.

<!-- ch15-p046 -->
> “My knowledge of such evils,” says Dr. Simon, the medical officer of the Privy Council and editor in chief of the Reports on Public Health, “may excuse the profound misgiving with which I regard any large industrial employment of adult women.”[^15.52]

[^15.52]: Cited above, p. 37.

<!-- ch15-p047 -->
“Happy indeed,” exclaims Mr. Baker, the factory inspector, in his official report, “happy indeed will it be for the manufacturing districts of England, when every married woman having a family is prohibited from working in any textile works at all.”[^15.53]

[^15.53]: “Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct., 1862,” p. 59. Mr. Baker used to be a doctor.

<!-- ch15-p048 -->
F. Engels, in his “Lage der Arbeitenden Klasse Englands” [The Condition of the Working Class in England], and other writers have described so thoroughly the moral degradation caused by the capitalist exploitation of women and children that I need only mention the subject here. But there is also the intellectual desolation that is artificially produced by turning immature human beings into mere machines for making surplus-value. This state of mind is clearly different from the natural ignorance that leaves the mind fallow without destroying its capacity for development, its natural fertility. In the end, this desolation forced even the English Parliament to make elementary education a compulsory condition for the “productive” employment of children under 14 years in every industry subject to the Factory Acts. The spirit of capitalist production stands out clearly in several things: in the ridiculous wording of the so-called education clauses in the Factory Acts; in the lack of any administrative machinery, a lack that again makes the compulsion an illusion; in the manufacturers’ own opposition to these education clauses; and in the tricks and dodges they use to evade them.

<!-- ch15-p049 -->
> “For this the legislature is alone to blame, by having passed a delusive law, which, while it would seem to provide that the children employed in factories shall be *educated,* contains no enactment by which that professed end can be secured. It provides nothing more than that the children shall on certain days of the week, and for a certain number of hours (three) in each day, be inclosed within the four walls of a place called a school, and that the employer of the child shall receive weekly a certificate to that effect signed by a person designated by the subscriber as a schoolmaster or schoolmistress.”[^15.54]

[^15.54]: L. Horner in “Reports of Insp. of Fact. for 30th June, 1857,” p. 17.

<!-- ch15-p050 -->
Before the amended Factory Act of 1844 was passed, it was not unusual for the schoolmaster or schoolmistress to sign the certificates of school attendance with a cross, because they themselves could not write.

<!-- ch15-p051 -->
> “On one occasion, on visiting a place called a school, from which certificates of school attendance, had issued, I was so struck with the ignorance of the master, that I said to him: ‘Pray, sir, can you read?’ His reply was: ‘Aye, summat [somewhat]!’ and as a justification of his right to grant certificates, he added: ‘At any rate, I am before [ahead of] my scholars.’”

<!-- ch15-p052 -->
When the Bill of 1844 was being prepared, the inspectors did not fail to point out the disgraceful state of the places called schools, whose certificates they were obliged to accept as compliance with the law. But all they managed to obtain was this: that since the passing of the Act of 1845,

<!-- ch15-p053 -->
> the figures in the school certificate must be filled up in the handwriting of the schoolmaster, who must also sign his Christian and surname in full.”[^15.55]

[^15.55]: L. Horner in “Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct., 1855,” pp. 18, 19.

<!-- ch15-p054 -->
Sir John Kincaid, factory inspector for Scotland, reports experiences of the same kind.

<!-- ch15-p055 -->
> “The first school we visited was kept by a Mrs. Ann Killin. Upon asking her to spell her name, she straightway made a mistake, by beginning with the letter C, but correcting herself immediately, she said her name began with a K. On looking at her signature, however, in the school certificate books, I noticed that she spelt it in various ways, while her handwriting left no doubt as to her unfitness to teach. She herself also acknowledged that she could not keep the register ... In a second school I found the schoolroom 15 feet long, and 10 feet wide, and counted in this space 75 children, who were gabbling something unintelligible”[^15.56] But it is not only in the miserable places above referred to that the children obtain certificates of school attendance without having received instruction of any value, for in many schools where there is a competent teacher, his efforts are of little avail from the distracting crowd of children of all ages, from infants of 3 years old and upwards; his livelihood, miserable at the best, depending on the pence received from the greatest number of children whom it is possible to cram into the space. To this is to be added scanty school furniture, deficiency of books, and other materials for teaching, and the depressing effect upon the poor children themselves of a close, noisome atmosphere. I have been in many such schools, where I have seen rows of children doing absolutely nothing; and this is certified as school attendance, and, in statistical returns, such children are set down as being educated.”[^15.57]

[^15.56]: Sir John Kincaid in “Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct., 1858,” pp. 31, 32.

[^15.57]: L. Horner in “Reports, &c., for 31st Oct., 1857,” pp. 17, 18.

<!-- ch15-p056 -->
In Scotland the manufacturers do all they can to manage without the children who are obliged to attend school.

<!-- ch15-p057 -->
> “It requires no further argument to prove that the educational clauses of the Factory Act, being held in such disfavour among mill-owners, tend in a great measure to exclude that class of children alike from the employment and the benefit of education contemplated by this Act.”[^15.58]

[^15.58]: Sir J. Kincaid in “Reports, &c., 31st Oct., 1856,” p. 66

<!-- ch15-p058 -->
This looks horribly grotesque in print works, which are regulated by a special Act. Under that Act,

<!-- ch15-p059 -->
> “every child, before being employed in a print work must have attended school for at least 30 days, and not less than 150 hours, during the six months immediately preceding such first day of employment, and during the continuance of its employment in the print works, it must attend for a like period of 30 days, and 150 hours during every successive period of six months.... The attendance at school must be between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. No attendance of less than 2½ hours, nor more than 5 hours on any one day, shall be reckoned as part of the 150 hours. Under ordinary circumstances the children attend school morning and afternoon for 30 days, for at least 5 hours each day, and upon the expiration of the 30 days, the statutory total of 150 hours having been attained, having, in their language, made up their book, they return to the print work, where they continue until the six months have expired, when another instalment of school attendance becomes due, and they again seek the school until the book is again made up.... Many boys having attended school for the required number of hours, when they return to school after the expiration of their six months’ work in the print work, are in the same condition as when they first attended school as print-work boys, that they have lost all they gained by their previous school attendance.... In other print works the children’s attendance at school is made to depend altogether upon the exigencies [demands] of the work in the establishment. The requisite number of hours is made up each six months, by instalments consisting of from 3 to 5 hours at a time, spreading over, perhaps, the whole six months.... For instance, the attendance on one day might be from 8 to 11 a.m., on another day from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m., and the child might not appear at school again for several days, when it would attend from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m.; then it might attend for 3 or 4 days consecutively, or for a week, then it would not appear in school for 3 weeks or a month, after that upon some odd days at some odd hours when the operative who employed it chose to spare it; and thus the child was, as it were, buffeted from school to work, from work to school, until the tale [count] of 150 hours was told.”[^15.59]

[^15.59]: A. Redgrave in “Rep. of Insp. of Fact., 31st. Oct., 1857,” pp. 41-42. In the industries where the Factory Act proper (not the Print Works Act referred to in the text) has been in force for some time, the obstacles in the way of the education clauses have been overcome in recent years. In industries not under the Act, the views of Mr. J. Geddes, a glass manufacturer, are still widely held. He told Mr. White, one of the Inquiry Commissioners: “As far as I can see, the greater amount of education which a part of the working-class has enjoyed for some years past is an evil. It is dangerous, because it makes them independent.” (“Children’s Empl. Comm., Fourth Report,” London, 1865, p. 253.)

<!-- ch15-p060 -->
By adding women and children in excessive numbers to the ranks of the workers, machinery at last breaks down the resistance that the male workers in the manufacturing period still put up against the despotism of capital.[^15.60]

[^15.60]: “Mr. E., a manufacturer ... informed me that he employed females exclusively at his power-looms ... gives a decided preference to married females, especially those who have families at home dependent on them for support; they are attentive, docile, more so than unmarried females, and are compelled to use their utmost exertions to procure the necessaries of life. Thus are the virtues, the peculiar virtues of the female character to be perverted to her injury – thus all that is most dutiful and tender in her nature is made a means of her bondage and suffering.” (Ten Hours’ Factory Bill. The Speech of Lord Ashley, March 15th, London, 1844, p. 20.)

#### B. Prolongation of the Working day

<!-- ch15-p061 -->
If machinery is the most powerful means of increasing the productivity of labor – that is, of shortening the working time needed to produce a commodity – then in the hands of capital it becomes the most powerful means, in the industries it first invades, of lengthening the working day beyond all limits set by human nature. On the one hand, it creates new conditions that let capital give free rein to this constant tendency of its own. On the other hand, it creates new motives that sharpen capital's appetite for the labor of others.

<!-- ch15-p062 -->
In the first place, in the form of machinery, the implements of labor become automatic: things that move and work independently of the worker. From then on they are an industrial perpetual-motion machine, which would go on producing forever if it did not meet certain natural obstacles in the weak bodies and the strong wills of its human attendants. The automaton, as capital, and because it is capital, is given intelligence and will in the person of the capitalist. It is therefore filled with the longing to reduce to a minimum the resistance put up by that repellent yet elastic natural barrier, man.[^15.61] This resistance is also lessened by the apparent lightness of machine work, and by the more pliant and docile character of the women and children employed on it.[^15.62]

[^15.61]: “Since the general introduction of machinery, human nature has been forced far beyond its average strength.” (Rob. Owen: “Observations on the Effects of the Manufacturing System,” 2nd Ed., London, 1817.)

[^15.62]: The English, who tend to take the earliest form of appearance of a thing for the cause of its existence, are in the habit of blaming the long hours of work in factories on the widespread kidnapping of children from workhouses and orphanages, which capitalists practiced when the factory system was in its infancy. By means of this robbery they obtained material for exploitation that could not resist. Thus, for instance, Fielden, himself a manufacturer, says: “It is evident that the long hours of work were brought about by the circumstance of so great a number of destitute children being supplied from different parts of the country, that the masters were independent of the hands, and that having once established the custom by means of the miserable materials they had procured in this way, they could impose it on their neighbours with the greater facility.” (J. Fielden: “The Curse of the Factory System,” London, 1836, p. 11.) On the labor of women, Saunders, the factory inspector, says in his report of 1844: “Amongst the female operatives there are some women who, for many weeks in succession, except for a few days, are employed from 6 a. m. till midnight, with less than 2 hours for meals, so that on 5 days of the week they have only 6 hours left out of the 24, for going to and from their homes and resting in bed.”

<!-- ch15-p063 -->
As we saw, the productivity of machinery is inversely proportional to the value it transfers to the product. The longer the life of the machine, the greater the mass of products over which the value it passes on is spread, and the smaller the share of that value added to each single commodity. But the active lifetime of a machine clearly depends on the length of the working day, or on the duration of the daily labor process multiplied by the number of days for which the process is carried on.

<!-- ch15-p064 -->
The wear and tear of a machine is not exactly proportional to its working time. And even if it were, a machine working 16 hours a day for 7½ years covers as long a working period as the same machine would if it worked only 8 hours a day for 15 years, and passes no more value on to the total product. But in the first case the value of the machine would be reproduced twice as fast as in the second, and by using the machine in this way the capitalist would absorb in 7½ years as much surplus-value as he would absorb in 15 in the second case.

<!-- ch15-p065 -->
The material wear and tear of a machine is of two kinds. One kind comes from use, as coins wear away by circulating. The other comes from not being used, as a sword rusts when left in its sheath. This second kind is due to the elements. The first kind is more or less directly proportional to the use of the machine, the second to a certain extent inversely proportional to it.[^15.63]

[^15.63]: “Occasion... injury to the delicate moving parts of metallic mechanism by inaction.” (Ure, cited above, p. 281.)

<!-- ch15-p066 -->
But besides the material wear and tear, a machine also undergoes what we may call a moral depreciation. It loses exchange-value (the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for), either because machines of the same sort are produced more cheaply than it, or because better machines come into competition with it.[^15.64] In both cases, however young and full of life the machine may be, its value is no longer fixed by the labor actually materialized in it, but by the labor-time needed to reproduce either it or the better machine. So it has lost value, more or less. The shorter the period needed to reproduce its total value, the smaller the danger of moral depreciation; and the longer the working day, the shorter that period. When machinery is first introduced into an industry, new methods of reproducing it more cheaply follow blow upon blow,[^15.65] and so do improvements that affect not only individual parts and details of the machine, but its entire construction. It is therefore in the early days of the life of machinery that this special incentive to lengthen the working day is felt most sharply.[^15.66]

[^15.64]: The Manchester Spinner (*Times*, 26th Nov., 1862), mentioned before, says on this subject: “It (namely, the “allowance for deterioration of machinery”) is also intended to cover the loss which is constantly arising from the superseding of machines before they are worn out, by others of a new and better construction.”

[^15.65]: “It has been estimated, roughly, that the first individual of a newly-invented machine will cost about five times as much as the construction of the second.” (Babbage, cited above, p. 349.)

[^15.66]: “The improvements which took place not long ago in frames for making patent net were so great that a machine in good repair which had cost £1,200, sold a few years after for £60 ... improvements succeeded each other so rapidly, that machines which had never been finished were abandoned in the hands of their makers, because new improvements had superseded their utility.” (Babbage, cited above, p. 233.) So in these stormy, go-ahead times the tulle manufacturers soon extended the working day, by using double sets of workers, from the original 8 hours to 24.

<!-- ch15-p067 -->
Given the length of the working day, and all other circumstances remaining the same, exploiting twice the number of workers requires doubling not only the part of constant capital invested in machinery and buildings, but also the part laid out on raw material and auxiliary materials. Lengthening the working day, on the other hand, allows production on an extended scale without any change in the amount of capital laid out on machinery and buildings.[^15.67] So not only does surplus-value increase, but the outlay needed to obtain it decreases. It is true that this happens, more or less, with every lengthening of the working day. But in the case we are considering, the change is more marked, because the capital turned into instruments of labor predominates to a greater degree.[^15.68] The development of the factory system fixes an ever-growing part of the capital in a form in which, on the one hand, its value is capable of continual self-expansion, and in which, on the other hand, it loses both use-value (the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties) and exchange-value whenever it loses contact with living labor. “When a labourer,” said Mr. Ashworth, a cotton magnate, to Professor Nassau W. Senior, “lays down his spade, he renders useless, for that period, a capital worth eighteen-pence. When one of our people leaves the mill, he renders useless a capital that has cost £100,000.”[^15.69] Just imagine! Making “useless,” for a single moment, a capital that has cost £100,000! It is truly monstrous that a single one of our people should ever leave the factory! The increased use of machinery, as Senior clearly sees after the instruction he received from Ashworth, makes an ever-greater lengthening of the working day “desirable.”[^15.70]

[^15.67]: “It is self-evident, that, amid the ebbings and flowings of the markets and the alternate expansions and contractions of demand, occasions will constantly recur, in which the manufacturer may employ additional floating capital without employing additional fixed capital... if additional quantities of raw material can be worked up without incurring an additional expense for buildings and machinery.” (R. Torrens: “On Wages and Combination.” London, 1834, p. 64.)

[^15.68]: I mention this circumstance only for the sake of completeness, because I shall not consider the rate of profit, that is, the ratio of the surplus-value to the total capital advanced, until I come to the third book.

[^15.69]: Senior, “Letters on the Factory Act.” London, 1837, pp. 13, 14.

[^15.70]: “The great proportion of fixed to circulating capital ... makes long hours of work desirable.” With the increased use of machinery, etc., “the motives to long hours of work will become greater, as the only means by which a large proportion of fixed capital can be made profitable.” (cited above, pp. 11-13.) “There are certain expenses upon a mill which go on in the same proportion whether the mill be running short or full time, as, for instance, rent rates, and taxes, insurance against fire, wages of several permanent servants, deterioration of machinery, with various other charges upon a manufacturing establishment, the proportion of which to profits increases as the production decreases.” (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct., 1862,” p. 19.)

<!-- ch15-p068 -->
Machinery produces relative surplus-value – surplus-value obtained by shortening necessary labor-time (by making workers' necessities cheaper through higher productivity), so that more of a working day of given length is surplus labor. It does this not only by directly lowering the value of labor-power, and by cheapening labor-power indirectly through cheapening the commodities that go into its reproduction; when machinery is first introduced sporadically into an industry, it also does it by converting the labor employed by the owner of that machinery into labor of a higher degree and greater effectiveness, by raising the social value of the article produced above its individual value, and so enabling the capitalist to replace the value of a day's labor-power with a smaller part of the value of a day's product. During this transition period, when the use of machinery is a sort of monopoly, the profits are therefore exceptional, and the capitalist tries to exploit to the full “the sunny time of this his first love,” by lengthening the working day as much as possible. The size of the profit sharpens his appetite for more profit.

<!-- ch15-p069 -->
As the use of machinery becomes more general in a particular industry, the social value of the product sinks to its individual value, and the law asserts itself that surplus-value does not arise from the labor-power that the machinery has replaced, but from the labor-power actually employed in working with the machinery. Surplus-value arises from variable capital alone – the part of capital spent on labor-power, which reproduces its own value and also produces surplus-value, so that its size varies. And we saw that the amount of surplus-value depends on two factors, namely the rate of surplus-value (the ratio of surplus-value to variable capital, s/v) and the number of workers employed at the same time. Given the length of the working day, the rate of surplus-value is determined by the relative duration of the necessary labor and of the surplus labor in a day. The number of workers employed at the same time depends, for its part, on the ratio of the variable to the constant capital. Now, however much the use of machinery may increase surplus labor at the expense of necessary labor by raising the productivity of labor, it clearly achieves this result only by reducing the number of workers employed by a given amount of capital. It converts what was formerly variable capital, invested in labor-power, into machinery, which, being constant capital, does not produce surplus-value. It is impossible, for instance, to squeeze as much surplus-value out of 2 workers as out of 24. If each of these 24 men gives only one hour of surplus labor in 12, the 24 men together give 24 hours of surplus labor, while 24 hours is the total labor of the two men. Hence the application of machinery to the production of surplus-value contains a contradiction that is built into it. For of the two factors of the surplus-value created by a given amount of capital, one, the rate of surplus-value, cannot be increased except by reducing the other, the number of workers. This contradiction comes to light as soon as the general use of machinery in a given industry makes the value of the machine-made commodity regulate the value of all commodities of the same sort. And it is this contradiction that in its turn drives the capitalist, without his being conscious of the fact,[^15.71] to lengthen the working day excessively, so that he may make up for the decrease in the relative number of workers exploited by an increase not only of the relative but of the absolute surplus labor.

[^15.71]: Why the capitalist, and also the political economists who are steeped in his views, are unconscious of this built-in contradiction will become clear from the first part of the third book.

<!-- ch15-p070 -->
So if, on the one hand, the capitalist use of machinery supplies new and powerful motives for lengthening the working day excessively, and radically changes both the methods of labor and the character of the social working organism in such a way as to break down all opposition to this tendency, then on the other hand it produces a surplus working population,[^15.72] which is forced to submit to the dictates of capital. It produces this population partly by opening up to the capitalist new layers of the working class that were previously out of his reach, and partly by setting free the workers it replaces. Hence that remarkable phenomenon in the history of modern industry: machinery sweeps away every moral and natural limit on the length of the working day. Hence, too, the economic paradox that the most powerful instrument for shortening labor-time becomes the most unfailing means of placing every moment of the worker's time, and of his family's, at the disposal of the capitalist, for the purpose of expanding the value of his capital. “If,” dreamed Aristotle, the greatest thinker of antiquity, “if every tool, when summoned, or even of its own accord, could do the work that befits it, just as the creations of Daedalus moved of themselves, or the tripods of Hephaestos went of their own accord to their sacred work, if the weavers’ shuttles were to weave of themselves, then there would be no need either of apprentices for the master workers, or of slaves for the lords.”[^15.73] And Antipatros, a Greek poet of the time of Cicero, hailed the invention of the water-wheel for grinding grain, an invention that is the elementary form of all machinery, as the giver of freedom to female slaves and the bringer back of the golden age.[^15.74] Oh! those heathens! As the learned Bastiat, and before him the still wiser MacCulloch, have discovered, they understood nothing of political economy and Christianity. They did not, for example, grasp that machinery is the surest means of lengthening the working day. They perhaps excused the slavery of one on the ground that it was a means to the full development of another. But to preach the slavery of the masses so that a few crude and half-educated upstarts might become “eminent spinners,” “extensive sausage-makers,” and “influential shoe-black dealers” – to do this, they lacked the phrenological bump of Christianity.

[^15.72]: One of Ricardo's greatest merits is that he saw in machinery not only the means of producing commodities, but also the means of creating a “redundant population.”

[^15.73]: F. Biese. “Die Philosophie des Aristoteles,” Vol. 2. Berlin, 1842, p. 408.

[^15.74]: I give below Stolberg's translation of this poem, because, quite in the spirit of earlier quotations about division of labor, it brings out the opposition between the views of the ancients and those of the moderns. “Spare the hand that grinds the corn, Oh, miller girls, and softly sleep. Let Chanticleer [the rooster] announce the morn in vain! Deo [Demeter] has commanded the work of the girls to be done by the Nymphs, and now they skip lightly over the wheels, so that the shaken axles revolve with their spokes and pull round the load of the revolving stones. Let us live the life of our fathers, and let us rest from work and enjoy the gifts that the Goddess sends us.”

    “Schonet der mahlenden Hand, o Müllerinnen, und schlafet Sanft! es verkünde der Hahn euch den Morgen umsonst! Däo hat die Arbeit der Midchen den Nymphen befohlen, Und itzt hüpfen sic leicht über die Räder dahin, Daß die erschütterten Achsen mit ihren Speichen sich wälzen, Und im Kreise die Last drehen des wälzenden Steins. Laßt uns leben das Leben der Väter, und laBt uns der Gaben Arbeitslos uns freun, welche die Göttin uns schenkt.”

    (Gedichte aus dem Griechischen übersetzt von Christian Graf zu Stolberg, Hamburg, 1782.)

#### C. Intensification of Labor

<!-- ch15-p071 -->
Machinery in the hands of capital produces an immoderate lengthening of the working day. This leads to a reaction on the part of society, whose very sources of life are threatened, and from there to a normal working day whose length is fixed by law. From then on, a phenomenon we have already met with, namely the intensification of labor, grows to great importance. Our analysis of absolute surplus-value dealt mainly with the extension or duration of labor, and took its intensity as given. We now go on to consider how more intensified labor is substituted for labor of longer duration, and the degree of that more intensified labor.

<!-- ch15-p072 -->
It is self-evident that as the use of machinery spreads, and as a special class of workers used to machinery gathers experience, the speed and intensity of labor increase as a natural consequence. Thus in England, for half a century, the lengthening of the working day went hand in hand with the increasing intensity of factory labor. Nevertheless, the reader will clearly see the following. Where labor is not carried on by fits and starts, but repeated day after day with unvarying uniformity, a point must inevitably be reached where extending the working day and intensifying the labor exclude one another. Lengthening the working day then becomes compatible only with a lower degree of intensity, and a higher degree of intensity only with a shorter working day. The gradually surging revolt of the working class compelled Parliament to shorten the hours of labor by law, and to begin by imposing a normal working day on factories proper. As soon as that happened, and so as soon as an increased production of surplus-value by lengthening the working day was stopped once and for all, capital threw itself with all its might into producing relative surplus-value, by hurrying on the further improvement of machinery. At the same time a change took place in the nature of relative surplus-value. Generally speaking, relative surplus-value is produced by raising the productive power of the worker, so that he can produce more in a given time with the same expenditure of labor. Labor-time goes on transferring the same value to the total product as before, but this unchanged amount of exchange-value is spread over more use-value; hence the value of each single commodity falls. It is otherwise, however, as soon as the hours of labor are shortened by law. The immense impetus this gives to the development of productive power, and to economy in the means of production, imposes on the worker an increased expenditure of labor in a given time, a heightened tension of labor-power, and a closer filling up of the pores of the working day, or condensation of labor, to a degree that can be reached only within the limits of the shortened working day. From then on, this condensation of a greater mass of labor into a given period counts for what it really is: a greater quantity of labor. Besides a measure of its extension, that is, its duration, labor now acquires a measure of its intensity, or of the degree of its condensation or density.[^15.75] The denser hour of the ten hours' working day contains more labor, that is, more expended labor-power, than the more porous hour of the twelve hours' working day. So the product of one of the denser hours has as much value as the product of 1 1/5 of the more porous hours, or more. Leaving aside the increased yield of relative surplus-value through the higher productivity of labor, the same mass of value is now produced for the capitalist by, say, 3 1/3 hours of surplus labor and 6 2/3 hours of necessary labor, as was produced before by four hours of surplus labor and eight hours of necessary labor.

[^15.75]: There are, of course, always differences in the intensity of labor in various industries. But, as Adam Smith has shown, these differences are partly compensated by minor circumstances peculiar to each sort of labor. Labor-time as a measure of value is not affected in this case, however, except insofar as the duration of labor and the degree of its intensity are two opposite and mutually exclusive expressions for one and the same quantity of labor.

<!-- ch15-p073 -->
We now come to the question: How is labor intensified?

<!-- ch15-p074 -->
The first effect of shortening the working day follows from a self-evident law: the efficiency of labor-power is in inverse ratio to the length of time over which it is spent. Hence, within certain limits, what is lost by shortening the duration is gained through the increased tension of labor-power. Moreover, the way the capitalist pays the worker ensures that the worker really does spend more labor-power.[^15.76] In industries such as potteries, where machinery plays little or no part, the introduction of the Factory Acts has strikingly shown that merely shortening the working day increases to a wonderful degree the regularity, uniformity, order, continuity, and energy of the labor.[^15.77] It seemed doubtful, however, whether this effect was produced in the factory proper, where the worker's dependence on the continuous and uniform motion of the machinery had already created the strictest discipline. Hence, when the reduction of the working day to less than twelve hours was being debated in 1844, the employers almost unanimously declared

[^15.76]: Especially through piece-work, a form we shall examine in Part VI. of this book.

[^15.77]: See “Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st October, 1865.”

<!-- ch15-p075 -->
> “that their overlookers in the different rooms took good care that the hands lost no time,” that “the extent of vigilance and attention on the part of the workmen was hardly capable of being increased,” and, therefore, that the speed of the machinery and other conditions remaining unaltered, “to expect in a well-managed factory any important result from increased attention of the workmen was an absurdity.”[^15.78]

[^15.78]: Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 1844 and the quarter ending 30th April, 1845, pp. 20-21.

<!-- ch15-p076 -->
Experiments contradicted this assertion. Mr. Robert Gardner reduced the hours of labor in his two large factories at Preston from twelve to eleven hours a day, starting on the 20th April, 1844. After about a year's working the result was that “the same amount of product for the same cost was received, and the workpeople as a whole earned in eleven hours as much wages as they did before in twelve.”[^15.79] I pass over the experiments made in the spinning and carding rooms, because they went together with an increase of 2% in the speed of the machines. But in the weaving department, where, moreover, many sorts of patterned fancy articles were woven, there was not the slightest change in the conditions of the work. The result was: “From 6th January to 20th April, 1844, with a twelve hours’ day, average weekly wages of each hand 10s. 1½d., from 20th April to 29th June, 1844, with day of eleven hours, average weekly wages 10s. 3½d.”[^15.80] Here we have more produced in eleven hours than before in twelve, and entirely because the workers applied themselves more steadily and used their time more economically. While they got the same wages and gained one hour of free time, the capitalist got the same amount produced and saved the cost of coal, gas, and other such items for one hour. Similar experiments, with the same success, were carried out in the mills of Messrs. Horrocks and Jacson.[^15.81]

[^15.79]: Cited above, p. 19. Since the wages for piece-work were unchanged, the weekly wages depended on the quantity produced.

[^15.80]: Cited above, p. 20.

[^15.81]: The moral element played an important part in the experiments above. The workers told the factory inspector: “We work with more spirit, we have the reward ever before us of getting away sooner at night, and one active and cheerful spirit pervades the whole mill, from the youngest piecer to the oldest hand, and we can greatly help each other.” (Cited above, p. 21.)

<!-- ch15-p077 -->
To begin with, the shortening of the hours of labor creates the subjective conditions for condensing labor, by enabling the worker to exert more strength in a given time. As soon as that shortening becomes compulsory, machinery becomes, in the hands of capital, the objective means, systematically used, for squeezing out more labor in a given time. This is done in two ways: by increasing the speed of the machinery, and by giving the worker more machinery to tend. Improved construction of the machinery is necessary, partly because without it greater pressure cannot be put on the worker, and partly because the shortened hours of labor force the capitalist to keep the strictest watch over the cost of production. The improvements in the steam-engine have increased the piston speed. At the same time, by means of a greater economy of power, they have made it possible to drive more machinery with the same engine, with the same or even a smaller consumption of coal. The improvements in the transmitting mechanism have lessened friction. They have also reduced the diameter and weight of the shafting to a constantly decreasing minimum, and this is what so strikingly distinguishes modern machinery from the older kind. Finally, the improvements in the working machines have had several effects. In some cases they have reduced the machines' size while increasing their speed and efficiency, as in the modern power-loom. In others they have enlarged the framework and at the same time increased the extent and number of the working parts, as in spinning-mules. Or they have added to the speed of these working parts by imperceptible changes of detail, such as those which ten years ago increased the speed of the spindles in self-acting mules by one-fifth.

<!-- ch15-p078 -->
In England the reduction of the working day to 12 hours dates from 1832. In 1836 a manufacturer stated:

<!-- ch15-p079 -->
> “The labour now undergone in the factories is much greater than it used to be ... compared with thirty or forty years ago ... owing to the greater attention and activity required by the greatly increased speed which is given to the machinery.”[^15.82]

[^15.82]: John Fielden, cited above, p. 32.

<!-- ch15-p080 -->
In 1844 Lord Ashley, now Lord Shaftesbury, made the following statements in the House of Commons, backed by documentary evidence:

<!-- ch15-p081 -->
> “The labour performed by those engaged in the processes of manufacture, is three times as great as in the beginning of such operations. Machinery has executed, no doubt, the work that would demand the sinews of millions of men; but it has also prodigiously multiplied the labour of those who are governed by its fearful movements.... In 1815, the labour of following a pair of mules spinning cotton of No. 40 – reckoning 12 hours to the working day – involved a necessity of walking 8 miles. In 1832, the distance travelled in following a pair of mules, spinning cotton yarn of the same number, was 20 miles, and frequently more. In 1835” (query – 1815 or 1825?) “the spinner put up daily, on each of these mules, 820 stretches, making a total of 1,640 stretches in the course of the day. In 1832, the spinner put up on each mule 2,200 stretches, making a total of 4,400. In 1844, 2,400 stretches, making a total of 4,800; and in some cases the amount of labour required is even still greater.... I have another document sent to me in 1842, stating that the labour is progressively increasing ‒ increasing not only because the distance to be travelled is greater, but because the quantity of goods produced is multiplied, while the hands are fewer in proportion than before; and, moreover, because an inferior species of cotton is now often spun, which it is more difficult to work.... In the carding-room there has also been a great increase of labour. One person there does the work formerly divided between two. In the weaving-room, where a vast number of persons are employed, and principally females ... the labour has increased within the last few years fully 10 per cent., owing to the increased speed of the machinery in spinning. In 1838, the number of hanks spun per week was 18,000, in 1843 it amounted to 21,000. In 1819, the number of picks in power-loom-weaving per minute was 60 – in 1842 it was 140, showing a vast increase of labour.”[^15.83]

[^15.83]: Lord Ashley, cited above, pp. 6-9, passim.

<!-- ch15-p082 -->
At that time the English manufacturers asserted that any further progress in that direction was impossible, and therefore that every further reduction of the hours of labor meant less production. In the face of this remarkable intensity of labor, already reached in 1844 under the Twelve Hours' Act, there appeared to be a justification for this assertion. The apparent correctness of their reasons will be best shown by the following statement made at the time by Leonard Horner, the factory inspector, their ever watchful censor.

<!-- ch15-p083 -->
> “Now, as the quantity produced must, in the main, be regulated by the speed of the machinery, it must be the interest of the mill-owner to drive it at the utmost rate of speed consistent with these following conditions, viz., the preservation of the machinery from too rapid deterioration; the preservation of the quality of the article manufactured; and the capability of the workman to follow the motion without a greater exertion than he can sustain for a constancy [continuously]. One of the most important problems, therefore, which the owner of a factory has to solve is to find out the maximum speed at which he can run, with a due regard to the above conditions. It frequently happens that he finds he has gone too fast, that breakages and bad work more than counterbalance the increased speed, and that he is obliged to slacken his pace. I therefore concluded, that as an active and intelligent mill-owner would find out the safe maximum, it would not be possible to produce as much in eleven hours as in twelve. I further assumed that the operative paid by piecework, would exert himself to the utmost consistent with the power of continuing at the same rate.”[^15.84]

[^15.84]: Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for Quarter ending 30th September, 1844, and from 1st October, 1844, to 30th April, 1845, p. 20.

<!-- ch15-p084 -->
Horner therefore concluded that reducing the working hours below twelve would necessarily reduce production.[^15.85] Ten years later he himself cites his opinion of 1845 as proof of how much he had underestimated, in that year, the elasticity of machinery and of human labor-power, both of which are stretched to an extreme at the same time by the compulsory shortening of the working day.

[^15.85]: Cited above, p. 22.

<!-- ch15-p085 -->
We now come to the period that follows the introduction of the Ten Hours' Act in 1847 into the English cotton, woolen, silk, and flax mills.

<!-- ch15-p086 -->
> “The speed of the spindles has increased upon throstles 500, and upon mules 1,000 revolutions a minute, i.e., the speed of the throstle spindle, which in 1839 was 4,500 times a minute, is now (1862) 5,000; and of the mule spindle, that was 5,000, is now 6,000 times a minute, amounting in the former case to one-tenth, and in the second case to one-fifth additional increase.”[^15.86]

[^15.86]: “Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st October, 1862,” p. 62.

<!-- ch15-p087 -->
James Nasmyth, the eminent civil engineer of Patricroft, near Manchester, explained in a letter to Leonard Horner, written in 1852, the nature of the improvements in the steam-engine made between 1848 and 1852. He first remarks that the horse-power of steam-engines, which the official returns always estimate according to the power of similar engines in 1828[^15.87], is only nominal, and can serve only as an index of their real power. Then he goes on to say:

[^15.87]: This was changed in the “Parliamentary Return” of 1862. There the actual horse-power of the modern steam engines and water wheels appears instead of the nominal horse-power. The doubling spindles, too, are no longer included among the spinning spindles (as they were in the “Returns” of 1839, 1850, and 1856). Further, for woolen mills the number of “gigs” [machines for raising the nap on cloth] is added; a distinction is made between jute and hemp mills on the one hand and flax mills on the other; and finally stocking-weaving is included in the report for the first time.

<!-- ch15-p088 -->
> “I am confident that from the same weight of steam-engine machinery, we are now obtaining at least 50 per cent. more duty or work performed on the average, and that in many cases the identical steam-engines which in the days of the restricted speed of 220 feet per minute, yielded 50 horsepower, are now yielding upwards of 100...” “The modern steam-engine of 100 horse-power is capable of being driven at a much greater force than formerly, arising from improvements in its construction, the capacity and construction of the boilers, &c....” “Although the same number of hands are employed in proportion to the horse-power as at former periods, there are fewer hands employed in proportion to the machinery.”[^15.88] “In the year 1850, the factories of the United Kingdom employed 134,217 nominal horse-power to give motion to 25,638,716 spindles and 301,445 looms. The number of spindles and looms in 1856 was respectively 33,503,580 of the former, and 369,205 of the latter, which, reckoning the force of the nominal horse-power required to be the same as in 1850, would require a force equal to 175,000 horses, but the actual power given in the return for 1856 is 161,435, less by above 10,000 horses than, calculating upon the basis of the return of 1850, the factories ought to have required in 1856.”[^15.89] “The facts thus brought out by the Return (of 1856) appear to be that the factory system is increasing rapidly; that although the same number of hands are employed in proportion to the horse-power as at former periods, there are fewer hands employed in proportion to the machinery; that the steam-engine is enabled to drive an increased weight of machinery by economy of force and other methods, and that an increased quantity of work can be turned off by improvements in machinery, and in methods of manufacture, by increase of speed of the machinery, and by a variety of other causes.”[^15.90]

[^15.88]: “Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st October, 1856,” pp. 13-14, 20 and 1852, p. 23.

[^15.89]: Cited above, pp. 14-15.

[^15.90]: Cited above, p. 20.

<!-- ch15-p089 -->
> “The great improvements made in machines of every kind have raised their productive power very much. Without any doubt, the shortening of the hours of labour... gave the impulse to these improvements. The latter, combined with the more intense strain on the workman, have had the effect, that at least as much is produced in the shortened (by two hours or one-sixth) working day as was previously produced during the longer one.”[^15.91]

[^15.91]: “Reports, &c., for 31st October, 1858,” pp. 9-10. Compare “Reports, &c., for 30th April, 1860,” p. 30 and following.

<!-- ch15-p090 -->
One fact is enough to show how greatly the wealth of the manufacturers grew along with the more intense exploitation of labor-power. From 1838 to 1850 the average proportional increase in English cotton and other factories was 32%, while from 1850 to 1856 it amounted to 86%.

<!-- ch15-p091 -->
But however great the progress of English industry had been during the 8 years from 1848 to 1856 under a working day of 10 hours, it was far surpassed during the next period of 6 years, from 1856 to 1862. In silk factories, for instance, there were 1,093,799 spindles in 1856 and 1,388,544 in 1862; there were 9,260 looms in 1856 and 10,709 in 1862. But the number of factory workers was 56,131 in 1856 and 52,429 in 1862. So the spindles increased by 26.9% and the looms by 15.6%, while the number of factory workers fell by 7%. In 1850 worsted mills employed 875,830 spindles; in 1856, 1,324,549 (an increase of 51.2%); and in 1862, 1,289,172 (a decrease of 2.7%). But if we deduct the doubling spindles, which figure in the numbers for 1856 but not in those for 1862, we find that after 1856 the number of spindles stayed nearly stationary. On the other hand, after 1850 the speed of the spindles and looms was in many cases doubled. The number of power-looms in worsted mills was 32,617 in 1850, 38,956 in 1856, and 43,048 in 1862. The number of factory workers was 79,737 in 1850, 87,794 in 1856, and 86,063 in 1862. Included in these, however, were the children under 14 years of age: 9,956 in 1850, 11,228 in 1856, and 13,178 in 1862. So, despite the greatly increased number of looms in 1862 compared with 1856, the total number of workers employed fell, and the number of children exploited rose.[^15.92]

[^15.92]: “Reports of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct., 1862,” pp. 100 and 130.

<!-- ch15-p092 -->
On the 27th April, 1863, Mr. Ferrand said in the House of Commons:

<!-- ch15-p093 -->
> “I have been informed by delegates from 16 districts of Lancashire and Cheshire, in whose behalf I speak, that the work in the factories is, in consequence of the improvements in machinery, constantly on the increase. Instead of as formerly one person with two helps tenting [tending] two looms, one person now tents three looms without helps, and it is no uncommon thing for one person to tent four. Twelve hours’ work, as is evident from the facts adduced, is now compressed into less than 10 hours. It is therefore self-evident, to what an enormous extent the toil of the factory operative has increased during the last 10 years.”[^15.93]

[^15.93]: On 2 modern power-looms a weaver now makes 26 pieces of a certain quality, length, and breadth in a week of 60 hours, while on the old power-looms he could make no more than 4 such pieces. Soon after 1850, the cost of weaving a piece of such cloth had already fallen from 2s. 9d. to 5 1/8d.

    “Thirty years ago (1841) one spinner with three placers was not required to attend to more than one pair of mules with 300-324 spindles. At the present time (1871) he has to mind with the help of 5 piecers 2,200 spindles, and produces not less than seven times as much yarn as in 1841.” (Alex. Redgrave, Factory Inspector – in the *Journal of Arts*, 5th January, 1872.)

<!-- ch15-p094 -->
So, although the Factory Inspectors constantly and rightly praise the results of the Acts of 1844 and 1850, they admit that the shortening of the hours of labor has already called forth an intensification of labor so great that it injures the worker's health and his capacity for work.

<!-- ch15-p095 -->
> “In most of the cotton, worsted, and silk mills, an exhausting state of excitement necessary to enable the workers satisfactorily to mind the machinery, the motion of which has been greatly accelerated within the last few years, seems to me not unlikely to be one of the causes of that excess of mortality from lung disease, which Dr. Greenhow has pointed out in his recent report on this subject.”[^15.94]

[^15.94]: “Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct., 1861,” pp. 25, 26.

<!-- ch15-p096 -->
There cannot be the slightest doubt about the following. As soon as a lengthening of the hours of labor is forbidden once and for all, a tendency drives capital to make up for it by systematically raising the intensity of labor, and to turn every improvement in machinery into a more perfect means of exhausting the worker. This tendency must soon lead to a state of things in which a reduction of the hours of labor will again be inevitable.[^15.95] On the other hand, the rapid advance of English industry from 1848 to the present day, under a day of 10 hours, surpasses the advance made from 1833 to 1847, when the day was 12 hours long, by far more than that advance surpasses the advance made in the half century after the factory system was first introduced, when the working day had no limits.[^15.96]

[^15.95]: The agitation for a working day of 8 hours has now (1867) begun among the factory workers in Lancashire.

[^15.96]: The following few figures show the increase in the “factories” of the United Kingdom since 1848: Quantity Exported. **1848.**Quantity Exported. **1851.**Quantity Exported. **1860.**Quantity Exported. **1865.COTTON**Cotton yarnlbs. 135,831,162lbs. 143,966,106lbs. 197,343,655lbs. 103,751,455Sewing thread—lbs. 4,392,176lbs. 6,297,554lbs. 4,648,611Cotton clothyds. 1,091,373,930yds. 1,543,161,789yds. 2,776,218,427yds. 2,015,237,851**FLAX & HEMP**Yarnlbs. 11,722,182lbs. 18,841,326lbs. 31,210,612lbs. 36,777,334Clothyds. 88,901,519yds. 129,106,753yds. 143,996,773yds. 247,012.529**SILK**Yarnlbs. 466,825lbs. 462,513lbs. 897,402lbs. 812,589Cloth—yds. 1,181,455yds. 1,307,293yds. 2,869,837**WOOL**Woollen and Worsted yarns—lbs. 14,670,880lbs. 27,533,968lbs. 31,669,267Cloth—yds. 151,231,153yds. 190,371,507yds. 278,837,418
