    See the Blue books “Statistical Abstract of the United Kingdom,” Nos. 8 and 13. London, 1861 and 1866. In Lancashire the number of mills increased by only 4 percent between 1839 and 1850, by 19 percent between 1850 and 1856, and by 33 percent between 1856 and 1862. Meanwhile, in each of the above periods of 11 years, the number of persons employed in them increased absolutely but fell relatively. (See “Rep. of Insp. of Fact., for 31st Oct., 1862,” p. 63.) The cotton trade is the dominant trade in Lancashire. We can form an idea of the enormous scale of the cotton trade in that district when we consider that it takes up 45.2 percent of the total number of textile factories in the United Kingdom, 83.3 percent of the spindles, 81.4 percent of the power-looms, 72.6 percent of the mechanical horse-power, and 58.2 percent of the total number of persons employed. (Cited above, pp. 62-63.)

### Section 4: The Factory

<!-- ch15-p097 -->
At the beginning of this chapter we looked at what we may call the body of the factory, that is, machinery organized into a system. We saw there how machinery, by annexing the labor of women and children, increases the number of human beings who form the material for capitalist exploitation. We saw how it confiscates the whole of the worker’s disposable time by stretching the hours of labor beyond all measure. And we saw how, finally, its progress, which allows an enormous increase of production in shorter and shorter periods, serves as a means of systematically getting more work done in a shorter time, or of exploiting labor-power more intensely. We now turn to the factory as a whole, and to the factory in its most perfect form.

<!-- ch15-p098 -->
Dr. Ure, the Pindar of the automatic factory, describes it, on the one hand, as

<!-- ch15-p099 -->
> “Combined co-operation of many orders of workpeople, adult and young, in tending with assiduous skill, a system of productive machines, continuously impelled by a central power” (the prime mover); on the other hand, as “a vast automaton, composed of various mechanical and intellectual organs, acting in uninterrupted concert for the production of a common object, all of them being subordinate to a self-regulated moving force.”

<!-- ch15-p100 -->
These two descriptions are far from identical. In the first, the collective worker, or social body of labor, appears as the dominant subject, and the mechanical automaton as the object. In the second, the automaton itself is the subject, and the workers are merely conscious organs, set alongside the unconscious organs of the automaton and, together with them, subordinated to the central moving power. The first description applies to every possible use of machinery on a large scale. The second is characteristic of its use by capital, and therefore of the modern factory system. Ure therefore prefers to describe the central machine, from which the motion comes, not only as an automaton but as an autocrat. “In these spacious halls the benignant power of steam summons around him his myriads of willing menials.”[^15.97]

[^15.97]: Ure, cited above, p. 18.

<!-- ch15-p101 -->
Along with the tool, the worker’s skill in handling it passes over to the machine. The capabilities of the tool are freed from the limits that are inseparable from human labor-power. This sweeps away the technical foundation on which the division of labor in manufacture is based. So in the automatic factory, the hierarchy of specialized workers that characterizes manufacture is replaced by a tendency to equalize and reduce to one and the same level every kind of work that the minders of the machines have to do;[^15.98] in place of the artificially produced differences between the detail workers, there step the natural differences of age and sex.

[^15.98]: Ure, cited above, P. 3 1. See Karl Marx, cited above, pp. 140-141.

<!-- ch15-p102 -->
To the extent that division of labor reappears in the factory, it is primarily a distribution of the workers among the specialized machines. It is also a distribution of masses of workers, who are not, however, organized into groups, among the various departments of the factory, in each of which they work at a number of similar machines placed together. So their cooperation is only simple. The organized group peculiar to manufacture is replaced by the connection between the head worker and his few assistants. The essential division is into workers who are actually employed on the machines (among whom are included a few who look after the engine), and mere attendants of these workers (almost exclusively children). More or less all the “Feeders,” who supply the machines with the material to be worked, are counted among the attendants. In addition to these two principal classes, there is a class of persons, unimportant in numbers, whose job is to look after the whole of the machinery and repair it from time to time: engineers, mechanics, joiners, etc. This is a superior class of workers, some of them scientifically educated, others brought up to a trade. It is distinct from the class of factory workers, and merely lumped together with it.[^15.99] This division of labor is purely technical.

[^15.99]: It looks very much like deliberate misleading by statistics (misleading that could be proved in detail in other cases too) when the English factory legislation excludes from its operation the class of workers last mentioned in the text, while the parliamentary returns expressly include in the category of factory workers not only engineers, mechanics, etc., but also managers, salesmen, messengers, warehousemen, packers, etc., in short everybody except the owner of the factory himself.

<!-- ch15-p103 -->
To work at a machine, the worker should be taught from childhood, so that he may learn to adapt his own movements to the uniform and unceasing motion of an automaton. When the machinery as a whole forms a system of many different machines, working at the same time and in concert, the cooperation based on it requires the distribution of various groups of workers among the different kinds of machines. But the use of machinery does away with the need to fix this distribution permanently, in the way manufacture does, by constantly tying a particular man to a particular function.[^15.100] Since the motion of the whole system does not come from the worker but from the machinery, people can be changed at any time without interrupting the work. The most striking proof of this is the *relay system* (a system of shifts in which workers, especially children, were switched in and out at different times, which made the legal hours hard to check), which the manufacturers put into operation during their revolt from 1848-1850. Lastly, young people learn machine work so quickly that there is no need to bring up a special class of factory workers to be employed exclusively by machinery.[^15.101] As for the work of the mere attendants, it can to some extent be replaced in the mill by machines,[^15.102] and because it is extremely simple, it allows a rapid and constant change of the individuals burdened with this drudgery.

[^15.100]: Ure admits this. He says that “in case of need” the workers can be moved at the manager’s will from one machine to another, and he exclaims in triumph: “Such a change is in flat contradiction with the old routine, that divides the labour, and to one workman assigns the task of fashioning the head of a needle, to another the sharpening of the point.” He would have done much better to ask himself why this “old routine” is departed from in the automatic factory only “in case of need.”

[^15.101]: When distress is very great, as for instance during the American Civil War, the factory worker is now and then set by the bourgeois to do the roughest of work, such as road-making, etc. The English “ateliers nationaux” [national workshops] of 1862 and the following years, set up for the benefit of the destitute cotton workers, differ from the French ones of 1848 in this: in the French ones, the workers had to do unproductive work at the expense of the state; in the English ones, they had to do productive municipal work to the advantage of the bourgeois, and at that, more cheaply than the regular workers, with whom they were thus thrown into competition. “The physical appearance of the cotton operatives is unquestionably improved. This I attribute ... as to the men, to outdoor labour on public works.” (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1863,” p. 59.) The writer is referring here to the Preston factory workers, who were employed on Preston Moor.

[^15.102]: An example: the various mechanical devices introduced into woolen mills since the Act of 1844 to replace the labor of children. As soon as it happens that the manufacturers’ own children have to go through a course of schooling as helpers in the mill, this almost unexplored territory of mechanics will soon make remarkable progress. “Of machinery, perhaps self-acting mules are as dangerous as any other kind. Most of the accidents from them happen to little children, from their creeping under the mules to sweep the floor whilst the mules are in motion. Several ‘minders’ have been fined for this offence, but without much general benefit. If machine makers would only invent a self-sweeper, by whose use the necessity for these little children to creep under the machinery might be prevented, it would be a happy addition to our protective measures.” (“Reports of Insp. of Fact. for 31st. Oct., 1866,” p. 63.)

<!-- ch15-p104 -->
So although, technically speaking, machinery throws the old system of division of labor overboard, that system hangs on in the factory as a traditional habit handed down from manufacture. Afterwards capital systematically remolds it and establishes it in a more hideous form, as a means of exploiting labor-power. The lifelong specialty of handling one and the same tool now becomes the lifelong specialty of serving one and the same machine. Machinery is misused in order to turn the worker, from his very childhood, into a part of a detail machine.[^15.103] In this way, not only are the costs of his reproduction considerably reduced, but at the same time his helpless dependence on the factory as a whole, and therefore on the capitalist, is made complete. Here as everywhere else, we must distinguish between the increased productivity due to the development of the social process of production and the increased productivity due to the capitalist exploitation of that process. In handicrafts and manufacture, the worker makes use of a tool; in the factory, the machine makes use of him. There, the movements of the instrument of labor come from him; here, it is the movements of the machine that he must follow. In manufacture the workers are parts of a living mechanism. In the factory we have a lifeless mechanism that is independent of the worker, who becomes its mere living appendage.

[^15.103]: So much, then, for Proudhon’s wonderful idea: he “construes” machinery not as a synthesis of instruments of labor, but as a synthesis of detail operations for the benefit of the worker himself.

<!-- ch15-p105 -->
> “The miserable routine of endless drudgery and toil in which the same mechanical process is gone through over and over again, is like the labour of Sisyphus. The burden of labour, like the rock, keeps ever falling back on the worn-out labourer.”[^15.104]

[^15.104]: F. Engels, cited above, p. 217. Even an ordinary and optimistic Free-trader like Mr. Molinari goes so far as to say: “Un homme s’use plus vite en surveillant, quinze heures par jour, l’évolution uniforme d’un mécanisme, qu’en exercant, dans le même espace de temps, sa force physique. Ce travail de surveillance qui servirait peut-être d’utile gymnastique à l’intelligence, s’il n’était pas trop prolongé, détruit à la longue, par son excès, et l’intelligence, et le corps même.” [A man wears out faster by watching the uniform movement of a mechanism for fifteen hours a day than by using his physical strength for the same length of time. This work of watching, which might perhaps serve as useful exercise for the mind if it did not go on too long, in the long run destroys, by its excess, both the mind and the body itself.] (G. de Molinari: “Études Économiques.” Paris, 1846.)

<!-- ch15-p106 -->
At the same time that factory work exhausts the nervous system to the utmost, it does away with the many-sided play of the muscles and confiscates every atom of freedom, both in bodily and in intellectual activity.[^15.105] Even the lightening of the labor becomes a sort of torture, since the machine does not free the worker from work, but deprives the work of all interest. Every kind of capitalist production, insofar as it is not only a labor process but also a process of creating surplus-value, has this in common: it is not the worker who employs the instruments of labor, but the instruments of labor that employ the worker. But it is only in the factory system that this inversion for the first time acquires a technical and tangible reality. By being turned into an automaton, the instrument of labor confronts the worker, during the labor process, in the shape of capital, of dead labor, which dominates living labor-power and pumps it dry. The separation of the intellectual powers of production from manual labor, and the conversion of those powers into the might of capital over labor, is, as we have already shown, finally completed by modern industry built on the foundation of machinery. The special skill of each individual, insignificant factory worker vanishes as an infinitely small quantity before the science, the gigantic physical forces, and the mass of labor that are embodied in the factory mechanism and that, together with that mechanism, make up the power of the “master.” So this “master,” in whose brain the machinery and his monopoly of it are inseparably united, contemptuously tells his “hands,” whenever he falls out with them:

[^15.105]: F. Engels, cited above, p. 216.

<!-- ch15-p107 -->
> “The factory operatives should keep in wholesome remembrance the fact that theirs is really a low species of skilled labour; and that there is none which is more easily acquired, or of its quality more amply remunerated, or which by a short training of the least expert can be more quickly, as well as abundantly, acquired.... The master’s machinery really plays a far more important part in the business of production than the labour and the skill of the operative, which six months’ education can teach, and a common labourer can learn.”[^15.106]

[^15.106]: “The Master Spinners’ and Manufacturers’ Defence Fund. Report of the Committee.” Manchester, 1854, p. 17. We shall see later that the “master” can sing quite another song when he is threatened with the loss of his “living” automaton.

<!-- ch15-p108 -->
The technical subordination of the worker to the uniform motion of the instruments of labor, and the peculiar makeup of the body of workers, consisting as it does of individuals of both sexes and of all ages, give rise to a barrack discipline. In the factory this discipline is worked out into a complete system. It fully develops the labor of overseeing mentioned earlier, and so divides the workers into factory workers and overseers, into the privates and sergeants of an industrial army. “The main difficulty [in the automatic factory] ... lay ... above all in training human beings to renounce their desultory [irregular] habits of work, and to identify themselves with the unvarying regularity of the complex automaton. To devise and administer a successful code of factory discipline, suited to the necessities of factory diligence, was the Herculean enterprise, the noble achievement of Arkwright! Even at the present day, when the system is perfectly organised and its labour lightened to the utmost, it is found nearly impossible to convert persons past the age of puberty, into useful factory hands.”[^15.107] In the factory code, capital, like a private legislator and at his own good will, formulates his autocracy over his workers. This code comes without the division of responsibility that the bourgeoisie approves of so much in other matters, and without the representative system that it approves of even more. It is only the capitalist caricature of the social regulation of the labor process that becomes necessary in cooperation on a large scale and in the common use of instruments of labor, especially of machinery. The overseer’s book of penalties takes the place of the slave-driver’s lash. All punishments naturally come down to fines and deductions from wages, and the law-giving talent of the factory Lycurgus arranges matters so that breaking his laws is, if possible, more profitable to him than keeping them.[^15.108] Here we shall merely touch on the material conditions under which factory labor is carried on. Every organ of sense is injured equally by the artificially raised temperature, by the dust-laden air, and by the deafening noise, not to mention the danger to life and limb among the thickly crowded machinery, which, with the regularity of the seasons, issues its list of the killed and wounded in the industrial battle.[^15.109] Economy in the social means of production, matured and forced as in a hothouse by the factory system, is turned, in the hands of capital, into systematic robbery of what the worker needs for life while he is at work: robbery of space, light, and air, and of protection for his person against the dangerous and unhealthy accompaniments of the production process, not to mention robbery of facilities for the worker’s comfort.[^15.110] Is Fourier wrong when he calls factories “tempered bagnos [convict prisons]”?[^15.111]

[^15.107]: Ure, cited above, p. 15. Anyone who knows the life history of Arkwright will never call this barber-genius “noble.” Of all the great inventors of the 18th century, he was beyond dispute the greatest thief of other people’s inventions and the meanest fellow.

[^15.108]: “The slavery in which the bourgeoisie has bound the proletariat [the class of wage workers], comes nowhere more plainly into daylight than in the factory system. In it all freedom comes to an end both at law and in fact. The workman must be in the factory at half past five. If he come a few minutes late, he is punished; if he come 10 minutes late, he is not allowed to enter until after breakfast, and thus loses a quarter of a day’s wage. He must eat, drink and sleep at word of command.... The despotic bell calls him from his bed, calls him from breakfast and dinner. And how does he fare in the mill? There the master is the absolute law-giver. He makes what regulations he pleases; he alters and makes additions to his code at pleasure; and if he insert the veriest nonsense, the courts say to the workman: Since you have entered into this contract voluntarily, you must now carry it out .... These workmen are condemned to live, from their ninth year till their death, under this mental and bodily torture.” (F. Engels, cited above, p. 217, and following.) What “the courts say,” I will illustrate with two examples. The first occurred at Sheffield at the end of 1866. In that town a worker had bound himself for 2 years to a steelworks. After a quarrel with his employer he left the works, and declared that under no circumstances would he work for that employer any more. He was prosecuted for breach of contract and sentenced to two months’ imprisonment. (If the employer breaks the contract, he can be proceeded against only in a civil action, and risks nothing but money damages.) After the worker had served his two months, the employer invited him to return to the works, as the contract required. The worker said no: he had already been punished for the breach. The employer prosecuted again, and the court condemned him again, although one of the judges, Mr. Shee, publicly denounced this as a legal monstrosity, by which a man can be punished periodically, as long as he lives, over and over again for the same offense or crime. This judgment was given not by the “Great Unpaid,” the provincial Dogberries (after the constable in Shakespeare’s *Much Ado About Nothing*), but by one of the highest courts of justice in London. — [Added *in the 4th German edition. — This* has now been done away with. With few exceptions, for example when public gas-works are involved, the worker in England is now put on an equal footing with the employer in case of breach of contract and can be sued only in a civil action. — F. E.] The second case occurred in Wiltshire at the end of November 1863. About 30 power-loom weavers, employed by one Harrup, a cloth manufacturer at Leower’s Mill, Westbury Leigh, went on strike because master Harrup had the agreeable habit of making deductions from their wages for being late in the morning: 6d. for 2 minutes, 1s. for 3 minutes, and 1s. 6d. for ten minutes. This works out at 9s. per hour and £4 10s. 0d. per day, while the weavers’ wages, averaged over a year, never exceeded 10s. to 12s. a week. Harrup also appointed a boy to announce the starting time with a whistle, which he often blew before six o’clock in the morning. If the workers were not all there at the moment the whistle stopped, the doors were closed, and those workers who were outside were fined. And as there was no clock on the premises, the unfortunate workers were at the mercy of the young Harrup-inspired timekeeper. The workers on strike, mothers of families as well as girls, offered to go back to work if the timekeeper were replaced by a clock and a more reasonable scale of fines were introduced. Harrup summoned 19 women and girls before the magistrates for breach of contract. To the utter indignation of everyone present, they were each fined 6d., plus 2s. 6d. for costs. A crowd of people followed Harrup out of the court, hissing him. A favorite practice of manufacturers is to punish the workers by making deductions from their wages for faults in the material worked on. In 1866 this method gave rise to a general strike in the English pottery districts. The reports of the Ch. Empl. Com. (1863-1866) give cases where the worker not only receives no wages, but, through his labor and the penal regulations, ends up as the debtor of his worthy employer into the bargain. The recent cotton crisis also supplied edifying examples of the shrewdness the factory autocrats showed in making deductions from wages. Mr. R. Baker, the Inspector of Factories, says: “I have myself had lately to direct prosecutions against one cotton mill occupier for having in these pinching and painful times deducted 10d. a piece from some of the young workers employed by him, for the surgeon’s certificate (for which he himself had only paid 6d.), when only allowed by the law to deduct 3d., and by custom nothing at all .... And I have been informed of another, who, in order to keep without [outside] the law, but to attain the same object, charges the poor children who work for him a shilling each, as a fee for learning them the art and mystery of cotton spinning, so soon as they are declared by the surgeon fit and proper persons for that occupation. There may therefore be undercurrent causes for such extraordinary exhibitions as strikes, not only wherever they arise, but particularly at such times as the present, which without explanation, render them inexplicable to the public understanding.” He is referring here to a strike of power-loom weavers at Darwen, June, 1863. (“Reports of Insp. of Fact. for 30 April, 1863,” pp. 50-51.) The reports always go beyond their official dates.

[^15.109]: The protection that the Factory Acts give against dangerous machinery has had a beneficial effect. “But ... there are other sources of accident which did not exist twenty years since; one especially, viz., the increased speed of the machinery. Wheels, rollers, spindles and shuttles are now propelled at increased and increasing rates; fingers must be quicker and defter in their movements to take up the broken thread, for, if placed with hesitation or carelessness, they are sacrificed.... A large number of accidents are caused by the eagerness of the workpeople to get through their work expeditiously. It must be remembered that it is of the highest importance to manufacturers that their machinery should be in motion, i.e., producing yarns and goods. Every minute’s stoppage is not only a loss of power, but of production, and the workpeople are urged by the overlookers, who are interested in the quantity of work turned off, to keep the machinery in motion, and it is no less important to those of the operatives who are paid by the weight or piece, that the machines should be kept in motion. Consequently, although it is strictly forbidden in many, nay in most factories, that machinery should be cleaned while in motion, it is nevertheless the constant practice in most, if not in all, that the workpeople do, unreproved, pick out waste, wipe rollers and wheels, &c., while their frames are in motion. Thus from this cause only, 906 accidents have occurred during the six months.... Although a great deal of cleaning is constantly going on day by day, yet Saturday is generally the day set apart for the thorough cleaning of the machinery, and a great deal of this is done while the machinery is in motion.” Since cleaning is not paid for, the workers try to get it done as quickly as possible. Hence “the number of accidents which occur on Fridays, and especially on Saturdays, is much larger than on any other day. On the former day the excess is nearly 12 per cent. over the average number of the four first days of the week, and on the latter day the excess is 25 per cent. over the average of the preceding five days; or, if the number of working-hours on Saturday being taken into account — 7½ hours on Saturday as compared with 10½ on other days — there is an excess of 65 per cent. on Saturdays over the average of the other five days.” (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1866,” pp. 9, 15, 16, 17.)

[^15.110]: In Part I. of Book III. I shall give an account of a recent campaign by the English manufacturers against the clauses in the Factory Acts that protect the “hands” against dangerous machinery. For now, let this one quotation from the official report of Leonard Horner be enough: “I have heard some mill-owners speak with inexcusable levity of some of the accidents; such, for instance, as the loss of a finger being a trifling matter. A working-man’s living and prospects depend so much upon his fingers, that any loss of them is a very serious matter to him. When I have heard such inconsiderate remarks made, I have usually put this question: Suppose you were in want of an additional workman, and two were to apply, both equally well qualified in other respects, but one had lost a thumb or a forefinger, which would you engage? There never was a hesitation as to the answer....” The manufacturers have “mistaken prejudices against what they have heard represented as a pseudo-philanthropic legislation.” (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1855.”) These manufacturers are clever folk, and not without reason were they enthusiastic for the slave-holders’ rebellion.

[^15.111]: In the factories that have been subject longest to the Factory Acts, with their compulsory limitation of the hours of labor and other regulations, many of the older abuses have vanished. The very improvement of the machinery demands, to a certain extent, “improved construction of the buildings,” and this is an advantage to the workers. (See “Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct., 1863,” p. 109.)

### Section 5: The Strife Between Workman and Machine

<!-- ch15-p109 -->
The struggle between the capitalist and the wage worker goes back to the very origin of capital. It raged on throughout the whole manufacturing period.[^15.112] But only since machinery was introduced has the worker fought against the instrument of labor itself, the material embodiment of capital. He revolts against this particular form of the means of production, seeing it as the material basis of the capitalist mode of production.

[^15.112]: See, among others, John Houghton: “Husbandry and Trade Improved.” London, 1727. “The Advantages of the East India Trade, 1720.” John Bellers, cited above. “The masters and their workmen are, unhappily, in a perpetual war with each other. The invariable object of the former is to get their work done as cheaply as possible; and they do not fail to employ every artifice to this purpose, whilst the latter are equally attentive to every occasion of distressing their masters into a compliance with higher demands.” (“An Enquiry into the Causes of the Present High Price of Provisions,” pp. 61-62. The author, the Rev. Nathaniel Forster, is entirely on the side of the workers.)

<!-- ch15-p110 -->
In the 17th century, workers in nearly all of Europe revolted against the ribbon-loom, a machine for weaving ribbons and trimmings, called in Germany Bandmühle [ribbon mill], Schnurmühle [cord mill], and Mühlenstuhl [mill loom]. These machines were invented in Germany. Abbé Lancellotti, in a work that appeared in Venice in 1636 but was written in 1579, says the following:

<!-- ch15-p111 -->
> “Anthony Müller of Danzig saw about 50 years ago in that town, a very ingenious machine, which weaves 4 to 6 pieces at once. But the Mayor being apprehensive that this invention might throw a large number of workmen on the streets, caused the inventor to be secretly strangled or drowned.”

<!-- ch15-p112 -->
In Leyden this machine was not used until 1629. There the riots of the ribbon-weavers finally forced the Town Council to ban it.

<!-- ch15-p113 -->
> “In hac urbe,” says Boxhorn (Inst. Pol., 1663), referring to the introduction of this machine into Leyden, “ante hos viginti circiter annos instrumentum quidam invenerunt textorium, quo solus plus panni et facilius conficere poterat, quan plures aequali tempore. Hinc turbae ortae et querulae textorum, tandemque usus hujus instrumenti a magistratu prohibitus est.” [In this town, about twenty years ago, some people invented a weaving instrument with which one person alone could make more cloth, and more easily, than several people in the same time. From this arose disturbances and complaints by the weavers, until at last the Town Council banned the use of this instrument.]

<!-- ch15-p114 -->
In 1632, 1639, etc., the States General of Holland issued various decrees that more or less banned this loom. Finally, by the decree of the 15th December, 1661, they allowed it to be used under certain conditions. It was also banned in Cologne in 1676, at the same time that its introduction into England was causing disturbances among the workers. An imperial Edict of 19th Feb., 1685, forbade its use throughout all Germany. In Hamburg it was burnt in public by order of the Senate. The Emperor Charles VI., on 9th Feb., 1719, renewed the edict of 1685, and not until 1765 was its use openly allowed in the Electorate of Saxony. This machine, which shook Europe to its foundations, was in fact the forerunner of the mule and the power-loom, and of the industrial revolution of the 18th century. It let a totally inexperienced boy set the whole loom, with all its shuttles, in motion simply by moving a rod backwards and forwards. In its improved form it produced from 40 to 50 pieces at once.

<!-- ch15-p115 -->
About 1630, a wind-driven sawmill put up near London by a Dutchman fell victim to the violence of the crowd. Even as late as the beginning of the 18th century, sawmills driven by water overcame the opposition of the people, which Parliament supported, only with great difficulty. In 1758 Everet put up the first wool-shearing machine driven by water-power; no sooner was it built than it was set on fire by 100,000 people who had been thrown out of work. Fifty thousand workers who had until then lived by carding wool petitioned Parliament against Arkwright’s scribbling mills and carding engines. During the first 15 years of this century, the English manufacturing districts saw an enormous destruction of machinery, caused chiefly by the use of the power-loom and known as the Luddite movement. It gave the anti-Jacobin governments of a Sidmouth, a Castlereagh, and the like, a pretext for the most reactionary and forcible measures. It took both time and experience before the workers learned to distinguish between machinery and its use by capital, and to direct their attacks not against the material instruments of production, but against the way in which they are used.[^15.113]

[^15.113]: In old-fashioned branches of manufacture, the revolts of the workers against machinery, even to this day, sometimes take a savage form, as in the case of the Sheffield file cutters in 1865.

<!-- ch15-p116 -->
The struggles about wages in manufacture presuppose manufacture, and are in no sense directed against its existence. The opposition to setting up new manufacturing workshops comes from the guilds and the privileged towns, not from the workers. So the writers of the manufacturing period treat the division of labor mainly as a means of making up, in effect, for a shortage of workers, and not as a means of actually displacing those in work. This distinction is self-evident. Suppose someone says that 100 millions of people would be needed in England to spin, with the old spinning-wheel, the cotton that is now spun with mules by 500,000 people. This does not mean that the mules took the place of those millions, who never existed. It means only that many millions of workers would be needed to replace the spinning machinery. If, on the other hand, we say that in England the power-loom threw 800,000 weavers onto the streets, we do not mean existing machinery that would have to be replaced by a definite number of workers. We mean a number of weavers who existed and were actually replaced or displaced by the looms. During the manufacturing period, handicraft labor, though altered by the division of labor, was still the basis. The demands of the new colonial markets could not be met, because the town workers handed down from the middle ages were relatively few. And manufacture proper opened up new fields of production to the rural population, driven from the land by the break-up of the feudal system. At that time, therefore, the division of labor and cooperation in the workshops were seen more from their positive side: that they made the workers more productive.[^15.114] Long before the period of modern industry, cooperation and the concentration of the instruments of labor in the hands of a few gave rise to great, sudden and forcible revolutions in the modes of production, and as a result in the conditions of existence and the means of employment of the rural populations. This happened in numerous countries where these methods were applied in agriculture. But this struggle at first takes place more between the large and the small landowners than between capital and wage labor. On the other hand, when the workers are displaced by instruments of labor, by sheep, horses, etc., force is in this case used directly, in the first instance, as the prelude to the industrial revolution. First the workers are driven from the land, and then come the sheep. Land grabbing on a great scale, such as was carried out in England, is the first step in creating a field for setting up agriculture on a great scale.[^15.115] So this overturning of agriculture looks at first more like a political revolution.

[^15.114]: Sir James Steuart also understands machinery entirely in this sense. “Je considère donc les machines comme des moyens d’augmenter (virtuellement) le nombre des gens industrieux qu’on n’est pas obligé de nourrir.... En quoi l’effet d’une machine diffère-t-il de celui de nouveaux habitants?” [So I consider machines as means of increasing (virtually) the number of industrious people whom one is not obliged to feed.... In what way does the effect of a machine differ from that of new inhabitants?] (French trans. t. I., l. I., ch. XIX.) Petty is more naïve: he says it replaces “Polygamy.” The point of view above can be accepted, at the most, only for some parts of the United States. On the other hand: “machinery can seldom be used with success to abridge [shorten] the labour of an individual; more time would be lost in its construction than could be saved by its application. It is only really useful when it acts on great masses, when a single machine can assist the work of thousands. It is accordingly in the most populous countries, where there are most idle men, that it is most abundant.... It is not called into use by a scarcity of men, but by the facility with which they can be brought to work in masses.” (Piercy Ravenstone: “Thoughts on the Funding System and its Effects.” London, 1824, p. 45.)

[^15.115]: *[Note in the 4th German edition.* — This applies to Germany too. Wherever large-scale agriculture exists in our country, and so particularly in the East, it has become possible only as a result of the clearing of the estates (“Bauernlegen”), a practice which became widespread in the 16th century, and especially so after 1648. — *F. E.*]

<!-- ch15-p117 -->
The instrument of labor, once it takes the form of a machine, immediately becomes a competitor of the worker himself.[^15.116] From then on, the self-expansion of capital by means of machinery is directly proportional to the number of workers whose means of livelihood that machinery has destroyed. The whole system of capitalist production rests on the fact that the worker sells his labor-power as a commodity. Division of labor specializes this labor-power by reducing it to skill in handling a particular tool. As soon as handling this tool becomes the work of a machine, the use-value of the worker’s labor-power vanishes, and its exchange-value with it. The worker becomes unsaleable, like paper money taken out of currency by law. Machinery in this way makes part of the working class superfluous, that is, no longer immediately necessary for the self-expansion of capital. This part either goes under in the unequal contest of the old handicrafts and branches of manufacture with machinery, or else floods all the more easily entered branches of industry, swamps the labor-market, and pushes the price of labor-power below its value. The workers are told, as a great consolation, first, that their sufferings are only temporary (“a temporary inconvenience”), and secondly, that machinery takes over the whole of a given field of production only by degrees, so that the extent and intensity of its destructive effect is lessened. The first consolation cancels out the second. When machinery takes over an industry by degrees, it produces chronic misery among the factory workers who compete with it. Where the change is rapid, the effect is acute and felt by great masses. History shows no tragedy more horrible than the gradual dying out of the English hand-loom weavers, a dying out that stretched over several decades and was finally sealed in 1838. Many of them died of starvation; many, with families, barely survived for a long time on 2½ d. a day.[^15.117] On the other hand, the English cotton machinery had an acute effect in India. The Governor General reported in 1834-35:

[^15.116]: “Machinery and labour are in constant competition.” Ricardo, cited above, p. 479.

[^15.117]: In England, before the passing of the Poor Law of 1833, the competition between hand-weaving and power-weaving was dragged out by topping up wages, which had fallen well below the minimum, with parish relief. “The Rev. Mr. Turner was, in 1827, rector of Wilmslow in Cheshire, a manufacturing district. The questions of the Committee of Emigration, and Mr. Turner’s answers, show how the competition of human labour is maintained against machinery. ‘Question: Has not the use of the power-loom superseded the use of the hand-loom? Answer: Undoubtedly; it would have superseded them much more than it has done, if the hand-loom weavers were not enabled to submit to a reduction of wages.’ ‘Question: But in submitting he has accepted wages which are insufficient to support him, and looks to parochial [parish] contribution as the remainder of his support? Answer: Yes, and in fact the competition between the hand-loom and the power-loom is maintained out of the poor-rates.’ Thus degrading pauperism [the condition of the lowest layer of the surplus population] or expatriation, is the benefit which the industrious receive from the introduction of machinery, to be reduced from the respectable and in some degree independent mechanic [skilled craftsman], to the cringing wretch who lives on the debasing bread of charity. This they call a temporary inconvenience.” (“A Prize Essay on the Comparative Merits of Competition and Co-operation.” London, 1834, p. 29.)

<!-- ch15-p118 -->
> “The misery hardly finds a parallel in the history of commerce. The bones of the cotton-weavers are bleaching the plains of India.”

<!-- ch15-p119 -->
No doubt, in turning them out of this “temporal” world, the machinery caused them no more than “a temporary inconvenience.” For the rest, since machinery is constantly seizing on new fields of production, its temporary effect is really permanent. The capitalist mode of production as a whole gives the instruments of labor and the product a character of independence and estrangement in relation to the worker. So, by means of machinery, this character is developed into a thorough antagonism.[^15.118] That is why it is with the arrival of machinery that the worker for the first time revolts brutally against the instruments of labor.

[^15.118]: “The same cause which may increase the revenue of the country” (that is, as Ricardo explains in the same passage, the revenues of landlords and capitalists, whose wealth, from the economic point of view, forms the Wealth of the Nation), “may at the same time render the population redundant and deteriorate the condition of the labourer.” (Ricardo, cited above, p. 469.) “The constant aim and the tendency of every improvement in machinery is, in fact, to do away entirely with the labour of man, or to lessen its price by substituting the labour of women and children for that of grown-up men, or of unskilled for that of skilled workmen.” (Ure, cited above, t. I., p. 35.)

<!-- ch15-p120 -->
The instrument of labor strikes down the worker. This direct antagonism between the two shows most strongly wherever newly introduced machinery competes with handicrafts or branches of manufacture handed down from former times. But even in modern industry, the constant improvement of machinery and the development of the automatic system have a similar effect.

<!-- ch15-p121 -->
> “The object of improved machinery is to diminish manual labour, to provide for the performance of a process or the completion of a link in a manufacture by the aid of an iron instead of the human apparatus.”[^15.119] “The adaptation of power to machinery heretofore [until now] moved by hand, is almost of daily occurrence ... the minor improvements in machinery having for their object economy of power, the production of better work, the turning off more work in the same time, or in supplying the place of a child, a female, or a man, are constant, and although sometimes apparently of no great moment, have somewhat important results.”[^15.120] “Whenever a process requires peculiar dexterity and steadiness of hand, it is withdrawn, as soon as possible, from the cunning workman, who is prone to irregularities of many kinds, and it is placed in charge of a peculiar mechanism, so self-regulating that a child can superintend it.”[^15.121] “On the automatic plan skilled labour gets progressively superseded.”[^15.122] “The effect of improvements in machinery, not merely in superseding the necessity for the employment of the same quantity of adult labour as before, in order to produce a given result, but in substituting one description of human labour for another, the less skilled for the more skilled, juvenile for adult, female for male, causes a fresh disturbance in the rate of wages.”[^15.123] “The effect of substituting the self-acting mule for the common mule, is to discharge the greater part of the men spinners, and to retain adolescents and children.”[^15.124]

[^15.119]: “Rep. Insp. Fact. for 31st October, 1858,” p. 43.

[^15.120]: “Rep. Insp. Fact. for 31st October, 1856,” p. 15.

[^15.121]: Ure, cited above, p. 19. “The great advantage of the machinery employed in brick-making consists in this, that the employer is made entirely independent of skilled labourers.” (“Ch. Empl. Comm. V. Report,” London, 1866, p. 130, n. 46.) Mr. A. Sturrock, superintendent of the machine department of the Great Northern Railway, says about the building of locomotives, etc.: “Expensive English workmen are being less used every day. The production of the workshops of England is being increased by the use of improved tools and these tools are again served by a low class of labour.... Formerly their skilled labour necessarily produced all the parts of engines. Now the parts of engines are produced by labour with less skill, but with good tools. By tools, I mean engineer’s machinery, lathes, planing machines, drills, and so on.” (“Royal Com. on Railways,” London, 1867, Minutes of Evidence, n. 17, 862 and 17, 863.)

[^15.122]: Ure, cited above, p. 20.

[^15.123]: Ure, cited above, p. 321.

[^15.124]: Ure, cited above, p. 23.

<!-- ch15-p122 -->
The factory system has an extraordinary power of expansion, owing to accumulated practical experience, to the mechanical means at hand, and to constant technical progress. We saw this proved by the giant strides the system made under the pressure of a shortened working day. But who, in 1860, the peak year of the English cotton industry, would have dreamt of the galloping improvements in machinery, and the matching displacement of working people, that the American Civil War spurred on during the following 3 years? A couple of examples from the Reports of the Inspectors of Factories will be enough on this point. A Manchester manufacturer states:

<!-- ch15-p123 -->
> “We formerly had 75 carding engines, now we have 12, doing the same quantity of work.... We are doing with fewer hands by 14, at a saving in wages of £10 a-week. Our estimated saving in waste is about 10% in the quantity of cotton consumed.” “In another fine-spinning mill in Manchester, I was informed that through increased speed and the adoption of some self-acting processes, a reduction had been made, in number, of a fourth in one department, and of above half in another, and that the introduction of the combing machine in place of the second carding, had considerably reduced, the number of hands formerly employed in the carding-room.”

<!-- ch15-p124 -->
Another spinning mill is estimated to make a saving of labor of 10%. The Messrs. Gilmour, spinners at Manchester, state: “In our blowing-room department we consider our expense with new machinery is fully one-third less in wages and hands ... in the jack-frame and drawing-frame room, about one-third less in expense, and likewise one-third less in hands; in the spinning room about one-third less in expenses. But this is not all; when our yarn goes to the manufacturers, it is so much better by the application of our new machinery, that they will produce a greater quantity of cloth, and cheaper than from the yarn produced by old machinery.”[^15.125] Mr. Redgrave adds in the same Report:

[^15.125]: “Rep. Insp. Fact., 31st Oct., 1863,” pp. 108,109.

<!-- ch15-p125 -->
> “The reduction of hands against increased production is, in fact, constantly taking place, in woollen mills the reduction commenced some time since, and is continuing; a few days since, the master of a school in the neighbourhood of Rochdale said to me, that the great falling off in the girls’ school is not only caused by the distress, but by the changes of machinery in the woollen mills, in consequence of which a reduction of 70 short-timers had taken place.”[^15.126]

[^15.126]: Cited above, p. 109. During the crisis, machinery improved rapidly. This allowed the English manufacturers, immediately after the end of the American Civil War, and almost in no time, to glut the markets of the world again. During the last six months of 1866, cloth was almost unsaleable. Then began the shipping of goods on consignment to India and China, which naturally made the glut worse. At the beginning of 1867 the manufacturers turned to their usual way out of the difficulty, namely, cutting wages by 5 percent. The workers resisted, and said that the only remedy was to work short time, 4 days a week; and their theory was the correct one. After holding out for some time, the self-elected captains of industry had to make up their minds to short time, with reduced wages in some places, and without in others.

<!-- ch15-p126 -->
The following table shows the total result of the mechanical improvements in the English cotton industry due to the American Civil War.

<!-- ch15-p127 -->

<!-- ch15-p128 -->
So between 1861 and 1868, 338 cotton factories disappeared. In other words, more productive machinery on a larger scale was concentrated in the hands of a smaller number of capitalists. The number of power-looms fell by 20,663; but since their product grew in the same period, an improved loom must have produced more than an old one. Lastly, the number of spindles rose by 1,612,541, while the number of factory workers fell by 50,505. The “temporary” misery that the cotton crisis inflicted on the workers was made worse, and turned from temporary into permanent, by the rapid and persistent progress of machinery.

<!-- ch15-p129 -->
But machinery does not only act as a competitor who beats the worker and is constantly on the point of making him superfluous. It is also a power hostile to him, and capital proclaims it as such from the rooftops and uses it as such. It is the most powerful weapon for putting down strikes, those periodic revolts of the working class against the autocracy of capital.[^15.127] According to Gaskell, the steam-engine was from the very first an antagonist of human power. It was an antagonist that let the capitalist trample on the growing demands of the workers, who threatened the newly born factory system with a crisis.[^15.128] One could write a whole history of the inventions made since 1830 for the sole purpose of supplying capital with weapons against the revolts of the working class. First among these in importance stands the self-acting mule, because it opened a new epoch in the automatic system.[^15.129]

[^15.127]: “The relation of master and man in the blown-flint bottle trades amounts to a chronic strike.” Hence the push given to the manufacture of pressed glass, in which the chief operations are done by machinery. One firm in Newcastle, which formerly produced 350,000 lbs. of blown-flint glass, now produces 3,000,500 lbs. of pressed glass in its place. (“Ch. Empl. Comm., Fourth Rep.,” 1865, pp. 262-263.)

[^15.128]: Gaskell. “The Manufacturing Population of England,” London, 1833, pp. 3, 4.

[^15.129]: W. Fairbairn discovered several very important applications of machinery to the building of machines, as a result of strikes in his own workshops.

<!-- ch15-p130 -->
Nasmyth, the inventor of the steam-hammer, gives the following evidence before the Trades’ Union Commission about the improvements he made in machinery and introduced as a result of the widespread and long strikes of the engineers in 1851.

<!-- ch15-p131 -->
> “The characteristic feature of our modern mechanical improvements, is the introduction of self-acting tool machinery. What every mechanical workman has now to do, and what every boy can do, is not to work himself but to superintend the beautiful labour of the machine. The whole class of workmen that depend exclusively on their skill, is now done away with. Formerly, I employed four boys to every mechanic. Thanks to these new mechanical combinations, I have reduced the number of grown-up men from 1,500 to 750. The result was a considerable increase in my profits.”

<!-- ch15-p132 -->
Ure says of a machine used in calico printing:

<!-- ch15-p133 -->
> “At length capitalists sought deliverance from this intolerable bondage” [namely the terms of their contracts with the workers, which in their eyes were burdensome] “in the resources of science, and were speedily re-instated in their legitimate rule, that of the head over the inferior members.”

<!-- ch15-p134 -->
Speaking of an invention for dressing warps, he says:

<!-- ch15-p135 -->
> “Then the combined malcontents, who fancied themselves impregnably entrenched behind the old lines of division of labour, found their flanks turned and their defences rendered useless by the new mechanical tactics, and were obliged to surrender at discretion [unconditionally].”

<!-- ch15-p136 -->
About the invention of the self-acting mule, he says:

<!-- ch15-p137 -->
> “A creation destined to restore order among the industrious classes.... This invention confirms the great doctrine already propounded, that when capital enlists science into her service, the refractory [unruly] hand of labour will always be taught docility.”[^15.130]

[^15.130]: Ure, cited above, pp. 368-370

<!-- ch15-p138 -->
Ure’s work appeared 30 years ago, when the factory system was still relatively little developed. Even so, it still expresses the spirit of the factory perfectly, not only through its open cynicism, but also through the naïveté with which it blurts out the stupid contradictions of the capitalist brain. For instance, after setting out the “doctrine” stated above, that capital, with the help of science taken into its pay, always reduces the refractory hand of labor to docility, he grows indignant because

<!-- ch15-p139 -->
> “it (physico-mechanical science) has been accused of lending itself to the rich capitalist as an instrument for harassing the poor.”

<!-- ch15-p140 -->
After preaching a long sermon to show how good the rapid development of machinery is for the working classes, he warns them that by their obstinacy and their strikes they speed up that development.

<!-- ch15-p141 -->
> “Violent revulsions of this nature,” he says, “display short-sighted man in the contemptible character of a self-tormentor.”

<!-- ch15-p142 -->
A few pages earlier he says the opposite.

<!-- ch15-p143 -->
> “Had it not been for the violent collisions and interruptions resulting from erroneous views among the factory operatives, the factory system would have been developed still more rapidly and beneficially for all concerned.” Then he exclaims again: “Fortunately for the state of society in the cotton districts of Great Britain, the improvements in machinery are gradual.” “It” (improvement in machinery) “is said to lower the rate of earnings of adults by displacing a portion of them, and thus rendering their number superabundant as compared with the demand for their labour. It certainly augments the demand for the labour of children and increases the rate of *their* wages.”

<!-- ch15-p144 -->
On the other hand, this same dispenser of consolation defends the low wages of children on the ground that they keep parents from sending their children into the factory at too early an age. His whole book is a defense of a working day of unlimited length. That Parliament should forbid children of 13 years to be exhausted by working 12 hours a day reminds his liberal soul of the darkest days of the Middle Ages. This does not stop him from calling on the factory workers to thank Providence, who by means of machinery has given them the leisure to think of their “immortal interests.”[^15.131]

[^15.131]: Ure, cited above, pp. 368, 7, 370, 280, 281, 321, 370, 475.

### Section 6: The Theory of Compensation as Regards the Workpeople Displaced by Machinery

<!-- ch15-p145 -->
James Mill, MacCulloch, Torrens, Senior, John Stuart Mill, and a whole series of other bourgeois political economists insist on the following: all machinery that displaces workers at the same time, and necessarily, sets free an amount of capital large enough to employ the very same workers.[^15.132]

[^15.132]: Ricardo was at first also of this opinion. But later he expressly withdrew it, with the scientific impartiality and love of truth that were typical of him. See the work cited above, ch. xxxi. “On Machinery.”

<!-- ch15-p146 -->
Suppose a capitalist employs 100 workers in a carpet factory, at £30 a year each. So the variable capital he lays out each year amounts to £3,000. Suppose also that he dismisses 50 of his workers, and employs the remaining 50 with machinery that costs him £1,500. To keep things simple, we leave out buildings, coal, etc. Suppose further that the raw material used up each year costs £3,000, both before and after the change.[^15.133] Is any capital set free by this metamorphosis, this change of form? Before the change, of the total sum of £6,000, half was constant capital and half variable capital. After the change it consists of £4,500 constant capital (£3,000 raw material and £1,500 machinery) and £1,500 variable capital. Instead of being one half of the total capital, the variable capital is only one quarter of it. Instead of being set free, part of the capital is here locked up in such a way that it is no longer exchanged for labor-power: variable capital has been changed into constant capital. Other things remaining unchanged, the capital of £6,000 can in future employ no more than 50 men. With each improvement in the machinery, it will employ fewer. Now suppose the newly introduced machinery had cost less than the labor-power and tools it displaced. If, for instance, it had cost only £1,000, instead of £1,500, then a variable capital of £1,000 would have been converted into constant capital and locked up, and a capital of £500 would have been set free. Supposing wages unchanged, this £500 would form a fund large enough to employ about 16 of the 50 men dismissed; indeed, fewer than 16, for in order to be employed as capital, part of this £500 must now itself become constant capital. That leaves only the rest to be laid out in labor-power.

[^15.133]: Note well: my illustration follows exactly the lines of those given by the economists named above.

<!-- ch15-p147 -->
But suppose, besides, that making the new machinery gives work to a greater number of mechanics. Can that be called compensation to the carpet-makers who have been thrown onto the streets? At best, building the machinery employs fewer men than using it displaces. The sum of £1,500 that used to represent the wages of the dismissed carpet-makers now represents, in the shape of machinery: (1) the value of the means of production used in building that machinery, (2) the wages of the mechanics employed in building it, and (3) the surplus-value that falls to the share of their “master.” Further, the machinery need not be renewed until it is worn out. Hence, to keep the increased number of mechanics in constant employment, one carpet manufacturer after another must displace workers with machines.

<!-- ch15-p148 -->
In fact, the apologists do not mean this sort of setting free.

<!-- ch15-p149 -->
What they have in mind is the means of subsistence of the liberated workers. In the example above, it cannot be denied that the machinery not only liberates 50 men, and so places them at others' disposal, but at the same time withdraws from their consumption, and sets free, means of subsistence to the value of £1,500. Machinery cuts the workers off from their means of subsistence: that is a simple fact, and by no means a new one. In the language of economics, therefore, this fact amounts to saying that machinery liberates means of subsistence for the worker, or converts those means into capital for employing him. The way you put it, you see, is everything. Nominibus mollire licet mala [It is allowed to soften evils with names].

<!-- ch15-p150 -->
This theory implies that the £1,500 worth of means of subsistence was capital, which was being expanded by the labor of the 50 men who were dismissed. It implies, consequently, that this capital falls out of employment as soon as the men begin their forced holidays. It implies that the capital never rests until it has found a new investment, where these same 50 men can once again consume it productively. It implies, therefore, that sooner or later the capital and the workers must come together again, and that the compensation is then complete. And it implies that the sufferings of the workers displaced by machinery are therefore as passing as the riches of this world.

<!-- ch15-p151 -->
In relation to the dismissed workers, the £1,500 worth of means of subsistence never was capital. What really faced them as capital was the sum of £1,500, which was later laid out in machinery. Looking closer, we see that this sum represented part of the carpets the 50 dismissed men produced in a year. They received this part as wages from their employer, in money instead of in kind. With the carpets, now in the form of money, they bought means of subsistence to the value of £1,500. So for them these means were not capital but commodities. And with regard to these commodities, they were not wage workers but buyers. The machinery “freed” them from their means of purchase, and this changed them from buyers into non-buyers. Hence a reduced demand for those commodities – voilà tout [that's all]. If this fall in demand is not made up by a rise from some other quarter, the market price of the commodities falls. If this state of things lasts for some time and spreads, workers employed in producing these commodities are dismissed. Part of the capital that used to go into producing necessary means of subsistence has to be reproduced in another form. While prices fall and capital is being displaced, the workers employed in producing necessary means of subsistence are in their turn “freed” from part of their wages. So our apologists, with their cut-and-dried law of supply and demand, do not prove that when machinery frees the worker from his means of subsistence, it at the same time converts those means into capital for employing him further. On the contrary, they prove that machinery throws workers onto the streets, not only in the branch of production where it is introduced, but also in the branches where it is not introduced.

<!-- ch15-p152 -->
The real facts, which the optimism of the economists turns into a travesty, are as follows. When the machinery drives the workers out of the workshop, they are thrown onto the labor market. There they add to the number of workers at the capitalists' disposal. In Part VII of this book we shall see that this effect of machinery, which, as we have seen, is presented as a compensation to the working class, is on the contrary a most frightful scourge. For the present I will say only this. The workers thrown out of work in any branch of industry can no doubt look for employment in some other branch. If they find it, and so renew the bond between themselves and the means of subsistence, this happens only through a new and additional capital that is looking for investment. It does not happen at all through the capital that used to employ them and was later converted into machinery. And even if they do find employment, what poor prospects they have! Crippled as they are by the division of labor, these poor devils are worth so little outside their old trade that they cannot get into any industries except a few of an inferior kind, which are over-supplied with underpaid workers.[^15.134] Further, every branch of industry attracts a new stream of men each year. These men provide a contingent from which to fill vacancies and to draw a supply for expansion. As soon as machinery sets free part of the workers employed in a given branch of industry, these reserve men are also diverted into new channels of employment and absorbed in other branches. Meanwhile the original victims, during the period of transition, for the most part starve and perish.

[^15.134]: A follower of Ricardo, answering the insipid remarks of J. B. Say, observes on this point: “Where division of labour is well developed, the skill of the labourer is available only in that particular branch in which it has been acquired; he himself is a sort of machine. It does not therefore help matters one jot, to repeat in parrot fashion, that things have a tendency to find their level. On looking around us we cannot but see, that they are unable to find their level for a long time; and that when they do find it, the level is always lower than at the commencement of the process.” (“An Inquiry into those Principles Respecting the Nature of Demand,” etc., London 1821, p. 72.)

<!-- ch15-p153 -->
It is an undoubted fact that machinery, as such, is not responsible for “setting free” the worker from the means of subsistence. In the branch it seizes on, it makes production cheaper and greater, and at first it makes no change in the mass of means of subsistence produced in other branches. Hence, after machinery is introduced, society has as much of the necessaries of life as before, if not more, for the workers thrown out of work; and that is quite apart from the enormous share of the annual produce wasted by the non-workers. And this is the point our apologists rely on! The contradictions and antagonisms inseparable from the capitalist employment of machinery do not exist, they say, since they do not arise out of machinery as such, but out of its capitalist employment! So, since machinery, considered by itself, shortens the hours of labor, but lengthens them in the service of capital; since in itself it lightens labor, but raises the intensity of labor when capital employs it; since in itself it is a victory of man over the forces of Nature, but in the hands of capital makes man the slave of those forces; since in itself it increases the wealth of the producers, but in the hands of capital makes them paupers ‒ for all these reasons and others besides, says the bourgeois economist without more ado, it is as clear as noonday that all these contradictions are a mere semblance of reality, and that in fact they have neither an actual nor a theoretical existence. In this way he spares himself all further racking of his brain. What is more, he implicitly declares that his opponent is stupid enough to fight, not against the capitalist employment of machinery, but against machinery itself.

<!-- ch15-p154 -->
No doubt he is far from denying that temporary inconvenience may result from the capitalist use of machinery. But where is the medal without its reverse side! To him, any employment of machinery except by capital is an impossibility. So, with him, the exploitation of the worker by the machine is the same thing as the exploitation of the machine by the worker. Therefore, by his reasoning, whoever exposes the real state of things in the capitalist employment of machinery is against employing machinery in any way, and is an enemy of social progress![^15.135] This is exactly the reasoning of the celebrated Bill Sykes (the murderer in Dickens's *Oliver Twist*). “Gentlemen of the jury, no doubt the throat of this traveling salesman has been cut. But that is not my fault, it is the fault of the knife. Must we, for such a temporary inconvenience, abolish the use of the knife? Only consider! Where would agriculture and trade be without the knife? Is it not as beneficial in surgery as it is expert in anatomy? And a willing helper at the feast table besides? If you abolish the knife – you hurl us back into the depths of barbarism.”[^15.136]

[^15.135]: MacCulloch, among others, is a past master of this pretentious idiocy. “If,” he says, with the put-on innocence of a child of 8 years, “if it be advantageous, to develop the skill of the workman more and more, so that he is capable of producing, with the same or with a less quantity of labour, a constantly increasing quantity of commodities, it must also be advantageous, that he should avail himself of the help of such machinery as will assist him most effectively in the attainment of this result.” (MacCulloch: “Princ. of Pol. Econ.,” London 1830, p. 166.)

[^15.136]: “The inventor of the spinning machine has ruined India, a fact, however, that touches us but little.” A. Thiers: De la propriété. — M. Thiers here confuses the spinning machine with the power-loom, “a fact, however, that touches us but little.”

<!-- ch15-p155 -->
Machinery necessarily throws men out of work in the industries into which it is introduced. Yet, despite this, it may bring about an increase of employment in other industries. This effect, however, has nothing in common with the so-called theory of compensation. Since every article produced by a machine is cheaper than a similar article produced by hand, we deduce the following infallible law. If the total quantity of an article produced by machinery is equal to the total quantity of the same article previously produced by a handicraft or by manufacture, and now made by machinery, then the total labor spent is reduced. The new labor spent on the instruments of labor, on the machinery, on the coal, and so on, must necessarily be less than the labor displaced by using the machinery. Otherwise the product of the machine would be as dear as the product of manual labor, or dearer. But in fact the total quantity of the article produced by machinery with a reduced number of workers does not stay equal to the total quantity of the hand-made article it has displaced: it far exceeds it. Suppose that 400,000 yards of cloth have been produced on power-looms by fewer weavers than could weave 100,000 yards by hand. The quadrupled product contains four times as much raw material. Hence the production of raw material must be quadrupled. But with the instruments of labor, such as buildings, coal, machinery, and so on, it is different. The additional labor needed to produce them can increase only up to a certain limit. That limit varies with the difference between the quantity of the machine-made article and the quantity of the same article that the same number of workers could make by hand.

<!-- ch15-p156 -->
Hence, as the use of machinery spreads in a given industry, the immediate effect is to increase production in the other industries that supply the first with means of production. How far this provides employment for a greater number of men depends, given the length of the working day and the intensity of labor, on the composition of the capital employed, that is, on the ratio of its constant part to its variable part. This ratio, in turn, varies considerably with the extent to which machinery has already seized on those trades, or is seizing on them at the time. The number of men condemned to work in coal and metal mines grew enormously because of the progress of the English factory system. But during the last few decades this increase in numbers has been slower, because of the use of new machinery in mining.[^15.137] A new type of worker springs into life along with the machine, namely its maker. We have already learned that machinery has taken over even this branch of production, on a scale that grows greater every day.[^15.138] As to raw material,[^15.139] there is not the least doubt about what the rapid strides of cotton spinning did. They not only pushed on the growth of cotton in the United States with tropical luxuriance, and with it the African slave trade, but also made the breeding of slaves the chief business of the border slave-states. When the first census of slaves was taken in the United States, in 1790, their number was 697,000; in 1861, it had nearly reached four millions. On the other hand, it is no less certain that the rise of the English woolen factories, together with the gradual conversion of cropland into sheep pasture, brought about the surplus of agricultural workers that led to their being driven in masses into the towns. Ireland has reduced its population by nearly one half during the last twenty years. At this moment it is undergoing the process of reducing the number of its inhabitants still further, so as to suit exactly the requirements of its landlords and of the English woolen manufacturers.

[^15.137]: According to the census of 1861 (Vol. II., London, 1863), the number of people employed in coal mines in England and Wales amounted to 246,613. Of these, 73,545 were under and 173,067 were over 20 years. Of those under 20, 835 were between 5 and 10 years old, 30,701 between 10 and 15 years, and 42,010 between 15 and 19 years. The number employed in iron, copper, lead, tin, and other mines of every description was 319, 222.

[^15.138]: In England and Wales, in 1861, 60,807 persons were employed in making machinery. This number includes the employers and their clerks, etc., and also all agents and business people connected with this industry. It excludes the makers of small machines, such as sewing-machines, etc., and also the makers of the working parts of machines, such as spindles. The total number of civil engineers was 3,329.

[^15.139]: Since iron is one of the most important raw materials, let me state here that in 1861 there were in England and Wales 125,771 working iron founders, of whom 123,430 were males and 2,341 females. Of the males, 30,810 were under and 92,620 over 20 years.

<!-- ch15-p157 -->
When machinery is applied to any of the preliminary or intermediate stages that the object of labor (the material being worked on) has to pass through on its way to completion, the yield of material in those stages increases. At the same time, the demand for labor increases in the handicrafts or branches of manufacture that the products of the machines supply. Spinning by machinery, for example, supplied yarn so cheaply and so abundantly that the hand-loom weavers were at first able to work full time without any increased outlay. Their earnings accordingly rose.[^15.140] Hence a flow of people into the cotton-weaving trade. In the end, the 800,000 weavers whom the Jenny, the throstle and the mule had called into existence were overwhelmed by the power-loom. In the same way, because machinery produced clothing materials in abundance, the number of tailors, seamstresses and needlewomen kept increasing until the sewing-machine appeared.

[^15.140]: “A family of four grown-up persons, with two children as winders, earned at the end of the last, and the beginning of the present century, by ten hours’ daily labour, £4 a week. If the work was very pressing, they could earn more.... Before that, they had always suffered from a deficient supply of yarn.” (Gaskell, cited above, pp. 25-27.)

<!-- ch15-p158 -->
In proportion as machinery, with the help of a relatively small number of workers, increases the mass of raw materials, intermediate products, instruments of labor, etc., the working-up of these raw materials and intermediate products splits into countless branches. Social production becomes more varied. The factory system carries the social division of labor immeasurably further than manufacture does, because it raises the productivity of the industries it seizes on to a far higher degree.

<!-- ch15-p159 -->
The immediate result of machinery is to increase surplus-value and the mass of products in which surplus-value is embodied. And as the things consumed by the capitalists and their dependents become more plentiful, so do these layers of society themselves. Their growing wealth, together with the relatively smaller number of workers needed to produce the necessaries of life, gives rise to the means of satisfying new luxurious wants, at the same time as those wants arise. A larger portion of society's produce is changed into surplus produce, and a larger part of the surplus produce is supplied for consumption in many refined forms. In other words, the production of luxuries increases.[^15.141] The refined and varied forms of the products are also due to new relations with the markets of the world, relations that modern industry creates. Not only are greater quantities of foreign luxury articles exchanged for home products. A greater mass of foreign raw materials, ingredients, and intermediate products is also used as means of production in the home industries. Because of these relations with the markets of the world, the demand for labor increases in the carrying trades (shipping and transport), which split up into numerous varieties.[^15.142]

[^15.141]: F. Engels, in “Lage, &c.,” points out the miserable condition of a large number of those who work on these very luxury articles. See also numerous instances in the “Reports of the Children’s Employment Commission.”

[^15.142]: In 1861, in England and Wales, there were 94,665 sailors in the merchant service.

<!-- ch15-p160 -->
The means of production and subsistence increase, while the number of workers falls relatively. This causes an increased demand for labor in making canals, docks, tunnels, bridges, and so on: works that can bear fruit only in the far future. Entirely new branches of production are also formed, creating new fields of labor. They arise as the direct result either of machinery or of the general industrial changes that machinery brings about. But even in the most developed countries, the place these branches occupy in total production is far from important. The number of workers they employ is directly proportional to the demand these industries create for the crudest kind of manual labor. At present the chief industries of this kind are gas-works, telegraphs, photography, steam navigation, and railways. According to the census of 1861 for England and Wales, we find 15,211 persons in the gas industry (gas-works, production of mechanical apparatus, employees of the gas companies, etc.); 2,399 in telegraphy; 2,366 in photography; 3,570 in steam navigation; and in railways, 70,599, of whom about 28,000 are made up of the unskilled “navvies” (laborers who dig and build the earthworks), employed more or less permanently, together with the whole administrative and commercial staff. So the total number of persons employed in these five new industries is 94,145.

<!-- ch15-p161 -->
Lastly, the extraordinary productivity of modern industry, accompanied as it is by both a more extensive and a more intense exploitation of labor-power in all other spheres of production, allows a larger and larger part of the working class to be employed unproductively. As a consequence, it allows the ancient domestic slaves to be reproduced, on a constantly extending scale, under the name of a servant class, which includes men-servants, women-servants, lackeys, etc. According to the census of 1861, the population of England and Wales was 20,066,244: 9,776,259 males and 10,289,965 females. From this population let us deduct all who are too old or too young for work; all unproductive women, young persons and children; the “ideological” classes, such as government officials, priests, lawyers, soldiers, etc.; further, all whose only occupation is to consume the labor of others in the form of rent, interest, etc.; and lastly, paupers, vagabonds, and criminals. There remain, in round numbers, eight millions of both sexes and of every age. That number includes every capitalist who is in any way engaged in industry, trade, or finance. Among these 8 millions are:

<!-- ch15-p162 -->
