[^15.143]: Of these, only 177,596 are males above 13 years of age.

[^15.144]: Of these, 30,501 are females.

[^15.145]: Of these, 137,447 are males. The 1,208,648 includes no one who does not serve in private houses. Between 1861 and 1870 the number of male servants nearly doubled, rising to 267,671. In the year 1847 there were 2,694 gamekeepers (for the landlords' game preserves); in 1869 there were 4,921. In everyday speech, the young servant girls in the houses of the London lower middle class are called “slaveys.”

<!-- ch15-p164 -->
All the persons employed in textile factories and in mines, taken together, number 1,208,442. Those employed in textile factories and metal industries, taken together, number 1,039,605. In both cases they are fewer than the modern domestic slaves. What a splendid result of the capitalist exploitation of machinery!

### Section 7: Repulsion and Attraction of Workpeople by the Factory System. Crises in the Cotton Trade

<!-- ch15-p165 -->
All political economists of any standing admit that the introduction of new machinery has a disastrous effect on the workers in the old handicrafts and branches of manufacture with which this machinery at first competes. Almost all of them lament the slavery of the factory worker. And what is the great trump card they play? That machinery, once the horrors of the period of its introduction and development have died down, in the long run increases the number of the slaves of labor instead of reducing it! Yes, political economy revels in the hideous theory, hideous to every “philanthropist” who believes in the eternal, Nature-ordained necessity of capitalist production, that after a period of growth and transition, even its crowning success, the factory system based on machinery, grinds down more workers than it throws on the streets when it is first introduced.[^15.146]

[^15.146]: Ganilh, on the contrary, considers that the final result of the factory system is an absolutely smaller number of factory workers, at whose expense a larger number of “gens honnêtes” [respectable people] live and develop their well-known “perfectibilité perfectible” [perfectible perfectibility]. Little as he understands the movement of production, he at least feels that machinery must be a very fatal institution if its introduction turns busy workers into paupers, and its development calls more slaves of labor into existence than it has done away with. The idiocy of his standpoint can only be brought out in his own words: “Les classes condamnées à produire et à consommer diminuent, et les classes qui dirigent le travail, qui soulagent, consolent, et éclairent toute la population, se multiplient ... et s’approprient tous les bienfaits qui résultent de la diminution des frais du travail, de l’abondance des productions, et du bon marché des consommations. Dans cette direction, l’espéce humaine s’élève aux plus hautes conceptions du génie, pénètre dans les profoundeurs mystérieuses de la religion, établit les principes salutaires de la morale (which consists in ‘s’approprier tous les beinfaits,’ etc.), les lois tutélaires de la liberté (liberty of ‘les classes condamnées à produire?’) et du pouvoir, de l’obéissance et de la justice, du devoir et de la l’humanité.” [The classes condemned to produce and to consume grow fewer, and the classes that direct labor, that relieve, console and enlighten the whole population, multiply ... and take for themselves all the benefits that come from the lower costs of labor, from the abundance of products and from the cheapness of consumer goods. In this way the human species rises to the highest creations of genius, reaches into the mysterious depths of religion, and lays down the beneficial principles of morality, the laws that protect liberty, and power, obedience and justice, duty and humanity.] For this drivel, see “Des Systèmes d’Economie Politique, &c., Par M. Ch. Ganilh,” 2ème ed., Paris, 1821, t. I, p. 224, and see p. 212.

<!-- ch15-p166 -->
It is true that in some cases, as we saw from the examples of English worsted and silk factories, a huge extension of the factory system may, at a certain stage of its development, go along with a decrease in the number of factory workers employed that is not only relative but absolute. In the year 1860 Parliament ordered a special census of all the factories in the United Kingdom. In the parts of Lancashire, Cheshire, and Yorkshire that made up the district of Mr. Baker, the factory inspector, there were 652 factories. 570 of these contained 85,622 power-looms and 6,819,146 spindles (not counting doubling spindles), used 27,439 horse-power (steam) and 1,390 (water), and employed 94,119 persons. In the year 1865 the same factories contained 95,163 looms and 7,025,031 spindles, had a steam-power of 28,925 horses and a water-power of 1,445 horses, and employed 88,913 persons. So between 1860 and 1865 looms increased by 11%, spindles by 3%, and engine-power by 3%, while the number of persons employed decreased by 5½%.[^15.147] Between 1852 and 1862 the English woolen industry expanded considerably, while the number of workers employed in it stayed almost the same,

[^15.147]: “Reports of Insp. of Fact., 31 Oct., 1865,” p. 58 and following. At the same time, however, employment for a larger number of workers was ready in 110 new mills with 11,625 looms, 628,576 spindles and 2,695 total horse-power of steam and water (cited above).

<!-- ch15-p167 -->
> “showing how greatly the introduction of new machines had superseded the labour of preceding periods.”[^15.148]

[^15.148]: “Reports, &c., for 31 Oct., 1862,” p. 79. At the end of 1871 Mr. A. Redgrave, the factory inspector, gave a lecture at Bradford, in the New Mechanics’ Institution, in which he said: “What has struck me for some time past is the altered appearance of the woollen factories. Formerly they were filled with women and children, now machinery seems to do all the work. At my asking for an explanation of this from a manufacturer, he gave me the following: ‘Under the old system I employed 63 persons; after the introduction of improved machinery I reduced my hands to 33, and lately, in consequence of new and extensive alterations, I have been in a position to reduce those 33 to 13’.”

<!-- ch15-p168 -->
In certain cases the increase in the number of workers employed is only apparent. That is, it does not come from the extension of factories already established, but from the gradual takeover of connected trades. For instance, between 1838 and 1856 power-looms increased, and so did the workers who ran them. In the cotton trade this was simply due to the growth of that branch of industry. But in the other trades it was due to steam-power being applied to the carpet-loom, the ribbon-loom, and the linen-loom, which had previously been worked by human muscle.[^15.149] So the increase of the workers in these latter trades was merely a symptom of a reduction in the total number employed. Finally, we have looked at this question entirely apart from the fact that everywhere except in the metal industries, young persons (under 18), women and children make up the predominant part of the class of factory workers.

[^15.149]: See “Reports, &c., 31 Oct., 1856,” p. 16.

<!-- ch15-p169 -->
Nevertheless, despite the mass of workers actually displaced and virtually replaced by machinery, we can understand how factory workers may become more numerous than the manufacturing workers and craftsmen who have been displaced, through the building of more mills and the extension of old ones in a given industry. Suppose, for example, that in the old mode of production a capital of £500 is employed weekly, two-fifths of it constant and three-fifths variable capital. That is, £200 is laid out in means of production, and £300, say £1 per man, in labor-power. When machinery is introduced, the composition of this capital changes. We will suppose it now consists of four-fifths constant and one-fifth variable capital, which means that only £100 is now laid out in labor-power. As a result, two-thirds of the workers are dismissed. If the business now expands, and the total capital employed grows to £1,500 under unchanged conditions, the number of workers employed will increase to 300, just as many as before the machinery was introduced. If the capital grows further to £2,000, 400 men will be employed, or one-third more than under the old system. Their numbers have in fact increased by 100. But relatively, that is, in proportion to the total capital advanced, they have decreased by 800, for under the old conditions the £2,000 capital would have employed 1,200 men instead of 400. So a relative decrease in the number of workers is consistent with an actual increase. We assumed above that while the total capital increases, its composition stays the same, because the conditions of production stay constant. But we have already seen that with every advance in the use of machinery, the constant part of capital increases (the part that consists of machinery, raw material, etc.), while the variable part, the part laid out in labor-power, decreases. We also know that in no other system of production is improvement so continuous, and the composition of the capital employed so constantly changing, as in the factory system. However, these changes are continually interrupted by periods of rest, during which the factories merely expand in quantity on the existing technical basis. During such periods the number of factory workers increases. Thus in 1835 the total number of workers in the cotton, woolen, worsted, flax, and silk factories of the United Kingdom was only 354,684, while in 1861 the power-loom weavers alone (of both sexes and all ages, from eight years up) numbered 230,654. Certainly, this growth looks less important when we consider that in 1838 the hand-loom weavers with their families still numbered 800,000,[^15.150] not to mention those thrown out of work in Asia and on the Continent of Europe.

[^15.150]: “The sufferings of the hand-loom weavers were the subject of an inquiry by a Royal Commission, but although their distress was acknowledged and lamented, the amelioration [improvement] of their condition was left, and probably necessarily so, to the chances and changes of time, which it may now be hoped” [20 years later!] “have nearly obliterated those miseries, and not improbably by the present great extension of the power-loom.” (“Rep. Insp. of Fact., 31 Oct., 1856,” p. 15.)

<!-- ch15-p170 -->
In the few remarks I still have to make on this point, I shall refer to some relations that actually exist, but whose existence our theoretical investigation has not yet revealed.

<!-- ch15-p171 -->
As long as the factory system spreads in a given branch of industry at the expense of the old handicrafts or of manufacture, the result is as certain as the result of a battle between an army equipped with breech-loading rifles and one armed with bows and arrows. This first period, in which machinery conquers its field of action, is of decisive importance because of the extraordinary profits it helps to produce. These profits are not only a source of faster accumulation (accumulation of capital: turning surplus-value back into capital, so that capital grows). They also attract into the favored sphere of production a large part of the additional social capital that is constantly being created and is always on the lookout for new investments. The special advantages of this first period of fast and furious activity are felt in every branch of production that machinery invades. But as soon as the factory system has gained a certain breadth of footing and a definite degree of maturity, and especially as soon as its technical basis, machinery, is itself produced by machinery; as soon as coal mining and iron mining, the metal industries, and the means of transport have been revolutionized; as soon, in short, as the general conditions needed for production by the modern industrial system have been established, this mode of production acquires an elasticity. It gains a capacity for sudden expansion by leaps and bounds, which meets no limit except the supply of raw material and the sale of the produce. On the one hand, the immediate effect of machinery is to increase the supply of raw material, in the way, for example, that the cotton gin increased the production of cotton.[^15.151] On the other hand, the cheapness of the articles produced by machinery, and the improved means of transport and communication, provide the weapons for conquering foreign markets. By ruining handicraft production in other countries, machinery forcibly turns them into fields for supplying its raw material. In this way East India was compelled to produce cotton, wool, hemp, jute, and indigo for Great Britain.[^15.152] In all countries where it has taken root, modern industry constantly makes a part of the workers “supernumerary” (surplus to need). In this way it spurs emigration and the colonization of foreign lands, which are thereby turned into settlements for growing the raw material of the mother country, just as Australia, for example, was turned into a colony for growing wool.[^15.153] A new and international division of labor springs up, a division suited to the requirements of the chief centers of modern industry. It turns one part of the globe into a chiefly agricultural field of production, for supplying the other part, which remains a chiefly industrial field. This revolution is bound up with radical changes in agriculture, which we need not look into further here.[^15.154]

[^15.151]: Other ways in which machinery affects the production of raw material will be mentioned in the third book.

<!-- ch15-p177 -->
The enormous power of expanding by jumps that is built into the factory system, and that system's dependence on the markets of the world, necessarily give rise to feverish production. This is followed by overfilling of the markets, and then the shrinking of the markets cripples production. The life of modern industry becomes a series of periods of moderate activity, prosperity, overproduction, crisis and stagnation. Machinery makes the employment of the factory workers, and so their conditions of life, uncertain and unstable. Because of these periodic changes of the industrial cycle, this uncertainty and instability become normal. Except in the periods of prosperity, the most furious struggle rages among the capitalists over each one's share of the markets. This share is directly proportional to the cheapness of the product. This struggle breeds rivalry in the use of improved machinery to replace labor-power, and of new methods of production. Besides this, there also comes a time in every industrial cycle when an attempt is made to force wages down below the value of labor-power, in order to cheapen commodities.[^15.155]

[^15.155]: In an appeal to the Trade Societies of England made in July, 1866, by the shoemakers of Leicester, who had been thrown on the streets by a lock-out, it is stated: “Twenty years ago the Leicester shoe trade was revolutionised by the introduction of riveting in the place of stitching. At that time good wages could be earned. Great competition was shown between the different firms as to which could turn out the neatest article. Shortly afterwards, however a worse kind of competition sprang up, namely, that of underselling one another in the market. The injurious consequences soon manifested themselves in reductions of wages, and so sweepingly quick was the fall in the price of labour, that many firms now pay only one half of the original wages. And yet, though wages sink lower and lower, profits appear, with each alteration in the scale of wages, to increase.” The manufacturers use even bad times to make exceptional profits by cutting wages excessively, that is, by directly robbing the worker of means of subsistence. One example (it refers to the crisis in the Coventry silk weaving): “From information I have received from manufacturers as well as workmen, there seems to be no doubt that wages have been reduced to a greater extent than either the competition of the foreign producers, or other circumstances have rendered necessary ... the majority of weavers are working at a reduction of 30 to 40 per cent. in their wages. A piece of ribbon for making which the weaver got 6s. or 7s. five years back, now only brings them 3s. 3d. or 3s. 6d.; other work is now priced at 2s. and 2s. 3d. which was formerly priced at 4s. and 4s. 3d. The reduction in wage seems to have been carried to a greater extent than is necessary for increasing demand. Indeed, the reduction in the cost of weaving, in the case of many descriptions of ribbons, has not been accompanied by any corresponding reduction in the selling price of the manufactured article.” (Mr. F. D. Longe’s Report. “Ch. Emp. Com., V. Rep., 1866,” p. 114, 1.)

<!-- ch15-p178 -->
So a necessary condition for the growth of the number of factory workers is a proportionally much faster growth of the amount of capital invested in mills. This growth, however, depends on the ebb and flow of the industrial cycle. Besides, it is constantly interrupted by technical progress, which at one time virtually takes the place of new workers, and at another actually displaces old ones. This qualitative change in mechanical industry continually discharges workers from the factory, or shuts its doors against the fresh stream of recruits. Meanwhile the purely quantitative extension of the factories absorbs not only the men thrown out of work, but also fresh contingents. So the workers are continually both repelled and attracted, hustled from pillar to post, while at the same time the sex, age, and skill of the recruits constantly change.

<!-- ch15-p179 -->
The lot of the factory workers will be best shown by a rapid survey of the course of the English cotton industry.

<!-- ch15-p180 -->
From 1770 to 1815 this trade was depressed or stagnant for 5 years only. During this period of 45 years the English manufacturers had a monopoly of machinery and of the markets of the world. From 1815 to 1821 depression; 1822 and 1823 prosperity; 1824 repeal of the laws against Trades’ Unions, great extension of factories everywhere; 1825 crisis; 1826 great misery and riots among the factory workers; 1827 slight improvement; 1828 great increase in power-looms and in exports; 1829 exports, especially to India, surpass all former years; 1830 glutted markets, great distress; 1831 to 1833 continued depression, the East India Company loses its monopoly of the trade with India and China; 1834 great increase of factories and machinery, shortage of workers. The new poor law encourages the migration of agricultural laborers into the factory districts. The country districts are swept clean of children. White slave trade; 1835 great prosperity, while at the same time the hand-loom weavers starve; 1836 great prosperity; 1837 and 1838 depression and crisis; 1839 revival; 1840 great depression, riots, the military called out; 1841 and 1842 frightful suffering among the factory workers; 1842 the manufacturers lock the workers out of the factories in order to force the repeal of the Corn Laws (the tariffs on imported grain). The factory workers stream in thousands into the towns of Lancashire and Yorkshire, are driven back by the military, and their leaders are brought to trial at Lancaster; 1843 great misery; 1844 revival; 1845 great prosperity; 1846 continued improvement at first, then reaction. Repeal of the Corn Laws; 1847 crisis, general reduction of wages by 10 and more percent in honor of the “big loaf”; 1848 continued depression; Manchester under military protection; 1849 revival; 1850 prosperity; 1851 falling prices, low wages, frequent strikes; 1852 improvement begins, strikes continue, the manufacturers threaten to import foreign workers; 1853 increasing exports. Strike for 8 months, and great misery at Preston; 1854 prosperity, glutted markets; 1855 news of failures streams in from the United States, Canada, and the Eastern markets; 1856 great prosperity; 1857 crisis; 1858 improvement; 1859 great prosperity, increase in factories; 1860 peak of the English cotton trade, the Indian, Australian, and other markets so glutted with goods that even in 1863 they had not absorbed the whole lot; the French Treaty of Commerce, enormous growth of factories and machinery; 1861 prosperity continues for a time, reaction, the American Civil War, cotton famine: 1862 to 1863 complete collapse.

<!-- ch15-p181 -->
The history of the cotton famine is too characteristic for us not to dwell on it for a moment. From the signs of the state of the world markets in 1860 and 1861, we see that the cotton famine came in the nick of time for the manufacturers, and was to some extent to their advantage. This fact was acknowledged in the reports of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, proclaimed in Parliament by Palmerston and Derby, and confirmed by events.[^15.156] No doubt, among the 2,887 cotton mills in the United Kingdom in 1861, there were many small ones. According to the report of Mr. A. Redgrave, out of the 2,109 mills included in his district, 392, or 19%, used less than ten horse-power each; 345, or 16%, used 10 H. P. and less than 20 H. P.; while 1,372 used more than 20 H. P.[^15.157] Most of the small mills were weaving sheds built during the period of prosperity after 1858, mostly by speculators, one of whom supplied the yarn, another the machinery, a third the buildings. They were run by men who had been overseers, or by other persons of small means. Most of these small manufacturers went under. The same fate would have overtaken them in the commercial crisis that was put off only by the cotton famine. Although they made up one-third of the total number of manufacturers, their mills absorbed a much smaller part of the capital invested in the cotton trade. As to the extent of the stoppage, reliable estimates show that in October 1862, 60.3% of the spindles and 58% of the looms were standing idle. This refers to the cotton trade as a whole, and of course needs considerable adjustment for individual districts. Only very few mills worked full time (60 hours a week); the rest worked at intervals. Even in the few cases where full time was worked, at the usual rate of piece wages (wages paid per piece of work done), the weekly wages of the factory workers necessarily shrank. This was because good cotton was replaced by bad: Sea Island by Egyptian (in fine spinning mills), American and Egyptian by Surat, and pure cotton by mixtures of waste and Surat. The shorter fiber of the Surat cotton and its dirty condition, the greater fragility of the thread, and the use of all sorts of heavy ingredients instead of flour in sizing the warps all had the same effects. They lowered the speed of the machinery, or the number of looms one weaver could tend, increased the labor caused by defects in the machinery, and reduced piece wages by reducing the amount of product turned out. Where Surat cotton was used, the loss to the factory workers on full time amounted to 20, 30, and more percent. But besides this, most of the manufacturers cut the rate of piece wages by 5, 7½, and 10 percent. We can therefore imagine the situation of those workers who were employed for only 3, 3½ or 4 days a week, or for only 6 hours a day. Even in 1863, after a comparative improvement had set in, the weekly wages of spinners and of weavers were 3s. 4d., 3s. 10d., 4s. 6d. and 5s. 1d.[^15.158] Yet even in this miserable state of things, the inventive spirit of the employer never stood still, but busied itself with making deductions from wages. To some extent these were imposed as a penalty for defects in the finished article that were really due to his bad cotton and his unsuitable machinery. Moreover, where the manufacturer owned the workers' cottages, he paid himself his rents by deducting them from these miserable wages. Mr. Redgrave tells us of self-acting minders (factory workers who manage a pair of self-acting mules)

[^15.156]: Compare “Reports of Insp. of Fact., 31st October, 1862,” p. 30.

[^15.157]: Cited above, p. 19.

[^15.158]: “Rep. Insp. of Fact., 31st October, 1863,” pp. 41-45.

<!-- ch15-p182 -->
> “earning at the end of a fortnight’s full work 8s. 11d., and that from this sum was deducted the rent of the house, the manufacturer, however, returning half the rent as a gift. The minders took away the sum of 6s. 11d. In many places the self-acting minders ranged from 5s. to 9s. per week, and the weavers from 2s. to 6s. per week, during the latter part of 1862.”[^15.159]

[^15.159]: Cited above, pp. 41-42

<!-- ch15-p183 -->
Even when the factory workers were on short time, the rent was often deducted from their wages.[^15.160] No wonder that in some parts of Lancashire a kind of famine fever broke out. But more characteristic than all this was the revolution in the process of production that was carried out at the expense of the workers. Experimenta in corpore vili [experiments on a worthless body], like those of anatomists on frogs, were formally made.

[^15.160]: Cited above, p. 57.

<!-- ch15-p184 -->
> “Although,” says Mr. Redgrave, “I have given the actual earnings of the operatives in the several mills, it does not follow that they earn the same amount week by week. The operatives are subject to great fluctuation from the constant experimentalising of the manufacturers ... the earnings of the operatives rise and fall with the quality of the cotton mixings; sometimes they have been within 15 per cent. of former earnings, and then, in a week or two, they have fallen off from 50 to 60 per cent.”[^15.161]

[^15.161]: Cited above, pp. 50-51.

<!-- ch15-p185 -->
These experiments were not made solely at the expense of the worker's means of subsistence. His five senses also had to pay the penalty.

<!-- ch15-p186 -->
> “The people who are employed in making up Surat cotton complain very much. They inform me, on opening the bales of cotton there is an intolerable smell, which causes sickness.... In the mixing, scribbling and carding rooms, the dust and dirt which are disengaged, irritate the air passages, and give rise to cough and difficulty of breathing. A disease of the skin, no doubt from the irritation of the dirt contained in the Surat cotton, also prevails.... The fibre being so short, a great amount of size [paste used to stiffen the thread], both animal and vegetable, is used.... Bronchitis is more prevalent owing to the dust. Inflammatory sore throat is common, from the same cause. Sickness and dyspepsia [indigestion] are produced by the frequent breaking of the weft, when the weaver sucks the weft through the eye of the shuttle.” On the other hand, the substitutes for flour were a Fortunatus’ purse (the never-emptying purse of the old tale) to the manufacturers, because they increased the weight of the yarn. They caused “15 lbs. of raw material to weigh 26 lbs. after it was woven.”[^15.162]

[^15.162]: Cited above, pp. 62-63.

<!-- ch15-p187 -->
In the Report of Inspectors of Factories for 30th April, 1864, we read the following:

<!-- ch15-p188 -->
> “The trade is availing itself of this resource at present to an extent which is even discreditable. I have heard on good authority of a cloth weighing 8 lbs. which was made of 5 1/4 lbs. cotton and 2 3/4 lbs. size; and of another cloth weighing 5 1/4 lbs., of which 2 lbs. was size. These were ordinary export shirtings. In cloths of other descriptions, as much as 50 per cent. size is sometimes added; so that a manufacturer may, and does truly boast, that he is getting rich by selling cloth for less money per pound than he paid for the mere yarn of which they are composed.”[^15.163]

[^15.163]: “Rep. &c., 30th April, 1864,” p. 27.

<!-- ch15-p189 -->
But the workers had to suffer from more than the experiments of the manufacturers inside the mills, and of the municipalities outside; more than reduced wages and lack of work, want and charity, and the speeches of praise from lords and commons.

<!-- ch15-p190 -->
> “Unfortunate females who, in consequence of the cotton famine, were at its commencement thrown out of employment, and have thereby become outcasts of society; and now, though trade has revived, and work is plentiful, continue members of that unfortunate class, and are likely to continue so. There are also in the borough more youthful prostitutes than I have known for the last 25 years.”[^15.164]

[^15.164]: From a letter of Mr. Harris, Chief Constable of Bolton, in “Rep. of Insp. of Fact., 31st October, 1865,” pp. 61-62.

<!-- ch15-p191 -->
So in the first 45 years of the English cotton trade, from 1770 to 1815, we find only 5 years of crisis and stagnation; but this was the period of monopoly. The second period, from 1815 to 1863, counts in its 48 years only 20 years of revival and prosperity against 28 of depression and stagnation. Between 1815 and 1830 competition with the continent of Europe and with the United States sets in. After 1833 the extension of the Asiatic markets is forced through by “destruction of the human race” (the wholesale wiping out of Indian hand-loom weavers). After the repeal of the Corn Laws, from 1846 to 1863, there are 8 years of moderate activity and prosperity against 9 years of depression and stagnation. The condition of the adult male factory workers, even during the years of prosperity, may be judged from the note below.[^15.165]

[^15.165]: In an appeal dated 1863 by the factory workers of Lancashire, etc., for the purpose of forming a society for organized emigration, we find the following: “That a large emigration of factory workers is now absolutely essential to raise them from their present prostrate condition, few will deny; but to show that a continuous stream of emigration is at all times demanded, and, without which it is impossible for them to maintain their position in ordinary times, we beg to call attention to the subjoined facts: — In 1814 the official value of cotton goods exported was £17,665,378, whilst the real marketable value was £20,070,824. In 1858 the official value of cotton goods exported, was £182,221,681; but the real or marketable value was only £43,001,322, being a ten-fold quantity sold for little more than double the former price. To produce results so disadvantageous to the country generally, and to the factory workers in particular, several causes have co-operated, which, had circumstances permitted, we should have brought more prominently under your notice; suffice it for the present to say that the most obvious one is the constant redundancy of labour, without which a trade so ruinous in its effects never could have been carried on, and which requires a constantly extending market to save it from annihilation. Our cotton mills may be brought to a stand by the periodical stagnations of trade, which, under present arrangements, are as inevitable as death itself; but the human mind is constantly at work, and although we believe we are under the mark in stating that six millions of persons have left these shores during the last 25 years, yet, from the natural increase of population, and the displacement of labour to cheapen production, a large percentage of the male adults in the most prosperous times find it impossible to obtain work in factories on any conditions whatever.” (“Reports of Insp. of Fact., 30th April 1863,” pp. 51-52.) In a later chapter we shall see how our friends the manufacturers tried, during the catastrophe in the cotton trade, to prevent the emigration of the factory workers by every means, including State interference.

### Section 8: Revolution Effected in Manufacture, Handicrafts, and Domestic Industry by Modern Industry

#### A. Overthrow of Cooperation Based on Handicraft and on the Division of Labor

<!-- ch15-p192 -->
We have seen how machinery does away with cooperation based on handicrafts, and with manufacture based on the division of handicraft labor. An example of the first kind is the mowing-machine: it replaces cooperation between mowers. A striking example of the second kind is the needle-making machine. According to Adam Smith, 10 men in his day, working in cooperation, made over 48,000 needles a day. A single needle-machine, on the other hand, makes 145,000 in a working day of 11 hours. One woman or one girl supervises four such machines, and so produces close to 600,000 needles in a day, and more than 3,000,000 in a week.[^15.166] When a single machine takes the place of cooperation or of manufacture, it may itself serve as the basis of an industry of a handicraft character. Still, such a return to handicrafts is only a transition to the factory system. As a rule, the factory system appears as soon as a mechanical motive power, such as steam or water, replaces human muscles for driving the machines. Here and there, but in any case only for a time, an industry may be carried on on a small scale by means of mechanical power. This is done by hiring steam-power, as in some of the Birmingham trades, or by using small caloric-engines, as in some branches of weaving.[^15.167] In the Coventry silk-weaving industry the experiment of “cottage factories” was tried. An engine-house was built in the center of a square surrounded by rows of cottages, and the engine was connected by shafts with the looms in the cottages. In all cases the power was hired at so much per loom. The rent was payable weekly, whether the looms worked or not. Each cottage held from 2 to 6 looms; some belonged to the weaver, some were bought on credit, some were hired. The struggle between these cottage factories and the factory proper lasted over 12 years. It ended with the complete ruin of the 300 cottage factories.[^15.168] Wherever the nature of the process did not involve production on a large scale, the new industries that have sprung up in the last few decades, such as envelope making, steel-pen making, etc., have as a general rule passed first through the handicraft stage and then through the manufacturing stage, as short phases of transition to the factory stage. The transition is very difficult where making the article by manufacture consists not of a series of graduated processes but of a great number of disconnected ones. This circumstance was a great obstacle to setting up steel-pen factories. Nevertheless, about 15 years ago, a machine was invented that automatically performed 6 separate operations at once. The first steel-pens were supplied by the handicraft system, in the year 1820, at £7 4s. the gross; in 1830 manufacture supplied them at 8s.; and today the factory system supplies them to the trade at from 2 to 6d. the gross.[^15.169]

[^15.166]: “Ch. Empl. Comm. III. Report, 1864,” p. 108, n. 447.

[^15.167]: In the United States this kind of restoration of handicrafts based on machinery is frequent. Therefore, when the inevitable transition to the factory system takes place, the concentration that follows will, compared with Europe and even with England, stride on in seven-league boots.

[^15.168]: See “Rep. of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1865,” p. 64.

[^15.169]: Mr. Gillott built the first large-scale steel-pen factory in Birmingham. As early as 1851 it produced over 180,000,000 pens a year, and consumed 120 tons of steel. Birmingham has the monopoly of this industry in the United Kingdom, and at present produces thousands of millions of steel-pens. According to the Census of 1861, the number of persons employed was 1,428, of whom 1,268 were females from 5 years of age upwards.

#### B. Reaction of the Factory System on Manufacture and Domestic Industries

<!-- ch15-p193 -->
Along with the development of the factory system, and of the revolution in agriculture that goes with it, production in all the other branches of industry not only expands but also changes its character. The factory system carries out the principle of analyzing the process of production into its constituent phases, and of solving the problems this poses by applying mechanics, chemistry, and the whole range of the natural sciences. This principle now becomes the determining principle everywhere. Hence machinery squeezes its way into the manufacturing industries, first for one detail process, then for another. In this way the solid crystal of their organization, based on the old division of labor, is dissolved and gives way to constant changes. Independently of this, a radical change takes place in the composition of the collective worker, a change in the persons working in combination. In contrast with the manufacturing period, the division of labor is from then on based, wherever possible, on employing women, children of all ages, and unskilled workers, in one word, on cheap labor, as it is characteristically called in England. This is the case not only with all large-scale production, whether it uses machinery or not, but also with the so-called domestic industry, whether carried on in the workers' houses or in small workshops. This modern so-called domestic industry has nothing in common, except the name, with the old-fashioned domestic industry. The existence of the old kind presupposes independent urban handicrafts, independent peasant farming, and above all a dwelling-house for the worker and his family. That old-fashioned industry has now been turned into an outside department of the factory, the manufacturing workshop, or the warehouse. Besides the factory workers, the manufacturing workers, and the craftsmen, whom it concentrates in large masses in one place and commands directly, capital also sets in motion another army by means of invisible threads: the workers in the domestic industries, who live in the large towns and are also scattered over the face of the country. An example: the shirt factory of Messrs. Tillie at Londonderry, which employs 1,000 factory workers in the factory itself, and 9,000 people spread up and down the country and working in their own houses.[^15.170]

[^15.170]: “Ch. Empl. Comm. II. Rep. 1864,” p. LXVIII., n. 415.

<!-- ch15-p194 -->
The exploitation of cheap and immature labor-power is carried out more shamelessly in modern manufacture than in the factory proper. This is because the technical foundation of the factory system, namely the replacement of muscular power by machines and the light character of the labor, is almost entirely absent in manufacture. At the same time, women and over-young children are exposed, in a most unconscionable way, to the influence of poisonous or harmful substances. This exploitation is more shameless in the so-called domestic industry than in manufacture. The reasons are these: the workers' power of resistance decreases as they are scattered; a whole series of plundering parasites push their way in between the employer and the worker; a domestic industry always has to compete either with the factory system or with manufacture in the same branch of production; poverty robs the worker of the conditions most essential to his labor, of space, light, and ventilation; employment becomes more and more irregular; and, finally, in these last refuges of the masses made “redundant” by modern industry and agriculture, competition for work reaches its maximum. Economy in the means of production was first carried out systematically in the factory system. There, from the very beginning, it went hand in hand with the most reckless squandering of labor-power and with robbery of the conditions normally needed for labor. This economy now shows its antagonistic and murderous side more and more in a given branch of industry, the less the social productive power of labor and the technical basis for a combination of processes are developed in that branch.

#### C. Modern Manufacture

<!-- ch15-p195 -->
I now go on to illustrate the principles laid down above with a few examples. In fact, the reader already knows numerous instances from the chapter on the working day. In the hardware manufacture of Birmingham and its neighborhood, 30,000 children and young persons, besides 10,000 women, are employed, mostly in very heavy work. They are to be seen there in the unhealthy brass-foundries, button factories, and enameling, galvanizing, and lacquering works.[^15.171] Because of the excessive labor of their workers, both adult and non-adult, certain London houses where newspapers and books are printed have earned the ill-omened name of “slaughterhouses.”[^15.172] Similar excesses occur in book-binding, where the victims are chiefly women, girls, and children. Young persons have to do heavy work in rope-walks (long sheds where rope is made) and night-work in salt mines, candle manufacturing workshops, and chemical works. Young people are worked to death turning the looms in silk weaving, where it is not carried on by machinery.[^15.173] One of the most shameful, the dirtiest, and the worst-paid kinds of labor, and one for which women and young girls are preferred, is the sorting of rags. It is well known that Great Britain, apart from its own immense store of rags, is the central market for the rag trade of the whole world. Rags flow in from Japan, from the most remote states of South America, and from the Canary Islands. But the chief sources of supply are Germany, France, Russia, Italy, Egypt, Turkey, Belgium, and Holland. They are used for manure, for stuffing bedding, for shoddy (cloth made from shredded rags), and as the raw material of paper. The rag-sorters are the medium through which small-pox and other infectious diseases spread, and they themselves are the first victims.[^15.174] A classic example of overwork, of hard and unsuitable labor, and of its brutalizing effects on the worker from childhood on, is found not only in coal-mining and among miners generally, but also in tile and brick making. In this industry, in England, the recently invented machinery is used only here and there. Between May and September the work lasts from 5 in the morning till 8 in the evening, and where the drying is done in the open air it often lasts from 4 in the morning till 9 in the evening. Work from 5 in the morning till 7 in the evening is considered “reduced” and “moderate.” Both boys and girls of 6, and even of 4, years of age are employed. They work the same number of hours as the adults, often longer. The work is hard, and the summer heat adds to the exhaustion. In a certain tile-field at Mosley, for example, a young woman 24 years of age used to make 2,000 tiles a day, with the help of 2 little girls who carried the clay for her and stacked the tiles. These girls carried 10 tons a day up the slippery sides of the clay pits, from a depth of 30 feet, and then for a distance of 210 feet.

[^15.171]: And now, if you please, children are employed at file-cutting in Sheffield.

[^15.172]: “Ch. Empl. Comm., V. Rep. 1866,” p. 3, n. 24; p. 6, n. 55, 56; p. 7, n. 59, 60.

[^15.173]: Cited above, pp. 114, 115, n. 6, 7. The commissioner rightly remarks that although as a rule machines take the place of men, here young persons literally replace machines.

[^15.174]: See the Report on the rag trade, and numerous details in “Public Health, VIII. Rep.” London 1866, app., pp. 196, 208.

<!-- ch15-p196 -->
> “It is impossible for a child to pass through the purgatory of a tile-field without great moral degradation... the low language, which they are accustomed to hear from their tenderest years, the filthy, indecent, and shameless habits, amidst which, unknowing, and half wild, they grow up, make them in after-life lawless, abandoned, dissolute.... A frightful source of demoralisation is the mode of living. Each moulder, who is always a skilled labourer, and the chief of a group, supplies his 7 subordinates with board and lodging in his cottage. Whether members of his family or not, the men, boys, and girls all sleep in the cottage, which contains generally two, exceptionally 3 rooms, all on the ground floor, and badly ventilated. These people are so exhausted after the day’s hard work, that neither the rules of health, of cleanliness, nor of decency are in the least observed. Many of these cottages are models of untidiness, dirt, and dust.... The greatest evil of the system that employs young girls on this sort of work consists in this: that, as a rule, it chains them fast from childhood for the whole of their after-life to the most abandoned rabble. They become rough, foul-mouthed boys, before Nature has taught them that they are women. Clothed in a few dirty rags, the legs naked far above the knees, hair and face besmeared with dirt, they learn to treat all feelings of decency and of shame with contempt. During meal-times they lie at full length in the fields, or watch the boys bathing in a neighbouring canal. Their heavy day’s work at length completed, they put on better clothes, and accompany the men to the public houses [pubs].”

<!-- ch15-p197 -->
That heavy drinking is widespread from childhood on among the whole of this class is only natural.

<!-- ch15-p198 -->
> “The worst is that the brickmakers despair of themselves. You might as well, said one of the better kind to a chaplain of Southallfield, try to raise and improve the devil as a brickie, sir!”[^15.175]

[^15.175]: “Ch. Empl. Comm. V. Rep., 1866,” pp. xvi-xviii, n. 86-97, and pp. 130-133, n. 39-71. See also III. Rep., 1864, pp. 48, 56.

<!-- ch15-p199 -->
As to the way in which capital economizes on the requisites of labor (the things labor needs) in modern manufacture (in which I include all larger workshops, except factories proper), official and very ample material on the subject is to be found in the Public Health Reports IV. (1863) and VI. (1864). The description of the workshops, especially those of the London printers and tailors, goes beyond the most loathsome fantasies of our romance writers. The effect on the workers' health is self-evident. Dr. Simon, the chief medical officer of the Privy Council and the official editor of the “Public Health Reports,” says:

<!-- ch15-p200 -->
> “In my fourth Report (1863) I showed how it is practically impossible for the workpeople to insist upon that which is their first sanitary right, viz., the right that, no matter what the work for which their employer brings them together, the labour, so far as it depends upon him, should be freed from all avoidably unwholesome conditions. I pointed out that while the workpeople are practically incapable of doing themselves this sanitary justice, they are unable to obtain any effective support from the paid administrations of the sanitary police [public health authorities].... The life of myriads of workmen and workwomen is now uselessly tortured and shortened by the never-ending physical suffering that their mere occupation begets.”[^15.176]

[^15.176]: “Public Health. Sixth Rep.,” London 1864, pp. 29, 31.

<!-- ch15-p201 -->
To illustrate how the workrooms affect the state of health, Dr. Simon gives the following table of mortality.[^15.177]

[^15.177]: Cited above, p. 30. Dr. Simon remarks that the mortality among the London tailors and printers between the ages of 25 and 35 is in fact much greater. The reason is that the employers in London bring in from the country a great number of young people up to 30 years of age, as “apprentices” and “improvers,” who come in order to be perfected in their trade. These figure in the census as Londoners. They swell the number of heads on which the London death-rate is calculated, without adding proportionally to the number of deaths there. Most of them in fact return to the country, especially in cases of severe illness. (Cited above.)

#### D. Modern Domestic Industry

<!-- ch15-p205 -->
I now come to the so-called domestic industry. To get an idea of the horrors of this sphere, in which capital carries on its exploitation in the background of modern mechanical industry, one must go to the apparently quite idyllic trade of nail-making,[^15.178] carried on in a few remote villages of England. Here, however, it will be enough to give a few examples from those branches of the lace-making and straw-plaiting industries that are not yet carried on with the help of machinery, and that do not yet compete with branches carried on in factories or in manufacturing workshops.

[^15.178]: I mean here hammered nails, as distinguished from nails cut out and made by machinery. See “Child. Empl. Comm., Third Rep.,” pp. xi., xix., n. 125-130, p. 52, n. 11, p. 114, n. 487, p. 137, n. 674.

<!-- ch15-p206 -->
Of the 150,000 persons employed in England in the production of lace, about 10,000 come under the authority of the Factory Act, 1861. Almost all of the remaining 140,000 are women, young persons, and children of both sexes, though the male sex is weakly represented. The state of health of this cheap material for exploitation can be seen from the following table, computed by Dr. Trueman, physician to the Nottingham General Dispensary. Out of 686 female patients who were lace-makers, most of them between the ages of 17 and 24, the number with consumption (tuberculosis) was:

<!-- ch15-p207 -->
1852. – 1 in 45. 1857. – 1 in 13.\
1853. – 1 in 28. 1858. – 1 in 15.\
1854. – 1 in 17. 1859. – 1 in 9.\
1856. – 1 in 15. 1861. – 1 in 8.[^15.179]

[^15.179]: “Ch. Empl. Comm., II. Rep.,” p. xxii, n. 166.

<!-- ch15-p208 -->
This progress in the rate of consumption ought to satisfy the most optimistic believer in progress, and the biggest peddler of lies among the Free-trade traveling salesmen of Germany.

<!-- ch15-p209 -->
The Factory Act of 1861 regulates the actual making of the lace, insofar as it is done by machinery, and this is the rule in England. The branches we are now about to examine, looking only at the workers who work at home and not at those who work in manufacturing workshops or warehouses, fall into two divisions, namely (1) finishing and (2) mending. Finishing gives the final touches to the machine-made lace, and includes numerous sub-divisions.

<!-- ch15-p210 -->
Lace finishing is done either in what are called “mistresses’ houses,” or by women in their own houses, with or without the help of their children. The women who keep the “mistresses’ houses” are themselves poor. The workroom is in a private house. The mistresses take orders from manufacturers or from warehousemen, and employ as many women, girls, and young children as the size of their rooms and the fluctuating demand of the business will allow. The number of workwomen employed in these workrooms varies from 20 to 40 in some, and from 10 to 20 in others. The average age at which the children start work is six years, but in many cases it is below five. The usual working hours are from 8 in the morning till eight in the evening, with 1½ hours for meals, which are taken at irregular intervals and often in the foul workrooms. When business is brisk, the labor often lasts from 8 or even 6 o’clock in the morning till 10, 11, or 12 o’clock at night. In English barracks the regulation space allotted to each soldier is 500-600 cubic feet, and in the military hospitals 1,200 cubic feet. But in those finishing sties there are only 67 to 100 cubic feet to each person. At the same time, gas-lights consume the oxygen of the air. To keep the lace clean, the children are often forced to take off their shoes, even in winter, although the floor is tiled or flagged.

<!-- ch15-p211 -->
> “It is not at all uncommon in Nottingham to find 14 to 20 children huddled together in a small room, of, perhaps, not more than 12 feet square, and employed for 15 hours out of the 24, at work that of itself is exhausting, from its weariness and monotony, and is besides carried on under every possible unwholesome condition.... Even the very youngest children work with a strained attention and a rapidity that is astonishing, hardly ever giving their fingers rest or glowering their motion. If a question be asked them, they never raise their eyes from their work from fear of losing a single moment.”

<!-- ch15-p212 -->
The mistresses use the “long stick” as a stimulant more and more as the working hours are lengthened.

<!-- ch15-p213 -->
> “The children gradually tire and become as restless as birds towards the end of their long detention at an occupation that is monotonous, eye-straining, and exhausting from the uniformity in the posture of the body. Their work is like slavery.”[^15.180]

[^15.180]: “Ch. Empl. Comm., II. Rep., 1864,” pp. xix., xx., xxi.

<!-- ch15-p214 -->
When women and their children work at home, which nowadays means in a hired room, often in an attic, things are, if possible, still worse. This sort of work is given out within a radius of 80 miles around Nottingham. When the children leave the warehouses at 9 or 10 o’clock at night, they are often given a bundle of lace to take home with them and finish. The Pharisee of a capitalist, represented by one of his servants, accompanies this act, of course, with the oily phrase: “That’s for mother.” Yet he knows well enough that the poor children must sit up and help.[^15.181]

[^15.181]: Cited above, pp. xxi., xxii.

<!-- ch15-p215 -->
Pillow lace-making is carried on in England chiefly in two agricultural districts. One is the Honiton lace district, which stretches from 20 to 30 miles along the south coast of Devonshire and includes a few places in North Devon. The other takes in a great part of the counties of Buckingham, Bedford, and Northampton, and also the neighboring parts of Oxfordshire and Huntingdonshire. The work is usually carried on in the cottages of the farm laborers. Many manufacturers employ more than 3,000 of these lace-makers, who are chiefly children and young persons, exclusively of the female sex. The state of things described for lace finishing is repeated here, except that instead of the “mistresses’ houses” we find what are called “lace-schools,” kept by poor women in their cottages. The children work in these schools from their fifth year, and often earlier, until their twelfth or fifteenth year. During the first year the very young ones work from four to eight hours, and later on from six in the morning till eight and ten o’clock at night.

<!-- ch15-p216 -->
> “The rooms are generally the ordinary living rooms of small cottages, the chimney stopped up to keep out draughts, the inmates kept warm by their own animal heat alone, and this frequently in winter. In other cases, these so-called school-rooms are like small store-rooms without fire-places.... The over-crowding in these dens and the consequent vitiation [fouling] of the air are often extreme. Added to this is the injurious effect of drains, privies [outdoor toilets], decomposing substances, and other filth usual in the purlieus [surroundings] of the smaller cottages.” With regard to space: “In one lace-school 18 girls and a mistress, 35 cubic feet to each person; in another, where the smell was unbearable, 18 persons and 24½ cubic feet per head. In this industry are to be found employed children of 2 and 2½ years.”[^15.182]

[^15.182]: Cited above, pp. xxix., xxx.

<!-- ch15-p217 -->
Where lace-making ends in the counties of Buckingham and Bedford, straw-plaiting begins, and it extends over a large part of Hertfordshire and the western and northern parts of Essex. In 1861 there were 40,043 persons employed in straw-plaiting and straw-hat making. Of these, 3,815 were males of all ages, and the rest females, of whom 14,913, including about 7,000 children, were under 20 years of age. In place of the lace-schools we find here the “straw-plait schools.” The children generally begin their instruction in straw-plaiting in their 4th year, often between their 3rd and 4th year. Education, of course, they get none. The children themselves call the elementary schools “natural schools,” to distinguish them from these blood-sucking institutions. In these they are kept at work simply to get through the task prescribed by their half-starved mothers, generally 30 yards a day. These same mothers often make them work at home after school is over, till 10, 11, and 12 o’clock at night. The straw cuts their mouths, with which they constantly moisten it, and their fingers. Dr. Ballard gives it as the general opinion of the whole body of medical officers in London that 300 cubic feet is the minimum proper space for each person in a bedroom or workroom. But in the straw-plait schools space is allotted more sparingly than in the lace-schools: “12 2/3, 17, 18½ and below 22 cubic feet for each person.”

<!-- ch15-p218 -->
> “The smaller of these numbers, says one of the commissioners, Mr. White, represents less space than the half of what a child would occupy if packed in a box measuring 3 feet in each direction.”

<!-- ch15-p219 -->
That is how the children enjoy life till the age of 12 or 14. The wretched, half-starved parents think of nothing but getting as much as possible out of their children. As soon as the children are grown up, they do not care a farthing for their parents, and naturally so, and they leave them.

<!-- ch15-p220 -->
> “It is no wonder that ignorance and vice abound in a population so brought up.... Their morality is at the lowest ebb,... a great number of the women have illegitimate children, and that at such an immature age that even those most conversant with criminal statistics are astounded.”[^15.183]

[^15.183]: Cited above, pp. xi., xii.

<!-- ch15-p221 -->
And the homeland of these model families is the model Christian country for Europe; so at least says Count Montalembert, certainly a competent authority on Christianity!

<!-- ch15-p222 -->
Miserable as they are, wages in the above industries (the maximum wages of a child in the straw-plait schools rise in rare cases to 3 shillings) are reduced far below their nominal amount by the truck system, which prevails everywhere, but especially in the lace districts.[^15.184]

[^15.184]: “Child. Empl. Comm., I. Rep. 1863,” p. 185.

#### E. Passage of Modern Manufacture, and Domestic Industry into Modern Mechanical Industry. The Hastening of this Revolution by the Application of the Factory Acts to those Industries

<!-- ch15-p223 -->
The cheapening of labor-power, by sheer abuse of the labor of women and children, by sheer robbery of every normal condition needed for working and living, and by the sheer brutality of overwork and night-work, at last runs into natural obstacles that cannot be crossed. So do the cheapening of commodities and capitalist exploitation in general, when they are based on these methods. As soon as this point is at last reached – and it takes many years – the hour has struck for the introduction of machinery, and for the rapid conversion, from then on, of the scattered domestic industries and also of branches of manufacture into factory industries.

<!-- ch15-p224 -->
The production of clothing offers an example of this movement on the most colossal scale. According to the classification of the Children’s Employment Commission, this industry includes straw-hat makers, ladies’-hat makers, cap-makers, tailors, milliners and dressmakers, shirt-makers, corset-makers, glove-makers, shoemakers, and many minor branches as well, such as the making of neck-ties, collars, etc. In 1861, the number of females employed in these industries in England and Wales came to 586,299. Of these, at least 115,242 were under 20, and 16,650 under 15 years of age. The number of these women workers in the United Kingdom in 1861 was 750,334. The number of males employed in England and Wales in hat-making, shoemaking, glove-making and tailoring was 437,969. Of these, 14,964 were under 15 years, 89,285 between 15 and 20, and 333,117 over 20 years. Many of the smaller branches are not included in these figures. But take the figures as they stand. Then, according to the census of 1861, we have for England and Wales alone a total of 1,024,277 persons, about as many as are absorbed by agriculture and cattle breeding. We begin to understand what becomes of the immense quantities of goods conjured up by the magic of machinery, and of the enormous masses of workers that this machinery sets free.

<!-- ch15-p225 -->
The production of clothing is carried on partly in manufacturing workshops whose workrooms merely reproduce that division of labor whose membra disjecta [scattered limbs] were found ready to hand. It is carried on partly by small master craftsmen. These, however, no longer work for individual consumers, as they used to, but for manufacturing workshops and warehouses, and to such an extent that whole towns and stretches of country often carry on certain branches, such as shoemaking, as a specialty. Finally, it is carried on, on a very great scale, by the so-called domestic workers, who form an outside department of the manufacturing workshops, the warehouses, and even the workshops of the smaller employers.[^15.185]

[^15.185]: In England, millinery and dressmaking are for the most part carried on at the employer’s premises, partly by women workers who live there, partly by women who live elsewhere.

<!-- ch15-p226 -->
The raw material, etc., is supplied by mechanical industry. The mass of cheap human material (taillable à merci et miséricorde [taxable at will and at mercy]) is made up of the individuals “liberated” by mechanical industry and improved agriculture. The manufacturing workshops of this kind owed their origin chiefly to the capitalist’s need to have at hand an army, fully equipped, ready to meet any increase in demand.[^15.186] All the same, these manufacturing workshops allowed the scattered handicrafts and domestic industries to go on existing as a broad foundation. The great production of surplus-value in these branches of labor, and the steady cheapening of their articles, were and are due chiefly to the minimum wages paid, no more than is needed to vegetate miserably, and to the stretching of working time to the maximum that the human organism can endure. It was in fact by the cheapness of human sweat and human blood, turned into commodities, that the markets were constantly being extended, and are still extended every day. This was especially the case with England’s colonial markets, where English tastes and habits also prevail. At last the critical point was reached. The basis of the old method – sheer brutality in exploiting the workers, accompanied more or less by a systematic division of labor – was no longer enough for the expanding markets and for the even faster-expanding competition among the capitalists. The hour struck for the coming of machinery. The decisively revolutionary machine is the sewing-machine: the machine that attacks equally the whole of the countless branches of this sphere of production, dressmaking, tailoring, shoemaking, sewing, hat-making, and many others.

[^15.186]: Mr. White, a commissioner, visited a military clothing manufacturing workshop that employed 1,000 to 1,200 persons, almost all females, and a shoe manufacturing workshop with 1,300 persons. Of these, nearly one half were children and young persons.

<!-- ch15-p227 -->
Its immediate effect on the workers is like that of all machinery that has seized on new branches of trade since the rise of modern industry. Children who are too young are cast adrift. The wages of the machine workers rise compared with those of the home workers, many of whom belong to the poorest of the poor. The wages of the better-placed craftsman, with whom the machine competes, sink. The new machine workers are exclusively girls and young women. With the help of mechanical force, they destroy the monopoly that male labor had over the heavier work, and they drive many old women and very young children out of the lighter work. The overpowering competition crushes the weakest of the manual workers. The fearful increase in deaths from starvation in London during the last 10 years runs parallel with the spread of machine sewing.[^15.187] The new women workers turn the machines by hand and foot, or by hand alone, sometimes sitting, sometimes standing, according to the weight, size, and special make of the machine, and they spend a great deal of labor-power. Their occupation is unhealthy because of the long hours, although in most cases these are not as long as under the old system. Wherever the sewing-machine settles into narrow, already overcrowded workrooms, it adds to the unhealthy influences.

[^15.187]: An example. The Registrar-General’s weekly report of deaths dated 26th Feb., 1864, contains 5 cases of death from starvation. On the same day *The Times* reports another case. Six victims of starvation in one week!

<!-- ch15-p228 -->
“The effect,” says Mr. Lord, “on entering low-ceiled workrooms in which 30 to 40 machine hands are working is unbearable.... The heat, partly due to the gas stoves used for warming the irons, is horrible.... Even when moderate hours of work, i.e., from 8 in the morning till 6 in the evening, prevail in such places, yet 3 or 4 persons fall into a swoon [faint] regularly every day.”[^15.188]

[^15.188]: “Child. Empl. Comm., Second Rep., 1864,” p. lxvii., n. 406-9, p. 84, n. 124, p. lxxiii, n. 441, p. 68, n. 6, p. 84, n. 126, p. 78, n. 85, p. 76, n. 69, p. lxxii, n. 483.

<!-- ch15-p229 -->
The revolution in industrial methods, which is the necessary result of the revolution in the instruments of production, is carried out through a medley of transition forms. These forms vary according to how far the sewing-machine has spread in one branch of industry or another, how long it has been in operation, the previous condition of the workers, whether manufacture, handicrafts or domestic industry predominates, the rent of the workrooms,[^15.189] etc. In dressmaking, for instance, the labor was for the most part already organized, chiefly by simple cooperation, and there the sewing-machine at first was merely a new factor in that manufacturing industry. In tailoring, shirtmaking, shoemaking, etc., all the forms are mixed together. Here we find the factory system proper. There, middlemen receive the raw material from the capitalist in chief, and group from 10 to 50 or more women workers around their sewing-machines, in “chambers” and “garrets.” Finally, as is always the case with machinery when it is not organized into a system and can also be used on a dwarfish scale, craftsmen and domestic workers, along with their families, or with a little extra labor from outside, use their own sewing-machines.[^15.190] The system actually prevalent in England is this: the capitalist concentrates a large number of machines on his premises, and then distributes the product of those machines among the domestic workers for further working up.[^15.191] The variety of the transition forms, however, does not hide the tendency toward conversion into the factory system proper. This tendency is fed by the very nature of the sewing-machine, whose many uses push forward the concentration, under one roof and one management, of branches of a trade that used to be separate. It is also favored by the fact that preparatory needlework, and certain other operations, are most conveniently done on the premises where the machine is at work. It is favored, too, by the inevitable expropriation (taking away people’s property, here their means of production) of the hand sewers, and of the domestic workers who work with their own machines. This fate has already in part overtaken them. The constantly increasing amount of capital invested in sewing-machines[^15.192] spurs on the production of machine-made articles and gluts the markets with them, and so gives the domestic workers the signal to sell their machines. The overproduction of the sewing-machines themselves causes their producers, badly in need of sales, to rent them out at so much a week, and so to crush the small owners of machines by their deadly competition.[^15.193] Constant changes in the construction of the machines, and their ever-increasing cheapness, make the older makes lose value day by day. This lets them be sold in great numbers, at absurd prices, to large capitalists, who alone can thus use them at a profit. Finally, here as in all similar revolutions, the replacement of man by the steam-engine gives the finishing blow. At first, the use of steam power meets with merely technical difficulties, such as unsteadiness in the machines, difficulty in controlling their speed, rapid wear and tear of the lighter machines, etc., all of which experience soon overcomes.[^15.194] If, on the one hand, the concentration of many machines in large manufacturing workshops leads to the use of steam power, on the other hand the competition of steam with human muscles hastens the concentration of workers and machines in large factories. Thus England is at present experiencing the conversion of manufacture, of handicrafts, and of domestic work into the factory system. It is experiencing this not only in the colossal industry of making clothing, but in most of the other trades mentioned above. And this comes after each of those forms of production, totally changed and disorganized under the influence of modern industry, has long since reproduced, and even outdone, all the horrors of the factory system, without sharing in any of the elements of social progress that the factory system contains.[^15.195]

[^15.189]: “The rental of premises required for workrooms seems the element which ultimately determines the point; and consequently it is in the metropolis, that the old system of giving work out to small employers and families has been longest retained, and earliest returned to.” (cited above, p. 83, n. 123.) The last statement in this quotation refers only to shoemaking.

[^15.190]: In glove-making and other industries where the condition of the workers can hardly be told apart from that of paupers, this does not happen.

[^15.191]: Cited above, p. 83, n. 122.

[^15.192]: In the wholesale boot and shoe trade of Leicester alone, 800 sewing-machines were already in use in 1864.

[^15.193]: Cited above, p. 84, n. 124.

[^15.194]: Examples: the Army Clothing Depot at Pimlico, London, the shirt factory of Tillie and Henderson at Londonderry, and the clothes factory of Messrs. Tait at Limerick, which employs about 1,200 workers.

[^15.195]: “Tendency to Factory System” (cited above, p. lxvii). “The whole employment is at this time in a state of transition, and is undergoing the same Change as that effected in the lace trade, weaving, &c.” (cited above, n. 405.) “A complete revolution” (cited above, p. xlvi., n. 318). At the time of the Child. Empl. Comm. of 1840, stocking making was still done by manual labor. Since 1846 various kinds of machines have been introduced, and these are now driven by steam. In 1862 the total number of persons of both sexes and of all ages from 3 years upwards employed in stocking making in England was about 129,000. According to the Parliamentary Return of the 11th February, 1862, only 4,063 of these were working under the Factory Acts.

<!-- ch15-p230 -->
This industrial revolution, which takes place spontaneously, is artificially helped along by the extension of the Factory Acts to all industries in which women, young persons and children are employed. The compulsory regulation of the working day – its length, its pauses, its beginning and end – the system of relays of children, the exclusion of all children under a certain age, etc., make necessary, on the one hand, more machinery[^15.196] and the replacement of muscles by steam as the motive power.[^15.197] On the other hand, to make up for the lost time, the means of production used in common expand: the furnaces, buildings, etc. In one word, there is a greater concentration of the means of production and a correspondingly greater gathering of workers. In fact, the chief objection, urged again and again and passionately on behalf of each manufacture threatened with the Factory Act, is this: that in order to continue the business on the old scale, a greater outlay of capital will be necessary. But as for labor in the so-called domestic industries and in the intermediate forms between them and manufacture, as soon as limits are put on the working day and on the employment of children, those industries go to the wall. Unlimited exploitation of cheap labor-power is the sole foundation of their power to compete.

[^15.196]: Thus, for example, in the earthenware trade, Messrs. Cochrane, of the Britain Pottery, Glasgow, report: “To keep up our quantity we have gone extensively into machines wrought by unskilled labour, and every day convinces us that we can produce a greater quantity than by the old method.” (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1865,” p. 13.) “The effect of the Fact. Acts is to force on the further introduction of machinery” (cited above, pp. 13-14).

[^15.197]: Thus, after the extension of the Factory Act to the potteries, there was a great increase of power-jiggers in place of hand-moved jiggers.

<!-- ch15-p231 -->
One of the essential conditions for the existence of the factory system, especially when the length of the working day is fixed, is certainty in the result, that is, the production of a given quantity of commodities, or of a given useful effect, in a given time. The statutory pauses in the working day, moreover, assume that periodic and sudden stopping of the work does no harm to the article in the process of production. This certainty in the result, and this possibility of interrupting the work, are of course easier to achieve in the purely mechanical industries than in those in which chemical and physical processes play a part, as, for instance, in the earthenware trade, in bleaching, dyeing, baking, and in most of the metal industries. Wherever there is a working day with no limit on its length, wherever there is night-work and unrestricted waste of human life, there the slightest obstacle that the nature of the work puts in the way of a change for the better is soon looked on as an everlasting barrier set up by Nature. No poison kills vermin more surely than the Factory Act removes such everlasting barriers. No one made a greater outcry over “impossibilities” than our friends the earthenware manufacturers. In 1864, however, they were brought under the Act, and within sixteen months every “impossibility” had vanished.

<!-- ch15-p232 -->
> “The improved method,” called forth by the Act, “of making slip [liquid clay] by pressure instead of by evaporation, the newly-constructed stoves for drying the ware in its green [unfired] state, &c., are each events of great importance in the pottery art, and mark an advance which the preceding century could not rival.... It has even considerably reduced the temperature of the stoves themselves with a considerable saving of fuel, and with a readier effect on the ware.”[^15.198]

[^15.198]: “Report of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1865,” pp. 96 and 127.

<!-- ch15-p233 -->
In spite of every prophecy, the cost-price of earthenware did not rise, but the quantity produced did, and to such an extent that exports for the twelve months ending December, 1865, exceeded the average of the preceding three years in value by £138,628. In the manufacture of matches it was thought to be an indispensable requirement that boys, even while gulping down their dinner, should go on dipping the matches in melted phosphorus, whose poisonous vapor rose into their faces. The Factory Act (1864) made saving time a necessity, and so forced into existence a dipping machine whose vapor could not come into contact with the workers.[^15.199] In the same way, at the present time, in those branches of the lace manufacture not yet subject to the Factory Act, it is maintained that meal-times cannot be regular, because the various kinds of lace need different periods to dry, and these periods vary from three minutes up to an hour and more. To this the Children’s Employment Commissioners answer:

[^15.199]: The introduction of this and other machinery into match-making caused 230 young persons, in one department alone, to be replaced by 32 boys and girls of 14 to 17 years of age. This saving in labor was carried still further in 1865, by the use of steam power.

<!-- ch15-p234 -->
> “The circumstances of this case are precisely analogous to that of the paper-stainers, dealt with in our first report. Some of the principal manufacturers in the trade urged that in consequence of the nature of the materials used, and their various processes, they would be unable, without serious loss, to stop for meal-times at any given moment. But it was seen from the evidence that, by due care and previous arrangement, the apprehended difficulty would be got over; and accordingly, by clause 6 of section 6 of the Factory Acts Extension Act, passed during this Session of Parliament, an interval of eighteen months is given to them from the passing of the Act before they are required to conform to the meal hours, specified by the Factory Acts.”[^15.200]

[^15.200]: “Ch. Empl. Comm., 11. Rep., 1864,” p. ix., n. 50.

<!-- ch15-p235 -->
The Act had hardly been passed when our friends the manufacturers discovered:

<!-- ch15-p236 -->
> “The inconveniences we expected to arise from the introduction of the Factory Acts into our branch of manufacture, I am happy to say, have not arisen. We do not find the production at all interfered with; in short, we produce more in the same time.”[^15.201]

[^15.201]: “Rep. of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1865,” p. 22.

<!-- ch15-p237 -->
Clearly the English legislature – which certainly no one will dare to reproach with an overdose of genius – has been led by experience to the conclusion that a simple compulsory law is enough to enact away all the so-called impediments, opposed by the nature of the process, to the restriction and regulation of the working day. Hence, when the Factory Act is introduced into a given industry, a period varying from six to eighteen months is fixed, within which the manufacturers are obliged to remove all technical impediments to the working of the Act. Mirabeau’s “Impossible! ne me dites jamais ce bête de mot!” [Impossible! Never say that stupid word to me!] applies particularly well to modern technology. But though the Factory Acts thus artificially ripen the material elements needed for the conversion of the manufacturing system into the factory system, at the same time, because they make a greater outlay of capital necessary, they hasten the decline of the small employers and the concentration of capital.[^15.202]

[^15.202]: “But it must be borne in mind that those improvements, though carried out fully in some establishments, are by no means general, and are not capable of being brought into use in many of the old manufactories without an expenditure of capital beyond the means of many of the present occupiers.” “I cannot but rejoice,” writes Sub-Inspector May, “that notwithstanding the temporary disorganisation which inevitably follows the introduction of such a measure (as the Factory Act Extension Act), and is, indeed, directly indicative of the evils which it was intended to remedy, &c.” (Rep. of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1865.)

<!-- ch15-p238 -->
Besides the purely technical impediments that can be removed by technical means, the irregular habits of the workers themselves obstruct the regulation of the hours of labor.
