This is especially the case where piece wages predominate, and where time lost in one part of the day or week can be made good by later overtime or by night-work, a process that brutalizes the adult worker and ruins his wife and children.[^15.203] Although this lack of regularity in the expenditure of labor-power is a natural and crude reaction against the tedium of monotonous drudgery, it also originates, to a much greater degree, in anarchy in production, an anarchy that in its turn presupposes unbridled exploitation of labor-power by the capitalist. Besides the general periodic changes of the industrial cycle, and the special fluctuations in the markets to which each industry is subject, we may also count what is called “the season.” It depends either on the periodic return of the times of year that favor navigation, or on fashion and the sudden placing of large orders that have to be carried out in the shortest possible time. The habit of giving such orders becomes more frequent with the extension of railways and telegraphs.

[^15.203]: With blast furnaces, for instance, “work towards the end of the week being generally much increased in duration in consequence of the habit of the men of idling on Monday and occasionally during a part or the whole of Tuesday also.” (“Child. Empl. Comm., III. Rep.,” p. vi.) “The little masters generally have very irregular hours. They lose two or three days, and then work all night to make it up.... They always employ their own children, if they have any.” (cited above, p. vii.) “The want of regularity in coming to work, encouraged by the possibility and practice of making up for this by working longer hours.” (cited above, p. xviii.) “In Birmingham ... an enormous amount of time is lost ... idling part of the time, slaving the rest.” (cited above, p. xi.)

<!-- ch15-p239 -->
> “The extension of the railway system throughout the country has tended very much to encourage giving short notice. Purchasers now come up from Glasgow, Manchester, and Edinburgh once every fortnight or so to the wholesale city warehouses which we supply, and give small orders requiring immediate execution, instead of buying from stock as they used to do. Years ago we were always able to work in the slack times, so as to meet demand of the next season, but now no one can say beforehand what will be the demand then.”[^15.204]

[^15.204]: “Child. Empl. Comm., IV., Rep.,” p. xxxii., “The extension of the railway system is said to have contributed greatly to this custom of giving sudden orders, and the consequent hurry, neglect of meal-times, and late hours of the workpeople.” (cited above, p. xxxi.)

<!-- ch15-p240 -->
In those factories and manufacturing workshops that are not yet subject to the Factory Acts, the most fearful overwork prevails periodically during what is called the season, as a result of sudden orders. In the outside department of the factory, of the manufacturing workshop, and of the warehouse, the so-called domestic workers, whose employment is irregular at the best of times, depend entirely for their raw material and their orders on the whims of the capitalist. In this industry the capitalist is not held back by any concern about the depreciation of his buildings and machinery, and he risks nothing by a stoppage of work except the skin of the worker himself. Here, then, he sets to work systematically to form an industrial reserve force that shall be ready at a moment’s notice. During one part of the year he decimates this force by the most inhuman toil; during the other part, he lets it starve for lack of work.

<!-- ch15-p241 -->
> “The employers avail themselves of the habitual irregularity in the homework, when any extra work is wanted at a push, so that the work goes on till 11, and 12 p.m. or 2 a.m., or as the usual phrase is, “all hours,” and that in localities where “the stench is enough to knock you down, you go to the door, perhaps, and open it, but shudder to go further.”[^15.205] “They are curious men,” said one of the witnesses, a shoemaker, speaking of the masters, “they think it does a boy no harm to work too hard for half the year, if he is nearly idle for the other half.”[^15.206]

[^15.205]: “Ch. Empl. Comm, IV. Rep.,” pp. xxxv., n. 235, 237.

[^15.206]: “Ch. Empl. Comm. IV. Rep.,” p. 127, n. 56.

<!-- ch15-p242 -->
In the same way as technical impediments, those “usages which have grown with the growth of trade” were, and still are, proclaimed by interested capitalists to be obstacles due to the nature of the work. This was a favorite cry of the cotton lords at the time when they were first threatened with the Factory Acts. Although their industry depends on navigation more than any other, experience has proved them false. Since then, the Factory inspectors have treated every pretended obstruction to business as a mere sham.[^15.207] The thoroughly conscientious investigations of the Children’s Employment Commission prove the following: that the effect of regulating the hours of work, in some industries, was to spread the mass of labor previously employed more evenly over the whole year;[^15.208] that this regulation was the first rational bridle on the murderous, meaningless whims of fashion,[^15.209] whims that fit so badly with the system of modern industry; that the development of ocean navigation and of the means of communication generally has swept away the technical basis on which season-work really rested;[^15.210] and that all other so-called unconquerable difficulties vanish before larger buildings, additional machinery, an increase in the number of workers employed,[^15.211] and the changes that all these cause in the way the wholesale trade is conducted.[^15.212] But for all that, capital never becomes reconciled to such changes – and its own representatives admit this over and over again – except “under the pressure of a General Act of Parliament”[^15.213] for the compulsory regulation of the hours of labor.

[^15.207]: “With respect to the loss of trade by non-completion of shipping orders in time, I remember that this was the pet argument of the factory masters in 1832 and 1833. Nothing that can be advanced now on this subject, could have the force that it had then, before steam had halved all distances and established new regulations for transit. It quite failed at that time of proof when put to the test, and again it will certainly fail should it have to be tried.” (“Reports of Insp. of Fact., 31 Oct., 1862,” pp. 54, 55.)

[^15.208]: “Ch. Empl. Comm. IV. Rep.,” p. xviii, n. 118.

[^15.209]: As far back as 1699, John Bellers remarked: “The uncertainty of fashions does increase necessitous poor. It has two great mischiefs in it. 1st, The journeymen are miserable in winter for want of work, the mercers [cloth dealers] and master-weavers not daring to lay out their stocks to keep the journeymen employed before the spring comes, and they know what the fashion will then be; 2ndly, In the spring the journeymen are not sufficient, but the master-weavers must draw in many prentices [apprentices], that they may supply the trade of the kingdom in a quarter or half a year, which robs the plough of hands, drains the country of labourers, and in a great part stocks the city with beggars, and starves some in winter that are ashamed to beg.” (“Essays about the Poor, Manufactures, &c.,” p. 9.)

[^15.210]: “Ch. Empl. Comm. V. Rep.,” p. 171, n. 34.

[^15.211]: The evidence of some Bradford export-houses is as follows: “Under these circumstances, it seems clear that no boys need be worked longer than from 8 a.m. to 7 or 7.30 p.m., in making up. It is merely a question of extra hands and extra outlay. If some masters were not so greedy, the boys would not work late; an extra machine costs only £16 or £18; much of such over-time as does occur is to be referred to an insufficiency of appliances, and a want of space.” “Ch. Empl. Comm. V. Rep.,” p. 171, n. 35, 36, 38.

[^15.212]: Cited above. A London manufacturer, who in other respects regards the compulsory regulation of the hours of labor as a protection for the workers against the manufacturers, and for the manufacturers themselves against the wholesale trade, states: “The pressure in our business is caused by the shippers, who want, e.g., to send the goods by sailing vessel so as to reach their destination at a given season, and at the same time want to pocket the difference in freight between a sailing vessel and a steamship, or who select the earlier of two steamships in order to be in the foreign market before their competitors.”

[^15.213]: “This could be obviated,” says a manufacturer, “at the expense of an enlargement of the works under the pressure of a General Act of Parliament.” Cited above, p. x., n. 38.

### Section 9: The Factory Acts. Sanitary and Educational Clauses of the same. Their General Extension in England

<!-- ch15-p243 -->
Factory legislation is the first conscious and methodical reaction of society against the form that the process of production developed spontaneously. As we have seen, it is just as much the necessary product of modern industry as cotton yarn, self-actors, and the electric telegraph. Before we move on to how that legislation was extended in England, we shall look briefly at certain clauses in the Factory Acts that do not concern the hours of work.

<!-- ch15-p244 -->
Apart from their wording, which makes them easy for the capitalist to evade, the sanitary clauses are extremely meager. In fact, they are limited to provisions for whitewashing the walls, for ensuring cleanliness in a few other matters, for ventilation, and for protection against dangerous machinery. In the third book we shall come back to the fanatical opposition of the employers to those clauses that made them spend a little on appliances to protect the limbs of their workers. That opposition throws a fresh and glaring light on the Free-trade dogma, according to which, in a society of conflicting interests, each individual necessarily furthers the common good by seeking nothing but his own personal advantage! One example is enough. The reader knows that during the last 20 years the flax industry has expanded greatly, and that with this expansion the number of scutching mills in Ireland has increased. In 1864 there were 1,800 of these mills in that country. Regularly in autumn and winter, women and “young persons” are taken from field labor to feed flax into the rollers of the scutching mills. They are the wives, sons, and daughters of the neighboring small farmers, a class of people wholly unused to machinery. The accidents, in both number and kind, are without any parallel in the history of machinery. In one scutching mill, at Kildinan, near Cork, there were six fatal accidents and sixty mutilations between 1852 and 1856. Every one of them could have been prevented by the simplest appliances, at the cost of a few shillings. Dr. W. White, the certifying surgeon for factories at Downpatrick, states in his official report dated the 15th December, 1865:

<!-- ch15-p245 -->
> “The serious accidents at the scutching mills are of the most fearful nature. In many cases a quarter of the body is torn from the trunk, and either involves death, or a future of wretched incapacity and suffering. The increase of mills in the country will, of course, extend these dreadful results, and it will be a great boon if they are brought under the legislature. I am convinced that by proper supervision of scutching mills a vast sacrifice of life and limb would be averted.”[^15.214]

[^15.214]: Cited above, p. xv., n. 72. and following.

<!-- ch15-p246 -->
What could show the character of the capitalist mode of production better than the need to force on it, by Acts of Parliament, the simplest appliances for keeping things clean and healthy? In the potteries the Factory Act of 1864 “has whitewashed and cleansed upwards of 200 workshops, after a period of abstinence from any such cleaning, in many cases of 20 years, and in some, entirely,” (this is the “abstinence” of the capitalist!) “in which were employed 27,800 artisans, hitherto breathing through protracted days and often nights of labour, a mephitic [foul and poisonous] atmosphere, and which rendered an otherwise comparatively innocuous occupation, pregnant with disease and death. The Act has improved the ventilation very much.”[^15.215]

[^15.215]: “Rep. Insp. Fact., 31st October, 1865,” p. 127.

<!-- ch15-p247 -->
At the same time, this part of the Act shows strikingly that the capitalist mode of production, by its very nature, rules out all rational improvement beyond a certain point. It has been stated over and over again that the English doctors agree unanimously: where the work is continuous, 500 cubic feet is the very least space that should be allowed for each person. Now, if the Factory Acts, through their compulsory provisions, indirectly speed up the conversion of small workshops into factories, and so indirectly attack the property rights of the smaller capitalists and assure a monopoly to the great ones, then in the same way, if it were made compulsory to provide the proper space for each worker in every workshop, thousands of small employers would be expropriated directly, at a single stroke! The very root of the capitalist mode of production would be attacked, that is, the self-expansion of all capital, large or small, by means of the “free” purchase and consumption of labor-power. So factory legislation comes to a deadlock in front of these 500 cubic feet of breathing space. The sanitary officers, the industrial inquiry commissioners, the factory inspectors all harp, over and over again, on the need for those 500 cubic feet, and on the impossibility of wringing them out of capital. In fact, they are thereby declaring that consumption and other lung diseases among the workers are necessary conditions for the existence of capital.[^15.216]

[^15.216]: Experiments have found that with each breath of average intensity, a healthy average person uses up about 25 cubic inches of air, and takes about 20 breaths each minute. Hence the air each person breathes in during 24 hours is about 720,000 cubic inches, or 416 cubic feet. Clearly, however, air that has been breathed once cannot serve for the same process again until it has been purified in the great workshop of Nature. According to the experiments of Valentin and Brunner, it appears that a healthy man gives off about 1,300 cubic inches of carbonic acid per hour. This would mean about 8 ounces of solid carbon given off from the lungs in 24 hours. “Every man should have at least 800 cubic feet.” (Huxley.)

<!-- ch15-p248 -->
Paltry as the education clauses of the Act appear on the whole, they still proclaim elementary education to be an indispensable condition for employing children.[^15.217] Their success proved for the first time that it is possible to combine education and gymnastics[^15.218] with manual labor, and so also to combine manual labor with education and gymnastics. By questioning the schoolmasters, the factory inspectors soon found out that the factory children learned quite as much as the regular day pupils, and often more, although they received only half as much schooling.

[^15.217]: Under the English Factory Act, parents cannot send their children under 14 years of age into factories controlled by the Act unless they also let them receive elementary education at the same time. The manufacturer is responsible for compliance with the Act. “Factory education is compulsory, and it is a condition of labour.” (“Rep. Insp. Fact., 31st Oct., 1865,” p. 111.)

[^15.218]: On the very good results of combining gymnastics (and drill, in the case of boys) with compulsory education for factory children and pauper pupils, see the speech of N. W. Senior at the seventh annual congress of “The National Association for the Promotion of Social Science,” in “Report of Proceedings, &c.,” London 1863, pp. 63, 64, and also the “Rep. Insp. Fact., 31st Oct., 1865,” pp. 118, 119, 120, 126, and following.

<!-- ch15-p249 -->
> “This can be accounted for by the simple fact that, with only being at school for one half of the day, they are always fresh, and nearly always ready and willing to receive instruction. The system on which they work, half manual labour, and half school, renders each employment a rest and a relief to the other; consequently, both are far more congenial to the child, than would be the case were he kept constantly at one. It is quite clear that a boy who has been at school all the morning, cannot (in hot weather particularly) cope with one who comes fresh and bright from his work.”[^15.219]

[^15.219]: “Rep. Insp. Fact., 31st Oct., 1865,” p. 118. A silk manufacturer naively states to the Children’s Employment Commissioners: “I am quite sure that the true secret of producing efficient workpeople is to be found in uniting education and labour from a period of childhood. Of course the occupation must not be too severe, nor irksome, or unhealthy. But of the advantage of the union I have no doubt. I wish my own children could have some work as well as play to give variety to their schooling.” (“Ch. Empl. Comm. V. Rep.,” p. 82, n. 36.)

<!-- ch15-p250 -->
More on this point can be found in Senior’s speech at the Social Science Congress at Edinburgh in 1863. There he shows, among other things, how the monotonous and uselessly long school hours of upper-class and middle-class children uselessly add to the teacher’s labor, “while he not only fruitlessly but absolutely injuriously, wastes the time, health, and energy of the children.”[^15.220] As Robert Owen has shown us in detail, the germ of the education of the future sprouted from the factory system. That education will, for every child over a given age, combine productive labor with instruction and gymnastics. It will do this not only as one way of making production more efficient, but as the only way of producing fully developed human beings.

[^15.220]: Senior, cited above, p. 66. Modern industry, once it has reached a certain level, can also revolutionize people’s minds, through the revolution it brings about in the mode of production and in the social conditions of production. This is strikingly shown by comparing Senior’s speech in 1863 with his fierce attack on the Factory Act of 1833. It is also shown by comparing the views of the congress mentioned above with the fact that in certain country districts of England poor parents are forbidden, on pain of death by starvation, to educate their children. For example, Mr. Snell reports that it is a common occurrence in Somersetshire that, when a poor person claims parish relief, he is forced to take his children out of school. Mr. Wollarton, the clergyman at Feltham, also tells of cases where all relief was refused to certain families “because they were sending their children to school!”

<!-- ch15-p251 -->
Modern industry, as we have seen, uses technical means to sweep away the manufacturing division of labor, under which each man is bound hand and foot for life to a single detail-operation. At the same time, the capitalist form of that industry reproduces this same division of labor in a still more monstrous shape. In the factory proper, it does so by turning the worker into a living appendage of the machine. Everywhere outside the factory, it does so partly by the scattered use of machinery and machine workers,[^15.221] and partly by re-establishing the division of labor on a new basis, through the general introduction of the labor of women and children and of cheap unskilled labor.

[^15.221]: Wherever handicraft-machines driven by men compete, directly or indirectly, with more developed machines driven by mechanical power, a great change takes place for the worker who drives the machine. At first the steam-engine replaces this worker; afterwards he must replace the steam-engine. As a result, the strain and the amount of labor-power spent become monstrous, especially for the children who are condemned to this torture. Thus Mr. Longe, one of the commissioners, found boys from 10 to 15 years old in and around Coventry employed in driving the ribbon-looms, not to mention younger children who had to drive smaller machines. “It is extraordinarily fatiguing work. The boy is a mere substitute for steam power.” (“Ch. Empl. Comm. V, Rep. 1866;” p. 114, n. 6.) On the fatal consequences of “this system of slavery,” as the official report calls it, see the source cited above, p. 114 and following.

<!-- ch15-p252 -->
The antagonism between the manufacturing division of labor and the methods of modern industry makes itself forcibly felt. Among other ways, it shows itself in a frightful fact. A great part of the children employed in modern factories and manufacturing workshops are riveted from their earliest years to the simplest manipulations, and exploited for years, without being taught a single kind of work that would later make them of use, even in the same manufacturing workshop or factory. In the English letter-press printing trade, for example, there used to be a system, like the one in the old branches of manufacture and handicrafts, of moving the apprentices up from easy work to more and more difficult work. They went through a course of teaching until they were finished printers. Every one of them had to be able to read and write: their trade required it. All this was changed by the printing machine. It employs two kinds of workers. One kind is adults, tenters (machine minders). The other is boys, mostly from 11 to 17 years of age, whose sole business is either to spread the sheets of paper under the machine or to take the printed sheets from it. They perform this weary task, in London especially, for 14, 15, and 16 hours at a stretch, on several days in the week, and often for 36 hours, with only 2 hours’ rest for meals and sleep.[^15.222] A great part of them cannot read, and they are, as a rule, utter savages and very extraordinary creatures.

[^15.222]: Cited above, p. 3, n. 24.

<!-- ch15-p253 -->
> “To qualify them for the work which they have to do, they require no intellectual training; there is little room in it for skill, and less for judgment; their wages, though rather high for boys, do not increase proportionately as they grow up, and the majority of them cannot look for advancement to the better paid and more responsible post of machine minder, because while each machine has but one minder, it has at least two, and often four boys attached to it.”[^15.223]

[^15.223]: Cited above, P. 7, n. 60.

<!-- ch15-p254 -->
As soon as they get too old for such child’s work, that is, at about 17 at the latest, they are dismissed from the printing establishments. They become recruits for crime. Several attempts to find them work elsewhere came to nothing because of their ignorance and brutality, and their mental and physical degradation.

<!-- ch15-p255 -->
As with the division of labor inside the manufacturing workshops, so it is with the division of labor inside society. As long as handicraft and manufacture form the general groundwork of social production, the producer’s subjection to one branch alone, the breaking up of the many-sided variety of his work,[^15.224] is a necessary step in the development. On that groundwork, each separate branch of production finds through experience the form that suits it technically, slowly perfects that form, and, as soon as it has reached a given degree of maturity, quickly crystallizes it. Apart from new raw materials supplied by trade, the only thing that causes a change here and there is the gradual alteration of the instruments of labor. But their form, too, once experience has fixed it for good, turns to stone. This is proved by the fact that in many cases they were handed down in the same form from one generation to another for thousands of years. It is a telling feature that, even down into the eighteenth century, the different trades were called “mysteries” (mystères).[^15.225] No one but those duly initiated could get into their secrets. Modern industry tore away the veil that hid from men their own social process of production, and that turned the various, spontaneously divided branches of production into so many riddles, not only to outsiders but even to the initiated. Modern industry followed the principle of breaking each process down into its component movements, without any regard to whether a human hand could carry them out. This principle created the new modern science of technology. The varied, apparently unconnected, and petrified forms of the industrial processes now broke down into so many conscious and systematic applications of natural science to obtaining given useful effects. Technology also discovered the few main basic forms of motion that every productive action of the human body necessarily takes, however varied the instruments used. In just the same way, the science of mechanics sees in the most complicated machinery nothing but the continual repetition of the simple mechanical powers.

[^15.224]: “In some parts of the Highlands of Scotland, not many years ago, every peasant, according to the Statistical Account, made his own shoes of leather tanned by himself. Many a shepherd and cottar [cottager, farm tenant] too, with his wife and children, appeared at Church in clothes which had been touched by no hands but their own, since they were shorn from the sheep and sown in the flaxfield. In the preparation of these, it is added, scarcely a single article had been purchased, except the awl, needle, thimble, and a very few parts of the iron-work employed in the weaving. The dyes, too, were chiefly extracted by the women from trees, shrubs and herbs.” (Dugald Stewart’s “Works,” Hamilton’s Ed., Vol. viii., pp. 327-328.)

[^15.225]: In the celebrated “Livre des métiers” [Book of the Trades] of Etienne Boileau, we find the rule that a journeyman, on being admitted among the masters, had to swear “to love his brethren with brotherly love, to support them in their respective trades, not wilfully to betray the secrets of the trade, and besides, in the interests of all, not to recommend his own wares by calling the attention of the buyer to defects in the articles made by others.”

<!-- ch15-p256 -->
Modern industry never looks on the existing form of a process as final, or treats it as final. So the technical basis of that industry is revolutionary, while all earlier modes of production were essentially conservative.[^15.226] By means of machinery, chemical processes, and other methods, it is constantly changing not only the technical basis of production but also the functions of the worker and the social combinations of the labor process. In doing so it also revolutionizes, at the same time, the division of labor within society, and it keeps hurling masses of capital and of workers from one branch of production into another. So modern industry, by its very nature, requires variation of labor, fluidity of function, all-round mobility of the worker. But on the other hand, in its capitalist form, it reproduces the old division of labor with its fossilized specializations. We have seen how this absolute contradiction between the technical needs of modern industry and the social character built into its capitalist form does away with all fixity and security in the worker’s situation. We have seen how it constantly threatens, by taking away his instruments of labor, to snatch his means of subsistence out of his hands,[^15.227] and to make him superfluous by suppressing his detail-function. We have seen, too, how this antagonism vents its rage in creating that monstrosity, an industrial reserve army, kept in misery so as to be always at capital’s disposal. It vents its rage in the endless human sacrifices from among the working class, in the most reckless squandering of labor-power, and in the devastation caused by a social anarchy that turns every economic advance into a social disaster. This is the negative side. On the one hand, variation of work now imposes itself in the manner of an overpowering natural law, and with the blindly destructive action of a natural law that meets with resistance[^15.228] at every point. But on the other hand, modern industry, through its catastrophes, makes it necessary to recognize variation of work as a fundamental law of production, and with it the worker’s fitness for varied work, and with that the greatest possible development of his varied abilities. It becomes a question of life and death for society to adapt the mode of production to the normal working of this law. Indeed, modern industry compels society, on pain of death, to replace the detail worker of today with the fully developed individual. The detail worker of today is held in the grip of lifelong repetition of one and the same trivial operation, and so reduced to the mere fragment of a man. The fully developed individual is fit for a variety of labors and ready to face any change of production, and for him the different social functions he performs are just so many ways of giving free play to his own natural and acquired powers.

[^15.226]: “The bourgeoisie cannot exist without continually revolutionising the instruments of production, and thereby the relations of production and all the social relations. Conservation, in an unaltered form, of the old modes of production was on the contrary the first condition of existence for all earlier industrial classes. Constant revolution in production, uninterrupted disturbance of all social conditions, everlasting uncertainty and agitation, distinguish the bourgeois epoch from all earlier ones. All fixed, fast-frozen relations, with their train of ancient and venerable prejudices and opinions, are swept away, all new formed ones become antiquated before they can ossify. All that is solid melts into air, all that is holy is profaned, and man is at last compelled to face with sober senses his real conditions of life, and his relations with his kind.” (F. Engels und Karl Marx: “Manifest der Kommunistischen Partei.” London 1848, p. 5.)

[^15.227]: “You take my life When you do take the means whereby I live.” Shakespeare.

[^15.228]: A French worker, on his return from San-Francisco, writes as follows: “I never could have believed, that I was capable of working at the various occupations I was employed on in California. I was firmly convinced that I was fit for nothing but letter-press printing.... Once in the midst of this world of adventurers, who change their occupation as often as they do their shirt, egad, I did as the others. As mining did not turn out remunerative enough, I left it for the town, where in succession I became typographer, slater, plumber, &c. In consequence of thus finding out that I am fit to any sort of work, I feel less of a mollusk and more of a man.” (A. Corbon, “De l’enseignement professionnel,” 2ème ed., p. 50.)

<!-- ch15-p257 -->
One step already taken spontaneously toward bringing about this revolution is the founding of technical and agricultural schools, and of “écoles d’enseignement professionnel” [schools of vocational education], in which the children of working men receive a little instruction in technology and in the practical handling of the various implements of labor. The Factory Act, that first and meager concession wrung from capital, goes no further than combining elementary education with work in the factory. Even so, there can be no doubt that when the working class comes to power, as it inevitably must, technical instruction, both theoretical and practical, will take its proper place in the working-class schools. There is also no doubt that such revolutionary ferments, whose final result is the abolition of the old division of labor, are diametrically opposed to the capitalist form of production and to the economic position of the worker that corresponds to that form. But the historical development of the antagonisms built into a given form of production is the only way in which that form of production can be dissolved and a new form established. “Ne sutor ultra crepidam” [Let the shoemaker not go beyond his shoe] – this *nec plus ultra* [very height] of handicraft wisdom became sheer nonsense from the moment the watchmaker Watt invented the steam-engine, the barber Arkwright the throstle, and the working jeweler Fulton the steamship.[^15.229]

[^15.229]: John Bellers, a true phenomenon in the history of political economy, saw very clearly at the end of the 17th century the need to abolish the present system of education and division of labor, which breed hypertrophy (overgrowth) and atrophy (wasting away) at the two opposite extremes of society. Among other things he says this: “An idle learning being little better than the learning of idleness.... Bodily labour, it’s a primitive institution of God.... Labour being as proper for the bodies’ health as eating is for its living; for what pains a man saves by ease, he will find in disease.... Labour adds oil to the lamp of life, when thinking inflames it.... A childish silly employ” (a warning, this, given by foresight, against the Basedows and their modern imitators) “leaves the children’s minds silly,” (“Proposals for Raising a Colledge of Industry of all Useful Trades and Husbandry.” London, 1696, pp. 12, 14, 18.)

<!-- ch15-p258 -->
As long as factory legislation is confined to regulating labor in factories, manufacturing workshops, etc., it is regarded as a mere interference with capital’s rights of exploitation. But when it comes to regulating the so-called “home-labour,”[^15.230] it is at once seen as a direct attack on the patria potestas, on parental authority. The tender-hearted English Parliament long pretended to shrink from taking this step. But the force of facts at last compelled it to admit that modern industry, by overturning the economic foundation of the traditional family and of the family labor that went with it, had also loosened all traditional family ties. The rights of the children had to be proclaimed. The final report of the Children’s Employment Commission of 1866 states:

[^15.230]: This kind of labor goes on mostly in small workshops, as we have seen in the lace-making and straw-plaiting trades, and as could be shown in more detail from the metal trades of Sheffield, Birmingham, etc.

<!-- ch15-p259 -->
> “It is unhappily, to a painful degree, apparent throughout the whole of the evidence, that against no persons do the children of both sexes so much require protection as against their parents.” The system of unlimited exploitation of children’s labor in general, and of the so-called home-labor in particular, is “maintained only because the parents are able, without check or control, to exercise this arbitrary and mischievous power over their young and tender offspring.... Parents must not possess the absolute power of making their children mere ‘machines to earn so much weekly wage....’ The children and young persons, therefore, in all such cases may justifiably claim from the legislature, as a natural right, that an exemption should be secured to them, from what destroys prematurely their physical strength, and lowers them in the scale of intellectual and moral beings.”[^15.231]

[^15.231]: “Ch. Empl. Comm., V. Rep.,” p. xxv., n. 162, and II. Rep., p. xxxviii., n, 285, 289, p. xxv., xxvi., n. 191.

<!-- ch15-p260 -->
However, it was not the misuse of parental authority that created the capitalist exploitation of children’s labor, whether direct or indirect. On the contrary, it was the capitalist mode of exploitation that swept away the economic basis of parental authority, and so made its exercise degenerate into a mischievous misuse of power. Under the capitalist system, the breaking up of the old family ties may seem terrible and disgusting. Nevertheless, modern industry gives an important part in the process of production, outside the domestic sphere, to women, to young persons, and to children of both sexes. In doing so it creates a new economic foundation for a higher form of the family and of the relations between the sexes. Of course, it is just as absurd to hold the Germanic-Christian form of the family to be absolute and final as it would be to give that character to the ancient Roman, the ancient Greek, or the Eastern forms, which, besides, taken together form a series in historical development. Moreover, it is obvious that the collective working group is made up of individuals of both sexes and all ages, and that this fact must necessarily, under suitable conditions, become a source of humane development. In its spontaneously developed, brutal, capitalist form, though, where the worker exists for the process of production and not the process of production for the worker, that fact is a pestilent source of corruption and slavery.[^15.232]

[^15.232]: “Factory labour may be as pure and as excellent as domestic labour, and perhaps more so.” (“Rep. Insp. of Fact., 31st October, 1865,” p. 129.)

<!-- ch15-p261 -->
It became necessary to generalize the Factory Acts, to transform them from an exceptional law covering mechanical spinning and weaving, those first creations of machinery, into a law affecting social production as a whole. As we have seen, this necessity arose from the way modern industry developed historically. In the wake of that industry, the traditional form of manufacture, of handicraft, and of domestic industry is entirely revolutionized. Manufacture keeps passing into the factory system, and handicrafts into manufacture. And lastly, the spheres of handicraft and of the domestic industries become, in what is, comparatively speaking, a wonderfully short time, dens of misery in which capitalist exploitation is given free rein for its wildest excesses. Two circumstances finally tip the scale. First, there is the constantly recurring experience that capital, as soon as it is subjected to legal control at one point, makes up for it all the more recklessly at other points.[^15.233] Second, there is the cry of the capitalists for equality in the conditions of competition, that is, for equal restraint on all exploitation of labor.[^15.234] On this point let us listen to two heart-broken cries. Messrs. Cooksley of Bristol, manufacturers of nails, chains, etc., introduced the regulations of the Factory Act into their business of their own accord.

[^15.233]: “Rep. Insp. of Fact., 31st October, 1865,” pp. 27-32.

[^15.234]: Many examples can be found in “Rep. of Insp. of Fact.”

<!-- ch15-p262 -->
> “As the old irregular system prevails in neighbouring works, the Messrs. Cooksley are subject to the disadvantage of having their boys enticed to continue their labour elsewhere after 6 p.m. ‘This,’ they naturally say, ‘is an unjustice and loss to us, as it exhausts a portion of the boy’s strength, of which we ought to have the full benefit’.”[^15.235]

[^15.235]: “Ch. Empl. Comm., V. Rep.,” p. x., n. 35.

<!-- ch15-p263 -->
Mr. J. Simpson (a paper-box and bag maker, London) states before the commissioners of the Children’s Employment Commission:

<!-- ch15-p264 -->
> “He would sign any petition for it” (legislative interference)... “As it was, he always felt restless at night, when he had closed his place, lest others should be working later than him and getting away his orders.”[^15.236]

[^15.236]: “Ch. Empl. Comm., V. Rep.,” p. ix., n. 28.

<!-- ch15-p265 -->
Summing up, the Children’s Employment Commission says:

<!-- ch15-p266 -->
> “It would be unjust to the larger employers that their factories should be placed under regulation, while the hours of labour in the smaller places in their own branch of business were under no legislative restriction. And to the injustice arising from the unfair conditions of competition, in regard to hours, that would be created if the smaller places of work were exempt, would be added the disadvantage to the larger manufacturers, of finding their supply of juvenile and female labour drawn off to the places of work exempt from legislation. Further, a stimulus would be given to the multiplication of the smaller places of work, which are almost invariably the least favourable to the health, comfort, education, and general improvement of the people.”[^15.237]

[^15.237]: Cited above, p. xxv., n. 165-167. On the advantages of large-scale industries compared with small-scale ones, see “Ch. Empl. Comm., III. Rep.,” p. 13, n. 144, p. 25, n. 121, p. 26, n. 125, p. 27, n. 140, etc.

<!-- ch15-p267 -->
In its final report the Commission proposes to bring more than 1,400,000 children, young persons, and women under the Factory Act. About half of that number are exploited in small industries and by the so-called home-work.[^15.238] It says,

[^15.238]: The trades proposed to be brought under the Act were the following: lace-making, stocking-weaving, straw-plaiting, the manufacture of clothing with its many subdivisions, artificial flower-making, shoemaking, hat-making, glove-making, tailoring, all metal works from blast furnaces down to needle works, etc., paper-mills, glassworks, tobacco factories, India-rubber works, braid-making (for weaving), hand carpet-making, umbrella and parasol making, the manufacture of spindles and spools, letterpress printing, book-binding, the manufacture of stationery (including paper bags, cards, colored paper, etc.), rope-making, the manufacture of jet ornaments, brick-making, silk manufacture by hand, Coventry weaving, salt works, tallow chandlers (candle-makers), cement works, sugar refineries, biscuit-making, various industries connected with timber, and other mixed trades.

<!-- ch15-p268 -->
> “But if it should seem fit to Parliament to place the whole of that large number of children, young persons and females under the protective legislation above adverted to ... it cannot be doubted that such legislation would have a most beneficent effect, not only upon the young and the feeble, who are its more immediate objects, but upon the still larger body of adult workers, who would in all these employments, both directly and indirectly, come immediately under its influence. It would enforce upon them regular and moderate hours; it would lead to their places of work being kept in a healthy and cleanly state; it would therefore husband and improve that store of physical strength on which their own well-being and that of the country so much depends; it would save the rising generation from that overexertion at an early age which undermines their constitutions and leads to premature decay; finally, it would ensure them – at least up to the age of 13 – the opportunity of receiving the elements of education, and would put an end to that utter ignorance ... so faithfully exhibited in the Reports of our Assistant Commissioners, and which cannot be regarded without the deepest pain, and a profound sense of national degradation.”[^15.239]

[^15.239]: Cited above, p. xxv., n. 169.

<!-- ch15-p269 -->
The Tory Cabinet[^15.240] announced in the Speech from the Throne, on February 5, 1867, that it had drawn up the proposals of the Industrial Commission of Inquiry[^15.241] as Bills. To get that far had taken another twenty years of *experimentum in corpore vili* [experiment on a worthless body]. As early as 1840 a Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry on children’s labor had been appointed. Its Report, in 1842, unfolded, in the words of Nassau W. Senior,

[^15.240]: Here (from “The Tory Cabinet...... to “Nassau W. Senior”) the English text has been altered in conformity with the 4th German edition. — Ed.

[^15.241]: The Factory Acts Extension Act was passed on August 12, 1867. It regulates all foundries, smithies, and metal manufactories, including machine shops; and also glass-works, paper mills, gutta-percha and India-rubber works, tobacco manufactories, letter-press printing and book-binding works, and, lastly, all workshops employing more than 50 persons. The Hours of Labour Regulation Act, passed on August 17, 1867, regulates the smaller workshops and the so-called domestic industries. I shall return to these Acts and to the new Mining Act of 1872 in Volume II.

<!-- ch15-p270 -->
> “the most frightful picture of avarice, selfishness and cruelty on the part of masters and of parents, and of juvenile and infantile misery, degradation and destruction ever presented.... It may be supposed that it describes the horrors of a past age. But there is unhappily evidence that those horrors continue as intense as they were. A pamphlet published by Hardwicke about 2 years ago states that the abuses complained of in 1842 are in full bloom at the present day. It is a strange proof of the general neglect of the morals and health of the children of the working-class, that this report lay unnoticed for 20 years, during which the children, ‘bred up without the remotest sign of comprehension as to what is meant by the term morals, who had neither knowledge, nor religion, nor natural affection,’ were allowed to become the parents of the present generation.”[^15.242]

[^15.242]: Senior, “Social Science Congress,” pp. 55-58.

<!-- ch15-p271 -->
Social conditions had changed, so Parliament could not risk shelving the demands of the Commission of 1862, as it had shelved those of the Commission of 1840. So in 1864, when the Commission had published no more than part of its reports, the earthenware industries (including the potteries), the makers of paperhangings (wallpaper), matches, cartridges, and caps, and the fustian cutters were brought under the Acts already in force in the textile industries. In the Speech from the Throne, on 5th February, 1867, the Tory Cabinet of the day announced that it would bring in Bills based on the final recommendations of the Commission, which had finished its work in 1866.

<!-- ch15-p272 -->
On the 15th August, 1867, the Factory Acts Extension Act received the Royal Assent, and on the 21st August the Workshops’ Regulation Act did too. The first of these Acts dealt with large industries, the second with small ones.

<!-- ch15-p273 -->
The Factory Acts Extension Act applies to blast-furnaces, iron and copper mills, foundries, machine shops, metal-manufacturing workshops, gutta-percha works, paper mills, glass-works, tobacco-manufacturing workshops, letter-press printing (including newspapers), and book-binding. In short, it applies to all industrial establishments of these kinds in which 50 individuals or more are employed at the same time, and for not less than 100 days during the year.

<!-- ch15-p274 -->
To give an idea of how wide a field the Workshops’ Regulation Act covers in practice, we quote the following passages from its interpretation clause (the clause that defines its terms):

<!-- ch15-p275 -->
> “*Handicraft* shall mean any manual labour exercised by way of trade, or for purposes of gain in, or incidental to, the making any article or part of an article, or in, or incidental to, the altering, repairing, ornamenting, finishing, or otherwise adapting for sale any article.”

<!-- ch15-p276 -->
> “*Workshop* shall mean any room or place whatever in the open air or undercover, in which any handicraft is carried on by any child, young person, or woman, and to which and over which the person by whom such child, young person, or woman is employed, has the right of access and control.”

<!-- ch15-p277 -->
> “*Employed* shall mean occupied in any handicraft, whether for wages or not, under a master or under a parent as herein defined.”

<!-- ch15-p278 -->
> “*Parent* shall mean parent, guardian, or person, having the custody of, or control over, any... child or young person.”

<!-- ch15-p279 -->
Clause 7 imposes a penalty for employing children, young persons, and women against the provisions of the Act. It makes liable to fines not only the occupier of the workshop, whether a parent or not, but even

<!-- ch15-p280 -->
> “the parent of, or the person deriving any direct benefit from the labour of, or having the control over, the child, young person or woman.”

<!-- ch15-p281 -->
The Factory Acts Extension Act, which covers the large establishments, departs from the Factory Act through a crowd of vicious exceptions and cowardly compromises with the employers.

<!-- ch15-p282 -->
The Workshops’ Regulation Act, wretched in all its details, remained a dead letter in the hands of the municipal and local authorities who were responsible for enforcing it. In 1871 Parliament took this power away from them and handed it to the Factory Inspectors, so that at a single stroke it added more than one hundred thousand workshops, and three hundred brickworks, to the inspectors’ field. But at the same time care was taken not to add more than eight assistants to their staff, which was already too small.[^15.243]

[^15.243]: The “personnel” of this staff consisted of 2 inspectors, 2 assistant inspectors and 41 sub-inspectors. Eight more sub-inspectors were appointed in 1871. The total cost of administering the Acts in England, Scotland, and Ireland for the year 1871-72 came to no more than £25,347, including the legal costs of prosecuting employers who had broken the law.

<!-- ch15-p283 -->
What strikes us, then, in the English legislation of 1867 is, on the one hand, the necessity that forced the parliament of the ruling classes to adopt in principle measures so extraordinary, and on so great a scale, against the excesses of capitalist exploitation. On the other hand, it is the hesitation, the repugnance, and the bad faith with which that parliament went about the task of carrying those measures into practice.

<!-- ch15-p284 -->
The Inquiry Commission of 1862 also proposed new regulation of the mining industry. Mining differs from other industries by one exceptional feature: in it, the interests of landlord and capitalist join hands. The antagonism between these two interests had been favorable to Factory legislation. On the other hand, the absence of that antagonism is enough to explain the delays and trickery of the legislation on mines.

<!-- ch15-p285 -->
The Inquiry Commission of 1840 had made revelations so terrible and so shocking, and causing such a scandal all over Europe, that Parliament passed the Mining Act of 1842 to salve its conscience. In that Act it limited itself to forbidding the employment underground in mines of children under 10 years of age and of females.

<!-- ch15-p286 -->
Then another Act, the Mines’ Inspecting Act of 1860, provides that mines shall be inspected by public officials appointed specially for that purpose, and that boys between the ages of 10 and 12 years shall not be employed unless they have a school certificate, or go to school for a certain number of hours. This Act was a complete dead letter, because of the ridiculously small number of inspectors, their meager powers, and other causes that will become clear as we go on.

<!-- ch15-p287 -->
One of the most recent Blue books on mines is the “Report from the Select Committee on Mines, together with &c. Evidence, 23rd July, 1866.” This Report is the work of a Parliamentary Committee chosen from members of the House of Commons, with the power to summon and examine witnesses. It is a thick folio volume, in which the Report itself takes up only five lines, saying in effect that the committee has nothing to say, and that more witnesses must be examined!

<!-- ch15-p288 -->
The way the witnesses are examined reminds one of the cross-examination of witnesses in English courts of justice. There the lawyer tries, by impudent, unexpected, ambiguous and tangled questions, asked without any connection, to intimidate, surprise, and confuse the witness, and to force a meaning onto the answers he squeezes out of him. In this inquiry the members of the committee are themselves the cross-examiners, and among them are both mine-owners and mine exploiters; the witnesses are mostly working coal miners. The whole farce is too typical of the spirit of capital for me not to give a few extracts from this Report. To keep it short, I have arranged them in classes. I may also add that in the English Blue books every question and its answer are numbered.

<!-- ch15-p289 -->
**1. Employment in mines of boys of 10 years and upwards.** – In the mines the work, including going and returning, usually lasts 14 or 15 hours, sometimes even from 3, 4 and 5 o’clock a.m. till 5 and 6 o’clock p.m. (n. 6, 452, 83). The adults work in two shifts, of eight hours each; but there is no such alternation for the boys, because of the expense (n. 80, 203, 204). The younger boys are mainly employed in opening and shutting the ventilating doors in the various parts of the mine; the older ones are employed on heavier work, carrying coal, etc. (n. 122, 739, 1747). They work these long hours underground until their 18th or 22nd year, when they are put to miner’s work proper (n. 161). Children and young persons are at present treated worse, and worked harder, than at any earlier period (n. 1663-1667). The miners almost unanimously demand an act of Parliament forbidding the employment in mines of children under 14. And now Hussey Vivian (himself an exploiter of mines) asks:

<!-- ch15-p290 -->
> “Would not the opinion of the workman depend upon the poverty of the workman’s family?” Mr. Bruce: “Do you not think it would be a very hard case, where a parent had been injured, or where he was sickly, or where a father was dead, and there was only a mother, to prevent a child between 12 and 14 earning 1s. 7d. a day for the good of the family? ... You must lay down a general rule? ... Are you prepared to recommend legislation which would prevent the employment of children under 12 and 14, whatever the state of their parents might be?” “Yes.” (ns. 107-110). Vivian: “Supposing that an enactment were passed preventing the employment of children under the age of 14, would it not be probable that ... the parents of children would seek employment for their children in other directions, for instance, in manufacture?” “Not generally I think” (n. 174). Kinnaird: “Some of the boys are keepers of doors?” “Yes.” “Is there not generally a very great draught every time you open a door or close it?” “Yes, generally there is.” “It sounds a very easy thing, but it is in fact rather a painful one?” “He is imprisoned there just the same as if he was in a cell of a gaol [jail].” Bourgeois Vivian: “Whenever a boy is furnished with a lamp cannot he read?” “Yes, he can read, if he finds himself in candles [pays for his own candles].... I suppose he would be found fault with if he were discovered reading; he is there to mind his business, he has a duty to perform, and he has to attend to it in the first place, and I do not think it would be allowed down the pit.” (ns. 139, 141, 143, 158, 160).

<!-- ch15-p291 -->
**II. Education.** – The working miners want a law for the compulsory education of their children, as in factories. They declare that the clauses of the Act of 1860 which require a school certificate to be obtained before boys of 10 and 12 years of age are employed are quite illusory. The examination of the witnesses on this subject is truly comical.

<!-- ch15-p292 -->
> “Is it (the Act) required more against the masters or against the parents?” “It is required against both I think.” “You cannot say whether it is required against one more than against the other?” “No; I can hardly answer that question.” (ns. 115, 116). “Does there appear to be any desire on the part of the employers that the boys should have such hours as to enable them to go to school?” “No; the hours are never shortened for that purpose.” (n. 137) Mr. Kinnaird: “Should you say that the colliers [coal miners] generally improve their education; have you any instances of men who have, since they began to work, greatly improved their education, or do they not rather go back, and lose any advantage that they may have gained?” “They generally become worse: they do not improve; they acquire bad habits; they get on to drinking and gambling and such like, and they go completely to wreck.” (n. 211.) “Do they make any attempt of the kind (for providing instruction) by having schools at night?” “There are few collieries where night schools are held, and perhaps at those collieries a few boys do go to those schools; but they are so physically exhausted that it is to no purpose that they go there.” (n. 454.) “You are then,” concludes the bourgeois, “against education?” “Most certainly not; but,” etc. (n. 443.) “But are they (the employers) not compelled to demand them (school certificates)?” “By law they are; but I am not aware that they are demanded by the employers.” “Then it is your opinion, that this provision of the Act as to requiring certificates, is not generally carried out in the collieries?” “It is not carried out.” (ns. 443, 444.) “Do the men take a great interest in this question (of education)?” “The majority of them do.” (n. 717.) “Are they very anxious to see the law enforced?” “The majority are.” (n. 718.) “Do you think that in this country any law that you pass ... can really be effectual unless the population themselves assist in putting it into operation?” “Many a man might wish to object to employing a boy, but he would perhaps become marked by it.” (n. 720.) “Marked by whom?” “By his employers.” (n. 721.) “Do you think that the employers would find any fault with a man who obeyed the law... ?” “I believe they would.” (n. 722.) “Have you ever heard of any workman objecting to employ a boy between 10 and 12, who could not write or read?” “It is not left to men’s option.” (n. 123.) “Would you call for the interference of Parliament?” “I think that if anything effectual is to be done in the education of the colliers’ children, it will have to be made compulsory by Act of Parliament.” (n. 1634.) “Would you lay that obligation upon the colliers only, or all the workpeople of Great Britain?” “I came to speak for the colliers.” (n. 1636.) “Why should you distinguish them (colliery boys) from other boys?” “Because I think they are an exception to the rule.” (n. 1638.) “In what respect?” “In a physical respect.” (n. 1639.) “Why should education be more valuable to them than to other classes of lads?” “I do not know that it is more valuable; but through the over-exertion in mines there is less chance for the boys that are employed there to get education, either at Sunday schools, or at day schools.” (n. 1640.) “It is impossible to look at a question of this sort absolutely by itself?” (n. 1644.) “Is there a sufficiency of schools?” – “No”... (n. 1646). “If the State were to require that every child should be sent to school, would there be schools for the children to go to?” “No; but I think if the circumstances were to spring up, the schools would be forthcoming.” (n. 1647.) “Some of them (the boys) cannot read and write at all, I suppose?” “The majority cannot... The majority of the men themselves cannot.” (ns. 705, 725.)

<!-- ch15-p293 -->
**III. Employment of women.** – Since 1842 women have no longer been employed underground, but they are occupied on the surface loading the coal, etc., drawing the tubs to the canals and railway wagons, sorting, etc. Their numbers have increased considerably during the last three or four years. (n. 1727.) They are mostly the wives, daughters, and widows of the working miners, and their ages range from 12 to 50 or 60 years. (ns. 645, 1779.)

<!-- ch15-p294 -->
> “What is the feeling among the working miners as to the employment of women?” “I think they generally condemn it.” (n. 648.) “What objection do you see to it?” “I think it is degrading to the sex.” (n. 649.) “There is a peculiarity of dress?” “Yes ... it is rather a man’s dress, and I believe in some cases, it drowns all sense of decency.” “Do the women smoke?” “Some do.” “And I suppose it is very dirty work?” “Very dirty.” “They get black and grimy?” “As black as those who are down the mines ... I believe that a woman having children (and there are plenty on the banks [the surface at the pit-head] that have) cannot do her duty to her children.” (ns. 650-654, 701.) “Do you think that those widows could get employment anywhere else, which would bring them in as much wages as that (from 8s. to 10s. a week)?” “I cannot speak to that.” (n. 709.) “You would still be prepared, would you,” (flint-hearted fellow!) “to prevent their obtaining a livelihood by these means?” “I would.” (n. 710.) “What is the general feeling in the district ... as to the employment of women?” “The feeling is that it is degrading; and we wish as miners to have more respect to the fair sex than to see them placed on the pit bank... Some part of the work is very hard; some of these girls have raised as much as 10 tons of stuff a day.” (ns. 1715,1717.) “Do you think that the women employed about the collieries are less moral than the women employed in the factories?” “...the percentage of bad ones may be a little more ... than with the girls in the factories.” (n. 1237.) “But you are not quite satisfied with the state of morality in the factories?” “No.” (n. 1733.) “Would you prohibit the employment of women in factories also?” “No, I would not.” (n. 1734.) “Why not?” “I think it a more honourable occupation for them in the mills.” (n. 1735.) “Still it is injurious to their morality, you think?” “Not so much as working on the pit bank; but it is more on the social position I take it; I do not take it on its moral ground alone. The degradation, in its social bearing on the girls, is deplorable in the extreme. When these 400 or 500 girls become colliers’ wives, the men suffer greatly from this degradation, and it causes them to leave their homes and drink.” (n. 1736.) “You would be obliged to stop the employment of women in the ironworks as well, would you not, if you stopped it in the collieries?” “I cannot speak for any other trade.” (n. 1737.) “Can you see any difference in the circumstances of women employed in ironworks, and the circumstances of women employed above ground in collieries?” “I have not ascertained anything as to that.” (n. 1740.) “Can you see anything that makes a distinction between one class and the other?” “I have not ascertained that, but I know from house to house visitation, that it is a deplorable state of things in our district....” (n. 1741.) “Would you interfere in every case with the employment of women where that employment was degrading?” “It would become injurious, I think, in this way: the best feelings of Englishmen have been gained from the instruction of a mother. ...” (n. 1750.) “That equally applies to agricultural employments, does it not?” “Yes, but that is only for two seasons, and we have work all the four seasons.” (n. 1751.) “They often work day and night, wet through to the skin, their constitution undermined and their health ruined.” “You have not inquired into that subject perhaps?” “I have certainly taken note of it as I have gone along, and certainly I have seen nothing parallel to the effects of the employment of women on the pit bank.... It is the work of a man... a strong man.” (ns. 1753, 1793, 1794.) “Your feeling upon the whole subject is that the better class of colliers who desire to raise themselves and humanise themselves, instead of deriving help from the women, are pulled down by them?” “Yes.” (n. 1808.) After some more crooked questions from these bourgeois, the secret of their “sympathy” for widows, poor families, etc., finally comes out. “The coal proprietor appoints certain gentlemen to take the oversight of the workings, and it is their policy, in order to receive approbation [approval], to place things on the most economical basis they can, and these girls are employed at from 1s. up to 1s. 6d. a day, where a man at the rate of 2s. 6d. a day would have to be employed.” (n. 1816.)

<!-- ch15-p295 -->
**IV. Coroner’s inquests. –**

<!-- ch15-p296 -->
> “With regard to coroner’s inquests in your district, have the workmen confidence in the proceedings at those inquests when accidents occur?” “No; they have not.” (n. 360.) “Why not?” “Chiefly because the men who are generally chosen, are men who know nothing about mines and such like.” “Are not workmen summoned at all upon the juries?” “Never but as witnesses to my knowledge.” “Who are the people who are generally summoned upon these juries?” “Generally tradesmen in the neighbourhood ... from their circumstances they are sometimes liable to be influenced by their employers ... the owners of the works. They are generally men who have no knowledge, and can scarcely understand the witnesses who are called before them, and the terms which are used and such like.” “Would you have the jury composed of persons who had been employed in mining?” “Yes, partly... they (the workmen) think that the verdict is not in accordance with the evidence given generally.” (ns. 361, 364, 366, 368, 371, 375.) “One great object in summoning a jury is to have an impartial one, is it not?” “Yes, I should think so.” “Do you think that the juries would be impartial if they were composed to a considerable extent of workmen?” “I cannot see any motive which the workmen would have to act partially ... they necessarily have a better knowledge of the operations in connexion with the mine.” “You do not think there would be a tendency on the part of the workmen to return unfairly severe verdicts?” “No, I think not.” (ns. 378, 379, 380.)

<!-- ch15-p297 -->
**V. False weights and measures.** – The workers demand to be paid weekly instead of every two weeks, and by weight instead of by the cubic contents of the tubs. They also demand protection against the use of false weights, etc. (n. 1071.)

<!-- ch15-p298 -->
> “If the tubs were fraudulently increased, a man could discontinue working by giving 14 days’ notice?” “But if he goes to another place, there is the same thing going on there.” (n. 1071.) “But he can leave that place where the wrong has been committed?” “It is general; wherever he goes, he has to submit to it.” (n. 1072.) “Could a man leave by giving 14 days’ notice?” “Yes.” (n. 1073.) And yet they are not satisfied!

<!-- ch15-p299 -->
**VI. Inspection of mines.** – Casualties from explosions are not the only things the workers suffer from. (n. 234, and following.)

<!-- ch15-p300 -->
> “Our men complained very much of the bad ventilation of the collieries ... the ventilation is so bad in general that the men can scarcely breathe; they are quite unfit for employment of any kind after they have been for a length of time in connexion with their work; indeed, just at the part of the mine where I am working, men have been obliged to leave their employment and come home in consequence of that ... some of them have been out of work for weeks just in consequence of the bad state of the ventilation where there is not explosive gas ... there is plenty of air generally in the main courses, yet pains are not taken to get air into the workings where men are working.” “Why do you not apply to the inspector?” “To tell the truth there are many men who are timid on that point; there have been cases of men being sacrificed and losing their employment in consequence of applying to the inspector.” “Why is he a marked man for having complained?” “Yes...... And he finds it difficult to get employment in another mine?” “Yes.” “Do you think the mines in your neighbourhood are sufficiently inspected to insure a compliance with the provisions of the Act?” “No; they are not inspected at all ... the inspector has been down just once in the pit, and it has been going seven years.... In the district to which I belong there are not a sufficient number of inspectors. We have one old man more than 70 years of age to inspect more than 130 collieries.” “You wish to have a class of sub-inspectors?” “Yes.” (ns. 234, 241, 251, 254, 274, 275, 554, 276, 293.) “But do you think it would be possible for Government to maintain such an army of inspectors as would be necessary to do all that you want them to do, without information from the men?” “No, I should think it would be next to impossible....” “It would be desirable the inspectors should come oftener?” “Yes, and without being sent for.” (n. 280, 277.) “Do you not think that the effect of having these inspectors examining the collieries so frequently would be to shift the responsibility (!) of supplying proper ventilation from the owners of the collieries to the Government officials?” “No, I do not think that, I think that they should make it their business to enforce the Acts which are already in existence.” (n. 285.) “When you speak of sub-inspectors, do you mean men at a less salary, and of an inferior stamp to the present inspectors?” “I would not have them inferior, if you could get them otherwise.” (n. 294.) “Do you merely want more inspectors, or do you want a lower class of men as an inspector?” “A man who would knock about, and see that things are kept right; a man who would not be afraid of himself.” (n. 295.) “If you obtained your wish in getting an inferior class of inspectors appointed, do you think that there would be no danger from want of skill, &c?” “I think not, I think that the Government would see after that, and have proper men in that position.” (n. 297.)

<!-- ch15-p301 -->
In the end this kind of examination becomes too much even for the chairman of the committee, and he breaks in with the remark:

<!-- ch15-p302 -->
> “You want a class of men who would look into all the details of the mine, and would go into all the holes and corners, and go into the real facts ... they would report to the chief inspector, who would then bring his scientific knowledge to bear on the facts they have stated?” (ns. 298, 299.) “Would it not entail very great expense if all these old workings were kept ventilated?” “Yes, expense might be incurred, but life would be at the same time protected.” (n. 531.)

<!-- ch15-p303 -->
A working miner objects to the 17th section of the Act of 1860. He says,

<!-- ch15-p304 -->
> “At the present time, if the inspector of mines finds a part of the mine unfit to work in, he has to report it to the mine-owner and the Home Secretary. After doing that, there is given to the owner 20 days to look over the matter; at the end of 20 days he has the power to refuse making any alteration in the mine; but, when he refuses, the mine-owner writes to the Home Secretary, at the same time nominating five engineers, and from those five engineers named by the mine-owner himself, the Home Secretary appoints one, I think, as arbitrator, or appoints arbitrators from them; now we think in that case the mine-owner virtually appoints his own arbitrator.” (n. 581.)

<!-- ch15-p305 -->
Bourgeois examiner, himself a mine-owner:

<!-- ch15-p306 -->
> “But ... is this a merely speculative objection?” (n. 586.) “Then you have a very poor opinion of the integrity of mining engineers?” “It is most certainly unjust and inequitable.” (n. 588.) “Do not mining engineers possess a sort of public character, and do not you think that they are above making such a partial decision as you apprehend?” “I do not wish to answer such a question as that with respect to the personal character of those men. I believe that in many cases they would act very partially indeed, and that it ought not to be in their hands to do so, where men’s lives are at stake.” (n. 589.)

<!-- ch15-p307 -->
This same bourgeois is not ashamed to ask this question: “Do you not think that the mine-owner also suffers loss from an explosion?” And finally: “Are not you workmen in Lancashire able to take care of your own interests without calling in the Government to help you?” “No.” (n. 1042.)

<!-- ch15-p308 -->
In the year 1865 there were 3,217 coal mines in Great Britain, and 12 inspectors. A Yorkshire mine-owner himself calculates (*Times*, 26th January, 1867) that, leaving aside the inspectors’ office work, which takes up all their time, each mine can be visited by an inspector only once in ten years. No wonder that explosions have increased steadily, both in number and in extent (sometimes with a loss of 200-300 men), during the last ten years. These are the beauties of “free” capitalist production! *[This sentence has been added to the English text in conformity with the 4th German edition. – Ed.*]

<!-- ch15-p309 -->
The very defective Act passed in 1872 is the first that regulates the hours of labor of the children employed in mines, and that makes exploiters and owners, to a certain extent, responsible for so-called accidents.

<!-- ch15-p310 -->
The Royal Commission appointed in 1867 to inquire into the employment of children, young persons, and women in agriculture has published some very important reports. Several attempts have been made to apply the principles of the Factory Acts to agriculture, though in a modified form, but so far they have failed completely. All I wish to draw attention to here is that there exists an irresistible tendency towards the general application of those principles.

<!-- ch15-p311 -->
If the general extension of factory legislation to all trades, to protect the working class both in mind and body, has become inevitable, then on the other hand, as we have already pointed out, that extension speeds up the general conversion of numerous isolated small industries into a few combined industries carried on on a large scale. It therefore speeds up the concentration of capital and the exclusive dominance of the factory system. It destroys both the ancient and the transitional forms behind which the rule of capital is still partly hidden, and replaces them with the direct and open rule of capital; but in doing so it also makes the direct opposition to this rule general. In each individual workshop it enforces uniformity, regularity, order, and economy. Yet, through the immense spur that the limitation and regulation of the working day give to technical improvement, it increases the anarchy and the catastrophes of capitalist production as a whole, the intensity of labor, and the competition of machinery with the worker. By destroying small-scale and domestic industries, it destroys the last refuge of the “redundant population,” and with it the only remaining safety-valve of the whole social mechanism. By maturing the material conditions and the combination of the processes of production on a social scale, it matures the contradictions and antagonisms of the capitalist form of production. In this way it provides, along with the elements for forming a new society, the forces for exploding the old one.[^15.244]

[^15.244]: Robert Owen was the father of Cooperative Factories and Stores. But, as remarked before, he in no way shared his followers’ illusions about the importance of these isolated elements of transformation. He not only made the factory system, in practice, the sole foundation of his experiments, but also declared that system to be, in theory, the starting-point of the social revolution. Herr Vissering, Professor of Political Economy in the University of Leyden, appears to have a suspicion of this. In his “Handboek van Practische Staatshuishoudkunde, 1860-62,” which repeats all the platitudes of vulgar economics (economics that only describes and defends the surface appearances of the system, without investigating its real relations), he strongly supports handicrafts against the factory system.

    **[*****Added in the 4th German edition*** — The “hopelessly bewildering tangle of contradictory enactments” (S. 314) (present volume, p. 284) which English legislation brought to life through the mutually conflicting Factory Acts, the Factory Acts Extension Act and the Workshops’ Act finally became intolerable. So all the laws on this subject were codified in the Factory and Workshop Act of 1878. Of course no detailed critique of this English industrial code now in force can be given here. The following remarks will have to do. The Act covers:

    1) **Textile Mills**. Here everything stays about as it was: children more than 10 years of age may work 5½ hours a day; or 6 hours and Saturday off; young persons and women, 10 hours on 5 days, and at most 6½ on Saturday.

    2) **Non-Textile Factories**. Here the regulations are brought closer than before to those of No. 1, but there are still several exceptions that favor the capitalists, and in certain cases these may be widened by special permission of the Home Secretary.

    3) **Workshops**, defined roughly as in the former Act. As for the children, young workers and women employed there, the workshops are about on a par with the non-textile factories, but again the conditions are easier in details.

    4) **Workshops** in which no children or young workers are employed, but only persons of both sexes above the age of 18; this category enjoys still easier conditions.

    5) **Domestic Workshops**, where only members of the family are employed, in the family dwelling: still more elastic regulations, and at the same time the restriction that the inspector, without special permission of the ministry or a court, may enter only rooms not also used for living in; and lastly unrestricted freedom for straw-plaiting and lace- and glove-making by members of the family. With all its defects this Act, together with the Swiss Federal Factory Law of March 23, 1877, is still by far the best piece of legislation in this field. Comparing it with that Swiss federal law is of particular interest, because the comparison clearly shows the merits and faults of the two legislative methods — the English, “historical” method, which steps in when occasion requires, and the continental method, which is built up on the traditions of the French Revolution and generalizes more. Unfortunately, because there are too few inspection staff, the English code is still largely a dead letter as far as its application to workshops is concerned. *— F. E.*]

### Section 10: Modern Industry and Agriculture

<!-- ch15-p312 -->
The revolution that modern industry has brought about in agriculture, and in the social relations of agricultural producers, will be investigated later on. Here we shall only point out a few results in advance. If the use of machinery in agriculture is for the most part free from the harmful physical effects it has on the factory worker, its action in pushing out the workers is more intense, and meets less resistance, as we shall see later in detail. In the counties of Cambridge and Suffolk, for example, the area of cultivated land has grown very much within the last 20 years (up to 1868). In the same period the rural population has shrunk, not only relatively, but absolutely. In the United States agricultural machines as yet replace workers only virtually. In other words, they allow the farmer to cultivate a larger area, but do not actually drive out the workers employed. In 1861 the number of persons employed in England and Wales in the manufacture of agricultural machines was 1,034, while the number of agricultural workers employed in using agricultural machines and steam-engines was no more than 1,205.

<!-- ch15-p313 -->
In agriculture, modern industry has a more revolutionary effect than anywhere else, for this reason: it wipes out the peasant, that bulwark of the old society, and puts the wage worker in his place. So the desire for social change and the class antagonisms are brought to the same level in the country as in the towns. The irrational, old-fashioned methods of farming are replaced by scientific ones. Capitalist production completely tears apart the old bond that held agriculture and manufacture together in their infancy.
