But at the same time it creates the material conditions for a higher synthesis in the future, namely the union of agriculture and industry on the basis of the more perfected forms that each has acquired during their temporary separation. Capitalist production gathers the population in great centers and makes the town population ever more dominant. In this way, on the one hand, it concentrates the historical motive power of society. On the other hand, it disturbs the circulation of matter between man and the soil, that is, it prevents the return to the soil of those of its elements that man consumes in the form of food and clothing. So it violates the conditions necessary for the lasting fertility of the soil. By this action it destroys, at the same time, the health of the town worker and the intellectual life of the rural worker.[^15.245] But while it upsets the conditions that grew up naturally for maintaining that circulation of matter, it imperiously demands that this circulation be restored as a system, as a regulating law of social production, and in a form fit for the full development of the human race. In agriculture as in manufacture, the transformation of production under the rule of capital means, at the same time, the martyrdom of the producer. The instrument of labor becomes the means of enslaving, exploiting, and impoverishing the worker. The social combination and organization of labor processes is turned into an organized way of crushing out the worker's individual vitality, freedom, and independence. The scattering of the rural workers over larger areas breaks their power of resistance, while concentration increases the power of resistance of the town factory workers. In modern agriculture, as in the urban industries, the increased productivity and quantity of the labor set in motion are bought at the cost of laying waste labor-power itself and consuming it by disease. Moreover, all progress in capitalist agriculture is progress in the art not only of robbing the worker, but of robbing the soil. All progress in increasing the fertility of the soil for a given time is progress towards ruining the lasting sources of that fertility. The more a country, like the United States, for example, starts its development on the foundation of modern industry, the more rapid is this process of destruction.[^15.246] Capitalist production, therefore, develops technology, and the combining of various processes into a social whole, only by sapping the original sources of all wealth – the soil and the worker.

[^15.245]: “You divide the people into two hostile camps of clownish boors and emasculated dwarfs. Good heavens! a nation divided into agricultural and commercial interests, calling itself sane; nay, styling itself enlightened and civilised, not only in spite of, but in consequence of this monstrous and unnatural division.” (David Urquhart, cited above, p. 119.) This passage shows, at one and the same time, the strength and the weakness of the kind of criticism that knows how to judge and condemn the present, but not how to understand it.

[^15.246]: See Liebig: “Die Chemie in ihrer Anwendung auf Agricultur und Physiologie,” 7. Auflage, 1862, and especially the “Einleitung in die Naturgesetze des Feldbaus,” in the 1st Volume. To have developed, from the point of view of natural science, the negative, that is, destructive, side of modern agriculture is one of Liebig’s immortal merits. His summary of the history of agriculture, too, although not free from gross errors, contains flashes of light. It is a pity, however, that he ventures on such haphazard assertions as the following: “By greater pulverising and more frequent ploughing, the circulation of air in the interior of porous soil is aided, and the surface exposed to the action of the atmosphere is increased and renewed; but it is easily seen that the increased yield of the land cannot be proportional to the labour spent on that land, but increases in a much smaller proportion. This law,” adds Liebig, “was first enunciated by John Stuart Mill in his ‘Principles of Pol. Econ.,’ Vol. 1, p. 17, as follows: ‘That the produce of land increases, *caeteris paribus* [other things being equal], in a diminishing ratio to the increase of the labourers employed’ (Mill here introduces in an erroneous form the law enunciated by Ricardo’s school, for since the ‘decrease of the labourers employed,’ kept even pace in England with the advance of agriculture, the law discovered in, and applied to, England, could have no application to that country, at all events), ‘is the universal law of agricultural industry.’ This is very remarkable, since Mill was ignorant of the reason for this law.” (Liebig, cited above, Bd. I., p. 143 and Note.) Leaving aside Liebig’s wrong interpretation of the word “labour,” by which he understands something quite different from what political economy means by it, it is in any case “very remarkable” that he should make Mr. John Stuart Mill the first to put forward a theory that was first published by James Anderson in A. Smith’s day, and was repeated in various works down to the beginning of the 19th century. It is a theory that Malthus, that master of plagiarism (the whole of his population theory is a shameless plagiarism), took over as his own in 1815; that West developed at the same time as Anderson and independently of him; that Ricardo, in the year 1817, connected with the general theory of value, after which it went around the world as Ricardo’s theory; that James Mill, the father of John Stuart Mill, vulgarized in 1820; and that, finally, John Stuart Mill and others reproduced as a dogma already quite commonplace and known to every schoolboy. It cannot be denied that John Stuart Mill owes his authority, which is at all events “remarkable,” almost entirely to such mix-ups.

# Part 5: Production of Absolute and Relative Surplus-Value

## Chapter 16: Absolute and Relative Surplus- Value

<!-- ch16-p001 -->
In considering the labor process, we began (see Chapter VII.) by treating it in the abstract, apart from its historical forms, as a process between man and Nature. (The labor process is the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things.) We stated there: “If we examine the whole labour-process, from the point of view of its result, it is plain that both the instruments and the subject of labour [the material worked on] are means of production, and that the labour itself is productive labour.” (Means of production are the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things.) And in Note 2, on the same page, we added: “This method of determining, from the standpoint of the labour-process alone, what is productive labour, is by no means directly applicable to the case of the capitalist process of production.” We now go on to develop this subject further.

<!-- ch16-p002 -->
To the extent that the labor process is purely individual, one and the same worker unites in himself all the functions that later become separated. When an individual takes hold of natural objects to make his living, no one controls him but himself. Later he is controlled by others. A single man cannot act upon Nature without calling his own muscles into play under the control of his own brain. Just as in the natural body head and hand serve each other, so the labor process unites the labor of the hand with that of the head. Later on they part company and even become deadly enemies. The product stops being the direct product of the individual and becomes a social product, produced in common by a collective worker, that is, by a combination of workers, each of whom takes only a part, greater or smaller, in handling the object of their labor. As the cooperative character of the labor process becomes more and more marked, our notion of productive labor, and of its agent, the productive worker, necessarily becomes wider as a consequence. To labor productively, it is no longer necessary for you to do manual work yourself; it is enough if you are an organ of the collective worker and perform one of its subordinate functions. The first definition of productive labor given above, a definition drawn from the very nature of the production of material objects, still remains correct for the collective worker, considered as a whole. But it no longer holds good for each member taken individually.

<!-- ch16-p003 -->
On the other hand, however, our notion of productive labor also becomes narrower. Capitalist production is not merely the production of commodities; it is essentially the production of surplus-value. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, that is, sold, not for the producer's own use. Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it.) The worker produces, not for himself, but for capital. (Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger.) So it is no longer enough that he should simply produce. He must produce surplus-value. Only the worker who produces surplus-value for the capitalist, and so works for the self-expansion of capital, is productive. If we may take an example from outside the sphere of producing material objects: a schoolmaster is a productive worker when, besides belaboring the heads of his pupils, he works like a horse to enrich the owner of the school. That the owner has laid out his capital in a teaching factory instead of a sausage factory does not change the relation. So the notion of a productive worker implies not merely a relation between work and useful effect, between worker and product of labor, but also a specific, social relation of production. It is a relation that has arisen historically and that stamps the worker as the direct means of creating surplus-value. To be a productive worker is therefore not a piece of luck, but a misfortune. In Book IV, which deals with the history of the theory, it will be seen more clearly that the classical political economists have at all times made the production of surplus-value the distinguishing mark of the productive worker. (Political economy is the science of economics as it was then called; classical political economy means the economists from Petty to Ricardo who investigated the real relations of production.) Hence their definition of a productive worker changes with their understanding of the nature of surplus-value. Thus the Physiocrats insist that only agricultural labor is productive, since that alone, they say, yields a surplus-value. And they say so because, for them, surplus-value exists only in the form of rent.

<!-- ch16-p004 -->
Lengthening the working day beyond the point at which the worker would have produced just an equivalent for the value of his labor-power, and capital's appropriation of that surplus labor: this is the production of absolute surplus-value. (The working day is the total hours a worker works in a day. Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist. The value of labor-power is the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker, and to raise the next generation of workers, able to work. Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) The production of absolute surplus-value forms the general groundwork of the capitalist system, and the starting-point for the production of relative surplus-value. Relative surplus-value presupposes that the working day is already divided into two parts, necessary labor and surplus labor. To lengthen the surplus labor, the necessary labor is shortened by methods that let the equivalent of the wages be produced in less time. (Wages are the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself.) The production of absolute surplus-value turns solely on the length of the working day; the production of relative surplus-value revolutionizes through and through the technical processes of labor and the makeup of society. It therefore presupposes a specific mode, the capitalist mode of production. This mode, along with its methods, means, and conditions, arises and develops spontaneously on the foundation provided by the formal subjection of labor to capital. In the course of this development, the formal subjection is replaced by the real subjection of labor to capital.

<!-- ch16-p005 -->
It will be enough merely to mention certain intermediate forms, in which surplus labor is not squeezed out of the producer by direct compulsion, nor has the producer himself yet been formally subjected to capital. In such forms capital has not yet gained direct control of the labor process. Alongside independent producers who carry on their handicrafts and agriculture in the traditional old-fashioned way, there stands the usurer or the merchant, with his usurer's capital or merchant's capital, feeding on them like a parasite. Where this form of exploitation predominates in a society, it rules out the capitalist mode of production; but this form may serve as a transition to that mode, as it did toward the close of the Middle Ages. Finally, as modern “domestic industry” shows, some intermediate forms are reproduced here and there in the background of modern industry, though their whole appearance is totally changed. (Modern industry is large-scale production based on machinery and the factory system.)

<!-- ch16-p006 -->
On the one hand, the mere formal subjection of labor to capital is enough for the production of absolute surplus-value. For example, it is enough that craftsmen who previously worked on their own account, or as apprentices of a master, should become wage workers under the direct control of a capitalist. On the other hand, we have seen how the methods of producing relative surplus-value are at the same time methods of producing absolute surplus-value. Indeed, more than that: the excessive lengthening of the working day turned out to be the peculiar product of modern industry. Generally speaking, the specifically capitalist mode of production stops being a mere means of producing relative surplus-value as soon as that mode has conquered an entire branch of production, and still more so as soon as it has conquered all the important branches. It then becomes the general, socially predominant form of production. As a special method of producing relative surplus-value, it remains effective only, first, insofar as it seizes on industries that previously were only formally subject to capital, that is, insofar as it is propagandist; and second, insofar as the industries it has already taken over continue to be revolutionized by changes in the methods of production.

<!-- ch16-p007 -->
From one standpoint, any distinction between absolute and relative surplus-value appears illusory. Relative surplus-value is absolute, since it compels the absolute lengthening of the working day beyond the labor-time necessary for the worker's own existence. Absolute surplus-value is relative, since it requires such a development of the productivity of labor as will allow the necessary labor-time to be confined to a part of the working day. (The productivity of labor is how much a given amount of labor produces in a given time.) But if we keep in mind how surplus-value behaves, this appearance of identity vanishes. Once the capitalist mode of production is established and has become general, the difference between absolute and relative surplus-value makes itself felt whenever there is a question of raising the rate of surplus-value. (The rate of surplus-value is the ratio of surplus-value to variable capital (s/v), that is, of surplus labor to necessary labor; it is also called the degree of exploitation of labor-power.) Assuming that labor-power is paid for at its value, we face this alternative. Given the productivity of labor and its normal intensity, the rate of surplus-value can be raised only by actually lengthening the working day. On the other hand, given the length of the working day, that rise can be brought about only by a change in the relative magnitudes of the parts of the working day, namely necessary labor and surplus labor. And if wages are not to fall below the value of labor-power, such a change presupposes a change either in the productivity or in the intensity of labor.

<!-- ch16-p008 -->
If the worker needs all his time to produce the necessary means of subsistence for himself and his kind, he has no time left in which to work free of charge for others. (Means of subsistence are the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live.) Without a certain degree of productivity in his labor, he has no such spare time at his disposal. Without such spare time, there is no surplus labor, and therefore no capitalists, no slave-owners, no feudal lords, in a word, no class of large proprietors.[^16.1]

[^16.1]: “The very existence of the master-capitalists, as a distinct class, is dependent on the productiveness of industry.” (Ramsay, cited above, p. 206.) “If each man’s labour were but enough to produce his own food, there could be no property.” (Ravenstone, cited above, p. 14, 15.)

<!-- ch16-p009 -->
So we may say that surplus-value rests on a natural basis. But this is permissible only in the very general sense that there is no natural obstacle absolutely preventing one man from unloading from himself the labor needed for his own existence and loading it onto another, any more than, for instance, unconquerable natural obstacles prevent one man from eating the flesh of another.[^16.2] No mystical ideas must in any way be attached to this historically developed productivity of labor, as sometimes happens. Only after men have raised themselves above the level of animals, and when therefore their labor has to some extent been socialized, does a state of things arise in which the surplus labor of one becomes a condition of existence for another. At the dawn of civilization the productivity that labor has acquired is small, but so too are the wants, which develop with the means of satisfying them and through those means. Further, at that early period, the part of society that lives on the labor of others is infinitely small compared with the mass of direct producers. As the productivity of labor progresses, that small part of society grows both absolutely and relatively.[^16.3] Besides, capital, with the relations that go with it, springs up from an economic soil that is the product of a long process of development. The productivity of labor that serves as its foundation and starting-point is a gift, not of nature, but of a history embracing thousands of centuries.

[^16.2]: According to a recent calculation, there are still at least 4,000,000 cannibals in those parts of the earth that have already been explored.

[^16.3]: “Among the wild Indians in America, almost everything is the labourer’s, 99 parts of a hundred are to be put upon the account of labour. In England, perhaps, the labourer has not 2/3.” (The Advantages of the East India Trade, &c., p. 73.)

<!-- ch16-p010 -->
Apart from the greater or lesser degree of development in the form of social production, the productivity of labor is tied down by physical conditions. These can all be traced back to the constitution of man himself (race, etc.) and to surrounding nature. The external physical conditions fall into two great economic classes: (1) natural wealth in means of subsistence, that is, a fruitful soil, waters teeming with fish, etc., and (2) natural wealth in the instruments of labor, such as waterfalls, navigable rivers, wood, metal, coal, etc. At the dawn of civilization, it is the first class that tips the scale; at a higher stage of development, it is the second. Compare, for example, England with India, or, in ancient times, Athens and Corinth with the shores of the Black Sea.

<!-- ch16-p011 -->
The fewer the natural wants that urgently demand satisfaction, and the greater the natural fertility of the soil and the more favorable the climate, the less is the labor-time necessary for maintaining and reproducing the producer. So much greater, therefore, can be the excess of his labor for others over his labor for himself. Diodorus remarked on this long ago in the case of the ancient Egyptians.

<!-- ch16-p012 -->
> “It is altogether incredible how little trouble and expense the bringing up of their children causes them. They cook for them the first simple food at hand; they also give them the lower part of the papyrus stem to eat, so far as it can be roasted in the fire, and the roots and stalks of marsh plants, some raw, some boiled and roasted. Most of the children go without shoes and unclothed, for the air is so mild. Hence a child, until he is grown up, costs his parents not more, on the whole, than twenty drachmas. It is this, chiefly, which explains why the population of Egypt is so numerous, and, therefore, why so many great works can be undertaken.”[^16.4]

[^16.4]: Diodorus, cited above, l. I., c. 80.

<!-- ch16-p013 -->
Nevertheless, the grand structures of ancient Egypt are due less to the size of its population than to the large proportion of it that was freely available. Just as the individual worker can do more surplus labor the smaller his necessary labor-time is, so it is with the working population. The smaller the part of it that is needed for producing the necessary means of subsistence, the greater is the part that can be set to do other work.

<!-- ch16-p014 -->
So, once capitalist production is assumed, with all other circumstances remaining the same and the length of the working day given, the quantity of surplus labor will vary with the physical conditions of labor, especially with the fertility of the soil. But it by no means follows from this that the most fruitful soil is the best suited for the growth of the capitalist mode of production. This mode is based on man's mastery over nature. Where nature is too lavish, she “keeps him in hand, like a child in leading-strings [strings used to guide a small child learning to walk].” She does not force on him any need to develop himself.[^16.5] It is not the tropics with their lush vegetation, but the temperate zone, that is the mother-country of capital. It is not the mere fertility of the soil, but the differentiation of the soil, the variety of its natural products, and the changes of the seasons, that form the physical basis for the social division of labor. And these, by changes in the natural surroundings, spur man on to multiply his wants, his capabilities, and his means and modes of labor. It is the necessity of bringing a natural force under the control of society, of economizing it, of appropriating or subduing it on a large scale by the work of man's hand, that first plays the decisive part in the history of industry. Examples are the irrigation works in Egypt,[^16.6] Lombardy, and Holland, or in India and Persia. There, irrigation by means of artificial canals not only supplies the soil with the water it cannot do without, but also carries down to it mineral fertilizers, in the form of sediment from the hills. The secret of the flourishing state of industry in Spain and Sicily under the rule of the Arabs lay in their irrigation works.[^16.7]

[^16.5]: “The first (natural wealth) as it is most noble and advantageous, so doth it make the people careless, proud, and given to all excesses; whereas the second enforceth vigilancy, literature, arts and policy.” (England’s Treasure by Foreign Trade. Or the Balance of our Foreign Trade is the Rule of our Treasure. Written by Thomas Mun of London, merchant, and now published for the common good by his son John Mun. London, 1669, p. 181, 182.) “Nor can I conceive a greater curse upon a body of people, than to be thrown upon a spot of land, where the productions for subsistence and food were, in great measure, spontaneous, and the climate required or admitted little care for raiment [clothing] and covering... there may be an extreme on the other side. A soil incapable of produce by labour is quite as bad as a soil that produces plentifully without any labour.” (An Inquiry into the Present High Price of Provisions. London 1767, p. 10.)

[^16.6]: The need to predict the rise and fall of the Nile created Egyptian astronomy, and with it the rule of the priests as directors of agriculture. “Le solstice est le moment de l’année ou commence la crue du Nil, et celui que les Egyptiens ont du observer avec le plus d’attention.... C’était cette année tropique qu’il leur importait de marquer pour se diriger dans leurs opérations agricoles. Ils durent donc chercher dans le ciel un signe apparent de son retour.” [The solstice is the moment of the year when the Nile flood begins, and the one the Egyptians had to watch with the greatest attention .... It was this tropical year that they needed to mark, to guide themselves in their farming work. So they had to look in the sky for a visible sign of its return.] (Cuvier: Discours sur les révolutions du globe, ed. Hoefer, Paris, 1863, p. 141.)

[^16.7]: One of the material bases of the state's power over the small, unconnected producing organisms in India was the regulation of the water supply. The Muslim rulers of India understood this better than their English successors. It is enough to recall the famine of 1866, which cost the lives of more than a million Hindus in the district of Orissa, in the Bengal presidency.

<!-- ch16-p015 -->
Favorable natural conditions alone give us only the possibility, never the reality, of surplus labor, nor, therefore, of surplus-value and a surplus-product. The result of differences in the natural conditions of labor is this: the same quantity of labor satisfies a different mass of needs in different countries,[^16.8] and consequently, under circumstances that are otherwise similar, the necessary labor-time is different. These conditions affect surplus labor only as natural limits, that is, by fixing the points at which labor for others can begin. As industry advances, these natural limits recede. In the midst of our West European society, where the worker buys the right to work for his own livelihood only by paying for it in surplus labor, the idea easily takes root that it is an inherent quality of human labor to provide a surplus-product.[^16.9] But consider, for example, an inhabitant of the eastern islands of the Asiatic Archipelago, where sago grows wild in the forests.

[^16.8]: “There are no two countries which furnish an equal number of the necessaries of life in equal plenty, and with the same quantity of labour. Men’s wants increase or diminish with the severity or temperateness of the climate they live in; consequently, the proportion of trade which the inhabitants of different countries are obliged to carry on through necessity cannot be the same, nor is it practicable to ascertain the degree of variation farther than by the degrees of Heat and Cold; from whence one may make this general conclusion, that the quantity of labour required for a certain number of people is greatest in cold climates, and least in hot ones; for in the former men not only want more clothes, but the earth more cultivating than in the latter.” (An Essay on the Governing Causes of the Natural Rate of Interest. London 1750. p. 60.) The author of this epoch-making anonymous work is J. Massy. Hume took his theory of interest from it.

[^16.9]: “Chaque travail doit (this also appears to be one of the *droits et devoirs du citoyen* [rights and duties of the citizen]) laisser un excédent.” [All labor must leave a surplus] Proudhon.

<!-- ch16-p016 -->
> “When the inhabitants have convinced themselves, by boring a hole in the tree, that the pith is ripe, the trunk is cut down and divided into several pieces, the pith is extracted, mixed with water and filtered: it is then quite fit for use as sago. One tree commonly yields 300 lbs., and occasionally 500 to 600 lbs. There, then, people go into the forests, and cut bread for themselves, just as with us they cut fire-wood.”[^16.10]

[^16.10]: F. Schouw: “Die Erde, die Pflanze und der Mensch,” 2. Ed. Leipz. 1854, p. 148.

<!-- ch16-p017 -->
Suppose now that such an eastern bread-cutter needs 12 working hours a week to satisfy all his wants. Nature's direct gift to him is plenty of leisure time. Before he can use this leisure time productively for himself, a whole series of historical events is required. Before he spends it in surplus labor for strangers, compulsion is necessary. If capitalist production were introduced, the honest fellow would perhaps have to work six days a week in order to take for himself the product of one working day. The bounty of Nature does not explain why he would then have to work 6 days a week, or why he must provide 5 days of surplus labor. It explains only why his necessary labor-time would be limited to one day a week. But in no case would his surplus-product arise from some mysterious quality inherent in human labor.

<!-- ch16-p018 -->
Thus not only the historically developed social productivity of labor, but also its natural productivity, appears to be the productivity of the capital with which that labor is incorporated.

<!-- ch16-p019 -->
Ricardo never concerns himself with the origin of surplus-value. He treats it as something inherent in the capitalist mode of production, a mode which, in his eyes, is the natural form of social production. Whenever he discusses the productivity of labor, he looks in it not for the cause of surplus-value, but for the cause that determines the magnitude of that value. His school, on the other hand, has openly proclaimed the productivity of labor to be the originating cause of profit (read: surplus-value). This at any rate is progress compared with the mercantilists. They, for their part, derived the excess of the price over the cost of production of the product from the act of exchange, from the product being sold above its value. (Price is the money name of the value, that is, the labor, embodied in a commodity.) Nevertheless, Ricardo's school simply dodged the problem; they did not solve it. In fact these bourgeois economists saw by instinct, and rightly so, that it is very dangerous to stir too deeply the burning question of the origin of surplus-value. (Bourgeois means belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it.) But what are we to think of John Stuart Mill, who, half a century after Ricardo, solemnly claims to be superior to the mercantilists by clumsily repeating the wretched evasions of Ricardo's earliest vulgarizers?

<!-- ch16-p020 -->
Mill says:

<!-- ch16-p021 -->
> “The cause of profit is that labour produces more than is required for its support.”

<!-- ch16-p022 -->
So far, nothing but the old story; but Mill, wishing to add something of his own, goes on:

<!-- ch16-p023 -->
> “To vary the form of the theorem; the reason why capital yields a profit, is because food, clothing, materials and tools, last longer than the time which was required to produce them.”

<!-- ch16-p024 -->
Here he confuses the duration of labor-time with the duration of its products. On this view, a baker whose product lasts only a day could never extract the same profit from his workers as a machine-maker whose products last for 20 years and more. Of course it is very true that if a bird's nest did not last longer than the time it takes to build, birds would have to do without nests.

<!-- ch16-p025 -->
Once this fundamental truth is established, Mill establishes his own superiority over the mercantilists.

<!-- ch16-p026 -->
> “We thus see,” he proceeds, “that profit arises, not from the incident of exchange, but from the productive power of labour; and the general profit of the country is always what the productive power of labour makes it, whether any exchange takes place or not. If there were no division of employments, there would be no buying or selling, but there would still be profit.”

<!-- ch16-p027 -->
For Mill, then, exchange, buying and selling, those general conditions of capitalist production, are a mere incident, and there would always be profits even without the purchase and sale of labor-power!

<!-- ch16-p028 -->
“If,” he continues, “the labourers of the country collectively produce twenty per cent more than their wages, profits will be twenty per cent, whatever prices may or may not be.” On the one hand, this is a rare bit of tautology; for if workers produce a surplus-value of 20% for the capitalist, his profit will be to the total wages of the workers as 20:100. On the other hand, it is absolutely false to say that “profits will be 20%.” They will always be less, because they are calculated on the *sum total* of the capital advanced. If, for example, the capitalist has advanced £500, of which £400 is laid out in means of production and £100 in wages, and if the rate of surplus-value is 20%, the rate of profit will be 20:500, that is, 4% and not 20%.

<!-- ch16-p029 -->
Next comes a splendid example of Mill's way of handling the different historical forms of social production.

<!-- ch16-p030 -->
> “I assume, throughout, the state of things which, where the labourers and capitalists are separate classes, prevails, with few exceptions, universally; namely, that the capitalist advances the whole expenses, including the entire remuneration of the labourer.”

<!-- ch16-p031 -->
A strange optical illusion, to see everywhere a state of things that as yet exists on our earth only as an exception.[^16.11] But let us finish – Mill is willing to concede,

[^16.11]: In earlier editions of *Capital* the quotation from John Stuart Mill, “I assume throughout...of the labourer,” had been given incorrectly: the words “where the labourers and capitalists are separate classes” had been left out. In a letter dated November 28, 1878, Marx pointed this out to Danielson, the Russian translator of *Capital*, and added: “The next two sentences, viz. ‘Strange optical illusion to see everywhere a state of things which as yet exists only exceptionally on our earth. But let us finish’ ‒ should be deleted and the following sentence substituted:

    “Mr. Mill is good enough to believe that this state of things is not an absolute necessity, even in that economic system in which ‘labourers and capitalists are separate classes.’”

    The content of this note is taken from the *Volksausgabe* [People's Edition]. The quotation from Mill is from his *Principles of Political Economy*, Book II, Chap XV, 5.

<!-- ch16-p032 -->
> “that he should do so is not a matter of inherent necessity.” On the contrary: “the labourer might wait, until the production is complete, for all that part of his wages which exceeds mere necessaries: and even for the whole, if he has funds in hand sufficient for his temporary support. But in the latter case, the labourer is to that extent really a capitalist in the concern, by supplying a portion of the funds necessary for carrying it on.”

<!-- ch16-p033 -->
Mill might have gone further and added that the worker who advances to himself not only the necessaries of life but also the means of production is in reality nothing but his own wage worker. He might also have said that the American peasant proprietor is only a serf who does forced labor for himself instead of for his lord.

<!-- ch16-p034 -->
After thus proving clearly that even if capitalist production did not exist, it would still always exist, Mill is consistent enough to show, on the contrary, that it does not exist even when it does exist.

<!-- ch16-p035 -->
> “And even in the former case” (when the worker is a wage worker to whom the capitalist advances all the necessaries of life, he, the worker), “may be looked upon in the same light,” (that is, as a capitalist), “since, contributing his labour at less than the market-price, (!) he may be regarded as lending the difference (?) to his employer and receiving it back with interest, &c.”[^16.12]

[^16.12]: J. St. Mill. Principles of Pol. Econ. London 1868, p. 252-53 passim.

<!-- ch16-p036 -->
In reality, the worker advances his labor free of charge to the capitalist for, say, one week, in order to receive the market price at the end of the week, etc.; and it is this, according to Mill, that turns him into a capitalist. On a level plain, simple mounds look like hills; and the imbecile flatness of today's bourgeoisie is to be measured by the height of its great intellects.

## Chapter 17: Changes of Magnitude in the Price of Labor-Power and in Surplus-Value

<!-- ch17-p001 -->
The value of labor-power is determined by the value of the necessities of life that the average worker habitually requires. (Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist. Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) The quantity of these necessities is known at any given period in a given society, and so it can be treated as a constant magnitude. What changes is the value of this quantity. Besides this, two other factors help determine the value of labor-power. One is the cost of developing that power, and this cost varies with the mode of production. The other is its natural diversity: the difference between the labor-power of men and of women, of children and of adults. The use of these different sorts of labor-power, a use that is in its turn made necessary by the mode of production, makes a great difference in the cost of maintaining the worker's family, and in the value of the labor-power of the adult male. Both these factors, however, are left out of the following investigation.[^17.1]

[^17.1]: *Note in the 3rd German edition*. — The case considered at pages 321-324 is of course left out here. — *F. E.*

<!-- ch17-p002 -->
I assume (1) that commodities are sold at their value; (2) that the price of labor-power rises above its value now and then, but never sinks below it. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer's own use. Price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity.)

<!-- ch17-p003 -->
On these assumptions, we have seen that the relative magnitudes of surplus-value and of the price of labor-power are determined by three circumstances. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it.) These are: (1) the length of the working day, or the extensive magnitude of labor (the working day is the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor); (2) the normal intensity of labor, its intensive magnitude, by which a given quantity of labor is spent in a given time; (3) the productivity of labor, by which the same amount of labor yields, in a given time, a greater or smaller amount of product, depending on how far the conditions of production have developed. Clearly, very different combinations are possible. One of the three factors may be constant and two variable, or two constant and one variable, or, lastly, all three may vary at the same time. And the number of these combinations grows further because, when these factors vary at the same time, the amount and direction of their variations may differ. In what follows, only the chief combinations are considered.

### Section 1: Length of the Working day and Intensity of Labor Constant. Productiveness of Labor Variable

<!-- ch17-p004 -->
On these assumptions, the value of labor-power and the magnitude of surplus-value are determined by three laws.

<!-- ch17-p005 -->
*(1.)* A working day of given length always creates the same amount of value, no matter how the productivity of labor may vary, and with it the mass of the product and the price of each single commodity produced.

<!-- ch17-p006 -->
Say the value created by a working day of 12 hours is six shillings. The mass of articles produced varies with the productivity of labor. But the only result is that the value represented by six shillings is spread over a greater or smaller number of articles.

<!-- ch17-p007 -->
*(2.)* Surplus-value and the value of labor-power vary in opposite directions. A change in the productivity of labor, whether an increase or a decrease, causes a change in the opposite direction in the value of labor-power, and in the same direction in surplus-value.

<!-- ch17-p008 -->
The value created by a working day of 12 hours is a constant quantity, say six shillings. This constant quantity is the sum of the surplus-value plus the value of labor-power, which is the value the worker replaces with an equivalent. It is self-evident that if a constant quantity consists of two parts, neither of them can increase without the other decreasing. Let the two parts be equal at the start: 3 shillings value of labor-power, 3 shillings surplus-value. Then the value of labor-power cannot rise from three shillings to four without the surplus-value falling from three shillings to two. And the surplus-value cannot rise from three shillings to four without the value of labor-power falling from three shillings to two. So under these circumstances no change can take place in the absolute magnitude of either the surplus-value or the value of labor-power without a change, at the same time, in their relative magnitudes, that is, in their size relative to each other. It is impossible for them both to rise or both to fall at the same time.

<!-- ch17-p009 -->
Further, the value of labor-power cannot fall, and so surplus-value cannot rise, without a rise in the productivity of labor. For instance, in the case above, the value of labor-power cannot sink from three shillings to two unless an increase in the productivity of labor makes it possible to produce in 4 hours the same quantity of necessities that previously took 6 hours to produce. On the other hand, the value of labor-power cannot rise from three shillings to four without a decrease in the productivity of labor, so that eight hours become necessary to produce the same quantity of necessities that six hours used to be enough for. It follows that an increase in the productivity of labor causes a fall in the value of labor-power and a resulting rise in surplus-value. On the other hand, a decrease in that productivity causes a rise in the value of labor-power and a fall in surplus-value.

<!-- ch17-p010 -->
In formulating this law, Ricardo overlooked one circumstance. A change in the magnitude of the surplus-value or surplus labor causes a change in the opposite direction in the magnitude of the value of labor-power, or in the quantity of necessary labor. (Necessary labor is the part of the working day in which the worker produces the equivalent of the value of their own labor-power, that is, of their wages. Surplus labor is the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist.) But it by no means follows that they vary in the same proportion. They do increase or decrease by the same quantity. But their proportional increase or decrease depends on their original magnitudes, before the change in the productivity of labor took place. Suppose the value of labor-power is 4 shillings, or the necessary labor-time 8 hours, and the surplus-value is 2 shillings, or the surplus labor 4 hours. Then suppose that, as a result of an increase in the productivity of labor, the value of labor-power falls to 3 shillings, or the necessary labor to 6 hours. The surplus-value will then rise to 3 shillings, or the surplus labor to 6 hours. The same quantity, 1 shilling or 2 hours, is added in one case and subtracted in the other. But the proportional change of magnitude is different in each case. The value of labor-power falls from 4 shillings to 3, that is, by 1/4 or 25%, while the surplus-value rises from 2 shillings to 3, that is, by 1/2 or 50%. So it follows that the proportional increase or decrease in surplus-value that results from a given change in the productivity of labor depends on the original magnitude of the part of the working day that is embodied in surplus-value. The smaller that part, the greater the proportional change; the greater that part, the smaller the proportional change.

<!-- ch17-p011 -->
*(3.)* An increase or decrease in surplus-value is always the result, and never the cause, of the corresponding decrease or increase in the value of labor-power.[^17.2]

[^17.2]: To this third law MacCulloch has made, among others, this absurd addition: that a rise in surplus-value, without a fall in the value of labor-power, can come about through the abolition of taxes payable by the capitalist. But abolishing such taxes makes no change whatever in the quantity of surplus-value that the capitalist squeezes out of the worker at first hand. It alters only the proportion in which that surplus-value is divided between himself and third persons. So it makes no change whatever in the relation between surplus-value and the value of labor-power. MacCulloch's exception therefore proves only that he has misunderstood the rule, a misfortune that happens to him as often in vulgarizing Ricardo as it happens to J. B. Say in vulgarizing Adam Smith.

<!-- ch17-p012 -->
The working day is constant in magnitude and is represented by a value of constant magnitude. To every change in the magnitude of surplus-value there corresponds an opposite change in the value of labor-power. And the value of labor-power cannot change except as a result of a change in the productivity of labor. Under these conditions, then, it clearly follows that every change of magnitude in surplus-value arises from an opposite change of magnitude in the value of labor-power. We have already seen that there can be no change of absolute magnitude in the value of labor-power and in surplus-value without a change in their relative magnitudes. So now it follows that no change in their relative magnitudes is possible without a previous change in the absolute magnitude of the value of labor-power.

<!-- ch17-p013 -->
According to the third law, a change in the magnitude of surplus-value presupposes a movement in the value of labor-power, and this movement is brought about by a change in the productivity of labor. The limit of this change is given by the altered value of labor-power. Nevertheless, even when circumstances allow the law to operate, secondary movements may occur. For example, suppose that, as a result of the increased productivity of labor, the value of labor-power falls from 4 shillings to 3, or the necessary labor-time from 8 hours to 6. The price of labor-power may then possibly fall no lower than 3s. 8d., 3s. 6d., or 3s. 2d., and so the surplus-value may rise no higher than 3s. 4d., 3s. 6d., or 3s. 10d. How far the price falls, with 3 shillings (the new value of labor-power) as its lowest limit, depends on the relative weight thrown into the scale by the pressure of capital on the one side and the resistance of the worker on the other. (Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger.)

<!-- ch17-p014 -->
The value of labor-power is determined by the value of a given quantity of necessities. It is the value, not the mass, of these necessities that varies with the productivity of labor. It is possible, however, that an increase in productivity may let both the worker and the capitalist take for themselves a greater quantity of these necessities at the same time, without any change in the price of labor-power or in surplus-value. Suppose the value of labor-power is 3 shillings, and the necessary labor-time amounts to 6 hours, and the surplus-value is likewise 3 shillings, and the surplus labor 6 hours. If the productivity of labor were then doubled without altering the ratio of necessary labor to surplus labor, there would be no change of magnitude in surplus-value or in the price of labor-power. The only result would be that each of them would represent twice as many use-values as before (a use-value is the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties), these use-values being twice as cheap as before. Although labor-power would be unchanged in price, it would be above its value. If, however, the price of labor-power had fallen, not to 1s. 6d., the lowest point possible given its new value, but to 2s. 10d. or 2s. 6d., this lower price would still represent an increased mass of necessities. In this way, with an increasing productivity of labor, the price of labor-power can keep on falling, and yet this fall can go along with a constant growth in the mass of the worker's means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live). But even in such a case, the fall in the value of labor-power would cause a corresponding rise of surplus-value, and so the gulf between the worker's position and the capitalist's would keep widening.[^17.3]

[^17.3]: “When an alteration takes place in the productiveness of industry, and that either more or less is produced by a given quantity of labour and capital, the proportion of wages [the price paid for labor-power] may obviously vary, whilst the quantity, which that proportion represents, remains the same, or the quantity may vary, whilst the proportion remains the same.” (“Outlines of Political Economy, &c.,” p. 67.)

<!-- ch17-p015 -->
Ricardo was the first to formulate accurately the three laws stated above. But he falls into the following errors. (1) He takes the special conditions under which these laws hold good to be the general and only conditions of capitalist production. He knows of no change either in the length of the working day or in the intensity of labor, so for him there can be only one variable factor, namely the productivity of labor. (2) This error damages his analysis much more than (1): like the other economists, he has not investigated surplus-value as such, that is, independently of its particular forms, such as profit, rent, etc. So he mixes up the laws of the rate of surplus-value with the laws of the rate of profit. The rate of profit is, as we have already said, the ratio of the surplus-value to the total capital advanced. The rate of surplus-value is the ratio of the surplus-value to the variable part of that capital. Assume that a capital C of £500 is made up of raw material, instruments of labor, etc. (c), to the amount of £400, and of wages (v) to the amount of £100. (Wages are the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself.) Assume further that the surplus-value (s) = £100. Then we have rate of surplus-value s/v = £100/£100 = 100%. But the rate of profit s/c = £100/£500 = 20%. It is obvious, besides, that the rate of profit may depend on circumstances that in no way affect the rate of surplus-value. I shall show in Book III. that, with a given rate of surplus-value, we may have any number of rates of profit, and that various rates of surplus-value may, under given conditions, be expressed in a single rate of profit.

### Section 2: Working day Constant. Productiveness of Labor Constant. Intensity of Labor Variable

<!-- ch17-p016 -->
Increased intensity of labor means that more labor is spent in a given time. So a working day of more intense labor is embodied in more products than a day of less intense labor, the length of each day being the same. It is true that increased productivity of labor will also supply more products in a given working day. But in that case the value of each single product falls, because it costs less labor than before. In the case of greater intensity, that value stays unchanged, because each article costs the same labor as before. Here we have an increase in the number of products without a fall in their individual prices: as their number increases, so does the sum of their prices. But in the case of increased productivity, a given value is spread over a greater mass of products. So, with the length of the working day constant, a day's labor of increased intensity will be embodied in an increased value and, if the value of money stays unchanged, in more money. The value created varies with how far the intensity of labor departs from the normal intensity in that society. So a given working day no longer creates a constant value but a variable one. In a day of 12 hours of ordinary intensity, the value created is, say, 6 shillings, but with increased intensity the value created may be 7, 8, or more shillings. Clearly, if the value created by a day's labor increases from, say, 6 to 8 shillings, then the two parts into which this value is divided, namely the price of labor-power and surplus-value, may both increase at the same time, either equally or unequally. They may both increase at the same time from 3 shillings to 4. Here, the rise in the price of labor-power does not necessarily mean that the price has risen above the value of labor-power. On the contrary, the rise in price may go along with a fall in value. This happens whenever the rise in the price of labor-power does not make up for its increased wear and tear.

<!-- ch17-p017 -->
We know that, with temporary exceptions, a change in the productivity of labor causes no change in the value of labor-power, and so none in the magnitude of surplus-value, unless the products of the industries affected are articles that the workers habitually consume. In the present case this condition no longer applies. For when the change is either in the duration or in the intensity of labor, there is always a corresponding change in the magnitude of the value created, whatever the nature of the article in which that value is embodied.

<!-- ch17-p018 -->
If the intensity of labor were to increase at the same time and equally in every branch of industry, then the new, higher degree of intensity would become the normal degree for the society, and so would cease to be taken into account. But even then, the intensity of labor would still differ from country to country, and would modify how the law of value applies internationally. The more intense working day of one nation would be represented by a greater sum of money than the less intense day of another nation.[^17.4]

[^17.4]: “All things being equal, the English manufacturer can turn out a considerably larger amount of work in a given time than a foreign manufacturer, so much as to counterbalance the difference of the working days, between 60 hours a week here, and 72 or 80 elsewhere.” (Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct., 1855, p. 65.) The surest possible means of reducing this qualitative difference between the English and the Continental working hour would be a law that shortened, quantitatively, the length of the working day in Continental factories.

### Section 3: Productiveness and Intensity of Labor Constant. Length of the Working day Variable

<!-- ch17-p019 -->
The working day may vary in two ways. It may be made either longer or shorter. From our present data, and within the limits of the assumptions made above, we obtain the following laws:

<!-- ch17-p020 -->
*(1.)* The working day creates a greater or smaller amount of value in proportion to its length. So it creates a variable, not a constant, quantity of value.

<!-- ch17-p021 -->
*(2.)* Every change in the relation between the magnitudes of surplus-value and of the value of labor-power arises from a change in the absolute magnitude of the surplus labor, and so of the surplus-value.

<!-- ch17-p022 -->
*(3.)* The absolute value of labor-power can change only as a result of the effect that the lengthening of surplus labor has on the wear and tear of labor-power. So every change in this absolute value is the effect, but never the cause, of a change in the magnitude of surplus-value.

<!-- ch17-p023 -->
We begin with the case in which the working day is shortened.

<!-- ch17-p024 -->
*(1.)* Under the conditions given above, a shortening of the working day leaves the value of labor-power, and with it the necessary labor-time, unaltered. It reduces the surplus labor and the surplus-value. Along with the absolute magnitude of the surplus-value, its relative magnitude also falls, that is*,* its magnitude relative to the value of labor-power, whose magnitude stays unaltered. Only by lowering the price of labor-power below its value could the capitalist protect himself from loss.

<!-- ch17-p025 -->
All the usual arguments against shortening the working day assume that it takes place under the conditions we have supposed here. But in reality the very opposite is the case: a change in the productivity and intensity of labor either comes before a shortening of the working day or immediately follows it.[^17.5]

[^17.5]: “There are compensating circumstances ... which the working of the Ten Hours' Act has brought to light.” (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact. for 31st Oct. 1848,” p. 7.)

<!-- ch17-p026 -->
*(2.)* Lengthening of the working day. Let the necessary labor-time be 6 hours, or the value of labor-power 3 shillings; let the surplus labor also be 6 hours, or the surplus-value 3 shillings. The whole working day then amounts to 12 hours and is embodied in a value of 6 shillings. Now, if the working day is lengthened by 2 hours and the price of labor-power stays unaltered, the surplus-value increases both absolutely and relatively. Although there is no absolute change in the value of labor-power, it suffers a relative fall. Under the conditions assumed in 1. there could be no change of relative magnitude in the value of labor-power without a change in its absolute magnitude. Here, on the contrary, the change of relative magnitude in the value of labor-power is the result of the change of absolute magnitude in surplus-value.

<!-- ch17-p027 -->
The value in which a day's labor is embodied increases with the length of that day. So clearly the surplus-value and the price of labor-power may both increase at the same time, by either equal or unequal quantities. This increase of both at the same time is therefore possible in two cases: one, an actual lengthening of the working day; the other, an increase in the intensity of labor without such lengthening.

<!-- ch17-p028 -->
When the working day is prolonged, the price of labor-power may fall below its value, although that price stays nominally unchanged or even rises. The value of a day's labor-power is, as will be remembered, estimated from its normal average duration, or from the normal length of life among the workers, and from the corresponding normal conversions of the body's organized matter into motion,[^17.6] in keeping with human nature. Up to a certain point, the increased wear and tear of labor-power that is inseparable from a lengthened working day may be made up for by higher wages. But beyond this point the wear and tear increases in geometrical progression, multiplying at every step, and every condition needed for the normal reproduction and functioning of labor-power is suppressed. The price of labor-power and the degree of its exploitation cease to be quantities that can be measured against each other.

[^17.6]: “The amount of labour which a man had undergone in the course of 24 hours might be approximately arrived at by an examination of the chemical changes which had taken place in his body, changed forms in matter indicating the anterior [earlier] exercise of dynamic force.” (Grove: “On the Correlation of Physical Forces.”)

### Section 4: Simultaneous Variations in the Duration, Productiveness, and Intensity of Labor

<!-- ch17-p029 -->
Clearly, a large number of combinations are possible here. Any two of the factors may vary while the third stays constant, or all three may vary at once. They may vary to the same or to different degrees, in the same or in opposite directions, so that the changes cancel each other out, either wholly or in part. Even so, analyzing every possible case is easy in view of the results given in I., II., and III. The effect of every possible combination can be found by treating each factor in turn as variable, and the other two as constant for the time being. So we shall take note, and briefly at that, of only two important cases.

#### A. Diminishing Productiveness of Labor with a Simultaneous Lengthening of the Working day

<!-- ch17-p030 -->
When we speak of a falling productivity of labor, we mean here a fall in those industries whose products determine the value of labor-power. An example is the fall that results from the soil becoming less fertile, and from the corresponding rise in the price of its products. Take the working day at 12 hours and the value it creates at 6 shillings, of which one half replaces the value of labor-power and the other forms the surplus-value. Suppose that, because the products of the soil have become dearer, the value of labor-power rises from 3 shillings to 4, and so the necessary labor-time from 6 hours to 8. If there is no change in the length of the working day, the surplus labor would fall from 6 hours to 4, and the surplus-value from 3 shillings to 2. If the day is lengthened by 2 hours, that is, from 12 hours to 14, the surplus labor stays at 6 hours and the surplus-value at 3 shillings[^17.*1], but the surplus-value decreases compared with the value of labor-power, as measured by the necessary labor-time. If the day is lengthened by 4 hours, namely from 12 hours to 16, the proportional magnitudes of surplus-value and value of labor-power, of surplus labor and necessary labor, stay unchanged. But the absolute magnitude of surplus-value rises from 3 shillings to 4, and that of the surplus labor from 6 hours to 8, an increase of 33 1/3%. So, with a falling productivity of labor and a simultaneous lengthening of the working day, the absolute magnitude of surplus-value may stay unaltered while its relative magnitude decreases. Its relative magnitude may stay unchanged while its absolute magnitude increases. And, provided the day is lengthened enough, both may increase.

[^17.*1]: Earlier English translations have “6 sh.” instead of 3 shillings. A reader pointed this error out to us; we have looked into it, checked it against the 1872 German Edition, and duly corrected an obvious error.

<!-- ch17-p031 -->
In the period between 1799 and 1815, the rising price of provisions in England led to a nominal rise in wages, although real wages, expressed in the necessities of life, fell. From this fact West and Ricardo drew the conclusion that the fall in the productivity of agricultural labor had brought about a fall in the rate of surplus-value. They made this assumed fact, which existed only in their imaginations, the starting-point of important investigations into the relative magnitudes of wages, profits, and rent. But in actual fact, surplus-value had at that time increased in both absolute and relative magnitude, thanks to the increased intensity of labor and to the lengthening of the working day. This was the period in which the right to prolong the hours of labor to an outrageous extent was established;[^17.7] the period that was especially marked by accelerated accumulation of capital here, by pauperism there.[^17.8] (Accumulation of capital means turning surplus-value back into capital, so that capital grows. Pauperism is the condition of the lowest layer of the surplus population, unable to find work and dependent on poor relief.)

[^17.7]: “Corn and labour rarely march quite abreast; but there is an obvious limit, beyond which they cannot be separated. With regard to the unusual exertions made by the labouring classes in periods of dearness, which produce the fall of wages noticed in the evidence” (namely, before the Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry, 1814-15), “they are most meritorious in the individuals, and certainly favour the growth of capital. But no man of humanity could wish to see them constant and unremitted. They are most admirable as a temporary relief; but if they were constantly in action, effects of a similar kind would result from them, as from the population of a country being pushed to the very extreme limits of its food.” (Malthus: “Inquiry into the Nature and Progress of Rent,” London, 1815, p. 48, note.) All honor to Malthus for stressing the lengthening of the hours of labor, a fact he draws attention to elsewhere in his pamphlet as well, while Ricardo and others, in the face of the most notorious facts, make an unchanging length of the working day the foundation of all their investigations. But the conservative interests that Malthus served kept him from seeing something. An unlimited prolongation of the working day, combined with an extraordinary development of machinery and the exploitation of women and children, was bound to make a great part of the working class “supernumerary,” particularly as soon as the war should cease and England's monopoly in the markets of the world should come to an end. It was, of course, far more convenient, and far more in keeping with the interests of the ruling classes, whom Malthus worshipped like a true priest, to explain this “over-population” by the eternal laws of Nature, rather than by the historical laws of capitalist production.

[^17.8]: “A principal cause of the increase of capital, during the war, proceeded from the greater exertions, and perhaps the greater privations of the labouring classes, the most numerous in every society. More women and children were compelled by necessitous circumstances, to enter upon laborious occupations, and former workmen were, from the same cause, obliged to devote a greater portion of their time to increase production.” (Essays on Pol. Econ., in which are illustrated the principal causes of the present national distress. London, 1830, p. 248.)

#### B. Increasing Intensity and Productiveness of Labor with Simultaneous Shortening of the Working day

<!-- ch17-p032 -->
Increased productivity and greater intensity of labor both have the same effect. They both increase the mass of articles produced in a given time. So both shorten the part of the working day that the worker needs to produce his means of subsistence or their equivalent. The minimum length of the working day is fixed by this part, which is necessary but able to shrink. If the whole working day were to shrink to the length of this part, surplus labor would vanish, an outcome utterly impossible under the rule of capital. Only by abolishing the capitalist form of production could the working day be reduced to the necessary labor-time. But even in that case, necessary labor-time would expand its limits. On the one hand, this is because the notion of “means of subsistence” would expand considerably, and the worker would lay claim to an altogether different standard of life. On the other hand, it is because a part of what is now surplus labor would then count as necessary labor; I mean the labor of forming a fund for reserve and accumulation.

<!-- ch17-p033 -->
The more the productivity of labor increases, the more the working day can be shortened; and the more the working day is shortened, the more the intensity of labor can increase. From the point of view of society, productivity increases in the same ratio as the economy of labor. This economy, in its turn, includes not only economy in the means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things), but also the avoidance of all useless labor. The capitalist mode of production on the one hand enforces economy in each individual business. On the other hand, through its anarchic system of competition, it gives rise to the most outrageous waste of labor-power and of society's means of production, not to mention the creation of a vast number of jobs that are at present indispensable, but in themselves superfluous.

<!-- ch17-p034 -->
Given the intensity and productivity of labor, the time that society must devote to material production is shorter, and so the time at its disposal for the free development, intellectual and social, of the individual is greater, in proportion as the work is more and more evenly divided among all the able-bodied members of society, and as any particular class is more and more deprived of the power to shift the natural burden of labor from its own shoulders onto those of another layer of society. In this direction, the shortening of the working day finally finds a limit in the generalization of labor. In capitalist society, free time is gained for one class by turning the whole lifetime of the masses into labor-time.

## Chapter 18: Various Formula for the Rate of Surplus-Value

<!-- ch18-p001 -->
We have seen that the rate of surplus-value (surplus-value being the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it) is represented by the following formulas:

<!-- ch18-p002 -->
```text
     Surplus-value      s           Surplus-value          Surplus-labour
I.                                                     =
    Variable Capital (  v ) =  Value of labour-power      Necessary labour
```

<!-- ch18-p003 -->
The first two of these formulas express, as a ratio of values, what the third expresses as a ratio of the times during which those values are produced. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) These formulas complement one another, and they are strictly precise and correct. We therefore find them worked out in classical political economy in substance, but not consciously. (Political economy was the science of economics as it was then called; classical political economy means the economists from Petty to Ricardo who investigated the real relations of production.) There we meet with the following derived formulas.

<!-- ch18-p004 -->
```text
     Surplus-labour              Surplus-value           Surplus-product
II.                      =                           =
      Working day             Value of the Product         Total Product
```

<!-- ch18-p005 -->
Here one and the same ratio is expressed as a ratio of labor-times, as a ratio of the values in which those labor-times are embodied, and as a ratio of the products in which those values exist. It is of course understood that “Value of the Product” means only the value newly created in a working day (the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor), leaving out the constant part of the value of the product.

<!-- ch18-p006 -->
In all of these formulas (II.), the actual degree of exploitation of labor, or the rate of surplus-value, is expressed falsely. Let the working day be 12 hours. Then, making the same assumptions as in earlier examples, the real degree of exploitation of labor is represented in the following proportions.

<!-- ch18-p007 -->
```text
  6 hours surplus-labour        Surplus-value of 3 sh.
                           =                              = 100%
6 hours necessary labour       Variable Capital of 3 sh.
From formulae II. we get very differently,
  6 hours surplus-labour         Surplus-value of 3 sh.
                             =                           = 50%
 Working day of 12 hours         Value created of 6 sh.
```

<!-- ch18-p008 -->
In reality, these derived formulas express only the proportion in which the working day, or the value produced by it, is divided between capitalist and worker. If they are to be treated as direct expressions of the degree of self-expansion of capital (capital being value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger), the following mistaken law would hold good: Surplus labor or surplus-value can never reach 100%.[^18.1] Surplus labor (the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist) is only a fraction of the working day, or surplus-value is only a fraction of the value created. So the surplus labor must necessarily always be less than the working day, or the surplus-value always less than the total value created. But to reach the ratio of 100:100 they must be equal. For the surplus labor to absorb the whole day (that is, an average day of any week or year), the necessary labor must sink to zero. (Necessary labor is the part of the working day in which the worker produces the equivalent of the value of their own labor-power, that is, of their wages.) But if the necessary labor vanishes, so does the surplus labor, since the surplus labor is only a function of the necessary labor. The ratio

[^18.1]: For example, in “Dritter Brief an v. Kirchmann von Rodbertus. Widerlegung der Ricardo’schen Lehre von der Grundrente und Begrundung einer neuen Rententheorie.” Berlin, 1851. I shall return to this letter later on. In spite of its mistaken theory of rent, it sees through the nature of capitalist production.

    NOTE ADDED IN THE 3RD GERMAN EDITION: From this it can be seen how favorably Marx judged his predecessors whenever he found real progress in them, or new and sound ideas. Since then, the publication of Rodbertus’ letters to Rud. Meyer has shown that Marx’s acknowledgment above needs to be restricted to some extent. In those letters this passage occurs:

    “Capital must be rescued not only from labor, but from itself, and that will be best effected, by treating the acts of the industrial capitalist as economic and political functions, that have been delegated to him with his capital, and by treating his profit as a form of salary, because we still know no other social organisation. But salaries may be regulated, and may also be reduced if they take too much from wages. The irruption [violent bursting in] of Marx into Society, as I may call his book, must be warded off.... Altogether, Marx’s book is not so much an investigation into capital, as a polemic against the present form of capital, a form which he confounds with the concept itself of capital.” (“Briefe, &c., von Dr. Robertus-Jagetzow, herausgg. von Dr. Rud. Meyer,” Berlin, 1881, I, Bd. P.111, 46. Brief von Rodbertus.) Such were the ideological commonplaces into which the bold attack Rodbertus made in his “social letters” finally dwindled. — *F. E.*

<!-- ch18-p009 -->
Surplus labor or Surplus-value\
Working day Value created

<!-- ch18-p010 -->
can therefore never reach the limit 100/100, still less rise to 100 + x/100. But this is not so for the rate of surplus-value, the real degree of exploitation of labor. Take, for example, the estimate of L. de Lavergne. According to it, the English agricultural worker gets only 1/4, and the capitalist (farmer), on the other hand, 3/4 of the product[^18.2] or its value, leaving aside the question of how the booty is later divided between the capitalist, the landlord, and others. According to this, the surplus labor of the English agricultural worker is to his necessary labor as 3:1, which gives a rate of exploitation of 300%.

[^18.2]: Of course, the part of the product that merely replaces the constant capital advanced is left out of this calculation. (Constant capital is the part of capital spent on means of production. Its value is passed on to the product but does not grow.) Mr. L. de Lavergne, a blind admirer of England, tends to estimate the capitalist’s share too low rather than too high.

<!-- ch18-p011 -->
Through the use of formulas II., the favorite method of treating the working day as fixed in length became a settled habit, because in these formulas surplus labor is always compared with a working day of given length. The same holds good when only the division of the value produced is kept in view. The working day that has already been realized in a given value must necessarily be a day of given length.

<!-- ch18-p012 -->
There is a habit of representing surplus-value and value of labor-power as fractions of the value created. (Labor-power is a person’s capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist. The value of labor-power is the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker, and to raise the next generation of workers, able to work.) This habit originates in the capitalist mode of production itself, and its meaning will be revealed later. It hides the very transaction that characterizes capital, namely the exchange of variable capital for living labor-power, and the resulting exclusion of the worker from the product. (Variable capital is the part of capital spent on labor-power. It reproduces its own value and also produces surplus-value, so its size varies.) Instead of the real fact, we get the false appearance of an association, in which worker and capitalist divide the product in proportion to the different elements that each of them contributes to making it.[^18.3]

[^18.3]: All well-developed forms of capitalist production are forms of cooperation (many workers working together, side by side, in the same or connected processes, under one capitalist’s command). So nothing is easier, of course, than to ignore their antagonistic character and to turn them, with a word, into some form of free association. A. de Laborde does this in “De l’Esprit d’Association dans tous les intérêts de la communauté”. Paris 1818. H. Carey, the Yankee, occasionally performs this conjuring trick with equal success, even with the relations that result from slavery.

<!-- ch18-p013 -->
Moreover, formulas II. can at any time be turned back into formulas I. If, for instance, we have

<!-- ch18-p014 -->
Surplus labor of 6 hours\
Working day of 12 hours

<!-- ch18-p015 -->
then the necessary labor-time is 12 hours minus the surplus labor of 6 hours, and we get the following result,

<!-- ch18-p016 -->
```text
  Surplus-labour of 6 hours       100
                             =
Necessary labour of 6 hours       100
```

<!-- ch18-p017 -->
There is a third formula, which I have already anticipated now and then; it is

<!-- ch18-p018 -->
```text
            Surplus-value             Surplus-labour        Unpaid labour
III.                             =                      =
       Value of labour-power         Necessary labour        Paid labour
```

<!-- ch18-p019 -->
After the investigations we have given above, it is no longer possible to be misled by the formula

<!-- ch18-p020 -->
Unpaid labor,\
Paid labor

<!-- ch18-p021 -->
into concluding that the capitalist pays for labor and not for labor-power. This formula is only a popular expression for

<!-- ch18-p022 -->
Surplus labor,\
Necessary labor

<!-- ch18-p023 -->
The capitalist pays the value of the labor-power, so far as price coincides with value. (A price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity.) In exchange he receives the disposal of the living labor-power itself. His usufruct, his right to use it, is spread over two periods. During one period the worker produces a value that is only equal to the value of his labor-power; he produces its equivalent. This the capitalist receives in return for advancing the price of the labor-power, a product ready-made in the market.
