During the other period, the period of surplus labor, the use of the labor-power creates a value for the capitalist that costs him no equivalent.[^18.4] This expenditure of labor-power comes to him free of charge. It is in this sense that surplus labor can be called unpaid labor.

[^18.4]: Although the Physiocrats could not see through the mystery of surplus-value, this much was clear to them, namely that it is “une richesse indépendante et disponible qu’il (the owner) n’a point achetée et qu’il vend.” [a wealth that is independent and available, which he ... has not bought and which he sells] (Turgot: “Réflexions sur la Formation et la Distribution des Richesses,” p.11.)

<!-- ch18-p024 -->
Capital, therefore, is not only, as Adam Smith says, the command over labor. It is essentially the command over unpaid labor. All surplus-value, whatever particular form (profit, interest, or rent) it may later crystallize into, is in substance the materialization of unpaid labor. The secret of the self-expansion of capital comes down to the power to dispose of a definite quantity of other people’s unpaid labor.

# Part 6: Wages

## Chapter 19: The Transformation of the Value (and Respective Price) of Labor-Power into Wages

<!-- ch19-p001 -->
On the surface of bourgeois society (bourgeois: belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it), the worker's wage appears as the price of labor: a certain amount of money paid for a certain amount of labor. So people speak of the value of labor, and they call its expression in money its necessary or natural price. (A price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity.) On the other hand, they speak of the market prices of labor, that is, prices that swing above or below its natural price.

<!-- ch19-p002 -->
But what is the value of a commodity? It is the objective form of the social labor spent in producing it. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, that is, sold, not for the producer's own use.) And how do we measure the size of this value? By the amount of labor it contains. How, then, is the value of, for example, a 12 hour working day to be fixed? By the 12 working hours contained in a working day of 12 hours. That is an absurd tautology.[^19.1] (The working day is the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor.)

[^19.1]: “Mr. Ricardo ingeniously enough avoids a difficulty which, on a first view, threatens to encumber his doctrine — that value depends on the quantity of labour employed in production. If this principle is rigidly adhered to, it follows that the value of labour depends on the quantity of labour employed in producing it — which is evidently absurd. By a dexterous turn, therefore, Mr. Ricardo makes the value of labour depend on the quantity of labour required to produce wages; or, to give him the benefit of his own language, he maintains, that the value of labour is to be estimated by the quantity of labour required to produce wages; by which he means the quantity of labour required to produce the money or commodities given to the labourer. This is similar to saying, that the value of cloth is estimated, not by the quantity of labour bestowed on its production, but by the quantity of labour bestowed on the production of the silver, for which the cloth is exchanged.” — “A Critical Dissertation on the Nature, &c., of Value,” pp. 50, 51.

<!-- ch19-p003 -->
To be sold as a commodity on the market, labor must in any case exist before it is sold. But if the worker could give it an independent, objective existence, he would be selling a commodity and not labor.[^19.2]

[^19.2]: “If you call labour a commodity, it is not like a commodity which is first produced in order to exchange, and then brought to market where it must exchange with other commodities according to the respective quantities of each which there may be in the market at the time; labour is created the moment it is brought to market; nay, it is brought to market before it is created.” — “Observations on Certain Verbal Disputes,” etc., pp. 75, 76.

<!-- ch19-p004 -->
Apart from these contradictions, a direct exchange of money, that is, of realized labor, for living labor (living labor: the labor of workers now at work) would do one of two things. Either it would abolish the law of value, which only begins to develop freely on the basis of capitalist production, or it would abolish capitalist production itself, which rests directly on wage labor. For example, the working day of 12 hours is embodied in a money-value of 6s. Either equivalents are exchanged, and then the worker receives 6s. for 12 hours' labor; the price of his labor would be equal to the price of his product. In this case he produces no surplus-value for the buyer of his labor. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it.) The 6s. are not turned into capital (capital: value that is used to make more value, money that is advanced in order to come back larger), and the basis of capitalist production vanishes. But it is on this very basis that he sells his labor, and that his labor is wage labor. Or else he receives less than 6s. for 12 hours' labor, that is, less than 12 hours' labor. Twelve hours' labor is exchanged for 10, 6, etc., hours' labor. This equating of unequal amounts does more than just abolish the way value is fixed. A self-destroying contradiction of this kind cannot in any way even be stated or formulated as a law.[^19.3]

[^19.3]: “Treating labour as a commodity, and capital, the produce of labour, as another, then, if the values of these two commodities were regulated by equal quantities of labour, a given amount of labour would ... exchange for that quantity of capital which had been produced by the same amount of labour; antecedent labour would ... exchange for the same amount as present labour. But the value of labour in relation to other commodities ... is determined not by equal quantities of labour.” — E. G. Wakefield in his edition of Adam Smith’s “Wealth of Nations,” Vol. I., London, 1836, p. 231, note.

<!-- ch19-p005 -->
It is no use trying to derive the exchange of more labor for less from their difference in form, the one being realized and the other living.[^19.4] This is all the more absurd because the value of a commodity is fixed not by the amount of labor actually realized in it, but by the amount of living labor necessary to produce it. Say a commodity represents 6 working hours. If an invention is made by which it can be produced in 3 hours, the value even of the commodity already produced falls by half. It now represents 3 hours of social labor instead of the 6 formerly necessary. It is the amount of labor required to produce a commodity, not the realized form of that labor, that fixes the amount of its value.

[^19.4]: “There has to be a new agreement” (a new edition of the social contract!) “that whenever there is an exchange of work done for work to be done, the latter” (the capitalist) “is to receive a higher value than the former” (the worker). — Simonde (de Sismondi), “De la Richesse Commerciale,” Geneva, 1803, Vol I, p. 37.

<!-- ch19-p006 -->
What comes directly face to face with the owner of money on the market is in fact not labor, but the worker. What the worker sells is his labor-power (a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything). As soon as his labor actually begins, it has already stopped belonging to him, so he can no longer sell it. Labor is the substance and the built-in measure of value, but it has no value itself.[^19.5]

[^19.5]: “Labour the exclusive standard of value ... the creator of all wealth, no commodity.” Thomas Hodgskin, “Popul. Polit. Econ.,” p. 186.

<!-- ch19-p007 -->
In the expression “value of labor,” the idea of value is not only completely wiped out, but actually turned upside down. It is an expression as imaginary as the value of the earth. These imaginary expressions, however, arise from the relations of production themselves. They are categories for the forms of appearance of essential relations. That things often present themselves upside down in their appearance is fairly well known in every science except political economy (the science of economics as it was then called).[^19.6]

[^19.6]: On the other hand, trying to explain such expressions as mere poetic license only shows how powerless the analysis is. That is why, in answer to Proudhon's phrase, “Labour is called value, not as being a commodity itself, but in view of the values supposed to be potentially embodied in it. The value of labour is a figurative expression,” etc., I remarked: “In labour, commodity, which is a frightful reality, he (Proudhon) sees nothing but a grammatical ellipsis. The whole of existing society, then, based upon labour commodity, is henceforth based upon a poetic license, on a figurative expression. Does society desire to eliminate all the inconveniences which trouble it, it has only to eliminate all the ill-sounding terms. Let it change the language, and for that it has only to address itself to the Academy and ask it for a new edition of its dictionary.” (Karl Marx, “Misère de la Philosophie,” pp. 34, 35.) It is, naturally, even more convenient to understand nothing at all by value. Then one can easily fit everything under this category. So, for example, J. B. Say: “What is value?” Answer: “That which a thing is worth”; and what is “price”? Answer: “The value of a thing expressed in money.” And why does agriculture have a value? Answer: “Because one sets a price on it.” So value is what a thing is worth, and the land has its “value” because its value is “expressed in money.” This is, anyhow, a very simple way of explaining the why and the wherefore of things.

<!-- ch19-p008 -->
Classical political economy (the economists from Petty to Ricardo who investigated the real relations of production) borrowed the category “price of labor” from everyday life without further criticism, and then simply asked: how is this price determined? It soon recognized that changes in the relation of demand and supply explained nothing about the price of labor, as about the price of all other commodities, except its changes, that is, the swings of the market price above or below a certain average. If demand and supply balance, then, all other conditions remaining the same, prices stop swinging. But then demand and supply also stop explaining anything. At the moment when demand and supply are in balance, the price of labor is its natural price, determined independently of the relation of demand and supply. And how this price is determined is precisely the question. Or else a longer period of swings in the market price is taken, for example a year, and the swings are found to cancel each other out, leaving a mean average quantity, a relatively constant magnitude. This, naturally, had to be determined by something other than its own variations, which cancel each other out. This price, which always wins out in the end over the accidental market prices of labor and regulates them, this “necessary price” (the Physiocrats) or “natural price” of labor (Adam Smith) can, as with all other commodities, be nothing else than its value expressed in money. In this way political economy expected to break through the accidental prices of labor to the value of labor. As with other commodities, this value was then determined by the cost of production. But what is the cost of production of the worker, that is, the cost of producing or reproducing the worker himself? Without noticing it, political economy put this question in place of the original one, because the search for the cost of production of labor as such went round in a circle and never got anywhere. So what economists call the value of labor is in fact the value of labor-power, as it exists in the worker's person, and labor-power is as different from its function, labor, as a machine is from the work it performs. (The value of labor-power is the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker, and to raise the next generation of workers, able to work.) Busy with the difference between the market price of labor and its so-called value, with the relation of this value to the rate of profit and to the values of the commodities produced by means of labor, etc., the economists never discovered that the course of the analysis had led not only from the market prices of labor to its presumed value, but had led to this value of labor itself being broken down into the value of labor-power. Classical economics never became aware of the results of its own analysis. It accepted the categories “value of labor,” “natural price of labor,” etc., uncritically, as final and adequate expressions for the value-relation under consideration. So, as will be seen later, it was led into hopeless confusion and contradiction, while it gave the vulgar economists (economists who only describe and defend the surface appearances of the system, without investigating its real relations) a secure base of operations for their shallowness, which on principle worships appearances only.

<!-- ch19-p009 -->
Let us next see how the value (and price) of labor-power present themselves in this transformed condition, as wages.

<!-- ch19-p010 -->
We know that the daily value of labor-power is calculated on a certain length of the worker's life, and that a certain length of working day, in turn, corresponds to this. Assume that the usual working day is 12 hours, and the daily value of labor-power is 3s., the expression in money of a value that embodies 6 hours of labor. If the worker receives 3s., then he receives the value of his labor-power functioning through 12 hours. Now, if this value of a day's labor-power is expressed as the value of a day's labor itself, we get the formula: Twelve hours' labor has a value of 3s. In this way the value of labor-power determines the value of labor, or, expressed in money, its necessary price. If, on the other hand, the price of labor-power differs from its value, then in the same way the price of labor differs from its so-called value.

<!-- ch19-p011 -->
Since the value of labor is only an irrational expression for the value of labor-power, it follows, of course, that the value of labor must always be less than the value it produces. For the capitalist always makes labor-power work longer than is necessary to reproduce its own value. In the example above, the value of the labor-power that functions through 12 hours is 3s., a value that takes 6 hours to reproduce. The value that the labor-power produces, on the other hand, is 6s., because it in fact functions for 12 hours, and the value it produces depends not on its own value but on the length of time it is in action. So we get a result that seems absurd at first sight: labor that creates a value of 6s. has a value of 3s.[^19.7]

[^19.7]: Compare “Zur Kritik &c.,” p. 40, where I state that this problem will be solved in the part of that work that deals with Capital: “How does production, on the basis of exchange-value [the proportion in which one commodity trades for others] determined simply by labour-time, lead to the result that the exchange-value of labour is less than the exchange-value of its product?”

<!-- ch19-p012 -->
We see, further: the value of 3s., which pays for only part of the working day, that is, 6 hours' labor, appears as the value or price of the whole working day of 12 hours, which therefore includes 6 hours that are not paid for. So the wage form wipes out every trace of the division of the working day into necessary labor and surplus labor, into paid and unpaid labor. (Necessary labor is the part of the working day in which the worker produces the equivalent of the value of their own labor-power, that is, of their wages. Surplus labor is the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist.) All labor appears as paid labor. Under the corvée (forced unpaid labor that peasants had to perform for a lord), the worker's labor for himself and his forced labor for his lord are separated in space and time in the clearest possible way. In slave labor, even the part of the working day in which the slave is only replacing the value of his own means of existence, in which he therefore in fact works for himself alone, appears as labor for his master. All the slave's labor appears as unpaid labor.[^19.8] In wage labor, on the contrary, even surplus labor, or unpaid labor, appears as paid. There, the property relation hides the slave's labor for himself; here, the money relation hides the unrewarded labor of the wage worker.

[^19.8]: The “Morning Star,” a London Free-trade paper, naive to the point of silliness, protested again and again during the American Civil War, with all the moral indignation man is capable of, that the Black man in the “Confederate States” worked absolutely for nothing. It should have compared the daily cost of such a Black man with that of the free worker in the East End of London.

<!-- ch19-p013 -->
Hence we can understand the decisive importance of the transformation of the value and price of labor-power into the form of wages, or into the value and price of labor itself. This form of appearance makes the actual relation invisible, and indeed shows the direct opposite of that relation. It forms the basis of all the legal notions of both worker and capitalist, of all the mystifications of the capitalist mode of production, of all its illusions about freedom, and of all the apologetic dodges of the vulgar economists.

<!-- ch19-p014 -->
If history took a long time to get to the bottom of the mystery of wages, nothing, on the other hand, is easier to understand than the necessity, the reason for the existence, of this phenomenon.

<!-- ch19-p015 -->
At first, the exchange between capital and labor presents itself to the mind in the same guise as the buying and selling of all other commodities. The buyer gives a certain sum of money, the seller an article of a nature different from money. The legal mind sees in this, at most, a material difference, expressed in the legally equivalent formula: “Do ut des, do ut facias, facio ut des, facio ut facias.”[^19.9]

[^19.9]: I give so that you may give; I give so that you may do; I do so that you may give; I do so that you may do.

<!-- ch19-p016 -->
Furthermore, since exchange-value and use-value are in their very nature magnitudes that cannot be measured against each other, the expressions “value of labor” and “price of labor” do not seem more irrational than the expressions “value of cotton” and “price of cotton.” (Exchange-value is the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for. Use-value is the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties.) Moreover, the worker is paid after he has given his labor. In its function as means of payment (money used to settle a debt after goods have changed hands on credit), money realizes afterwards the value or price of the article supplied, that is, in this particular case, the value or price of the labor supplied. Finally, the use-value that the worker supplies to the capitalist is not in fact his labor-power, but its function, some definite useful labor, the work of tailoring, shoemaking, spinning, etc. (Useful labor is labor of a particular kind, such as tailoring or weaving, that makes a particular useful thing.) That this same labor is, on the other hand, the universal value-creating element, and so has a property by which it differs from all other commodities, is beyond the grasp of the ordinary mind.

<!-- ch19-p017 -->
Let us put ourselves in the place of the worker who receives, for 12 hours' labor, say, the value produced by 6 hours' labor, say 3s. For him, in fact, his 12 hours' labor is the means of buying the 3s. The value of his labor-power may vary with the value of his usual means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live), from 3 to 4 shillings, or from 3 to 2 shillings. Or, if the value of his labor-power stays constant, its price may rise to 4s. or fall to 2s., as a result of changing relations of demand and supply. He always gives 12 hours of labor. So every change in the amount of the equivalent that he receives necessarily appears to him as a change in the value or price of his 12 hours' work. This circumstance misled Adam Smith, who treated the working day as a constant quantity,[^19.10] into asserting that the value of labor is constant, although the value of the means of subsistence may vary, and the same working day may therefore represent itself in more or less money for the worker.

[^19.10]: Adam Smith only incidentally mentions the variation of the working day, when he is referring to piece wages (wages paid per piece of work done).

<!-- ch19-p018 -->
Let us consider, on the other hand, the capitalist. He wants to receive as much labor as possible for as little money as possible. In practice, therefore, the only thing that interests him is the difference between the price of labor-power and the value that its function creates. But then, he tries to buy all commodities as cheaply as possible, and always explains his profit by simple cheating, by buying below value and selling above it. Hence he never comes to see that if such a thing as the value of labor really existed, and he really paid this value, no capital would exist: his money would not be turned into capital.

<!-- ch19-p019 -->
Moreover, the actual movement of wages shows phenomena which seem to prove that what is paid is not the value of labor-power, but the value of its function, of labor itself. We may reduce these phenomena to two great classes: 1.) Change of wages as the length of the working day changes. One might as well conclude that what is paid is not the value of a machine but the value of its working, because it costs more to hire a machine for a week than for a day. 2.) The individual difference in the wages of different workers who do the same kind of work. We find this individual difference, but are not deceived by it, in the system of slavery, where labor-power itself is sold frankly and openly, without any beating about the bush. Only, in the slave system, the advantage of a labor-power above the average, and the disadvantage of a labor-power below the average, affects the slave-owner; in the wage labor system, it affects the worker himself, because his labor-power is, in the one case, sold by himself, in the other, by a third person.

<!-- ch19-p020 -->
For the rest, between the form of appearance, “value and price of labor,” or “wages,” and the essential relation that shows itself in it, namely the value and price of labor-power, the same difference holds that holds between all phenomena and their hidden basis. The forms of appearance arise directly and spontaneously as current ways of thinking; the hidden basis must first be discovered by science. Classical political economy almost touches the true relation of things, but without consciously formulating it. It cannot do this as long as it sticks in its bourgeois skin.

## Chapter 20: Time-Wages

<!-- ch20-p001 -->
Wages (the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself) in turn take many forms. This fact cannot be seen in the ordinary economic treatises, which care only about the material side of the question and ignore every difference of form. However, an account of all these forms belongs to the special study of wage labor, and therefore not to this work. Still, the two basic forms must be briefly worked out here.

<!-- ch20-p002 -->
As the reader will remember, labor-power (a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything; it is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist) is sold for a definite period of time. Hence the converted form in which the daily, weekly, etc., value of labor-power presents itself is that of time wages, and so of day wages, etc. (Here value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time. The value of labor-power is the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker, and to raise the next generation of workers, able to work.)

<!-- ch20-p003 -->
Next we should note that the laws set out in the 17th chapter, on the changes in the relative magnitudes of the price of labor-power and of surplus-value, turn into laws of wages by a simple change of form. Here price means the money name of the value (the labor) embodied in a commodity, and surplus-value means the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it. In the same way, the distinction between the exchange-value of labor-power (the proportion in which it, like any commodity, trades for others) and the sum of the necessaries of life into which this value is converted now reappears as the distinction between nominal and real wages. It would be useless to repeat here, for the form of appearance, what has already been worked out for the substance underlying it. So we limit ourselves to a few points that are characteristic of time wages.

<!-- ch20-p004 -->
The sum of money[^20.1] that the worker receives for his daily or weekly labor makes up the amount of his nominal wages, or of his wages estimated in value. But clearly, depending on the length of the working day (the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor), that is, depending on the amount of actual labor supplied each day, the same daily or weekly wage may represent very different prices of labor, that is, very different sums of money for the same quantity of labor.[^20.2] So in considering time wages we must again distinguish between the total of the daily or weekly wages, etc., and the price of labor. How, then, are we to find this price, that is, the money-value of a given quantity of labor? The average price of labor is found by dividing the average daily value of labor-power by the average number of hours in the working day. If, for example, the daily value of labor-power is 3 shillings, the value of the product of 6 working hours, and if the working day is 12 hours, then the price of 1 working hour is 3/12 shillings = 3d. The price of the working hour found in this way serves as the unit of measure for the price of labor.

[^20.1]: The value of money itself is always assumed here to be constant.

[^20.2]: “The price of labour is the sum paid for a given quantity of labour.” (Sir Edward West, “Price of Corn and Wages of Labour,” London, 1836, p. 67.) West is the author of the anonymous “Essay on the Application of Capital to Land.” by a Fellow of the University College of Oxford, London, 1815. It is an epoch-making work in the history of political economy (the science of economics as it was then called).

<!-- ch20-p005 -->
It follows, therefore, that the daily and weekly wages, etc., may stay the same although the price of labor falls constantly. If, for example, the usual working day is 10 hours and the daily value of labor-power is 3s., the price of the working hour is 3 3/5d. It falls to 3d. as soon as the working day rises to 12 hours, and to 2 2/5d as soon as it rises to 15 hours. Despite all this, daily or weekly wages remain unchanged. Conversely, the daily or weekly wages may rise although the price of labor stays constant or even falls. If, for example, the working day is 10 hours and the daily value of labor-power is 3 shillings, the price of one working hour is 3 3/5d. If, because trade has increased, the worker works 12 hours, with the price of labor staying the same, his daily wage now rises to 3 shillings 7 1/5 d. without any change in the price of labor. The same result might follow if it were the intensive amount of labor that increased, instead of its extensive amount.[^20.3] So a rise in the nominal daily or weekly wages may go along with a price of labor that stays put or falls. The same holds for the income of the worker's family, as soon as the quantity of labor spent by the head of the family is increased by the labor of the members of his family. There are, therefore, ways of lowering the price of labor that do not depend on reducing the nominal daily or weekly wages.[^20.4]

[^20.3]: “The wages of labour depend upon the price of labour and the quantity of labour performed.... An increase in the wages of labour does not necessarily imply an enhancement of the price of labour. From fuller employment, and greater exertions, the wages of labour may be considerably increased, while the price of labour may continue the same.” (West, op. cit., pp. 67, 68, 112.) West, however, brushes off the main question, “How is the price of labour determined?”, with mere commonplaces.

[^20.4]: This is seen by the author of the “Essay on Trade and Commerce”, whom we have often quoted, the fanatical spokesman of the industrial bourgeoisie (the capitalist class) of the 18th century, although he puts the matter in a confused way: “It is the quantity of labour and not the price of it” (he means by this the nominal daily or weekly wages) “that is determined by the price of provisions and other necessaries: reduce the price of necessaries very low, and of course you reduce the quantity of labour in proportion. Master manufacturers know that there are various ways of raising and felling the price of labour, besides that of altering its nominal amount.” (op. cit., pp. 48, 61.) In his “Three Lectures on the Rate of Wages,” London, 1830, in which N. W. Senior makes use of West's work without naming it, Senior says: “The labourer is principally interested in the amount of wages” (p. 14). That is to say, the worker is principally interested in what he receives, the nominal sum of his wages, not in what he gives, the amount of labor!

<!-- ch20-p006 -->
As a general law it follows that, if the amount of daily or weekly labor, etc., is given, the daily or weekly wages depend on the price of labor. That price itself varies either with the value of labor-power or with the gap between its price and its value. If, on the other hand, the price of labor is given, the daily or weekly wages depend on the quantity of daily or weekly labor.

<!-- ch20-p007 -->
The unit of measure for time wages, the price of the working hour, is the value of a day's labor-power divided by the number of hours in the average working day. Let the average working day be 12 hours, and the daily value of labor-power 3 shillings, the value of the product of 6 hours of labor. Under these conditions the price of a working hour is 3d., and the value produced in it is 6d. If the worker is now employed for less than 12 hours (or less than 6 days in the week), for example only 6 or 8 hours, then at this price of labor he receives only 2s. or 1s. 6d. a day.[^20.5] On our assumption he must work 6 hours a day on average just to produce a day's wage that matches the value of his labor-power. On the same assumption he works only half of every hour for himself and half for the capitalist. So clearly he cannot get for himself the value of the product of 6 hours if he is employed for less than 12 hours. In earlier chapters we saw the destructive results of overwork. Here we find the sources of the suffering that comes to the worker from not being employed enough.

[^20.5]: The effect of such an abnormal cut in employment is quite different from that of a general shortening of the working day enforced by law. The former has nothing to do with the absolute length of the working day, and can occur just as well in a working day of 15 hours as in one of 6 hours. In the first case the normal price of labor is calculated on the worker working 15 hours a day on average, in the second on his working 6 hours a day on average. So the result is the same if in the one case he is employed for only 7½ hours, and in the other for only 3 hours.

<!-- ch20-p008 -->
Suppose the hourly wage is fixed in such a way that the capitalist does not bind himself to pay a day's or a week's wage, but only to pay wages for the hours during which he chooses to employ the worker. Then he can employ him for less time than the time originally used as the basis for calculating the hourly wage, the unit of measure of the price of labor. Since this unit is fixed by the ratio

<!-- ch20-p009 -->
daily value of labor-power\
working day of a given number of hours’

<!-- ch20-p010 -->
it naturally loses all meaning as soon as the working day stops containing a definite number of hours. The connection between paid and unpaid labor is destroyed. The capitalist can now squeeze a certain quantity of surplus labor (the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist) out of the worker without allowing him the labor-time necessary for his own subsistence. He can wipe out all regularity of employment. To suit his own convenience, whims, and interest of the moment, he can make the most enormous overwork alternate with a partial or total stop of work. On the pretense of paying “the normal price of labour,” he can lengthen the working day abnormally without any matching compensation to the worker. Hence the perfectly rational revolt in 1860 of the London workers in the building trades against the capitalists' attempt to impose this sort of hourly wage on them. The legal limitation of the working day puts an end to such mischief. It does not, of course, put an end to the reduced employment caused by the competition of machinery, by changes in the quality of the workers employed, and by crises, partial or general.

<!-- ch20-p011 -->
With a rising daily or weekly wage, the price of labor may stay nominally constant and yet fall below its normal level. This happens every time the working day is lengthened beyond its customary length while the price of labor (reckoned per working hour) stays constant. If in the fraction:

<!-- ch20-p012 -->
daily value of labor-power\
working day

<!-- ch20-p013 -->
the denominator increases, the numerator increases still faster. The value of labor-power, as it depends on its wear and tear, increases with the length of time that labor-power is at work, and it increases faster than that time does. In many branches of industry where time wages are the general rule and there are no legal limits to working time, a habit has therefore grown up on its own of treating the working day as normal only up to a certain point, for example up to the end of the tenth hour (“normal working day,” “the day's work,” “the regular hours of work”). Beyond this limit the working time is overtime, and, taking the hour as the unit of measure, it is paid better (“extra pay”), although often in a ridiculously small proportion.[^20.6] Here the normal working day exists as a fraction of the actual working day, and the actual working day, often throughout the whole year, lasts longer than the normal one.[^20.7] In various British industries, the increase in the price of labor when the working day is extended beyond a certain normal limit takes such a shape that the low price of labor during the so-called normal time forces the worker to work during the better-paid overtime, if he wants to earn an adequate wage at all.[^20.8] Legal limitation of the working day puts an end to these amenities.[^20.9]

[^20.6]: “The rate of payment for overtime (in lace-making) is so small, from ½ d. and ¾ d. to 2d. per hour, that it stands in painful contrast to the amount of injury produced to the health and stamina of the workpeople.... The small amount thus earned is also often obliged to be spent in extra nourishment.” (“Child.Empl.Com., II. Rep.,” p. xvi., n. 117.)

[^20.7]: For example, in paper-staining, before the Factory Act was recently introduced into this trade. “We work on with no stoppage for meals, so that the day’s work of 10½ hours is finished by 4:30 p.m., and all after that is over-time, and we seldom leave off working before 6 p.m., so that we are really working over-time the whole year round.” (Mr. Smith’s “Evidence in Child. Empl. Com., 1. Rep.,” p. 125.)

[^20.8]: For example, in the Scottish bleaching works. “In some parts of Scotland this trade” (before the introduction of the Factory Act in 1862) “was carried on by a system of over-time, i.e., ten hours a day were the regular hours of work, for which a nominal wage of 1s. 2d. per day was paid to a man, there being every day over-time for three or four hours, paid at the rate of 3d. per hour. The effect of this system ... a man could not earn more than 8s. per week when working the ordinary hours ... without over-time they could not earn a fair day’s wages.” (“Rept. of Insp. of Factories,” April 30th, 1863, p. 10.) “The higher wages, for getting adult males to work longer hours, are a temptation too strong to be resisted.” (“Rept. of Insp. of Fact.,” April 30th, 1848, p. 5.) The book-binding trade in the City of London employs a great many young girls from 14 to 15 years old, under indentures (apprenticeship contracts) that lay down certain definite hours of labor. Nevertheless, in the last week of each month they work until 10, 11, 12, or 1 o’clock at night, along with the older workers, in very mixed company. “The masters tempt them by extra pay and supper,” which they eat in nearby public houses. The great debauchery this produces among these “young immortals” (“Children’s Employment Comm., V. Rept.,” p. 44, n. 191) is made up for by the fact that, among other things, many Bibles and religious books are bound by them.

[^20.9]: See “Reports of Insp. of Fact.,” 30th April, 1863, p. 10. Judging the state of things very accurately, the London workers employed in the building trades declared, during the great strike and lock-out of 1860, that they would accept wages by the hour only on two conditions: (1), that, together with the price of the working hour, a normal working day of 9 and 10 hours respectively should be fixed, and that the price of the hour for the 10 hours' working day should be higher than that for the hour of the 9 hours' working day; (2), that every hour beyond the normal working day should be counted as overtime and paid proportionally more.

<!-- ch20-p014 -->
It is a generally known fact that, in any branch of industry, the longer the working days, the lower the wages.[^20.10] A. Redgrave, factory inspector, illustrates this with a comparative review of the 20 years from 1839-1859. According to it, wages rose in the factories under the 10 Hours Law, while they fell in the factories where work lasted 14 to 15 hours a day.[^20.11]

[^20.10]: “It is a very notable thing, too, that where long hours are the rule, small wages are also so.” (“Report of Insp. of Fact.,” 31st. Oct., 1863, p. 9.) “The work which obtains the scanty pittance of food, is, for the most part, excessively prolonged.” (“Public Health, Sixth Report,” 1864, p. 15.)

[^20.11]: “Report of Inspectors of Fact.,” 30th April, 1860, pp. 31, 32.

<!-- ch20-p015 -->
From the law, “the price of labour being given, the daily or weekly wage depends on the quantity of labour expended,” it follows, first of all, that the lower the price of labor, the greater the quantity of labor must be, or the longer the working day must be, for the worker to secure even a miserable average wage. Here the low price of labor acts as a spur to the extension of labor-time.[^20.12]

[^20.12]: The hand nail-makers in England, for example, have to work 15 hours a day because of the low price of labor, in order to hammer out their miserable weekly wage. “It’s a great many hours in a day (6 a.m. to 8 p.m.), and he has to work hard all the time to get 11 d. or 1s., and there is the wear of the tools, the cost of firing, and something for waste iron to go out of this, which takes off altogether 2½d. or 3d.” (“Children’s Employment Com., III. Report,” p. 136, n. 671.) In the same working time the women earn a week's wage of only 5 shillings. (Cited above, p. 137, n. 674.)

<!-- ch20-p016 -->
On the other hand, the extension of working time in its turn produces a fall in the price of labor, and with it a fall in the day's or week's wages.

<!-- ch20-p017 -->
The fixing of the price of labor by:

<!-- ch20-p018 -->
daily value of labor-power\
working day of a given number of hours

<!-- ch20-p019 -->
shows that merely lengthening the working day lowers the price of labor, if no compensation steps in. But the same circumstances that allow the capitalist to lengthen the working day in the long run also allow him at first, and force him in the end, to lower the price of labor nominally, until the total price of the increased number of hours falls, and therefore the daily or weekly wage too. It is enough here to point to two circumstances. If one man does the work of 1½ or 2 men, the supply of labor increases, although the supply of labor-power on the market stays constant. The competition this creates among the workers allows the capitalist to beat down the price of labor, while the falling price of labor, on the other hand, allows him to screw up working time still further.[^20.13] Soon, however, this command over abnormal quantities of unpaid labor, that is, quantities beyond the average social amount, becomes a source of competition among the capitalists themselves. Part of the price of the commodity (a thing produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer's own use) consists of the price of labor. The unpaid part of the labor-price need not be counted in the price of the commodity. It can be given away to the buyer. This is the first step competition leads to. The second step it drives to is to leave out of the selling price of the commodity at least part of the abnormal surplus-value created by lengthening the working day as well. In this way an abnormally low selling price of the commodity arises, at first here and there, and becomes fixed by degrees. From then on this lower selling price becomes the constant basis of a miserable wage for an excessive working time, just as it was originally the product of these very circumstances. This movement is only pointed out here, since the analysis of competition does not belong to this part of our subject. Nevertheless, the capitalist may, for a moment, speak for himself. “In Birmingham there is so much competition of masters one against another that many are obliged to do things as employers that they would otherwise be ashamed of; and yet no more money is made, but only the public gets the benefit.”[^20.14] The reader will remember the two sorts of London bakers. One sort sold bread at its full price (the “full-priced” bakers), the other below its normal price (“the under-priced,” “the undersellers”). The “full-priced” bakers denounced their rivals before the Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry: “They only exist now by first defrauding the public, and next getting 18 hours’ work out of their men for 12 hours’ wages.... The unpaid labour of the men was made ... the source whereby the competition was carried on, and continues so to this day.... The competition among the master bakers is the cause of the difficulty in getting rid of night-work. An underseller, who sells his bread below the cost-price according to the price of flour, must make it up by getting more out of the labour of the men.... If I got only 12 hours’ work out of my men, and my neighbor got 18 or 20, he must beat me in the selling price. If the men could insist on payment for over-work, this would be set right.... A large number of those employed by the undersellers are foreigners and youths, who are obliged to accept almost any wages they can obtain.”[^20.15]

[^20.13]: If a factory worker, for example, refused to work the customary long hours, “he would very shortly be replaced by somebody who would work any length of time, and thus be thrown out of employment.” (“Reports of Inspectors of Factories,” 30th April, 1848. Evidence, p. 39, n. 58.) “If one man performs the work of two... the rate of profits will generally be raised ... in consequence of the additional supply of labour having diminished its price.” (Senior, cited above, p. 15.)

[^20.14]: “Children’s Employment Com., III Rep.,” Evidence, p. 66, n. 22.

[^20.15]: “Report, &c., Relative to the Grievances Complained of by the Journeymen Bakers.” London, 1862, p. 411, and same source, Evidence, notes 479, 359, 27. In any case the full-priced bakers, as was mentioned above, and as their spokesman, Bennett, himself admits, make their men “generally begin work at 11 p.m. ... up to 8 o’clock the next morning.... They are then engaged all day long ... as late as 7 o’clock in the evening.” (Cited above, p. 22.)

<!-- ch20-p020 -->
This lament is also interesting because it shows how only the appearance of the relations of production is mirrored in the capitalist's brain. The capitalist does not know that the normal price of labor also includes a definite quantity of unpaid labor, and that this very unpaid labor is the normal source of his gain. The category of surplus labor-time does not exist for him at all, since it is included in the normal working day, which he thinks he has paid for in the day's wages. But overtime does exist for him: the lengthening of the working day beyond the limits that correspond to the usual price of labor. Face to face with his underselling competitor, he even insists on extra pay for this overtime. Again he does not know that this extra pay includes unpaid labor, just as the price of the customary hour of labor does. For example, the price of one hour of the 12 hours' working day is 3d., say the value-product (the new value created by labor in a given period, as distinct from the old value transferred from the means of production) of half a working hour, while the price of the overtime working hour is 4d., or the value-product of 2/3 of a working hour. In the first case the capitalist takes for himself one-half of the working hour without paying for it, in the second case one-third.

## Chapter 21: Piece Wages

<!-- ch21-p001 -->
Wages by the piece are nothing other than a converted form of wages by time, just as wages by time are a converted form of the value or price of labor-power. (Time wages are wages paid by the hour, day, or week; piece wages are wages paid per piece of work done. Wages are the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself. Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist. Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time. Price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity. The value of labor-power is the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker, and to raise the next generation of workers, able to work.)

<!-- ch21-p002 -->
With piece wages it seems at first sight as if the use-value (the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties) bought from the worker were not the functioning of his labor-power, living labor (the labor of workers now at work), but labor already realized in the product. It also seems as if the price of this labor were determined not, as with time wages, by the fraction

<!-- ch21-p003 -->
daily value of labor-power\
the working day of a given number of hours

<!-- ch21-p004 -->
but by the producer's capacity for work.[^21.1]

[^21.1]: “The system of piece-work illustrates an epoch in the history of the working-man; it is halfway between the position of the mere day-labourer depending upon the will of the capitalist and the co-operative artisan, who in the not distant future promises to combine the artisan and the capitalist in his own person. Piece-workers are in fact their own masters, even whilst working upon the capital of the employer.” (John Watts: “Trade Societies and Strikes, Machinery and Co-operative Societies.” Manchester, 1865, pp. 52, 53.) I quote this little work because it is a real cesspool of every apologetic commonplace that rotted long ago. This same Mr. Watts once dealt in Owenism (the socialism of Robert Owen), and in 1842 he published another pamphlet, “Facts and Fictions of Political Economists,” in which, among other things, he declares that “property is robbery.” That was long ago.

<!-- ch21-p005 -->
Faith in this appearance ought to get its first severe shock from the fact that both forms of wages exist side by side, at the same time, in the same branches of industry; for example,

<!-- ch21-p006 -->
> “the compositors [typesetters] of London, as a general rule, work by the piece, time-work being the exception, while those in the country work by the day, the exception being work by the piece. The shipwrights of the port of London work by the job or piece, while those of all other parts work by the day.”[^21.2]

[^21.2]: T. J. Dunning: “Trades’ Unions and Strikes,” London, 1860, p. 22.

<!-- ch21-p007 -->
In the same saddlery shops of London, often for the same work, the French are paid piece wages and the English time wages. In those regular factories in which piece wages predominate throughout, particular kinds of work are unsuited to this form of wage, and so they are paid by time.[^21.3] But it is, moreover, self-evident that the difference in the form in which wages are paid alters nothing in their essential nature, although one form may be more favorable to the development of capitalist production than the other.

[^21.3]: How the existence of these two forms of wage side by side, at the same time, favors the employers' cheating: “A factory employs 400 people, the half of which work by the piece, and have a direct interest in working longer hours. The other 200 are paid by the day, work equally long with the others, and get no more money for their over-time.... The work of these 200 people for half an hour a day is equal to one person’s work for 50 hours, or 5/6’s of one person’s labour in a week, and is a positive gain to the employer.” (“Reports of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1860,” p. 9.) “Over-working to a very considerable extent still prevails; and, in most instances, with that security against detection and punishment which the law itself affords. I have in many former reports shown ... the injury to workpeople who are not employed on piece-work, but receive weekly wages.” (Leonard Horner in “Reports of Insp. of Fact.,” 30th April, 1859, pp. 8, 9.)

<!-- ch21-p008 -->
Let the ordinary working day contain 12 hours, of which 6 are paid and 6 unpaid. (The working day is the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor.) Let its value-product be 6 shillings, so that the value-product of one hour's labor is 6d. (The value-product is the new value created by labor in a given period, as distinct from the old value transferred from the means of production.) Let us suppose that experience has shown the following. A worker who works with the average intensity and skill, and who therefore in fact spends only the time socially necessary to produce an article, supplies 24 pieces in 12 hours, either separate products or measurable parts of a continuous whole. (Socially necessary labor-time is the time needed to produce an article under the normal conditions of production of the day, with the average skill and intensity of labor.) Then the value of these 24 pieces, after subtracting the part of constant capital contained in them, is 6 shillings, and the value of a single piece is 3d. (Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger. Constant capital is the part of capital spent on means of production. Its value is passed on to the product but does not grow.) The worker receives 1 ½d. per piece, and so earns 3 shillings in 12 hours. With time wages, it makes no difference whether we assume that the worker works 6 hours for himself and 6 hours for the capitalist, or half of every hour for himself and the other half for the capitalist. Just so, here it makes no difference whether we say that each single piece is half paid for and half unpaid, or that the price of 12 pieces is the equivalent only of the value of the labor-power, while surplus-value is embodied in the other 12 pieces. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it.)

<!-- ch21-p009 -->
The form of piece wages is just as irrational as that of time wages. In our example, two pieces of a commodity, after subtracting the value of the means of production used up in them, are worth 6d., as the product of one hour. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, that is, sold, not for the producer's own use. Means of production are the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things.) Yet the worker receives a price of 3d. for them. In fact, piece wages do not distinctly express any relation of value. So it is not a question of measuring the value of the piece by the working time embodied in it. On the contrary, it is a question of measuring the working time the worker has spent by the number of pieces he has produced. With time wages, labor is measured by its immediate duration; with piece wages, by the quantity of products in which the labor has embodied itself during a given time.[^21.4] The price of labor-time itself is finally determined by the equation: value of a day's labor = daily value of labor-power. So piece wages are only a modified form of time wages.

[^21.4]: “Wages can be measured in two ways: either by the duration of the labour, or by its product.” (“Abrégé élémentaire des principes de l’économie politique.” Paris, 1796, p. 32.) The author of this anonymous work is G. Garnier.

<!-- ch21-p010 -->
Let us now look a little more closely at the characteristic features of piece wages.

<!-- ch21-p011 -->
Here the quality of the labor is controlled by the work itself, which must be of average perfection if the piece-price is to be paid in full. From this point of view, piece wages become the most fruitful source of wage cuts and capitalist cheating.

<!-- ch21-p012 -->
They give the capitalist an exact measure of the intensity of labor. (Intensity of labor is how much labor is packed into a given time, that is, how hard and fast people must work.) Only the working time embodied in an amount of commodities fixed in advance by experiment counts as socially necessary working time, and is paid as such. So in the larger workshops of the London tailors, a certain piece of work, a waistcoat for example, is called an hour, or half an hour, with the hour at 6d. Practice shows how much the average product of one hour is. With new fashions, repairs, etc., a contest arises between employer and worker over whether a particular piece of work is one hour, and so on, until here too experience decides. It is the same in the London furniture workshops, etc. If the worker does not have the average capacity, and so cannot supply a certain minimum of work per day, he is dismissed.[^21.5]

[^21.5]: “So much weight of cotton is delivered to him” (the spinner), “and he has to return by a certain time, in lieu of it, a given weight of twist or yarn, of a certain degree of fineness, and he is paid so much per pound for all that he so returns. If his work is defective in quality, the penalty falls on him, if less in quantity than the minimum fixed for a given time, he is dismissed and an abler operative procured.” (Ure, cited above, p. 317.)

<!-- ch21-p013 -->
Since the form of wage itself here controls the quality and intensity of the work, supervision of labor becomes largely superfluous. So piece wages form the basis of the modern “domestic labour” described earlier, and also of a hierarchically organized system of exploitation and oppression. This system has two basic forms. On the one hand, piece wages make it easier for parasites to step in between the capitalist and the wage worker: the “sub-letting of labour.” These middlemen's gain comes entirely from the difference between the labor-price that the capitalist pays and the part of that price that they actually allow to reach the worker.[^21.6] In England this system is called, characteristically, the “sweating system.” On the other hand, piece wages allow the capitalist to make a contract at so much per piece with the head worker – in manufacturing workshops with the chief of some group, in mines with the man who cuts the coal, in the factory with the actual machine-worker – at a price for which the head worker himself takes on the hiring and paying of his assistants. (Manufacture is the stage and form of capitalist production, roughly from the mid-16th to the late 18th century, based on handicraft work divided among many workers in one workshop.) Here the exploitation of the worker by capital is carried out through the exploitation of the worker by the worker.[^21.7]

[^21.6]: “It is when work passes through several hands, each of which is to take its share of profits, while only the last does the work, that the pay which reaches the workwoman is miserably disproportioned.” (“Child. Emp. Comm. II Report,” p. lxx., n. 424.)

[^21.7]: Even Watts, the apologist, remarks: “It would be a great improvement to the system of piece-work, if all the men employed on a job were partners in the contract, each according to his abilities, instead of one man being interested in over-working his fellows for his own benefit.” (cited above, p. 53.) On the vileness of this system, compare “Child. Emp. Comm., Rep. III.,” p. 66, n. 22, p. 11, n. 124, p. xi, n. 13, 53, 59, etc.

<!-- ch21-p014 -->
With piece wages, it is naturally in the worker's personal interest to strain his labor-power as intensely as possible. This makes it easier for the capitalist to raise the normal degree of intensity of labor.[^21.8] It is moreover now in the worker's personal interest to lengthen the working day, since that raises his daily or weekly wages.[^21.9] This gradually brings on a reaction like the one already described for time wages, not to mention that lengthening the working day, even if the piece wage stays constant, necessarily includes a fall in the price of labor.

[^21.8]: This spontaneous result is often helped along artificially. For example, in the Engineering Trade of London a customary trick is “the selecting of a man who possesses superior physical strength and quickness, as the principal of several workmen, and paying him an additional rate, by the quarter or otherwise, with the understanding that he is to exert himself to the utmost to induce the others, who are only paid the ordinary wages, to keep up to him ... without any comment this will go far to explain many of the complaints of stinting the action, superior skill, and working-power, made by the employers against the men” (in Trades-Unions. Dunning, cited above, pp. 22, 23). Since the author is himself a worker and secretary of a Trades’ Union, this might be taken for exaggeration. But the reader may compare the “highly respectable” “Cyclopedia of Agriculture” of J. C. Morton, Art., the article “Labourer,” where this method is recommended to the farmers as an approved one.

[^21.9]: “All those who are paid by piece-work ... profit by the transgression of the legal limits of work. This observation as to the willingness to work over-time is especially applicable to the women employed as weavers and reelers.” (“Rept. of Insp. of Fact., 30th April, 1858,” p. 9.) “This system” (piece-work), “so advantageous to the employer ... tends directly to encourage the young potter greatly to over-work himself during the four or five years during which he is employed in the piece-work system, but at low wages.... This is ... another great cause to which the bad constitutions of the potters are to be attributed.” (“Child. Empl. Comm. 1. Rept.,” p. xiii.)

<!-- ch21-p015 -->
With time wages, with few exceptions, the same wage holds for the same kind of work. With piece wages, on the other hand, although the price of the working time is measured by a certain quantity of product, the day's or week's wage will vary with the individual differences between workers: one supplies only the minimum product in a given time, another the average, a third more than the average. So as regards actual earnings there is great variety, according to the different skill, strength, energy, staying-power, etc., of the individual workers.[^21.10] Of course this does not alter the general relations between capital and wage labor. First, the individual differences balance one another out in the workshop as a whole, which thus supplies the average product in a given working time, and the total wages paid will be the average wages of that particular branch of industry. Second, the proportion between wages and surplus-value remains unchanged, since the mass of surplus labor supplied by each particular worker corresponds to the wage he receives. (Surplus labor is the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist.) But the wider scope that piece wages give to individuality tends to develop, on the one hand, that individuality, and with it the workers' sense of liberty, independence, and self-control, and on the other hand, their competition with one another. So piece-work tends, while raising individual wages above the average, to lower this average itself. But where a particular rate of piece wage had long been fixed by tradition, so that lowering it presented special difficulties, the employers in such exceptional cases sometimes resorted to forcibly turning it into time wages. Hence, for example, a great strike among the ribbon-weavers of Coventry in 1860.[^21.11] Finally, piece wages are one of the main supports of the hour system described in the preceding chapter.[^21.12]

[^21.10]: “Where the work in any trade is paid for by the piece at so much per job ... wages may very materially differ in amount.... But in work by the day there is generally an uniform rate ... recognized by both employer and employed as the standard of wages for the general run of workmen in the trade.” (Dunning, cited above, p. 17.)

[^21.11]: “The work of the journeyman-artisans will be ruled by the day or by the piece. These master-artisans know about how much work a journeyman-artisan can do per day in each craft, and often pay them in proportion to the work which they do; the journey men, therefore, work as much as they can, in their own interest, without any further inspection.” (Cantillon, “Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en général,” Amst. Ed., 1756, pp. 185 and 202. The first edition appeared in 1755.) Cantillon, from whom Quesnay, Sir James Steuart & A. Smith have drawn heavily, already presents piece wages here as simply a modified form of time wages. The French edition of Cantillon claims in its title to be a translation from the English. But the English edition, “The Analysis of Trade, Commerce, &c.,” by Philip Cantillon, late of the city of London, Merchant, is not only of later date (1759), but shows by its contents that it is a later and revised edition. For example, in the French edition Hume is not yet mentioned, while in the English edition, on the other hand, Petty hardly appears any longer. The English edition is less important theoretically, but it contains many details specifically about English trade, the bullion trade, etc., that are missing from the French text. So the words on the title-page of the English edition, according to which the work is “taken chiefly from the manuscript of a very ingenious gentleman, deceased, and adapted, &c.,” seem to be a pure fiction, of a kind very common at that time.

[^21.12]: “How often have we seen, in some workshops, many more workers recruited than the work actually called for? On many occasions, workers are recruited in anticipation of future work, which may never materialize. Because they are paid by piece wages, it is said that no risk is incurred, since any loss of time will be charged against the unemployed.” (H. Gregoir: “Les Typographes devant le Tribunal correctionnel de Bruxelles,” Brusseles, 1865, p. 9.)

<!-- ch21-p016 -->
From what has been shown so far, it follows that piece wages are the form of wages most in harmony with the capitalist mode of production. Although they are by no means new – they appear officially, side by side with time wages, in the French and English labor statutes of the 14th century – they only win a larger field of action during the period of manufacture properly so called. In the stormy youth of modern industry, especially from 1797 to 1815, they served as a lever for lengthening the working day and lowering wages. (Modern industry is large-scale production based on machinery and the factory system.) Very important materials on the fluctuation of wages during that period can be found in the Blue books: “Report and Evidence from the Select Committee on Petitions respecting the Corn Laws” (Parliamentary Session of 1813-14), and “Report from the Lords’ Committee, on the State of the Growth, Commerce, and Consumption of Grain, and all Laws relating thereto” (Session of 1814-15). Here we find documentary evidence of the constant lowering of the price of labor from the beginning of the anti-Jacobin War (the war against revolutionary France). In the weaving industry, for example, piece wages had fallen so low that, despite the very great lengthening of the working day, the daily wages were then lower than before.

<!-- ch21-p017 -->
> “The real earnings of the cotton weaver are now far less than they were; his superiority over the common labourer, which at first was very great, has now almost entirely ceased. Indeed... the difference in the wages of skillful and common labour is far less now than at any former period.”[^21.13]

[^21.13]: “Remarks on the Commercial Policy of Great Britain,” London, 1815.

<!-- ch21-p018 -->
The following passage, taken from a work that sides with the landlords and farmers, shows how little the greater intensity and extension of labor through piece wages benefited the agricultural proletariat (the proletariat is the class of wage workers, who own nothing they can live by except their labor-power):

<!-- ch21-p019 -->
> “By far the greater part of agricultural operations is done by people who are hired for the day or on piece-work. Their weekly wages are about 12s., and although it may be assumed that a man earns on piece-work under the greater stimulus to labour, 1s. or perhaps 2s. more than on weekly wages, yet it is found, on calculating his total income, that his loss of employment, during the year, outweighs this gain...Further, it will generally be found that the wages of these men bear a certain proportion to the price of the necessary means of subsistence [the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live], so that a man with two children is able to bring up his family without recourse to parish relief.”[^21.14]

[^21.14]: “A Defense of the Landowners and Farmers of Great Britain,” 1814, pp. 4, 5

<!-- ch21-p020 -->
Malthus remarked at that time, referring to the facts published by Parliament:

<!-- ch21-p021 -->
> “I confess that I see, with misgiving, the great extension of the practice of piece-wage. Really hard work during 12 or 14 hours of the day, or for any longer time, is too much for any human being.”[^21.15]

[^21.15]: Malthus, “Inquiry into the Nature and Progress of Rent,” London, 1815.

<!-- ch21-p022 -->
In the workshops under the Factory Acts, piece wages become the general rule, because there capital can increase the effectiveness of the working day only by intensifying labor.[^21.16]

[^21.16]: “Those who are paid by piece-work ... constitute probably four-fifths of the workers in the factories.” “Report of Insp. of Fact.,” 30th April, 1858.

<!-- ch21-p023 -->
As the productivity of labor changes, the same amount of product represents a varying working time. (Productivity of labor is how much a given amount of labor produces in a given time.) So the piece wage varies too, for it is the money expression of a definite working time. In our example above, 24 pieces were produced in 12 hours, while the value of the product of the 12 hours was 6s., the daily value of the labor-power 3s., the price of the labor-hour 3d., and the wage for one piece ½d. One piece absorbed half an hour's labor. Now suppose that the same working day supplies 48 pieces instead of 24, because the productivity of labor has doubled, and that all other circumstances remain unchanged. Then the piece wage falls from 1 ½d. to 3/4d., as every piece now represents only 1/4 of a working-hour, instead of ½. 24 by 1½d. = 3s., and in the same way 48 by 3/4d. = 3s. In other words, the piece wage is lowered in the same proportion as the number of pieces produced in the same time rises,[^21.17] and so in the same proportion as the working time spent on the same piece falls. This change in the piece wage, so far purely nominal, leads to constant battles between capitalist and labor. The battles arise either because the capitalist uses it as a pretext for actually lowering the price of labor, or because the increased productive power of labor is accompanied by an increased intensity of labor. Or they arise because the worker takes the appearance of piece wages seriously (namely, that his product is paid for, and not his labor-power), and so revolts against a lowering of wages that is not accompanied by a lowering of the selling price of the commodity.

[^21.17]: “The productive power of his spinning-machine is accurately measured, and the rate of pay for work done with it decreases with, though not as, the increase of its productive power.” (Ure, cited above, p. 317.) Ure himself cancels this last apologetic phrase again. The lengthening of the mule causes some increase of labor, he admits. So the labor does not diminish in the same ratio as its productivity increases. Further: “By this increase the productive power of the machine will be augmented one-fifth. When this event happens the spinner will not be paid at the same rate for work done as he was before, but as that rate will not be diminished in the ratio of one-fifth, the improvement will augment his money earnings for any given number of hours’ work,” but “the foregoing statement requires a certain modification.... The spinner has to pay something additional for juvenile aid out of his additional sixpence, accompanied by displacing a portion of adults” (cited above, p. 321), which in no way tends to raise wages.

<!-- ch21-p024 -->
> “The operatives...carefully watch the price of the raw material and the price of manufactured goods, and are thus enabled to form an accurate estimate of their master’s profits.”[^21.18]

[^21.18]: H. Fawcett: “The Economic Position of the British labourer.” Cambridge and London, 1865, p. 178.

<!-- ch21-p025 -->
The capitalist rightly knocks such pretensions on the head as gross errors about the nature of wage labor.[^21.19] He cries out against this usurping attempt to lay taxes on the advance of industry, and declares flatly that the productivity of labor does not concern the worker at all.[^21.20]

[^21.19]: In the “London Standard” of October 26, 1861, there is a report of proceedings by the firm of John Bright & Co. before the Rochdale magistrates “to prosecute for intimidation the agents of the Carpet Weavers Trades’ Union. Bright’s partners had introduced new machinery which would turn out 240 yards of carpet in the time and with the labour (!) previously required to produce 160 yards. The workmen had no claim whatever to share in the profits made by the investment of their employer’s capital in mechanical improvements. Accordingly, Messrs. Bright proposed to lower the rate of pay from 1½d. per yard to 1d., leaving the earnings of the men exactly the same as before for the same labour. But there was a nominal reduction, of which the operatives, it is asserted, had not fair warning beforehand.”

[^21.20]: “Trades’ Unions, in their desire to maintain wages, endeavor to share in the benefits of improved machinery.” (Quelle horreur! [How horrible!]) “... the demanding higher wages, because labour is abbreviated, is in other words the endeavor to establish a duty on mechanical improvements.” (“On Combination of Trades,” new ed., London, 1834, p. 42.)

## Chapter 22: National Differences of Wages

<!-- ch22-p001 -->
In the 17th chapter we dealt with the many combinations that may bring about a change in the magnitude of the value of labor-power. Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist. The value of labor-power is the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker (and to raise the next generation of workers) able to work; means of subsistence are the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live. We considered this magnitude either absolutely or relatively, that is, compared with surplus-value (the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it). On the other hand, the amount of the means of subsistence in which the price of labor is realized might in turn fluctuate independently of the changes in this price, or differently from them.[^22.1] As we have already said, simply translating the value of labor-power, or its price, as the case may be, into the outward form of wages turns all these laws into laws of the fluctuations of wages. (Wages are the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself.) What appears in these fluctuations of wages within a single country as a series of changing combinations may appear in different countries as differences between national wages that exist at the same time. So when we compare wages in different nations, we must take into account all the factors that determine changes in the amount of the value of labor-power: the price and the extent of the prime necessities of life, as they have developed naturally and historically; the cost of training the workers; the part played by the labor of women and children; the productivity of labor; and its extensive and intensive magnitude. Even the most superficial comparison requires first reducing the average day-wage for the same trades, in different countries, to a uniform working day (the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor). After the day-wages have been reduced to the same terms in this way, the time wage must again be translated into the piece wage. (Time wages are wages paid by the hour, day, or week; piece wages are wages paid per piece of work done.) For only the piece wage can be a measure both of the productivity of labor (how much a given amount of labor produces in a given time) and of the intensity of labor (how much labor is packed into a given time, that is, how hard and fast people must work).

[^22.1]: “It is not accurate to say that wages” (here he is dealing with wages as expressed in money) “are increased, because they purchase more of a cheaper article.” (David Buchanan in his edition of Adam Smith’s “Wealth of Nations,” 1814, Vol. 1, p. 417, note.)

<!-- ch22-p002 -->
In every country there is a certain average intensity of labor. Below it, the labor spent producing a commodity (a thing produced in order to be exchanged, that is, sold, not for the producer's own use) takes more than the socially necessary time, and so does not count as labor of normal quality. The socially necessary labor-time is the time needed to produce an article under the normal conditions of production of the day, with the average skill and intensity of labor. In a given country, only a degree of intensity above the national average affects the measuring of value by the mere length of the working time. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) This is not the case on the world market, whose component parts are the individual countries. The average intensity of labor changes from country to country: here it is greater, there less. These national averages form a scale whose unit of measure is the average unit of universal labor. So the more intense national labor, compared with the less intense, produces more value in the same time, and this value is expressed in more money.

<!-- ch22-p003 -->
But in its international application, the law of value is modified still further by the fact that on the world market the more productive national labor also counts as the more intense, so long as competition does not force the more productive nation to lower the selling price of its commodities to the level of their value.

<!-- ch22-p004 -->
The more capitalist production develops in a country, the more the national intensity and productivity of labor there rise above the international level.[^22.2] (Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger.) So the different quantities of commodities of the same kind that different countries produce in the same working time have unequal international values. These values are expressed in different prices, that is, in sums of money that vary according to the international values. (A price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity.) The relative value of money will therefore be lower in the nation with a more developed capitalist mode of production than in the nation with a less developed one. It follows, then, that nominal wages, the equivalent of labor-power expressed in money, will also be higher in the first nation than in the second. But this does not at all prove that the same holds for real wages, that is, for the means of subsistence placed at the disposal of the worker.

[^22.2]: We shall inquire elsewhere into the circumstances, connected with productivity, that may modify this law for individual branches of industry.

<!-- ch22-p005 -->
But even apart from these relative differences in the value of money in different countries, it will often be found that the daily or weekly, etc., wage in the first nation is higher than in the second, while the relative price of labor, that is, the price of labor compared both with surplus-value and with the value of the product, stands higher in the second than in the first.[^22.3]

[^22.3]: In his polemic against Adam Smith, James Anderson remarks: “It deserves, likewise, to be remarked, that although the apparent price of Labour is usually lower in poor countries, where the produce of the soil, and grain in general, is cheap; yet it is in fact for the most part really higher than in other countries. For it is not the wages that is given to the labourer per day that constitutes the real price of labour, although it is its apparent price.
