The real price is that which a certain quantity of work performed actually costs the employer; and considered in this light, labour is in almost all cases cheaper in rich countries than in those that are poorer, although the price of grain and other provisions is usually much lower in the last than in the first.... Labour estimated by the day is much lower in Scotland than in England.... Labour by the piece is generally cheaper in England.” (James Anderson, “Observations on the Means of Exciting a Spirit of National Industry,” etc., Edin. 1777, pp. 350, 351.) On the contrary, low wages in their turn make labor dear. “Labour being dearer in Ireland than it is in England ... because the wages are so much lower.” (N. 2079 in “Royal Commission on Railways, Minutes,” 1867.)

<!-- ch22-p006 -->
J. W. Cowell, a member of the Factory Commission of 1833, made a careful investigation of the spinning trade and came to the conclusion that

<!-- ch22-p007 -->
> “in England wages are virtually lower to the capitalist, though higher to the operative than on the Continent of Europe.”[^22.4]

[^22.4]: (Ure, op. cit., p. 314.)

<!-- ch22-p008 -->
The English Factory Inspector Alexander Redgrave, in his report of Oct. 31st, 1866, uses comparative statistics on continental states to prove that, in spite of lower wages and much longer working time, continental labor is dearer than English labor in proportion to the product. An English manager of a cotton factory in Oldenburg declares that the working time there lasted from 5:30 a.m. to 8 p.m., Saturdays included. He also declares that the workers there, when under English overseers, did not supply quite as much product in this time as the English did in 10 hours, and under German overseers much less. Wages are much lower than in England, in many cases 50%, but the number of workers in proportion to the machinery was much greater, in certain departments in the proportion of 5:3.

<!-- ch22-p009 -->
Mr. Redgrave gives very full details on the Russian cotton factories. The data were given to him by an English manager who had until recently been employed there. On this Russian soil, so fruitful of every infamy, the old horrors of the early days of English factories are in full swing. The managers are, of course, English, since the native Russian capitalist is of no use in the factory business. Despite all the overwork, continued day and night, and despite the most shameful underpayment of the workers, Russian manufacture manages to vegetate only because foreign competition is prohibited.

<!-- ch22-p010 -->
In conclusion, I give a comparative table of Mr. Redgrave's on the average number of spindles per factory and per spinner in the different countries of Europe. He himself remarks that he collected these figures a few years ago, and that since then the size of the factories and the number of spindles per worker in England have increased. He assumes, however, that the continental countries mentioned have made roughly equal progress, so that the figures given would still have their value for purposes of comparison.

<!-- ch22-p011 -->
```text
AVERAGE NUMBER OF SPINDLES PER FACTORY
England  , average of spindles per factory     12,600
France  , average of spindles per factory      1,500
Prussia,  average of spindles per factory      1,500
Belgium  , average of spindles per factory     4,000
Saxony  , average of spindles per factory      4,500
Austria,  average of spindles per factory      7,000
Switzerland  , average of spindles per factory 8,000
```

<!-- ch22-p012 -->
**AVERAGE NUMBER OF PERSONS EMPLOYED TO SPINDLES**

<!-- ch22-p013 -->
```text
France                                         one person to 14 spindles
Russia                                         one person to 28 spindles
Prussia                                        one person to 37 spindles
Bavaria                                        one person to 46 spindles
Austria                                        one person to 49 spindles
Belgium                                        one person to 50 spindles
Saxony                                         one person to 50 spindles
Switzerland                                    one person to 55 spindles
Smaller States of Germany                      one person to 55 spindles
Great Britain                                  one person to 74 spindles
```

<!-- ch22-p014 -->
“This comparison,” says Mr. Redgrave, “is yet more unfavorable to Great Britain, inasmuch as there is so large a number of factories in which weaving by power is carried on in conjunction with spinning” (while in the table the weavers are not subtracted), “and the factories abroad are chiefly spinning factories; if it were possible to compare like with like, strictly, I could find many cotton spinning factories in my district in which mules containing 2,200 spindles are minded [tended] by one man (the minder) and two assistants only, turning off [producing] daily 220 lbs. of yarn, measuring 400 miles in length.”[^22.5]

[^22.5]: (“Reports of Insp. of Fact.,” 31st Oct., 1866, pp. 31-37, passim.)

<!-- ch22-p015 -->
It is well known that English companies have undertaken the building of railways in Eastern Europe as well as in Asia, and that in building them they have employed a certain number of English workers side by side with the native workers. Practical necessity has thus forced them to take into account the national difference in the intensity of labor, but this has brought them no loss. Their experience shows that even if the level of wages corresponds more or less to the average intensity of labor, the relative price of labor generally moves in the opposite direction.

<!-- ch22-p016 -->
In an “Essay on the Rate of Wages,”[^22.6] one of his first economic writings, H. Carey tries to prove that the wages of the different nations are directly proportional to the degree of productivity of the national working days. His aim is to draw from this international relation the conclusion that wages everywhere rise and fall in proportion to the productivity of labor. Our whole analysis of the production of surplus-value shows that this conclusion is absurd. It would be absurd even if Carey himself had proved his premises, instead of shuffling a confused mass of statistical material back and forth in his usual uncritical and superficial fashion. The best of it is that he does not claim that things actually are as they ought to be according to his theory. For, he says, State intervention has falsified the natural economic relations. Therefore, according to him, the different national wages must be reckoned as if the part of each that goes to the State in the form of taxes came to the worker himself. Ought not Mr. Carey to consider further whether those “State expenses” are not the “natural” fruits of capitalist development? The reasoning is quite worthy of the man who first declared the relations of capitalist production to be eternal laws of nature and reason, whose free, harmonious working is disturbed only by the intervention of the State, and who did so in order to discover afterwards that the diabolical influence of England on the world market (an influence which, it appears, does not spring from the natural laws of capitalist production) makes State intervention necessary, that is, the protection of those laws of nature and reason by the State, otherwise known as the System of Protection (protective tariffs). He discovered further that the theorems of Ricardo and others, in which existing social antagonisms and contradictions are formulated, are not the ideal product (the product in the realm of ideas) of the real economic movement. On the contrary, he discovered that the real antagonisms of capitalist production in England and elsewhere are the result of the theories of Ricardo and others! Finally he discovered that it is, in the last resort, trade that destroys the inborn beauties and harmonies of the capitalist mode of production. One step further and he will, perhaps, discover that the one evil in capitalist production is capital itself. Only a man with such an atrocious lack of the critical faculty and such fake learning deserved, in spite of his Protectionist heresy, to become the secret source of the harmonious wisdom of a Bastiat, and of all the other Free-trade optimists of today.

[^22.6]: “Essay on the Rate of Wages, with an Examination of the Causes of the Differences in the Condition of the Labouring Population throughout the World,” Philadelphia, 1835.

# Part 7: The Accumulation of Capital

<!-- pt7-p001 -->
The first step taken by the amount of value that is going to function as capital is the conversion of a sum of money into means of production and labor-power. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time. Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger. Means of production are the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things. Labor-power is a person’s capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist.) This conversion takes place in the market, within the sphere of circulation (the exchange of commodities through money: selling and buying). The second step, the process of production, is complete as soon as the means of production have been turned into commodities (things produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer’s own use) whose value is greater than that of their component parts. So their value contains the capital originally advanced, plus a surplus-value (the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it). These commodities must then be thrown into circulation. They must be sold and their value realized in money, and this money must be turned into capital afresh, and so on, over and over again. This circular movement, in which the same phases are continually gone through one after another, forms the circulation of capital.

<!-- pt7-p002 -->
The first condition of accumulation (the accumulation of capital: turning surplus-value back into capital, so that capital grows) is that the capitalist must have managed to sell his commodities, and to turn the greater part of the money so received back into capital. In the following pages we shall assume that capital circulates in its normal way. The detailed analysis of the process will be found in Book II.

<!-- pt7-p003 -->
The capitalist who produces surplus-value, that is, who extracts unpaid labor directly from the workers and fixes it in commodities, is indeed the first to appropriate this surplus-value, but by no means its final owner. He has to share it with capitalists, with landowners, etc., who perform other functions in the complex whole of social production. Surplus-value, therefore, splits up into various parts. Its fragments fall to various categories of persons and take various forms, independent of one another, such as profit, interest, merchants’ profit, rent, etc. Only in Book III. can we take up these modified forms of surplus-value.

<!-- pt7-p004 -->
On the one hand, then, we assume that the capitalist sells the commodities he has produced at their value. We do not concern ourselves either with the new forms that capital takes on while in the sphere of circulation, or with the concrete conditions of reproduction hidden under these forms. On the other hand, we treat the capitalist producer as the owner of the entire surplus-value, or, better perhaps, as the representative of all who share the booty with him. So we first of all consider accumulation from an abstract point of view, that is, as a mere phase in the actual process of production.

<!-- pt7-p005 -->
To the extent that accumulation takes place, the capitalist must have succeeded in selling his commodities and in turning the money from the sale back into capital. Moreover, the breaking-up of surplus-value into fragments changes neither its nature nor the conditions under which it becomes an element of accumulation. Whatever share of surplus-value the industrial capitalist keeps for himself or gives up to others, he is the one who appropriates it in the first instance. So we assume no more than what actually takes place. On the other hand, the simple fundamental form of the process of accumulation is obscured by the incidental process of circulation that brings it about, and by the splitting-up of surplus-value. So an exact analysis of the process demands that we disregard, for a time, all phenomena that hide the play of its inner mechanism.

## Chapter 23: Simple Reproduction

<!-- ch23-p001 -->
Whatever the form of the process of production in a society, it must be a continuous process; it must keep going periodically through the same phases. A society can no more stop producing than it can stop consuming. So when it is viewed as a connected whole, and as flowing on with constant renewal, every social process of production is at the same time a process of reproduction.

<!-- ch23-p002 -->
The conditions of production are also those of reproduction. No society can go on producing, in other words no society can reproduce, unless it constantly turns a part of its products back into means of production, or elements of new products. All other circumstances remaining the same, the only way it can reproduce its wealth and keep it at one level is by replacing the means of production (that is, the instruments of labor, the raw material, and the auxiliary substances used up in the course of the year) with an equal quantity of articles of the same kind. These must be separated from the mass of the year’s products and thrown afresh into the process of production. So a definite portion of each year’s product belongs to the domain of production. This portion is destined for productive consumption from the very first, and for the most part it exists in the shape of articles totally unfit for individual consumption.

<!-- ch23-p003 -->
If production is capitalist in form, so too will reproduction be. Just as in capitalist production the labor process (the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things) figures only as a means toward the self-expansion of capital, so in capitalist reproduction it figures only as a means of reproducing the value advanced as capital, that is, as self-expanding value. It is only because his money constantly functions as capital that a man wears the economic guise of a capitalist. If, for instance, a sum of £100 has been turned into capital this year and has produced a surplus-value of £20, it must go on repeating the same operation next year and in the years after. As a periodic increase of the capital advanced, or periodic fruit of capital in process, surplus-value takes on the form of a revenue flowing out of capital.[^23.1]

[^23.1]: “Mais ces riches, qui consomment les produits du travail des autres, ne peuvent les obtenir que par des échanges [purchases of commodities]. S’ils donnent cependant leur richesse acquise et accumulée en retour contre ces produits nouveaux qui sont l’objet de leur fantaisie, ils semblent exposés à épuiser bientôt leur fonds de réserve; ils ne travaillent point, avons-nous dit, et ils ne peuvent même travailler; on croirait donc que chaque jour doit voir diminuer leurs vieilles richesses, et que lorsqu’il ne leur en restera plus, rien ne sera offert en échange aux ouvriers qui travaillent exclusivement pour eux.... Mais dans l’ordre social, la richesse a acquis la propriété de se reproduire par le travail d’autrui, et sans que son propriétaire y concoure. La richesse, comme le travail, et par le travail, donne un fruit annuel qui peut être détruit chaque année sans que le riche en devienne plus pauvre. Ce fruit est le *revenu* qui naît du *capital*.” [But these rich people, who consume the products of the labor of others, can obtain them only by exchanges. Yet if they give their acquired and accumulated wealth in return for these new products, which are the object of their fancy, they seem exposed to using up their reserve fund soon. They do not work at all, we have said, and they cannot even work. So one would think that each day must see their old wealth shrink, and that when none of it is left to them, nothing will be offered in exchange to the workers who work exclusively for them.... But in the social order, wealth has acquired the property of reproducing itself through the labor of others, and without its owner taking part. Wealth, like labor, and through labor, yields a yearly fruit that can be destroyed every year without the rich man becoming any poorer. This fruit is the *revenue* that arises from *capital*.] (Sismondi: “Nouv. Princ. d’Econ. Pol.” Paris, 1819, t. I, pp. 81-82.)

<!-- ch23-p004 -->
If this revenue serves the capitalist only as a fund for his consumption, and is spent as periodically as it is gained, then, other things being equal, simple reproduction will take place. And although this reproduction is a mere repetition of the process of production on the old scale, this mere repetition, or continuity, still gives the process a new character, or rather, makes some apparent characteristics disappear that it had as an isolated, discontinuous process.

<!-- ch23-p005 -->
The purchase of labor-power for a fixed period is the prelude to the process of production. This prelude is constantly repeated when the agreed term comes to an end, when a definite period of production, such as a week or a month, has passed. But the worker is not paid until after he has spent his labor-power and realized in commodities not only its value, but surplus-value. So he has produced not only surplus-value, which for the present we regard as a fund to meet the private consumption of the capitalist. He has also produced the fund out of which he himself is paid, the variable capital, before it flows back to him in the shape of wages (the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself). (Variable capital is the part of capital spent on labor-power. It reproduces its own value and also produces surplus-value, so its size varies.) And he stays employed only as long as he keeps reproducing this fund. Hence that formula of the economists, mentioned in Chapter XVIII, which represents wages as a share in the product itself.[^23.2] What flows back to the worker in the shape of wages is a portion of the product that he continuously reproduces. The capitalist, it is true, pays him in money, but this money is merely the changed form of the product of his labor. While he is turning a portion of the means of production into products, a portion of his earlier product is being turned into money. It is his labor of last week, or of last year, that pays for his labor-power this week or this year. The illusion created by money stepping in between vanishes at once if, instead of taking a single capitalist and a single worker, we take the class of capitalists and the class of workers as a whole. The capitalist class constantly gives the working class order-notes, in the form of money, on a portion of the commodities that the workers produced and the capitalists appropriated. The workers just as constantly give these order-notes back to the capitalist class, and in this way get their share of their own product. The transaction is veiled by the commodity form of the product and the money form of the commodity. (The money form is the form of value in which one commodity, gold, has become the universal equivalent.)

[^23.2]: “Wages as well as profits are to be considered, each of them, as really a portion of the finished product.” (Ramsay, cited above, p. 142.) “The share of the product which comes to the labourer in the form of wages.” (J. Mill, “Eléments, &c.” Translated by Parissot. Paris, 1823, p. 34.)

<!-- ch23-p006 -->
So variable capital is only a particular historical form of appearance of the fund for providing the necessaries of life, or the labor fund, which the worker needs to maintain himself and his family, and which, whatever the system of social production, he must himself produce and reproduce. If the labor fund constantly flows to him in the form of money that pays for his labor, it is because the product he has created constantly moves away from him in the form of capital. But all this does not change the fact that it is the worker’s own labor, realized in a product, that the capitalist advances to him.[^23.3] Let us take a peasant who is bound to do compulsory service for his lord. He works on his own land, with his own means of production, for, say, 3 days a week. On the 3 other days he does forced work on the lord’s estate. He constantly reproduces his own labor fund, which in his case never takes the form of a money payment for his labor, advanced by another person. But in return, his unpaid forced labor for the lord, for its part, never takes on the character of voluntary paid labor. If one fine morning the lord takes for himself the land, the cattle, the seed, in a word, the means of production of this peasant, the peasant will from then on be obliged to sell his labor-power to the lord. Other things being equal, he will labor 6 days a week as before, 3 for himself and 3 for his lord, who from then on becomes a wage-paying capitalist. As before, he will use up the means of production as means of production and transfer their value to the product. As before, a definite portion of the product will go to reproduction. But from the moment the forced labor is changed into wage labor, from that moment the labor fund, which the peasant himself goes on producing and reproducing as before, takes the form of a capital advanced by the lord in the form of wages. The bourgeois economist (bourgeois: belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it), whose narrow mind cannot separate the form of appearance from the thing that appears, shuts his eyes to the fact that even nowadays the labor fund crops up in the form of capital only here and there on the face of the earth.[^23.4]

[^23.3]: “When capital is employed in advancing to the workman his wages, it adds nothing to the funds for the maintenance of labour.” (Cazenove in note to his edition of Malthus’ “Definitions in Pol. Econ.” London, 1853, p. 22.)

[^23.4]: “The wages of labour are advanced by capitalists in the case of less than one fourth of the labourers of the earth.” (Rich. Jones: “Textbook of Lectures on the Pol. Econ. of Nations.” Hertford, 1852, p. 36.)

<!-- ch23-p007 -->
Variable capital, it is true, loses its character of a value advanced out of the capitalist’s funds[^23.5] only when we view the process of capitalist production in the flow of its constant renewal. But that process must have had a beginning of some kind. So from our present standpoint it seems likely that the capitalist, once upon a time, came into possession of money through some accumulation that took place independently of the unpaid labor of others, and that this, therefore, was how he was able to go to the market as a buyer of labor-power. However this may be, the mere continuity of the process, simple reproduction, brings about some other wonderful changes, which affect not only the variable capital but the total capital.

[^23.5]: “Though the manufacturer” (that is, the worker) “has his wages advanced to him by his master, he in reality costs him no expense, the value of these wages being generally reserved, together with a profit, in the improved value of the subject [the material worked on] upon which his labour is bestowed.” (A. Smith, cited above, Book II. ch. III, p. 311.)

<!-- ch23-p008 -->
If a capital of £1,000 produces a surplus-value of £200 a year, and if this surplus-value is consumed every year, then clearly at the end of 5 years the surplus-value consumed will amount to 5 × £200, or the £1,000 originally advanced. If only a part, say one half, were consumed, the same result would follow at the end of 10 years, since 10 × £100= £1,000. General Rule: The value of the capital advanced, divided by the surplus-value consumed each year, gives the number of years, or reproduction periods, at the end of which the capital originally advanced has been consumed by the capitalist and has disappeared. The capitalist thinks that he is consuming the product of the unpaid labor of others, that is, the surplus-value, and keeping his original capital intact; but what he thinks cannot change the facts. After a certain number of years, the capital value he then owns is equal to the sum total of the surplus-value he appropriated during those years, and the total value he has consumed is equal to that of his original capital. It is true that he has in hand a capital whose amount has not changed, and part of which, namely the buildings, machinery, etc., was already there when the work of his business began. But what we are dealing with here is not the material elements of that capital, but its value. When a person runs through all his property by taking on debts equal to the value of that property, clearly his property represents nothing but the sum total of his debts. And so it is with the capitalist. When he has consumed the equivalent of his original capital, the value of his present capital represents nothing but the total amount of the surplus-value he appropriated without payment. Not a single atom of the value of his old capital still exists.

<!-- ch23-p009 -->
Apart, then, from all accumulation, the mere continuity of the process of production, in other words simple reproduction, sooner or later and of necessity turns every capital into accumulated capital, or capitalized surplus-value. Even if that capital was originally acquired by the personal labor of the one who employs it, sooner or later it becomes value appropriated without an equivalent: the unpaid labor of others, materialized either in money or in some other object. We saw in Chapters IV.-VI. that turning money into capital requires something more than the production and circulation of commodities. We saw that on the one side the possessor of value or money, and on the other the possessor of the value-creating substance; on the one side the possessor of the means of production and subsistence, and on the other the possessor of nothing but labor-power, must face each other as buyer and seller. (Means of subsistence are the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live.) So the separation of labor from its product, of subjective labor-power from the objective conditions of labor, was the real foundation in fact, and the starting-point, of capitalist production.

<!-- ch23-p010 -->
But what at first was only a starting-point becomes, through the mere continuity of the process, through simple reproduction, the distinctive result of capitalist production, constantly renewed and made permanent. On the one hand, the process of production constantly turns material wealth into capital, into means of creating more wealth and means of enjoyment for the capitalist. On the other hand, the worker leaves the process as he entered it: a source of wealth, but without any means of making that wealth his own. Since his own labor, before he enters the process, has already been alienated from him by the sale of his labor-power, and has been appropriated by the capitalist and incorporated into capital, it must, during the process, be realized in a product that does not belong to him. Since the process of production is also the process by which the capitalist consumes labor-power, the worker’s product is constantly turned not only into commodities but into capital: into value that sucks up the value-creating power, into means of subsistence that buy the person of the worker, into means of production that command the producers.[^23.6] So the worker constantly produces material, objective wealth, but in the form of capital, of an alien power that dominates and exploits him. And the capitalist just as constantly produces labor-power, but in the form of a subjective source of wealth, separated from the objects in which and through which alone it can be realized. In short, he produces the worker, but as a wage worker.[^23.7] This constant reproduction, this perpetuation of the worker, is the indispensable condition of capitalist production.

[^23.6]: “This is a remarkably peculiar property of productive labour. Whatever is productively consumed is capital and it becomes capital by consumption.” (James Mill, cited above, p. 242.) James Mill, however, never got onto the track of this “remarkably peculiar property.”

[^23.7]: “It is true indeed, that the first introducing a manufacture employs many poor, but they cease not to be so, and the continuance of it makes many.” (“Reasons for a Limited Exportation of Wool.” London, 1677, p. 19.) “The farmer now absurdly asserts, that he keeps the poor. They are indeed kept in misery.” (“Reasons for the Late Increase of the Poor Rates: or a Comparative View of the Prices of Labour and Provisions.” London, 1777, p. 31.)

<!-- ch23-p011 -->
The worker consumes in two ways. While producing, he consumes the means of production by his labor and turns them into products with a higher value than that of the capital advanced. This is his productive consumption. It is at the same time the consumption of his labor-power by the capitalist who bought it. On the other hand, the worker turns the money paid to him for his labor-power into means of subsistence: this is his individual consumption. So the worker’s productive consumption and his individual consumption are totally distinct. In the first, he acts as the motive power of capital and belongs to the capitalist. In the second, he belongs to himself and performs his necessary vital functions outside the process of production. The result of the one is that the capitalist lives; of the other, that the worker lives.

<!-- ch23-p012 -->
When we dealt with the working day (the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor), we saw that the worker is often forced to make his individual consumption a mere incident of production. In such a case, he supplies himself with necessaries in order to maintain his labor-power, just as coal and water are supplied to the steam-engine and oil to the wheel. His means of consumption are then merely the means of consumption required by a means of production. His individual consumption is directly productive consumption. This, however, appears to be an abuse that does not belong to the essence of capitalist production.[^23.8]

[^23.8]: Rossi would not protest so loudly against this, if he had really seen into the secret of “productive consumption.”

<!-- ch23-p013 -->
The matter looks quite different when we consider, not the single capitalist and the single worker, but the capitalist class and the working class; not an isolated process of production, but capitalist production in full swing and on its actual social scale. By turning part of his capital into labor-power, the capitalist increases the value of his entire capital. He kills two birds with one stone. He profits not only by what he receives from the worker, but also by what he gives to him. The capital given in exchange for labor-power is turned into necessaries. By consuming these, the existing workers reproduce their muscles, nerves, bones, and brains, and new workers are begotten. Within the limits of what is strictly necessary, therefore, the individual consumption of the working class turns the means of subsistence, which capital gave in exchange for labor-power, back into fresh labor-power that capital can exploit. It is the production and reproduction of that means of production so indispensable to the capitalist: the worker himself. So the individual consumption of the worker, whether it goes on inside the workshop or outside it, whether it is part of the process of production or not, is a factor in the production and reproduction of capital. In the same way, cleaning machinery is such a factor, whether it is done while the machinery is running or while it is standing still. The fact that the worker consumes his means of subsistence for his own purposes, and not to please the capitalist, makes no difference to the matter. A beast of burden's eating is no less a necessary factor in the process of production because the beast enjoys what it eats. The maintenance and reproduction of the working class is, and must always remain, a necessary condition for the reproduction of capital. But the capitalist may safely leave this to the worker's instincts of self-preservation and of propagation. All the capitalist cares about is to cut the worker's individual consumption down, as far as possible, to what is strictly necessary. He is far from imitating those brutal South Americans who force their workers to eat the more nourishing kind of food rather than the less nourishing kind.[^23.9]

[^23.9]: “The labourers in the mines of S. America, whose daily task (the heaviest perhaps in the world) consists in bringing to the surface on their shoulders a load of metal weighing from 180 to 200 pounds, from a depth of 450 feet, live on bread and beans only; they themselves would prefer the bread alone for food, but their masters, who have found out that the men cannot work so hard on bread, treat them like horses, and compel them to eat beans; beans, however, are relatively much richer in bone-earth (phosphate of lime) than is bread.” (Liebig, cited above, vol. 1., p. 194, note.)

<!-- ch23-p014 -->
Hence both the capitalist and his ideological representative, the political economist, count as productive only that part of the worker's individual consumption which is needed to perpetuate the class. That part must take place so that the capitalist may have labor-power to consume. Whatever the worker consumes for his own pleasure beyond that part is, in their view, unproductive consumption.[^23.10] If the accumulation of capital were to cause a rise of wages and an increase in the worker's consumption, without any increase in capital's consumption of labor-power, the additional capital would be consumed unproductively.[^23.11] In reality, the individual consumption of the worker is unproductive as far as he himself is concerned, for it reproduces nothing but the needy individual. It is productive for the capitalist and for the State, since it produces the power that creates their wealth.[^23.12]

[^23.10]: James Mill, cited above, p. 238

[^23.11]: “If the price of labour should rise so high that, notwithstanding the increase of capital, no more could be employed, I should say that such increase of capital would be still unproductively consumed.” (Ricardo, cited above, p. 163.)

[^23.12]: “The only productive consumption, properly so called, is the consumption or destruction of wealth” (he means the means of production) “by capitalists with a view to reproduction.... The workman ... is a productive consumer to the person who employs him, and to the State, but not, strictly speaking, to himself.” (Malthus’ “Definitions, &c.,” p. 30.)

<!-- ch23-p015 -->
From a social point of view, therefore, the working class, even when it is not directly engaged in the labor process, is just as much an appendage of capital as the ordinary instruments of labor are. Even its individual consumption is, within certain limits, a mere factor in the process of production. That process, however, takes good care that these self-conscious instruments do not leave it in the lurch. As fast as they make their product, it removes it from their pole to the opposite pole, that of capital. On the one hand, individual consumption provides the means for their maintenance and reproduction. On the other hand, by using up the necessaries of life, it makes sure that the worker keeps reappearing in the labor market. The Roman slave was held by chains; the wage worker is bound to his owner by invisible threads. The appearance of independence is kept up by a constant change of employers, and by the *fictio juris* [legal fiction] of a contract.

<!-- ch23-p016 -->
In earlier times, capital turned to legislation whenever necessary, to enforce its property rights over the free worker. For instance, down to 1815, mechanics employed in machine-making were forbidden to emigrate from England, under heavy pains and penalties.

<!-- ch23-p017 -->
The reproduction of the working class brings with it the accumulation of skill, which is handed down from one generation to the next.[^23.13] To what extent the capitalist counts the existence of such a skilled class among the factors of production that belong to him by right, and to what extent he actually regards it as the reality of his variable capital, becomes clear as soon as a crisis threatens him with its loss. As a result of the civil war in the United States and the cotton famine that came with it, most of the cotton factory workers in Lancashire were, as is well known, thrown out of work. Both from the working class itself and from other ranks of society, there arose a cry for State aid, or for voluntary national collections, so that the “superfluous” hands could emigrate to the colonies or to the United States. Thereupon *The Times* published, on the 24th March, 1863, a letter from Edmund Potter, a former president of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce. In the House of Commons this letter was rightly called the manufacturers' manifesto.[^23.14] We pick out here a few characteristic passages, in which the property rights of capital over labor-power are shamelessly asserted.

[^23.13]: “The only thing, of which one can say, that it is stored up and prepared beforehand, is the skill of the labourer.... The accumulation and storage of skilled labour, that most important operation, is, as regards the great mass of labourers, accomplished without any capital whatever.” (Th. Hodgskin: “Labour Defended, &c.,” p. 13.)

[^23.14]: “That letter might be looked upon as the manifesto of the manufacturers.” (Ferrand: “Motion on the Cotton Famine.” H.o.C., 27th April, 1863.)

<!-- ch23-p018 -->
> “He” (the man out of work) “may be told the supply of cotton-workers is too large ... and ... must ... in fact be reduced by a third, perhaps, and that then there will be a healthy demand for the remaining two-thirds.... Public opinion... urges emigration.... The master cannot willingly see his labour supply being removed; he may think, and perhaps justly, that it is both wrong and unsound.... But if the public funds are to be devoted to assist emigration, he has a right to be heard, and perhaps to protest.”

<!-- ch23-p019 -->
Mr. Potter then shows how useful the cotton trade is; how the “trade has undoubtedly drawn the surplus-population [the workers made ‘surplus’ to capital's needs for the time being] from Ireland and from the agricultural districts”; how immense its extent is; how in the year 1860 it yielded 5/13 ths of the total English exports; and how, after a few years, it will expand again, through the widening of the market, especially the Indian market, and by calling forth a plentiful supply of cotton at 6d. per lb. He then continues:

<!-- ch23-p020 -->
> “Some time ..., one, two, or three years, it may be, will produce the quantity.... The question I would put then is this – Is the trade worth retaining? Is it worth while to keep the machinery (he means the living labor machines) in order, and is it not the greatest folly to think of parting with that? I think it is. I allow that the workers are not a property, not the property of Lancashire and the masters; but they are the strength of both; they are the mental and trained power which cannot be replaced for a generation; the mere machinery which they work might much of it be beneficially replaced, nay improved, in a twelvemonth.[^23.15] Encourage or allow (!) the working-power to emigrate, and what of the capitalist?... Take away the cream of the workers, and fixed capital will depreciate in a great degree, and the floating will not subject itself to a struggle with the short supply of inferior labour.... We are told the workers wish it” (emigration). “Very natural it is that they should do so.... Reduce, compress the cotton trade by taking away its working power and reducing their wages expenditure, say one-fifth, or five millions, and what then would happen to the class above, the small shopkeepers; and what of the rents, the cottage rents.... Trace out the effects upwards to the small farmer, the better householder, and ... the landowner, and say if there could be any suggestion more suicidal to all classes of the country than by enfeebling a nation by exporting the best of its manufacturing population, and destroying the value of some of its most productive capital and enrichment .... I advise a loan (of five or six millions sterling), ... extending it may be over two or three years, administered by special commissioners added to the Boards of Guardians in the cotton districts, under special legislative regulations, enforcing some occupation or labour, as a means of keeping up at least the moral standard of the recipients of the loan... can anything be worse for landowners or masters than parting with the best of the workers, and demoralising and disappointing the rest by an extended depletive emigration, a depletion of capital and value in an entire province?”

[^23.15]: Let us not forget that this same capital sings quite a different song under ordinary circumstances, when the question is one of cutting wages. Then the employers cry out with one voice: “The factory operatives should keep in wholesome remembrance the fact that theirs is really a low species of skilled labour, and that there is none which is more easily acquired, or of its quality more amply remunerated, or which, by a short training of the least expert, can be more quickly, as well as abundantly, acquired ... The master’s machinery” (which, we now learn, can be replaced with advantage in 12 months) “really plays a far more important part in the business of production than the labour and skill of the operative” (who now cannot be replaced in under 30 years), “which six months’ education can reach, and a common labourer can learn.” (See earlier, p. 423.)

<!-- ch23-p021 -->
Potter, the chosen mouthpiece of the manufacturers, distinguishes two sorts of “machinery.” Each belongs to the capitalist. One stands in his factory; the other is housed outside the factory at night and on Sundays, in cottages. The one is lifeless, the other living. The lifeless machinery not only wears out and loses value from day to day, but a great part of it becomes outdated so quickly, through constant technical progress, that it can be replaced with advantage by new machinery after a few months. The living machinery, on the contrary, gets better the longer it lasts, and the more the skill handed down from one generation to the next accumulates. *The Times* answered the cotton lord as follows:

<!-- ch23-p022 -->
> “Mr. Edmund Potter is so impressed with the exceptional and supreme importance of the cotton masters that, in order to preserve this class and perpetuate their profession, he would keep half a million of the labouring class confined in a great moral workhouse against their will. ‘Is the trade worth retaining?’ asks Mr. Potter. ‘Certainly by all honest means it is,’ we answer. ‘Is it worth while keeping the machinery in order?’ again asks Mr. Potter. Here we hesitate. By the ‘machinery’ Mr. Potter means the human machinery, for he goes on to protest that he does not mean to use them as an absolute property. We must confess that we do not think it ‘worth while,’ or even possible, to keep the human machinery in order – that is to shut it up and keep it oiled till it is wanted. Human machinery will rust under inaction, oil and rub it as you may. Moreover, the human machinery will, as we have just seen, get the steam up of its own accord, and burst or run amuck in our great towns. It might, as Mr. Potter says, require some time to reproduce the workers, but, having machinists and capitalists at hand, we could always find thrifty, hard, industrious men wherewith to improvise more master manufacturers than we can ever want. Mr. Potter talks of the trade reviving ‘in one, two, or three years,’ and he asks us not ‘to encourage or allow (!) the working power to emigrate.’[^23.16] He says that it is very natural the workers should wish to emigrate; but he thinks that in spite of their desire, the nation ought to keep this half million of workers with their 700,000 dependents, shut up in the cotton districts; and as a necessary consequence, he must of course think that the nation ought to keep down their discontent by force, and sustain them by alms – and upon the chance that the cotton masters may some day want them.... The time is come when the great public opinion of these islands must operate to save this ‘working power’ from those who would deal with it as they would deal with iron, and coal, and cotton.”

[^23.16]: Parliament did not vote a single farthing in aid of emigration. It simply passed some Acts that empowered the municipal corporations to keep the factory workers in a half-starved state, that is, to exploit them at less than the normal wages. On the other hand, when the cattle disease broke out 3 years later, Parliament broke wildly with its customs and voted, straight off, millions to compensate the millionaire landlords, whose farmers in any case came off without loss, thanks to the rise in the price of meat. The bull-like bellowing of the landed proprietors at the opening of Parliament in 1866 showed that a man can worship the cow Sabala without being a Hindu, and can turn himself into an ox without being a Jupiter.

<!-- ch23-p023 -->
*The Times'* article was merely an exercise in wit. In fact, the “great public opinion” shared Mr. Potter's opinion that the factory workers are part of the movable fittings of a factory. Their emigration was prevented. They were locked up in that “moral workhouse,” the cotton districts, and they form, as before, “the strength” of the cotton manufacturers of Lancashire.

<!-- ch23-p024 -->
Capitalist production, therefore, reproduces, by itself, the separation between labor-power and the means of labor. In doing so, it reproduces and perpetuates the condition for exploiting the worker. It constantly forces him to sell his labor-power in order to live, and it enables the capitalist to buy labor-power in order to enrich himself.[^23.17] It is no longer a mere accident that capitalist and worker face each other in the market as buyer and seller. It is the process itself that constantly hurls the worker back onto the market as a seller of his labor-power, and that constantly turns his own product into a means by which another man can buy him. In reality, the worker belongs to capital before he has sold himself to capital. His economic bondage[^23.18] is both brought about and concealed by the periodic sale of himself, by his change of masters, and by the ups and downs in the market price of labor-power.[^23.19]

[^23.17]: “L’ouvrier demandait de la subsistence pour vivre, le chef demandait du travail pour gagner.” [The worker asked for the means of subsistence in order to live; the boss asked for labor in order to make a profit] (Sismondi, cited above, p. 91.)

[^23.18]: A crudely clumsy form of this bondage exists in the county of Durham. This is one of the few counties where circumstances do not guarantee the farmer undisputed property rights over the farm laborer. The mining industry gives the laborer some choice. In this county, unlike elsewhere, the farmer rents only farms that have laborers' cottages on them. The rent of the cottage is part of the wages. These cottages are known as “hinds’ houses.” They are let to the laborers in return for certain feudal services, under a contract called “bondage.” Among other things, this contract binds the laborer, during the time he is employed elsewhere, to leave someone, say his daughter, etc., to take his place. The laborer himself is called a “bondsman.” This relationship also shows, from quite a new angle, how the worker's individual consumption becomes consumption on behalf of capital ‒ or productive consumption: “It is curious to observe that the very dung of the hind and bondsman is the perquisite [perk] of the calculating lord ... and the lord will allow no privy [outdoor toilet] but his own to exist in the neighbourhood, and will rather give a bit of manure here and there for a garden than bate [give up] any part of his seigneurial right.” (“Public Health, Report VII., 1864,” p. 188.)

[^23.19]: Let us not forget that, in the case of the labor of children, etc., even the formality of a voluntary sale disappears.

<!-- ch23-p025 -->
Capitalist production, therefore, seen as a continuous connected process, as a process of reproduction, produces not only commodities, not only surplus-value. It also produces and reproduces the capitalist relation: on the one side the capitalist, on the other the wage worker.[^23.20]

[^23.20]: “Capital pre-supposes wage labour, and wage labour pre-supposes capital. One is a necessary condition to the existence of the other; they mutually call each other into existence. Does an operative in a cotton-factory produce nothing but cotton goods? No, he produces capital. He produces values that give fresh command over his labour, and that, by means of such command, create fresh values.” (Karl Marx: “Lohnarbeit und Kapital,” in the *Neue Rheinische Zeitung*: No. 266, 7th April, 1849.) The articles published under that title in the *N. Rh. Z.* are parts of some lectures I gave on that subject in 1847, in the German “Arbeiter-Verein” [Workers' Association] at Brussels. Their publication was interrupted by the February revolution.

## Chapter 24: Conversion of Surplus-Value into Capital

### Section 1: Capitalist Production on a Progressively Increasing Scale. Transition of the Laws of Property that Characterize Production of Commodities into Laws of Capitalist Appropriation

<!-- ch24-p001 -->
So far we have investigated how surplus-value comes out of capital; now we have to see how capital arises out of surplus-value. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it. Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger.) Using surplus-value as capital, turning it back into capital, is called accumulation of capital.[^24.1]

[^24.1]: “Accumulation of capital; the employment of a portion of revenue as capital.” (Malthus: “Definitions, &c.,” ed. Cazenove, p. 11.) “Conversion of revenue into capital,” (Malthus: “Princ. of Pol. Econ “ 2nd Ed., London. 1836, p. 320.)

<!-- ch24-p002 -->
First let us look at this transaction from the standpoint of the individual capitalist. Suppose a spinner has advanced a capital of £10,000. Four-fifths of it (£8,000) are laid out in cotton, machinery, etc., and one-fifth (£2,000) in wages (the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself). Let him produce 240,000 lbs. of yarn a year, with a value of £2,000. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) The rate of surplus-value is 100%. (The rate of surplus-value is the ratio of surplus-value to variable capital, s/v, that is, of surplus labor to necessary labor; it is also called the degree of exploitation of labor-power.) At this rate, the surplus-value lies in the surplus product, or net product, of 40,000 lbs. of yarn. This is one-sixth of the gross product, with a value of £2,000, which will be realized by a sale. £2,000 is £2,000. In this sum of money we can neither see nor smell a trace of surplus-value. When we know that a given value is surplus-value, we know how its owner came by it; but that does not change the nature either of value or of money.

<!-- ch24-p003 -->
To turn this additional sum of £2,000 into capital, the master-spinner will, all circumstances remaining as before, advance four-fifths of it (£1,600) to buy cotton, etc., and one-fifth (£400) to buy additional spinners. These spinners will find in the market the necessities of life whose value the master has advanced to them.

<!-- ch24-p004 -->
Then the new capital of £2,000 functions in the spinning mill, and in its turn brings in a surplus-value of £400.

<!-- ch24-p005 -->
The capital value was originally advanced in the money form. The surplus-value, on the other hand, is originally the value of a definite portion of the gross product. If this gross product is sold, turned into money, the capital value regains its original form. From this moment on, the capital value and the surplus-value are both sums of money, and they are turned back into capital in exactly the same way. The capitalist lays out both the one and the other to buy commodities that put him in a position to start making his goods afresh, and this time on an extended scale. (A commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged (sold), not for the producer's own use.) But to be able to buy those commodities, he must find them ready in the market.

<!-- ch24-p006 -->
His own yarns circulate only because he brings his annual product to market, as all other capitalists likewise do with their commodities. But before coming to market, these commodities were part of the general annual product. They were part of the total mass of objects of every kind into which the sum of the individual capitals, that is, the total capital of society, had been converted in the course of the year, and of which each capitalist had in hand only a fractional part. The transactions in the market only carry out the exchange of the individual parts of this annual product among themselves, moving them from one hand to another. They can neither increase the total annual production nor change the nature of the objects produced. Hence the use that can be made of the total annual product depends entirely on its own composition, and in no way on circulation (the exchange of commodities through money: selling and buying).

<!-- ch24-p007 -->
The annual production must, in the first place, supply all those objects (use-values) from which the material parts of capital used up in the course of the year have to be replaced. (A use-value is the usefulness of a thing: what it can be used for, which comes from its physical properties.) When these objects are deducted, what remains is the net product or surplus product, in which the surplus-value lies. And what does this surplus product consist of? Only of things meant to satisfy the wants and desires of the capitalist class, things which therefore go into the capitalists' consumption fund? If that were so, the cup of surplus-value would be drained to the very dregs, and nothing but simple reproduction would ever take place. (Simple reproduction is production repeated on the same scale, with the capitalist consuming all the surplus-value.)

<!-- ch24-p008 -->
To accumulate, a portion of the surplus product must be turned into capital. But, short of a miracle, we can turn into capital only such articles as can be used in the labor process (that is, means of production), and such further articles as are suitable for keeping the worker alive (that is, means of subsistence). (The labor process is the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things.) So a part of the annual surplus labor must have been spent on producing additional means of production and subsistence, over and above the amount of these things needed to replace the capital advanced. (Surplus labor is the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist.) In a word, surplus-value can be turned into capital only because the surplus product, whose value it is, already contains the material elements of new capital.[^24.2]

[^24.2]: Here we take no account of export trade, by which a nation can change articles of luxury into either means of production or means of subsistence, and the other way round. To examine the object of our investigation intact, free from all disturbing side circumstances, we must treat the whole world as one nation, and assume that capitalist production is established everywhere and has taken possession of every branch of industry.

<!-- ch24-p009 -->
Now, for these elements actually to function as capital, the capitalist class needs additional labor. If the exploitation of the workers already employed does not increase, either extensively or intensively, then additional labor-power must be found. (Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist.) The mechanism of capitalist production provides for this in advance. It turns the working class into a class dependent on wages, a class whose ordinary wages are enough not only to maintain it but to make it grow. Capital need only combine this additional labor-power, which the working class supplies every year in the shape of workers of all ages, with the surplus means of production contained in the annual product, and the conversion of surplus-value into capital is complete. Seen concretely, accumulation comes down to the reproduction of capital on an extended scale. The circle in which simple reproduction moves changes its form and, to use Sismondi's expression, turns into a spiral.[^24.3]

[^24.3]: Sismondi's analysis of accumulation suffers from a great defect: he is content, to too great an extent, with the phrase “conversion of revenue into capital,” without getting to the bottom of the material conditions of this operation.

<!-- ch24-p010 -->
Let us now go back to our illustration. It is the old story: Abraham begat Isaac, Isaac begat Jacob, and so on. The original capital of £10,000 brings in a surplus-value of £2,000, which is capitalized. The new capital of £2,000 brings in a surplus-value of £400. This too is capitalized, turned into a second additional capital, which in its turn produces a further surplus-value of £80. And so the ball keeps rolling.

<!-- ch24-p011 -->
Here we leave out of account the portion of the surplus-value that the capitalist consumes. Just as little does it concern us, for the moment, whether the additional capital is joined on to the original capital or separated from it to function independently; or whether the same capitalist who accumulated it employs it, or hands it over to another. Only this we must not forget: alongside the newly formed capital, the original capital goes on reproducing itself and producing surplus-value, and the same is true of all accumulated capital and of the additional capital it gives rise to.

<!-- ch24-p012 -->
The original capital was formed by advancing £10,000. How did its owner come to possess it? “By his own labour and that of his forefathers,” the spokesmen of political economy (the science of economics as it was then called) answer with one voice.[^24.4] And in fact their assumption seems the only one consistent with the laws of the production of commodities.

[^24.4]: “Le travail primitif auquel son capital a dû sa naissance.” [The original labor to which his capital owed its birth] Sismondi, cited above, ed. Paris, t. I., p. 109.

<!-- ch24-p013 -->
But it is quite otherwise with the additional capital of £2,000. We know perfectly well how that came into being. There is not one single atom of its value that does not owe its existence to unpaid labor. The means of production with which the additional labor-power is combined, as well as the necessities that keep the workers alive, are nothing but component parts of the surplus product, of the tribute that the capitalist class exacts every year from the working class. Though the capitalist class uses a portion of that tribute to buy the additional labor-power even at its full price, so that equivalent is exchanged for equivalent, the transaction is still, for all that, only the old trick of every conqueror who buys commodities from the conquered with the money he has robbed from them. (Price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity.)

<!-- ch24-p014 -->
If the additional capital employs the person who produced it, this producer must not only go on increasing the value of the original capital, but must buy back the fruits of his earlier labor with more labor than they cost. Viewed as a transaction between the capitalist class and the working class, it makes no difference that additional workers are employed by means of the unpaid labor of the workers employed before. The capitalist may even turn the additional capital into a machine that throws the producers of that capital out of work and replaces them by a few children. In every case the working class, by the surplus labor of one year, creates the capital meant to employ additional labor in the following year.[^24.5] And this is what is called: creating capital out of capital.

[^24.5]: “Labour creates capital before capital employs labour.” E. G. Wakefield, “England and America,” London, 1833, Vol. II, p. 110.

<!-- ch24-p015 -->
The accumulation of the first additional capital of £2,000 presupposes a value of £10,000 that belonged to the capitalist by virtue of his “primitive labour,” and that he advanced. The second additional capital of £400, on the other hand, presupposes only the earlier accumulation of the £2,000, of which the £400 is the capitalized surplus-value. From then on, ownership of past unpaid labor is the only condition for appropriating living unpaid labor on a constantly increasing scale. (Living labor is the labor of workers now at work, as distinct from dead labor, the labor already embodied in means of production.) The more the capitalist has accumulated, the more he is able to accumulate.

<!-- ch24-p016 -->
Insofar as the surplus-value of which additional capital No. 1 consists is the result of buying labor-power with part of the original capital – a purchase that conformed to the laws of the exchange of commodities, and that, from a legal standpoint, presupposes nothing beyond the free disposal by the worker of his own capacities, and by the owner of money or commodities of the values that belong to him; insofar as additional capital No. 2, etc., is merely the result of No. 1, and therefore a consequence of the conditions above; insofar as each single transaction always conforms to the laws of the exchange of commodities, with the capitalist buying labor-power and the worker selling it, and, we will assume, at its real value; insofar as all this is true, clearly the laws of appropriation or of private property, laws based on the production and circulation of commodities, are turned by their own inner and inexorable dialectic into their very opposite. The exchange of equivalents, the original operation we started with, has now been turned round in such a way that there is only an apparent exchange. This is due, first, to the fact that the capital exchanged for labor-power is itself only a portion of the product of other people's labor, appropriated without an equivalent; and, second, to the fact that its producer must not only replace this capital, but replace it together with an added surplus. The relation of exchange between capitalist and worker becomes a mere appearance belonging to the process of circulation, a mere form, foreign to the real nature of the transaction, and only mystifying it. The constantly repeated purchase and sale of labor-power is now the mere form. What really takes place is this: the capitalist again and again appropriates, without an equivalent, a portion of the previously materialized labor of others, and exchanges it for a greater quantity of living labor. At first the rights of property seemed to us to be based on a man's own labor. At least, some such assumption was necessary, since only commodity-owners with equal rights faced each other, and the only means by which a man could come to possess the commodities of others was by parting with his own commodities; and these could be replaced by labor alone. Now, however, property turns out to be, on the side of the capitalist, the right to appropriate the unpaid labor of others or its product, and, on the side of the worker, the impossibility of appropriating his own product. The separation of property from labor has become the necessary consequence of a law that apparently started from their identity.[^24.6]

[^24.6]: The capitalist's property in the product of other people's labor “is a strict consequence of the law of appropriation, the fundamental principle of which was, on the contrary, the exclusive title of every labourer to the product of his own labour.” (Cherbuliez, “Richesse ou Pauvreté,” Paris, 1841, p. 58, where, however, the dialectical reversal is not properly developed.)

<!-- ch24-p017 -->
Therefore,[^24.7] however much the capitalist mode of appropriation may seem to fly in the face of the original laws of commodity production, it arises not from a violation of these laws but, on the contrary, from their application. Let us make this clear once more by briefly reviewing the successive phases of the movement whose culminating point is capitalist accumulation.

[^24.7]: The following passage (to p. 551 “laws of capitalist appropriation.”) has been added to the English text to conform with the 4th German edition.

<!-- ch24-p018 -->
We saw, in the first place, that the original conversion of a sum of values into capital was carried out in complete accordance with the laws of exchange. One party to the contract sells his labor-power, the other buys it. The seller receives the value of his commodity, and its use-value – labor – is thereby handed over to the buyer. The buyer then uses labor that equally belongs to him to transform means of production that already belong to him into a new product, which is likewise lawfully his.

<!-- ch24-p019 -->
The value of this product includes, first, the value of the used-up means of production. Useful labor (labor of a particular kind, such as tailoring or weaving, that makes a particular useful thing) cannot consume these means of production without transferring their value to the new product. But to be saleable, labor-power must be able to supply useful labor in the branch of industry in which it is to be employed.

<!-- ch24-p020 -->
The value of the new product further includes the equivalent of the value of the labor-power, together with a surplus-value. This is because the value of the labor-power – sold for a definite length of time, say a day, a week, etc. – is less than the value created by its use during that time. But the worker has received payment for the exchange-value of his labor-power (exchange-value being the proportion in which one commodity trades for others, for example how many coats a quantity of linen trades for), and by doing so has handed over its use-value – as happens in every sale and purchase.

<!-- ch24-p021 -->
This particular commodity, labor-power, has the peculiar use-value of supplying labor, and therefore of creating value; but that fact cannot affect the general law of commodity production. So if the magnitude of value advanced in wages is not merely found again in the product, but is found there increased by a surplus-value, this is not because the seller has been cheated, for he has really received the value of his commodity. It is due solely to the fact that the buyer has used this commodity up. (Magnitude of value means how much value a commodity has, measured by the socially necessary labor-time needed to produce it.)

<!-- ch24-p022 -->
The law of exchange requires equality only between the exchange-values of the commodities given in exchange for one another. From the very start it even presupposes a difference between their use-values, and it has nothing whatever to do with their consumption, which only begins after the deal is closed and carried out.

<!-- ch24-p023 -->
So the original conversion of money into capital is carried out in the most exact accordance with the economic laws of commodity production and with the right of property derived from them. Nevertheless, its result is:

<!-- ch24-p024 -->
(1) that the product belongs to the capitalist and not to the worker;

<!-- ch24-p025 -->
(2) that the value of this product includes, besides the value of the capital advanced, a surplus-value which costs the worker labor but costs the capitalist nothing, and which nonetheless becomes the legitimate property of the capitalist;

<!-- ch24-p026 -->
(3) that the worker has kept his labor-power and can sell it again if he can find a buyer.

<!-- ch24-p027 -->
Simple reproduction is only the periodic repetition of this first operation; each time, money is converted afresh into capital. So the law is not broken; on the contrary, it is merely enabled to operate continuously. “Several successive acts of exchange have only made the last represent the first” (Sismondi, “Nouveaux Principes, etc.,” p. 70).

<!-- ch24-p028 -->
And yet we have seen that simple reproduction is enough to stamp this first operation, insofar as it is thought of as an isolated process, with a totally changed character. “Of those who share the national income among themselves, the one side (the workers) acquire every year a fresh right to their share by fresh work; the others (the capitalists) have already acquired, by work done originally, a permanent right to their share” (Sismondi, cited above, pp. 110, 111). It is indeed notorious that the sphere of labor is not the only one in which primogeniture (the eldest son's right to inherit) works miracles.

<!-- ch24-p029 -->
Nor does it matter if simple reproduction is replaced by reproduction on an extended scale, by accumulation. In the first case the capitalist squanders the whole surplus-value on dissipation; in the second he shows his bourgeois virtue by consuming only a portion of it and converting the rest into money. (Bourgeois means belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it.)

<!-- ch24-p030 -->
The surplus-value is his property; it has never belonged to anyone else. If he advances it for the purposes of production, the advances come from his own funds, exactly as on the day when he first entered the market. The fact that this time the funds come from the unpaid labor of his workers makes absolutely no difference. If worker B is paid out of the surplus-value that worker A produced, then, in the first place, A supplied that surplus-value without having the just price of his commodity cut by a half-penny, and, in the second place, the transaction is no concern whatever of B's. What B claims, and has a right to claim, is that the capitalist should pay him the value of his labor-power. “Both were still gainers: the worker because he was advanced the fruits of his labour” (should read: of the unpaid labor of other workers) “before the work was done” (should read: before his own labor had borne fruit); “the employer *(le maître)* [the master], because the labour of this worker was worth more than his wages” (should read: produced more value than the value of his wages). (Sismondi, cited above, p. 135.)

<!-- ch24-p031 -->
To be sure, the matter looks quite different if we consider capitalist production in the unbroken flow of its renewal, and if, instead of the individual capitalist and the individual worker, we look at them in their totality: the capitalist class and the working class facing each other. But in doing so we would be applying standards entirely foreign to commodity production.

<!-- ch24-p032 -->
In commodity production, only buyer and seller face each other, independent of each other. The relations between them end on the day the term set in the contract they made expires. If the transaction is repeated, it is repeated as the result of a new agreement, which has nothing to do with the earlier one and which only by chance brings the same seller together again with the same buyer.

<!-- ch24-p033 -->
So if commodity production, or one of its associated processes, is to be judged according to its own economic laws, we must consider each act of exchange by itself, apart from any connection with the act of exchange before it and the one after it. And since sales and purchases are negotiated only between particular individuals, it is not admissible to look here for relations between whole social classes.

<!-- ch24-p034 -->
However long a series of periodic reproductions and earlier accumulations the capital functioning today may have passed through, it always keeps its original virginity. So long as the laws of exchange are observed in every single act of exchange, the mode of appropriation can be completely revolutionized without in any way affecting the property rights that correspond to commodity production. These same rights remain in force both at the outset, when the product belongs to its producer, who, exchanging equivalent for equivalent, can grow rich only by his own labor, and also in the period of capitalism, when social wealth becomes, to an ever-increasing degree, the property of those who are in a position to appropriate the unpaid labor of others continually and ever afresh.

<!-- ch24-p035 -->
This result becomes inevitable from the moment the worker himself freely sells labor-power as a commodity. But it is also only from then on that commodity production becomes general and the typical form of production; only from then on is every product produced for sale from the start, and does all the wealth produced pass through the sphere of circulation. Only when and where wage labor is its basis does commodity production impose itself on society as a whole; but only then and there, too, does it unfold all its hidden potential. To say that the arrival of wage labor adulterates commodity production is to say that commodity production must not develop if it is to remain unadulterated. To the extent that commodity production, in accordance with its own built-in laws, develops further into capitalist production, the property laws of commodity production change into the laws of capitalist appropriation.[^24.8]

[^24.8]: We may well, therefore, be astonished at the cleverness of Proudhon, who would abolish capitalist property by enforcing the eternal laws of property that are based on commodity production!

<!-- ch24-p036 -->
We have seen that even in the case of simple reproduction, all capital, whatever its original source, is turned into accumulated capital, capitalized surplus-value. But in the flood of production all the capital originally advanced becomes a vanishing quantity *(magnitudo evanescens* [vanishing magnitude], in the mathematical sense) compared with the directly accumulated capital, that is, with the surplus-value or surplus product that is turned back into capital, whether it functions in the hands of the one who accumulated it or in the hands of others. Hence political economy describes capital in general as “accumulated wealth” (converted surplus-value or revenue), “that is employed over again in the production of surplus-value,”[^24.9] and the capitalist as “the owner of surplus-value.”[^24.10] It is merely another way of expressing the same thing to say that all existing capital is accumulated or capitalized interest, for interest is a mere fragment of surplus-value.[^24.11]

[^24.9]: “Capital, viz., accumulated wealth employed with a view to profit.” (Malthus, cited above.) “Capital ... consists of wealth saved from revenue, and used with a view to profit.” (R. Jones: “An Introductory Lecture on Polit. Econ.,” London, 1833, p. 16.)

[^24.10]: “The possessors of surplus-produce or capital.” (“The Source and Remedy of the National Difficulties. A Letter to Lord John Russell.” London, 1821.)

[^24.11]: “Capital, with compound interest on every portion of capital saved, is so all engrossing that all the wealth in the world from which income is derived, has long ago become the interest on capital.” (London, *Economist,* 19th July, 1851.)

### Section 2: Erroneous Conception, by Political Economy, of Reproduction on a Progressively Increasing Scale

<!-- ch24-p037 -->
Before we investigate accumulation further, that is, the turning of surplus-value back into capital, we must brush aside an ambiguity that the classical economists brought in. (Classical political economy means the economists from Petty to Ricardo who investigated the real relations of production.)

<!-- ch24-p038 -->
The commodities that the capitalist buys with a part of the surplus-value for his own consumption do not serve the purpose of production or of creating value. In just the same way, the labor that he buys to satisfy his natural and social needs is not productive labor. By buying those commodities and that labor, he does not convert the surplus-value into capital. On the contrary, he consumes it, or spends it, as revenue. The old feudal nobility had a habitual way of life which, as Hegel rightly says, “consists in consuming what is in hand,” and which showed itself above all in the luxury of personal attendants. Against this way of life it was extremely important for bourgeois economics to proclaim the doctrine that accumulation of capital is the first duty of every citizen. It had to preach without ceasing that a man cannot accumulate if he eats up all his revenue, instead of spending a good part of it on acquiring additional productive workers, who bring in more than they cost. On the other hand, the economists had to fight against the popular prejudice that confuses capitalist production with hoarding (building up a hoard: money withdrawn from circulation and kept as a store of value).[^24.12] This prejudice imagines that accumulated wealth is either wealth that is rescued from being destroyed in its existing form, that is, from being consumed, or wealth that is withdrawn from circulation. Shutting money out of circulation would also shut out completely its self-expansion as capital, while piling up a hoard in the form of commodities would be sheer tomfoolery.[^24.13] The accumulation of commodities in great masses is the result either of over-production or of a stoppage of circulation.[^24.14] It is true that the popular mind is impressed by two sights. On the one hand, there is the mass of goods stored up for gradual consumption by the rich.[^24.15] On the other hand, there is the building up of reserve stocks. The latter is a phenomenon common to all modes of production, and we shall dwell on it for a moment when we come to analyze circulation. Classical economics is therefore quite right when it maintains that the consumption of surplus-products by productive, instead of by unproductive, workers is a characteristic feature of the process of accumulation. But at this point the mistakes also begin. Adam Smith has made it the fashion to represent accumulation as nothing more than the consumption of surplus-products by productive workers. That amounts to saying that capitalizing surplus-value consists merely in turning surplus-value into labor-power.
