[^24.12]: “No political economist of the present day can by saving mean mere hoarding: and beyond this contracted and insufficient proceeding, no use of the term in reference to the national wealth can well be imagined, but that which must arise from a different application of what is saved, founded upon a real distinction between the different kinds of labour maintained by it.” (Malthus, cited above, pp. 38, 39.)

[^24.13]: So, for example, Balzac, who studied every shade of greed so thoroughly, shows the old usurer Gobseck as being in his second childhood when he begins to heap up a hoard of commodities.

[^24.14]: “Accumulation of stocks ... non-exchange ... over-production.” (Th. Corbet, cited above, p. 104.)

[^24.15]: In this sense Necker speaks of the “objets de faste et de somptuosité,” [things of show and luxury] of which “le temps a grossi l’accummulation,” [time has swollen the accumulation] and which “les lois de propriété ont rassemblés dans une seule classe de la société.” [the laws of property have gathered together in a single class of society] (*Oeuvres de M. Necker*, Paris and Lausanne, 1789, t. ii., p. 291.)

<!-- ch24-p039 -->
Let us see what Ricardo, for example, says:

<!-- ch24-p040 -->
> “It must be understood that all the productions of a country are consumed; but it makes the greatest difference imaginable whether they are consumed by those who reproduce, or by those who do not reproduce another value. When we say that revenue is saved, and added to capital, what we mean is, that the portion of revenue, so said to be added to capital, is consumed by productive instead of unproductive labourers. There can be no greater error than in supposing that capital is increased by non-consumption.”[^24.16]

[^24.16]: Ricardo, cited above, p. 163, note.

<!-- ch24-p041 -->
There can be no greater error than the one that Ricardo and all later economists repeat after A. Smith, namely, that

<!-- ch24-p042 -->
> “the part of revenue, of which it is said, it has been added to capital, is consumed by productive labourers.”

<!-- ch24-p043 -->
According to this, all surplus-value that is changed into capital becomes variable capital (the part of capital spent on labor-power, which reproduces its own value and also produces surplus-value, so its size varies). This is far from being the case. The surplus-value, like the original capital, divides into constant capital (the part of capital spent on means of production, whose value is passed on to the product but does not grow) and variable capital, into means of production and labor-power. Labor-power is the form in which variable capital exists during the process of production. In this process the labor-power is itself consumed by the capitalist, while the means of production are consumed by the labor-power as it performs its function, labor. At the same time, the money paid to buy the labor-power is converted into necessaries, which are consumed, not by “productive labour,” but by the “productive labourer.” Through a fundamentally perverted analysis, Adam Smith arrives at the absurd conclusion that, even though each individual capital is divided into a constant and a variable part, the capital of society breaks down only into variable capital, that is, it is laid out exclusively in paying wages. For instance, suppose a cloth manufacturer converts £2,000 into capital. He lays out one portion in buying weavers, the other in woollen yarn, machinery, etc. But the people from whom he buys the yarn and the machinery pay for labor with a part of the purchase money, and so on, until the whole £2,000 are spent in paying wages, that is, until the entire product represented by the £2,000 has been consumed by productive workers. Clearly, the whole point of this argument lies in the words “and so on,” which send us from pillar to post. In truth, Adam Smith breaks off his investigation just where its difficulties begin.[^24.17]

[^24.17]: In spite of his “Logic,” John St. Mill never detects even a faulty analysis like this one when his predecessors make it, an analysis that, even from the bourgeois standpoint of the science, cries out to be corrected. In every case he records the confusion of his master’s thoughts with the dogmatism of a disciple. So here: “The capital itself in the long run becomes entirely wages, and when replaced by the sale of produce becomes wages again.”

<!-- ch24-p044 -->
The annual process of reproduction is easy to understand, so long as we look only at the sum total of the year’s production. But every single component of this product must be brought onto the market as a commodity, and there the difficulty begins. The movements of the individual capitals and of the personal revenues cross and mix with each other, and they are lost in the general change of places, in the circulation of society’s wealth. This dazzles the eye and sets very complicated problems to be solved. In the third part of Book II I shall give an analysis of how the facts really hang together. It is one of the great merits of the Physiocrats (a school of 18th-century French economists) that in their *Tableau économique* [Economic Table] they were the first to try to depict the year’s production in the shape in which it presents itself to us after passing through the process of circulation.[^24.18]

[^24.18]: In his description of the process of reproduction and of accumulation, Adam Smith in many ways not only made no advance, but even lost considerable ground, compared with his predecessors, especially the Physiocrats. Connected with the illusion mentioned in the text is the really wonderful dogma that he left as an inheritance to political economy: the dogma that the price of commodities is made up of wages, profit (interest) and rent, that is, of wages and surplus-value. Starting from this basis, Storch naively confesses, “Il est impossible de résoudre le prix nécessaire dans ses éléments les plus simples.” [It is impossible to break down the necessary price into its simplest elements.] (Storch, cited above, Petersb. Edit., 1815, t. ii., p. 141, note.) A fine science of economics this is, which declares it impossible to break down the price of a commodity into its simplest elements! This point will be investigated further in the seventh part of Book iii.

<!-- ch24-p045 -->
For the rest, it goes without saying that political economy, acting in the interests of the capitalist class, has not failed to exploit Adam Smith’s doctrine, namely, that the whole of that part of the surplus-product which is converted into capital is consumed by the working class.

### Section 3: Separation of Surplus-Value into Capital and Revenue. The Abstinence Theory

<!-- ch24-p046 -->
In the last chapter, we treated surplus-value (or the surplus-product) only as a fund for supplying the capitalist's individual consumption. In this chapter we have so far treated it only as a fund for accumulation. But it is neither the one nor the other alone: it is both together. The capitalist consumes one portion as revenue;[^24.19] the other is used as capital, that is, it is accumulated.

[^24.19]: The reader will notice that the word revenue is used in a double sense. First, it means surplus-value insofar as it is the fruit that capital yields periodically. Second, it means the part of that fruit which the capitalist periodically consumes, or adds to the fund that supplies his private consumption. I have kept this double meaning because it fits the language of the English and French economists.

<!-- ch24-p047 -->
So, given the mass of surplus-value, the larger one of these parts is, the smaller the other is. Other things being equal, the ratio between these parts determines the size of the accumulation. But it is the owner of the surplus-value, the capitalist alone, who makes the division. It is his deliberate act. The part of the tribute he extracts which he accumulates is said to be saved by him, because he does not eat it, that is, because he performs the function of a capitalist and enriches himself.

<!-- ch24-p048 -->
Except as personified capital, the capitalist has no historical value, and no right to that historical existence which, to use an expression of the witty Lichnowsky, “hasn’t got no date.” And only to that extent is the necessity of his own passing existence contained in the passing necessity of the capitalist mode of production. But insofar as he is personified capital, what drives him to act is not use-values and the enjoyment of them, but exchange-value and its increase. He is fanatically bent on making value expand itself, so he ruthlessly forces the human race to produce for production’s sake. In this way he forces the development of the productive powers of society. He creates those material conditions which alone can form the real basis of a higher form of society, a society whose ruling principle is the full and free development of every individual. Only as personified capital is the capitalist respectable. As such, he shares with the miser the passion for wealth as wealth. But what in the miser is a mere personal quirk is, in the capitalist, the effect of the social mechanism, of which he is only one of the wheels. Moreover, the development of capitalist production makes it constantly necessary to keep increasing the amount of capital laid out in a given industrial undertaking. And competition makes each individual capitalist feel the built-in laws of capitalist production as external laws that coerce him. It compels him to keep extending his capital constantly in order to preserve it, but he cannot extend it except by progressive accumulation.

<!-- ch24-p049 -->
So, insofar as his actions are a mere function of capital – capital which, in his person, is endowed with consciousness and a will – his own private consumption is a robbery committed against accumulation. In the same way, in double-entry book-keeping, the capitalist’s private spending is placed on the debit side of his account, against his capital. To accumulate is to conquer the world of social wealth, to increase the mass of human beings he exploits, and so to extend both the direct and the indirect rule of the capitalist.[^24.20]

[^24.20]: Taking as his text the usurer, that old-fashioned but ever-renewed specimen of the capitalist, Luther shows very aptly that the love of power is an element in the desire to get rich. “The heathen were able, by the light of reason, to conclude that a usurer is a double-dyed thief and murderer. We Christians, however, hold them in such honour, that we fairly worship them for the sake of their money.... Whoever eats up, robs, and steals the nourishment of another, that man commits as great a murder (so far as in him lies) as he who starves a man or utterly undoes him. Such does a usurer, and sits the while safe on his stool, when he ought rather to be hanging on the gallows, and be eaten by as many ravens as he has stolen guilders, if only there were so much flesh on him, that so many ravens could stick their beaks in and share it. Meanwhile, we hang the small thieves.... Little thieves are put in the stocks, great thieves go flaunting in gold and silk.... Therefore is there, on this earth, no greater enemy of man (after the devil) than a gripe-money [miser], and usurer, for he wants to be God over all men. Turks, soldiers, and tyrants are also bad men, yet must they let the people live, and confess that they are bad, and enemies, and do, nay [indeed], must, now and then show pity to some. But a usurer and money-glutton, such a one would have the whole world perish of hunger and thirst, misery and want, so far as in him lies, so that he may have all to himself, and every one may receive from him as from a God, and be his serf for ever. To wear fine cloaks, golden chains, rings, to wipe his mouth, to be deemed and taken for a worthy, pious man .... Usury is a great huge monster, like a werewolf, who lays waste all, more than any Cacus, Gerion or Antus. And yet decks himself out, and would be thought pious, so that people may not see where the oxen have gone, that he drags backwards into his den. But Hercules shall hear the cry of the oxen and of his prisoners, and shall seek Cacus even in cliffs and among rocks, and shall set the oxen loose again from the villain. For Cacus means the villain that is a pious usurer, and steals, robs, eats everything. And will not own that he has done it, and thinks no one will find him out, because the oxen, drawn backwards into his den, make it seem, from their foot-prints, that they have been let out. So the usurer would deceive the world, as though he were of use and gave the world oxen, which he, however, rends, and eats all alone... And since we break on the wheel, and behead highwaymen, murderers and housebreakers, how much more ought we to break on the wheel and kill.... hunt down, curse and behead all usurers.” (Martin Luther, cited above.)

<!-- ch24-p050 -->
But original sin is at work everywhere. As capitalist production, accumulation, and wealth develop, the capitalist stops being the mere incarnation of capital. He has a fellow-feeling for his own Adam, and his education gradually lets him smile at the passion for self-denial as a mere prejudice of the old-fashioned miser. The capitalist of the classical type condemns individual consumption as a sin against his function, as “abstinence” from accumulating. The modernized capitalist, by contrast, is capable of seeing accumulation as “abstinence” from pleasure.

<!-- ch24-p051 -->
> “Two souls, alas, do dwell within his breast;\
> The one is ever parting from the other.”[^24.21]

[^24.21]: See Goethe’s “Faust.”

<!-- ch24-p052 -->
At the historical dawn of capitalist production – and every capitalist upstart has to go through this historical stage personally – greed and the desire to get rich are the ruling passions. But the progress of capitalist production does not only create a world of delights. In speculation and the credit system, it also opens up a thousand sources of sudden enrichment. Once a certain stage of development has been reached, a conventional degree of extravagance, which is also a display of wealth and so a source of credit, becomes a business necessity for the “unfortunate” capitalist. Luxury becomes part of capital’s costs of putting on a show. Moreover, the capitalist does not get rich as the miser does, in proportion to his own personal labor and restricted consumption. He gets rich at the same rate as he squeezes out the labor-power of others and forces on the worker abstinence from all of life’s enjoyments. So the capitalist’s extravagance never has the genuine character of the open-handed feudal lord’s extravagance. On the contrary, behind it there always lurk the most sordid greed and the most anxious calculation. Even so, his spending grows with his accumulation, without the one necessarily restricting the other. But along with this growth, there develops at the same time in his breast a Faustian conflict between the passion for accumulation and the desire for enjoyment.

<!-- ch24-p053 -->
Dr. Aikin says in a work published in 1795:

<!-- ch24-p054 -->
> “The trade of Manchester may be divided into four periods. First, when manufacturers were obliged to work hard for their livelihood.”

<!-- ch24-p055 -->
They enriched themselves chiefly by robbing the parents whose children were bound to them as apprentices. The parents paid a high fee, while the apprentices were starved. On the other hand, average profits were low, and accumulating required extreme thrift. They lived like misers and were far from consuming even the interest on their capital.

<!-- ch24-p056 -->
> “The second period, when they had begun to acquire little fortunes, but worked as hard as before,” – for direct exploitation of labor costs labor, as every slave-driver knows – “and lived in as plain a manner as before.... The third, when luxury began, and the trade was pushed by sending out riders [traveling salesmen] for orders into every market town in the Kingdom.... It is probable that few or no capitals of £3,000 to £4,000 acquired by trade existed here before 1690. However, about that time, or a little later, the traders had got money beforehand [had money saved up], and began to build modern brick houses, instead of those of wood and plaster.”

<!-- ch24-p057 -->
Even in the early part of the 18th century, a Manchester manufacturer who set a pint of foreign wine before his guests exposed himself to the remarks and head-shaking of all his neighbors. Before the rise of machinery, a manufacturer’s evening spending at the pub where they all met never went beyond sixpence for a glass of punch and a penny for a twist of tobacco. Not until 1758, and this marks an epoch, was a person actually engaged in business seen with a carriage of his own.

<!-- ch24-p058 -->
> “The fourth period,” the last 30 years of the 18th century, “is that in which expense and luxury have made great progress, and was supported by a trade extended by means of riders and factors [agents] through every part of Europe.”[^24.22]

[^24.22]: Dr. Aikin: “Description of the Country from 30 to 40 miles round Manchester.” London, 1795, p. 182, and following.

<!-- ch24-p059 -->
What would the good Dr. Aikin say if he could rise from his grave and see the Manchester of today?

<!-- ch24-p060 -->
Accumulate, accumulate! That is Moses and the prophets! “Industry furnishes the material which saving accumulates.”[^24.23] Therefore save, save, that is, turn as much as possible of the surplus-value, or surplus-product, back into capital! Accumulation for accumulation’s sake, production for production’s sake: in this formula classical economics expressed the historical mission of the bourgeoisie, and it did not for a single instant fool itself about the birth-pangs of wealth.[^24.24] But what is the use of lamenting in the face of historical necessity? If, to classical economics, the proletarian – a member of the proletariat, the class of wage workers, who own nothing they can live by except their labor-power – is only a machine for producing surplus-value, then, on the other hand, the capitalist too is in its eyes only a machine for turning this surplus-value into additional capital. Political economy takes the historical function of the capitalist in bitter earnest. Malthus wanted to charm out of the capitalist’s breast the awful conflict between the desire for enjoyment and the chase after riches. So, around the year 1820, he argued for a division of labor that assigns the business of accumulating to the capitalist actually engaged in production, and the business of spending to the other sharers in surplus-value: to the landlords, the holders of government posts, the clergy with church incomes, etc. It is of the highest importance, he says,

[^24.23]: A. Smith, cited above, bk. iii., ch. iii.

[^24.24]: Even J. B. Say says: “Les épargnes des riches se font aux dépens des pauvres.” [the savings of the rich are made at the expense of the poor] “The Roman proletarian lived almost entirely at the expense of society.... It can almost be said that modern society lives at the expense of the proletarians, on what it keeps out of the remuneration of labour.” (Sismondi: “études, &c.,” t. i., p. 24.)

<!-- ch24-p061 -->
> “to keep separate the passion for expenditure and the passion for accumulation.”[^24.25]

[^24.25]: Malthus, cited above, pp. 319, 320.

<!-- ch24-p062 -->
The capitalists had long since become men of the world who liked to live well, and they raised a loud outcry. One of their spokesmen, a follower of Ricardo, cried out: What! Mr. Malthus preaches high rents, heavy taxes, etc., so that unproductive consumers can keep the spur constantly pressed into the side of the industrious! By all means production, production on an ever-growing scale, so goes the slogan; but

<!-- ch24-p063 -->
> “production will, by such a process, be held back far more than it is spurred on. Nor is it quite fair to keep a number of persons idle in this way, only to pinch others, who are likely, from their characters, if you can force them to work, to work with success.”[^24.26]

[^24.26]: “An Inquiry into those Principles Respecting the Nature of Demand, &c.,” p. 67.

<!-- ch24-p064 -->
Unfair as he finds it to spur on the industrial capitalist by taking the butter off his bread, he still thinks it necessary to cut the worker’s wages to a minimum “to keep him industrious.” Nor does he hide for a moment the fact that the appropriation of unpaid labor is the secret of surplus-value.

<!-- ch24-p065 -->
> “Increased demand on the part of the labourers means nothing more than their willingness to take less of their own product for themselves, and leave a greater part of it to their employers; and if it be said, that this begets glut [oversupply], by lessening consumption” (on the part of the workers), “I can only reply that glut is synonymous with large profits.”[^24.27]

[^24.27]: Cited above, p. 59.

<!-- ch24-p066 -->
The learned debate over how the booty pumped out of the worker might be divided between the industrial capitalist and the rich idler, with the most advantage to accumulation, fell silent in the face of the revolution of July (the 1830 revolution in France). Shortly afterwards, the town proletariat at Lyons rang the alarm bell of revolution, and the country proletariat in England began to set fire to farmyards and grain-stacks. On this side of the Channel Owenism began to spread; on the other side, St. Simonism and Fourierism. The hour of vulgar economics had struck. Vulgar economics means economists who only describe and defend the surface appearances of the system, without investigating its real relations. Exactly a year before Nassau W. Senior discovered at Manchester that the profit (including interest) of capital is the product of the last hour of the twelve, he had announced another discovery to the world.

<!-- ch24-p067 -->
> “I substitute,” he proudly says, “for the word capital, considered as an instrument of production, the word abstinence.”

<!-- ch24-p068 -->
Here is a matchless sample of the discoveries of vulgar economics! It puts a fawning phrase in the place of an economic category – *voilà tout* [that’s all].

<!-- ch24-p069 -->
> “When the savage,” says Senior, “makes bows, he exercises an industry, but he does not practise abstinence.”[^24.28]

[^24.28]: (Senior, “Principes fondamentaux del’Écon. Pol.” trad. Arrivabene. Paris, 1836, p. 308.) This was rather too much for the followers of the old classical school. “Mr. Senior has substituted for it” (the expression, labor and profit) “the expression labour and Abstinence. He who converts his revenue abstains from the enjoyment which its expenditure would afford him. It is not the capital, but the use of the capital productively, which is the cause of profits.” (John Cazenove, cited above, p. 130, Note.) John St. Mill, on the contrary, accepts Ricardo’s theory of profit on the one hand, and on the other hand takes over Senior’s “remuneration of abstinence.” He is as much at home in absurd contradictions as he feels at sea in the Hegelian contradiction, the source of all dialectic. It has never occurred to the vulgar economist to make the simple reflection that every human action may be viewed as “abstinence” from its opposite. Eating is abstinence from fasting, walking is abstinence from standing still, working is abstinence from idling, idling is abstinence from working, etc. These gentlemen would do well to ponder, once in a while, Spinoza’s “Determinatio est Negatio” [Determination is negation].

<!-- ch24-p070 -->
This explains how and why, in the earlier states of society, the implements of labor were made without abstinence on the part of the capitalist.

<!-- ch24-p071 -->
> “The more society progresses, the more abstinence is demanded,”[^24.29]

[^24.29]: Senior, cited above, p. 342.

<!-- ch24-p072 -->
Namely, from those who carry on the industry of appropriating the fruits of other people’s industry. All the conditions for carrying on the labor process are suddenly turned into so many acts of abstinence on the part of the capitalist. If the grain is not all eaten, but part of it is also sown – abstinence of the capitalist. If the wine is given time to mature – abstinence of the capitalist.[^24.30] The capitalist robs his own self whenever he “lends (!) the instruments of production to the labourer.” That is, he robs himself whenever he incorporates labor-power with them and uses them to extract surplus-value out of that labor-power, instead of eating them up, steam-engines, cotton, railways, manure, horses, and all; or, as the vulgar economist childishly puts it, instead of squandering “their value” on luxuries and other articles of consumption.[^24.31] How the capitalists as a class are to perform that feat is a secret that vulgar economics has so far stubbornly refused to reveal. Enough that the world still jogs on, solely through the self-punishment of this modern penitent of Vishnu, the capitalist. Not only accumulation, but the simple “conservation of a capital requires a constant effort to resist the temptation of consuming it.”[^24.32] So the simple dictates of humanity plainly require that the capitalist be released from this martyrdom and temptation, in the same way that the Georgian slave-owner was lately delivered, by the abolition of slavery, from his painful dilemma: whether to squander the surplus-product lashed out of his niggers entirely on champagne, or to turn part of it back into more niggers and more land.

[^24.30]: “No one ... will sow his wheat, for instance, and allow it to remain a twelve month in the ground, or leave his wine in a cellar for years, instead of consuming these things or their equivalent at once ... unless he expects to acquire additional value, &c.” (Scrope, “Polit. Econ.,” edit. by A. Potter, New York, 1841, pp. 133-134.)

[^24.31]: “La privation que s’impose le capitalisté, en prêtant [The deprivation the capitalist imposes on himself by lending ...] (this euphemism is used in order to identify, by the approved method of vulgar economics, the worker who is exploited with the industrial capitalist who exploits, and to whom other capitalists lend money) ses instruments de production au travailleur, au lieu d’en consacrer la valeur à son propre usage, en la transforment en objets d’utilité ou d’agrément.” [his instruments of production to the worker, instead of devoting their value to his own use by turning it into useful or pleasant objects] (G. de Molinari, cited above, p. 36.)

[^24.32]: “La conservation d’un capital exige ... un effort constant pour résister a la tentation de le consommer.” [The conservation of a capital requires ... a constant effort to resist the temptation to consume it.] (Courcelle-Seneuil, cited above, p. 57.)

<!-- ch24-p073 -->
In economic forms of society of the most varied kinds, there is not only simple reproduction but also, in varying degrees, reproduction on an extended scale. Gradually more is produced and more is consumed, and so more products have to be turned into means of production. But this process does not appear as accumulation of capital, or as the function of a capitalist, as long as the worker’s means of production, and with them his product and means of subsistence, do not confront him in the shape of capital.[^24.33] Richard Jones, who died a few years ago and succeeded Malthus in the chair of political economy at Haileybury College, discusses this point well in the light of two important facts. Since the great mass of the Hindu population are peasants who cultivate their land themselves, their products, their instruments of labor and their means of subsistence never take “the shape of a fund saved from revenue, which fund has, therefore, gone through a previous process of accumulation.”[^24.34] On the other hand, in those provinces where English rule has least disturbed the old system, the non-agricultural workers are employed directly by the magnates, to whom a portion of the agricultural surplus-product is handed over as tribute or rent. The magnates consume one portion of this product in kind. The workers turn another portion, for the magnates’ use, into luxury articles and similar things. The rest forms the wages of the workers, who own their implements of labor. Here, production and reproduction on an extended scale go on their way without any intervention from that odd saint, that knight of the woeful countenance, the capitalist “abstainer.”

[^24.33]: “The particular classes of income which yield the most abundantly to the progress of national capital, change at different stages of their progress, and are, therefore, entirely different in nations occupying different positions in that progress.... Profits ... unimportant source of accumulation, compared with wages and rents, in the earlier stages of society.... When a considerable advance in the powers of national industry has actually taken place, profits rise into comparative importance as a source of accumulation.” (Richard Jones, “Textbook, &c.,” pp. 16, 21.)

[^24.34]: Cited above, p. 36, and following.

### Section 4: Circumstances that, Independently of the Proportional Division of Surplus-Value into Capital and Revenue, Determine the Amount of Accumulation. Degree of Exploitation of Labor-Power. Productivity of Labor. Growing Difference in Amount Between Capital Employed and Capital Consumed. Magnitude of Capital Advanced

<!-- ch24-p074 -->
If the proportion in which surplus-value splits into capital and revenue is given, then the size of the capital accumulated clearly depends on the absolute size of the surplus-value. Suppose that 80 percent were capitalized and 20 percent eaten up. Then the accumulated capital will be £2,400 or £200, depending on whether the total surplus-value has amounted to £3,000 or £500. Hence all the circumstances that determine the mass of surplus-value also work to determine the size of the accumulation. We sum them up once again here, but only to the extent that they offer new points of view on accumulation.

<!-- ch24-p075 -->
It will be remembered that the rate of surplus-value depends, in the first place, on the degree of exploitation of labor-power. Political economy values this fact so highly that it sometimes treats the speeding-up of accumulation that comes from increased productivity of labor (how much a given amount of labor produces in a given time) as the same thing as its speeding-up through increased exploitation of the worker.[^24.35] In the chapters on the production of surplus-value we constantly assumed that wages are at least equal to the value of labor-power (the value of the means of subsistence needed to keep the worker, and to raise the next generation of workers, able to work). In practice, however, the forcible reduction of wages below this value plays too important a part for us not to stop on it for a moment. Within certain limits, it in fact turns the worker’s necessary consumption fund into a fund for the accumulation of capital.

[^24.35]: “Ricardo says: ‘In different stages of society the accumulation of capital or of the means of employing’ (that is, exploiting) ‘labour is more or less rapid, and must in all cases depend on the productive powers of labour. The productive powers of labour are generally greatest where there is an abundance of fertile land.’ If, in the first sentence, the productive powers of labour mean the smallness of that aliquot part [fractional part] of any produce that goes to those whose manual labour produced it, the sentence is nearly identical, because the remaining aliquot part is the fund whence capital can, if the *owner pleases,* be accumulated. But then this does not generally happen, where there is most fertile land.” (“Observations on Certain Verbal Disputes, &c.” pp. 74, 75.)

<!-- ch24-p076 -->
> “Wages,” says John Stuart Mill, “have no productive power; they are the price of a productive power. Wages do not contribute, along with labour, to the production of commodities, no more than the price of tools contributes along with the tools themselves. If labour could be had without purchase, wages might be dispensed with.”[^24.36]

[^24.36]: J. Stuart Mill: “Essays on Some Unsettled Questions of Political Economy,” London, 1844, p. 90.

<!-- ch24-p077 -->
But if the workers could live on air, they could not be bought at any price. So zero cost for them is a limit in the mathematical sense: always out of reach, although we can always get closer and closer to it. The constant tendency of capital is to force the cost of labor back toward this zero. A writer of the 18th century whom we have often quoted already, the author of the “Essay on Trade and Commerce,” only gives away the innermost secret soul of English capitalism when he declares that England’s historic mission is to force English wages down to the level of the French and the Dutch.[^24.37] Among other things, he says naively:

[^24.37]: “An Essay on Trade and Commerce,” London, 1770, P. 44. In the same way, *The Times* of December, 1866, and January, 1867, published certain outpourings from the heart of the English mine-owner. They pictured the happy lot of the Belgian miners, who asked for and received no more than was strictly necessary for them to live for their “masters.” The Belgian workers have to suffer much, but to figure in *The Times* as model workers! At the beginning of February, 1867, the answer came: a strike of the Belgian miners at Marchienne, put down with powder and lead.

<!-- ch24-p078 -->
> “But if our poor” (the technical term for workers) “will live luxuriously ... then labour must, of course, be dear ... When it is considered what luxuries the manufacturing populace consume, such as brandy, gin, tea, sugar, foreign fruit, strong beer, printed linens, snuff, tobacco, &c.”[^24.38]

[^24.38]: Cited above, pp. 44, 46.

<!-- ch24-p079 -->
He quotes the work of a Northamptonshire manufacturer, who moans, with eyes squinting heavenward:

<!-- ch24-p080 -->
> “Labour is one-third cheaper in France than in England; for their poor work hard, and fare hard, as to their food and clothing. Their chief diet is bread, fruit, herbs, roots, and dried fish; for they very seldom eat flesh; and when wheat is dear, they eat very little bread.”[^24.39] “To which may be added,” our essayist goes on, “that their drink is either water or other small liquors [weak drinks], so that they spend very little money.... These things are very difficult to be brought about; but they are not impracticable, since they have been effected both in France and in Holland.”[^24.40]

[^24.39]: The Northamptonshire manufacturer commits a pious fraud, pardonable in someone whose heart is so full. In name he compares the life of the English and the French manufacturing worker. But in the words just quoted he is painting the French agricultural workers, as he himself confesses in his confused way.

[^24.40]: Cited above, pp. 70, 71. *Note in the 3rd German edition:* today, thanks to the competition on the world market that has been established since then, we have advanced much further. “If China,” says Mr. Stapleton, M.P., to his constituents, “should become a great manufacturing country, I do not see how the manufacturing population of Europe could sustain the contest without descending to the level of their competitors.” (*Times,* Sept. 3, 1873, p. 8.) The goal English capital longs for is no longer Continental wages, but Chinese ones.

<!-- ch24-p081 -->
Twenty years later, an American humbug, the Yankee turned baron, Benjamin Thompson (*alias* Count Rumford), followed the same line of philanthropy, to the great satisfaction of God and man. His “Essays” are a cookbook, with recipes of every kind for replacing the worker’s ordinary, expensive food with some substitute. Here is a particularly successful recipe from this wonderful philosopher:

<!-- ch24-p082 -->
> “5 lbs. of barleymeal, 7½d.; 5 lbs. of Indian corn [maize], 6¼d.; 3d. worth of red herring, 1d. salt, 1d. vinegar, 2d. pepper and sweet herbs, in all 20¾.; make a soup for 64 men, and at the medium price of barley and of Indian corn ... this soup may be provided at ¼d., the portion of 20 ounces.”[^24.41]

[^24.41]: Benjamin Thompson: “Essays, Political, Economical, and Philosophical, &c.,” 3 vols., London, 1796-1802, vol. i., p. 294. In his “The State of the Poor, or an History of the Labouring Classes in England, &c.,” Sir F. M. Eden strongly recommends the Rumfordian beggar-soup to workhouse overseers. He reproachfully warns the English workers that “many poor people, particularly in Scotland, live, and that very comfortably, for months together, upon oat-meal and barley-meal, mixed with only water and salt.” (Cited above, vol. i, book i., ch. 2, p. 503.) The same sort of hints come in the 19th century. “The most wholesome mixtures of flour having been refused (by the English agricultural labourer)... in Scotland, where education is better, this prejudice is, probably, unknown.” (Charles H. Parry, M. D., “The Question of the Necessity of the Existing Corn Laws Considered.” London, 1816, p. 69.) This same Parry, however, complains that the English worker is now (1815) in a much worse condition than in Eden’s time (1797.)

<!-- ch24-p083 -->
As capitalist production advanced, the adulteration of food made Thompson’s ideal unnecessary.[^24.42] At the end of the 18th century and during the first ten years of the 19th, the English farmers and landlords enforced the absolute minimum of wages. They did it by paying the agricultural workers less than the minimum in the form of wages, and the rest in the form of parish relief. Here is an example of the comical way in which the English Dogberries (after the constable in Shakespeare) went about their “legal” fixing of a scale of wages:

[^24.42]: The reports of the last Parliamentary Commission on the adulteration of means of subsistence show that in England even the adulteration of medicines is the rule, not the exception. For example, 34 samples of opium were bought from as many different pharmacists in London and examined. 31 of them turned out to be adulterated with poppy heads, wheat-flour, gum, clay, sand, etc. Several did not contain an atom of morphine.

<!-- ch24-p084 -->
> “The squires of Norfolk had dined, says Mr. Burke, when they fixed the rate of wages; the squires of Berks [Berkshire] evidently thought the labourers ought not to do so, when they fixed the rate of wages at Speenhamland, 1795.... There they decide that ‘income (weekly) should be 3s. for a man,’ when the gallon or half-peck loaf of 8 lbs. 11 oz. is at 1s., and increase regularly till bread is 1s. 5d.; when it is above that sum decrease regularly till it be at 2s., and then his food *should be* 1/5 th less.”[^24.43]

[^24.43]: G. B. Newnham (barrister-at-law): “A Review of the Evidence before the Committee of the two Houses of Parliament on the Corn Laws.” London, 1815, p. 20, *note.*

<!-- ch24-p085 -->
Before the Committee of Inquiry of the House of Lords, 1814, a certain A. Bennett, a large farmer, magistrate, poor-law guardian, and wage-regulator, was asked:

<!-- ch24-p086 -->
> “Has any proportion of the value of daily labour been made up to the labourers out of the poors’ rate?” Answer: “Yes, it has; the weekly income of every family is made up to the gallon loaf (8 lbs. 11 oz.), and 3d. per head!... The gallon loaf per week is what we suppose sufficient for the maintenance of every person in the family for the week; and the 3d. is for clothes, and if the parish think proper to find [provide] clothes; the 3d. is deducted. This practice goes through all the western part of Wiltshire, and, I believe, throughout the country.”[^24.44] “For years,” exclaims a bourgeois author of that time, “they (the farmers) have degraded a respectable class of their countrymen, by forcing them to have recourse to the workhouse ... the farmer, while increasing his own gains, has prevented any accumulation on the part of his labouring dependents.”[^24.45]

[^24.44]: Cited above, pp. 19, 20.

[^24.45]: C. H. Parry, cited above, pp. 77, 69. The landlords, for their part, not only “indemnified” themselves for the Anti-Jacobin War, which they waged in the name of England, but made themselves enormously rich. Their rents doubled, tripled, quadrupled, “and in one instance, increased sixfold in eighteen years.” (Cited above, pp. 100, 101.)

<!-- ch24-p087 -->
The so-called domestic industry has shown what part is played in our day by direct robbery from the worker’s necessary consumption fund in the formation of surplus-value, and therefore of capital’s accumulation fund. (Ch. xv., sect. 8, c.) Further facts on this subject will be given later.

<!-- ch24-p088 -->
In every branch of industry, the part of constant capital that consists of instruments of labor must be enough for a certain number of workers (a number fixed by the size of the business). Even so, it by no means always necessarily grows in the same proportion as the quantity of labor employed. Suppose that in a factory 100 workers working 8 hours a day yield 800 working hours. If the capitalist wants to raise this total by one half, he can employ 50 more workers. But then he must also advance more capital, not just for wages but for instruments of labor. He might, however, also let the 100 workers work 12 hours instead of 8, and then the instruments of labor already on hand would be enough. They would simply be used up faster. So additional labor, produced by a greater strain on labor-power, can increase the surplus-product and surplus-value (that is, the material of accumulation) without a matching increase in the constant part of capital.

<!-- ch24-p089 -->
In the extractive industries, such as mines, etc., the raw materials form no part of the capital advanced. Here the object of labor is not a product of earlier labor. Nature provides it free of charge, as with metals, minerals, coal, stone, etc. In these cases constant capital consists almost entirely of instruments of labor, which can very well absorb an increased quantity of labor (day and night shifts of workers, for example). Other things being equal, the mass and the value of the product will rise in direct proportion to the labor spent. As on the first day of production, the two original makers of products, man and Nature, now turned into the creators of the material elements of capital, still work together. Thanks to the elasticity of labor-power, the field of accumulation has widened without any previous enlargement of constant capital.

<!-- ch24-p090 -->
In agriculture, the land under cultivation cannot be increased without advancing more seed and manure. But once this advance is made, the purely mechanical working of the soil itself has a marvelous effect on the amount of the product. So a greater quantity of labor, done by the same number of workers as before, increases the fertility without requiring any new advance in instruments of labor. Once again it is the direct action of man on Nature that becomes an immediate source of greater accumulation, without any new capital stepping in.

<!-- ch24-p091 -->
Finally, in what is called manufacturing industry, every additional expenditure of labor presupposes a matching additional expenditure of raw materials, but not necessarily of instruments of labor. And since extractive industry and agriculture supply manufacturing industry with its raw materials and with those of its instruments of labor, the additional product that extractive industry and agriculture have created without an additional advance of capital also works in favor of manufacturing industry.

<!-- ch24-p092 -->
General result: by taking into itself the two primary creators of wealth, labor-power and the land, capital gains a power of expansion. This power lets it increase the elements of its accumulation beyond the limits apparently set by its own size, or by the value and the mass of the already-produced means of production in which it exists.

<!-- ch24-p093 -->
Another important factor in the accumulation of capital is the degree of productivity of social labor.

<!-- ch24-p094 -->
As the productive power of labor increases, so does the mass of products in which a certain value, and therefore a surplus-value of a given size, is embodied. If the rate of surplus-value stays the same, or even falls, as long as it falls more slowly than the productive power of labor rises, the mass of the surplus-product increases. If the division of this product into revenue and additional capital stays the same, the capitalist’s consumption may therefore increase without any decrease in the accumulation fund. The relative size of the accumulation fund may even increase at the expense of the consumption fund, while the cheapening of commodities puts at the capitalist’s disposal as many means of enjoyment as before, or even more. But, as we have seen, the growing productivity of labor goes hand in hand with the cheapening of the worker, and therefore with a higher rate of surplus-value, even when real wages are rising. Real wages never rise in proportion to the productive power of labor. So the same value in variable capital sets in motion more labor-power, and therefore more labor. The same value in constant capital is embodied in more means of production, that is, in more instruments of labor, materials of labor, and auxiliary materials. So it also supplies more elements for producing both use-value and value, and with them more absorbers of labor. Therefore, even if the value of the additional capital stays the same or even shrinks, accumulation still speeds up. Not only does the scale of reproduction grow materially, but the production of surplus-value grows faster than the value of the additional capital.

<!-- ch24-p095 -->
The development of the productive power of labor also acts back on the original capital already engaged in the process of production. Part of the functioning constant capital consists of instruments of labor, such as machinery, etc., which are not used up, and so not reproduced or replaced by new ones of the same kind, until after long periods of time. But every year part of these instruments of labor perishes or reaches the limit of its productive working life. So in that year it reaches the time for its periodic reproduction, its replacement by new ones of the same kind. If the productivity of labor has increased while these instruments of labor were being used up (and it develops continually with the unbroken advance of science and technology), more efficient and (considering their greater efficiency) cheaper machines, tools, apparatus, etc., replace the old ones. The old capital is reproduced in a more productive form, quite apart from the constant small improvements in the instruments of labor already in use. The other part of constant capital, raw material and auxiliary substances, is constantly reproduced in less than a year; those produced by agriculture, mostly once a year. So every introduction of improved methods acts almost at the same time on the new capital and on the capital already at work. Every advance in Chemistry does more than multiply the number of useful materials and the useful applications of those already known, and so widen capital’s field of investment as capital grows. At the same time it teaches how to throw the excrements of the processes of production and consumption back into the cycle of the process of reproduction. In this way, without any previous outlay of capital, it creates new material for capital. Like the increased exploitation of natural wealth by merely straining labor-power harder, science and technology give capital a power of expansion that does not depend on the given size of the capital actually functioning. At the same time they act on that part of the original capital which has reached its stage of renewal. In passing into its new shape, this part takes in, free of charge, the social progress made while its old shape was being used up. Of course, this development of productive power goes along with a partial depreciation of functioning capital. To the extent that this depreciation is sharply felt in competition, the burden falls on the worker, in whose increased exploitation the capitalist looks for compensation.

<!-- ch24-p096 -->
Labor passes on to its product the value of the means of production it uses up. On the other hand, the value and mass of the means of production set in motion by a given quantity of labor increase as the labor becomes more productive. Although the same quantity of labor always adds only the same sum of new value to its products, the old capital value that labor passes on to the products still increases as the productivity of labor grows.

<!-- ch24-p097 -->
For example, an English spinner and a Chinese spinner may work the same number of hours with the same intensity. Then in a week they will both create equal values. But in spite of this equality, there will be an immense difference between the value of the week’s product of the Englishman, who works with a mighty automatic machine, and that of the Chinese spinner, who has only a spinning-wheel. In the time the Chinese spinner spins one pound of cotton, the Englishman spins several hundreds of pounds. A sum of old values many hundred times as great swells the value of the Englishman’s product. In it those old values reappear in a new, useful form, and so can function again as capital.

<!-- ch24-p098 -->
> “In 1782,” as Frederick Engels teaches us, “all the wool crop in England of the three preceding years, lay untouched for want of labourers, and so it must have lain, if newly invented machinery had not come to its aid and spun it.”[^24.46]

[^24.46]: Friedrich Engels, “Lage der arbeitenden Klasse in England,” p. 20.

<!-- ch24-p099 -->
Labor embodied in the form of machinery did not, of course, directly call a single man into life. But it made it possible for a smaller number of workers, adding relatively less living labor, not only to consume the wool productively and put new value into it, but also to preserve its old value in the form of yarn, etc. At the same time, it caused and stimulated increased reproduction of wool. It is the natural property of living labor to pass on old value while it creates new value. Hence, as the efficiency, extent, and value of its means of production increase, and so with the accumulation that goes along with the development of its productive power, labor keeps up and perpetuates an ever-growing capital value in an ever-new form.”[^24.47] This natural power of labor appears as a built-in property of capital, in which labor is incorporated, just as the productive forces of social labor appear as inherent properties of capital, and as the capitalists’ constant appropriation of surplus labor appears as a constant self-expansion of capital.

[^24.47]: Classical economics, because of a faulty analysis of the labor process and of the process of creating value, has never properly grasped this important element of reproduction, as can be seen in Ricardo. He says, for example, that whatever the change in productive power, “a million men always produce in manufactures the same value.” This is accurate if the length and degree of intensity of their labor are given. But it does not prevent (and this Ricardo overlooks in certain conclusions he draws) a million men whose labor has different degrees of productivity from turning very different masses of means of production into products, and so preserving very different masses of value in their products. As a result, the values of the products they yield may vary considerably. Ricardo, it may be noted in passing, tried in vain to use that very example to make clear to J. B. Say the difference between use-value (which he here calls wealth or material riches) and exchange-value. Say answers: “Quant à la difficulté qu’élève Mr. Ricardo en disant que, par des procédés mieux entendus un million de personnes peuvent produire deux fois, trois fois autant de richesses, sans produire plus de valeurs, cette difficulté n’est pas une lorsque l’on considére, ainsi qu’on le doit, la production comme un échange dans lequel on donne les services productifs de son travail, de sa terre, et de ses capitaux, pour obtenir des produits. C’est par le moyen de ces services productifs, que nous acquérons tous les produits qui sont au monde. Or... nous sommes d’autant plus riches, nos services productifs ont d’autant plus de valeur qu’ils obtiennent dans l’échange appelé production une plus grande quantité de choses utiles.” [As for the difficulty Mr. Ricardo raises when he says that, by better-understood methods, a million people can produce two times, three times as much wealth without producing more values, this difficulty is none when one considers, as one should, production as an exchange in which one gives the productive services of one’s labor, one’s land, and one’s capital in order to obtain products. It is by means of these productive services that we acquire all the products that are in the world. Now ... we are the richer, our productive services have the more value, the greater the quantity of useful things they obtain in the exchange called production.] (J. B. Say, “Lettres à M. Malthus,” Paris, 1820, pp. 168, 169.) The “difficulté” [difficulty] – it exists for him, not for Ricardo – that Say means to clear up is this: Why does the exchange-value of use-values not increase when their quantity increases because of an increased productive power of labor? Answer: the difficulty is met by calling use-value exchange-value, if you please. Exchange-value is a thing that is connected one way or another with exchange. So if production is called an exchange of labor and means of production for the product, it is as clear as day that you get more exchange-value in proportion as production yields more use-value. In other words, the more use-values, for example stockings, a working day (the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor) yields to the stocking-manufacturer, the richer he is in stockings. Suddenly, however, Say remembers that “with a greater quantity” of stockings their “price” (which of course has nothing to do with their exchange-value!) falls “parce que la concurrence les (les producteurs) oblige à donner les produits pour ce qu’ils leur coûtent... [because competition obliges them (the producers) to give up the products for what they cost them] But where does the profit come from, if the capitalist sells the commodities at cost-price? Never mind! Say declares that, as a result of increased productivity, everyone now receives two pairs of stockings in return for a given equivalent instead of one as before. The result he arrives at is precisely the proposition of Ricardo that he set out to disprove. After this mighty effort of thought, he triumphantly addresses Malthus in these words: “Telle est, monsieur, la doctrine bien liée, sans laquelle il est impossible, je le déclare, d’expliquer les plus grandes difficultés de l’économie politique, et notamment, comment il se peut qu’une nation soit plus riche lorsque ses produits diminuent de valeur, quoique la richesse soit de la valeur.” [Such, Sir, is the well-connected doctrine without which it is impossible, I declare, to explain the greatest difficulties of political economy, and in particular how it can be that a nation is richer when its products fall in value, although wealth is value.] (Cited above, p. 170.) An English economist remarks on the conjuring tricks of the same kind that appear in Say’s “Lettres”: “Those affected ways of talking make up in general that which M. Say is pleased to call his doctrine and which he earnestly urges Malthus to teach at Hertford, as it is already taught ‘dans plusieurs parties de l’Europe.’ He says, ‘Si vous trouvez une physionomie de paradoxe à toutes ces propositions, voyez les choses qu’elles expriment, et j’ose croire qu’elles vous paraîtront fort simples et fort raisonnables.’ [in several parts of Europe ... If you find all these propositions look like a paradox, look at the things they express, and I dare to believe that they will seem to you very simple and very reasonable] Doubtless, and in consequence of the same process, they will appear everything else, except original.” (“An Inquiry into those Principles Respecting the Nature of Demand, &c.,” pp. 116, 110.)

<!-- ch24-p100 -->
As capital grows, the difference between the capital employed and the capital consumed grows. In other words, there is an increase in the value and the material mass of the instruments of labor: buildings, machinery, drain-pipes, working cattle, and apparatus of every kind. These function for a longer or shorter time in processes of production that are constantly repeated, or serve to achieve particular useful effects, while they themselves wear out only gradually. So they lose their value only piece by piece, and so pass that value on to the product only bit by bit. To the same extent that these instruments of labor serve as makers of products without adding value to the product, that is, to the extent that they are wholly employed but only partly consumed, they perform, as we saw earlier, the same free service as the natural forces, water, steam, air, electricity, etc. This free service of past labor, when it is seized and filled with a soul by living labor, increases with the advancing stages of accumulation.

<!-- ch24-p101 -->
Past labor always disguises itself as capital. That is, the passive of the labor of A, B, C, etc., takes the form of the active of the non-worker X. Because of this, bourgeois and political economists are full of praise for the services of dead and gone labor, which, according to the Scottish genius MacCulloch, ought to receive a special remuneration in the shape of interest, profit, etc.[^24.48] So the powerful and ever-growing help that past labor gives to the living labor process, in the form of means of production, is credited to that form of past labor in which it is alienated from the worker himself as unpaid labor, that is, to its capitalist form. The practical agents of capitalist production and their petty, quibbling ideologists are as unable to think of the means of production as separate from the antagonistic social mask they wear today as a slave-owner is unable to think of the worker himself as distinct from his character as a slave.

[^24.48]: MacCulloch took out a patent on “wages of past labour” long before Senior did on “wages of abstinence.”

<!-- ch24-p102 -->
With a given degree of exploitation of labor-power, the mass of surplus-value produced is determined by the number of workers exploited at the same time. This number corresponds, although in varying proportions, to the size of the capital. So the more capital grows through successive accumulations, the more the sum of value grows that is divided into the consumption fund and the accumulation fund. The capitalist can therefore live a jollier life and at the same time show more “abstinence.” And finally, all the springs of production act with greater elasticity the more their scale extends with the mass of capital advanced.

### Section 5: The So-Called Labor Fund

<!-- ch24-p103 -->
We have shown in the course of this inquiry that capital is not a fixed magnitude. It is a part of social wealth that is elastic and constantly fluctuates with the division of fresh surplus-value into revenue and additional capital. We have also seen that, even when the magnitude of the functioning capital is given, the labor-power, the science, and the land (by which, in economic terms, we are to understand all the conditions of labor that Nature supplies independently of man) embodied in it form elastic powers of capital. Within certain limits, these allow capital a field of action independent of its own magnitude. In this inquiry we have left aside all effects of the process of circulation, effects which may give the same mass of capital very different degrees of efficiency. And since we assumed the limits set by capitalist production, that is, assumed the process of social production in a form that has developed by purely spontaneous growth, we left aside any more rational combination that could be carried out directly and systematically with the means of production and the mass of labor-power now available. Classical economics always loved to think of social capital as a fixed magnitude with a fixed degree of efficiency. But it was the arch-Philistine Jeremy Bentham, that dull, pedantic, leather-tongued oracle of the ordinary bourgeois intelligence of the 19th century, who first set up this prejudice as a dogma.[^24.49] Bentham is among philosophers what Martin Tupper (author of the popular verse book *Proverbial Philosophy*) is among poets. Both could only have been manufactured in England.[^24.50] In the light of his dogma, the commonest phenomena of the process of production, for example its sudden expansions and contractions, and indeed even accumulation itself, become completely inconceivable.[^24.51] Bentham himself, as well as Malthus, James Mill, MacCulloch, etc., used the dogma for an apologetic purpose, that is, in defense of the system. Above all they used it to represent one part of capital as a fixed magnitude, namely variable capital, the part that can be converted into labor-power. The material of variable capital, that is, the mass of means of subsistence it represents for the worker, or the so-called labor fund, was presented in a fable as a separate part of social wealth, fixed by natural laws and unchangeable. To set in motion the part of social wealth that is to function as constant capital, or, to put it in material form, as means of production, a definite mass of living labor is required. This mass is given by technology. But the number of workers required to set this mass of labor-power flowing is not given (it changes with the degree of exploitation of the individual labor-power). Nor is the price of this labor-power given. Only its minimum limit is given, and even that is very variable. The facts that lie at the bottom of this dogma are these. On the one hand, the worker has no right to interfere in the division of social wealth into means of enjoyment for the non-worker and means of production.[^24.52] On the other hand, only in favorable and exceptional cases does the worker have the power to enlarge the so-called labor fund at the expense of the “revenue” of the wealthy.

[^24.49]: Compare, among others, Jeremy Bentham: “Théorie des Peines et des Récompenses,” traduct. d’Et. Dumont, 3ème édit. Paris, 1826, t. II, L. IV., ch. II.

[^24.50]: Bentham is a purely English phenomenon. Not even excepting our own philosopher, Christian Wolff, never in any age or any country has the most homespun commonplace strutted about so self-satisfied. The principle of utility was not Bentham's discovery. He simply reproduced, in his dull way, what Helvétius and other Frenchmen had said with wit in the 18th century. To know what is useful for a dog, one must study dog-nature. This nature itself cannot be deduced from the principle of utility. Applying this to man: whoever wants to criticize all human acts, movements, relations, etc., by the principle of utility must first deal with human nature in general, and then with human nature as modified in each historical epoch. Bentham makes short work of it. With the driest naïveté he takes the modern shopkeeper, especially the English shopkeeper, as the normal man. Whatever is useful to this odd normal man, and to his world, is absolutely useful. This yard-measure, then, he applies to past, present, and future. The Christian religion, for example, is “useful,” “because it forbids in the name of religion the same faults that the penal code condemns in the name of the law.” Artistic criticism is “harmful,” because it disturbs worthy people in their enjoyment of Martin Tupper, etc. With such rubbish the brave fellow, whose motto was “nuila dies sine line!” [No day without a line!], has piled up mountains of books. If I had the courage of my friend Heinrich Heine, I would call Mr. Jeremy a genius in the way of bourgeois stupidity.

[^24.51]: “Political economists are too apt to consider a certain quantity of capital and a certain number of labourers as productive instruments of uniform power, or operating with a certain uniform intensity.... Those... who maintain ... that commodities are the sole agents of production ... prove that production could never be enlarged, for it requires as an indispensable condition to such an enlargement that food, raw materials, and tools should be previously augmented; which is in fact maintaining that no increase of production can take place without a previous increase, or, in other words, that an increase is impossible.” (S. Bailey: “Money and its Vicissitudes,” pp. 58 and 70.) Bailey criticizes the dogma mainly from the point of view of the process of circulation.

[^24.52]: John Stuart Mill, in his “Principles of Political Economy,” says: “The really exhausting and the really repulsive labours instead of being better paid than others, are almost invariably paid the worst of all.... The more revolting the occupation, the more certain it is to receive the minimum of remuneration.... The hardships and the earnings, instead of being directly proportional, as in any just arrangements of society they would be, are generally in an inverse ratio to one another.” To avoid misunderstanding, let me say this: although men like John Stuart Mill are to blame for the contradiction between their traditional economic dogmas and their modern tendencies, it would be very wrong to class them with the herd of vulgar economic apologists.

<!-- ch24-p104 -->
What silly tautology results from trying to present the capitalist limits of the labor fund as its natural and social limits can be seen, for example, in Professor Fawcett.[^24.53]

[^24.53]: H. Fawcett, Professor of Political Economy at Cambridge. “The Economic position of the British labourer.” London, 1865, p. 120.

<!-- ch24-p105 -->
> “The circulating capital of a country,” he says, “is its wage-fund. Hence, if we desire to calculate the average money wages received by each labourer, we have simply to divide the amount of this capital by the number of the labouring population.”[^24.54]

[^24.54]: I must remind the reader here that I was the first to use the categories “variable and constant capital.” Since the time of Adam Smith, political economy has confusedly mixed up the essential distinctions involved in these categories with the merely formal differences between fixed and circulating capital, which arise out of the process of circulation. For further details on this point, see Book II., Part II.

<!-- ch24-p106 -->
That is to say, we first add together the individual wages actually paid. Then we declare that the sum we get forms the total value of the “labor fund” fixed and granted to us by God and Nature. Lastly, we divide the sum thus obtained by the number of workers, to find out again how much may come to each on average. An uncommonly clever dodge, this. It did not stop Mr. Fawcett from saying in the same breath:

<!-- ch24-p107 -->
“The aggregate wealth which is annually saved in England, is divided into two portions; one portion is employed as capital to maintain our industry, and the other portion is exported to foreign countries... Only a portion, and perhaps, not a large portion of the wealth which is annually saved in this country, is invested in our own industry.[^24.55]

[^24.55]: Fawcett, cited above, pp. 122, 123.

<!-- ch24-p108 -->
The greater part of the surplus-product that accrues each year is embezzled from the English worker, because it is taken from him without any equivalent being returned. This greater part is thus used as capital, not in England, but in foreign countries. But along with the additional capital exported in this way, a part of the “labor fund” invented by God and Bentham is also exported.[^24.56]

[^24.56]: It might be said that not only capital, but also workers, in the form of emigrants, are exported from England every year. In the text, however, there is no question of the *peculium* [the small property a slave was allowed to keep] of the emigrants, a great part of whom are not workers. Farmers' sons make up a great part of them. The additional capital transported abroad each year to be put out at interest is in much greater proportion to the annual accumulation than the yearly emigration is to the yearly increase of population.

## Chapter 25: The General Law of Capitalist Accumulation

### Section 1: The Increased Demand for labor power that Accompanies Accumulation, the Composition of Capital Remaining the same

<!-- ch25-p001 -->
In this chapter we consider how the growth of capital (value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger) affects the lot of the working class. The most important factor in this inquiry is the composition of capital and the changes it goes through in the course of the process of accumulation (turning surplus-value back into capital, so that capital grows).

<!-- ch25-p002 -->
The composition of capital is to be understood in a two-fold sense. On the side of value, it is fixed by the proportion in which capital is divided into constant capital, or the value of the means of production, and variable capital, or the value of labor-power, the sum total of wages. Here value means what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time. The means of production are the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things. Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist. The value of labor-power is the value of the means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live) needed to keep the worker, and to raise the next generation of workers, able to work. Wages are the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself. On the side of material, as it functions in the process of production, all capital is divided into means of production and living labor-power. This second composition is fixed by the relation between the mass of the means of production employed, on the one hand, and the mass of labor needed to employ them, on the other. I call the first the *value-composition* of capital, and the second its *technical composition*.

<!-- ch25-p003 -->
There is a strict correlation between the two. To express it, I call the value composition of capital, insofar as it is determined by its technical composition and mirrors the changes in that technical composition, the *organic composition* of capital. Wherever I speak of the composition of capital without further qualification, its organic composition is always meant.

<!-- ch25-p004 -->
The many individual capitals invested in a particular branch of production have compositions that differ, more or less, from one another. The average of their individual compositions gives us the composition of the total capital in this branch of production. Lastly, the average of these averages, across all branches of production, gives us the composition of the total social capital of a country. In the last resort, it is with this alone that we are concerned in the investigation that follows.

<!-- ch25-p005 -->
Growth of capital involves growth of its variable part, the part invested in labor-power. A part of the surplus-value (the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it) that is turned into additional capital must always be turned back into variable capital, or additional labor fund. Let us suppose that, all other circumstances remaining the same, the composition of capital also remains constant (that is, that a definite mass of means of production always needs the same mass of labor-power to set it in motion). Then the demand for labor and the subsistence-fund of the workers clearly increase in the same proportion as the capital, and the faster the capital increases, the faster they increase. The capital produces a surplus-value every year, and one part of it is added to the original capital every year. This increment itself grows every year along with the growth of the capital already functioning. Lastly, under a special stimulus to getting rich, such as the opening of new markets, or of new spheres for investing capital as a result of newly developed social wants, etc., the scale of accumulation may be suddenly extended, merely by a change in the way the surplus-value or surplus-product is divided into capital and revenue. Because of all this, the requirements of accumulating capital may exceed the increase of labor-power or of the number of workers; the demand for workers may exceed the supply, and so wages may rise. Indeed, this must ultimately be the case if the conditions supposed above continue. For since more workers are employed in each year than in the year before, sooner or later a point must be reached at which the requirements of accumulation begin to outrun the customary supply of labor, and so a rise of wages takes place. A lament on this score was heard in England during the whole of the fifteenth century and the first half of the eighteenth. The more or less favorable circumstances in which the wage-working class supports and multiplies itself in no way alter the fundamental character of capitalist production. Simple reproduction (production repeated on the same scale, with the capitalist consuming all the surplus-value) constantly reproduces the capital relation itself, that is, the relation of capitalists on the one side and wage workers on the other. In the same way, reproduction on an extended scale, that is, accumulation, reproduces the capital relation on an extended scale: more capitalists, or larger capitalists, at this pole, more wage workers at that one. The reproduction of a mass of labor-power is, in fact, an essential part of the reproduction of capital itself. This labor-power must constantly re-incorporate itself into capital, for that capital's self-expansion. It cannot get free from capital, and its enslavement to capital is only concealed by the variety of individual capitalists to whom it sells itself. Accumulation of capital is, therefore, increase of the proletariat (the class of wage workers, who own nothing they can live by except their labor-power).[^25.1]

[^25.1]: Karl Marx, cited above. “A égalité d’oppression des masses, plus un pays a de prolétaires et plus il est riche.” [With the oppression of the masses being equal, the more proletarians a country has, the richer it is.] (Colins, “L’Economie Politique. Source des Révolutions et des Utopies, prétendues Socialistes.” Paris, 1857, t. III., p. 331.) Our “prolétarian” is, economically, none other than the wage worker who produces and increases capital, and who is thrown out on the streets as soon as he is superfluous to the needs of growth of “Monsieur capital,” as Pecqueur calls this person. “The sickly proletarian of the primitive forest” is a pretty Roscherian fancy. The primitive forester owns the primitive forest, and uses the primitive forest as his property with the freedom of an orangutan. So he is not a proletarian. He would only be one if the primitive forest exploited him, instead of being exploited by him. As far as his health is concerned, such a man would compare well, not only with the modern proletarian, but also with the syphilitic and scrofulous (tubercular) upper classes. But no doubt Herr Wilhelm Roscher means by “primitive forest” his native heath of Lüneburg.

<!-- ch25-p006 -->
Classical economics (the economists from Petty to Ricardo who investigated the real relations of production) grasped this fact so thoroughly that Adam Smith, Ricardo, etc., as mentioned earlier, inaccurately identified accumulation with the consumption of the whole capitalized part of the surplus-product by productive workers, or with its transformation into additional wage workers. As early as 1696 John Bellers says:

<!-- ch25-p007 -->
> “For if one had a hundred thousand acres of land and as many pounds in money, and as many cattle, without a labourer, what would the rich man be, but a labourer? And as the labourers make men rich, so the more labourers there will be, the more rich men ... the labour of the poor being the mines of the rich.”[^25.2]

[^25.2]: John Bellers, cited above, p. 2.

<!-- ch25-p008 -->
So too Bernard de Mandeville, at the beginning of the eighteenth century:

<!-- ch25-p009 -->
> “It would be easier, where property is well secured, to live without money than without poor; for who would do the work? ... As they [the poor] ought to be kept from starving, so they should receive nothing worth saving. If here and there one of the lowest class by uncommon industry, and pinching his belly, lifts himself above the condition he was brought up in, nobody ought to hinder him; nay, it is undeniably the wisest course for every person in the society, and for every private family to be frugal; but it is the interest of all rich nations, that the greatest part of the poor should almost never be idle, and yet continually spend what they get.... Those that get their living by their daily labour ... have nothing to stir them up to be serviceable but their wants which it is prudence to relieve, but folly to cure. The only thing then that can render the labouring man industrious, is a moderate quantity of money, for as too little will, according as his temper is, either dispirit or make him desperate, so too much will make him insolent and lazy.... From what has been said, it is manifest, that, in a free nation, where slaves are not allowed of, the surest wealth consists in a multitude of laborious poor; for besides, that they are the never-failing nursery of fleets and armies, without them there could be no enjoyment, and no product of any country could be valuable. “To make the society” [which of course consists of non-workers] “happy and people easier under the meanest circumstances, it is requisite that great numbers of them should be ignorant as well as poor; knowledge both enlarges and multiplies our desires, and the fewer things a man wishes for, the more easily his necessities may be supplied.”[^25.3]

[^25.3]: Bernard de Mandeville: “The Fable of the Bees,” 5th edition, London, 1728. Remarks, pp. 212, 213, 328. “Temperate living and constant employment is the direct road, for the poor, to rational happiness” [by which he most probably means long working days and scant means of subsistence], “and to riches and strength for the state” (namely, for the landlords, capitalists, and their political dignitaries and agents). (“An Essay on Trade and Commerce,” London, 1770, p. 54.)

<!-- ch25-p010 -->
What Mandeville, an honest, clear-headed man, had not yet seen is that the mechanism of the process of accumulation itself increases, along with the capital, the mass of the “labouring poor,” that is, the wage workers. They turn their labor-power into an increasing power of self-expansion of the growing capital, and even by doing so they must make eternal their relation of dependence on their own product, as personified in the capitalists.
