On this relation of dependence, Sir F. M. Eden, in his “The State of the Poor, an History of the Labouring Classes in England,” says,

<!-- ch25-p011 -->
> “the natural produce of our soil is certainly not fully adequate to our subsistence; we can neither be clothed, lodged nor fed but in consequence of some previous labour. A portion at least of the society must be indefatigably employed .... There are others who, though they ‘neither toil nor spin,’ can yet command the produce of industry, but who owe their exemption from labour solely to civilisation and order .... They are peculiarly the creatures of civil institutions,[^25.4] which have recognised that individuals may acquire property by various other means besides the exertion of labour.... Persons of independent fortune ... owe their superior advantages by no means to any superior abilities of their own, but almost entirely ... to the industry of others. It is not the possession of land, or of money, but the command of labour which distinguishes the opulent from the labouring part of the community .... This [scheme approved by Eden] would give the people of property sufficient (but by no means too much) influence and authority over those who ... work for them; and it would place such labourers, not in an abject or servile condition, but in such a state of easy and liberal dependence as all who know human nature, and its history, will allow to be necessary for their own comfort.”[^25.5]

[^25.4]: Eden should have asked: whose creatures, then, are “the civil institutions”? From his standpoint of legal illusion, he does not regard the law as a product of the material relations of production, but, the other way round, the relations of production as products of the law. Linguet overthrew Montesquieu’s illusory “Esprit des lois” with one word: “ L’esprit des lois, c’est la propriété.” [The spirit of the laws is property.]

[^25.5]: Eden, cited above, Vol. 1, book I., chapter 1, pp. 1, 2, and preface, p. xx.

<!-- ch25-p012 -->
Sir F. M. Eden, it may be noted in passing, is the only follower of Adam Smith during the eighteenth century who produced any work of importance.[^25.6]

[^25.6]: If the reader reminds me of Malthus, whose “Essay on Population” appeared in 1798, I remind him that this work, in its first form, is nothing more than a schoolboyish, superficial plagiarism of De Foe, Sir James Steuart, Townsend, Franklin, Wallace, etc., and does not contain a single sentence thought out by himself. The great sensation this pamphlet caused was due solely to party interest. The French Revolution had found passionate defenders in the United Kingdom. The “principle of population” had been slowly worked out in the eighteenth century. Then, in the midst of a great social crisis, it was proclaimed with drums and trumpets as the infallible antidote to the teachings of Condorcet, etc., and the English oligarchy greeted it with jubilation as the great destroyer of all hankerings after human development. Malthus, hugely astonished at his success, set about stuffing his book with materials superficially compiled, and adding to it new matter, not discovered but annexed by him. Note further: although Malthus was a parson of the English State Church, he had taken the monastic vow of celibacy — one of the conditions of holding a Fellowship in Protestant Cambridge University: “Socios collegiorum maritos esse non permittimus, sed statim postquam quis uxorem duxerit socius collegii desinat esse.” [We do not permit fellows of colleges to be married, but as soon as anyone has taken a wife, let him cease to be a fellow of the college.] (“Reports of Cambridge University Commission,” p. 172.) This circumstance favorably distinguishes Malthus from the other Protestant parsons. They have shrugged off the command of celibacy for the priesthood, and have taken “Be fruitful and multiply” as their special Biblical mission to such a degree that they generally contribute to the increase of population to a really unbecoming extent, while at the same time they preach the “principle of population” to the workers. It is characteristic that the economic fall of man, the Adam’s apple, the urgent appetite, “the checks which tend to blunt the shafts of Cupid,” as Parson Townsend waggishly puts it — that this delicate question was and is monopolized by the Reverends of Protestant Theology, or rather of the Protestant Church. With the exception of the Venetian monk Ortes, an original and clever writer, most of the teachers of population theory are Protestant parsons. For instance, Bruckner, “Théorie du Système animal,” Leyde, 1767, in which the whole subject of the modern population theory is exhausted, and to which the passing quarrel between Quesnay and his pupil, the elder Mirabeau, supplied ideas on the same topic; then Parson Wallace, Parson Townsend, Parson Malthus and his pupil, the arch-Parson Thomas Chalmers, to say nothing of lesser reverend scribblers in this line. Originally, political economy (the science of economics as it was then called) was studied by philosophers like Hobbes, Locke, Hume; by businessmen and statesmen like Thomas More, Temple, Sully, De Witt, North, Law, Vanderlint, Cantillon, Franklin; and especially, and with the greatest success, by medical men like Petty, Barbon, Mandeville, Quesnay. Even in the middle of the eighteenth century, the Rev. Mr. Tucker, a notable economist of his time, apologized for meddling with the things of Mammon. Later on, and in truth with this very “Principle of population,” the hour of the Protestant parsons struck. Petty regarded the population as the basis of wealth, and was, like Adam Smith, an outspoken enemy of parsons. As if he had a presentiment of their bungling interference, he says “that Religion best flourishes when the Priests are most mortified [held down by self-denial], as was before said of the Law, which best flourisheth when lawyers have least to do.” So he advises the Protestant priests, if they will not, once and for all, follow the Apostle Paul and “mortify” themselves by celibacy, “not to breed more Churchmen than the Benefices [paid church posts], as they now stand shared out, will receive, that is to say, if there be places for about twelve thousand in England and Wales, it will not be safe to breed up 24,000 ministers, for then the twelve thousand which are unprovided for, will seek ways how to get themselves a livelihood, which they cannot do more easily than by persuading the people that the twelve thousand incumbents do poison or starve their souls, and misguide them in their way to Heaven.” (Petty: “A Treatise of Taxes and Contributions,” London, 1667, p. 57.) Adam Smith’s position with the Protestant priesthood of his time is shown by the following. In “A Letter to A. Smith, L.L.D. On the Life, Death, and Philosophy of his Friend, David Hume. By one of the People called Christians,” 4th Edition, Oxford, 1784, Dr. Horne, Bishop of Norwich, reproves Adam Smith: because in a published letter to Mr. Strahan he “embalmed his friend David” (namely, Hume); because he told the world how “Hume amused himself on his deathbed with Lucian and Whist”; and because he even had the impudence to write of Hume: “I have always considered him, both in his life-time and since his death, as approaching as nearly to the idea of a perfectly wise and virtuous man, as, perhaps, the nature of human frailty will permit.” The bishop cries out in a passion: “Is it right in you, Sir, to hold up to our view as ‘perfectly wise and virtuous,’ the *character* and *conduct* of one, who seems to have been possessed with an incurable antipathy to all that is called *Religion;* and who strained every nerve to explode, suppress and extirpate the spirit of it among men, that its very name, if he could effect it, might no more be had in remembrance?” (cited above, p. 8.) “But let not the lovers of truth be discouraged. Atheism cannot be of long continuance.” (P. 17.) Adam Smith, “had the atrocious wickedness to propagate atheism through the land (viz., by his “Theory of Moral Sentiments”). Upon the whole, Doctor, your meaning is good; but I think you will not succeed this time. You would persuade us, by the example of *David Hume, Esq.,* that atheism is the only cordial for low spirits, and the proper antidote against the fear of death.... You may smile over *Babylon* in ruins and congratulate the hardened *Pharaoh* on his overthrow in the Red Sea.” (cited above, pp. 21, 22.) One orthodox individual among Adam Smith’s college friends writes after his death: “Smith’s well-placed affection for Hume ... hindered him from being a Christian.... When he met with honest men whom he liked ... he would believe almost anything they said. Had he been a friend of the worthy ingenious Horrox he would have believed that the moon some times disappeared in a clear sky without the interposition of a cloud.... He approached to republicanism in his political principles.” (“The Bee.” By James Anderson, 18 Vols., Vol. 3, pp. 166, 165, Edinburgh, 1791-93.) Parson Thomas Chalmers suspects that Adam Smith invented the category of “unproductive labourers” solely for the Protestant parsons, in spite of their blessed work in the vineyard of the Lord.

<!-- ch25-p013 -->
Under the conditions of accumulation supposed so far, which are the conditions most favorable to the workers, their relation of dependence on capital takes on a bearable form, or, as Eden says, an “easy and liberal” one. Instead of becoming more intensive as capital grows, this relation of dependence only becomes more extensive. That is, the sphere of capital's exploitation and rule merely extends along with its own dimensions and the number of its subjects. A larger part of the workers' own surplus-product, which is always increasing and is continually transformed into additional capital, comes back to them in the shape of means of payment. So they can widen the circle of their enjoyments, make some additions to their consumption-fund of clothes, furniture, etc., and lay by small reserve funds of money. But better clothing, food, and treatment, and a larger peculium [the small property a slave was allowed to keep], do away with the exploitation of the slave no more than they set aside the exploitation of the wage worker. A rise in the price of labor as a consequence of the accumulation of capital only means, in fact, that the length and weight of the golden chain the wage worker has already forged for himself allow it to be pulled less tight. In the controversies on this subject the chief fact has generally been overlooked, namely the defining characteristic of capitalist production. Labor-power is sold today not in order to satisfy the buyer's personal needs by its service or by its product. The buyer's aim is to increase his capital: to produce commodities (things produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer's own use) that contain more labor than he pays for, and so contain a portion of value that costs him nothing and that is nevertheless realized when the commodities are sold. Production of surplus-value is the absolute law of this mode of production. Labor-power can be sold only insofar as it preserves the means of production in their capacity as capital, reproduces its own value as capital, and yields, in unpaid labor, a source of additional capital.[^25.7] So the conditions of its sale, whether more or less favorable to the worker, include the necessity of its constant re-selling, and the constantly extended reproduction of all wealth in the shape of capital. Wages, as we have seen, by their very nature always imply that the worker performs a certain quantity of unpaid labor. Quite apart from the case of a rise of wages with a falling price of labor, etc., such an increase means at best only a quantitative reduction of the unpaid labor that the worker has to supply. This reduction can never reach the point at which it would threaten the system itself. Apart from violent conflicts over the rate of wages (and Adam Smith has already shown that in such a conflict, taken on the whole, the master is always master), a rise in the price of labor resulting from the accumulation of capital implies the following alternative:

[^25.7]: “The limit, however, to the employment of both the operative and the labourer is the same; namely, the possibility of the employer realising a *profit* on the produce of their industry. If the rate of wages is such as to reduce the master’s gains below the average profit of capital, he will cease to employ them, or he will only employ them on condition of submission to a reduction of wages.” (John Wade, cited above, p. 241.)

<!-- ch25-p014 -->
Either the price of labor keeps on rising, because its rise does not interfere with the progress of accumulation. There is nothing wonderful in this, for, says Adam Smith, “after these (profits) are diminished, stock may not only continue to increase, but to increase much faster than before.... A great stock, though with small profits, generally increases faster than a small stock with great profits.” (cited above, ii, p. 189.) In this case, clearly, a reduction in the unpaid labor in no way interferes with the extension of the domain of capital. – Or, on the other hand, accumulation slackens as a result of the rise in the price of labor, because the stimulus of gain is blunted. The rate of accumulation lessens; but as it lessens, the primary cause of its lessening vanishes, namely the disproportion between capital and exploitable labor-power. The mechanism of the capitalist production process removes the very obstacles that it temporarily creates. The price of labor falls again to a level corresponding to the needs of the self-expansion of capital, whether that level is below, the same as, or above the one that was normal before the rise of wages took place. So we see: in the first case, it is not a reduced rate of increase in labor-power, or in the working population, whether absolute or proportional, that makes capital excessive; on the contrary, it is the excess of capital that makes exploitable labor-power insufficient. In the second case, it is not an increased rate of increase in labor-power, or in the working population, whether absolute or proportional, that makes capital insufficient; on the contrary, it is the relative reduction of capital that makes exploitable labor-power, or rather its price, excessive. It is these absolute movements of the accumulation of capital that are reflected as relative movements of the mass of exploitable labor-power, and that therefore seem to be produced by that mass's own independent movement. To put it mathematically: the rate of accumulation is the independent, not the dependent, variable; the rate of wages is the dependent, not the independent, variable. Thus, when the industrial cycle is in its phase of crisis, a general fall in the price of commodities is expressed as a rise in the value of money; and in its phase of prosperity, a general rise in the price of commodities is expressed as a fall in the value of money. (Price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity.) The so-called currency school concludes from this that when prices are high too much money, and when prices are low too little[^25.8] money, is in circulation (the exchange of commodities through money: selling and buying). Their ignorance and complete misunderstanding of the facts[^25.9] are worthily matched by the economists who interpret the above phenomena of accumulation by saying that there are now too few, now too many wage workers.

[^25.8]: Note by the Institute of Marxism-Leninism to the Russian edition: The manuscript says “little” in the first case and “much” in the second; the correction has been made following the authorized French translation.

[^25.9]: Compare Karl Marx: “Zur Kritik der Politischen Oekonomie,” pp. 166, and following.

<!-- ch25-p015 -->
The law of capitalist production that lies at the bottom of the supposed “natural law of population” comes down simply to this. The correlation between accumulation of capital and rate of wages is nothing other than the correlation between the unpaid labor transformed into capital and the additional paid labor needed to set this additional capital in motion. So it is in no way a relation between two magnitudes independent of each other: on the one side, the magnitude of the capital; on the other, the number of the working population. It is rather, at bottom, only the relation between the unpaid and the paid labor of the same working population. If the quantity of unpaid labor supplied by the working class and accumulated by the capitalist class increases so rapidly that its conversion into capital requires an extraordinary addition of paid labor, then wages rise, and, all other circumstances remaining equal, the unpaid labor shrinks in proportion. But as soon as this shrinking touches the point at which the surplus labor (the part of the working day beyond necessary labor, in which the worker produces surplus-value for the capitalist) that nourishes capital is no longer supplied in normal quantity, a reaction sets in: a smaller part of revenue is capitalized, accumulation lags, and the upward movement of wages receives a check. So the rise of wages is confined within limits that not only leave the foundations of the capitalist system untouched, but also secure its reproduction on an extended scale. The law of capitalist accumulation, metamorphosed by economists into a supposed law of Nature, in reality merely states that the very nature of accumulation excludes every reduction in the degree of exploitation of labor, and every rise in the price of labor, which could seriously endanger the continual reproduction, on an ever-enlarging scale, of the capitalist relation. It cannot be otherwise in a mode of production in which the worker exists to satisfy the needs of self-expansion of existing values, instead of material wealth existing, the other way round, to satisfy the worker's needs of development. As in religion man is governed by the products of his own brain, so in capitalist production he is governed by the products of his own hand.[^25.10]

[^25.10]: “If we now return to our first inquiry, wherein it was shown that capital itself is only the result of human labour... it seems quite incomprehensible that man can have fallen under the domination of capital, his own product; can be subordinated to it; and as in reality this is beyond dispute the case, involuntarily the question arises: How has the labourer been able to pass from being master of capital — as its creator — to being its slave?” (Von Thünen, “Der isolierte Staat” Part ii., Section ii., Rostock, 1863, pp. 5, 6.) It is Thünen’s merit to have asked this question. His answer is simply childish.

### Section 2: Relative Diminution of the Variable Part of Capital Simultaneously with the Progress of Accumulation and of the Concentration that Accompanies it

<!-- ch25-p016 -->
According to the economists themselves, what leads to a rise in wages is neither the actual extent of social wealth nor the size of the capital already at work. It is only the constant growth of accumulation, and the speed of that growth. (Adam Smith, Book I., chapter 8.) So far, we have considered only one special phase of this process: the phase in which capital increases while the technical composition of capital stays constant. But the process goes beyond this phase.

<!-- ch25-p017 -->
Once the general basis of the capitalist system is given, a point is reached in the course of accumulation at which the development of the productivity of social labor (how much a given amount of labor produces in a given time) becomes the most powerful lever of accumulation.

<!-- ch25-p018 -->
> “The same cause,” says Adam Smith, “which raises the wages of labour, the increase of stock [capital], tends to increase its productive powers, and to make a smaller quantity of labour produce a greater quantity of work.”[^25.11]

[^25.11]: Adam Smith, “Enquiry into the Nature of ...”, Volume I.

<!-- ch25-p019 -->
Leave aside natural conditions, such as the fertility of the soil, etc. Leave aside, too, the skill of independent and isolated producers, which shows itself in the quality of their products rather than in their quantity. Apart from these, the degree of productivity of labor in a given society is expressed in the relative amount of means of production that one worker turns into products during a given time, with the same exertion of labor-power. The mass of means of production that he transforms in this way grows with the productivity of his labor. But these means of production play a double part. The increase of some is a consequence of the rising productivity of labor; the increase of others is a condition of it. For example, with the division of labor in manufacture, and with the use of machinery, more raw material is worked up in the same time. (Division of labor here means the splitting of the making of one product into many separate tasks, each done by a specialized worker. Manufacture is the stage and form of capitalist production, roughly from the mid-16th to the late 18th century, based on handicraft work divided among many workers in one workshop.) So a greater mass of raw material and auxiliary materials enters into the labor process, the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things. That is the consequence of the rising productivity of labor. On the other hand, the mass of machinery, beasts of burden, mineral fertilizers, drain-pipes, etc., is a condition of the rising productivity of labor. So too are the means of production concentrated in buildings, furnaces, means of transport, etc. But whether condition or consequence, the growing amount of the means of production, compared with the labor-power incorporated into them, is an expression of the growing productivity of labor. So the increase of this productivity shows itself in a decrease of the mass of labor in proportion to the mass of means of production it sets in motion, or in a decrease of the subjective factor of the labor process compared with the objective factor.

<!-- ch25-p020 -->
This change in the technical composition of capital, this growth in the mass of means of production compared with the mass of the labor-power that brings them to life, is reflected in turn in its value composition: the constant part of capital increases at the expense of its variable part. For example, at first 50 percent of a capital may be laid out in means of production, and 50 percent in labor-power; later on, with the development of the productivity of labor, 80 percent in means of production and 20 percent in labor-power, and so on. This law of the progressive increase of constant capital in proportion to variable capital is confirmed at every step (as already shown) by comparative analysis of the prices of commodities, whether we compare different economic epochs or different nations in the same epoch. One element of price represents only the value of the means of production, that is, the constant part of capital consumed. Its relative size is in direct proportion to the advance of accumulation. The other element of price pays for labor (the variable part of capital). Its relative size is in inverse proportion to the advance of accumulation.

<!-- ch25-p021 -->
However, this decrease in the variable part of capital compared with the constant part, or the altered value composition of capital, shows only approximately the change in the composition of its material parts. Suppose, for example, that the capital-value employed today in spinning is 7/8 constant and 1/8 variable, while at the beginning of the 18th century it was ½ constant and ½ variable. On the other hand, the mass of raw material, instruments of labor, etc., that a certain quantity of spinning labor consumes productively today is many hundred times greater than at the beginning of the 18th century. The reason is simply that, with the rising productivity of labor, not only does the mass of the means of production it consumes increase, but their value compared with their mass falls. So their value rises absolutely, but not in proportion to their mass. The growth of the difference between constant and variable capital is therefore much smaller than the growth of the difference between two masses: the mass of means of production into which the constant capital is converted, and the mass of labor-power into which the variable capital is converted. The first difference increases with the second, but to a smaller degree.

<!-- ch25-p022 -->
But if the progress of accumulation reduces the relative size of the variable part of capital, it by no means, in doing so, rules out the possibility of a rise in its absolute size. Suppose that a capital-value is at first divided into 50 percent constant and 50 percent variable capital, and later into 80 percent constant and 20 percent variable. If in the meantime the original capital, say £6,000, has grown to £18,000, its variable part has also grown. It was £3,000; it is now £3,600. But where before an increase of capital by 20 percent would have been enough to raise the demand for labor by 20 percent, now this same rise requires the original capital to be tripled.

<!-- ch25-p023 -->
In Part IV it was shown how the development of the productivity of social labor presupposes cooperation on a large scale (many workers working together, side by side, in the same or connected processes, under one capitalist's command); how only on this condition can division and combination of labor be organized, and the means of production be economized by concentration on a vast scale; how instruments of labor that by their very nature can only be used in common, such as a system of machinery, can be called into being; how huge natural forces can be pressed into the service of production; and how the process of production can be transformed into a technological application of science. Take the basis of the production of commodities, where the means of production are the property of private persons, and where the craftsman therefore either produces commodities in isolation from and independently of others, or sells his labor-power as a commodity because he lacks the means to work independently. On this basis, cooperation on a large scale can come about only through the growth of individual capitals, only in proportion as the means of social production and the means of subsistence are turned into the private property of capitalists. The basis of the production of commodities can allow production on a large scale only in the capitalist form. So a certain accumulation of capital in the hands of individual producers of commodities is the necessary precondition of the specifically capitalist mode of production. We therefore had to assume that this happens during the transition from handicraft to capitalist industry. It may be called primitive accumulation, because it is the historical basis, instead of the historical result, of specifically capitalist production. How it itself arises we need not ask here yet. It is enough that it forms the starting point. But all the methods for raising the social productive power of labor that are developed on this basis are at the same time methods for producing more surplus-value or surplus-product, which in its turn is the element out of which accumulation is formed. So they are at the same time methods for producing capital by means of capital, or methods for speeding up its accumulation. The continual turning of surplus-value back into capital now shows itself as the growing size of the capital that enters into the process of production. This in turn is the basis of a larger scale of production, of the methods for raising the productive power of labor that go with it, and of a faster production of surplus-value. So if a certain degree of accumulation of capital appears as a condition of the specifically capitalist mode of production, the capitalist mode of production in its turn causes a faster accumulation of capital. With the accumulation of capital, therefore, the specifically capitalist mode of production develops, and with the capitalist mode of production, the accumulation of capital. These two economic factors, in the compound ratio of the pushes they give each other, bring about that change in the technical composition of capital by which the variable part becomes smaller and smaller compared with the constant part.

<!-- ch25-p024 -->
Every individual capital is a larger or smaller concentration of means of production, with a matching command over a larger or smaller labor-army. Every accumulation becomes the means of new accumulation. As the mass of wealth that functions as capital increases, accumulation increases the concentration of that wealth in the hands of individual capitalists. In this way it widens the basis of production on a large scale and of the specific methods of capitalist production. Social capital grows through the growth of many individual capitals. All other circumstances remaining the same, individual capitals, and with them the concentration of the means of production, grow in proportion to the fraction of the total social capital that each forms. At the same time, portions of the original capitals break away and function as new independent capitals. Among other causes, the division of property within capitalist families plays a large part in this. So, with the accumulation of capital, the number of capitalists grows to a greater or lesser extent. Two points mark this kind of concentration, which grows directly out of accumulation, or rather is identical with it. First: the growing concentration of the social means of production in the hands of individual capitalists is limited, other things remaining equal, by the degree to which social wealth grows. Second: the part of social capital settled in each particular sphere of production is divided among many capitalists, who face one another as independent commodity-producers competing with each other. So accumulation, and the concentration that goes with it, are not only scattered over many points; the growth of each functioning capital is also thwarted by the formation of new capitals and the splitting-up of old ones. Accumulation therefore presents itself, on the one hand, as growing concentration of the means of production and of the command over labor; on the other, as repulsion of many individual capitals from one another.

<!-- ch25-p025 -->
This splitting-up of the total social capital into many individual capitals, or the repulsion of its fractions from one another, is counteracted by their attraction. This attraction does not mean that simple concentration of the means of production and of the command over labor which is identical with accumulation. It is concentration of capitals already formed: the destruction of their individual independence, the expropriation of capitalist by capitalist (expropriation means taking away people's property, here one capitalist's by another), the transformation of many small capitals into few large ones. This process differs from the first in that it presupposes only a change in the distribution of capital already at hand and functioning. So its field of action is not limited by the absolute growth of social wealth, by the absolute limits of accumulation. Capital grows in one place to a huge mass in a single hand because in another place it has been lost by many. This is centralization proper, as distinct from accumulation and concentration.

<!-- ch25-p026 -->
The laws of this centralization of capitals, or of the attraction of capital by capital, cannot be developed here. A brief hint at a few facts must be enough. The battle of competition is fought by making commodities cheaper. Other things being equal, the cheapness of commodities depends on the productivity of labor, and this in turn on the scale of production. So the larger capitals beat the smaller. It will be remembered, too, that with the development of the capitalist mode of production, the minimum amount of individual capital needed to carry on a business under its normal conditions increases. The smaller capitals therefore crowd into spheres of production that modern industry (large-scale production based on machinery and the factory system) has taken hold of only here and there, or incompletely. Here competition rages in direct proportion to the number, and in inverse proportion to the size, of the rival capitals. It always ends in the ruin of many small capitalists, whose capitals partly pass into the hands of their conquerors and partly vanish. Apart from this, an altogether new force comes into play with capitalist production: the credit system. In its first stages it creeps in stealthily as the humble assistant of accumulation, drawing by invisible threads, into the hands of individual or associated capitalists, the money resources that lie scattered in larger or smaller amounts over the surface of society. But it soon becomes a new and terrible weapon in the battle of competition, and is finally transformed into an enormous social mechanism for the centralization of capitals.

<!-- ch25-p027 -->
As capitalist production and accumulation develop, the two most powerful levers of centralization develop to the same degree: competition and credit. At the same time, the progress of accumulation increases the material that can be centralized, that is, the individual capitals. Meanwhile the expansion of capitalist production creates, on the one hand, the social need and, on the other, the technical means for those immense industrial undertakings that can only be carried out after capital has first been centralized. Today, therefore, the force of attraction drawing individual capitals together, and the tendency to centralization, are stronger than ever before. But if the relative extent and energy of the movement toward centralization is determined, to a certain degree, by the size of capitalist wealth and the superiority of the economic mechanism already reached, progress in centralization does not in any way depend on a positive growth in the size of social capital. And this is the specific difference between centralization and concentration, concentration being only another name for reproduction on an extended scale. Centralization may result from a mere change in the distribution of capitals already existing, from a simple change in the quantitative grouping of the parts of social capital. Here capital can grow into powerful masses in a single hand because there it has been withdrawn from many individual hands. In any given branch of industry, centralization would reach its extreme limit if all the individual capitals invested in it were fused into a single capital.[^25.12] In a given society, the limit would be reached only when the entire social capital was united in the hands of either a single capitalist or a single capitalist company.

[^25.12]: *Note in the 4th German edition.* — The latest English and American “trusts” are already striving toward this goal. They are trying to unite at least all the large-scale concerns in one branch of industry into one great joint-stock company with a practical monopoly. *F. E.*

<!-- ch25-p028 -->
Centralization completes the work of accumulation by enabling industrial capitalists to extend the scale of their operations. This result may be the consequence of accumulation or of centralization. Centralization may be accomplished by the violent method of annexation, when certain capitals become such overwhelming centers of attraction for others that they shatter the individual cohesion of those others and then draw the separate fragments to themselves. Or a number of capitals, already formed or in the process of forming, may be fused by the smoother process of organizing joint-stock companies. Whichever it is, the economic effect remains the same. Everywhere the increased scale of industrial establishments is the starting point for a more comprehensive organization of the collective work of many, for a wider development of their material motive forces. In other words, it is the starting point for the progressive transformation of isolated processes of production, carried on by customary methods, into processes of production that are socially combined and scientifically arranged.

<!-- ch25-p029 -->
But accumulation, the gradual increase of capital by reproduction as it passes from the circular to the spiral form, is clearly a very slow procedure compared with centralization, which has only to change the quantitative groupings of the parts of social capital. The world would still be without railways if it had had to wait until accumulation had brought a few individual capitals far enough to be adequate for building a railway. Centralization, on the contrary, accomplished this in the twinkling of an eye, by means of joint-stock companies. And while centralization thus intensifies and speeds up the effects of accumulation, it at the same time extends and speeds up those revolutions in the technical composition of capital that raise its constant part at the expense of its variable part, and so reduce the relative demand for labor.

<!-- ch25-p030 -->
The masses of capital fused together overnight by centralization reproduce and multiply as the others do, only faster, and so become new and powerful levers of social accumulation. So when we speak of the progress of social accumulation, we tacitly include – today – the effects of centralization.

<!-- ch25-p031 -->
The additional capitals formed in the normal course of accumulation (see Chapter XXIV, Section 1) serve especially as vehicles for exploiting new inventions and discoveries, and industrial improvements in general. But in time the old capital also reaches the moment of renewal from top to toe. It sheds its skin and is reborn, like the others, in a perfected technical form, in which a smaller quantity of labor is enough to set a larger quantity of machinery and raw materials in motion. This necessarily brings an absolute reduction in the demand for labor. Obviously, that reduction is all the greater, the more the capitals going through this process of renewal are already massed together by the movement of centralization.

<!-- ch25-p032 -->
On the one hand, therefore, the additional capital formed in the course of accumulation attracts fewer and fewer workers in proportion to its size. On the other hand, the old capital, periodically reproduced with a change of composition, repels more and more of the workers it formerly employed.

### Section 3: Progressive Production of a Relative surplus population or Industrial Reserve Army

<!-- ch25-p033 -->
The accumulation of capital at first appears to be only its growth in quantity. But, as we have seen, it takes place through a progressive qualitative change in its composition, through a constant increase of its constant part at the expense of its variable part.[^25.13]

[^25.13]: *Note in the 3rd German edition.* — In Marx’s copy there is a marginal note here: “Here note for working out later; if the extension is only quantitative, then for a greater and a smaller capital in the same branch of business the profits are as the magnitudes of the capitals advanced. If the quantitative extension induces qualitative change, then the rate of profit on the larger capital rises simultaneously.” *F. E.*

<!-- ch25-p034 -->
The specifically capitalist mode of production, the development of the productive power of labor that corresponds to it, and the change in the organic composition of capital that results from it do not merely keep pace with the advance of accumulation, or with the growth of social wealth. They develop much faster. This is because mere accumulation, the absolute increase of the total social capital, is accompanied by the centralization of the individual capitals that make up that total. It is also because the change in the technological composition of the additional capital goes hand in hand with a similar change in the technological composition of the original capital. So, as accumulation advances, the proportion of constant to variable capital changes. If it was originally, say, 1:1, it now becomes successively 2:1, 3:1, 4:1, 5:1, 7:1, etc. As a result, as the capital grows, instead of ½ of its total value, only 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, 1/8, etc., is turned into labor-power, and, on the other hand, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, 5/6, 7/8 into means of production. The demand for labor is determined not by the amount of capital as a whole, but by its variable part alone. So that demand falls progressively as the total capital increases, instead of rising in proportion to it, as was previously assumed. It falls relative to the magnitude of the total capital, and at an accelerating rate as this magnitude increases. As the total capital grows, its variable part, or the labor incorporated in it, does increase too, but in a constantly diminishing proportion. The pauses in between, in which accumulation works as a simple extension of production on a given technical basis, become shorter. It is not merely that an accelerated accumulation of the total capital, accelerated in a constantly growing progression, is needed to absorb an additional number of workers, or even, because of the constant metamorphosis of old capital, to keep employed those already at work. In its turn, this growing accumulation and centralization itself becomes a source of new changes in the composition of capital, of a still faster decrease of its variable part compared with its constant part. This accelerated relative decrease of the variable part goes along with the accelerated increase of the total capital, and moves faster than this increase. At the other pole, it takes the opposite form: an apparently absolute increase of the working population, an increase always moving faster than that of the variable capital or the means of employment. But in fact it is capitalist accumulation itself that constantly produces a relatively redundant population of workers, and produces it in direct proportion to its own energy and extent. That is, it produces a population larger than suffices for the average needs of the self-expansion of capital, and therefore a surplus population.

<!-- ch25-p035 -->
If we consider the social capital in its totality, the movement of its accumulation at one time causes periodic changes that affect it more or less as a whole, and at another time distributes its various phases simultaneously over the different spheres of production. In some spheres, a change in the composition of capital takes place without any increase in its absolute magnitude, as a result of simple centralization. In others, the absolute growth of capital is connected with an absolute decrease of its variable part, or of the labor-power it absorbs. In still others, capital goes on growing for a time on its given technical basis, and attracts additional labor-power in proportion to its growth, while at other times it undergoes organic change and reduces its variable part. In all spheres, the increase of the variable part of capital, and therefore of the number of workers it employs, is always connected with violent fluctuations and with the temporary production of surplus population. This may take the more striking form of the repulsion, or pushing out, of workers already employed. Or it may take the less obvious, but no less real, form of the greater difficulty of absorbing the additional working population through the usual channels.[^25.14] With the magnitude of the social capital already functioning and the degree of its increase, with the extension of the scale of production and the mass of workers set in motion, with the development of the productivity of their labor, and with the greater breadth and fullness of all sources of wealth, there is also an extension of the scale on which greater attraction of workers by capital is accompanied by their greater repulsion. The speed of the change in the organic composition of capital, and in its technical form, increases, and a growing number of spheres of production are drawn into this change, sometimes at the same time, sometimes by turns. So the working population, along with the accumulation of capital that it produces, also produces the means by which it is itself made relatively superfluous, turned into a relative surplus population. And it does this to an ever-increasing extent.[^25.15] This is a law of population peculiar to the capitalist mode of production. In fact, every particular historical mode of production has its own particular laws of population, historically valid within its limits, and only insofar as man has not interfered with them.

[^25.14]: The census of England and Wales shows: all persons employed in agriculture (landlords, farmers, gardeners, shepherds, etc., included): 1851, 2,011,447; 1861, 1,924,110. Fall, 87,337. Worsted manufacture: 1851, 102,714 persons; 1861, 79,242. Silk weaving: 1851, 111,940; 1861, 101,678. Calico-printing: 1851, 12,098; 1861, 12,556. That is a small rise, in the face of the enormous expansion of this industry, and it implies a great fall, proportionally, in the number of workers employed. Hat-making: 1851, 15,957; 1861, 13,814. Straw-hat and bonnet-making: 1851, 20,393; 1861, 18,176. Malting: 1851, 10,566; 1861, 10,677. Chandlery (candle-making), 1851, 4,949; 1861, 4,686. This fall is due, among other causes, to the increase in gas lighting. Comb-making: 1851, 2,038; 1861, 1,478. Sawyers: 1851, 30,552; 1861, 31,647 — a small rise as a result of the increase of sawing-machines. Nail-making: 1851, 26,940; 1861, 26,130 — a fall as a result of the competition of machinery. Tin and copper-mining: 1851, 31,360; 1861, 32,041. On the other hand: Cotton-spinning and weaving: 1851, 371,777; 1861, 456,646. Coal-mining: 1851, 183,389, 1861, 246,613, “The increase of labourers is generally greatest, since 1851, in such branches of industry in which machinery has not up to the present been employed with success.” (Census of England and Wales for 1861. Vol. III. London, 1863, p. 36.)

[^25.15]: *Added in the 4th German edition.* — Some of the leading economists of the classical school guessed at, rather than understood, the law of the progressive decrease in the relative magnitude of variable capital and its effect on the condition of the class of wage workers. The greatest service here was done by John Barton, although he, like all the rest, lumps together constant capital with fixed capital, and variable capital with circulating capital. He says:

    “The demand for labour depends on the increase of circulating, and not of fixed capital. Were it true that the proportion between these two sorts of capital is the same at all times, and in all circumstances, then, indeed, it follows that the number of labourers employed is in proportion to the wealth of the state. But such a proposition has not the semblance of probability. As arts are cultivated, and civilisation is extended, fixed capital bears a larger and larger proportion to circulating capital. The amount of fixed capital employed in the production of a piece of British muslin is at least a hundred, probably a thousand times greater than that employed in a similar piece of Indian muslin. And the proportion of circulating capital is a hundred or thousand times less ... the whole of the annual savings, added to the fixed capital, would have no effect in increasing the demand for labour.” (John Barton, “Observations on the Circumstances which Influence the Condition of the Labouring Classes of Society.” London, 1817, pp. 16, 17.) “The same cause which may increase the net revenue of the country may at the same time render the population redundant, and deteriorate the condition of the labourer.” (Ricardo, cited above, p. 469.) With increase of capital, “the demand [for labour] will be in a diminishing ratio.” (Same source, p. 480, Note.) “The amount of capital devoted to the maintenance of labour may vary, independently of any changes in the whole amount of capital.... Great fluctuations in the amount of employment, and great suffering may become more frequent as capital itself becomes more plentiful.” (Richard Jones, “An Introductory Lecture on Pol. Econ.,” London 1833, p. 13) “Demand [for labour] will rise ... not in proportion to the accumulation of the general capital. ... Every augmentation, therefore, in the national stock destined for reproduction, comes, in the progress of society, to have less and less influence upon the condition of the labourer.” (Ramsay, cited above, pp. 90, 91.)

<!-- ch25-p036 -->
But if a surplus working population is a necessary product of accumulation, or of the development of wealth on a capitalist basis, this surplus population in turn becomes the lever of capitalist accumulation, indeed even a condition of existence of the capitalist mode of production. It forms a disposable industrial reserve army, which belongs to capital just as absolutely as if capital had bred it at its own cost. Independently of the limits of the actual increase of population, it creates, for the changing needs of the self-expansion of capital, a mass of human material always ready for exploitation. With accumulation, and the development of the productivity of labor that goes with it, capital's power of sudden expansion grows too. It grows not merely because the elasticity of the capital already functioning increases; not merely because the absolute wealth of society expands, of which capital forms only an elastic part; not merely because credit, under every special stimulus, at once places an unusual part of this wealth at the disposal of production in the form of additional capital. It grows also because the technical conditions of the process of production themselves – machinery, means of transport, etc. – now allow masses of surplus-product to be turned into additional means of production at the greatest speed. The mass of social wealth, overflowing as accumulation advances and able to be turned into additional capital, throws itself frantically into old branches of production whose market suddenly expands, or into newly formed branches, such as railways, etc., the need for which grows out of the development of the old ones. In all such cases, it must be possible to throw great masses of men suddenly onto the decisive points without harming the scale of production in other spheres. Overpopulation supplies these masses. The course characteristic of modern industry, namely a ten-year cycle (interrupted by smaller oscillations) of periods of average activity, production at high pressure, crisis, and stagnation, depends on the constant formation, the greater or lesser absorption, and the re-formation of the industrial reserve army or surplus population. In their turn, the changing phases of the industrial cycle recruit the surplus population, and become one of the most energetic agents of its reproduction. This peculiar course of modern industry, which occurs in no earlier period of human history, was also impossible in the childhood of capitalist production. The composition of capital changed only very slowly. So, on the whole, its accumulation was matched by a corresponding growth in the demand for labor. Slow as the advance of accumulation was compared with that of more modern times, it ran up against the natural limits of the exploitable working population, limits that could be got rid of only by forcible means, which will be mentioned later. The expansion of the scale of production by fits and starts is the prelude to its equally sudden contraction. The contraction in turn calls forth the expansion, but the expansion is impossible without disposable human material, without an increase in the number of workers independent of the absolute growth of the population. This increase is brought about by the simple process that constantly “sets free” a part of the workers, by methods that reduce the number of workers employed in proportion to the increased production. The whole form of the movement of modern industry therefore depends on the constant transformation of a part of the working population into unemployed or half-employed workers. The superficiality of political economy shows itself in the fact that it looks on the expansion and contraction of credit, which is a mere symptom of the periodic changes of the industrial cycle, as their cause. Just as the heavenly bodies, once thrown into a certain definite motion, always repeat it, so it is with social production once it has been thrown into this movement of alternate expansion and contraction. Effects in their turn become causes, and the changing accidents of the whole process, which always reproduces its own conditions, take on the form of periodicity. Once this periodicity has become fixed, even political economy sees that the production of a relative surplus population – that is, surplus with regard to the average needs of the self-expansion of capital – is a necessary condition of modern industry.

<!-- ch25-p037 -->
> “Suppose,” says H. Merivale, formerly Professor of Political Economy at Oxford, later employed in the English Colonial Office, “suppose that, on the occasion of some of these crises, the nation were to rouse itself to the effort of getting rid by emigration of some hundreds of thousands of superfluous arms, what would be the consequence? That, at the first returning demand for labour, there would be a deficiency. However rapid reproduction may be, it takes, at all events, the space of a generation to replace the loss of adult labour. Now, the profits of our manufacturers depend mainly on the power of making use of the prosperous moment when demand is brisk, and thus compensating themselves for the interval during which it is slack. This power is secured to them only by the command of machinery and of manual labour. They must have hands ready by them, they must be able to increase the activity of their operations when required, and to slacken it again, according to the state of the market, or they cannot possibly maintain that pre-eminence in the race of competition on which the wealth of the country is founded.”[^25.16]

[^25.16]: H. Merivale. “Lectures on Colonisation and Colonies,” 1841, Vol. I , p. 146.

<!-- ch25-p038 -->
Even Malthus recognizes overpopulation as a necessity of modern industry, although, in his narrow way, he explains it by the absolute overgrowth of the working population, not by its becoming relatively more than is needed. He says:

<!-- ch25-p039 -->
> “Prudential habits with regard to marriage, carried to a considerable extent among the labouring class of a country mainly depending upon manufactures and commerce, might injure it.... From the nature of a population, an increase of labourers cannot be brought into market in consequence of a particular demand till after the lapse of 16 or 18 years, and the conversion of revenue into capital, by saving, may take place much more rapidly: a country is always liable to an increase in the quantity of the funds for the maintenance of labour faster than the increase of population.”[^25.17]

[^25.17]: Malthus, “Principles of Political Economy,” pp. 215, 319, 320. In this work, Malthus at last discovers, with Sismondi's help, the beautiful Trinity of capitalist production: over-production, over-population, over-consumption — three very delicate monsters, indeed. Compare F. Engels, “Umrisse zu einer Kritik der Nationalökonomie,” cited above, p. 107, and following.

<!-- ch25-p040 -->
After political economy has thus shown that the constant production of a relative surplus population of workers is a necessity of capitalist accumulation, she very aptly, in the guise of an old maid, puts into the mouth of her “beau ideal” [perfect model] of a capitalist the following words, addressed to those surplus workers whom their own creation of additional capital has thrown on the streets: –

<!-- ch25-p041 -->
> “We manufacturers do what we can for you, whilst we are increasing that capital on which you must subsist, and you must do the rest by accommodating your numbers to the means of subsistence.”[^25.18]

[^25.18]: Harriet Martineau, “A Manchester Strike,” 1832, p. 101.

<!-- ch25-p042 -->
Capitalist production can by no means be content with the quantity of disposable labor-power that the natural increase of population yields. For its free play it requires an industrial reserve army independent of these natural limits.

<!-- ch25-p043 -->
Up to this point we have assumed that the increase or decrease of the variable capital corresponds rigidly to the increase or decrease of the number of workers employed.

<!-- ch25-p044 -->
The number of workers commanded by capital may stay the same, or even fall, while the variable capital increases. This is the case if the individual worker supplies more labor, and his wages therefore increase, and this even though the price of labor stays the same or even falls, only more slowly than the mass of labor rises. In this case, an increase of variable capital becomes an index of more labor, but not of more workers employed. It is the absolute interest of every capitalist to press a given quantity of labor out of a smaller rather than a greater number of workers, if the cost is about the same. With the greater number, the outlay of constant capital increases in proportion to the mass of labor set in motion; with the smaller number, that increase is much smaller. The larger the scale of production, the stronger this motive. Its force increases with the accumulation of capital.

<!-- ch25-p045 -->
We have seen that the development of the capitalist mode of production and of the productive power of labor – at once the cause and the effect of accumulation – enables the capitalist, with the same outlay of variable capital, to set more labor in motion by greater exploitation (extensive or intensive) of each individual labor-power. We have also seen that the capitalist buys a greater mass of labor-power with the same capital as he progressively replaces skilled workers by less skilled ones, mature labor-power by immature, male by female, and that of adults by that of young persons or children.

<!-- ch25-p046 -->
So, on the one hand, as accumulation progresses, a larger variable capital sets more labor in motion without enlisting more workers. On the other hand, a variable capital of the same magnitude sets more labor in motion with the same mass of labor-power. And finally, it sets in motion a greater number of inferior labor-powers by displacing higher ones.

<!-- ch25-p047 -->
The production of a relative surplus population, or the setting free of workers, therefore goes on even faster than the technical revolution of the process of production, which accompanies the advance of accumulation and is accelerated by it. It also goes on faster than the corresponding decrease of the variable part of capital compared with the constant part. If the means of production, as they grow in extent and effective power, become means of employment for workers to a lesser extent, this state of things is in turn modified by the fact that, as the productivity of labor increases, capital increases its supply of labor faster than its demand for workers. The overwork of the employed part of the working class swells the ranks of the reserve, while, the other way round, the greater pressure that the reserve exerts on the employed through its competition forces them to submit to overwork and to subjection under the dictates of capital. Condemning one part of the working class to enforced idleness through the overwork of the other part, and the other way round, becomes a means of enriching the individual capitalists,[^25.19] and at the same time speeds up the production of the industrial reserve army on a scale that corresponds to the advance of social accumulation. How important this element is in the formation of the relative surplus population is shown by the example of England. Her technical means for saving labor are colossal. Nevertheless, if tomorrow morning labor in general were reduced to a rational amount, and adjusted to the different sections of the working class according to age and sex, the working population at hand would be absolutely insufficient to carry on national production on its present scale. The great majority of the workers who are now “unproductive” would have to be turned into “productive” ones.

[^25.19]: Even during the cotton famine of 1863, we find fierce denunciations of overwork in a pamphlet by the cotton-spinning factory workers of Blackburn. Because of the Factory Acts, this overwork of course affected only adult male workers. “The adult operatives at this mill have been asked to work from 12 to 13 hours per day, while there are hundreds who are compelled to be idle who would willingly work partial time, in order to maintain their families and save their brethren from a premature grave through being overworked.... We,” the pamphlet goes on to say, “would ask if the practice of working overtime by a number of hands, is likely to create a good feeling between masters and servants. Those who are worked overtime feel the injustice equally with those who are condemned to forced idleness. There is in the district almost sufficient work to give to all partial employment if fairly distributed. We are only asking what is right in requesting the masters generally to pursue a system of short hours, particularly until a better state of things begins to dawn upon us, rather than to work a portion of the hands overtime, while others, for want of work, are compelled to exist upon charity.” (“Reports of Insp. of Fact., Oct. 31, 1863,” p. 8.) The author of the “Essay on Trade and Commerce” grasps the effect of a relative surplus population on the employed workers with his usual unerring bourgeois instinct (bourgeois: belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it). “Another cause of idleness in this kingdom is the want of a sufficient number of labouring hands .... Whenever from an extraordinary demand for manufactures, labour grows scarce, the labourers feel their own consequence [importance], and will make their masters feel it likewise — it is amazing; but so depraved are the dispositions of these people, that in such cases a set of workmen have combined to distress the employer by idling a whole day together.” (“Essay, &c.,” pp. 27, 28.) The fellows were in fact hankering after a rise in wages.

<!-- ch25-p048 -->
Taken as a whole, the general movements of wages are regulated exclusively by the expansion and contraction of the industrial reserve army, and these in turn correspond to the periodic changes of the industrial cycle. So these movements are not determined by the variations in the absolute number of the working population, but by the changing proportions in which the working class is divided into active army and reserve army, by the increase or decrease in the relative amount of the surplus population, and by the extent to which it is at one time absorbed, at another set free. Modern industry has its ten-year cycles and periodic phases, and as accumulation advances these are, moreover, complicated by irregular oscillations that follow each other more and more quickly. For such an industry, that would indeed be a beautiful law which pretends to make the action of capital depend on the absolute variation of the population, instead of regulating the demand and supply of labor by the alternate expansion and contraction of capital, with the labor-market now appearing relatively under-full because capital is expanding, now again over-full because it is contracting. Yet this is the dogma of the economists. According to them, wages rise as a result of the accumulation of capital. The higher wages stimulate the working population to multiply faster, and this goes on until the labor-market becomes too full, and capital therefore becomes insufficient relative to the supply of labor. Wages fall, and now we have the other side of the medal. As a result of the fall in wages, the working population is little by little decimated, so that capital is again in excess relative to them. Or, as others explain it, falling wages and the corresponding increase in the exploitation of the worker speed up accumulation again, while at the same time the lower wages hold the growth of the working class in check. Then the time comes again when the supply of labor is less than the demand, wages rise, and so on. A beautiful mode of motion, this, for developed capitalist production! Before any positive increase of the population really fit for work could occur as a result of the rise in wages, the time during which the industrial campaign had to be carried through, the battle fought and won, would have passed again and again.

<!-- ch25-p049 -->
Between 1849 and 1859, a rise of wages that was practically insignificant, though accompanied by falling prices of grain, took place in the English agricultural districts. In Wiltshire, for example, weekly wages rose from 7s. to 8s.; in Dorsetshire, from 7s. or 8s. to 9s., etc. This was the result of an unusual exodus of the agricultural surplus population, caused by the demands of war, the vast extension of railroads, factories, mines, etc. The lower the wages, the higher the proportion in which even the most insignificant rise in them expresses itself. If the weekly wage, for example, is 20s. and it rises to 22s., that is a rise of 10 percent; but if it is only 7s. and it rises to 9s., that is a rise of 28 4/7 per cent., which sounds very fine. Everywhere the farmers were howling, and the London *Economist,* referring to these starvation wages, prattled quite seriously about “a general and substantial advance.”[^25.20] What did the farmers do now? Did they wait until, as a result of this brilliant remuneration, the agricultural workers had so increased and multiplied that their wages had to fall again, as prescribed by the dogmatic economic brain? They introduced more machinery, and in a moment the workers were redundant again, in a proportion satisfactory even to the farmers. There was now “more capital” laid out in agriculture than before, and in a more productive form. With this, the demand for labor fell, not only relatively, but absolutely.

[^25.20]: *Economist,* Jan. 21. 1860.

<!-- ch25-p050 -->
The economic fiction described above confuses the laws that regulate the general movement of wages, or the ratio between the working class – that is, the total labor-power – and the total social capital, with the laws that distribute the working population over the different spheres of production. Suppose, for example, that favorable circumstances make accumulation especially active in a particular sphere of production, and that profits there, being greater than average profits, attract additional capital. Then, of course, the demand for labor rises and wages rise too. The higher wages draw a larger part of the working population into the more favored sphere, until it is glutted with labor-power, and wages at length fall again to their average level, or below it if the pressure is too great. Then the immigration of workers into the branch of industry in question not only stops; it gives way to their emigration. Here the political economist thinks he sees the why and wherefore of an absolute increase of workers accompanying a rise in wages, and of a fall in wages accompanying an absolute increase of workers. But what he really sees is only the local oscillation of the labor-market in a particular sphere of production. He sees only the phenomena that accompany the distribution of the working population among the different spheres where capital is laid out, according to its changing needs.

<!-- ch25-p051 -->
During periods of stagnation and average prosperity, the industrial reserve army weighs down the active labor-army; during periods of over-production and frenzy, it holds the active army's claims in check. Relative surplus population is therefore the pivot on which the law of demand and supply of labor works. It confines this law's field of action within limits that suit the activity of exploitation and the domination of capital absolutely.

<!-- ch25-p052 -->
This is the place to return to one of the grand exploits of economic apologetics, the defense of the system. It will be remembered that if, through the introduction of new machinery or the extension of old, a portion of variable capital is turned into constant capital, the economic apologist interprets this operation, which “fixes” capital and by that very act sets workers “free,” in exactly the opposite way: he pretends that it sets capital free for the workers. Only now can one fully understand the effrontery of these apologists. What are set free are not only the workers immediately turned out by the machines, but also their future replacements in the rising generation, and the additional contingent that the usual extension of trade on the old basis would regularly absorb. They are now all “set free,” and every new bit of capital looking for employment can dispose of them. Whether it attracts them or others, the effect on the general demand for labor will be nil, if this capital is just enough to take out of the market as many workers as the machines threw onto it. If it employs a smaller number, the number of surplus workers increases; if it employs a greater number, the general demand for labor increases only by the excess of those employed over those “set free.” So the impulse that additional capital seeking an outlet would otherwise have given to the general demand for labor is in every case neutralized to the extent of the workers thrown out of work by the machine. That is to say, the mechanism of capitalist production so manages matters that the absolute increase of capital is accompanied by no corresponding rise in the general demand for labor. And this the apologist calls a compensation for the misery, the suffering, the possible death of the displaced workers during the transition period that banishes them into the industrial reserve army! The demand for labor is not identical with the increase of capital, nor the supply of labor with the increase of the working class. It is not a case of two independent forces working on each other. Les dés sont pipés [The dice are loaded].

<!-- ch25-p053 -->
Capital works on both sides at the same time. If its accumulation, on the one hand, increases the demand for labor, on the other it increases the supply of workers by “setting free” some of them. At the same time, the pressure of the unemployed forces those who are employed to furnish more labor, and so makes the supply of labor, to a certain extent, independent of the supply of workers. The action of the law of supply and demand of labor on this basis completes the despotism of capital. So, as soon as the workers learn the secret of how it comes about that, in the same measure as they work more, produce more wealth for others, and as the productive power of their labor increases, in that same measure even their function as a means of the self-expansion of capital becomes more and more precarious for them; as soon as they discover that the degree of intensity of the competition among themselves depends wholly on the pressure of the relative surplus population; as soon as they try, through Trades’ Unions, etc., to organize regular cooperation between employed and unemployed, in order to destroy or weaken the ruinous effects of this natural law of capitalist production on their class – just as soon, capital and its sycophant, political economy, cry out at the violation of the “eternal” and, so to speak, “sacred” law of supply and demand. Every combination of employed and unemployed disturbs the “harmonious” action of this law. But on the other hand, as soon as adverse circumstances (in the colonies, for example) prevent the creation of an industrial reserve army, and with it the absolute dependence of the working class on the capitalist class, capital, along with its commonplace Sancho Panza (the down-to-earth squire of Don Quixote), rebels against the “sacred” law of supply and demand, and tries to check its inconvenient action by forcible means and State interference.

### Section 4: Different Forms of the Relative surplus population. The General Law of Capitalistic Accumulation

<!-- ch25-p054 -->
The relative surplus population exists in every possible form. Every worker belongs to it during the time when he is only partly employed or wholly unemployed. Leaving aside the great forms that recur periodically, which the changing phases of the industrial cycle stamp on it – now an acute form during the crisis, then again a chronic form during dull times – it always has three forms: the floating, the latent, and the stagnant.

<!-- ch25-p055 -->
In the centers of modern industry – factories, manufacturing workshops, ironworks, mines, etc. – the workers are sometimes pushed out, and sometimes drawn in again in greater masses. On the whole the number of those employed increases, although in a constantly decreasing proportion to the scale of production. Here the surplus population exists in the floating form.

<!-- ch25-p056 -->
In the automatic factories, as in all the great workshops, where machinery enters as a factor, or where only the modern division of labor is carried out, large numbers of boys are employed up to the age of maturity. Once they reach that age, only a very small number continue to find work in the same branches of industry, while the majority are regularly dismissed. This majority forms an element of the floating surplus population, and it grows as those branches of industry expand. Part of them emigrates, and in fact follows capital that has emigrated. One consequence is that the female population grows faster than the male, as England bears witness. The natural increase in the number of workers does not satisfy the needs of the accumulation of capital, and yet all the time it is in excess of them. That is a contradiction built into the movement of capital itself. Capital wants larger numbers of young workers and a smaller number of adults. This contradiction is no more glaring than that other one: there are complaints of a shortage of workers, while at the same time many thousands are out of work, because the division of labor chains them to a particular branch of industry.[^25.21]

[^25.21]: During the last six months of 1866, 80-90,000 working people in London were thrown out of work. Yet the Factory Report for that same half year says: “It does not appear absolutely true to say that demand will always produce supply just at the moment when it is needed. It has not done so with labour, for much machinery has been idle last year for want of hands.” (“Rep. of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1866,” p. 81.)

<!-- ch25-p057 -->
Besides, capital consumes labor-power so fast that the worker, by the middle of his life, has already more or less completely used himself up. He falls into the ranks of the supernumeraries, the extra workers no longer needed, or he is pushed down from a higher step on the ladder to a lower one. It is precisely among the workers of modern industry that we meet the shortest length of life. Dr. Lee, Medical Officer of Health for Manchester, stated

<!-- ch25-p058 -->
> “that the average age at death of the Manchester ... upper middle class was 38 years, while the average age at death of the labouring class was 17; while at Liverpool those figures were represented as 35 against 15. It thus appeared that the well-to-do classes had a lease of life which was more than double the value of that which fell to the lot of the less favoured citizens.”[^25.22]

[^25.22]: Opening address to the Sanitary Conference, Birmingham, January 15th, 1875, by J. Chamberlain, Mayor of the town, now (1883) President of the Board of Trade.

<!-- ch25-p059 -->
To fit these circumstances, the absolute increase of this section of the proletariat must take place under conditions that swell their numbers, even though the individual members are used up quickly. Hence the generations of workers must be renewed rapidly (this law does not hold for the other classes of the population). This social need is met by early marriages, which are a necessary consequence of the conditions in which the workers of modern industry live. It is also met by the premium that the exploitation of children places on their production.

<!-- ch25-p060 -->
As soon as capitalist production takes possession of agriculture, and in proportion to how far it does so, the demand for an agricultural working population falls absolutely, while the accumulation of the capital employed in agriculture advances. And unlike in non-agricultural industries, this pushing-out of workers is not made up for by a greater drawing-in. Part of the agricultural population is therefore constantly on the point of passing over into an urban or manufacturing proletariat, and is on the lookout for circumstances favorable to this change. (Manufacture is used here in the sense of all non-agricultural industries.)[^25.23] So this source of relative surplus population is constantly flowing. But the constant flow toward the towns presupposes that in the countryside itself there is a constant latent surplus population. How large it is becomes visible only when its outlet channels open exceptionally wide. The agricultural worker is therefore pushed down to the minimum of wages, and always stands with one foot already in the swamp of pauperism (the condition of the lowest layer of the surplus population, unable to find work and dependent on poor relief).

[^25.23]: The census for 1861 gives 781 towns for England and Wales, which “contained 10,960,998 inhabitants, while the villages and country parishes contained 9,105,226. In 1851, 580 towns were distinguished, and the population in them and in the surrounding country was nearly equal. But while in the subsequent ten years the population in the villages and the country increased half a million, the population in the 580 towns increased by a million and a half (1,554,067). The increase of the population of the country parishes is 6.5 per cent., and of the towns 17.3 per cent. The difference in the rates of increase is due to the migration from country to town. Three-fourths of the total increase of population has taken place in the towns.” (“Census. &c.,” pp. 11 and 12.)

<!-- ch25-p061 -->
The third category of the relative surplus population, the stagnant, forms part of the active labor army, but its employment is extremely irregular. So it provides capital with an endless reservoir of labor-power that is available for use. Its living conditions sink below the average normal level of the working class, and this at once makes it the broad basis of special branches of capitalist exploitation. Its marks are the maximum of working time and the minimum of wages. We have already come to know its chief form under the heading of “domestic industry.” It constantly recruits itself from the surplus forces of modern industry and agriculture, and especially from those decaying branches of industry where handicraft is giving way to manufacture, and manufacture to machinery. Its extent grows as the creation of a surplus population advances along with the extent and energy of accumulation.
