But at the same time it forms an element of the working class that reproduces and perpetuates itself, and it takes a proportionally greater part in the general increase of that class than the other elements do. In fact, not only the number of births and deaths, but the absolute size of families, stand in inverse proportion to the level of wages, and therefore to the amount of means of subsistence that the different categories of workers have at their disposal. This law of capitalist society would sound absurd to savages, or even to civilized colonists. It calls to mind the boundless reproduction of animals that are individually weak and constantly hunted down.[^25.24]

[^25.24]: “Poverty seems favourable to generation.” (A. Smith.) According to the gallant and witty Abbé Galiani, this is even an especially wise arrangement of God: “Iddio af che gli uomini che esercitano mestieri di prima utilità nascono abbondantemente.” (Galiani, cited above, p. 78.) [God brings it about that men who carry on trades of the first usefulness are born in abundance] “Misery up to the extreme point of famine and pestilence, instead of checking, tends to increase population.” (S. Laing, “National Distress,” 1844, p. 69.) After Laing has illustrated this with statistics, he goes on: “If the people were all in easy circumstances, the world would soon be depopulated.”

<!-- ch25-p062 -->
Finally, the lowest sediment of the relative surplus population lives in the sphere of pauperism. Leaving out vagabonds, criminals, and prostitutes – in a word, the “dangerous” classes – this layer of society consists of three categories. First, those able to work. One need only glance quickly at the statistics of English pauperism to see that the number of paupers rises with every crisis and falls with every revival of trade. Second, orphans and pauper children. These are candidates for the industrial reserve army, and in times of great prosperity, for example 1860, they are quickly enrolled in large numbers in the active army of workers. Third, the demoralized and ragged, and those unable to work. These are chiefly people who go under because the division of labor has left them unable to adapt; people who have passed the normal age of a worker; and the victims of industry, whose number grows with the growth of dangerous machinery, of mines, chemical works, etc. – the mutilated, the sickly, the widows, etc. Pauperism is the hospital of the active labor army and the dead weight of the industrial reserve army. Its production is included in that of the relative surplus population, and its necessity in theirs. Along with the surplus population, pauperism forms a condition of capitalist production, and of the capitalist development of wealth. It is part of the overhead costs of capitalist production; but capital knows how to shift most of these from its own shoulders onto those of the working class and the lower middle class.

<!-- ch25-p063 -->
The greater the social wealth, the capital at work, and the extent and energy of its growth – and therefore also the absolute mass of the proletariat and the productivity of its labor – the greater is the industrial reserve army. The same causes that develop the expansive power of capital also develop the labor-power at its disposal. So the relative mass of the industrial reserve army grows with the potential energy of wealth. But the greater this reserve army is in proportion to the active labor army, the greater is the mass of a fixed, settled surplus population, whose misery is in inverse ratio to the torment of its labor. Finally, the larger the Lazarus layers of the working class (named after the beggar Lazarus in the Bible) and the industrial reserve army, the greater is official pauperism. *This is the absolute general law of capitalist accumulation.* Like all other laws, it is modified in its working by many circumstances, but analyzing them does not concern us here.

<!-- ch25-p064 -->
We can now see plainly how foolish is the economic wisdom that preaches to the workers that they should adjust their numbers to the needs of capital. The mechanism of capitalist production and accumulation constantly carries out this adjustment itself. The first word of this adaptation is the creation of a relative surplus population, or industrial reserve army. Its last word is the misery of ever-widening layers of the active army of labor, and the dead weight of pauperism.

<!-- ch25-p065 -->
There is a law by which, thanks to the advance in the productivity of social labor, an ever-growing quantity of means of production may be set in motion by an ever-shrinking expenditure of human power. In a capitalist society – where the worker does not employ the means of production, but the means of production employ the worker – this law is completely turned upside down, and is expressed thus: the higher the productivity of labor, the greater is the pressure of the workers on the means of employment, and so the more precarious becomes their condition of existence, namely the sale of their own labor-power to increase another's wealth, or for the self-expansion of capital. The fact that the means of production, and the productivity of labor, increase faster than the productive population therefore expresses itself, in capitalist terms, in the inverted form that the working population always increases faster than the conditions under which capital can employ this increase for its own self-expansion.

<!-- ch25-p066 -->
We saw in Part IV., when we analyzed the production of relative surplus-value (surplus-value obtained by shortening necessary labor-time, by making workers' necessities cheaper through higher productivity, so that more of a working day of given length is surplus labor), that within the capitalist system all methods for raising the social productivity of labor are carried out at the cost of the individual worker. All means for developing production turn into means of domination over the producers and of exploitation of them. They mutilate the worker into a fragment of a man and degrade him to the level of an appendage of a machine. They destroy every remnant of charm in his work and turn it into hated toil. They estrange him from the intellectual powers of the labor process in the same proportion as science is built into it as an independent power. They distort the conditions under which he works, and during the labor process they subject him to a despotism all the more hateful for its pettiness. They turn his lifetime into working time, and drag his wife and child beneath the wheels of the Juggernaut of capital. But all methods for producing surplus-value are at the same time methods of accumulation, and every extension of accumulation becomes in turn a means for developing those methods. It follows therefore that as capital accumulates, the lot of the worker, be his pay high or low, must grow worse. Finally, the law that always keeps the relative surplus population, or industrial reserve army, in balance with the extent and energy of accumulation – this law chains the worker to capital more firmly than the wedges of Vulcan chained Prometheus to the rock. It establishes an accumulation of misery that corresponds to the accumulation of capital. Accumulation of wealth at one pole is therefore at the same time accumulation of misery, agony of toil slavery, ignorance, brutality, and mental degradation at the opposite pole, that is, on the side of the class that produces its own product in the form of capital.[^25.25] Political economists state this antagonistic character of capitalist accumulation in various forms, although they confuse it with phenomena that are certainly to some extent similar, but are nevertheless essentially different and belong to pre-capitalist modes of production.

[^25.25]: “De jour en jour il devient donc plus clair que les rapports de production dans lesquels se meut la bourgeoisie n’ont pas un caractère un, un caractère simple, mais un caractère de duplicité; que dans les mêmes rapports dans lesquels se produit la richesse, la misère se produit aussi; que dans les mêmes rapports dans lesquels il y a développement des forces productives, il y a une force productive de répression; que ces rapports ne produisent la richesse bourgeoise, c’est-à-dire la richesse de la classe bourgeoise, qu’en anéantissant continuellement la richesse des membres intégrants de cette classe et en produisant un prolétariat toujours croissant.” [So from day to day it becomes clearer that the relations of production in which the bourgeoisie moves do not have a single, simple character, but a double character; that in the very same relations in which wealth is produced, poverty is produced too; that in the very same relations in which productive forces develop, there is also a productive force of repression; that these relations produce bourgeois wealth, that is, the wealth of the bourgeois class, only by continually wiping out the wealth of the individual members of this class and by producing an ever-growing proletariat] (Karl Marx: “Misère de la Philosophie,” p. 116.)

<!-- ch25-p067 -->
The Venetian monk Ortes, one of the great economic writers of the 18th century, treats the antagonism of capitalist production as a general natural law of social wealth.

<!-- ch25-p068 -->
> “In the economy of a nation, advantages and evils always balance one another (il bene ed il male economico in una nazione sempre all, istessa misura [economic good and evil in a nation always at the same measure]): the abundance of wealth with some people, is always equal to the want of it with others (la copia dei beni in alcuni sempre eguale alia mancanza di essi in altri [the abundance of goods in some always equal to the lack of them in others]): the great riches of a small number are always accompanied by the absolute privation of the first necessaries of life for many others. The wealth of a nation corresponds with its population, and its misery corresponds with its wealth. Diligence in some compels idleness in others. The poor and idle are a necessary consequence of the rich and active,” etc.[^25.26]

[^25.26]: G. Ortes: “Delia Economia Nazionale libri sei, 1777,” in Custodi, Parte Moderna, t. xxi, pp. 6, 9, 22, 25, etc. Ortes says, cited above, p. 32: “In luoco di progettar sistemi inutili per la felicità de’popoli, mi limiterò a investigare la regione della loro infelicità.” [Instead of drawing up useless schemes for making peoples happy, I shall limit myself to looking into the reasons for their unhappiness]

<!-- ch25-p069 -->
About 10 years after Ortes, the Church of England parson Townsend glorified misery, in a thoroughly brutal way, as a necessary condition of wealth.

<!-- ch25-p070 -->
> “Legal constraint (to labour) is attended with too much trouble, violence, and noise, whereas hunger is not only a peaceable, silent, unremitted pressure, but as the most natural motive to industry and labour, it calls forth the most powerful exertions.”

<!-- ch25-p071 -->
So everything depends on making hunger permanent among the working class, and according to Townsend, the principle of population, which is especially active among the poor, takes care of that.

<!-- ch25-p072 -->
> “It seems to be a law of Nature that the poor should be to a certain degree improvident” [that is, so improvident as to be born *without* a silver spoon in the mouth], “that there may always be some to fulfil the most servile, the most sordid, and the most ignoble offices in the community. The stock of human happiness is thereby much increased, whilst the more delicate are not only relieved from drudgery ... but are left at liberty without interruption to pursue those callings which are suited to their various dispositions ... it” [the Poor Law] “tends to destroy the harmony and beauty, the symmetry and order of that system which God and Nature have established in the world.”[^25.27] Where the Venetian monk found in the fate that makes misery eternal the very reason for the existence of Christian charity, celibacy, monasteries, and holy houses, the Protestant prebendary (a clergyman paid from a cathedral's income) finds in it an excuse for condemning the laws under which the poor had a right to a miserable public relief.

[^25.27]: “A Dissertation on the Poor Laws. By a Well-wisher of Mankind. (The Rev. J. Townsend) 1786,” republished London 1817, pp. 15, 39, 41. This “delicate” parson, from whose work just quoted, as well as from his “Journey through Spain,” Malthus often copies whole pages, himself borrowed the greater part of his doctrine from Sir James Steuart, though he alters Steuart in the borrowing. For example, Steuart says: “Here, in slavery, was a forcible method of making mankind diligent,” [for the non-workers] ... “Men were then forced to work” [that is, to work free of charge for others], “because they were slaves of others; men are now forced to work” [that is, to work free of charge for non-workers] “because they are the slaves of their necessities.” But he does not conclude from this, as the fat holder of paid church posts does, that the wage worker must always go hungry. On the contrary, he wants to increase their wants and to make the growing number of their wants a spur to their labor for the “more delicate.”

<!-- ch25-p073 -->
> “The progress of social wealth,” says Storch, “begets this useful class of society ... which performs the most wearisome, the vilest, the most disgusting functions, which takes, in a word, on its shoulders all that is disagreeable and servile in life, and procures thus for other classes leisure, serenity of mind and conventional” [c’est bon! (that's a good one!)] “dignity of character.”[^25.28]

[^25.28]: Storch, cited above, t. iii, p. 223.

<!-- ch25-p074 -->
Storch asks himself what, then, the progress of this capitalist civilization, with its misery and its degradation of the masses, really consists of, compared with barbarism. He finds only one answer: security!

<!-- ch25-p075 -->
> “Thanks to the advance of industry and science,” says Sismondi, “every labourer can produce every day much more than his consumption requires. But at the same time, whilst his labour produces wealth, that wealth would, were he called on to consume it himself, make him less fit for labour.” According to him, “men” [that is, non-workers] “would probably prefer to do without all artistic perfection, and all the enjoyments that manufacturers procure for us, if it were necessary that all should buy them by constant toil like that of the labourer.... Exertion today is separated from its recompense; it is not the same man that first works, and then reposes; but it is because the one works that the other rests.... The indefinite multiplication of the productive powers of labour can then only have for result the increase of luxury and enjoyment of the idle rich.”[^25.29]

[^25.29]: Sismondi, cited above, pp. 79, 80, 85.

<!-- ch25-p076 -->
Finally Destutt de Tracy, the fish-blooded bourgeois doctrinaire, blurts it out brutally:

<!-- ch25-p077 -->
> “In poor nations the people are comfortable, in rich nations they are generally poor.”[^25.30]

[^25.30]: Destutt de Tracy, cited above, p. 231: “Les nations pauvres, c’est là où le peuple est à son aise; et les nations riches, c’est là où il est ordinairement pauvre.” [The poor nations are where the people are comfortably off; and the rich nations are where they are usually poor]

### Section 5: Illustrations of the General Law of Capitalist Accumulation

#### A. England from 1846-1866

<!-- ch25-p078 -->
No period of modern society is as good for studying capitalist accumulation as the last 20 years. It is as if this period had found Fortunatus' purse (the magic purse of the old tale, which never runs empty). But of all countries, England again provides the classic example. This is because it holds first place in the world market, because capitalist production is fully developed here and nowhere else, and finally because the arrival of the Free-trade millennium since 1846 has cut off the last line of retreat of vulgar economics (economists who only describe and defend the surface appearances of the system, without investigating its real relations). The giant advance of production, with the second half of the 20-year period again far outstripping the first, has already been shown well enough in Part IV.

<!-- ch25-p079 -->
The absolute increase of the English population in the last half century was very great. Even so, the relative increase, or rate of growth, fell steadily, as the following table, taken from the census, shows.

<!-- ch25-p080 -->
Annual increase per cent. of the population of England and Wales in decimal numbers:

<!-- ch25-p081 -->
1811-1821 1.533 *per cent.*\
1821-1831 1.446 *per cent.*\
1831-1841 1.326 *per cent.*\
1841-1851 1.216 *per cent.*\
1851-1861 1.141 *per cent.*

<!-- ch25-p082 -->
Now let us look, on the other hand, at the increase of wealth. Here the movement of profit, rent of land, etc., which come under the income tax, gives the surest basis. In Great Britain from 1853 to 1864, profits liable to income tax (not counting farmers and some other categories) increased by 50.47%, or 4.58% as the yearly average,[^25.31] while the population increased by about 12% over the same period. The rise in the taxable rent of land (including houses, railways, mines, fisheries, etc.) from 1853 to 1864 came to 38%, or 3 5/12% a year. Under this heading, the following categories show the greatest increase:

[^25.31]: “Tenth Report of the Commissioners of H. M. Inland Revenue.” London, 1866. p. 38.

<!-- ch25-p083 -->
```text
Excess of annual income       Increase
of 1864 over that of 1853     per year
Houses          38.60%        3.50%
Quarries        84.76%        7.70%
Mines           68.85%        6.26%
Ironworks       39.92%        3.63%
Fisheries       57.37%        5.21%
Gasworks        126.02%       11.45%
Railways        83.29%        7.57%
```

<!-- ch25-p084 -->
If we divide the years from 1853 to 1864 into three sets of four consecutive years each, the rate at which income grows rises steadily.[^25.32] For income from profits, for example, it is 1.73% a year from 1853 to 1857; 2.74% from 1857-1861; and 9.30% a year for 1861-64. The total of the incomes of the United Kingdom that come under the income tax was £307,068,898 in 1856; £328,127,416 in 1859; £351,745,241 in 1862; £359,142,897 in 1863; £362,462,279 in 1864; and £385,530,020 in 1865.[^25.33]

[^25.32]: Same source.

[^25.33]: These figures are good enough for comparison, but taken in absolute terms they are false, since perhaps £100,000,000 of income goes undeclared every year. The Inland Revenue Commissioners complain in every one of their reports of systematic fraud, especially by the commercial and industrial classes. So, for example: “A Joint-stock company returns £6,000 as assessable profits, the surveyor raises the amount to £88,000, and upon that sum duty is ultimately paid. Another company which returns £190,000 is finally compelled to admit that the true return should be £250,000.” (Same source, p. 42.)

<!-- ch25-p085 -->
The accumulation of capital went hand in hand with its concentration and centralization. No official statistics of agriculture existed for England (they did for Ireland), but 10 counties supplied them voluntarily. These statistics showed that from 1851 to 1861 the number of farms of less than 100 acres had fallen from 31,583 to 26,597, so that 5,016 had been merged into larger farms.[^25.34] From 1815 to 1825 no personal estate worth more than £1,000,000 came under the succession duty (the tax on inheritances). From 1825 to 1855, however, 8 did, and 4 did from 1856 to June, 1859, that is, in 4½ years.[^25.35] But centralization is best seen from a short analysis of Income Tax Schedule D (profits, not counting farms, etc.) for the years 1864 and 1865. I note first that incomes from this source pay income tax on everything over £60. These taxable incomes in England, Wales and Scotland came to £95,844,222 in 1864, and to £105,435,579 in 1865.[^25.36] The number of persons taxed was 308,416 in 1864, out of a population of 23,891,009; in 1865 it was 332,431, out of a population of 24,127,003. The following table shows how these incomes were distributed in the two years:

[^25.36]: These are the net incomes after certain deductions allowed by law.

In 1855 the United Kingdom produced 61,453,079 tons of coal, worth £16,113,167; in 1864, 92,787,873 tons, worth £23,197,968. In 1855 it produced 3,218,154 tons of pig-iron, worth £8,045,385; in 1864, 4,767,951 tons, worth £11,919,877. In 1854 the length of railroads operating in the United Kingdom was 8,054 miles, with a paid-up capital of £286,068,794; in 1864 the length was 12,789 miles, with a paid-up capital of £425,719,613. In 1854 the total of the exports and imports of the United Kingdom was £268,210,145; in 1865 it was £489,923,285. The following table shows how exports moved:

In 1866 the cotton factory workers had their wages cut by 5 percent. In 1867 a similar move led to a strike of 20,000 men at Preston. *[Added in the 4th German* edition. — That was the prelude to the crisis which broke out immediately afterwards. — *F. E.]*

<!-- ch25-p094 -->
After these few examples, one can understand the cry of triumph of the Registrar-General of the British people:

<!-- ch25-p095 -->
> “Rapidly as the population has increased, it has not kept pace with the progress of industry and wealth.”[^25.38]

[^25.38]: “Census, &c.,” cited above, P. 11.

<!-- ch25-p096 -->
Let us now turn to the direct agents of this industry, the producers of this wealth: the working class.

<!-- ch25-p097 -->
> “It is one of the most melancholy features in the social state of this country,” says Gladstone, “that while there was a decrease in the consuming powers of the people, and while there was an increase in the privations and distress of the labouring class and operatives, there was at the same time a constant accumulation of wealth in the upper classes, and a constant increase of capital.”[^25.39]

[^25.39]: Gladstone in the House of Commons, Feb. 13th, 1843. *Times,* Feb. 14th, 1843 — “It is one of the most melancholy features in the social state of this country that we see, beyond the possibility of denial, that while there is at this moment a decrease in the consuming powers of the people, an increase of the pressure of privations and distress; there is at the same time a constant accumulation of wealth in the upper classes, an increase of the luxuriousness of their habits, and of their means of enjoyment.” (Hansard, 13th Feb.)

<!-- ch25-p098 -->
So spoke this oily minister in the House of Commons on February 13th, 1843. On April 16th, 1863, 20 years later, in the speech introducing his Budget, he said:

<!-- ch25-p099 -->
> “From 1842 to 1852 the taxable income of the country increased by 6 per cent.... In the 8 years from 1853 to 1861 it had increased from the basis taken in 1853 by 20 per cent.! The fact is so astonishing as to be almost incredible ... this intoxicating augmentation of wealth and power ... entirely confined to classes of property ... must be of indirect benefit to the labouring population, because it cheapens the commodities of general consumption. While the rich have been growing richer, the poor have been growing less poor. At any rate, whether the extremes of poverty are less, I do not presume to say.”[^25.40]

[^25.40]: Gladstone in the House of Commons, April 16th, 1863. *Morning Star,* April 17th.

<!-- ch25-p100 -->
What a lame anticlimax! If the working class has stayed “poor,” only “less poor,” in proportion as it produces “an intoxicating augmentation of wealth and power” for the wealthy class, then it has stayed relatively just as poor. If the extremes of poverty have not lessened, they have increased, because the extremes of wealth have. As for the cheapening of the means of subsistence, the official statistics, for example the accounts of the London Orphan Asylum, show a 20% rise in prices for the average of the three years 1860-1862, compared with 1851-1853. In the following three years, 1863-1865, the prices of meat, butter, milk, sugar, salt, coals, and a number of other necessary means of subsistence rose steadily.[^25.41] Gladstone's next Budget speech, of April 7th, 1864, is a Pindaric dithyramb (an ecstatic hymn of praise) on the advance of surplus-value-making and on the happiness of the people “tempered by poverty.” He speaks of masses “on the border” of pauperism, and of branches of trade in which “wages have not increased.” Finally he sums up the happiness of the working class in these words:

[^25.41]: See the official accounts in the Blue book: “Miscellaneous Statistics of the United Kingdom,” Part vi., London, 1866, pp. 260-273, passim. Instead of the statistics of orphan asylums, etc., the high-flown articles of the pro-government newspapers recommending dowries for the Royal children might also serve. There, the rising cost of the means of subsistence is never forgotten.

<!-- ch25-p101 -->
> “human life is but, in nine cases out of ten, a struggle for existence.”[^25.42]

[^25.42]: Gladstone, House of Commons, 7th April, 1864. — “The Hansard version runs: ‘Again, and yet more at large — what is human life, but, in the majority of cases, a struggle for existence.’ An English writer summed up the constant, glaring contradictions in Gladstone's Budget speeches of 1863 and 1864 with the following quotation from Boileau:

    “Voilà l’homme en effet. Il va du blanc au noir, Il condamne au matin ses sentiments du soir. Importun à tout autre, à soi-même incommode, Il change à tout moment d’esprit comme de mode.” [That is the man indeed: he goes from white to black. / In the morning he condemns what he felt in the evening. / A nuisance to everyone else, a burden to himself, / he changes his mind every moment, as he changes his fashions] (“The Theory of Exchanges, &c.,” London, 1864, p. 135.)

<!-- ch25-p102 -->
Professor Fawcett, who is not bound by official considerations as Gladstone is, declares flatly:

<!-- ch25-p103 -->
> “I do not, of course, deny that money wages have been augmented by this increase of capital (in the last ten years), but this apparent advantage is to a great extent lost, because many of the necessaries of life are becoming dearer” (he thinks this is because of the fall in value of the precious metals)... “the rich grow rapidly richer, whilst there is no perceptible advance in the comfort enjoyed by the industrial classes.... They (the workers) become almost the slaves of the tradesman, to whom they owe money.”[^25.43]

[^25.43]: H. Fawcett, cited above, pp. 67-82. As for the growing dependence of workers on the retail shopkeepers, this is the result of the frequent ups and downs and breaks in their employment.

<!-- ch25-p104 -->
In the chapters on the “working day” and “machinery,” the reader has seen under what conditions the British working class created an “intoxicating augmentation of wealth and power” for the propertied classes. There we were mainly concerned with the worker in his social function. But to make the law of accumulation fully clear, we must also look at his condition outside the workshop: his food and his housing. The limits of this book force us to deal mainly with the worst-paid part of the industrial proletariat and with the agricultural workers, who together make up the majority of the working class.

<!-- ch25-p105 -->
But first, a word on official pauperism, that is, on the part of the working class that has lost the condition of its existence (the sale of labor-power) and vegetates on public charity. The official list of paupers in England[^25.44] numbered 851,369 persons; in 1856, 877,767; in 1865, 971,433. Because of the cotton famine, it grew in the years 1863 and 1864 to 1,079,382 and 1,014,978. The crisis of 1866 hit London hardest. In this center of the world market, which has more people than the kingdom of Scotland, it caused pauperism to rise in 1866 by 19.5% compared with 1865 and by 24.4% compared with 1864, and to rise still more in the first months of 1867 compared with 1866. Two points stand out from an analysis of the statistics of pauperism. On the one hand, the rise and fall in the number of paupers reflects the periodic changes of the industrial cycle. On the other hand, the official statistics become more and more misleading about the real extent of pauperism, in proportion as the class struggle, and therefore the class consciousness of the workers, develop along with the accumulation of capital. For example, the brutal treatment of paupers, about which the English Press (*The Times, Pall Mall Gazette,* etc.) has cried out so loudly in the last two years, is nothing new. In 1844 F. Engels showed exactly the same horrors, and exactly the same short-lived, hypocritical outcries of “sensational literature.” But the frightful increase of “deaths by starvation” in London during the last ten years proves beyond doubt the growing horror with which working people regard the slavery of the workhouse, that place of punishment for misery.[^25.45]

[^25.44]: Wales is always included in England here.

[^25.45]: A peculiar light is thrown on the progress made since the time of Adam Smith by the fact that he still sometimes uses the word “workhouse” to mean the same as “manufactory” (a manufacturing workshop). For example, the opening of his chapter on the division of labor says: “those employed in every different branch of the work can often be collected into the same workhouse.”

#### B. The Badly Paid Strata of the British Industrial Class

<!-- ch25-p106 -->
During the cotton famine of 1862, the Privy Council put Dr. Smith in charge of an inquiry into how well the distressed factory workers in Lancashire and Cheshire were fed. His observations over many earlier years had led him to conclude that “to avert starvation diseases,” the daily food of an average woman ought to contain at least 3,900 grains of carbon with 180 grains of nitrogen, and the daily food of an average man at least 4,300 grains of carbon with 200 grains of nitrogen. For women, by his reckoning, that is about the same quantity of nutritive elements as is contained in 2 lbs. of good wheaten bread, and for men 1/9 more. For the weekly average of adult men and women, his figure was at least 28,600 grains of carbon and 1,330 grains of nitrogen. His calculation was confirmed in practice in a surprising way: it agreed with the miserable quantity of food to which want had forced down the consumption of the cotton factory workers. In December, 1862, this was 29,211 grains of carbon and 1,295 grains of nitrogen weekly.

<!-- ch25-p107 -->
In the year 1863, the Privy Council ordered an inquiry into the state of distress of the worst-fed part of the English working class. Dr. Simon, medical officer to the Privy Council, chose the above-mentioned Dr. Smith for this work. On the one hand, his inquiry covers the agricultural workers. On the other, it covers silk-weavers, needlewomen, kid-glovers, stocking-weavers, glove-weavers, and shoemakers. Except for the stocking-weavers, the people in these last categories live exclusively in towns. The inquiry made it a rule to select, in each category, the healthiest families, and those comparatively best off.

<!-- ch25-p108 -->
The general result was that

<!-- ch25-p109 -->
> “in only one of the examined classes of in-door operatives did the average nitrogen supply just exceed, while in another it nearly reached, the estimated standard of bare sufficiency [that is, sufficient to avert starvation diseases], and that in two classes there was defect – in one, a very large defect – of both nitrogen and carbon. Moreover, as regards the examined families of the agricultural population, it appeared that more than a fifth were with less than the estimated sufficiency of carbonaceous food, that more than one-third were with less than the estimated sufficiency of nitrogenous food, and that in three counties (Berkshire, Oxfordshire, and Somersetshire), insufficiency of nitrogenous food was the average local diet.”[^25.46]

[^25.46]: “Public Health. Sixth Report, 1864,” p. 13.

<!-- ch25-p110 -->
Among the agricultural workers, those of England, the wealthiest part of the United Kingdom, were the worst fed.[^25.47] Among the agricultural workers, the shortage of food fell, as a rule, chiefly on the women and children, for “the man must eat to do his work.” Still greater want ravaged the town workers examined.

[^25.47]: Cited above, p. 17.

<!-- ch25-p111 -->
> “They are so ill fed that assuredly among them there must be many cases of severe and injurious privation.”[^25.48]

[^25.48]: Cited above, p. 13.

<!-- ch25-p112 -->
(All this is “privation” on the part of the capitalist! That is, his “abstinence” from paying for the means of subsistence absolutely necessary for his “hands” merely to vegetate.)[^25.49]

[^25.49]: Cited above, Appendix, p. 232.

<!-- ch25-p113 -->
The following table shows how the above-named categories of workers, who live purely in towns, were fed. It compares them with the minimum assumed by Dr. Smith, and with the food allowance of the cotton factory workers at the time of their greatest distress:

<!-- ch25-p114 -->
```text
                           Average weekly
                                             Average weekly

                           carbon            nitrogen

                           28,876 grains     1,192 grains
occupations

                           28,211 grains     1,295 grains

allowed to the Lancashire
```
