<!-- ch25-p200 -->
> “To the insufficient quantity and miserable quality of the house accommodation generally had,” says Dr. Simon, in his official Health Report, “by our agricultural labourers, almost every page of Dr. Hunter’s report bears testimony. And gradually, for many years past, the state of the labourer in these respects has been deteriorating, house-room being now greatly more difficult for him to find, and, when found, greatly less suitable to his needs than, perhaps, for centuries had been the case. Especially within the last twenty or thirty years, the evil has been in very rapid increase, and the household circumstances of the labourer are now in the highest degree deplorable. Except in so far as they whom his labour enriches, see fit to treat him with a kind of pitiful indulgence, he is quite peculiarly helpless in the matter. Whether he shall find house-room on the land which he contributes to till, whether the house-room which he gets shall be human or swinish, whether he shall have the little space of garden that so vastly lessens the pressure of his poverty – all this does not depend on his willingness and ability to pay reasonable rent for the decent accommodation he requires, but depends on the use which others may see fit to make of their ‘right to do as they will with their own.’ However large may be a farm, there is no law that a certain proportion of labourers’ dwellings (much less of decent dwellings) shall be upon it; nor does any law reserve for the labourer ever so little right in that soil to which his industry is as needful as sun and rain.... An extraneous element weighs the balance heavily against him ... the influence of the Poor Law in its provisions concerning settlement and chargeability.[^25.100] Under this influence, each parish has a pecuniary interest in reducing to a minimum the number of its resident labourers: – for, unhappily, agricultural labour instead of implying a safe and permanent independence for the hardworking labourer and his family, implies for the most part only a longer or shorter circuit to eventual pauperism – a pauperism which, during the whole circuit, is so near, that any illness or temporary failure of occupation necessitates immediate recourse to parochial relief – and thus all residence of agricultural population in a parish is glaringly an addition to its poor-rates .... Large proprietors[^25.101] ... have but to resolve that there shall be no labourers’ dwellings on their estates, and their estates will thenceforth be virtually free from half their responsibility for the poor. How far it has been intended, in the English constitution and law, that this kind of unconditional property in land should be acquirable, and that a landlord ‘doing as he wills with his own,’ should be able to treat the cultivators of the soil as aliens, whom he may expel from his territory, is a question which I do not pretend to discuss.... For that (power) of eviction ... does not exist only in theory. On a very large scale it prevails in practice – prevails ... as a main governing condition in the household circumstances of agricultural labour.... As regards the extent of the evil, it may suffice to refer to the evidence which Dr. Hunter has compiled from the last census, that destruction of houses, notwithstanding increased local demands for them, had, during the last ten years, been in progress in 821 separate parishes or townships of England, so that irrespectively of persons who had been forced to become non-resident (that is in the parishes in which they work), these parishes and townships were receiving in 1861, as compared with 1851, a population 5 1/3 per cent. greater, into houseroom 4½ per cent. less... When the process of depopulation has completed itself, the result, says Dr. Hunter, is a show-village where the cottages have been reduced to a few, and where none but persons who are needed as shepherds, gardeners, or game-keepers, are allowed to live; regular servants who receive the good treatment usual to their class.[^25.102] But the land requires cultivation, and it will be found that the labourers employed upon it are not the tenants of the owner, but that they come from a neighbouring open village, perhaps three miles off, where a numerous small proprietary had received them when their cottages were destroyed in the close villages around. Where things are tending to the above result, often the cottages which stand, testify, in their unrepaired and wretched condition, to the extinction to which they are doomed. They are seen standing in the various stages of natural decay. While the shelter holds together, the labourer is permitted to rent it, and glad enough he will often be to do so, even at the price of decent lodging. But no repair, no improvement shall it receive, except such as its penniless occupants can supply. And when at last it becomes quite uninhabitable – uninhabitable even to the humblest standard of serfdom – it will be but one more destroyed cottage, and future poor-rates will be somewhat lightened. While great owners are thus escaping from poor-rates through the depopulation of lands over which they have control, the nearest town or open village receive the evicted labourers: the nearest, I say, but this “nearest” may mean three or four miles distant from the farm where the labourer has his daily toil. To that daily toil there will then have to be added, as though it were nothing, the daily need of walking six or eight miles for power of earning his bread. And whatever farm work is done by his wife and children, is done at the same disadvantage. Nor is this nearly all the toil which the distance occasions him. In the open village, cottage-speculators buy scraps of land, which they throng as densely as they can with the cheapest of all possible hovels. And into those wretched habitations (which, even if they adjoin the open country, have some of the worst features of the worst town residences) crowd the agricultural labourers of England.[^25.103].... Nor on the other hand must it be supposed that even when the labourer is housed upon the lands which he cultivates, his household circumstances are generally such as his life of productive industry would seem to deserve. Even on princely estates ... his cottage ... may be of the meanest description. There are landlords who deem any stye good enough for their labourer and his family, and who yet do not disdain to drive with him the hardest possible bargain for rent.[^25.104] It may be but a ruinous one-bedroomed hut, having no fire-grate, no privy [outdoor toilet], no opening window, no water supply but the ditch, no garden – but the labourer is helpless against the wrong.... And the Nuisances Removal Acts ... are ... a mere dead letter ... in great part dependent for their working on such cottage-owners as the one from whom his (the labourer’s) hovel is rented.... From brighter, but exceptional scenes, it is requisite in the interests of justice, that attention should again be drawn to the overwhelming preponderance of facts which are a reproach to the civilisation of England. Lamentable indeed, must be the case, when, notwithstanding all that is evident with regard to the quality of the present accommodation, it is the common conclusion of competent observers that even the general badness of dwellings is an evil infinitely less urgent than their mere numerical insufficiency. For years the over-crowding of rural labourers’ dwellings has been a matter of deep concern, not only to persons who care for sanitary good, but to persons who care for decent and moral life. For, again and again in phrases so uniform that they seem stereotyped, reporters on the spread of epidemic disease in rural districts, have insisted on the extreme importance of that over-crowding, as an influence which renders it a quite hopeless task, to attempt the limiting of any infection which is introduced. And again and again it has been pointed out that, notwithstanding the many salubrious [healthy] influences which there are in country life, the crowding which so favours the extension of contagious disease, also favours the origination of disease which is not contagious. And those who have denounced the over-crowded state of our rural population have not been silent as to a further mischief. Even where their primary concern has been only with the injury to health, often almost perforce they have referred to other relations on the subject. In showing how frequently it happens that adult persons of both sexes, married and unmarried, are huddled together in single small sleeping rooms, their reports have carried the conviction that, under the circumstances they describe, decency must always be outraged, and morality almost of necessity must suffer.[^25.105] Thus, for instance, in the appendix of my last annual report, Dr. Ord, reporting on an outbreak of fever at Wing, in Buckinghamshire, mentions how a young man who had come thither from Wingrave with fever, “in the first days of his illness slept in a room with nine other persons. Within a fortnight several of these persons were attacked, and in the course of a few weeks five out of the nine had fever, and one died...” From Dr. Harvey, of St. George’s Hospital, who, on private professional business, visited Wing during the time of the epidemic, I received information exactly in the sense of the above report.... “A young woman having fever, lay at night in a room occupied by her father and mother, her bastard child, two young men (her brothers), and her two sisters, each with a bastard child – 10 persons in all. A few weeks ago 13 persons slept in it.”[^25.106]

[^25.100]: In 1865 this law was improved to some extent. Experience will soon teach that tinkering of this sort is of no use.

[^25.101]: To understand what follows, we must remember that “Close Villages” are those owned by one or two large landlords, and “Open villages” are those whose land belongs to many smaller landlords. It is in the open villages that building speculators can build cottages and lodging-houses.

[^25.102]: A show-village of this kind looks very nice, but it is as unreal as the villages that Catherine II. saw on her journey to the Crimea. In recent times the shepherd too has often been banished from these show-villages. For example, near Market Harboro there is a sheep-farm of about 500 acres that employs the labor of only one man. To cut down the long trudges over these wide plains, the beautiful pastures of Leicester and Northampton, the shepherd used to get a cottage on the farm. Now they give him a thirteenth shilling a week for lodging, which he must find far away in an open village.

[^25.103]: “The labourers’ houses (in the open villages, which, of course, are always overcrowded) are usually in rows, built with their backs against the extreme edge of the plot of land which the builder could call his, and on this account are not allowed light and air, except from the front.” (Dr. Hunter’s Report, cited above, p. 135.) Very often the village beerseller or grocer is also the one who lets its houses. In that case the agricultural worker finds in him a second master, besides the farmer. He must be his customer as well as his tenant. “The hind [farm laborer] with his 10s. a week, minus a rent of £4 a year ... is obliged to buy at the seller’s own terms, his modicum of tea, sugar, flour, soap, candles, and beer.” (Cited above, p. 132.) These open villages are, in fact, the “penal settlements” of the English agricultural proletariat. Many of the cottages are simply lodging-houses, through which all the rabble of the neighborhood passes. The country worker and his family, who had often, in a truly wonderful way, kept a thoroughness and purity of character under the foulest conditions, go utterly to the devil in these places. It is, of course, the fashion among the aristocratic shylocks to shrug their shoulders like Pharisees at the building speculators, the small landlords, and the open villages. They know well enough that their “close villages” and “show-villages” are the birthplaces of the open villages, and could not exist without them. “The labourers ... were it not for the small owners, would, for by far the most part, have to sleep under the trees of the farms on which they work.” (Cited above, p. 135.) The system of “open” and “closed” villages prevails in all the Midland counties and throughout the East of England.

[^25.104]: “The employer ... is ... directly or indirectly securing to himself the profit on a man employed at 10s. a week, and receiving from this poor hind [farm laborer] £4 or £5 annual rent for houses not worth £20 in a really free market, but maintained at their artificial value by the power of the owner to say ‘Use my house, or go seek a hiring elsewhere without a character [reference] from me....’ Does a man wish to better himself, to go as a plate-layer [track-layer] on the railway, or to begin quarry-work, the same power is ready with ‘Work for me at this low rate of wages or begone at a week’s notice; take your pig with you, and get what you can for the potatoes growing in your garden.’ Should his interest appear to be better served by it, an enhanced rent is sometimes preferred in these cases by the owner (that is, the farmer) as the penalty for leaving his service.” (Dr. Hunter, cited above, p. 132.)

[^25.105]: “New married couples are no edifying study for grown-up brothers and sisters: and though instances must not be recorded, sufficient data are remembered to warrant the remark, that great depression and sometimes death are the lot of the female participator in the offence of incest.” (Dr. Hunter, cited above, p. 137.) A member of the rural police, who had for many years been a detective in the worst quarters of London, says of the girls of his village: “their boldness and shamelessness I never saw equalled during some years of police life and detective duty in the worst parts of London .... They live like pigs, great boys and girls, mothers and fathers, all sleeping in one room, in many instances.” (“Child. Empl. Com. Sixth Report, 1867,” p. 77 and following 155.)

[^25.106]: “Public Health. Seventh Report, 1865,” pp. 9, 14 passim.

<!-- ch25-p201 -->
Dr. Hunter investigated 5,375 cottages of agricultural workers, not only in the purely agricultural districts but in every county of England. Of these, 2,195 had only one bedroom (which was often used as the living-room as well), 2,930 had only two, and 250 had more than two. I will give a few samples picked from a dozen counties.

<!-- ch25-p202 -->
(1.) Bedfordshire

<!-- ch25-p203 -->
*Wrestlingworth.* The bedrooms are about 12 feet long and 10 broad, although many are smaller than this. The small one-story cottages are often divided by partitions into two bedrooms, and there is frequently one bed in a kitchen 5 feet 6 inches high. Rent, £3 a year. The tenants have to make their own outdoor toilets; the landlord supplies only a hole. As soon as one tenant has made a toilet, the whole neighborhood uses it. One house, belonging to a family called Richardson, was of a beauty quite beyond compare. “Its plaster walls bulged very like a lady’s dress in a curtsey. One gable end was convex, the other concave, and on this last, unfortunately, stood the chimney, a curved tube of clay and wood like an elephant’s trunk. A long stick served as prop to prevent the chimney from falling. The doorway and window were rhomboidal.” Of 17 houses visited, only 4 had more than one bedroom, and those four were overcrowded. The cottages with one bedroom housed 3 adults and 3 children, a married couple with 6 children, etc.

<!-- ch25-p204 -->
*Dunton.* Rents are high, from £4 to £5; the man’s weekly wage is 10s. The families hope to pay the rent through the straw-plaiting they do. The higher the rent, the more people must work together to pay it. Six adults, living with 4 children in one sleeping room, pay £3 10s. for it. The cheapest house in Dunton, 15 feet long on the outside and 10 broad, was let for £3. Only one of the houses investigated had 2 bedrooms. A little outside the village stood a house whose “tenants dunged against the house-side.” The lower 9 inches of its door had been eaten away by sheer rot. The doorway was a single opening, closed at night by a few bricks, cleverly pushed up after shutting and covered with some matting. Half a window, glass and frame, had gone the way of all flesh. Here, without furniture, 3 adults and 5 children were huddled together. Dunton is no worse than the rest of Biggleswade Union.

<!-- ch25-p205 -->
(2.) Berkshire

<!-- ch25-p206 -->
*Beenham.* In June, 1864, a man, his wife, and 4 children lived in a cot (a one-story cottage). A daughter came home from service with scarlet fever. She died. One child fell ill and died. The mother and one child were down with typhus when Dr. Hunter was called in. The father and one child slept outside. But here one could see how hard it was to keep the sick apart, for the linen of the fever-stricken household lay in the crowded marketplace of the miserable village, waiting to be washed. The rent of H.’s house was 1s. a week, with one bedroom for the man, his wife, and 6 children. One house was let for 8d. a week. It was 14 feet 6 inches long and 7 feet broad, with a kitchen 6 feet high. The bedroom had no window, fireplace, door, or opening, except into the lobby. There was no garden. A man lived here for a little while with two grown-up daughters and one grown-up son. The father and son slept on the bed, the girls in the passage. Each of the girls had a child while the family was living here, but one went to the workhouse to give birth and then came home.

<!-- ch25-p207 -->
(3.) Buckinghamshire

<!-- ch25-p208 -->
Here 30 cottages – on 1,000 acres of land – held about 130-140 persons. The parish of *Bradenham* covers 1,000 acres. In 1851 it had 36 houses and a population of 84 males and 54 females. This inequality of the sexes was partly put right by 1861, when there were 98 males and 87 females: an increase in 10 years of 14 men and 33 women. Meanwhile, the number of houses had fallen by one.

<!-- ch25-p209 -->
*Winslow.* A great part of this place is newly built, in good style. The demand for houses appears to be very marked, since very miserable cottages are let at 1s. to 1s. 3d. per week.

<!-- ch25-p210 -->
*Water Eaton.* Here, in view of the growing population, the landlords have destroyed about 20 percent of the existing houses. A poor worker, who had to walk about 4 miles to his work, was asked whether he could not find a cottage nearer. He answered: “No; they know better than to take a man in with my large family.”

<!-- ch25-p211 -->
*Tinker’s End,* near Winslow. A bedroom 11 feet long, 9 feet broad, and 6 feet 5 inches high at its highest point held 4 adults and 4 children. Another, 11 feet 3 inches by 9 feet, and 5 feet 10 inches high, housed 6 persons. Each of these families had less space than is considered necessary for a convict. No house had more than one bedroom, and not one of them had a back door. Water was very scarce. The weekly rent ran from 1s. 4d. to 2s. In 16 of the houses visited, only 1 man earned 10s. a week. Under the conditions just described, the amount of air for each person equals what he would have if he were shut up for the whole night in a box measuring 4 feet each way. But then, the ancient dens allowed a certain amount of unintended ventilation.

<!-- ch25-p212 -->
(4.) Cambridgeshire

<!-- ch25-p213 -->
*Gamblingay* belongs to several landlords. It contains the most wretched cottages to be found anywhere. There is much straw-plaiting. “A deadly lassitude, a hopeless surrendering up to filth,” reigns in Gamblingay. The neglect at its center turns into gangrene at its edges, north and south, where the houses are rotting to pieces. The absentee landlords bleed this poor slum too freely. The rents are very high. 8 or 9 persons are packed into one sleeping room; in 2 cases, 6 adults, each with 1 or 2 children, are in one small bedroom.

<!-- ch25-p214 -->
(5.) Essex

<!-- ch25-p215 -->
In this county, in many parishes, the number of persons and the number of cottages go down hand in hand. In no fewer than 22 parishes, however, the destruction of houses has not prevented the population from growing, or has not brought about the expulsion which generally happens under the name of “migration to towns.” In Fingringhoe, a parish of 3,443 acres, there were 145 houses in 1851, but in 1861 only 110. But the people did not want to go away, and even managed to increase under these circumstances. In 1851, 252 persons lived in 61 houses, but in 1861, 262 persons were squeezed into 49 houses. In Basilden, in 1851, 157 persons lived on 1,827 acres, in 35 houses; at the end of ten years there were 180 persons in 27 houses. In the parishes of Fingringhoe, South Fambridge, Widford, Basilden, and Ramsden Crags, 1,392 persons were living on 8,449 acres in 316 houses in 1851; in 1861, on the same area, there were 1,473 persons in 249 houses.

<!-- ch25-p216 -->
(6.) Herefordshire

<!-- ch25-p217 -->
This little county has suffered more from the “eviction-spirit” than any other in England. At Nadby the cottages are generally overcrowded, with only 2 bedrooms, and they belong for the most part to the farmers. The farmers easily let them for £3 or £4 a year, and paid a weekly wage of 9s.

<!-- ch25-p218 -->
(7.) Huntingdon

<!-- ch25-p219 -->
*Hartford* had 87 houses in 1851. Shortly after that, 19 cottages were destroyed in this small parish of 1,720 acres. The population was 452 in 1831, 382 in 1852, and 341 in 1861. 14 cottages, each with 1 bedroom, were visited. In one lived a married couple, 3 grown-up sons, 1 grown-up daughter, and 4 children – 10 in all; in another, 3 adults and 6 children. One of these rooms, in which 8 people slept, was 12 feet 10 inches long, 12 feet 2 inches broad, and 6 feet 9 inches high. On average, without subtracting anything for parts jutting into the room, this gave about 130 cubic feet per head. In the 14 sleeping rooms there were 34 adults and 33 children. These cottages seldom have gardens, but many of the occupants are able to farm small allotments at 10s. or 12s. per rood. These allotments are some distance from the houses, which have no toilets. The family “must either go to the allotment to deposit their ordures,” or, as happens in this place, if you will pardon the expression, “use a closet with a trough set like a drawer in a chest of drawers, and drawn out weekly and conveyed to the allotment to be emptied where its contents were wanted.” In Japan, the cycle of the conditions of life runs more decently than this.

<!-- ch25-p220 -->
(8.) Lincolnshire

<!-- ch25-p221 -->
*Langtoft.* A man lives here in Wright’s house with his wife, her mother, and 5 children. The house has a front kitchen, a scullery, and a bedroom over the front kitchen. The front kitchen and the bedroom measure 12 feet 2 inches by 9 feet 5 inches; the whole ground floor, 21 feet 2 inches by 9 feet 5 inches. The bedroom is an attic: the walls run together into the roof like a sugar-loaf, with a dormer window opening in front. “Why did he live here? On account of the garden? No; it is very small. Rent? High, 1s. 3d. per week. Near his work? No; 6 miles away, so that he walks daily, to and fro, 12 miles. He lived there, because it was a tenantable [livable] cot,” and because he wanted a cottage for himself alone, anywhere, at any price, and in any conditions. Here are the statistics of 12 houses in Langtoft, with 12 bedrooms, 38 adults, and 36 children.

<!-- ch25-p222 -->

(9.) Kent

<!-- ch25-p223 -->
*Kennington* was very seriously overpopulated in 1859, when diphtheria broke out and the parish doctor set up a medical inquiry into the condition of the poorer classes. He found that in this locality, where much labor is employed, various cottages had been destroyed and no new ones built. In one district stood four houses, called birdcages. Each had 4 rooms of the following dimensions in feet and inches:

<!-- ch25-p224 -->
Kitchen: 9 ft. 5 by 8 ft. 11 by 6 ft. 6

<!-- ch25-p225 -->
Scullery: 8 ft. 6 by 4 ft. 6 by 6 ft. 6

<!-- ch25-p226 -->
Bedroom: 8 ft. 5 by 5 ft. 10 by 6 ft. 3

<!-- ch25-p227 -->
Bedroom: 8 ft. 3 by 8 ft. 4 by 6 ft. 3

<!-- ch25-p228 -->
(10.) Northamptonshire

<!-- ch25-p229 -->
*Brinworth, Pickford and Floore:* in these villages, in the winter, 20-30 men were hanging about the streets for lack of work. The farmers do not always till the grain and turnip land enough, and the landlord has found it best to throw all his farms together into 2 or 3. Hence the lack of work. While on one side of the wall the land calls for labor, on the other side the cheated workers cast longing glances at it. Feverishly overworked in summer and half-starved in winter, it is no wonder if they say in their peculiar dialect that “the parson and gentlefolk seem frit [frightened] to death at them.”

<!-- ch25-p230 -->
At Floore there were cases, in one bedroom of the smallest size, of couples with 4, 5, or 6 children; of 3 adults with 5 children; of a couple with a grandfather and 6 children down with scarlet fever, etc. In two houses with two bedrooms there were two families, of 8 and 9 adults respectively.

<!-- ch25-p231 -->
(11.) Wiltshire

<!-- ch25-p232 -->
*Stratton.* 31 houses were visited, 8 with only one bedroom. Pentill, in the same parish: a cottage let at 1s. 3d. a week, with 4 adults and 4 children, had nothing good about it except the walls, from the floor of rough-hewn pieces of stone to the roof of worn-out thatch.

<!-- ch25-p233 -->
(12.) Worcestershire

<!-- ch25-p234 -->
House-destruction here is not quite so extreme. Yet from 1851 to 1861 the average number of inhabitants per house rose from 4.2 to 4.6.

<!-- ch25-p235 -->
*Badsey.* There are many cottages and little gardens here. Some of the farmers declare that the cottages are “a great nuisance here, because they bring the poor.” One gentleman stated:

<!-- ch25-p236 -->
“The poor are none the better for them; if you build 500 they will let fast enough, in fact, the more you build, the more they want”

<!-- ch25-p237 -->
(according to him, the houses give birth to the inhabitants, who then, by a law of Nature, press on “the means of housing”). Dr. Hunter remarks:

<!-- ch25-p238 -->
“Now these poor must come from somewhere, and as there is no particular attraction, such as doles, at Badsey, it must be repulsion from some other unfit place, which will send them here. If each could find an allotment near his work, he would not prefer Badsey, where he pays for his scrap of ground twice as much as the farmer pays for his.”

<!-- ch25-p239 -->
The continual migration to the towns, the continual formation of a surplus population in the countryside through the concentration of farms, the turning of arable land into pasture, machinery, etc., and the continual eviction of the agricultural population through the destruction of their cottages, all go hand in hand. The emptier the district is of people, the greater is its “relative surplus population,” the greater is their pressure on the means of employment, and the greater is the absolute excess of the agricultural population over the means of housing it. The greater, therefore, in the villages, is the local surplus population and the most disease-breeding packing together of human beings. The packing together of knots of people in scattered little villages and small country towns corresponds to the forcible draining of people from the surface of the land. The continual displacement of the agricultural workers, in spite of their falling numbers and the growing mass of their products, gives birth to their pauperism. Their pauperism is in the end a motive for their eviction and the chief source of their miserable housing, which breaks down their last power of resistance and makes them all the more slaves of the landowners and the farmers.[^25.107] Thus wages at their minimum become a law of Nature for them. On the other hand, the land, in spite of its constant “relative surplus population,” is at the same time underpopulated. This shows not only locally, at the points where the outflow of people to towns, mines, railroad-building, etc., is most marked. It can be seen everywhere, at harvest-time as well as in spring and summer, at those frequently recurring times when English agriculture, so careful and intensive, needs extra workers. There are always too many agricultural workers for the ordinary needs of cultivating the soil, and always too few for its exceptional or temporary needs.[^25.108] So we find in the official documents contradictory complaints, from the same places at the same time, of a shortage of labor and of an excess of it. The temporary or local shortage of labor brings about no rise in wages, but a forcing of the women and children into the fields, and exploitation at an ever lower age. As soon as the exploitation of the women and children takes place on a larger scale, it becomes in its turn a new means of making the male agricultural worker surplus and of keeping down his wage. In the east of England a beautiful fruit of this vicious circle thrives – the so-called gang system, to which I must briefly return here.[^25.109]

[^25.107]: “The heaven-born employment of the hind [farm laborer] gives dignity even to his position. He is not a slave, but a soldier of peace, and deserves his place in married men’s quarters to be provided by the landlord, who has claimed a power of enforced labour similar to that the country demands of the soldier. He no more receives market-price for his work than does the soldier. Like the soldier he is caught young, ignorant, knowing only his own trade, and his own locality. Early marriage and the operation of the various laws of settlement affect the one as enlistment and the Mutiny Act [the law governing army discipline] affect the other.” (Dr. Hunter, cited above, p. 132.) Sometimes an exceptionally soft-hearted landlord is moved by the solitude he has created. “It is a melancholy thing to stand alone in one’s country,” said Lord Leicester, when he was congratulated on the completion of Hookham. “I look around and not a house is to be seen but mine. I am the giant of Giant Castle, and have eat up all my neighbours.”

[^25.108]: A similar movement has been seen in France during the last ten years. In proportion as capitalist production there takes possession of agriculture, it drives the “surplus” agricultural population into the towns. Here too we find the housing and other conditions getting worse at the source of the surplus population. On the special “prolétariat foncier” [land proletariat] to which this system of parceling out the land has given rise, see, among others, the work of Colins, already quoted, and Karl Marx, “Der Achtzehnte Brumaire des Louis Bonaparte.” 2nd edition. Hamburg, 1869, pp. 56, etc. In 1846 the town population of France stood at 24.42, the agricultural at 75.58; in 1861, the town at 28.86, the agricultural at 71.14 percent. During the last 5 years the fall in the agricultural share of the population has been even more marked. As early as 1846, Pierre Dupont sang in his “Ouvriers”:

    Mal vêtus, logés dans des trous, Sous les combles, dans les décombres, Nous vivons avec les hiboux Et les larrons, amis des ombres. [Badly clothed, lodged in holes, under the eaves, in the ruins, we live with the owls and the thieves, friends of the shadows]

[^25.109]: “Sixth and last Report of the Children’s Employment Commission,” published at the end of March, 1867. It deals only with the agricultural gang system.

<!-- ch25-p240 -->
The gang system is found almost exclusively in the counties of Lincoln, Huntingdon, Cambridge, Norfolk, Suffolk, and Nottingham, and here and there in the neighboring counties of Northampton, Bedford, and Rutland. Lincolnshire will serve us as an example. A large part of this county is new land, formerly marsh, or even, as in others of the eastern counties just named, recently won from the sea. The steam-engine has worked wonders in draining it. What were once fens and sandbanks now bear a lush sea of grain and the highest of rents. The same holds for the alluvial lands won by human effort, as on the island of Axholme and in other parishes on the banks of the Trent. As the new farms arose, not only were no new cottages built: old ones were pulled down, and the supply of labor had to come from open villages miles away, by long roads that wound along the hillsides. Only there had the population formerly found shelter from the endless floods of winter. The workers who live on the farms of 400-1,000 acres (they are called “confined labourers”) are employed only on the kinds of agricultural work that are permanent, difficult, and done with the help of horses. For every 100 acres there is, on average, scarcely one cottage. A fen farmer, for example, gave evidence before the Commission of Inquiry:

<!-- ch25-p241 -->
> “I farm 320 acres, all arable land. I have not one cottage on my farm. I have only one labourer on my farm now. I have four horsemen lodging about. We get light work done by gangs.”[^25.110]

[^25.110]: “Child. Emp. Comm., VI. Report.” Evidence 173, p. 37.

<!-- ch25-p242 -->
The soil needs much light field labor, such as weeding, hoeing, certain kinds of manuring, removing stones, etc. This is done by the gangs, or organized bands, who live in the open villages.

<!-- ch25-p243 -->
The gang consists of 10 to 40 or 50 persons: women, young persons of both sexes (13-18 years of age, although the boys are for the most part dropped at the age of 13), and children of both sexes (6-13 years of age). At its head is the gang-master, always an ordinary agricultural worker, generally what is called a bad lot, a rascal, unsteady and drunken, but with a dash of enterprise and know-how. He is the recruiting-sergeant for the gang, which works under him, not under the farmer. He generally arranges piece-work with the farmer, and his income, which on average is not very much above that of an ordinary agricultural worker,[^25.111] depends almost entirely on the skill with which he manages to extract the greatest possible amount of labor from his gang in the shortest time. The farmers have discovered that women work steadily only under the direction of men, but that women and children, once set going, spend their life-force recklessly – as Fourier knew – while the adult male worker is shrewd enough to save his as much as he can. The gang-master goes from one farm to another, and so employs his gang for 6 to 8 months of the year. Employment by him is therefore much more profitable and more certain for the working families than employment by the individual farmer, who employs children only occasionally. This fact fastens his influence on the open villages so completely that children can generally be hired only through him. Hiring these children out individually, apart from the gang, is his second trade.

[^25.111]: Some gang-masters, however, have worked their way up to become farmers of 500 acres, or owners of whole rows of houses.

<!-- ch25-p244 -->
The “drawbacks” of the system are the overwork of the children and young persons, the enormous marches they make every day to and from the farms 5, 6, and sometimes 7 miles away, and finally the moral corruption of the gang. Although the gang-master, who in some districts is called “the driver,” is armed with a long stick, he uses it only seldom, and complaints of brutal treatment are exceptional. He is a democratic emperor, or a kind of Pied Piper of Hamelin. He must therefore be popular with his subjects, and he binds them to himself by the charms of the roving, vagabond life under his direction. Coarse freedom, noisy jollity, and the most obscene impudence make the gang attractive. Generally the gang-master settles up in a pub; then he returns home at the head of the procession, reeling drunk, propped up right and left by a strapping, domineering woman, while children and young persons bring up the rear, rowdy, singing teasing and bawdy songs. On the return journey, what Fourier calls “phanerogamie” [open coupling] is the order of the day. It is common for girls of 13 and 14 to be made pregnant by their male companions of the same age. The open villages that supply the gang’s recruits become Sodoms and Gomorrahs,[^25.112] and have twice as high a rate of illegitimate births as the rest of the kingdom. The moral character of girls brought up in these schools, once they are married women, was shown above. Their children, when opium does not finish them off, are born recruits of the gang.

[^25.112]: “Half the girls of Ludford have been ruined by going out” (in gangs). Cited above, p. 6, § 32.

<!-- ch25-p245 -->
The gang in the classic form just described is called the public, common, or tramping gang. For there are also private gangs. These are made up in the same way as the common gang, but have fewer members, and work not under a gang-master but under some old farm servant whom the farmer does not know how to employ in any better way. The vagabond fun has vanished here, but according to all witnesses the children are paid and treated worse.

<!-- ch25-p246 -->
The gang system, which has steadily grown in recent years,[^25.113] clearly does not exist for the sake of the gang-master. It exists to enrich the large farmers,[^25.114] and indirectly the landlords.[^25.115] For the farmer there is no more ingenious method of keeping his workers well below the normal level and yet always having an extra worker ready for extra work, of extracting the greatest possible amount of labor with the least possible amount of money,[^25.116] and of making adult male labor “redundant.” From what has already been explained, it will be understood why, on the one hand, a greater or lesser lack of work for the agricultural worker is admitted, while on the other hand the gang system is at the same time declared “necessary” because of the shortage of adult male labor and its migration to the towns.[^25.117] The cleanly weeded land and the uncleanly human weeds of Lincolnshire are pole and counterpole of capitalist production.[^25.118]

[^25.113]: “They (gangs) have greatly increased of late years. In some places they are said to have been introduced at comparatively late dates; in others where gangs ... have been known for many years ... more and younger children are employed in them.” (cited above, p. 79, § 174).

[^25.114]: “Small farmers never employ gangs.” “It is not on poor land, but on land which affords rent of from 40 to 50 shillings, that women and children are employed in the greatest numbers.” (cited above, pp. 17, 14.)

[^25.115]: One of these gentlemen found the taste of his rent so pleasing that he indignantly declared to the Commission of Inquiry that the whole fuss was due only to the name of the system. If, instead of “gang,” it were called “the Agricultural Juvenile Industrial Self-supporting Association,” everything would be all right.

[^25.116]: “Gang work is cheaper than other work; that is why they are employed,” says a former gang-master (cited above, p. 17, § 14). “The gang-system is decidedly the cheapest for the farmer, and decidedly the worst for the children,” says a farmer (cited above, p. 16, § 3.)

[^25.117]: “Undoubtedly much of the work now done by children in gangs used to be done by men and women. More men are out of work now where children and women are employed than formerly.” (cited above, p. 43, n. 202.) On the other hand, “the labour question in some agricultural districts, particularly the arable, is becoming so serious in consequence of emigration, and the facility afforded by railways for getting to large towns that I (the “I” is the steward of a great lord) think the services of children are most indispensable,” (cited above, p. 80, n. 180.) For the “labour question” in English agricultural districts, unlike in the rest of the civilized world, means the landlords’ and farmers’ question, namely: how is it possible, despite an ever-growing exodus of the country people, to keep up a sufficient relative surplus population in the countryside, and by means of it to keep the wages of the agricultural worker at a minimum?

[^25.118]: The “Public Health Report,” which deals with the gang system in passing when it treats children’s mortality, remains unknown to the press, and therefore to the English public. On the other hand, the last report of the “Child. Empl. Comm.” gave the press the sensational copy it always welcomes. While the Liberal press asked how the fine gentlemen and ladies, and the well-paid clergy of the State Church, who swarm in Lincolnshire, could allow such a system to arise on their estates, under their very eyes – they who send out special missions to the Antipodes “for the improvement of the morals of South Sea Islanders” — the more refined press confined itself to reflections on the coarse degradation of the agricultural population, who are capable of selling their children into such slavery! Under the accursed conditions to which these “delicate” people condemn the agricultural worker, it would not be surprising if he ate his own children. What is really wonderful is the healthy integrity of character that he has, in great part, kept. The official reports prove that the parents, even in the gang districts, loathe the gang system. “There is much in the evidence that shows that the parents of the children would, in many instances, be glad to be aided by the requirements of a legal obligation, to resist the pressure and the temptations to which they are often subject. They are liable to be urged, at times by the parish officers, at times by employers, under threats of being themselves discharged, to be taken to work at an age when ... school attendance ... would be manifestly to their greater advantage.... All that time and strength wasted; all the suffering from extra and unprofitable fatigue produced to the labourer and to his children; every instance in which the parent may have traced the moral ruin of his child to the undermining of delicacy by the over-crowding of cottages, or to the contaminating influences of the public gang, must have been so many incentives to feelings in the minds of the labouring poor which can be well understood, and which it would be needless to particularise. They must be conscious that much bodily and mental pain has thus been inflicted upon them from causes for which they were in no way answerable; to which, had it been in their power, they would have in no way consented; and against which they were powerless to struggle.” (cited above, p. xx., § 82, and xxiii., n. 96.)

#### F. Ireland

<!-- ch25-p247 -->
To finish this section, we must travel for a moment to Ireland. First, the main facts of the case.

<!-- ch25-p248 -->
In 1841 the population of Ireland had reached 8,222,664. By 1851 it had dwindled to 6,623,985; by 1861, to 5,850,309; by 1866, to 5½ millions, nearly its level in 1801. The decline began with the famine year, 1846, so that in less than twenty years Ireland lost more than 5/16ths of its people.[^25.119] Its total emigration from May, 1851, to July, 1865, numbered 1,591,487; the emigration during the years 1861-1865 was more than half-a-million. From 1851-1861 the number of inhabited houses fell by 52,990. From 1851-1861 the number of holdings of 15 to 30 acres rose by 61,000, and the number of holdings over 30 acres by 109,000, while the total number of all farms fell by 120,000. This fall, therefore, was due solely to the suppression of farms under 15 acres, that is, to their centralization.

[^25.119]: Population of Ireland: 1801, 5,319,867 persons; 1811, 6,084,996; 1821, 6,869,544; 1831, 7,828,347; 1841, 8,222,664.

<!-- ch25-p272 -->
England, a country with fully developed capitalist production, and above all an industrial country, would have bled to death from such a drain of population as Ireland has suffered. But Ireland is at present only an agricultural district of England, separated by a wide channel from the country to which it supplies grain, wool, cattle, and industrial and military recruits.

<!-- ch25-p273 -->
The depopulation of Ireland has thrown much of the land out of cultivation and has greatly reduced the produce of the soil.[^25.123] And in spite of the greater area given over to cattle breeding, the depopulation has brought about an absolute decline in some branches of cattle breeding, and in others an advance hardly worth mentioning and constantly interrupted by setbacks. Nevertheless, as the population fell in numbers, rents and farmers’ profits rose, although profits did not rise as steadily as rents. The reason for this is easy to understand. On the one hand, as small holdings were thrown together into large ones and arable land was changed into pasture, a larger part of the whole produce was turned into surplus-produce. The surplus-produce increased, although the total produce, of which it formed a fraction, decreased. On the other hand, the money value of this surplus-produce increased even faster than its mass, because of the rise in the English market price of meat, wool, etc., during the last 20 years, and especially during the last 10.

[^25.123]: If the product per acre also falls relatively, it must not be forgotten that for a century and a half England has indirectly exported the soil of Ireland, without even allowing its cultivators the means to replace the elements of the soil that had been exhausted.

<!-- ch25-p274 -->
The scattered means of production that serve the producers themselves as means of employment and of subsistence, without increasing their own value by absorbing the labor of others, are no more capital than a product consumed by its own producer is a commodity. If the mass of the means of production employed in agriculture fell along with the mass of the population, the mass of the capital employed in agriculture still increased. This is because a part of the means of production that were formerly scattered was concentrated and turned into capital.

<!-- ch25-p275 -->
The total capital of Ireland outside agriculture, employed in industry and trade, accumulated slowly during the last two decades, with great and constantly recurring fluctuations. All the more rapidly did the concentration of its individual parts develop. And however small its absolute increase, it had increased greatly in proportion to the shrinking population.

<!-- ch25-p276 -->
Here, then, before our own eyes and on a large scale, a process is revealed that orthodox economics could not have wished better for the support of its dogma: that misery springs from absolute surplus population, and that balance is restored by depopulation. This is a far more important experiment than the plague in the middle of the 14th century, which the Malthusians have praised so highly. Note further: only the naïveté of the schoolmaster could apply the standard of the 14th century to the conditions of production and population of the nineteenth century. But on top of that, this naïveté overlooked a fact. After the plague and the decimation that went with it, on this side of the Channel, in England, the agricultural population was freed and grew richer; on that side, in France, there followed greater servitude and more misery.[^25.124]

[^25.124]: Because Ireland is regarded as the promised land of the “principle of population,” Th. Sadler, before publishing his work on population, issued his famous book, “Ireland, its Evils and their Remedies.” 2nd edition, London, 1829. In it he compares the statistics of the individual provinces, and of the individual counties in each province, and proves that the misery there is not, as Malthus would have it, in proportion to the size of the population, but in inverse proportion to it.

<!-- ch25-p277 -->
The Irish famine of 1846 killed more than 1,000,000 people, but it killed poor devils only. It did not do the slightest damage to the wealth of the country. The exodus of the next 20 years, an exodus still constantly growing, did not decimate their means of production along with the human beings, as, for example, the Thirty Years’ War did. Irish genius discovered an altogether new way of spiriting a poor people thousands of miles away from the scene of its misery. The exiles transplanted to the United States send sums of money home every year as traveling expenses for those left behind. Every troop that emigrates one year draws another after it the next. So, instead of costing Ireland anything, emigration forms one of the most profitable branches of its export trade. Finally, it is a systematic process. It does not simply make a passing gap in the population, but every year sucks out of it more people than births replace, so that the absolute level of the population falls year by year.[^25.125]

[^25.125]: Between 1851 and 1874, the total number of emigrants came to 2,325,922.

<!-- ch25-p278 -->
What were the consequences for the Irish workers left behind and freed from the surplus population? That the relative surplus population is as great today as before 1846; that wages are just as low; that the oppression of the workers has increased; that misery is forcing the country toward a new crisis. The facts are simple. The revolution in agriculture has kept pace with emigration. The production of relative surplus population has more than kept pace with the absolute depopulation. A glance at table C. shows that the change of arable land to pasture must work even more sharply in Ireland than in England. In England the growing of green crops increases with the breeding of cattle; in Ireland, it decreases. While a large number of acres that were formerly tilled lie idle or are turned permanently into grass-land, a great part of the waste land and peat bogs that were formerly unused now serve to extend cattle-breeding. The smaller and medium farmers – I count among these all who do not farm more than 100 acres – still make up about 8/10ths of the whole number.[^25.126] One after another, and with a force unknown before, they are crushed by the competition of an agriculture run by capital, and so they continually supply new recruits to the class of wage workers. The one great industry of Ireland, linen manufacture, needs relatively few adult men. In spite of its expansion since the price of cotton rose in 1861-1866, it employs altogether only a comparatively insignificant part of the population. Like all other great modern industries, it constantly produces, through incessant fluctuations, a relative surplus population within its own sphere, even when the mass of human beings it absorbs increases absolutely. The misery of the agricultural population forms the pedestal for gigantic shirt-factories, whose armies of workers are, for the most part, scattered over the country. Here we meet again the system of domestic industry described above, which, in underpayment and overwork, possesses its own systematic means of creating superfluous workers. Finally, although the depopulation does not have such destructive consequences as it would have in a country with fully developed capitalist production, it does not go on without constantly reacting on the home market. The gap that emigration causes here limits not only the local demand for labor, but also the incomes of small shopkeepers, artisans, and tradespeople generally. Hence the fall in incomes between £60 and £100 in Table E.

[^25.126]: According to a table in Murphy’s “Ireland Industrial, Political and Social,” 1870, 94.6 percent of the holdings do not reach 100 acres, and 5.4 exceed 100 acres.

<!-- ch25-p279 -->
A clear account of the condition of the agricultural workers in Ireland can be found in the Reports of the Irish Poor Law Inspectors (1870).[^25.127] As officials of a government that is kept in power only by bayonets and by a state of siege, now open, now disguised, they have to observe all the caution in language that their colleagues in England scorn. In spite of this, however, they do not let their government lull itself with illusions. According to them, the rate of wages in the country, still very low, has risen 50-60 percent within the last 20 years, and now stands, on the average, at 6s. to 9s. per week. But behind this apparent rise is hidden an actual fall in wages, because it does not match at all the rise in price of the necessary means of subsistence that has taken place in the meantime. As proof, here is the following extract from the official accounts of an Irish workhouse.

[^25.127]: “Reports from the Poor Law Inspectors on the Wages of Agricultural Labourers in Dublin,” 1870. See also “Agricultural labourers (Ireland). Return, etc.” 8 March, 1861, London, 1862.

<!-- ch25-p280 -->
```text
      AVERAGE WEEKLY COST PER HEAD
Year ended        Provisions and
                                  Clothing. TOTAL.
                  Necessaries.
29th Sept., 1849. 1s. 3 1/4d.     3d.       1s. 6 1/4d.
29th Sept., 1869. 2s. 7 1/4d.     6d.       3s. 1 1/4d.
```

<!-- ch25-p281 -->
So the price of the necessary means of subsistence is fully twice, and the price of clothing exactly twice, what it was 20 years before.

<!-- ch25-p282 -->
Even apart from this disproportion, a mere comparison of the rate of wages expressed in gold would give a result far from accurate. Before the famine, the great mass of agricultural wages was paid in kind, and only the smallest part in money; today, payment in money is the rule. From this it follows that, whatever the amount of the real wage, its money rate must rise.

<!-- ch25-p283 -->
> “Previous to the famine, the labourer enjoyed his cabin ... with a rood, or half-acre or acre of land, and facilities for ... a crop of potatoes. He was able to rear his pig and keep fowl.... But they now have to buy bread, and they have no refuse upon which they can feed a pig or fowl, and they have consequently no benefit from the sale of a pig, fowl, or eggs.”[^25.128]

[^25.128]: Cited above, pp. 29, 1.

<!-- ch25-p284 -->
In fact, the agricultural workers used to be simply the smallest of the small farmers, and for the most part they formed a kind of rear-guard of the medium and large farms on which they found work. Only since the catastrophe of 1846 have they begun to form a section of the class of purely wage workers, a special class, connected with its employers only by money relations.

<!-- ch25-p285 -->
We know what their housing conditions were in 1846. Since then they have grown even worse. A part of the agricultural workers, though a part that grows smaller day by day, still lives on the farmers’ holdings in over-crowded huts, whose hideousness far surpasses the worst that the English agricultural workers showed us in this line. And this holds generally, with the exception of certain tracts of Ulster; in the south, in the counties of Cork, Limerick, Kilkenny, etc.; in the east, in Wicklow, Wexford, etc.; in the center of Ireland, in King’s and Queen’s County, Dublin, etc.; in the west, in Sligo, Roscommon, Mayo, Galway, etc.

<!-- ch25-p286 -->
> “The agricultural labourers’ huts,” an inspector cries out, “are a disgrace to the Christianity and to the civilisation of this country.”[^25.129]

[^25.129]: Cited above, p. 12.

<!-- ch25-p287 -->
To make these holes still more attractive to the workers, the pieces of land that have belonged to these huts from time immemorial are systematically confiscated.

<!-- ch25-p288 -->
> “The mere sense that they exist subject to this species of ban, on the part of the landlords and their agents, has ... given birth in the minds of the labourers to corresponding sentiments of antagonism and dissatisfaction towards those by whom they are thus led to regard themselves as being treated as ... a proscribed race.”[^25.130]

[^25.130]: Cited above, p. 12.

<!-- ch25-p289 -->
The first act of the agricultural revolution was to sweep away the huts standing on the field of labor. This was done on the largest scale, and as if in obedience to a command from on high. Thus many workers were forced to look for shelter in villages and towns. There they were thrown like refuse into garrets, holes, cellars, and corners, in the worst back slums. Thousands of Irish families found themselves suddenly transplanted into hotbeds of vice – families who, according to the testimony of the English (eaten up as the English are with national prejudice), are notable for their rare attachment to hearth and home, for their cheerfulness, and for the purity of their home life. The men now have to look for work from the neighboring farmers and are hired only by the day, and so under the most precarious form of wage. Hence

<!-- ch25-p290 -->
> “they sometimes have long distances to go to and from work, often get wet, and suffer much hardship, not unfrequently ending in sickness, disease and want.”[^25.131]

[^25.131]: Cited above, p. 25.

<!-- ch25-p291 -->
> “The towns have had to receive from year to year what was deemed to be the surplus labour of the rural division;”[^25.132] and then people still wonder that “there is still a surplus of labour in the towns and villages, and either a scarcity or a threatened scarcity in some of the country divisions.”[^25.133] The truth is that this shortage becomes noticeable only “in harvest-time, or during spring, or at such times as agricultural operations are carried on with activity; at other periods of the year many hands are idle;”[^25.134] that “from the digging out of the main crop of potatoes in October until the early spring following ... there is no employment for them;”[^25.135] and further, that during the busy times they “are subject to broken days and to all kinds of interruptions.”[^25.136]

[^25.132]: Cited above, p. 27.

[^25.133]: Cited above, p. 25.

[^25.134]: Cited above, p. 1.

[^25.135]: Cited above, pp. 31, 32.

[^25.136]: Cited above, p. 25.

<!-- ch25-p292 -->
These results of the agricultural revolution – that is, of the change of arable land into pasture, the use of machinery, the strictest saving of labor, etc. – are made still worse by the model landlords, who, instead of spending their rents in other countries, condescend to live in Ireland on their demesnes. So that the law of supply and demand may not be broken, these gentlemen draw their

<!-- ch25-p293 -->
> “labour-supply ... chiefly from their small tenants, who are obliged to attend when required to do the landlord’s work, at rates of wages, in many instances, considerably under the current rates paid to ordinary labourers, and without regard to the inconvenience or loss to the tenant of being obliged to neglect his own business at critical periods of sowing or reaping.”[^25.137]

[^25.137]: Cited above, p. 30.

<!-- ch25-p294 -->
The uncertainty and irregularity of employment, the constant return and long duration of gluts of labor – all these symptoms of a relative surplus population therefore appear in the reports of the Poor Law administration as so many hardships of the agricultural proletariat. It will be remembered that we met a similar spectacle among the English agricultural proletariat. But the difference is this. In England, an industrial country, the industrial reserve recruits itself from the country districts. In Ireland, an agricultural country, the agricultural reserve recruits itself from the towns, the cities of refuge of the agricultural workers who have been driven out. In England, the people agriculture has left over are turned into factory workers. In Ireland, those forced into the towns press on wages in the towns, but at the same time they remain agricultural workers, and are constantly sent back to the country districts in search of work.

<!-- ch25-p295 -->
The official inspectors sum up the material condition of the agricultural worker as follows:

<!-- ch25-p296 -->
> “Though living with the strictest frugality, his own wages are barely sufficient to provide food for an ordinary family and pay his rent” and he depends upon other sources for the means of clothing himself, his wife, and children.... The atmosphere of these cabins, combined with the other privations they are subjected to, has made this class particularly susceptible to low fever and pulmonary consumption [tuberculosis of the lungs].”[^25.138]

[^25.138]: Cited above, pp. 21, 13.

<!-- ch25-p297 -->
After this, it is no wonder that, according to the unanimous testimony of the inspectors, a gloomy discontent runs through the ranks of this class; that they long for the return of the past, loathe the present, despair of the future, give themselves up “to the evil influence of agitators,” and have only one fixed idea, to emigrate to America. This is the land of Cockaigne, the fabled land of plenty, into which the great Malthusian cure-all, depopulation, has transformed green Erin.

<!-- ch25-p298 -->
One example will show what a happy life the Irish factory worker leads:

<!-- ch25-p299 -->
> “On my recent visit to the North of Ireland,” says the English Factory Inspector, Robert Baker, “I met with the following evidence of effort in an Irish skilled workman to afford education to his children; and I give his evidence verbatim, as I took it from his mouth. That he was a skilled factory hand, may be understood when I say that he was employed on goods for the Manchester market. ‘Johnson. – I am a beetler [a worker who pounds linen cloth to finish it] and work from 6 in the morning till 11 at night, from Monday to Friday. Saturday we leave off at 6 p. m., and get three hours of it (for meals and rest). I have five children in all. For this work I get 10s. 6d. a week; my wife works here also, and gets 5s. a week. The oldest girl who is 12, minds the house. She is also cook, and all the servant we have. She gets the young ones ready for school. A girl going past the house wakes me at half past five in the morning. My wife gets up and goes along with me. We get nothing (to eat) before we come to work. The child of 12 takes care of the little children all the day, and we get nothing till breakfast at eight. At eight we go home. We get tea once a week; at other times we get stirabout [porridge], sometimes of oat-meal, sometimes of Indian meal [cornmeal], as we are able to get it. In the winter we get a little sugar and water to our Indian meal. In the summer we get a few potatoes, planting a small patch ourselves; and when they are done we get back to stirabout. Sometimes we get a little milk as it may be. So we go on from day to day, Sunday and week day, always the same the year round. I am always very much tired when I have done at night. We may see a bit of flesh meat sometimes, but very seldom. Three of our children attend school, for whom we pay 1d. a week a head. Our rent is 9d. a week. Peat for firing costs 1s. 6d. a fortnight at the very lowest.’”[^25.139]

[^25.139]: “Rept. of Insp. of Fact., 31st Oct., 1866,” p. 96.

<!-- ch25-p300 -->
Such are Irish wages, such is Irish life!

<!-- ch25-p301 -->
In fact, the misery of Ireland is again the topic of the day in England. At the end of 1866 and the beginning of 1867, one of the Irish land magnates, Lord Dufferin, set about solving it in *The Times.* “Wie menschlich von solch grossem Herrn!” [How human of so great a lord!]

<!-- ch25-p302 -->
From Table E. we saw that in 1864, out of £4,368,610 of total profits, three surplus-value makers pocketed only £262,819; but that in 1865, out of £4,669,979 total profits, the same three virtuosi of “abstinence” pocketed £274,528. In 1864, 26 surplus-value makers reached £646,377; in 1865, 28 surplus-value makers reached £736,448. In 1864, 121 surplus-value makers took £1,076,912; in 1865, 150 surplus-value makers, £1,320,906. In 1864, 1,131 surplus-value makers took £2,150,818, nearly half of the total annual profit; in 1865, 1,194 surplus-value makers, £2,418,833, more than half of the total annual profit. But the lion’s share of the yearly national rental that an inconceivably small number of land magnates in England, Scotland and Ireland swallow up is so monstrous that the wisdom of the English State does not think fit to supply the same statistical materials about the distribution of rents as about the distribution of profits. Lord Dufferin is one of those land magnates. That rent-rolls and profits can ever be “excessive,” or that their plethora is in any way connected with a plethora of the people’s misery, is, of course, an idea as “disreputable” as it is “unsound.” He keeps to facts. The fact, as he sees it, is that as the Irish population shrinks, the Irish rent-rolls swell; that depopulation benefits the landlords, and therefore also benefits the soil, and therefore the people, that mere accessory of the soil. He declares, therefore, that Ireland is still over-populated, and that the stream of emigration still flows too lazily. To be perfectly happy, Ireland must get rid of at least one-third of a million working men. Let no one imagine that this lord, a poet into the bargain, is a physician of the school of Sangrado, who, whenever he did not find his patient better, ordered bloodletting and more bloodletting, until the patient lost his sickness at the same time as his blood. Lord Dufferin demands a new bloodletting of only one-third of a million, instead of about two millions; in fact, without getting rid of these, the millennium in Erin cannot come. The proof is easily given.

<!-- ch25-p303 -->

<!-- ch25-p305 -->
From 1851 to 1861 centralization destroyed mainly farms of the first three categories, under 1 and not over 15 acres. These above all must disappear. This gives 307,058 “supernumerary” farmers, and, counting the families at the low average of 4 persons, 1,228,232 persons. On the extravagant supposition that one-fourth of these can be absorbed again after the agricultural revolution is complete, there remain 921,174 persons for emigration. Categories 4, 5, 6, of over 15 and not over 100 acres, are, as has long been known in England, too small for the capitalist cultivation of grain, and for sheep-breeding they are almost vanishing quantities. On the same supposition as before, therefore, there are a further 788,761 persons to emigrate; total, 1,709,532. And as l’appétit vient en mangeant [appetite comes with eating], Rentroll’s eyes will soon discover that Ireland, with 3½ millions, is still miserable, and miserable because she is over-populated. Therefore her depopulation must go still further, so that she may fulfill her true destiny, that of an English sheep-walk and cattle-pasture.”[^25.141]

[^25.141]: I shall show more fully in Vol. III. of this work, in the section on landed property, how the famine and its consequences have been deliberately exploited, both by the individual landlords and by the English legislature, to carry out the agricultural revolution by force and to thin the population of Ireland down to the proportion that satisfies the landlords. There I also return to the condition of the small farmers and the agricultural workers. For now, only one quotation. Nassau W. Senior says, among other things, in his posthumous work, “Journals, Conversations and Essays relating to Ireland.” 2 vols. London, 1868; Vol. II., p. 282: “Well,” said Dr. G., “we have got our Poor Law and it is a great instrument for giving the victory to the landlords. Another, and a still more powerful instrument is emigration.... No friend to Ireland can wish the war to be prolonged [between the landlords and the small Celtic farmers] — still less, that it should end by the victory of the tenants. The sooner it is over — the sooner Ireland becomes a grazing country, with the comparatively thin population which a grazing country requires, the better for all classes.” The English Corn Laws of 1815 secured Ireland the monopoly of the free import of grain into Great Britain. So they artificially favored the growing of grain. With the abolition of the Corn Laws in 1846, this monopoly was suddenly removed. Apart from all other circumstances, this event alone was enough to give a great push to the turning of Irish arable land into pasture, to the concentration of farms, and to the eviction of small cultivators. From 1815 to 1846 the fruitfulness of the Irish soil had been praised, and loudly proclaimed as destined by Nature herself for the growing of wheat. After that, English agronomists, economists, and politicians suddenly discover that it is good for nothing but producing forage. M. Léonce de Lavergne has hurried to repeat this on the other side of the Channel. It takes a “serious” man, in Lavergne’s style, to be caught by such childishness.

<!-- ch25-p306 -->
Like all good things in this bad world, this profitable method has its drawbacks. As rents accumulate in Ireland, the Irish accumulate in America at the same pace. The Irishman, driven out by sheep and ox, reappears on the other side of the ocean as a Fenian (a member of the Irish revolutionary brotherhood). And face to face with the old queen of the seas rises, more and more threatening, the young giant Republic:

<!-- ch25-p307 -->
*Acerba fata Romanos agunt*\
*Scelusque fraternae necis.*\
[Harsh fates drive the Romans on,\
and the crime of a brother’s murder]

# Part 8: Primitive Accumulation

## Chapter 26: The Secret of Primitive Accumulation

<!-- ch26-p001 -->
We have seen how money is changed into capital (value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger). We have seen how surplus-value is made through capital, and how more capital is made from surplus-value. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it.) But the accumulation of capital presupposes surplus-value. Surplus-value presupposes capitalist production. And capitalist production presupposes that considerable masses of capital and of labor-power already exist in the hands of producers of commodities. (Labor-power is a person's capacity to work, which the worker sells to the capitalist; a commodity is a thing produced in order to be exchanged, not for the producer's own use.) So the whole movement seems to turn in a vicious circle. We can only get out of it by supposing a primitive accumulation (what Adam Smith calls previous accumulation) that comes before capitalist accumulation: an accumulation that is not the result of the capitalist mode of production, but its starting point.

<!-- ch26-p002 -->
This primitive accumulation plays about the same part in political economy (the science of economics as it was then called) as original sin plays in theology. Adam bit the apple, and from then on sin fell on the human race. Its origin is supposed to be explained by telling it as a story from the past. Long, long ago there were two sorts of people. One was the diligent, intelligent, and, above all, thrifty elite. The other was lazy good-for-nothings, who spent all they had, and more, in wild living. The legend of theological original sin certainly tells us how man came to be condemned to eat his bread in the sweat of his brow. But the history of economic original sin shows us that there are people for whom this is by no means necessary. Never mind! And so it came about that the thrifty sort piled up wealth, and the lazy sort in the end had nothing to sell except their own skins. And from this original sin dates the poverty of the great majority, who, despite all their labor, have up to now nothing to sell but themselves; and the wealth of the few, which keeps growing although they stopped working long ago. Such insipid childishness is preached to us every day in defense of property. M. Thiers, for example, had the nerve to repeat it, with all the solemnity of a statesman, to the French people, who were once so witty. But as soon as the question of property comes up, it becomes a sacred duty to proclaim the mental food of the infant as the only thing fit for all ages and all stages of development. In actual history it is well known that conquest, enslavement, robbery, murder, in short force, play the great part. In the gentle chronicles of political economy, the idyllic has reigned since time immemorial. Right and “labour” were from the beginning the only means of getting rich, with the present year, of course, always excepted. In fact, the methods of primitive accumulation are anything but idyllic.

<!-- ch26-p003 -->
In themselves, money and commodities are no more capital than the means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things) and the means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live) are. They need to be transformed into capital. But this transformation itself can only take place under certain conditions, which come down to this: two very different kinds of owners of commodities must come face to face and into contact. On the one side are the owners of money, means of production, and means of subsistence, who are eager to increase the sum of values they own by buying other people's labor-power. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) On the other side are free workers, the sellers of their own labor-power, and therefore the sellers of labor. They are free workers in a double sense. They are not themselves part and parcel of the means of production, as slaves, bondsmen, etc. are. Nor do the means of production belong to them, as they do to peasant-proprietors. So they are free from, unencumbered by, any means of production of their own. With this split of the market for commodities into two poles, the basic conditions of capitalist production are given. The capitalist system presupposes the complete separation of the workers from all property in the means by which they can put their labor to work. Once capitalist production stands on its own legs, it not only maintains this separation but reproduces it on a constantly growing scale. So the process that clears the way for the capitalist system can be none other than the process that takes away from the worker the possession of his means of production. On the one side, this process turns the social means of subsistence and of production into capital. On the other, it turns the immediate producers into wage workers. The so-called primitive accumulation, therefore, is nothing else than the historical process of divorcing the producer from the means of production. It appears as primitive because it forms the prehistoric stage of capital and of the mode of production that corresponds to capital.

<!-- ch26-p004 -->
The economic structure of capitalist society has grown out of the economic structure of feudal society. The breaking up of feudal society set free the elements of capitalist society.

<!-- ch26-p005 -->
The immediate producer, the worker, could only dispose of his own person once he was no longer tied to the soil and no longer the slave, serf, or bondsman of another person. To become a free seller of labor-power, who takes his commodity wherever he finds a market, he also had to escape from the rule of the guilds, their rules for apprentices and journeymen, and the obstacles of their labor regulations. So the historical movement that changes the producers into wage workers appears, on the one hand, as their liberation from serfdom and from the chains of the guilds. This side alone exists for our bourgeois historians (bourgeois: belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it). But, on the other hand, these newly freed men became sellers of themselves only after they had been robbed of all their own means of production, and of all the guarantees of existence that the old feudal arrangements offered. And the history of this, their expropriation (the taking away of their property), is written in the annals of mankind in letters of blood and fire.

<!-- ch26-p006 -->
The industrial capitalists, these new potentates, had for their part to push aside not only the guild masters of the handicrafts, but also the feudal lords, who owned the sources of wealth. In this respect, their conquest of social power appears as the fruit of a victorious struggle on two fronts. It was a struggle against feudal lordship and its revolting privileges. And it was a struggle against the guilds and the chains they laid on the free development of production and the free exploitation of man by man. The chevaliers d’industrie [knights of industry, that is, swindlers], however, only managed to replace the chevaliers of the sword [knights] by making use of events in which they themselves had played no part at all. They rose by means as vile as those by which the Roman freedman once made himself the master of his *patronus* [patron, his former master].

<!-- ch26-p007 -->
The starting point of the development that produced the wage worker as well as the capitalist was the servitude of the worker. The advance consisted in a change in the form of this servitude, in the transformation of feudal exploitation into capitalist exploitation. To understand how this development proceeded, we need not go back very far. We do come across the first beginnings of capitalist production as early as the 14th or 15th century, here and there, in certain towns of the Mediterranean. But the capitalist era dates from the 16th century. Wherever it appears, serfdom has long since been abolished, and the highest achievement of the middle ages, the existence of sovereign towns, has long been in decline.

<!-- ch26-p008 -->
In the history of primitive accumulation, every revolution is epoch-making that acts as a lever for the capitalist class as it is being formed. But above all, the epoch-making moments are those when great masses of men are suddenly and forcibly torn from their means of subsistence and hurled onto the labor market as free and “unattached” proletarians (members of the proletariat, the class of wage workers, who own nothing they can live by except their labor-power). The expropriation of the agricultural producer, of the peasant, from the soil is the basis of the whole process. The history of this expropriation takes on different aspects in different countries. It runs through its various phases in a different order of succession, and at different periods. Only in England, which we take as our example, does it have the classic form.

<!-- ch26-p009 -->
[^26.1]

[^26.1]: In Italy, where capitalist production developed earliest, the breaking up of serfdom also took place earlier than elsewhere. There the serf was freed before he had gained any prescriptive right to the soil (a right based on long use). His freedom at once transformed him into a free proletarian, who, moreover, found his master ready and waiting for him in the towns, for the most part handed down as legacies from Roman times. About the end of the 15th century, the revolution of the world market destroyed Northern Italy's commercial supremacy. Then a movement in the reverse direction set in. The workers of the towns were driven all together into the countryside, and gave a push, never seen before, to small-scale farming, carried on in the form of gardening.

## Chapter 27: Expropriation of the Agricultural Population From the Land

<!-- ch27-p001 -->
In England, serfdom had practically disappeared in the last part of the 14th century. At that time, and to a still larger extent in the 15th century, the immense majority of the population[^27.1] consisted of free peasant proprietors, whatever the feudal title under which their right of property was hidden.
