On the larger lords’ estates, the old bailiff, himself a serf, was displaced by the free farmer. The wage workers of agriculture were partly peasants, who used their leisure time to work on the large estates, and partly an independent special class of wage workers, few in number both relatively and absolutely. In practice these last were also peasant farmers at the same time, since besides their wages they were allotted 4 or more acres of arable land, together with their cottages. Besides, they and the rest of the peasants had the right to use the common land, which gave pasture to their cattle and supplied them with timber, firewood, turf, etc.[^27.2] In all countries of Europe, feudal production is characterized by the division of the soil among the greatest possible number of sub-vassals. The power of the feudal lord, like that of the sovereign, depended not on the length of his rent roll but on the number of his subjects, and the number of his subjects depended on the number of peasant proprietors.[^27.3] So although after the Norman Conquest the land of England was divided into gigantic baronies, one of which often included some 900 of the old Anglo-Saxon lordships, it was strewn with small peasant properties, with great lords’ estates scattered among them only here and there. Such conditions, together with the prosperity of the towns so characteristic of the 15th century, made possible that wealth of the people which Chancellor Fortescue paints so eloquently in his “Laudes legum Angliae” [In Praise of the Laws of England]; but they ruled out the possibility of capitalist wealth.

[^27.1]: “The petty proprietors who cultivated their own fields with their own hands, and enjoyed a modest competence.... then formed a much more important part of the nation than at present. If we may trust the best statistical writers of that age, not less than 160,000 proprietors who, with their families, must have made up more than a seventh of the whole population, derived their subsistence from little freehold estates. The average income of these small landlords... was estimated at between £60 and £70 a year. It was computed that the number of persons who tilled their own land was greater than the number of those who farmed the land of others.” Macaulay: “History of England,” 10th ed., 1854, I. pp. 333, 334. Even in the last third of the 17th century, 4/5 of the English people were agricultural. (cited above, p. 413.) I quote Macaulay because, as a systematic falsifier of history, he plays down facts of this kind as much as he can.

[^27.2]: We must never forget that even the serf was not only the owner of the piece of land attached to his house, if only a tribute-paying owner, but also a co-possessor of the common land. “Le paysan (in Silesia, under Frederick II.) est serf.” Nevertheless, these serfs possess common lands. “On n’a pas pu encore engager les Silésiens au partage des communes, tandis que dans la Nouvelle Marche, il n’y a guère de village où ce partage ne soit exécuté avec le plus grand succès.” [The peasant ... is a serf. ... It has not yet been possible to persuade the Silesians to divide up the common lands, while in the Neumark there is hardly a village where this division has not been carried out with the greatest success.] (Mirabeau: “De la Monarchie Prussienne.” Londres, 1788, t. ii, pp. 125, 126.)

[^27.3]: Japan, with its purely feudal organization of landed property and its developed small-scale farming, gives a much truer picture of the European middle ages than all our history books, which are for the most part dictated by bourgeois prejudices. (Bourgeois means belonging to the capitalist class, or to society and thinking shaped by it.) It is very convenient to be “liberal” at the expense of the middle ages.

<!-- ch27-p002 -->
The prelude to the revolution that laid the foundation of the capitalist mode of production was played in the last third of the 15th century and the first decade of the 16th. A mass of free proletarians was hurled onto the labor market by the breaking-up of the bands of feudal retainers who, as Sir James Steuart well says, “everywhere uselessly filled house and castle.” (Proletarians are members of the proletariat: the class of wage workers, who own nothing they can live by except their labor-power.) The royal power, itself a product of bourgeois development, forcibly hastened the breaking-up of these bands of retainers in its striving for absolute sovereignty. Yet although it did so, it was by no means the only cause. In insolent conflict with king and parliament, the great feudal lords created an incomparably larger proletariat. They did it by forcibly driving the peasantry from the land, to which the peasants had the same feudal right as the lord himself, and by seizing the common lands. The direct impulse for these evictions came from the rapid rise of the Flemish wool manufacture and the corresponding rise in the price of wool in England. The old nobility had been devoured by the great feudal wars. The new nobility was the child of its time, a time for which money was the power of all powers. Its cry, therefore, was: turn arable land into sheep pastures! Harrison, in his “Description of England, prefixed to Holinshed’s Chronicles,” describes how the expropriation of small peasants is ruining the country. (Expropriation means taking away people’s property, here their land and means of production.) “What care our great encroachers?” The dwellings of the peasants and the cottages of the workers were razed to the ground or doomed to decay. “If,” says Harrison, “the old records of euerie manour be sought... it will soon appear that in some manour seventeene, eighteene, or twentie houses are shrunk... that England was neuer less furnished with people than at the present... Of cities and townes either utterly decaied or more than a quarter or half diminished, though some one be a little increased here or there; of townes pulled downe for sheepe-walks, and no more but the lordships now standing in them... I could saie somewhat.” The complaints of these old chroniclers are always exaggerated, but they faithfully reflect the impression that the revolution in the conditions of production made on the people of the time. If we compare the writings of Chancellor Fortescue and Thomas More, we see the gulf between the 15th and the 16th century. As Thornton rightly puts it, the English working class was thrown, without any transition, from its golden age into its iron age.

<!-- ch27-p003 -->
Legislation was terrified at this revolution. It had not yet reached that height of civilization where the “wealth of the nation” (that is, the formation of capital – value that is used to make more value – and the reckless exploitation and impoverishing of the mass of the people) counts as the *ultima Thule* [farthest limit] of all statecraft. In his history of Henry VII., Bacon says: “Inclosures at that time (1489) began to be more frequent, whereby arable land (which could not be manured [cultivated] without people and families) was turned into pasture, which was easily rid [handled] by a few herdsmen; and tenancies for years, lives, and at will (whereupon much of the yeomanry lived) were turned into demesnes. This bred a decay of people, and (by consequence) a decay of towns, churches, tithes, and the like... In remedying of this inconvenience the king’s wisdom was admirable, and the parliament’s at that time... they took a course to take away depopulating enclosures, and depopulating pasturage.” An Act of Henry VII., 1489, cap. 19, forbade the destruction of all “houses of husbandry” [farmhouses] to which at least 20 acres of land belonged. An Act, 25 Henry VIII., renewed the same law. Among other things, this Act states that many farms and large flocks of cattle, especially of sheep, are concentrated in the hands of a few men. As a result, it says, the rent of land has risen greatly and tillage has fallen off, churches and houses have been pulled down, and marvelous numbers of people have been deprived of the means to maintain themselves and their families. The Act therefore orders the rebuilding of the decayed farmsteads, and fixes a proportion between grain land and pasture land, etc. An Act of 1533 states that some owners possess 24,000 sheep, and limits the number anyone may own to 2,000.[^27.4] The cry of the people, and the legislation directed for 150 years after Henry VII. against the expropriation of the small farmers and peasants, were both equally fruitless. Bacon, without knowing it, reveals to us the secret of why they failed. “The device of King Henry VII.,” says Bacon, in his “Essays, Civil and Moral,” Essay 29, “was profound and admirable, in making farms and houses of husbandry of a standard; that is, maintained with such a proportion of land unto them as may breed a subject to live in convenient plenty, and no servile condition, and to keep the plough in the hands of the owners and not mere hirelings.”[^27.5] What the capitalist system demanded, on the other hand, was a degraded and almost servile condition of the mass of the people, their transformation into mercenaries, and the transformation of their means of labor into capital. During this period of transformation, legislation also tried to keep the 4 acres of land by the cottage of the agricultural wage worker, and forbade him to take lodgers into his cottage. In the reign of James I., in 1627, Roger Crocker of Front Mill was condemned for having built a cottage on the manor of Front Mill without 4 acres of land attached to it permanently. As late as the reign of Charles I., in 1638, a royal commission was appointed to enforce the old laws, especially the one about the 4 acres of land. Even in Cromwell’s time, building a house within 4 miles of London was forbidden unless it came with 4 acres of land. As late as the first half of the 18th century, complaint is made if the agricultural worker’s cottage does not have one or two acres of land attached to it. Nowadays he is lucky if it has a little garden, or if he may rent a few roods far away from his cottage. “Landlords and farmers,” says Dr. Hunter, “work here hand in hand. A few acres to the cottage would make the labourers too independent.”[^27.6]

[^27.4]: In his “Utopia,” Thomas More says that in England “your shepe that were wont to be so meke and tame, and so smal eaters, now, as I heare saye, be become so great devourers and so wylde that they eate up, and swallow downe, the very men themselfes.” “Utopia,” transl. by Robinson, ed. Arber, London, 1869, p. 41.

[^27.5]: Bacon shows the connection between a free, well-to-do peasantry and good infantry. “This did wonderfully concern the might and mannerhood [manliness] of the kingdom to have farms as it were of a standard sufficient to maintain an able body out of penury, and did in effect amortise [settle permanently] a great part of the lands of the kingdom unto the hold and occupation of the yeomanry or middle people, of a condition between gentlemen, and cottagers and peasants.... For it hath been held by the general opinion of men of best judgment in the wars.... that the principal strength of an army consisteth in the infantry or foot. And to make good infantry it requireth men bred, not in a servile or indigent fashion, but in some free and plentiful manner. Therefore, if a state run most to noblemen and gentlemen, and that the husbandman and ploughmen be but as their workfolk and labourers, or else mere cottagers (which are but hous’d beggars), you may have a good cavalry, but never good stable bands of foot.... And this is to be seen in France, and Italy, and some other parts abroad, where in effect all is noblesse or peasantry.... insomuch that they are inforced to employ mercenary bands of Switzers [Swiss] and the like, for their battalions of foot; whereby also it comes to pass that those nations have much people and few soldiers.” (“The Reign of Henry VII.” Verbatim reprint from Kennet’s England. Ed. 1719. London, 1870, p. 308.)

[^27.6]: Dr. Hunter, cited above, p. 134. “The quantity of land assigned (in the old laws) would now be judged too great for labourers, and rather as likely to convert them into small farmers.” (George Roberts: “The Social History of the People of the Southern Counties of England in Past Centuries.” London, 1856, pp. 184-185.)

<!-- ch27-p004 -->
In the 16th century, the process of forcible expropriation of the people received a new and frightful impulse from the Reformation and from the colossal plundering of church property that followed from it. At the time of the Reformation, the Catholic church was the feudal owner of a great part of the English land. The suppression of the monasteries, etc., hurled their inmates into the proletariat. The church estates were to a large extent given away to greedy royal favorites, or sold at a nominal price to speculating farmers and townspeople. These drove out the hereditary sub-tenants in a mass and threw their holdings together into one. The poorer folk’s legally guaranteed property in a part of the church’s tithes was silently confiscated.[^27.7] “Pauper ubique jacet” [The pauper lies everywhere], cried Queen Elizabeth after a journey through England. In the 43rd year of her reign the nation was obliged to recognize pauperism officially by introducing a poor-rate. (Pauperism is the condition of the lowest layer of the surplus population, unable to find work and dependent on poor relief.) “The authors of this law seem to have been ashamed to state the grounds of it, for [contrary to traditional usage] it has no preamble whatever.”[^27.8] By the 16th of Charles I., ch. 4, it was declared perpetual, and in fact it took a new and harsher form only in 1834.[^27.9] These immediate results of the Reformation were not its most lasting ones. The property of the church formed the religious bulwark of the traditional conditions of landed property. With its fall, these conditions could no longer hold.[^27.10]

[^27.7]: “The right of the poor to share in the tithe, is established by the tenour of ancient statutes.” (Tuckett, cited above, Vol. II., pg. 804-805.)

[^27.8]: William Cobbett: “A History of the Protestant Reformation,” § 471.

[^27.9]: The “spirit” of Protestantism can be seen from the following, among other things. In the south of England, certain landowners and well-to-do farmers put their heads together and drew up ten questions on the right interpretation of Elizabeth’s poor-law. They laid these before a celebrated jurist of that time, Sergeant Snigge (later a judge under James I.), for his opinion. “Question 9 — Some of the more wealthy farmers in the parish have devised a skilful mode by which all the trouble of executing this Act (the 43rd of Elizabeth) might be avoided. They have proposed that we shall erect a prison in the parish, and then give notice to the neighbourhood, that if any persons are disposed to farm the poor [take charge of the poor under contract] of this parish, they do give in sealed proposals, on a certain day, of the lowest price at which they will take them off our hands; and that they will be authorised to refuse to any one unless he be shut up in the aforesaid prison. The proposers of this plan conceive that there will be found in the adjoining counties, persons, who, being unwilling to labour and not possessing substance or credit to take a farm or ship, so as to live without labour, may be induced to make a very advantageous offer to the parish. If any of the poor perish under the contractor’s care, the sin will lie at his door, as the parish will have done its duty by them. We are, however, apprehensive that the present Act (43rd of Elizabeth) will not warrant a prudential measure of this kind; but you are to learn that the rest of the freeholders of the county, and of the adjoining county of B, will very readily join in instructing their members to propose an Act to enable the parish to contract with a person to lock up and work the poor; and to declare that if any person shall refuse to be so locked up and worked, he shall be entitled to no relief. This, it is hoped, will prevent persons in distress from wanting relief, and be the means of keeping down parishes.” (R. Blakey: “The History of Political Literature from the Earliest Times.” London, 1855, Vol. II., pp. 84-85.) In Scotland, serfdom was abolished some centuries later than in England. Even in 1698, Fletcher of Saltoun declared in the Scottish parliament: “The number of beggars in Scotland is reckoned at not less than 200,000. The only remedy that I, a republican on principle, can suggest, is to restore the old state of serfdom, to make slaves of all those who are unable to provide for their own subsistence.” Eden, cited above, Book I., ch. 1, pp. 60-61, says: “The decrease of villenage [serfdom] seems necessarily to have been the era of the origin of the poor. Manufactures and commerce are the two parents of our national poor.” Eden, like our Scottish republican on principle, errs only in this: it was not the abolition of villenage, but the abolition of the agricultural worker’s property in the soil, that made him a proletarian, and in the end a pauper. In France, where the expropriation was carried out in another way, the ordonnance of Moulins, 1571, and the Edict of 1656 correspond to the English poor-laws.

[^27.10]: Professor Rogers, although formerly Professor of Political Economy in the University of Oxford, the hotbed of Protestant orthodoxy, stresses in his preface to the “History of Agriculture” the fact that the Reformation pauperized the mass of the people. (Political economy is the science of economics as it was then called.)

<!-- ch27-p005 -->
Even in the last decade of the 17th century, the yeomanry, the class of independent peasants, were more numerous than the class of farmers. They had formed the backbone of Cromwell’s strength. Even by Macaulay’s own admission, they compared favorably with the drunken squires and with the squires’ servants, the country clergy, who had to marry their masters’ cast-off mistresses. About 1750 the yeomanry had disappeared,[^27.11] and in the last decade of the 18th century so had the last trace of the agricultural worker’s common land. Here we leave aside the purely economic causes of the agricultural revolution. We deal only with the forcible means employed.

[^27.11]: “A Letter to Sir T. C. Bunbury, Bart., on the High Price of Provisions. By a Suffolk Gentleman.” Ipswich, 1795, p. 4. Even the fanatical advocate of the system of large farms, the author of the “Inquiry into the Connexion between the Present Price of Provisions,” London, 1773, p. 139, says: “I most lament the loss of our yeomanry, that set of men who really kept up the independence of this nation; and sorry I am to see their lands now in the hands of monopolising lords, tenanted out to small farmers, who hold their leases on such conditions as to be little better than vassals ready to attend a summons on every mischievous occasion.”

<!-- ch27-p006 -->
After the restoration of the Stuarts, the landowners carried out by legal means an act of usurpation that was carried out everywhere on the Continent without any legal formality. They abolished the feudal tenure of land, that is, they got rid of all its obligations to the State. They “indemnified” the State by taxes on the peasantry and the rest of the mass of the people. They claimed for themselves the rights of modern private property in estates to which they had only a feudal title. And finally, they passed those laws of settlement (laws that let a parish send poor newcomers back to their parish of origin) which, with the necessary changes, had the same effect on the English agricultural worker as the edict of the Tatar Boris Godunof had on the Russian peasantry.

<!-- ch27-p007 -->
The “glorious Revolution” brought into power, along with William of Orange, the landlords and capitalists who appropriate surplus-value.[^27.12] (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it.) They opened the new era by practicing thefts of state lands on a colossal scale, thefts that until then had been carried out more modestly. These estates were given away, sold at a ridiculous figure, or even annexed to private estates by direct seizure.[^27.13] All this happened without the slightest regard for legal etiquette. The Crown lands appropriated by fraud in this way, together with the robbed Church estates (so far as these had not been lost again during the republican revolution), form the basis of the present-day princely domains of the English oligarchy.[^27.14] The bourgeois capitalists favored the operation with a view, among other things, to promoting free trade in land, to extending modern agriculture based on the large-farm system, and to increasing their supply of free agricultural proletarians ready to hand. Besides, the new landed aristocracy was the natural ally of the new bankocracy, of the newly hatched high finance, and of the large manufacturers, who then depended on protective duties. The English bourgeoisie acted for its own interest just as wisely as the Swedish bourgeoisie did. The Swedes reversed the process: hand in hand with their economic allies, the peasantry, they helped the kings take back the Crown lands from the oligarchy by force. This happened from 1604 on, under Charles X. and Charles XI.

[^27.12]: On the private moral character of this bourgeois hero, among other things: “The large grant of lands in Ireland to Lady Orkney, in 1695, is a public instance of the king’s affection, and the lady’s influence... Lady Orkney’s endearing offices are supposed to have been — fœda labiorum ministeria [foul services of the lips].” (In the Sloane Manuscript Collection, at the British Museum, No. 4224. The Manuscript is entitled: “The character and behaviour of King William, Sunderland, etc., as represented in Original Letters to the Duke of Shrewsbury from Somers Halifax, Oxford, Secretary Vernon, etc.” It is full of curiosities.)

[^27.13]: “The illegal alienation of the Crown Estates, partly by sale and partly by gift, is a scandalous chapter in English history... a gigantic fraud on the nation.” (F. W. Newman, “Lectures on Political Economy.” London, 1851, pp. 129, 130.) [For details of how the present large landowners of England came into their possessions, see “Our Old Nobility. By Noblesse Oblige.” London, 1879. — *F. E.*]

[^27.14]: Read, for example, E. Burke’s pamphlet on the ducal house of Bedford, whose offshoot was Lord John Russell, the “tomtit of Liberalism.”

<!-- ch27-p008 -->
Communal property – always distinct from the State property just dealt with – was an old Germanic institution that lived on under cover of feudalism. We have seen how the forcible seizure of this property, generally accompanied by the turning of arable land into pasture, begins at the end of the 15th century and extends into the 16th. But at that time the process was carried on by means of individual acts of violence, against which legislation fought in vain for a hundred and fifty years. The advance made by the 18th century shows itself in this: the law itself now becomes the instrument of the theft of the people’s land, although the large farmers use their own little independent methods as well.[^27.15] The parliamentary form of the robbery is that of Acts for enclosures of Commons. In other words, these are decrees by which the landlords grant themselves the people’s land as private property, decrees of expropriation of the people. Sir F. M. Eden, in his crafty special pleading, tries to present communal property as the private property of the great landlords who have taken the place of the feudal lords. But he refutes himself when he himself demands a “general Act of Parliament for the enclosure of Commons” (thereby admitting that a parliamentary *coup d’état* is needed to turn it into private property), and moreover calls on the legislature to compensate the expropriated poor.[^27.16]

[^27.15]: “The farmers forbid cottagers to keep any living creatures besides themselves and children, under the pretence that if they keep any beasts or poultry, they will steal from the farmers’ barns for their support; they also say, keep the cottagers poor and you will keep them industrious, &c., but the real fact I believe, is that the farmers may have the whole right of common to themselves.” (“A Political Inquiry into the Consequences of Enclosing Waste Lands.” London, 1785, p. 75.)

[^27.16]: Eden, cited above, preface.

<!-- ch27-p009 -->
While the place of the independent yeoman was taken by tenants at will – small farmers on yearly leases, a servile rabble dependent on the landlords’ pleasure – the systematic robbery of the Communal lands, next to the theft of the State domains, helped especially to swell those large farms that in the 18th century were called capital farms[^27.17] or merchant farms,[^27.18] and to “set free” the agricultural population as proletarians for manufacturing industry.

[^27.17]: “Capital Farms.” Two letters on the Flour Trade and the Dearness of Corn. By a person in business. London, 1767, pp. 19, 20.

[^27.18]: “Merchant Farms.” “An Enquiry into the Causes of the Present High Price of Provisions.” London, 1767, p. 11. Note.— This excellent work, which was published anonymously, is by the Rev. Nathaniel Forster.

<!-- ch27-p010 -->
The 18th century, however, did not yet recognize as fully as the 19th that national wealth and the poverty of the people are one and the same thing. Hence the very fierce debate in the economic literature of that time over the “enclosure of commons.” From the mass of material that lies before me, I give a few extracts that will throw a strong light on conditions at the time. “In several parishes of Hertfordshire,” writes one indignant person, “24 farms, numbering on the average 50-150 acres, have been melted up into three farms.”[^27.19] “In Northamptonshire and Leicestershire the enclosure of common lands has taken place on a very large scale, and most of the new lordships [estates], resulting from the enclosure, have been turned into pasturage, in consequence of which many lordships have not now 50 acres ploughed yearly, in which 1,500 were ploughed formerly. The ruins of former dwelling-houses, barns, stables, &c.,” are the only traces of the former inhabitants. “An hundred houses and families have in some open-field villages dwindled to eight or ten.... The landholders in most parishes that have been enclosed only 15 or 20 years, are very few in comparison of the numbers who occupied them in their open-field state. It is no uncommon thing for 4 or 5 wealthy graziers [livestock farmers] to engross [take over] a large enclosed lordship which was before in the hands of 20 or 30 farmers, and as many smaller tenants and proprietors. All these are hereby thrown out of their livings with their families and many other families who were chiefly employed and supported by them.”[^27.20] It was not only land lying waste, but often land that was cultivated in common, or held for a fixed rent paid to the community, that the neighboring landlords annexed on the pretext of enclosure. “I have here in view enclosures of open fields and lands already improved. It is acknowledged by even the writers in defence of enclosures that these diminished villages increase the monopolies of farms, raise the prices of provisions, and produce depopulation ... and even the enclosure of waste lands (as now carried on) bears hard on the poor, by depriving them of a part of their subsistence, and only goes towards increasing farms already too large.”[^27.21] “When,” says Dr. Price, “this land gets into the hands of a few great farmers, the consequence must be that the little farmers” (whom he earlier calls “a multitude of little proprietors and tenants, who maintain themselves and families by the produce of the ground they occupy by sheep kept on a common, by poultry, hogs, &c., and who therefore have little occasion to purchase any of the means of subsistence [the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live]”) “will be converted into a body of men who earn their subsistence by working for others, and who will be under a necessity of going to market for all they want.... There will, perhaps, be more labour, because there will be more compulsion to it.... Towns and manufactures will increase, because more will be driven to them in quest of places and employment. This is the way in which the engrossing [buying up] of farms naturally operates. And this is the way in which, for many years, it has been actually operating in this kingdom.”[^27.22] He sums up the effect of the enclosures like this: “Upon the whole, the circumstances of the lower ranks of men are altered in almost every respect for the worse. From little occupiers of land, they are reduced to the state of day-labourers and hirelings; and, at the same time, their subsistence in that state has become more difficult.”[^27.23] In fact, the seizure of the common lands, and the revolution in agriculture that went with it, hit the agricultural workers so hard that, even according to Eden, their wages began to fall below the minimum between 1765 and 1780, and began to be topped up by official poor-law relief. Their wages, he says, “were not more than enough for the absolute necessaries of life.”

[^27.19]: Thomas Wright: “A Short Address to the Public on the Monopoly of Large Farms,” 1779, pp. 2, 3.

[^27.20]: Rev. Addington: “Inquiry into the Reasons for or against Enclosing Open Fields,” London, 1772, pp. 37, 43 passim.

[^27.21]: Dr. R. Price, cited above, v. ii., p. 155. Forster, Addington, Kent, Price, and James Anderson should be read and compared with the miserable prattle of Sycophant MacCulloch in his catalogue: “The Literature of Political Economy,” London, 1845.

[^27.22]: Price, cited above, p. 147.

[^27.23]: Price, cited above, p. 159. We are reminded of ancient Rome. “The rich had got possession of the greater part of the undivided land. They trusted in the conditions of the time, that these possessions would not be again taken from them, and bought, therefore, some of the pieces of land lying near theirs, and belonging to the poor, with the acquiescence of their owners, and took some by force, so that they now were cultivating widely extended domains, instead of isolated fields. Then they employed slaves in agriculture and cattle-breeding, because freemen would have been taken from labour for military service. The possession of slaves brought them great gain, inasmuch as these, on account of their immunity from military service, could freely multiply and have a multitude of children. Thus the powerful men drew all wealth to themselves, and all the land swarmed with slaves. The Italians, on the other hand, were always decreasing in number, destroyed as they were by poverty, taxes, and military service. Even when times of peace came, they were doomed to complete inactivity, because the rich were in possession of the soil, and used slaves instead of freemen in the tilling of it.” (Appian: “Civil Wars,” I.7.) This passage refers to the time before the Licinian rogations (the proposed Roman laws limiting how much public land one person could hold). Military service, which did so much to hasten the ruin of the Roman plebeians, was also the chief means by which Charlemagne, as if in a hothouse, brought about the transformation of free German peasants into serfs and bondsmen.

<!-- ch27-p011 -->
Let us listen for a moment to a defender of enclosures, who is also an opponent of Dr. Price. “Nor is it a consequence that there must be depopulation, because men are not seen wasting their labour in the open field.... If, by converting the little farmers into a body of men who must work for others, more labour is produced, it is an advantage which the nation” (to which, of course, the “converted” ones do not belong) “should wish for ... the produce being greater when their joint labours are employed on one farm, there will be a surplus for manufactures, and by this means manufactures, one of the mines of the nation, will increase, in proportion to the quantity of corn [grain] produced.”[^27.24]

[^27.24]: “An Inquiry into the Connexion between the Present Price of Provisions, &c.,” pp. 124, 129. To the same effect, but with an opposite tendency: “Working-men are driven from their cottages and forced into the towns to seek for employment; but then a larger surplus is obtained, and thus capital is augmented.” (“The Perils of the Nation,” 2nd ed. London, 1843, p. 14.)

<!-- ch27-p012 -->
Sir F. M. Eden, a philanthropist and a Tory to boot, shows the stoical calm with which the political economist looks on at the most shameless violation of the “sacred rights of property” and the crudest acts of violence against persons, as soon as these are needed to lay the foundations of the capitalist mode of production. The whole series of thefts, outrages, and popular misery that went with the forcible expropriation of the people, from the last third of the 15th to the end of the 18th century, leads him merely to this comfortable conclusion: “The due proportion between arable land and pasture had to be established. During the whole of the 14th and the greater part of the 15th century, there was one acre of pasture to 2, 3, and even 4 of arable land. About the middle of the 16th century the proportion was changed of 2 acres of pasture to 2, later on, of 2 acres of pasture to one of arable, until at last the just proportion of 3 acres of pasture to one of arable land was attained.”

<!-- ch27-p013 -->
In the 19th century, the very memory of the connection between the agricultural worker and the communal property had, of course, vanished. To say nothing of more recent times, has the agricultural population received a farthing of compensation for the 3,511,770 acres of common land that were stolen from them between 1801 and 1831 and presented to the landlords by the landlords through parliamentary tricks?

<!-- ch27-p014 -->
Finally, the last process of wholesale expropriation of the agricultural population from the soil is the so-called clearing of estates, that is, sweeping the people off them. All the English methods considered so far culminated in “clearing.” As we saw in the picture of present-day conditions given in an earlier chapter, where there are no more independent peasants to get rid of, the “clearing” of cottages begins. So the agricultural workers no longer find, on the very soil they cultivate, even the space they need for their own housing. But what “clearing of estates” really and properly means, we learn only in the promised land of modern romantic literature, the Highlands of Scotland. There the process stands out for its systematic character, for the size of the scale on which it is carried out at one blow (in Ireland landlords have gone so far as to sweep away several villages at once; in Scotland areas as large as German principalities are dealt with), and finally for the peculiar form of property under which the embezzled lands were held.

<!-- ch27-p015 -->
The Highland Celts were organized in clans, each of which owned the land on which it was settled. The representative of the clan, its chief or “great man,” was only the owner of this property in name, just as the Queen of England is the owner in name of all the nation's soil. When the English government succeeded in suppressing the internal wars of these “great men,” and their constant raids into the Lowland plains, the chiefs of the clans by no means gave up their time-honored trade as robbers; they only changed its form. On their own authority they turned their nominal right into a right of private property, and since this brought them into conflict with their clansmen, they resolved to drive the clansmen out by open force. “A king of England might as well claim to drive his subjects into the sea,” says Professor Newman.[^27.25] This revolution began in Scotland after the last rising of the followers of the Pretender (the exiled Stuart claimant to the British throne). Its first phases can be followed in the writings of Sir James Steuart[^27.26] and James Anderson.[^27.27] In the 18th century the Gaels who had been hunted out were forbidden to emigrate from the country, the aim being to drive them by force to Glasgow and other manufacturing towns.[^27.28] As an example of the method[^27.29] used in the 19th century, the “clearing” carried out by the Duchess of Sutherland will be enough here. This person, well schooled in economics, resolved, on taking over her government, to carry out a radical cure and to turn the whole country into a sheep pasture. Its population had already been reduced to 15,000 by earlier processes of the same kind. From 1814 to 1820 these 15,000 inhabitants, about 3,000 families, were systematically hunted and rooted out. All their villages were destroyed and burned, all their fields turned into pasture. British soldiers enforced this eviction and came to blows with the inhabitants. One old woman was burned to death in the flames of the hut she refused to leave. In this way this fine lady took for herself 794,000 acres of land that had belonged to the clan since time immemorial. She assigned the expelled inhabitants about 6,000 acres on the seashore – 2 acres per family. Until then these 6,000 acres had lain waste and brought in no income to their owners. The Duchess, in the nobility of her heart, actually went so far as to rent them, at an average rent of 2s. 6d. per acre, to the clansmen, who for centuries had shed their blood for her family. She divided the whole of the stolen clan land into 29 great sheep farms, each inhabited by a single family, mostly English farm-servants brought in from outside. In the year 1835 the 15,000 Gaels had already been replaced by 131,000 sheep. The remnant of the original inhabitants, flung onto the seashore, tried to live by catching fish. They became amphibious and lived, as an English author says, half on land and half on water, and, with all that, only half on both.[^27.30]

[^27.25]: Cited above, p. 132.

[^27.26]: Steuart says: “If you compare the rent of these lands” (he wrongly includes in this economic category the tribute the taskmen paid to the clan chief) “with the extent, it appears very small. If you compare it with the numbers fed upon the farm, you will find that an estate in the Highlands maintains, perhaps, ten times as many people as another of the same value in a good and fertile province.” (Cited above, vol. i., ch. xvi., p. 104.)

[^27.27]: James Anderson: “Observations on the Means of Exciting a Spirit of National Industry, &c.,” Edinburgh, 1777.

[^27.28]: In 1860 people who had been expropriated by force were exported to Canada under false pretenses. Some fled to the mountains and nearby islands. The police pursued them; they came to blows with the police and escaped.

[^27.29]: “In the Highlands of Scotland,” says Buchanan, the commentator on Adam Smith, in 1814, “the ancient state of property is daily subverted.... The landlord, without regard to the hereditary tenant (a category wrongly used here), now offers his land to the highest bidder, who, if he is an improver, instantly adopts a new system of cultivation. The land, formerly overspread with small tenants or labourers, was peopled in proportion to its produce, but under the new system of improved cultivation and increased rents, the largest possible produce is obtained at the least possible expense: and the useless hands being, with this view, removed, the population is reduced, not to what the land will maintain, but to what it will employ. “The dispossessed tenants either seek a subsistence in the neighbouring towns,” &c. (David Buchanan: “Observations on, &c., A. Smith’s Wealth of Nations.” Edinburgh, 1814, vol. iv., p. 144.) “The Scotch grandees dispossessed families as they would grub up coppice-wood [undergrowth], and they treated villages and their people as Indians harassed with wild beasts do, in their vengeance, a jungle with tigers.... Man is bartered for a fleece or a carcase of mutton, nay, held cheaper.... Why, how much worse is it than the intention of the Moguls, who, when they had broken into the northern provinces of China, proposed in council to exterminate the inhabitants, and convert the land into pasture. This proposal many Highland proprietors have effected in their own country against their own countrymen.” (George Ensor: “An Inquiry Concerning the Population of Nations.” London, 1818, pp. 215, 216.)

[^27.30]: The present Duchess of Sutherland entertained Mrs. Beecher Stowe, author of “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” with great magnificence in London, to show her sympathy for the Black slaves of the American republic. This was a sympathy that she, along with her fellow aristocrats, prudently forgot during the Civil War, when every “noble” English heart beat for the slave-owner. At the time of that visit, I gave the facts about the Sutherland slaves in the *New York Tribune*. (Summarized in part by Carey in “The Slave Trade.” Philadelphia, 1853, pp. 203, 204.) My article was reprinted in a Scottish newspaper, and led to a fine dispute between that paper and the sycophants of the Sutherlands.

<!-- ch27-p016 -->
But the brave Gaels had to atone still more bitterly for their romantic, mountain-bred idolatry of the clan's “great men.” The smell of their fish rose to the noses of the great men. They sniffed some profit in it, and leased the seashore to the big fishmongers of London. For the second time the Gaels were hunted out.[^27.31]

[^27.31]: Interesting details on this fish trade can be found in Mr. David Urquhart’s Portfolio, new series. — Nassau W. Senior, in his posthumous work quoted earlier, calls “the proceedings in Sutherlandshire one of the most beneficent clearings since the memory of man.” (Cited above.)

<!-- ch27-p017 -->
But finally, part of the sheep pastures are turned into deer preserves. Everyone knows that there are no real forests in England. The deer in the parks of the great are demure domestic cattle, as fat as London aldermen. So Scotland is the last refuge of the “noble passion.” “In the Highlands,” says Somers in 1848, “new forests are springing up like mushrooms. Here, on one side of Gaick, you have the new forest of Glenfeshie; and there on the other you have the new forest of Ardverikie. In the same line you have the Black Mount, an immense waste also recently erected. From east to west – from the neighbourhood of Aberdeen to the crags of Oban – you have now a continuous line of forests; while in other parts of the Highlands there are the new forests of Loch Archaig, Glengarry, Glenmoriston, &c. Sheep were introduced into glens which had been the seats of communities of small farmers; and the latter were driven to seek subsistence on coarser and more sterile tracks of soil. Now deer are supplanting sheep; and these are once more dispossessing the small tenants, who will necessarily be driven down upon still coarser land and to more grinding penury [poverty]. Deer-forests[^27.32] and the people cannot co-exist. One or other of the two must yield. Let the forests be increased in number and extent during the next quarter of a century, as they have been in the last, and the Gaels will perish from their native soil... This movement among the Highland proprietors is with some a matter of ambition... with some love of sport... while others, of a more practical cast, follow the trade in deer with an eye solely to profit. For it is a fact, that a mountain range laid out in forest is, in many cases, more profitable to the proprietor than when let as a sheep-walk. ... The huntsman who wants a deer-forest limits his offers by no other calculation than the extent of his purse.... Sufferings have been inflicted in the Highlands scarcely less severe than those occasioned by the policy of the Norman kings. Deer have received extended ranges, while men have been hunted within a narrower and still narrower circle.... One after one the liberties of the people have been cloven down.... And the oppressions are daily on the increase.... The clearance and dispersion of the people is pursued by the proprietors as a settled principle, as an agricultural necessity, just as trees and brushwood are cleared from the wastes of America or Australia; and the operation goes on in a quiet, business-like way, &c.”[^27.33]

[^27.32]: The deer-forests of Scotland do not contain a single tree. The sheep are driven off the bare hills, then the deer are driven onto them, and this is called a deer-forest. There is not even any timber-planting or real forestry.

[^27.33]: Robert Somers: “Letters from the Highlands: or the Famine of 1847.” London, 1848, pp. 12-28 passim. These letters first appeared in *The Times*. The English economists, of course, explained the famine of the Gaels in 1847 by their over-population. At any rate, they “were pressing on their food-supply.” The “clearing of estates,” or as it is called in Germany, “Bauernlegen” [clearing away the peasants], occurred in Germany especially after the 30 years’ war, and led to peasant revolts as late as 1790 in Kursachsen [Electoral Saxony]. It was found especially in East Germany. In most of the Prussian provinces, Frederick II. for the first time secured property rights for the peasants. After the conquest of Silesia he forced the landlords to rebuild the huts, barns, etc., and to provide the peasants with cattle and tools. He wanted soldiers for his army and taxpayers for his treasury. As for the rest, the pleasant life that the peasant led under Frederick’s system of finance and his hodge-podge rule of despotism, bureaucracy, and feudalism can be seen from the following quotation from his admirer, Mirabeau: “Le lin fait donc une des grandes richesses du cultivateur dans le Nord de l’Allemagne. Malheureusement pour l’espèce humaine, ce n’est qu’une ressource contre la misère et non un moyen de bien-être. Les impôts directs, les corvées, les servitudes de tout genre, écrasent le cultivateur allemand, qui paie encore des impôts indirects dans tout ce qu’il achète.... et pour comble de ruine, il n’ose pas vendre ses productions où et comme il le veut; il n’ose pas acheter ce dont il a besoin aux marchands qui pourraient le lui livrer au meilleur prix. Toutes ces causes le ruinent insensiblement, et il se trouverait hors d’état de payer les impôts directs à l’échéance sans la filerie; elle lui offre une ressource, en occupant utilement sa femme, ses enfants, ses servants, ses valets, et lui-même; mais quelle pénible vie, même aidée de ce secours. En été, il travaille comme un forçat au labourage et à la récolte; il se couche à 9 heures et se lève à deux, pour suffire aux travaux; en hiver il devrait réparer ses forces par un plus grand repos; mais il manquera de grains pour le pain et les semailles, s’il se défait des denrées qu’il faudrait vendre pour payer les impôts. Il faut donc filer pour suppléer à ce vide.... il faut y apporter la plus grande assiduité. Aussi le paysan se couche-t-il en hiver à minuit, une heure, et se lève à cinq ou six; ou bien il se couche à neuf, et se lève à deux, et cela tous les jours de la vie si ce n’est le dimanche. Ces excès de veille et de travail usent la nature humaine, et de là vient qu’hommes et femmes vieillissent beaucoup plutôt dans les campagnes que dans les villes.” [So flax is one of the great sources of wealth for the farmer in the North of Germany. Unfortunately for the human race, it is only a defense against misery and not a means to well-being. Direct taxes, the corvées (forced unpaid labor that peasants had to perform for a lord), obligations of all kinds crush the German farmer, who also pays indirect taxes on everything he buys, ... and to complete his ruin, he dare not sell his produce where and as he wishes; he dare not buy what he needs from the merchants who could sell it to him at the best price. All these causes slowly ruin him, and when the direct taxes fall due, he would be unable to pay them without spinning; spinning offers him a resource, by giving useful work to his wife, his children, his servants, his farm-hands, and himself; but what a hard life, even with this help! In summer, he works like a convict at plowing and at harvest; he goes to bed at 9 o’clock and gets up at two to get through all his work; in winter he ought to restore his strength by resting longer; but he will run short of grain for his bread and his sowing if he gets rid of the products he would have to sell to pay the taxes. So he has to spin to fill this gap ... and he must do it with the greatest diligence. So in winter the peasant goes to bed at midnight or one o’clock, and gets up at five or six; or else he goes to bed at nine and gets up at two, and this every day of his life except Sunday. This excess of sleeplessness and work wears out human nature, and that is why men and women age much earlier in the country than in the towns.] (Mirabeau, cited above, t.III. pp. 212 and following.)

    *Note to the second edition.* In April 1866, 18 years after the publication of the work of Robert Somers quoted above, Professor Leone Levi gave a lecture before the Society of Arts on the transformation of sheep pastures into deer-forest. In it he describes how the devastation of the Scottish Highlands has advanced. Among other things, he says: “Depopulation and transformation into sheep-walks were the most convenient means for getting an income without expenditure... A deer-forest in place of a sheep-walk was a common change in the Highlands. The landowners turned out the sheep as they once turned out the men from their estates, and welcomed the new tenants — the wild beasts and the feathered birds.... One can walk from the Earl of Dalhousie’s estates in Forfarshire to John O’Groats, without ever leaving forest land.... In many of these woods the fox, the wild cat, the marten, the polecat, the weasel and the Alpine hare are common; whilst the rabbit, the squirrel and the rat have lately made their way into the country. Immense tracts of land, much of which is described in the statistical account of Scotland as having a pasturage in richness and extent of very superior description, are thus shut out from all cultivation and improvement, and are solely devoted to the sport of a few persons for a very brief period of the year.” The London *Economist* of June 2, 1866, says, “Amongst the items of news in a Scotch paper of last week, we read... ’One of the finest sheep farms in Sutherlandshire, for which a rent of £1,200 a year was recently offered, on the expiry of the existing lease this year, is to be converted into a deer-forest.’ Here we see the modern instincts of feudalism ... operating pretty much as they did when the Norman Conqueror... destroyed 36 villages to create the New Forest.... Two millions of acres... totally laid waste, embracing within their area some of the most fertile lands of Scotland. The natural grass of Glen Tilt was among the most nutritive in the county of Perth. The deer-forest of Ben Aulder was by far the best grazing ground in the wide district of Badenoch; a part of the Black Mount forest was the best pasture for black-faced sheep in Scotland. Some idea of the ground laid waste for purely sporting purposes in Scotland may be formed from the fact that it embraced an area larger than the whole county of Perth. The resources of the forest of Ben Aulder might give some idea of the loss sustained from the forced desolations. The ground would pasture 15,000 sheep, and as it was not more than one-thirtieth part of the old forest ground in Scotland ... it might, &c., ... All that forest land is as totally unproductive.... It might thus as well have been submerged under the waters of the German Ocean [the North Sea].... Such extemporised wildernesses or deserts ought to be put down by the decided interference of the Legislature.”

<!-- ch27-p018 -->
The plundering of the church’s property, the fraudulent transfer of the State domains, the robbery of the common lands, the seizure of feudal and clan property and its transformation into modern private property under conditions of reckless terrorism: these were just so many idyllic methods of primitive accumulation (the historical process that separated the producers from their means of production, above all by driving peasants off the land, and so created the conditions for capitalism). They conquered the field for capitalist agriculture, made the soil part and parcel of capital, and created for the town industries the necessary supply of a “free” and outlawed proletariat.

## Chapter 28: Bloody Legislation Against the Expropriated, from the End of the 15th Century. Forcing Down of Wages by Acts of Parliament

<!-- ch28-p001 -->
The proletariat (the class of wage workers, who own nothing they can live by except their labor-power) was created by the breaking up of the bands of feudal retainers and by the forcible expropriation of the people from the soil. (Expropriation means taking away people's property, here their land.) This “free” proletariat could not possibly be absorbed by the newborn manufacturing workshops as fast as it was thrown onto the world. (Manufacture is the stage and form of capitalist production, roughly from the mid-16th to the late 18th century, based on handicraft work divided among many workers in one workshop.) On the other hand, these men had suddenly been dragged out of their accustomed way of life, and they could not adapt themselves just as suddenly to the discipline of their new condition. They were turned in a mass into beggars, robbers, and vagabonds, partly from inclination, in most cases under the pressure of circumstances. Hence, at the end of the 15th century and during the whole of the 16th, there was a bloody legislation against vagabondage throughout Western Europe. The fathers of the present working class were punished for having been forced to turn into vagabonds and paupers. The law treated them as “voluntary” criminals, and assumed that it depended on their own good will to go on working under the old conditions, which no longer existed.

<!-- ch28-p002 -->
In England this legislation began under Henry VII.

<!-- ch28-p003 -->
**Henry VIII. 1530:** Beggars who are old and unable to work receive a beggar's license. On the other hand, able-bodied vagabonds get whipping and imprisonment. They are to be tied to the back of a cart and whipped until the blood streams from their bodies. Then they are to swear an oath to go back to their birthplace, or to where they have lived for the last three years, and to “put themselves to labour.” What grim irony! In 27 Henry VIII. the earlier statute is repeated, but made harsher with new clauses. For a second arrest for vagabondage, the whipping is to be repeated and half the ear sliced off. But at the third relapse, the offender is to be executed as a hardened criminal and an enemy of the common good.

<!-- ch28-p004 -->
**Edward VI.:** A statute of the first year of his reign, 1547, orders that if anyone refuses to work, he shall be condemned as a slave to the person who has denounced him as an idler. The master shall feed his slave on bread and water, weak broth, and whatever scraps of meat he thinks fit. He has the right to force him to do any work, however disgusting, with whip and chains. If the slave is absent for two weeks, he is condemned to slavery for life and is to be branded on the forehead or back with the letter S. If he runs away three times, he is to be executed as a felon. The master can sell him, leave him in his will, or hire him out as a slave, just like any other personal chattel (movable property) or cattle. If the slaves attempt anything against the masters, they too are to be executed. Justices of the peace, when informed, are to hunt the rascals down. If it turns out that a vagabond has been idling about for three days, he is to be taken to his birthplace, branded on the breast with a red-hot iron with the letter V, and set to work, in chains, in the streets or at some other labor. If the vagabond gives a false birthplace, he is then to become the slave for life of that place, of its inhabitants, or of its corporation, and to be branded with an S. Everyone has the right to take away the children of the vagabonds and keep them as apprentices, the young men until their 24th year, the girls until their 20th. If they run away, they are to become the slaves of their masters up to that age, and the masters can put them in irons, whip them, etc., if they like. Every master may put an iron ring round the neck, arms, or legs of his slave, so as to know him more easily and be more certain of him.[^28.1] The last part of this statute provides that certain poor people may be employed by a place or by persons who are willing to give them food and drink and to find them work. This kind of parish slave was kept up in England until far into the 19th century under the name of “roundsmen.”

[^28.1]: The author of the “Essay on Trade, etc.,” 1770, says: “In the reign of Edward VI. indeed the English seem to have set, in good earnest, about encouraging manufactures and employing the poor. This we learn from a remarkable statute which runs thus: ‘That all vagrants shall be branded, &c.’” Cited above, p. 5.

<!-- ch28-p005 -->
**Elizabeth, 1572:** Unlicensed beggars over 14 years of age are to be severely flogged and branded on the left ear, unless someone will take them into service for two years. If they repeat the offense and are over 18, they are to be executed, unless someone will take them into service for two years. But for the third offense they are to be executed without mercy as felons. Similar statutes: 18 Elizabeth, c. 13, and another of 1597.[^28.2]

[^28.2]: Thomas More says in his “Utopia”: “Therfore that on [one] covetous and unsatiable cormaraunte [cormorant] and very plage of his native contrey maye compasse aboute and inclose many thousand akers of grounde together within one pale [fence] or hedge, the husbandman [farmer] be thrust owte of their owne, or els either by coneyne [collusion] and fraude, or by violent oppression they be put besydes it [put out of it], or by wrongs and iniuries thei be so weried that they be compelled to sell all: by one meanes, therfore, or by other, either by hooke or crooke they muste needes departe awaye, poore, selye [helpless], wretched soules, men, women, husbands, wiues, fatherlesse children, widowes, wofull mothers with their yonge babes, and their whole household smal in substance, and muche in numbre, as husbandrye requireth many handes. Awaye thei trudge, I say, owte of their knowen accustomed houses, fyndynge no place to reste in. All their housholde stuffe, which is very little woorthe, thoughe it might well abide the sale: yet beeynge sodainely thruste owte, they be constrayned to sell it for a thing of nought. And when they haue wandered abrode tyll that be spent, what cant they then els doe but steale, and then iustly pardy [truly] be hanged, or els go about beggyng. And yet then also they be caste in prison as vagaboundes, because they go aboute and worke not: whom no man wyl set a worke though thei neuer so willyngly profre themselues therto.” Of these poor fugitives, who, as Thomas More says, were forced to steal, “7,200 great and petty thieves were put to death,” in the reign of Henry VIII. (Holinshed, “Description of England,” Vol. 1, p. 186.) In Elizabeth's time, “rogues were trussed up [hanged] apace, and that there was not one year commonly wherein three or four hundred were not devoured and eaten up by the gallowes.” (Strype’s “Annals of the Reformation and Establishment of Religion and other Various Occurrences in the Church of England during Queen Elizabeth’s Happy Reign.” Second ed., 1725, Vol. 2.) According to this same Strype, in Somersetshire, in one year, 40 persons were executed, 35 robbers burnt in the hand, 37 whipped, and 183 discharged as “incorrigible vagabonds.” Nevertheless, he is of the opinion that this large number of prisoners does not include even a fifth of the actual criminals, thanks to the negligence of the justices and the foolish compassion of the people; and the other counties of England were no better off in this respect than Somersetshire, while some were even worse.

<!-- ch28-p006 -->
**James 1:** Anyone wandering about and begging is declared a rogue and a vagabond. Justices of the peace in petty sessions are authorized to have them publicly whipped, and to imprison them for 6 months for the first offense and for 2 years for the second. While in prison they are to be whipped as much and as often as the justices of the peace think fit... Incorrigible and dangerous rogues are to be branded with an R on the left shoulder and set to hard labor, and if they are caught begging again, they are to be executed without mercy. These statutes stayed legally binding until the beginning of the 18th century, and were only repealed by 12 Anne, c. 23.

<!-- ch28-p007 -->
There were similar laws in France, where by the middle of the 17th century a kingdom of vagabonds (truands) had been set up in Paris. Even at the beginning of Louis XVI.’s reign (Ordinance of July 13th, 1777), every man in good health from 16 to 60 years of age is to be sent to the galleys if he is without means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live) and does not practice a trade. Of the same nature are the statute of Charles V. for the Netherlands (October, 1537), the first edict of the States and Towns of Holland (March 10, 1614), the “Plakaat” [proclamation] of the United Provinces (June 26, 1649), etc.

<!-- ch28-p008 -->
Thus the agricultural people were first forcibly expropriated from the soil, driven from their homes, and turned into vagabonds. Then they were whipped, branded, and tortured, by laws grotesquely terrible, into the discipline necessary for the wage system.

<!-- ch28-p009 -->
It is not enough that the conditions of labor are concentrated in a mass, in the shape of capital, at one pole of society, while at the other pole are grouped masses of men who have nothing to sell but their labor-power. (Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger. Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist.) Nor is it enough that they are compelled to sell it voluntarily. As capitalist production advances, it develops a working class which, by education, tradition, and habit, looks on the conditions of that mode of production as self-evident laws of Nature. Once the organization of the capitalist process of production is fully developed, it breaks down all resistance. The constant generation of a relative surplus population keeps the law of supply and demand of labor, and therefore keeps wages, in a rut that suits the wants of capital. (The relative surplus population is the workers made “surplus” to capital's needs for the time being, who serve as a reserve of available labor and press down on the employed. Wages are the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself.) The dull compulsion of economic relations completes the subjection of the worker to the capitalist. Direct force, outside economic conditions, is of course still used, but only in exceptional cases. In the ordinary run of things, the worker can be left to the “natural laws of production,” that is, to his dependence on capital, a dependence that springs from the conditions of production themselves and is guaranteed by them forever. It is otherwise during the historical birth of capitalist production. The bourgeoisie (the capitalist class), at its rise, wants and uses the power of the state to “regulate” wages, that is, to force them within the limits suitable for making surplus-value, to lengthen the working day, and to keep the worker himself in the normal degree of dependence. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it. The working day is the total hours a worker works in a day: necessary labor plus surplus labor.) This is an essential element of the so-called primitive accumulation: the historical process that separated the producers from their means of production, above all by driving peasants off the land, and so created the conditions for capitalism.

<!-- ch28-p010 -->
The class of wage workers arose in the latter half of the 14th century. Then, and in the following century, it formed only a very small part of the population, and its position was well protected by the independent peasant proprietors in the country and by the guild organization in the town. In country and town, master and workers stood close together socially. The subordination of labor to capital was only formal, that is, the mode of production itself had as yet no specifically capitalist character. Variable capital greatly outweighed constant capital. (Variable capital is the part of capital spent on labor-power; it reproduces its own value and also produces surplus-value, so its size varies. Constant capital is the part spent on means of production; its value is passed on to the product but does not grow.) Therefore the demand for wage labor grew rapidly with every accumulation of capital (turning surplus-value back into capital, so that capital grows), while the supply of wage labor followed only slowly. A large part of the national product, which was later changed into a fund for capitalist accumulation, still went at that time into the worker's consumption fund.

<!-- ch28-p011 -->
Legislation on wage labor (aimed from the first at the exploitation of the worker and, as it went on, always equally hostile to him)[^28.3] was started in England by the Statute of Labourers of Edward III., 1349. The ordinance of 1350 in France, issued in the name of King John, corresponds to it. English and French legislation run parallel and are identical in content. Insofar as the labor statutes aim at forcibly lengthening the working day, I do not return to them, since this point was dealt with earlier (Chap. X., Section 5).

[^28.3]: “Whenever the legislature attempts to regulate the differences between masters and their workmen, its counsellors are always the masters,” says A. Smith. “L’esprit des lois, c’est la propriété” [The spirit of the laws is property], says Linguet.

<!-- ch28-p012 -->
The Statute of Labourers was passed at the urgent request of the House of Commons. A Tory says naively:

<!-- ch28-p013 -->
> “Formerly the poor demanded such *high* wages as to threaten industry and wealth. Next, their wages are so *low* as to threaten industry and wealth equally and perhaps more, but in another way.”[^28.4] A fixed scale of wages was laid down by law for town and country, for piece-work and day-work. The agricultural workers were to hire themselves out by the year, the town workers “in open market.” It was forbidden, under pain of imprisonment, to pay higher wages than those fixed by the statute, but taking higher wages was punished more severely than giving them. [So also in Sections 18 and 19 of the Statute of Apprentices of Elizabeth, ten days' imprisonment is decreed for the one who pays the higher wages, but twenty-one days for the one who receives them.] A statute of 1360 increased the penalties and authorized the employers to extort labor at the legal rate of wages by corporal punishment. All combinations, contracts, oaths, etc., by which masons and carpenters bound themselves to one another were declared null and void. Coalition of the workers is treated as a heinous crime from the 14th century to 1825, the year the laws against Trades’ Unions were repealed. The spirit of the Statute of Labourers of 1349 and of its offshoots shows clearly in the fact that the State does indeed dictate a maximum of wages, but on no account a minimum.

[^28.4]: “Sophisms of Free Trade.” By a Barrister. London, 1850, p. 206. He adds maliciously: “We were ready enough to interfere for the employer, can nothing now be done for the employed?”

<!-- ch28-p014 -->
In the 16th century, as we know, the condition of the workers had become much worse. The money wage rose, but not in proportion to the depreciation of money and the corresponding rise in the prices of commodities (things produced in order to be exchanged, that is, sold, not for the producer's own use). So wages in reality fell. Nevertheless, the laws for keeping them down remained in force, together with the ear-clipping and branding of those “whom no one was willing to take into service.” The Statute of Apprentices, 5 Elizabeth, c. 3, empowered the justices of the peace to fix certain wages and to adjust them according to the time of year and the price of commodities. James I. extended these regulations of labor to weavers, spinners, and every possible category of worker as well.[^28.5] George II. extended the laws against coalitions of workers to the branches of manufacture. In the manufacturing period proper, the capitalist mode of production had become strong enough to make legal regulation of wages as impracticable as it was unnecessary. But the ruling classes did not want to be without the weapons of the old arsenal in case of need. Still, 8 George II. forbade journeymen tailors in and around London a day's wage higher than 2s. 7½d., except in cases of general mourning. Still, 13 George III., c. 68, handed the regulation of the wages of silk-weavers to the justices of the peace. Still, in 1706, it took two judgments of the higher courts to decide whether the orders of justices of the peace on wages also held good for non-agricultural workers. Still, in 1799, an act of Parliament ordered that the wages of the Scottish miners should continue to be regulated by a statute of Elizabeth and two Scottish acts of 1661 and 1671. How completely circumstances had changed in the meantime is proved by an event never heard of before in the English Lower House. In that place, where for more than 400 years laws had been made for the maximum beyond which wages absolutely must not rise, Whitbread in 1796 proposed a legal minimum wage for agricultural workers. Pitt opposed this, but confessed that the “condition of the poor was cruel.” Finally, in 1813, the laws for the regulation of wages were repealed. They were an absurd anomaly, since the capitalist regulated his factory by his own private legislation, and could use the poor-rates to make up the agricultural worker's wage to the indispensable minimum. The provisions of the labor statutes on contracts between employer and worker, on giving notice, and the like, allow only a civil action against an employer who breaks a contract, but on the contrary permit a criminal action against a worker who breaks one; and these provisions are still in full force at this hour (1873). The barbarous laws against Trades’ Unions fell in 1825 before the threatening attitude of the proletariat. Despite this, they fell only in part. Certain beautiful fragments of the old statute vanished only in 1859. Finally, the act of Parliament of June 29, 1871, made a pretense of removing the last traces of this class of legislation by giving Trades’ Unions legal recognition. But an act of Parliament of the same date (an act to amend the criminal law relating to violence, threats, and molestation) in fact re-established the former state of things in a new shape. By this Parliamentary sleight of hand, the means that the workers could use in a strike or lock-out were taken out of the laws common to all citizens and placed under exceptional penal legislation, whose interpretation fell to the employers themselves in their capacity as justices of the peace. Two years earlier, the same House of Commons and the same Mr. Gladstone, in the well-known straightforward fashion, had brought in a bill for the abolition of all exceptional penal legislation against the working class. But it was never allowed to go beyond the second reading, and the matter was dragged out in this way until at last the “great Liberal party,” by an alliance with the Tories, found the courage to turn against the very proletariat that had carried it into power. Not content with this treachery, the “great Liberal party” allowed the English judges, always obliging in the service of the ruling classes, to dig up again the earlier laws against “conspiracy” and to apply them to coalitions of workers. We see that the English Parliament gave up the laws against Strikes and Trades’ Unions only against its will and under the pressure of the masses, after it had itself, for 500 years, held, with shameless egoism, the position of a permanent Trades’ Union of the capitalists against the workers.

[^28.5]: A clause of Statute 2 James I., c. 6, shows us that certain clothmakers took it upon themselves, in their capacity as justices of the peace, to dictate the official wage scale in their own shops. In Germany, especially after the Thirty Years' War, statutes for keeping down wages were general. “The want [lack] of servants and labourers was very troublesome to the landed proprietors in the depopulated districts. All villagers were forbidden to let rooms to single men and women; all the latter were to be reported to the authorities and cast into prison if they were unwilling to become servants, even if they were employed at any other work, such as sowing seeds for the peasants at a daily wage, or even buying and selling corn. (Imperial privileges and sanctions for Silesia, I., 25.) For a whole century in the decrees of the small German potentates a bitter cry goes up again and again about the wicked and impertinent rabble that will not reconcile itself to its hard lot, will not be content with the legal wage; the individual landed proprietors are forbidden to pay more than the State had fixed by a tariff. And yet the conditions of service were at times better after war than 100 years later; the farm servants of Silesia had, in 1652, meat twice a week, whilst even in our century, districts are known where they have it only three times a year. Further, wages after the war were higher than in the following century.” (G. Freytag.)

<!-- ch28-p015 -->
During the very first storms of the revolution, the French bourgeoisie dared to take away from the workers the right of association that they had only just won. By a decree of June 14, 1791, they declared every coalition of the workers to be “an attempt against liberty and the declaration of the rights of man,” punishable by a fine of 500 livres, together with loss of the rights of an active citizen for one year.[^28.6] By means of State compulsion, this law confined the struggle between capital and labor within limits comfortable for capital, and it has outlived revolutions and changes of dynasty. Even the Reign of Terror left it untouched. It was struck out of the Penal Code only quite recently. Nothing is more characteristic than the pretext for this bourgeois *coup d’état.* “Granting,” says Chapelier, the reporter of the Select Committee on this law, “that wages ought to be a little higher than they are, ... that they ought to be high enough for him that receives them, to be free from that state of absolute dependence due to the want [lack] of the necessaries of life, and which is almost that of slavery,” yet, Chapelier goes on, the workers must not be allowed to come to any understanding about their own interests, nor to act in common and so lessen their “absolute dependence, which is almost that of slavery;” because, if you please, in doing this they injure “the freedom of their cidevant [former] masters, the present entrepreneurs,” and because a coalition against the despotism of the one-time masters of the corporations (the old trade guilds) is – guess what! – a restoration of the corporations abolished by the French constitution.[^28.7]

[^28.6]: Article I. of this law reads: “L’anéantissement de toute espèce de corporations du même état et profession étant l’une des bases fondamentales de la constitution française, il est défendu de les rétablir de fait sous quelque prétexte et sous quelque forme que ce soit.” Article IV. declares that if “des citoyens attachés aux mêmes professions, arts et métiers prenaient des délibérations, faisaient entre eux des conventions tendantes à refuser de concert ou à n’accorder qu’à un prix déterminé le secours de leur industrie ou de leurs travaux, les dites délibérations et conventions... seront déclarées inconstitutionnelles, attentatoires à la liberté et à la declaration des droits de l’homme, &c.;” this is felony, therefore, as in the old labor statutes. [Since the abolition of every kind of corporation (guild) of the same estate and profession is one of the foundations of the French constitution, it is forbidden to re-establish them in fact, under any pretext or in any form whatever. ... citizens belonging to the same professions, crafts, and trades hold discussions and make agreements among themselves aimed at refusing together to provide the services of their industry or their labors, or at providing them only at a fixed price, then the said discussions and agreements ... shall be declared unconstitutional, attacks on liberty and on the declaration of the rights of man, etc.] (“Révolutions de Paris,” Paris, 1791, t. III, p. 523.)

[^28.7]: Buchez et Roux: “Histoire Parlementaire,” t. x., p. 195.

## Chapter 29: Genesis of the Capitalist Farmer

<!-- ch29-p001 -->
We have now considered the forcible creation of a class of outlawed proletarians (the proletariat is the class of wage workers, who own nothing they can live by except their labor-power). We have considered the bloody discipline that turned them into wage workers, and the disgraceful action of the State, which used the police to speed up the accumulation of capital by raising the degree of exploitation of labor. (Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger. The accumulation of capital is turning surplus-value back into capital, so that capital grows.) The question remains: where did the capitalists come from in the first place? For the expropriation of the agricultural population (the taking away of their property, here their land) directly creates nothing but the greatest landed proprietors. As far as the genesis of the farmer is concerned, however, we can, so to speak, put our hand on it, because it is a slow process that unfolded over many centuries. The serfs, and the free small proprietors too, held land on very different terms of tenure, and so they were freed under very different economic conditions. In England the first form of the farmer is the bailiff, who was himself a serf. His position is similar to that of the old Roman *villicus* [estate overseer], only with a narrower field of action. During the second half of the 14th century he is replaced by a farmer whom the landlord provided with seed, cattle and implements. This farmer's condition is not very different from the peasant's. Only he exploits more wage labor. Soon he becomes a metayer, a half-farmer. He advances one part of the farm's stock, and the landlord advances the other. The two divide the total product in proportions fixed by contract. In England this form quickly disappears and gives way to the farmer proper.
