He makes his own capital breed by employing wage workers, and he pays a part of the surplus-product to the landlord as rent, in money or in kind. During the 15th century, as long as the independent peasant, and the farm-laborer who worked for himself as well as for wages, grew rich by their own labor, the farmer's circumstances and his field of production stayed equally middling. The agricultural revolution began in the last third of the 15th century and went on through almost the whole of the 16th (except, however, its last decade). It made the farmer rich just as fast as it made the mass of the agricultural people poor.[^29.1]

[^29.1]: Harrison in his “Description of England,” says “although peradventure [perhaps] foure pounds of old rent be improved to fortie, toward the end of his term, if he have not six or seven yeares rent lieng [lying] by him, fiftie or a hundred pounds, yet will the farmer thinke his gaines verie small.”

<!-- ch29-p002 -->
The seizure of the common lands let him greatly increase his stock of cattle, almost without cost, while they also gave him a richer supply of manure for tilling the soil. In the 16th century a very important element was added to this. At that time contracts for farms ran for a long time, often for 99 years. The steady fall in the value of the precious metals, and so of money, brought the farmers golden fruit. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time.) Apart from all the other circumstances discussed above, this fall lowered wages (the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself). Part of the wages was now added to the profits of the farm. The continuous rise in the price of grain, wool, meat, in a word of all agricultural produce, swelled the money capital of the farm without any action on his part. (Price is the money name of the value, the labor, embodied in a commodity.) Meanwhile the rent he paid, which was calculated on the old value of money, really shrank.[^29.2] So the farmers grew rich at the expense both of their laborers and of their landlords. No wonder, then, that by the end of the 16th century England had a class of capitalist farmers who were rich, considering the circumstances of the time.[^29.3]

[^29.2]: On how the depreciation of money in the 16th century affected the different classes of society, see “A Compendium of Briefe Examination of Certayne Ordinary Complaints of Divers of our Countrymen in these our Days,” by W. S. Gentleman (London 1581). Because this work is written as a dialogue, people for a long time believed Shakespeare wrote it, and even in 1751 it was published under his name. Its author is William Stafford. In one place the knight reasons as follows: *Knight*: You, my neighbor, the husbandman [farmer], you Maister Mercer [cloth merchant], and you Goodman Cooper [barrel-maker], with other artificers [craftsmen], may save yourselves metely [fairly] well. For as much as all things are dearer than they were, so much do you arise in the pryce of your wares and occupations that ye sell agayne. But we have nothing to sell whereby we might advance ye price there of, to countervaile [offset] those things that we must buy agayne.” In another place, the knight asks the doctor: “I pray you, what be those sorts that ye meane. And first, of those that ye thinke should have no losse thereby? *Doctor*: I mean all those that live by buying and selling, for as they buy deare, they sell thereafter. *Knight*: What is the next sort that ye say would win by it? *Doctor*: Marry [why], all such as have takings of fearmes [farms] in their owne manurance [cultivation] at the old rent, for where they pay after the olde rate they sell after the newe — that is, they paye for theire lande good cheape, and sell all things growing thereof deare. *Knight*: What sorte is that which, ye sayde should have greater losse hereby, than these men had profit? *Doctor*: It is all noblemen, gentlemen, and all other that live either by a stinted [fixed] rent or stypend, or do not manure [cultivate] the ground, or doe occupy no buying and selling.”

[^29.3]: In France, the régisseur, the steward and collector of dues for the feudal lords during the earlier part of the middle ages, soon became a man of business, who swindled his way into being a capitalist by extortion, cheating, etc. These régisseurs were sometimes noblemen themselves. For example, “C'est li compte que messire Jacques de Thoraine, chevalier chastelain sor Besançon rent és-seigneur tenant les comptes à Dijon pour monseigneur le duc et comte de Bourgoigne, des rentes appartenant à la dite chastellenie, depuis xxve jour de décembre MCCCLIX jusqu'au xxviiie jour de décembre MCCCLX.” [This is the account given by M. Jacques de Thoraisse, knight, and Lord of a manor near Besançon, to the lord who keeps the accounts at Dijon for his highness the Duke and Count of Burgundy, of the rents belonging to the said manor, from the 25th day of December 1359 to the 28th day of December 1360] (Alexis Monteil: “Traité de Matériaux Manuscrits etc.,” pp. 234, 235.) Here already it is clear how, in every sphere of social life, the lion's share falls to the middleman. In the economic sphere, for example, financiers, stock-exchange speculators, merchants and shopkeepers skim the cream. In civil matters, the lawyer fleeces his clients. In politics the representative counts for more than the voters, and the minister for more than the sovereign. In religion, God is pushed into the background by the “Mediator,” and the Mediator in turn is shoved back by the priests, the inevitable middlemen between the good shepherd and his sheep. In France, as in England, the great feudal territories were divided into countless small homesteads, but under conditions incomparably more favorable for the people. During the 14th century the farms, or *terriers*, arose. Their number grew constantly, to far beyond 100,000. They paid rents of from 1/12 to 1/5 of the product, in money or in kind. These farms were fiefs, sub-fiefs, etc. (lands held from a lord), according to the value and extent of the domains, and many of them contained only a few acres. But these farmers had, to some degree, rights of jurisdiction over the people living on the land; there were four grades. One can understand how the agricultural population was oppressed under all these petty tyrants. Monteil says that France once had 160,000 judges, where today 4,000 courts, including justices of the peace, are enough.

## Chapter 30: Reaction of the Agricultural Revolution on Industry. Creation of the Home- Market for Industrial Capital

<!-- ch30-p001 -->
The expropriation (taking away people's property, here their land and means of production) and expulsion of the agricultural population was intermittent, but it was renewed again and again. As we saw, it supplied the town industries with a mass of proletarians (members of the proletariat, the class of wage workers, who own nothing they can live by except their labor-power). These proletarians had no connection at all with the corporate guilds and were not bound by them. This fortunate circumstance makes old A. Anderson (not to be confused with James Anderson), in his “History of Commerce,” believe in the direct intervention of Providence. We must still stop for a moment on this element of primitive accumulation (the historical process that separated the producers from their means of production, above all by driving peasants off the land, and so created the conditions for capitalism). The thinning-out of the independent, self-supporting peasants did not only bring about the crowding together of the industrial proletariat, in the way that Geoffrey Saint Hilaire explained the condensing of cosmic matter at one place by its thinning-out at another.[^30.1] Although fewer people now worked the soil, it brought forth as much produce as before, or more. This was because the revolution in the conditions of landed property was accompanied by improved methods of cultivation, greater cooperation (many workers working together, side by side, in the same or connected processes, under one capitalist's command), concentration of the means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things), etc. It was also because the agricultural wage workers were not only driven harder[^30.2], but the field of production on which they worked for themselves shrank more and more. Therefore, when a part of the agricultural population was set free, their former means of nourishment were also set free. These were now turned into material elements of variable capital. (Capital is value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger. Variable capital is the part of capital spent on labor-power; it reproduces its own value and also produces surplus-value, so its size varies.) The peasant, expropriated and cast adrift, must buy their value from his new master, the industrial capitalist, in the form of wages. (Value is what commodities have in common that lets them be exchanged as equals: the human labor spent on them, counted by labor-time. Wages are the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself.) What holds for the means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live) also holds for the raw materials of industry that depend on home agriculture. They were turned into an element of constant capital (the part of capital spent on means of production; its value is passed on to the product but does not grow). Suppose, for example, that a part of the Westphalian peasants, who in the time of Frederick II all spun flax, were forcibly expropriated and hunted off the soil, and that the other part, who stayed, were turned into day laborers for large farmers. At the same time large establishments for flax-spinning and weaving spring up, and the men who have been “set free” now work in them for wages. The flax looks exactly as before. Not a fiber of it has changed, but a new social soul has popped into its body. It now forms a part of the constant capital of the master manufacturer. Before, it was divided among a number of small producers, who grew it themselves and spun it with their families on a small scale. Now it is concentrated in the hands of one capitalist, who sets others to spin and weave it for him. The extra labor spent in flax-spinning used to be realized in extra income for numerous peasant families, or perhaps, in Frederick II’s time, in taxes *pour le roi de Prusse* [for the King of Prussia]. Now it is realized in profit for a few capitalists. The spindles and looms, once scattered over the face of the country, are now crowded together in a few great labor-barracks, together with the workers and the raw material. And spindles, looms, and raw material have now been turned from means of independent existence for the spinners and weavers into means for commanding them and sucking unpaid labor out of them.[^30.3] Looking at the large manufacturing workshops and the large farms, one does not see that they arose from throwing many small centers of production into one, and that they were built up by expropriating many small independent producers. Nevertheless, the popular intuition was not wrong. In the time of Mirabeau, the lion of the Revolution, the great manufacturing workshops were still called *manufactures réunies*, workshops thrown into one, as we speak of fields thrown into one. Mirabeau says:

[^30.1]: In his “Notions de Philosophie Naturelle.” Paris, 1838.

[^30.2]: A point that Sir James Steuart emphasizes.

[^30.3]: “Je permettrai,” says the capitalist, “que vous ayez l’honneur de me servir, à condition que vous me donnez le peu qui vous reste pour la peine que je prends de vous commander.” [I will allow you ... to have the honor of serving me, on condition that you give me the little you have left in return for the trouble I take in commanding you] (J. J. Rousseau: “Discours sur l’Economie Politique.”)

<!-- ch30-p002 -->
> “We are only paying attention to the grand manufactories, in which hundreds of men work under a director and which are commonly called *manufactures réunies*. Those where a very large number of labourers work, each separately and on his own account, are hardly considered; they are placed at an infinite distance from the others. This is a great error, as the latter alone make a really important object of national prosperity.... The large workshop (manufacture réunie) will enrich prodigiously one or two entrepreneurs, but the labourers will only be journeymen, paid more or less, and will not have any share in the success of the undertaking. In the discrete workshop (manufacture separée), on the contrary, no one will become rich, but many labourers will be comfortable; the saving and the industrious will be able to amass a little capital, to put by a little for a birth of a child, for an illness, for themselves or their belongings. The number of saving and industrious labourers will increase, because they will see in good conduct, in activity, a means of essentially bettering their condition, and not of obtaining a small rise in wages that can never be of any importance of the future, and whose sole result is to place men in the position to live a little better, but only from day to day.... The large workshops, undertakings of certain private persons who pay labourers from day to day to work for their gain, may be able to put these private individuals at their ease, but they will never be an object worth the attention of governments. Discrete workshops, for the most part combined with cultivation of small holdings, are the only free ones.”[^30.4] The expropriation and eviction of a part of the agricultural population did not only set free the workers, their means of subsistence, and material for labor for industrial capital. It also created the home market.

[^30.4]: Mirabeau, cited above, t.III, pp.20-109 passim. Mirabeau considers the separate workshops more economical and productive than the “combined” ones, and sees the combined ones as merely artificial hothouse plants raised under government care. This is explained by the situation at that time of a great part of the manufacturing workshops on the Continent.

<!-- ch30-p003 -->
In fact, the events that turned the small peasants into wage workers, and turned their means of subsistence and of labor into material elements of capital, at the same time created a home market for capital. Before, the peasant family produced the means of subsistence and the raw materials, and for the most part consumed them itself. These raw materials and means of subsistence have now become commodities (things produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer's own use). The large farmer sells them, and he finds his market in the manufacturing workshops. Yarn, linen, coarse woolen goods: their raw materials had been within the reach of every peasant family, which had spun and woven them for its own use. Now they were turned into articles of manufacture, and the country districts at once served as markets for them. Until now, stray artisans had found many scattered customers in the numerous small producers working on their own account. These customers now concentrate into one great market, supplied by industrial capital.[^30.5] So, hand in hand with the expropriation of the self-supporting peasants, with their separation from their means of production, goes the destruction of rural domestic industry, the process of separation between manufacture and agriculture. And only the destruction of rural domestic industry can give the internal market of a country the extent and solidity that the capitalist mode of production requires. Still, the manufacturing period in the strict sense does not succeed in carrying out this transformation radically and completely. It will be remembered that manufacture in the strict sense (the stage and form of capitalist production, roughly from the mid-16th to the late 18th century, based on handicraft work divided among many workers in one workshop) conquers only part of the domain of national production. It always rests, as its ultimate basis, on the handicrafts of the towns and the domestic industry of the rural districts. If it destroys these in one form, in particular branches, at certain points, it calls them up again elsewhere, because it needs them to prepare raw material up to a certain point. It therefore produces a new class of small villagers. They work the soil as a side occupation, but their chief occupation is industrial labor, whose products they sell to the manufacturers, either directly or through merchants. This is one cause, though not the chief one, of a phenomenon that at first puzzles the student of English history.[^30.6] From the last third of the 15th century on, he finds constant complaints, broken only at certain intervals, about capitalist farming encroaching on the country districts and about the progressive destruction of the peasantry. On the other hand, he always finds this peasantry turning up again, though in smaller numbers and always under worse conditions. The chief reason is this: England is at one time chiefly a grower of grain, at another chiefly a breeder of cattle, in alternating periods, and the extent of peasant farming rises and falls with these periods. Modern industry (large-scale production based on machinery and the factory system) alone, and finally, supplies in machinery the lasting basis of capitalist agriculture. It alone expropriates the enormous majority of the agricultural population radically, and completes the separation between agriculture and rural domestic industry, tearing up that industry's roots, spinning and weaving.[^30.7] It therefore also, for the first time, conquers the entire home market for industrial capital.[^30.8]

[^30.5]: “Twenty pounds of wool converted unobtrusively into yearly clothing of a labourer’s family by its own industry in the intervals of other works — this makes no show; but bring it to market, send it to the factory, thence to the broker, thence to the dealer, and you will have great commercial operations, and nominal capital engaged to the amount of twenty times its value.... The working-class is thus emersed to support a wretched factory population, a parasitical shop-keeping class, and a fictitious commercial, monetary, and financial system.” (David Urquhart, cited above, p.120.)

[^30.6]: Cromwell’s time is an exception. As long as the Republic lasted, the mass of the English people, of all ranks, rose out of the degradation into which they had sunk under the Tudors.

[^30.7]: Tuckett is aware that the modern woolen industry has sprung, with the introduction of machinery, from manufacture proper and from the destruction of rural and domestic industries.

    “The plough, the yoke, were ‘the invention of gods, and the occupation of heroes’; are the loom, the spindle, the distaff, of less noble parentage. You sever the distaff and the plough, the spindle and the yoke, and you get factories and poor-houses, credit and panics, two hostile nations, agriculture and commercial.” (David Urquhart, cited above, p.122.)

    But now comes Carey and accuses England, and surely not without reason, of trying to turn every other country into a mere agricultural nation, whose manufacturer is to be England. He claims that Turkey has been ruined in this way, because “the owners and occupants of land have never been permitted by England to strengthen themselves by the formation of that natural alliance between the plough and the loom, the hammer and the harrow.” (“The Slave Trade,” p.125.) According to Carey, Urquhart himself is one of the chief agents in the ruin of Turkey, where he had spread Free-trade propaganda in the English interest. The best of it is that Carey, a great Russophile by the way, wants to prevent the process of separation by means of the very system of protection that speeds it up.

[^30.8]: Philanthropic English economists, like Mill, Rogers, Goldwin Smith, Fawcett, etc., and liberal manufacturers like John Bright & Co., ask the English landed proprietors, as God asked Cain about Abel, Where have our thousands of freeholders gone? But where do *you* come from, then? From the destruction of those freeholders. Why don’t you go on to ask, where have the independent weavers, spinners, and artisans gone?

## Chapter 31: The Genesis of the Industrial Capitalist

<!-- ch31-p001 -->
The industrial[^31.*1] capitalist did not come into being in the same gradual way as the farmer. No doubt many small guild-masters, and even more independent small artisans, or even wage workers, turned themselves into small capitalists, and then (by gradually extending their exploitation of wage labor and the accumulation that went with it) into full-blown capitalists. (Accumulation of capital means turning surplus-value back into capital, so that capital grows.) In the infancy of capitalist production, things often went as they had in the infancy of medieval towns. There the question of which of the escaped serfs should be master and which servant was largely decided by how early or how late they had fled. The snail's pace of this method in no way matched the commercial needs of the new world market that the great discoveries at the end of the 15th century had created. But the middle ages had handed down two distinct forms of capital (value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger). These forms mature in the most varied economic formations of society, and before the era of the capitalist mode of production they are considered capital quand même [all the same]. They are usurer's capital and merchant's capital.

[^31.*1]: Industrial is used here as opposed to agricultural. In the “categoric” sense, the farmer is an industrial capitalist just as much as the manufacturer is.

<!-- ch31-p002 -->
> “At present, all the wealth of society goes first into the possession of the capitalist ... he pays the landowner his rent, the labourer his wages [the price paid for labor-power], the tax and tithe gatherer their claims, and keeps a large, indeed the largest, and a continually augmenting share, of the annual produce of labour for himself. The capitalist may now be said to be the first owner of all the wealth of the community, though no law has conferred on him the right to this property... this change has been effected by the taking of interest on capital ... and it is not a little curious that all the law-givers of Europe endeavoured to prevent this by statutes, viz., statutes against usury.... The power of the capitalist over all the wealth of the country is a complete change in the right of property, and by what law, or series of laws, was it effected?”[^31.2]

[^31.2]: “The Natural and Artificial Rights of Property Contrasted.” London, 1832, pp. 98-99. The author of this anonymous work is “Th. Hodgskin.”

<!-- ch31-p003 -->
The author should have remembered that revolutions are not made by laws.

<!-- ch31-p004 -->
The money capital formed through usury and trade was prevented from turning into industrial capital: in the countryside by the feudal constitution, in the towns by the guild organization.[^31.3] These fetters vanished with the breakup of feudal society, with the expropriation (the taking away of people's property, here land and means of production) and partial eviction of the country population. The new manufacturing workshops were set up at seaports, or at inland points beyond the control of the old municipalities and their guilds. Hence, in England, a bitter struggle of the corporate towns against these new nurseries of industry.

[^31.3]: Even as late as 1794, the small cloth-makers of Leeds sent a deputation to Parliament with a petition for a law forbidding any merchant to become a manufacturer. (Dr. Aikin, cited above.)

<!-- ch31-p005 -->
The discovery of gold and silver in America; the extermination of the native population, its enslavement, and its entombment in the mines; the beginning of the conquest and looting of the East Indies; the turning of Africa into a game preserve for the commercial hunting of Black people: these signaled the rosy dawn of the era of capitalist production. These idyllic proceedings are the chief elements of primitive accumulation (the historical process that separated the producers from their means of production, above all by driving peasants off the land, and so created the conditions for capitalism). Close on their heels comes the commercial war of the European nations, with the whole globe as its stage. It begins with the revolt of the Netherlands against Spain, takes on giant dimensions in England's Anti-Jacobin War, and is still going on in the opium wars against China, etc.

<!-- ch31-p006 -->
The different elements of primitive accumulation are now distributed, more or less in chronological order, over Spain, Portugal, Holland, France, and England in particular. In England at the end of the 17th century, they come together in a systematic combination that takes in the colonies, the national debt, the modern system of taxation, and the protectionist system. These methods depend in part on brute force, for example the colonial system. But they all use the power of the State, the concentrated and organized force of society, to speed up, hothouse fashion, the process by which the feudal mode of production is transformed into the capitalist mode, and to shorten the transition. Force is the midwife of every old society pregnant with a new one. It is itself an economic power.

<!-- ch31-p007 -->
W. Howitt, a man who makes a specialty of Christianity, says of the Christian colonial system:

<!-- ch31-p008 -->
> “The barbarities and desperate outrages of the so-called Christian race, throughout every region of the world, and upon every people they have been able to subdue, are not to be paralleled by those of any other race, however fierce, however untaught, and however reckless of mercy and of shame, in any age of the earth.”[^31.4]

[^31.4]: William Howitt: “Colonisation and Christianity: A Popular History of the Treatment of the Natives by the Europeans in all their Colonies.” London, 1838, p. 9. There is a good compilation on the treatment of the slaves in Charles Comte, “Traité de la Législation.” 3me éd. Bruxelles, 1837. One must study this subject in detail to see what the bourgeoisie (the capitalist class) makes of itself and of the worker wherever it can, without restraint, model the world after its own image.

<!-- ch31-p009 -->
The history of the colonial administration of Holland – and Holland was the leading capitalist nation of the 17th century –

<!-- ch31-p010 -->
> “is one of the most extraordinary relations of treachery, bribery, massacre, and meanness”[^31.5]

[^31.5]: Thomas Stamford Raffles, former Lieutenant-Governor of that island: “The History of Java,” London, 1817.

<!-- ch31-p011 -->
Nothing is more characteristic than their system of stealing men to get slaves for Java. The men-stealers were trained for this purpose. The thief, the interpreter, and the seller were the chief agents in this trade, and native princes were the chief sellers. The young people who were stolen were thrown into the secret dungeons of Celebes until they were ready to be sent to the slave-ships. An official report says:

<!-- ch31-p012 -->
> “This one town of Macassar, *e.g.*, is full of secret prisons, one more horrible than the other, crammed with unfortunates, victims of greed and tyranny fettered in chains, forcibly torn from their families.”

<!-- ch31-p013 -->
To secure Malacca, the Dutch bribed the Portuguese governor. He let them into the town in 1641. They hurried at once to his house and assassinated him, so as to “abstain” from paying £21,875, the price of his treason. Wherever they set foot, devastation and depopulation followed. Banjuwangi, a province of Java, had over 80,000 inhabitants in 1750, and only 18,000 in 1811. Sweet commerce!

<!-- ch31-p014 -->
The English East India Company, as is well known, obtained not only political rule in India but also the exclusive monopoly of the tea trade, as well as of the Chinese trade in general, and of the transport of goods to and from Europe. But the coastal trade of India and between the islands, as well as the internal trade of India, was the monopoly of the higher employees of the company. The monopolies of salt, opium, betel, and other commodities (things produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer's own use) were inexhaustible mines of wealth. The employees themselves fixed the price and plundered the unhappy Hindus at will. The Governor-General took part in this private trade. His favorites received contracts on terms under which they, cleverer than the alchemists, made gold out of nothing. Great fortunes sprang up like mushrooms in a day; primitive accumulation went on without a shilling being advanced. The trial of Warren Hastings swarms with such cases. Here is one instance. A contract for opium was given to a certain Sullivan just as he was leaving on an official mission to a part of India far away from the opium district. Sullivan sold his contract to one Binn for £40,000. Binn sold it the same day for £60,000, and the final buyer, who carried out the contract, declared that even after all this he made an enormous gain. According to one of the lists laid before Parliament, the Company and its employees got £6,000,000 from the Indians as gifts from 1757-1766. Between 1769 and 1770, the English manufactured a famine by buying up all the rice and refusing to sell it again except at fabulous prices.[^31.6]

[^31.6]: In the year 1866 more than a million Hindus died of hunger in the province of Orissa alone. Nevertheless, an attempt was made to enrich the Indian treasury by the price at which the necessities of life were sold to the starving people.

<!-- ch31-p015 -->
The treatment of the native peoples was, naturally, most frightful in plantation colonies meant only for export trade, such as the West Indies, and in rich and well-populated countries that were given over to plunder, such as Mexico and India. But even in the colonies properly so called, the Christian character of primitive accumulation stayed true to itself. Those sober virtuosos of Protestantism, the Puritans of New England, by decrees of their assembly in 1703 set a bounty of £40 on every Indian scalp and every captured Native American; in 1720 a bounty of £100 on every scalp; in 1744, after Massachusetts-Bay had proclaimed a certain tribe rebels, the following prices: for a male scalp of 12 years and upwards £100 (new currency), for a male prisoner £105, for women and children prisoners £50, for scalps of women and children £50. Some decades later, the colonial system took its revenge on the descendants of the pious pilgrim fathers, who had grown rebellious in the meantime. At English instigation and for English pay they were tomahawked by Native Americans. The British Parliament proclaimed bloodhounds and scalping to be “means that God and Nature had given into its hand.”

<!-- ch31-p016 -->
The colonial system ripened trade and navigation as in a hothouse. The “societies Monopolia” of Luther were powerful levers for the concentration of capital (the growth of individual capitals through accumulation). The colonies secured a market for the budding manufacturing workshops, and, through the monopoly of that market, an increased accumulation. The treasures captured outside Europe by open looting, enslavement, and murder flowed back to the mother country and were turned into capital there. Holland, which was the first to develop the colonial system fully, already stood at the peak of its commercial greatness in 1648. It was

<!-- ch31-p017 -->
> “in almost exclusive possession of the East Indian trade and the commerce between the south-east and north-west of Europe. Its fisheries, marine and branches of manufacture surpassed those of any other country. The total capital of the Republic was probably more important than that of all the rest of Europe put together.” Gülich forgets to add that by 1648 the people of Holland were more overworked, poorer, and more brutally oppressed than those of all the rest of Europe put together.

<!-- ch31-p018 -->
Today industrial supremacy carries commercial supremacy with it. In the period of manufacture properly so called, on the other hand, it is commercial supremacy that gives industrial predominance. (Manufacture is the stage and form of capitalist production, roughly from the mid-16th to the late 18th century, based on handicraft work divided among many workers in one workshop.) Hence the dominant role that the colonial system played at that time. It was “the strange God” who perched himself on the altar side by side with the old Gods of Europe, and one fine day, with a shove and a kick, tumbled them all down in a heap. It proclaimed the making of surplus-value to be the sole end and aim of humanity. (Surplus-value is the extra value that workers produce beyond the value of their own labor-power, which the capitalist keeps without paying for it.)

<!-- ch31-p019 -->
The system of public credit, that is, of national debts, whose origin we find in Genoa and Venice as early as the Middle Ages, took possession of Europe in general during the manufacturing period. The colonial system, with its sea trade and commercial wars, served as a hothouse for it. So it first took root in Holland. National debts, that is, the alienation (the selling off) of the state – whether despotic, constitutional, or republican – put their stamp on the capitalist era. The only part of the so-called national wealth that actually passes into the collective possession of modern peoples is their national debt.[^31.7] Hence, as a necessary consequence, the modern doctrine that a nation becomes the richer the more deeply it is in debt. Public credit becomes the creed of capital. And with the rise of national debt-making, lack of faith in the national debt takes the place of the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, which may not be forgiven.

[^31.7]: William Cobbett remarks that in England all public institutions are called “royal”; to make up for this, however, there is the “national” debt.

<!-- ch31-p020 -->
The public debt becomes one of the most powerful levers of primitive accumulation. As if with the stroke of a magician's wand, it gives barren money the power to breed, and so turns it into capital, without its having to expose itself to the troubles and risks that cannot be separated from its use in industry, or even in usury. The state's creditors actually give nothing away, for the sum they lend is turned into public bonds that are easily sold, and these go on functioning in their hands just as so much hard cash would. But there is more. Apart from the class of lazy annuitants (people who live on the yearly interest) created in this way, and from the improvised wealth of the financiers, the middlemen between the government and the nation – and apart also from the tax-farmers (private collectors of taxes), merchants, and private manufacturers, to whom a good part of every national loan does the service of a capital fallen from heaven – the national debt has given rise to joint-stock companies, to dealings in negotiable securities of all kinds, and to agiotage, in a word to stock-exchange gambling and the modern bankocracy.

<!-- ch31-p021 -->
At their birth, the great banks, decorated with national titles, were only associations of private speculators. These placed themselves at the side of governments and, thanks to the privileges they received, were in a position to advance money to the State. Hence the accumulation of the national debt has no surer measure than the successive rise in the stock of these banks, whose full development dates from the founding of the Bank of England in 1694. The Bank of England began by lending its money to the Government at 8%. At the same time Parliament empowered it to coin money out of the same capital, by lending it again to the public in the form of banknotes. It was allowed to use these notes for discounting bills, making advances on commodities, and buying the precious metals. It was not long before this credit-money, made by the bank itself, became the coin in which the Bank of England made its loans to the State and paid the interest on the public debt on the State's behalf. It was not enough that the bank gave with one hand and took back more with the other; even while it was receiving, it remained the eternal creditor of the nation down to the last shilling advanced. Gradually it inevitably became the storehouse of the country's metallic hoard (money withdrawn from circulation and kept as a store of value), and the center of gravity of all commercial credit. What effect the sudden rise of this brood of bankocrats, financiers, rentiers, brokers, stock-jobbers, etc., had on their contemporaries is proved by the writings of that time, for example by Bolingbroke's.[^31.8]

[^31.8]: “Si les Tartares inondaient l’Europe aujourd’hui, il faudrait bien des affaires pour leur faire entendre ce que c’est qu’un financier parmi nous.” [If the Tartars flooded into Europe today, it would take a great deal of trouble to make them understand what a financier is among us.] Montesquieu, “Esprit des lois,” t. iv., p. 33, ed. Londres, 1769.

<!-- ch31-p022 -->
With the national debt there arose an international credit system, which often hides one of the sources of primitive accumulation in this or that people. Thus the villainies of the Venetian system of robbery formed one of the secret foundations of the capital-wealth of Holland, to which Venice in her decline lent large sums of money. So it was too between Holland and England. By the beginning of the 18th century the Dutch manufacturing workshops had been far outstripped. Holland had ceased to be the leading nation in trade and industry. One of its main lines of business from 1701-1776, therefore, is the lending out of enormous amounts of capital, especially to its great rival England. The same thing is going on today between England and the United States. A great deal of capital that appears today in the United States without any birth certificate was, yesterday, in England, the capitalized blood of children.

<!-- ch31-p023 -->
The national debt is backed by the public revenue, which must cover the yearly interest payments, etc. So the modern system of taxation was the necessary complement of the system of national loans. The loans let the government meet extraordinary expenses without the taxpayers feeling it immediately, but as a consequence they make higher taxes necessary. On the other hand, the rise in taxes caused by the accumulation of debts contracted one after another forces the government always to turn to new loans for new extraordinary expenses. Modern fiscal policy, whose pivot is the taxes on the most necessary means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live), which raise their price, thus carries within itself the germ of automatic growth. Overtaxation is not an accident, but rather a principle. In Holland, therefore, where this system was first introduced, the great patriot DeWitt praised it in his “Maxims” as the best system for making the wage worker submissive, frugal, hardworking, and overburdened with labor. Here, however, we are less concerned with its destructive effect on the condition of the wage worker than with the forcible expropriation that results from it: the expropriation of peasants, artisans, and, in a word, all elements of the lower middle class. On this there are not two opinions, even among the bourgeois economists. Its expropriating effect is heightened still further by the system of protection, which forms one of its integral parts.

<!-- ch31-p024 -->
The great part that the public debt, and the fiscal system that goes with it, has played in the capitalization of wealth and the expropriation of the masses has led many writers, such as Cobbett, Doubleday and others, to look for the fundamental cause of the misery of modern peoples in this, wrongly.

<!-- ch31-p025 -->
The system of protection was an artificial means of manufacturing manufacturers, of expropriating independent workers, of turning the national means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things) and of subsistence into capital, and of forcibly cutting short the transition from the medieval to the modern mode of production. The European states tore one another to pieces over the patent of this invention. Once they had entered the service of the surplus-value makers, they did not merely make their own people pay for this purpose, indirectly through protective duties and directly through export bounties. They also forcibly rooted out all industry in their dependent countries, as England, for example, did with the Irish wool manufacture. On the continent of Europe, following Colbert's example, the process was much simplified. Here the primitive industrial capital came in part directly out of the state treasury. “Why,” cries Mirabeau, “why go so far to seek the cause of the manufacturing glory of Saxony before the war? 180,000,000 of debts contracted by the sovereigns!”[^31.9]

[^31.9]: Mirabeau, cited above, t. vi., p. 101.

<!-- ch31-p026 -->
Colonial system, public debts, heavy taxes, protection, commercial wars, etc.: these children of the true manufacturing period grow to gigantic size during the infancy of modern industry (large-scale production based on machinery and the factory system). Its birth is announced by a great slaughter of the innocents. Like the royal navy, the factories were recruited by means of the press-gang (the gangs that seized men by force for service). Sir F. M. Eden is blasé about the horrors of the expropriation of the agricultural population from the soil, from the last third of the 15th century to his own time. He rejoices with all self-satisfaction in this process, “essential” for establishing capitalist agriculture and “the due proportion between arable and pasture land.” Yet he does not show the same economic insight about the necessity of child-stealing and child-slavery for transforming manufacturing exploitation into factory exploitation, and for establishing the “true relation” between capital and labor-power. (Labor-power is a person's capacity to work: the mental and physical abilities a human being uses when producing anything. It is this capacity, not labor itself, that the worker sells to the capitalist.) He says:

<!-- ch31-p027 -->
> “It may, perhaps, be worthy the attention of the public to consider, whether any manufacture, which, in order to be carried on successfully, requires that cottages and workhouses should be ransacked for poor children; that they should be employed by turns during the greater part of the night and robbed of that rest which, though indispensable to all, is most required by the young; and that numbers of both sexes, of different ages and dispositions, should be collected together in such a manner that the contagion of example cannot but lead to profligacy and debauchery; will add to the sum of individual or national felicity?”[^31.10]

[^31.10]: Eden, cited above, Vol. I., Book II., Ch. 1., p. 421.

<!-- ch31-p028 -->
> “In the counties of Derbyshire, Nottinghamshire, and more particularly in Lancashire,” says Fielden, “the newly-invented machinery was used in large factories built on the sides of streams capable of turning the water-wheel. Thousands of hands were suddenly required in these places, remote from towns; and Lancashire, in particular, being, till then, comparatively thinly populated and barren, a population was all that she now wanted. The small and nimble fingers of little children being by very far the most in request, the custom instantly sprang up of procuring *apprentices* from the different parish workhouses of London, Birmingham, and elsewhere. Many, many thousands of these little, hapless creatures were sent down into the north, being from the age of 7 to the age of 13 or 14 years old. The custom was for the master to clothe his apprentices and to feed and lodge them in an “apprentice house” near the factory; overseers were appointed to see to the works, whose interest it was to work the children to the utmost, because their pay was in proportion to the quantity of work that they could exact. Cruelty was, of course, the consequence. ... In many of the manufacturing districts, but particularly, I am afraid, in the guilty county to which I belong [Lancashire], cruelties the most heart-rending were practised upon the unoffending and friendless creatures who were thus consigned to the charge of master-manufacturers; they were harassed to the brink of death by excess of labour ... were flogged, fettered and tortured in the most exquisite refinement of cruelty; ... they were in many cases starved to the bone while flogged to their work and ... even in some instances ... were driven to commit suicide.... The beautiful and romantic valleys of Derbyshire, Nottinghamshire and Lancashire, secluded from the public eye, became the dismal solitudes of torture, and of many a murder. The profits of manufacturers were enormous; but this only whetted the appetite that it should have satisfied, and therefore the manufacturers had recourse to an expedient that seemed to secure to them those profits without any possibility of limit; they began the practice of what is termed “night-working,” that is, having tired one set of hands, by working them throughout the day, they had another set ready to go on working throughout the night; the day-set getting into the beds that the night-set had just quitted, and in their turn again, the night-set getting into the beds that the day-set quitted in the morning. It is a common tradition in Lancashire, that the beds *never get cold.*”[^31.11]

[^31.11]: John Fielden, cited above, pp. 5, 6. On the earlier infamies of the factory system (production in which a system of machines, driven by a central power source, does the work and workers attend the machines), compare Dr. Aikin (1795), cited above, p. 219, and Gisborne: “Enquiry into the Duties of Men,” 1795 Vol. II. When the steam-engine moved the factories from the country waterfalls into the middle of towns, the “abstemious” surplus-value maker found the child-material ready to hand, without being forced to fetch slaves from the workhouses. When Sir R. Peel (father of the “minister of plausibility”) brought in his bill for the protection of children in 1815, Francis Horner, leading light of the Bullion Committee and intimate friend of Ricardo, said in the House of Commons: “It is notorious, that with a bankrupt’s effects, a gang, if he might use the word, of these children had been put up to sale, and were advertised publicly as part of the property. A most atrocious instance had been brought before the Court of King’s Bench two years before, in which a number of these boys, apprenticed by a parish in London to one manufacturer, had been transferred to another, and had been found by some benevolent persons in a state of absolute famine. Another case more horrible had come to his knowledge while on a [Parliamentary] Committee ... that not many years ago, an agreement had been made between a London parish and a Lancashire manufacturer, by which it was stipulated, that with every 20 sound children one idiot should be taken.”

<!-- ch31-p029 -->
With the development of capitalist production during the manufacturing period, the public opinion of Europe had lost the last remnant of shame and conscience. The nations bragged cynically of every infamy that served them as a means of capitalist accumulation. Read, for example, the naïve Annals of Commerce of the worthy A. Anderson. Here it is trumpeted as a triumph of English statecraft that at the Peace of Utrecht England extorted from the Spaniards, by the Asiento Treaty, the privilege of being allowed to carry on the trade in Black people between Africa and Spanish America as well, a trade that until then it had carried on only between Africa and the English West Indies. England thereby acquired the right to supply Spanish America until 1743 with 4,800 Black people a year. At the same time, this threw an official cloak over British smuggling. Liverpool grew fat on the slave trade. This was its method of primitive accumulation. And even to the present day, Liverpool “respectability” is the Pindar, the praise-singer, of the slave trade, which – compare the work of Aikin [1795] already quoted – “has coincided with that spirit of bold adventure which has characterised the trade of Liverpool and rapidly carried it to its present state of prosperity; has occasioned vast employment for shipping and sailors, and greatly augmented the demand for the manufactures of the country” (p. 339). Liverpool employed in the slave trade, in 1730, 15 ships; in 1751, 53; in 1760, 74; in 1770, 96; and in 1792, 132.[^31.12]

[^31.12]: In 1790 there were ten slaves for every free man in the English West Indies, fourteen for one in the French, and twenty-three for one in the Dutch. (Henry Brougham: “An Inquiry into the Colonial Policy of the European Powers.” Edin. 1803, vol. II., p. 74.)

<!-- ch31-p030 -->
While the cotton industry introduced child-slavery in England, in the United States it gave a stimulus to the transformation of the earlier, more or less patriarchal slavery into a system of commercial exploitation. In fact, the veiled slavery of the wage workers in Europe needed, as its pedestal, slavery pure and simple in the new world.

<!-- ch31-p031 -->
Tantae molis erat [So much effort did it take] to establish the “eternal laws of Nature” of the capitalist mode of production; to complete the process of separation between workers and the conditions of labor; to transform, at one pole, the social means of production and subsistence into capital, and at the opposite pole, the mass of the population into wage workers, into “free labouring poor,” that artificial product of modern society.[^31.13] If money, according to Augier,[^31.14] “comes into the world with a congenital blood-stain on one cheek,” capital comes dripping from head to foot, from every pore, with blood and dirt.[^31.15]

[^31.13]: The phrase “labouring poor” is found in English legislation from the moment when the class of wage workers becomes noticeable. This term is used in opposition, on the one hand, to the “idle poor,” beggars, etc., on the. out and out vulgar bourgeois. “The laws of commerce are the laws of Nature, and therefore the laws of God.” (E. Burke, cited above, pp. 31, 32.) No wonder that, true to the laws of God and of Nature, he always sold himself in the best market. A very good portrait of this Edmund Burke, during his liberal period, can be found in the writings of the Rev. Mr. Tucker. Tucker was a parson and a Tory, but otherwise an honorable man and a competent political economist. In the face of the infamous cowardice of character that reigns today, and believes most devoutly in “the laws of commerce,” it is our bounden duty to brand, again and again, the Burkes, who differ from their successors in only one thing — talent.

[^31.14]: Marie Angier: “Du Crédit Public.” Paris, 1842.

[^31.15]: “Capital is said by a Quarterly Reviewer to fly turbulence and strife, and to be timid, which is very true; but this is very incompletely stating the question. Capital eschews no profit, or very small profit, just as Nature was formerly said to abhor a vacuum. With adequate profit, capital is very bold. A certain 10 per cent. will ensure its employment anywhere; 20 per cent. certain will produce eagerness; 50 per cent., positive audacity; 100 per cent. will make it ready to trample on all human laws; 300 per cent., and there is not a crime at which it will scruple, nor a risk it will not run, even to the chance of its owner being hanged. If turbulence and strife will bring a profit, it will freely encourage both. Smuggling and the slave-trade have amply proved all that is here stated.” (T. J. Dunning, cited above, pp. 35, 36.)

## Chapter 32: Historical Tendency of Capitalist Accumulation

<!-- ch32-p001 -->
What does the primitive accumulation of capital, that is, its historical origin, come down to? (Capital means value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger.) To the extent that it is not the direct transformation of slaves and serfs into wage workers, and therefore a mere change of form, it means only the expropriation of the immediate producers, that is, the breaking up of private property based on the labor of its owner. Private property, as the opposite of social, collective property, exists only where the means of labor and the external conditions of labor belong to private individuals. But private property has a different character depending on whether these private individuals are workers or not workers. The countless shades that it shows at first sight correspond to the in-between stages that lie between these two extremes. The worker's private property in his means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things) is the foundation of small-scale industry, whether agricultural, manufacturing, or both. Small-scale industry, in turn, is an essential condition for the development of social production and of the free individuality of the worker himself. Of course, this small-scale mode of production also exists under slavery, serfdom, and other states of dependence. But it flourishes, it lets loose all its energy, it reaches its adequate classical form, only where the worker is the private owner of his own means of labor, which he sets in motion himself: the peasant of the land he cultivates, the artisan of the tool he handles like a virtuoso. This mode of production presupposes that the land is cut up into small plots and that the other means of production are scattered. Just as it excludes the concentration of these means of production, it also excludes cooperation, division of labor within each separate process of production, the control over the forces of Nature and their productive application by society, and the free development of the social productive powers. (Cooperation means many workers working together, side by side, in the same or connected processes, under one capitalist's command. Division of labor means the splitting of the making of one product into many separate tasks, each done by a specialized worker.) This mode of production is compatible only with a system of production, and a society, that move within narrow and more or less primitive limits. To make it last forever would be, as Pecqueur rightly says, “to decree universal mediocrity”. At a certain stage of development, it brings into being the material means of its own dissolution. From that moment new forces and new passions spring up in the heart of society; but the old social organization chains them and holds them down. It must be wiped out; it is wiped out. Its destruction is the transformation of the individualized and scattered means of production into socially concentrated ones, of the dwarf-sized property of the many into the huge property of the few. It is the expropriation of the great mass of the people from the soil, from the means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live), and from the means of labor. This terrible and painful expropriation of the mass of the people forms the prelude to the history of capital. It includes a series of methods of force, and of these we have reviewed only those that marked an epoch as methods of the primitive accumulation of capital. The expropriation of the immediate producers was carried out with merciless vandalism, spurred on by the most infamous, the most sordid, the pettiest, the most meanly hateful passions. Self-earned private property, which is based, so to speak, on the fusing together of the isolated, independent working individual with the conditions of his labor, is pushed out by capitalist private property, which rests on the exploitation of the nominally free labor of others, that is, on wage labor.[^32.1]

[^32.1]: “Nous sommes dans une condition tout-à-fait nouvelle de la societé... nous tendons a séparer toute espèce de propriété d’avec toute espèce de travail.” [We are in an entirely new condition of society ... we tend to separate every kind of property from every kind of labor] (Sismondi: “Nouveaux Principes d’Econ. Polit.” t.II, p.434.)

<!-- ch32-p002 -->
As soon as this process of transformation has broken up the old society enough, from top to bottom; as soon as the workers are turned into proletarians (members of the proletariat, the class of wage workers, who own nothing they can live by except their labor-power), and their means of labor into capital; as soon as the capitalist mode of production stands on its own feet: then the further socialization of labor, and the further transformation of the land and other means of production into socially exploited and therefore common means of production, as well as the further expropriation of private owners, take on a new form. What is now to be expropriated is no longer the worker working for himself, but the capitalist who exploits many workers. This expropriation is carried out by the working of the built-in laws of capitalist production itself, by the centralization of capital. One capitalist always kills many. Hand in hand with this centralization, or this expropriation of many capitalists by a few, other things develop on an ever-growing scale. These are the cooperative form of the labor process (the process of work itself, in which people use tools on materials to make useful things), the conscious technical application of science, and the methodical cultivation of the soil. They are also the transformation of the instruments of labor into instruments of labor that can only be used in common, and the economizing of all means of production by using them as the means of production of combined, socialized labor. And they are the entanglement of all peoples in the net of the world market, and with this, the international character of the capitalist regime. Along with the constantly shrinking number of the magnates of capital, who usurp and monopolize all the advantages of this process of transformation, the mass of misery, oppression, slavery, degradation, and exploitation grows. But with this there also grows the revolt of the working class, a class always increasing in numbers, and disciplined, united, and organized by the very mechanism of the process of capitalist production itself. The monopoly of capital becomes a fetter on the mode of production that has sprung up and flourished along with it and under it. Centralization of the means of production and socialization of labor at last reach a point where they become incompatible with their capitalist shell. This shell is burst apart. The death knell of capitalist private property sounds. The expropriators are expropriated.

<!-- ch32-p003 -->
The capitalist mode of appropriation, which is the result of the capitalist mode of production, produces capitalist private property. This is the first negation of individual private property, as founded on the labor of the owner. But capitalist production gives birth, with the relentlessness of a law of Nature, to its own negation. It is the negation of the negation. This does not re-establish private property for the producer, but gives him individual property based on what the capitalist era has acquired: that is, on cooperation and the possession in common of the land and of the means of production.

<!-- ch32-p004 -->
Turning scattered private property, arising from individual labor, into capitalist private property is, naturally, a process incomparably more drawn-out, violent, and difficult than turning capitalist private property, which in practice already rests on socialized production, into socialized property. In the first case, we had the expropriation of the mass of the people by a few usurpers; in the second, we have the expropriation of a few usurpers by the mass of the people.[^32.2]

[^32.2]: The advance of industry, whose involuntary promoter is the bourgeoisie [the capitalist class], replaces the isolation of the labourers, due to competition, by their revolutionary combination, due to association. The development of Modern Industry [large-scale production based on machinery and the factory system], therefore, cuts from under its feet the very foundation on which the bourgeoisie produces and appropriates products. What the bourgeoisie, therefore, produces, above all, are its own grave-diggers. Its fall and the victory of the proletariat are equally inevitable.... Of all the classes that stand face-to-face with the bourgeoisie today, the proletariat alone is a really revolutionary class. The other classes perish and disappear in the face of Modern Industry, the proletariat is its special and essential product.... The lower middle classes, the small manufacturers, the shopkeepers, the artisan, the peasant, all these fight against the bourgeoisie, to save from extinction their existence as fractions of the middle class... they are reactionary, for they try to roll back the wheel of history. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, “Manifest der Kommunistischen Partei,” London, 1848, pp. 9, 11.

## Chapter 33: The Modern Theory of Colonization[^33.1]

<!-- ch33-p001 -->
Political economy (the science of economics as it was then called) confuses, on principle, two very different kinds of private property. One rests on the producers’ own labor, the other on employing the labor of others. It forgets that the second is not only the direct opposite of the first, but grows absolutely only on its grave. In Western Europe, the home of political economy, the process of primitive accumulation (the historical process that separated the producers from their means of production, above all by driving peasants off the land, and so created the conditions for capitalism) is more or less complete. Here the capitalist regime has either directly conquered the whole field of national production, or, where economic conditions are less developed, it at least indirectly controls those layers of society which belong to the outdated mode of production but go on existing side by side with it, slowly decaying. To this ready-made world of capital (value that is used to make more value: money that is advanced in order to come back larger), the political economist applies the ideas of law and property he inherited from a pre-capitalist world. He does so with all the more anxious zeal and all the more pious oiliness, the more loudly the facts cry out against his ideology. It is different in the colonies. There the capitalist regime everywhere collides with the resistance of the producer, who owns his own conditions of labor and uses that labor to enrich himself instead of the capitalist. The contradiction between these two diametrically opposed economic systems shows itself here in practice, as a struggle between them. Where the capitalist has the power of the mother-country behind him, he tries to clear out of his way, by force, the modes of production and appropriation based on the producer’s independent labor. In the mother-country, the sycophant of capital, the political economist, is driven by his interest to proclaim that the capitalist mode of production is in theory identical with its opposite. That same interest drives him in the colonies to come clean and to proclaim aloud the antagonism between the two modes of production. To this end, he proves that the development of the social productive power of labor, cooperation (many workers working together, side by side, in the same or connected processes, under one capitalist’s command), division of labor (the splitting of the making of one product into many separate tasks, each done by a specialized worker), the use of machinery on a large scale, etc., are impossible without the expropriation of the workers (taking away people’s property, here land and means of production) and the matching transformation of their means of production (the tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials used in producing things) into capital. In the interest of the so-called national wealth, he looks for artificial means to make sure the people stay poor. Here his apologist’s armor crumbles off, bit by bit, like rotten touchwood. It is the great merit of E. G. Wakefield to have discovered, not anything new about the Colonies,[^33.2] but in the Colonies the truth about the conditions of capitalist production in the mother country. The system of protective tariffs, at its origin,[^33.3] tried to manufacture capitalists artificially in the mother-country. In the same way, Wakefield’s theory of colonization, which England tried for a time to enforce by Acts of Parliament, tried to manufacture wage workers in the Colonies. This he calls “systematic colonisation.”

[^33.1]: We deal here with real Colonies, virgin soils colonized by free immigrants. Economically speaking, the United States are still only a Colony of Europe. Besides, this category also includes old plantations where the abolition of slavery has completely changed the earlier conditions.

[^33.2]: Wakefield’s few glimpses on the subject of modern colonization were fully anticipated by Mirabeau Pere, the physiocrat, and even much earlier by English economists.

[^33.3]: Later, it became a temporary necessity in the international competitive struggle. But whatever its motive, the consequences remain the same.

<!-- ch33-p002 -->
First of all, Wakefield discovered that in the Colonies, owning money, means of subsistence (the food, clothing, housing, and other necessities a person needs to live), machines, and other means of production does not yet stamp a man as a capitalist if the counterpart is missing: the wage worker, the other man who is forced to sell himself of his own free will. He discovered that capital is not a thing, but a social relation between persons, set up by means of things.[^33.4] Mr. Peel, he moans, took with him from England to Swan River, West Australia, means of subsistence and of production worth £50,000. Mr. Peel had the foresight to bring with him, as well, 300 persons of the working class, men, women, and children. Once he arrived at his destination, “Mr. Peel was left without a servant to make his bed or fetch him water from the river.”[^33.5] Unhappy Mr. Peel, who provided for everything except the export of English modes of production to Swan River!

[^33.4]: “A negro is a negro. In certain circumstances he becomes a slave. A mule is a machine for spinning cotton. Only under certain circumstances does it become capital. Outside these circumstances, it is no more capital than gold is intrinsically money, or sugar is the price [the money name of the value embodied in a commodity] of sugar.... Capital is a social relation of production. It is a historical relation of production.” (Karl Marx, “Lohnarbeit und Kapital,” *N. Rh. Z*., No.266, April 7, 1849.)

[^33.5]: E. G. Wakefield: “England and America,” vol.ii. p.33.

<!-- ch33-p003 -->
To understand the following discoveries of Wakefield, two preliminary remarks are needed. We know that the means of production and subsistence, as long as they remain the property of the immediate producer, are not capital. They become capital only under circumstances in which they serve at the same time as means of exploiting and subjugating the worker. But in the head of the political economist this capitalist soul of theirs is so closely wedded to their material substance that he christens them capital under all circumstances, even when they are its exact opposite. So it is with Wakefield. Further: when the means of production are split up into the individual property of many independent workers, working on their own account, he calls this the equal division of capital. The political economist is like the feudal lawyer. The feudal lawyer stuck the labels supplied by feudal law onto purely monetary relations.

<!-- ch33-p004 -->
“If,” says Wakefield, “all members of the society are supposed to possess equal portions of capital... no man would have a motive for accumulating more capital than he could use with his own hands. This is to some extent the case in new American settlements, where a passion for owning land prevents the existence of a class of labourers for hire.”[^33.6] So as long as the worker can accumulate for himself (and he can do this as long as he remains the owner of his means of production), capitalist accumulation (turning surplus-value back into capital, so that capital grows) and the capitalist mode of production are impossible. The class of wage workers, which they cannot do without, is missing. How, then, in old Europe, was the worker expropriated from his conditions of labor? How, that is, did capital and wage labor come to exist side by side? By a social contract of a quite original kind. “Mankind have adopted a... simple contrivance for promoting the accumulation of capital,” which, of course, had floated in their imagination since the time of Adam as the sole and final purpose of their existence: “they have divided themselves into owners of capital and owners of labour.... The division was the result of concert and combination.”[^33.7] In a word: the mass of mankind expropriated itself in honor of the “accumulation of capital.” Now one would think that this instinct of self-denying fanaticism would have full play especially in the Colonies, the only place where the men and conditions exist that could turn a social contract from a dream into reality. But why, then, should “systematic colonisation” be called in to replace its opposite, spontaneous, unregulated colonization? But ‒ but ‒ “In the Northern States of the American Union; it may be doubted whether so many as a tenth of the people would fall under the description of hired labourers.... In England... the labouring class compose the bulk of the people.”[^33.8] Indeed, working humanity’s urge to expropriate itself for the glory of capital barely exists, so much so that slavery, according to Wakefield himself, is the only natural basis of Colonial wealth. His systematic colonization is a mere last resort, since he unfortunately has to deal with free men, not with slaves. “The first Spanish settlers in Saint Domingo did not obtain labourers from Spain. But, without labourers, their capital must have perished, or at least, must soon have been diminished to that small amount which each individual could employ with his own hands. This has actually occurred in the last Colony founded by England – the Swan River Settlement – where a great mass of capital, of seeds, implements, and cattle, has perished for want of labourers to use it, and where no settler has preserved much more capital than he can employ with his own hands.”[^33.9]

[^33.6]: Cited above, p.17.

[^33.7]: Cited above, vol.i, p.18.

[^33.8]: Cited above, pp.42, 43, 44.

[^33.9]: Cited above, vol.ii, p.5.

<!-- ch33-p005 -->
We have seen that the expropriation of the mass of the people from the soil forms the basis of the capitalist mode of production. The essence of a free colony, on the contrary, is this: the bulk of the soil is still public property, so every settler on it can turn part of it into his private property and individual means of production, without preventing later settlers from doing the same.[^33.10] This is the secret both of the colonies’ prosperity and of their deep-rooted vice: their opposition to the establishment of capital. “Where land is very cheap and all men are free, where every one who so pleases can easily obtain a piece of land for himself, not only is labour very dear, as respects the labourer’s share of the produce, but the difficulty is to obtain combined labour at any price.”[^33.11]

[^33.10]: “Land, to be an element of colonisation, must not only be waste, but it must be public property, liable to be converted into private property.” (Cited above, Vol.II, p.125.)

[^33.11]: Cited above, Vol.I, p.247.

<!-- ch33-p006 -->
In the colonies the separation of the worker from the conditions of labor and from their root, the soil, does not exist, or exists only here and there, or on too limited a scale. So neither does the separation of agriculture from industry exist, nor the destruction of the peasants’ household industry. Where, then, is the internal market for capital to come from? “No part of the population of America is exclusively agricultural, excepting slaves and their employers who combine capital and labour in particular works. Free Americans, who cultivate the soil, follow many other occupations. Some portion of the furniture and tools which they use is commonly made by themselves. They frequently build their own houses, and carry to market, at whatever distance, the produce of their own industry. They are spinners and weavers; they make soap and candles, as well as, in many cases, shoes and clothes for their own use. In America the cultivation of land is often the secondary pursuit of a blacksmith, a miller or a shopkeeper.”[^33.12] With such odd people as these, where is the “field of abstinence” for the capitalists?

[^33.12]: Cited above, pp.21, 22.

<!-- ch33-p007 -->
The great beauty of capitalist production is this: it not only constantly reproduces the wage worker as a wage worker, but also always produces, in proportion to the accumulation of capital, a relative surplus population of wage workers (workers made “surplus” to capital’s needs for the time being, who serve as a reserve of available labor and press down on the employed). In this way the law of the supply and demand of labor is kept in the right groove, the ups and downs of wages (the price paid for labor-power, which appears, wrongly, as the price of labor itself) are penned within limits that suit capitalist exploitation, and finally the worker’s social dependence on the capitalist, that indispensable requirement, is secured. This is an unmistakable relation of dependence. Yet at home, in the mother-country, the smug political economist can turn it, as if by magic, into a relation of free contract between buyer and seller, between equally independent owners of commodities (things produced in order to be exchanged, or sold, not for the producer’s own use): the owner of the commodity capital and the owner of the commodity labor. But in the colonies this pretty fancy is torn apart. Here the absolute population grows much faster than in the mother-country, because many workers enter this world as ready-made adults, and yet the labor-market is always short of workers. The law of the supply and demand of labor falls to pieces. On the one hand, the old world constantly throws in capital, thirsting for exploitation and “abstinence”; on the other, the regular reproduction of the wage worker as wage worker runs into obstacles of the most impertinent kind, some of them impossible to overcome. What becomes of the production of wage workers who are surplus in proportion to the accumulation of capital? The wage worker of today is tomorrow an independent peasant, or a craftsman working for himself. He vanishes from the labor-market, but not into the workhouse. Wage workers are constantly turning into independent producers, who work for themselves instead of for capital, and enrich themselves instead of the capitalist gentlemen. This in turn has a very perverse effect on the conditions of the labor-market. Not only does the degree of exploitation of the wage worker stay indecently low. On top of that, the wage worker loses, along with the relation of dependence, the feeling of dependence on the abstemious capitalist as well. Hence all the inconveniences that our E. G. Wakefield paints so stoutly, so eloquently, so touchingly. The supply of wage labor, he complains, is neither constant, nor regular, nor sufficient. “The supply of labour is always not only small but uncertain.”[^33.13] “Though the produce divided between the capitalist and the labourer be large, the labourer takes so great a share that he soon becomes a capitalist.... Few, even those whose lives are unusually long, can accumulate great masses of wealth.”[^33.14] The workers flatly refuse to allow the capitalist to abstain from paying for the greater part of their labor. It does him no good if he is cunning enough to import his own wage workers from Europe with his own capital. They soon “cease... to be labourers for hire; they... become independent landowners, if not competitors with their former masters in the labour-market.”[^33.15] Think of the horror! The excellent capitalist has imported from Europe, in the flesh and with his own good money, his own competitors! The end of the world has come! No wonder Wakefield laments that the wage workers in the colonies have no dependence at all, and no feeling of dependence either. Because of the high wages, says his disciple Merivale, there is in the colonies “the urgent desire for cheaper and more subservient labourers – for a class to whom the capitalist might dictate terms, instead of being dictated to by them.... In ancient civilised countries the labourer, though free, is by a law of Nature dependent on capitalists; in colonies this dependence must be created by artificial means.”[^33.16]

[^33.13]: Cited above, Vol.II, p.116

[^33.14]: Cited above, Vol.I, p.131.

[^33.15]: Cited above, Vol.II, p.5.

[^33.16]: Merivale, cited above, Vol.II, pp.235-314 passim. Even the mild Free Trade vulgar economist Molinari (vulgar economics: economists who only describe and defend the surface appearances of the system, without investigating its real relations) says: “Dans les colonies où l’esclavage a été aboli sans que le travail forcé se trouvait remplacé par une quantité équivalente de travail libre, on a vu s’opérer la contre-partie du fait qui se réalise tous les jours sous nos yeux. On a vu les simples travailleurs exploiter à leur tour les entrepreneurs d’industrie, exiger d’eux des salaires hors de toute proportion avec la part légitime qui leur revenait dans le produit. Les planteurs, ne pouvant obtenir de leurs sucres un prix suffisant pour couvrir la hausse de salaire, ont été obligés de fournir l’excédant, d’abord sur leurs profits, ensuite sur leurs capitaux mêmes. Une foule de planteurs ont été ruinés de la sorte, d’autres ont fermé leurs ateliers pour échapper à une ruine imminente.... Sans doute, il vaut mieux voir périr des accumulations de capitaux que des générations d’hommes [how generous Mr. Molinari!]: mais ne vaudrait-il pas mieux que ni les uns ni les autres périssent? [In the colonies where slavery has been abolished without the forced labor being replaced by an equivalent quantity of free labor, we have seen the reverse of what happens every day before our eyes. We have seen simple workers exploit the industrial entrepreneurs in their turn, demanding from them wages out of all proportion to the legitimate share in the product that was due to them. The planters, unable to get a price for their sugar high enough to cover the rise in wages, were obliged to make up the difference, first out of their profits, then out of their capital itself.
