A great many planters have been ruined in this way; others have closed their workshops to escape the ruin that threatened them ... No doubt it is better to see accumulations of capital perish than generations of men ... but would it not be better if neither perished?] (Molinari, cited above, pp.51,52.) Mr. Molinari, Mr. Molinari! What then becomes of the ten commandments, of Moses and the prophets, of the law of supply and demand, if in Europe the “entrepreneur” can cut down the worker’s legitimate part, and in the West Indies the worker can cut down the entrepreneur’s? And what, if you please, is this “legitimate part,” which, as you yourself show, the capitalist in Europe neglects to pay every day? Over there, in the colonies where the workers are so “simple” as to “exploit” the capitalist, Mr. Molinari feels a strong itch to use the police to set on the right road the law of supply and demand, which elsewhere works automatically.

<!-- ch33-p008 -->
What, according to Wakefield, is the consequence of this unfortunate state of things in the colonies? A “barbarising tendency of dispersion” of producers and of national wealth.[^33.17] When the means of production are parceled out among countless owners, each working on his own account, this destroys, along with the centralization of capital (the joining of already existing capitals into fewer, bigger ones), the whole foundation of combined labor. Every drawn-out undertaking that stretches over several years and demands an outlay of fixed capital is prevented from being carried out. In Europe, capital invests without a moment’s hesitation, for the working class is its living accessory, always in excess, always available. But in the colonies! Wakefield tells an extremely mournful anecdote. He was talking with some capitalists of Canada and the state of New York, where the wave of immigrants often stagnates and leaves behind a sediment of “supernumerary” workers. “Our capital,” says one of the characters in the melodrama, “was ready for many operations which require a considerable period of time for their completion; but we could not begin such operations with labour which, we knew, would soon leave us. If we had been sure of retaining the labour of such emigrants, we should have been glad to have engaged it at once, and for a high price: and we should have engaged it, even though we had been sure it would leave us, provided we had been sure of a fresh supply whenever we might need it.”[^33.18]

[^33.17]: Wakefield, cited above, Vol.II, p.52.

[^33.18]: Cited above, pp.191, 192.

<!-- ch33-p009 -->
Wakefield sets English capitalist agriculture and its “combined” labor against the scattered farming of American peasants. After that, he unwittingly gives us a glimpse of the other side of the medal. He depicts the mass of the American people as well-off, independent, enterprising, and comparatively cultured, while “the English agricultural labourer is miserable wretch, a pauper.... In what country, except North America and some new colonies, do the wages of free labour employed in agriculture much exceed a bare subsistence for the labourer? ... Undoubtedly, farm-horses in England, being a valuable property, are better fed than English peasants.”[^33.19] But never mind: national wealth is, once again, by its very nature identical with the misery of the people.

[^33.19]: Cited above, Vol.I, p.47, 246.

<!-- ch33-p010 -->
How, then, is the anti-capitalist cancer of the colonies to be healed? If people were willing to turn all the soil from public into private property at one blow, they would certainly destroy the root of the evil, but also – the colonies. The trick is to kill two birds with one stone. Let the Government put an artificial price on the virgin soil, a price independent of the law of supply and demand. It must be a price that forces the immigrant to work a long time for wages before he can earn enough money to buy land and turn himself into an independent peasant.[^33.20] The sale of land at a price that is relatively prohibitive for the wage workers produces a fund. This fund of money, squeezed out of the wages of labor by violating the sacred law of supply and demand, the Government is in turn to use, in proportion as it grows, to import have-nothings from Europe into the colonies, and so keep the wage labor market full for the capitalists. Under these circumstances, tout sera pour le mieux dans le meilleur des mondes possibles [everything will be for the best in the best of all possible worlds]. This is the great secret of “systematic colonisation.” By this plan, Wakefield cries in triumph, “the supply of labour *must* be constant and regular, because, first, as no labourer would be able to procure land until he had worked for money, all immigrant labourers, working for a time for wages and in combination, would produce capital for the employment of more labourers; secondly, because every labourer who left off working for wages and became a landowner would, by purchasing land, provide a fund for bringing fresh labour to the colony.”[^33.21] The price of the soil imposed by the State must, of course, be a “sufficient price,” that is, so high “as to prevent the labourers from becoming independent landowners until others had followed to take their place.”[^33.22] This “sufficient price for the land” is nothing but a roundabout, polite name for the ransom that the worker pays the capitalist for permission to retire from the wage labor market to the land. First, he must create “capital” for the capitalist, so that the capitalist can exploit more workers with it. Then he must put, at his own expense, a *locum tenens* [stand-in] on the labor market, whom the Government sends across the sea for the benefit of his old master, the capitalist.

[^33.20]: “C’est, ajoutez-vous, grâce à l’appropriation du sol et des capitaux que l’homme, qui n’a que ses bras, trouve de l’occupation et se fait un revenu... c’est au contraire, grâce à l’appropriation individuelle du sol qu’il se trouve des hommes n’ayant que leurs bras.... Quand vous mettez un homme dans le vide, vous vous emparez de l’atmosphère. Ainsi faites-vous, quand vous vous emparez du sol.... C’est le mettre dans le vide le richesses, pour ne la laisser vivre qu’à votre volonté.” [It is, you add, thanks to the appropriation of the soil and of capital that the man who has nothing but his arms finds work and makes an income for himself ... but on the contrary, it is thanks to the individual appropriation of the soil that there are men who have nothing but their arms. ... When you put a man in a vacuum, you seize the air. That is what you do when you seize the soil ... It is putting him in a vacuum of wealth, so as to let him live only at your will.] (Collins, cited above, t.III, pp.268-71, passim.)

[^33.21]: Wakefield, cited above, Vol.II, p.192.

[^33.22]: Cited above, p.45.

<!-- ch33-p011 -->
It is very characteristic that the English Government for years practiced this method of “primitive accumulation,” which Mr. Wakefield prescribed expressly for use in the colonies. The fiasco was, of course, as complete as that of Sir Robert Peel’s Bank Act. The stream of emigration was merely diverted from the English colonies to the United States. Meanwhile, the advance of capitalist production in Europe, together with growing Government pressure, has made Wakefield’s recipe unnecessary. On the one hand, the enormous and ceaseless stream of people driven to America year after year leaves behind a stationary sediment in the east of the United States. There the wave of immigration from Europe throws people onto the labor-market faster than the wave of emigration westwards can wash them away. On the other hand, the American Civil War brought in its train a colossal national debt, and with it the pressure of taxes, the rise of the vilest financial aristocracy, the squandering of a huge part of the public land on speculative companies for the exploitation of railways, mines, etc., in short, the most rapid centralization of capital. So the great republic has ceased to be the promised land for emigrant workers. Capitalist production advances there with giant strides, even though wages have not yet been lowered, and the wage worker has not yet been made dependent, anywhere near the normal European level. The Government has shamelessly lavished uncultivated colonial land on aristocrats and capitalists, as even Wakefield loudly denounced. Especially in Australia,[^33.23] this has produced an ample “relative surplus labouring population.” It did so together with the stream of people that the gold diggings attract, and with the competition that imported English commodities cause even to the smallest craftsman. As a result, almost every mail brings the Job’s news (bad news, like the messages brought to Job) of a “glut of the Australia labour-market,” and in some places prostitution flourishes as wantonly as in the London Haymarket.

[^33.23]: As soon as Australia became her own lawmaker, she passed, of course, laws favorable to the settlers, but the squandering of the land, already carried out by the English Government, stands in the way. “The first and main object at which new Land Act of 1862 aims is to give increased facilities for the settlement of the people.” (“The Land Law of Victoria,” by the Hon. C. G. Duffy, Minister of Public Lands, London, 1862.)

<!-- ch33-p012 -->
However, we are not concerned here with the conditions of the colonies. The only thing that interests us is the secret that the political economy of the old world discovered in the new world and proclaimed from the housetops: that the capitalist mode of production and accumulation, and therefore capitalist private property, have as their fundamental condition the destruction of self-earned private property; in other words, the expropriation of the worker.

<!-- ch33-p013 -->
**End of Book I**
